passages.heading: Course Modification Proposal Walkthrough
passages.text:
Course Modification Proposal Walkthrough
Course Modification Proposal Walkthrough
This guide provides step-by-step procedural instructions for completing and submitting a Course Modification Proposal in Kuali. It focuses on navigating the form, including what to select or enter in each field.
The guide is organized by proposal section (panel), so you can jump directly to a section when you need help.
This guide does not provide guidance on course content or academic decisions. Consult your department and applicable curriculum committees for questions about developing the course itself.
Related toolkit entry: Specialization Modification Proposal Walkthrough

passages.heading: Understand URI’s Curricular Process
passages.text:
Familiarize yourself with URI’s curricular process before beginning your proposal. This will help you understand the steps involved in the curricular process and accurately estimate how long your proposal may take to reach approval.
How the Curriculum Process Works
Related toolkit entry: How the Curriculum Process Works
Approval Calendar
Related toolkit entry: Approval Calendar

passages.heading: Make Sure You Can Access Kuali CM
passages.text:
You will need access to Kuali Curriculum Management (Kuali CM) to propose any curricular item.
Kuali Basics
Related toolkit entry: Kuali Basics

passages.heading: Choose the Right Proposal Type
passages.text:
Some course proposal types can be easily confused. If you are unsure which type applies, review these common examples.
Table columns: If you want to… | Use…
If you want to…: Make a Temporary Course a Permanent Course which appears in the Academic Catalog | Use…: Course Modification Proposal
If you want to…: Create a new cross-listing to accompany an existing course | Use…: Course Modification Proposal
If you want to…: Add a new topic to an open-ended topics course | Use…: New Course Proposal if the course is a GCH course No proposal needed for any other subject code. Contact Enrollment Services to add the new topic.
If you want to…: Add a new topic to a permanent topics course | Use…: Course Modification Proposal
If you want to…: Create a new 500-level section of a course to accompany the 400-level | Use…: New Course Proposal

passages.heading: Start the Proposal
passages.text:
From your browser, navigate to Kuali Curriculum Management (CM).
Select Curriculum to open your Dashboard .
Related toolkit entry: Dashboard
From the left-hand navigation menu, select Courses.
On the Courses page, use the search bar at the top to find the course you would like to modify. You can search by:
Course code (e.g., COM100)
Course title (e.g., Communication Fundamentals)
Keywords found in the course title, description, or anywhere in the course form.
Once you locate the course, select it to open the current version
With the current course open, select Propose Changes in the upper-right corner of the window.
A window will appear prompting you to select Create a new version or Create a new revision. Always select Create a new version.
The following sections of this walkthrough are grouped by section of the proposal form.

passages.heading: Course Modification Proposal
passages.text:
This is where you will indicate the changes you are proposing to make to the course.
Select the type(s) of change: Check Major, Minor, or both, depending on the changes you are proposing. If you’re not sure which category applies, that’s okay! Select an option to view the list of changes included in that category.
Select the specific change(s): From the list(s) that appear, check the box next to each Major and/or Minor change you are proposing.

passages.heading: Change the course description
passages.text:
Modify the description of a course. For example: Introduces students to the principles of environmental sustainability, with emphasis on climate change, resource management, and sustainable practices and their applications in modern society.
See Course Description
Related toolkit entry: Course Description

passages.heading: Add or change a modality
passages.text:
Add: Add a new modality to a course (e.g., add an in-person option to an online course). Change: Change the modality in which a course is offered (e.g., change an in-person course to online).
See Modality
Related toolkit entry: Modality

passages.heading: Change the method of instruction
passages.text:
Change the method of instruction for a course (e.g., Lecture to Seminar or Lecture to Lecture and Recitation).
See Method of Instruction
Related toolkit entry: Method of Instruction

passages.heading: Change the course number to a new hundred level
passages.text:
Change a course number to a different hundred level (e.g., BIO318 to BIO418).
See Course Number
Related toolkit entry: Course Number

passages.heading: Add new general education outcomes
passages.text:
Add GE outcomes to a course that does not currently have any, or add a new GE outcome to a course that already has been approved for GE (this may involve replacing an existing outcome, or adding a second outcome to a course currently approved for only one).
See General Education Outcomes
Related toolkit entry: General Education Outcomes

passages.heading: Add new topic to GCH course
passages.text:
Because GCH courses carry General Education outcomes, each new topic must be reviewed by the General Education Committee.
See GCH Topics
Related toolkit entry: GCH Topics

passages.heading: Change the grading method of a GE course
passages.text:
All GE outcomes must have a grading method of Letter Grades, with the exception of D1 which can also be graded as S/U. Therefore, this only applies to D1 courses.
See Grading Method
Related toolkit entry: Grading Method

passages.heading: Change number of fixed credits
passages.text:
Change the number of fixed credits for a course (e.g., 3 to 4 credits).
See Credits.
Related toolkit entry: Credits

passages.heading: Change fixed credits to a credit range
passages.text:
Change a course with fixed credits (e.g., 3 credits) to a credit range (e.g., 3–4 credits or 1–3 credits).
See Credits

passages.heading: Change the credit range outside of current range
passages.text:
Change a course’s credit range from 3–6 credits to a range that falls outside of 3–6 credits (e.g., 1–6, 3–12, or 1–12).
See Credits

passages.heading: Change varied credits to a fixed credit outside of current range
passages.text:
Change a course with a credit range (e.g., 3–6 credits) to a fixed number of credits outside the current range (e.g., 2 credits or 7 credits).
See Credits

passages.heading: Add graduate credit to a 400-level course
passages.text: Allow a 400-level course to count for graduate credit, either as an elective in a graduate program or for double counting in an ABM program.

passages.heading: Delete course
passages.text: Remove the course from the University’s course offerings, the catalog, and inactivate it in eCampus.

passages.heading: Change course title
passages.text:
Introduction to Digital Media and Design Fundamentals
SeeCourse Title
Related toolkit entry: Course Title

passages.heading: Change academic home (department / college)
passages.text: Move a course from one department or college to another.

passages.heading: Remove a modality
passages.text:
Remove one of the modalities in which a course is currently offered, so that the course is offered in only one modality (in-person / online)
See Modality

passages.heading: Change prerequisites
passages.text: Add, remove, or change a course prerequisite.

passages.heading: Change subject code
passages.text: Change the subject code assigned to a course, such as changing BIO to CMB.

passages.heading: Add a cross-listing
passages.text:
Add a new cross-listed subject code to a course. For example: MBA545 becomes MBA545(BUS545), or MBA543(BUS543) adds FIN543, becoming MBA543 (BUS543, FIN543).
SeeCross-listed Course
Related toolkit entry: Cross-listed Course

passages.heading: Remove a cross-listing
passages.text:
Remove an existing cross-listed subject code from a course. For example: MBA543(BUS543, FIN543) becomes MBA543(BUS543).
SeeCross-listed Course

passages.heading: Remove general education outcomes
passages.text: Remove one or more general education outcomes from a course.

passages.heading: Change temporary course to permanent
passages.text:
Make a temporary course permanent so that it can continue to be offered beyond the two times permitted within the two years after approval.
See Temporary Course
Related toolkit entry: Temporary Course

passages.heading: Change open ended topic course type (permanent topics vs. temporary topics)
passages.text:
Change whether an open-ended course is offered with permanent topics or temporary topics. Permanent topics are listed in the course description, while temporary topics are not.
See Topics Course
Related toolkit entry: Topics Course

passages.heading: Change grading method of a non-GE course
passages.text:
Change whether a non-General Education course is graded using letter grades, S/U grading, or both.
See Grading Method

passages.heading: Change course number within the hundred level
passages.text: Change a course number while keeping it within the same hundred level (e.g., BIO101 to BIO105).

passages.heading: Change credit range inside of the current range
passages.text:
Narrow a course’s credit range without changing its existing minimum or maximum credits (e.g., 1–6 credits to 2–5 credits).
See Credits

passages.heading: Change varied credits to fixed credits within current range
passages.text:
Change a course with a credit range to a fixed number of credits that falls within the current range (e.g., 3–6 credits to 4 credits).
See Credits

passages.heading: Change course repeat criteria
passages.text:
Change the conditions under which a course may be repeated for credit.
See Repeat Criteria
Related toolkit entry: Repeat Criteria

passages.heading: Remove graduate credit from a 400-level course
passages.text:
Remove the option for a 400-level course to count for graduate credit.
Rationale Briefly describe the rationale for the proposed changes.
🔽 The following field will appear only if a syllabus is required based on the checkboxes selected above.
Syllabus Upload the course syllabus here.

passages.heading: Contact Information
passages.text:
Complete the following fields with your contact information.
Proposer Name Your name is automatically populated based on your Kuali account.
Proposer Title Enter your university role.
Proposer Email Enter your URI email address. This is the email reviewers will use if they have questions about your proposal.

passages.heading: Course Administration
passages.text:
Effective Term & Year Select the term and year in which you intend the course to become effective. If the effective term entered at proposal submission has missed the deadline by the time it reaches the Faculty Senate, this field will be automatically updated to the next available semester.
Academic Career This field will already be populated. Leave the selection as is unless one of the following applies:
The course number or level is changing. For example, an undergraduate-level course is becoming a graduate-level course, or vice versa.
The course is moving from the Traditional Calendar to the Accelerated Online Calendar, or vice versa.
Changing the Academic Calendar?
Good to know: If a course is already approved for online instruction, you do not need a proposal to offer it in the other academic calendar, as long as it will remain online. You can simply contact Enrollment Services to schedule the course in the other calendar.
A proposal is required when the change also involves a change in modality (for example, changing from online to in-person).
Which situation applies to you?

passages.heading: Adding an Accelerated Online (7-week) section of a course already approved for online instruction?
passages.text: No proposal is needed as long as there are no other changes to the course. Contact Enrollment Services to schedule the course in the Accelerated Online Calendar.

passages.heading: Adding a Traditional (14-week) online section of a course already approved for online instruction in the Accelerated Online Calendar?
passages.text: No proposal is needed as long as there are no other changes to the course. Contact Enrollment Services to schedule the course in the Traditional Calendar.

passages.heading: Adding an Accelerated Online (7-week) section of a course currently approved only for in-person instruction?
passages.text:
A proposal is required because you are adding a new modality. On the proposal, keep the original 14-week calendar radio button selected under Academic Calendar. In your rationale, explain that you intend to continue offering the course in the Traditional Calendar while also adding an online section to the Accelerated Online Calendar.
Example: “We want to continue to offer this course in the Traditional Calendar, as well as add an online section to the Accelerated Online Calendar.”

passages.heading: Adding an in-person section to a course currently approved only for the Accelerated Online (7-week) Calendar?
passages.text:
A proposal is required because you are adding a new modality. On the proposal, keep the original 7-week accelerated calendar radio button selected under Academic Calendar. In your rationale, explain that you intend to continue offering the course in the Accelerated Online Calendar while also adding an in-person section to the Traditional Calendar.
Example: “We want to continue to offer this course in the Accelerated Online Calendar, as well as add an in-person section to the Traditional Calendar.”
College This field will already be populated. Leave the selection as is unless you have checked Change academic home (department/college) in the first section of the form.
Department This field will already be populated. Leave the selection as is unless you have checked Change academic home (department/college) in the first section of the form.
🔽 The following field will appear only if Change academic home was checked.
Letter(s) of support from outgoing department / college. Upload confirmation from the original department/college that they are in support of the course moving to a new academic home.
Honors Program This field will already be populated. Leave the selection as is.

passages.heading: Adding an in-person section to a course currently approved only for the Accelerated Online (7-week) Calendar?
passages.text:
🔽 The following field will appear only if “Yes” is chosen for Honors Program.
Honors Type This field will already be populated. Leave the selection as is.
General Education This field will already be populated. Leave the selection as is unless you have checked Add new general education outcomes (and the course was not GE previously), or Remove general education outcomes in the first section of the form.

passages.heading: Course Information
passages.text:
Subject Code This field will already be populated. Leave the selection as is unless you have checked Change subject code in the first section of the form.
Remember: The subject code must be owned by the College and Department previously entered in the form.
Number This field will already be populated. Leave the selection as is unless you have checked Change course number within the hundred level or Change course number to a new hundred level in the first section of the form. A few reminders:
The course numbering system is found in UM 8.30.10.
Temporary course numbers end with an “X”
Grand Challenge course numbers end with a “G”
Is this a 400-level course available for graduate credit? This field will already be populated. Leave the selection as is unless you have checked Add graduate credit to a 400-level course or Remove graduate from a 400-level course in the first section of the form.
Course Title This field will already be populated. Leave the selection as is unless you have checked Change course title in the first section of the form.

passages.heading: Course Information
passages.text:
Abbreviated Course Title This field will already be populated. Leave the selection as is unless you have checked Change course title in the first section of the form.
Course Description This field will already be populated. Leave the selection as is unless you are changing the course description, the general education outcomes, the grading method, the repeat criteria, the credits or credit range, removing or adding 400-level for graduate credit, the prerequisites, the cross-listing(s), or the repeat criteria. (Click on the Course Description link for more information).
Supporting Materials Optional. Use this file upload to provide additional information that may be helpful to review committees before the proposal enters the approval workflow.

passages.heading: Modality, Method of Instruction, and Prerequisites
passages.text:
Modality This field will already be populated. Leave the selection as is unless you have checked Add or change a modality in the first section of the form.
Method of Instruction This field will already be populated. Leave the selection as is unless you have checked Change the method of instruction in the first section of the form.
Note that “Online” is not a method of instruction; it was removed from the list of methods of instruction in 2025. If this still remains entered in your proposal, please change it.
If the course has multiple methods of instruction, select the first as Primary and all additional methods as Secondary.
If the course has two or more methods of instruction, indicate how the methods are divided. This information is important for Enrollment Services; omitting it may delay final approval.
Requisites Confirm the prerequisites in this textbox. Copy them exactly as they are listed in the description unless you have checked Change prerequisites in the first section of the form.

passages.heading: Cross-listed Courses
passages.text:
Is this a cross-listed course? This field will already be populated. Leave the selection as is unless you have checked Add a cross-listing or Remove a cross-listing in the first section of the form.
🔽 The following fields will appear only if “Yes” is chosen for Is this a cross-listed course?
Cross-listed course(s) for eCampus Make sure all cross-listed courses are entered (existing and proposed)
Cross-listed course(s) for the Catalog Make sure all cross-listed courses are entered here as well (existing and proposed).
Cross-listed Department(s) Make sure all departments are entered here which belong to the cross-listed courses (existing and proposed).
Letter(s) of support from cross-listed departments For new courses and course modifications, the “parent” department (the department associated with the course code on the proposal) must provide a letter of support from each cross-listed department.
🔽 The following fields will appear only if Remove a cross-listing is checked in the first section of the form.
Letter(s) of support from removed cross-listed department(s) Upload confirmation and support from the department of the proposed removed cross-listed course.

passages.heading: Cross-listed Courses
passages.text:
What if my cross-listed course code belongs to the same department as the parent course code? For example, MCE and ISE are both in the Department of Mechanical, Industrial & Systems Engineering.
Just upload a document stating: “Both subject codes belong to the same department.”

passages.heading: Grading Method, Credits, and Repeat Criteria
passages.text:
Credits This field will already be populated. Leave the selection as is unless you have checked one of the following in the first section of the form:
Change number of fixed credits
Change fixed credits to a credit range
Change the credit range outside of current range
Change varied credits to a fixed credit outside of current range
Change credit range inside of the current range
Change varied credits to fixed credits within current range
Grading Method Select letter grades, S/U, or both.
Can this course be repeated for credit? Select Yes or No.
🔽 The following fields will appear only if “Yes” is chosen for Can this course be repeated for credit?
Maximum times course may be taken: Enter max number of times.
Maximum credits allowed: Enter the maximum number of credits a student may earn for the course. For example, a 3-credit course that may be taken three times for credit has a maximum of 9 credits.
Can students repeat within the same term? Select Yes or No.
🔽 The following field will appear only if “Yes” is chosen for Can students repeat within the same term?
Maximum credits allowed per term: Enter the maximum number of credits a student may earn from this course within a single term.

passages.heading: General Education Outcomes
passages.text:
🔽 This section will appear only if Yes is chosen from General Education.
If this course is already approved for general education, the following fields will already be populated.
Proposers do not need to fill out the outcome tables for outcomes already approved. However, tables for new outcomes need to be filled out according to the requirements.
Learning Outcome 1 Select the appropriate learning outcome from the dropdown and complete the table for your first outcome.
Learning Outcome 2 Courses must have at least one General Education learning outcome and may have up to two. Based on your selection for Learning Outcome 1, the applicable options will be available in this dropdown. If you are not adding a second outcome, leave this field blank.
If selected, complete the table for your second outcome.
Is this a grand challenge? Select Yes or No.

passages.heading: Grand Challenge
passages.text:
🔽 This section will appear only if the course is for general education credit, and if Yes is chosen for Is this a grand challenge?
If this course is already approved for the Grand Challenge, you do not need to complete the following fields. Because Grand Challenge courses were established before Kuali, some fields may not have existing information. If you are required to enter something in a text field in order to submit the proposal to workflow, you may enter “—”.
GRAND CHALLENGE: Explain how the course title, syllabus, and assignments demonstrate the contemporary challenge addressed by the course.
INTERDISCIPLINARY: Explain how the course incorporates at least two disciplinary perspectives and provides opportunities for students to make interdisciplinary connections through assignments, activities, and/or experiences.
INTERDISCIPLINARY: Provide an abbreviated reading list organized by discipline that demonstrates the course’s disciplinary perspectives, and explain how each disciplinary perspective is integrated into major course assignments and activities.

passages.heading: Grand Challenge
passages.text:
ETHICS: Identify the ethical framework that allows students to weigh/evaluate issues. This topic needs to show up explicitly in the course schedule.
ETHICS: List the readings pertaining to ethics.
ETHICS: Describe how ethics is incorporated in some/all of the assignments and activities.

passages.heading: Submit to the Workflow
passages.text:
Once you have finalized your proposal draft:
Select Leave Edit Mode in the upper-right corner of the screen, just below the orange bar.
Select Submit for Approval to submit the proposal to the workflow.

passages.heading: So, what happens now?
passages.text: Your proposal will automatically be sent to the appropriate review committees. You may be contacted within Kuali Comments by the committees with questions to the proposal (an email will notify you automatically). You can also return to your proposal from your dashboard at any time to view the workflow status.

passages.text:
Grading Method
Tags: courses
Short Description: The method used to assign grades for a course, such as letter grades or S/U.
Grading Method

passages.heading: Letter Grades
passages.text:
A grading method in which student performance is evaluated using letter grades from A (Superior) through F (Failure), with each grade assigned a quality point value used to calculate GPA.
8.53.10 Student grades are defined as follows: A – Superior B – Good C – Fair D – Low grade, passing F – Failure 8.53.11 Grades shall be given quality point values as follows: A = 4.00 points A- = 3.70 points B+ = 3.30 points B = 3.00 points B- = 2.70 points C+ = 2.30 points C = 2.00 points C- = 1.70 points D+ = 1.30 points D = 1.00 points F = 0 points U = 0 points U* = not calculated in GPA

passages.heading: S/U Grades
passages.text:
Certain courses do not lend themselves to precise grading. For these courses, only S (satisfactory) or U (unsatisfactory) is given to all students enrolled. S/U courses are labeled as such in the course descriptions in this catalog. S/U courses are not counted as courses taken under the Pass-Fail option.
D1 is the only General Education outcome that can be graded using S/U or Letter Grades. All other outcomes must be graded by Letter Grades.

passages.heading: Kuali’s “Rules” Gadget
passages.text:
Kuali’s “Rules” Gadget
Kuali’s “Rules” Gadget
How to input Courses Approved for Double Counting in your ABM Specialization form.
Whether you are creating a new ABM, or modifying an existing, you will be asked to input all courses approved for double counting in a “Rules” gadget.

passages.heading: Adding Double-Counted Courses
passages.text:
Click Use Rule Categories checkbox
Click + Add Rules
In the blank box next to A, click the drop-down carrot, and select Double-Count.
In the next blank box, click the drop-down carrot, and select minimum number of credits from.
In the next blank box, click the drop-down carrot, and select selected courses.
Enter the total number of double-counted course credits in the Credits box. In the Courses box, list all courses that may be used toward these credits.
If the ABM allows only a certain number of credits from the courses specified, you can end here and move on to the next section of your form.

passages.heading: Adding Approved Course Statements
passages.text:
If you would like to add a statement indicating that other courses may be considered for double-counting with input from an advisor, program director, or other appropriate individual, follow these steps:
Click the plus (+) sign underneath the blue Update Logic button.
You will now see a blank box labeled with the letter B. In this box, click the drop-down carrot, and select Free form text.
Enter the text to accompany the courses selected.
Text Examples:
“Other 400-level ENG courses approved for graduate credit may be chosen in consultation with the program director.”
“Any 500-level CSF course approved by the advisor.”
“Nine credits may be double counted for the ABM Degree. Only 500­-level courses and 400­-level courses designated for graduate credit are eligible to be double counted.”

passages.heading: New Temporary & Permanent Course Email
passages.text:
New Temporary & Permanent Course Email
Date: January 29, 2027 (2027-01-29)
Tags: Temp Course Email
New Temporary & Permanent Course Email
The New Temporary & Permanent Course Email is distributed to all faculty, deans, and associate and assistant deans on the last weekday of each month. Recipients then have seven days to submit comments to the CASC Chair, GEC Chair, or Dean of the Graduate School regarding any potential or perceived content overlap involving a new temporary or permanent course.
The email serves two purposes:
Provides notice of upcoming Faculty Senate review. Courses included in the email have already been reviewed and approved by their respective College Curriculum Committees and will next be reviewed by the appropriate Faculty Senate Curriculum Committee: CASC, GEC, or Graduate Council.
Provides an opportunity to identify potential content overlap. College Curriculum Committees may review the courses included in the email to identify any potential or perceived overlap with courses offered or proposed by other colleges. Any concerns can then be raised before the courses proceed to Faculty Senate Curriculum Committee review.

passages.heading: Start the Proposal
passages.text:
From your browser, navigate to Kuali Curriculum Management (CM).
Select Curriculum to open your Dashboard .

From the left-hand navigation menu, select Programs.
On the Programs page, select + New Program in the upper-right corner.
The following sections of this walkthrough are grouped by section of the proposal form.

passages.heading: Contact Information
passages.text:
Complete the following fields with your contact information.
Proposer Name Your name is automatically populated based on your Kuali account.
Proposer Title Enter your university role.
Proposer Email Enter your URI email address. This is the email reviewers will use if they have questions about your proposal.
Additional Proposer(s) Use this section to identify additional individuals who can speak to the proposed program. Individuals listed here will not receive Kuali notifications or have access to edit the proposal. Their inclusion simply provides transparency to the reviewing committees about who else is involved in or can speak to the proposal.

passages.heading: Program Information
passages.text:
Effective Term & Year Select the term and year in which you intend the program to become effective. If the selected effective term has passed the applicable deadline by the time the proposal reaches the Faculty Senate, it will automatically be updated to the next available term.
First Graduation Term Select the term and year in which you anticipate the first students will graduate with this credential.
Credential Type Select the type of credential you are proposing: Degree, Major, Minor, or Certificate.
Level Select the level of the program: Undergraduate, Graduate, or Dual Currently, the only Dual Degree program offered at URI is the Pharm.D.
Academic Calendar Select the academic calendar for the program: Accelerated 7-week through URI Online, or Traditional 14-week with Summer and J-Term Sessions.
Program Locations Select all locations where the program will be offered.
College Select the college in which the program is housed.
Department Select the department in which the program is housed.
CIP Code Enter the specific CIP code that applies to your program. You can search for your program’s code here.

passages.heading: Program Information
passages.text:
Is this interdisciplinary? The intent of this question is to identify whether the program is jointly owned by multiple academic departments. If yes, the percentage of ownership assigned to each department must be provided in the curriculum worksheet.
🔽 The following field will appear only if “Yes” is chosen for Is this interdisciplinary?
Additional Department(s) and College(s) Enter departments sharing ownership of this program.
🔽 The following field will appear only if Degree or Major is chosen for Credential Type.
Degree e.g., Bachelor of Arts
🔽 The following field will appear only if Major is chosen for Credential Type.
Major e.g., Music
Academic Program Title Major or full degree name, followed by a dash and the degree abbreviation. e.g., Music - BA
Program Description See Program Description for formatting guidance.
Related toolkit entry: Program Description
Admission Requirements See Admission Requirements for criteria

passages.heading: New Temporary & Permanent Course Email
passages.text:
New Temporary & Permanent Course Email
Date: April 30, 2027 (2027-04-30)
Tags: Temp Course Email
New Temporary & Permanent Course Email
The New Temporary & Permanent Course Email is distributed to all faculty, deans, and associate and assistant deans on the last weekday of each month. Recipients then have seven days to submit comments to the CASC Chair, GEC Chair, or Dean of the Graduate School regarding any potential or perceived content overlap involving a new temporary or permanent course.
The email serves two purposes:
Provides notice of upcoming Faculty Senate review. Courses included in the email have already been reviewed and approved by their respective College Curriculum Committees and will next be reviewed by the appropriate Faculty Senate Curriculum Committee: CASC, GEC, or Graduate Council.
Provides an opportunity to identify potential content overlap. College Curriculum Committees may review the courses included in the email to identify any potential or perceived overlap with courses offered or proposed by other colleges. Any concerns can then be raised before the courses proceed to Faculty Senate Curriculum Committee review.

passages.heading: Degree or Major Program Requirements
passages.text:
An undergraduate student’s field of study is called the “major” (UM 8.20.40)
A graduate student’s field of study is called the “program” (UM 8.20.40)
Undergraduate programs are required to have a minimum or 120 credits, and a maximum of 148 (UM 8.21.10)
Undergraduate programs shall include at least 6 credits of free electives (UM 8.21.10)
General Education requirements shall apply to all undergraduate programs (UM 8.21.11)
A cumulative average of at least 2.00 is required to graduate from all undergraduate degrees. (UM 8.22.10)
Master’s degree programs with thesis require a minimum of 30 credits. 18 must be from content-based courses, 6 must be thesis courses. (GSM 7.44.1)
Master’s degree programs without thesis require a minimum of 30 credits. (GSM 7.45.1)
Doctoral students must complete a Program of Study with a minimum of 64 credit hours beyond the undergraduate degree (GSM 7.54) (See GSM sections 7.54 and 7.21)

passages.heading: Minor Requirements
passages.text:
18 or more credits of related studies offered by one or more departments or programs and sponsored by a faculty member. (UM 8.20.50)
At least 12 credits at the 200-level or above ( UM 8.20.51)
At least 8 credits must be earned at URI (UM 8.20.51)
Minimum GPA average of 2.0 must be earned in the minor’s required courses (UM 8.20.51)
A maximum of two courses can apply to both the major and minor field of study (UM 8.20.52)

passages.heading: Certificate Requirements
passages.text:
Undergraduate certificates generally require 15-21 credits of coursework (UM 8.20.70)
Undergraduate certificates are available to degree seeking and certificate-only seeking undergraduate students (UM 8.20.70)
Undergraduate certificate courses may not be pass/fail (UM 8.20.71)
Graduate certificates require 12 credits minimum, 16 credits maximum. (GSM Appendix J.1.1)
Post-master’s graduate certificates require 12 credits minimum, 18 credits maximum. (GSM Appendix J.1.1)

passages.heading: Faculty Senate Executive Committee
passages.text: Faculty Senate Executive Committee

passages.heading: Faculty Senate Executive Committee
passages.text:
Through RI General Law §16-32-10, academic responsibility at URI is delegated to the President and the Faculty Senate. The Faculty Senate Executive Committee (FSEC) serves as the steering committee of the Senate. It represents the Senate in meetings with other University bodies and with the Provost, the President, and the URI Board of Trustees. Meetings of the FSEC are held weekly to coordinate the Senate’s business and its committees and address concerns within its jurisdiction.
For the description of the powers and duties of the Executive Committee, please see University Manual Appendix C: By-laws of the Faculty Senate, Section 4.1 – 4.9.

passages.heading: What is Kuali Curriculum Management?
passages.text: Kuali Curriculum Management (CM) is the system used at URI to manage university-wide curricula, the curriculum approval process, and the official academic catalog.

passages.heading: Kuali vs. Catalog vs. eCampus
passages.text:
Kuali CM is the cloud-based system used to manage the curriculum approval process through forms and workflow.
The URI Academic Catalog is built in Kuali and pulls information directly from all course, program, and specialization records.
Kuali CM integrates with eCampus . When a course is approved in Kuali, the information is sent to eCampus and updated for a future term.

passages.heading: Why does this matter?
passages.text: Information entered into Kuali curricular forms (course, program, and specialization proposals) flows directly into the catalog and eCampus. It is essential that proposals are written clearly and leave no room for interpretation.

passages.heading: Access & Logging into Kuali
passages.text:
Access to Kuali CM is limited to faculty, Deans, and select administrators and staff. Only faculty members are permitted to submit proposals.
To request access or learn how to log in, visit the Faculty Senate’s Kuali Access page.

passages.heading: University Manual Appendix C: By-Laws of the Faculty Senate, Section 4.40
passages.text: The Committee for Research and Creative Activities (henceforth referred to as the “full committee”) shall consist of six faculty senators and five non-senator research-active faculty) and students active, experienced, or concerned with various aspects of research, creative, and scholarly efforts at URI. The Vice President for Research and Economic Development (VPRED) shall be an ex officio (non-voting) member of the committee. The FSEC shall appoint six senators, and the VPRED shall appoint five research-active non- senators. #23-24-21

passages.heading: University Manual Appendix C: By-Laws of the Faculty Senate, Section 4.40
passages.text:
The full committee shall serve as the representative voice of the university community in all matters related to research, creative, and scholarly activities. It shall seek to improve the environment for research at URI in all ways possible. The Chair of the full committee shall serve as an ex-officio voting member of the Intellectual Property Committee (See University Manual section 5.30.10). The full committee shall form from its membership, a subcommittee, the Competitive Grants Subcommittee, the chair of which shall be appointed from the members of the full committee. The full committee shall meet at least once a month and present reports to the Faculty Senate in December and April and more often as needed. The Competitive Grants Subcommittee shall report to the Faculty Senate at least once annually. #17-18-18, #21-22-37 , #23-24-21, #24-25-19

Faculty Senate meetings are scheduled monthly from 3:00 – 5:00PM during the academic year. Sponsored receptions typically follow the meetings. These are great opportunities to build collegial relationships and network with colleagues from other disciplines. Special Meetings may be called upon due notice.

Please check this page often for up-to-date meeting locations and Zoom links. passages.text: Online and Distance Learning

passages.heading: Online and Distance Learning
passages.text:
The purpose of the Joint Committee on Online and Distance Learning (JCODL) is to propose, examine, and recommend institutional policies and practices for developing, planning, and evaluating online and distance learning with a focus on quality, sustainability, and connection to the University’s mission, with approval of the Faculty Senate and Provost. Further, JCODL, considers faculty training, quality in delivery of online offerings, student learning outcomes, and ADA compliance regarding online and distance learning, as well as develops and implements strategic plans for online courses, certificate, and degree programs. (University Manual 5.78.10 – 5.78.11).

passages.heading: Space Allocation Committee
passages.text: Space Allocation Committee

passages.heading: Space Allocation Committee
passages.text: The Space Allocation Committee (SAC) shall consider the present and future space needs of the University community, including new projects falling below the State’s Capital Improvement Plan project threshold. The committee will provide recommendations regarding space allocations requested to meet the programmatic needs of the University’s colleges and divisions. In making its recommendations, SAC shall consider future priorities of the University with respect to space, take into account the University’s academic priorities and strategic initiatives, and communicate with the Division of Research and Economic Development, the Campus Master Plan Review Team (5.40.10-5.40-13), the Joint Classroom Steering Committee (5.85.10-5.85.12), and the Strategic Budget and Planning Council (5.55.10 – 5.55.14) as needed. The Vice President of Administration and Finance shall review and approve space allocation recommendations prior to implementation.

passages.heading: What is a temporary course?
passages.text:
In UM 8.80.12, a temporary course is one that must meet one or more of the following:
It is experimental in nature. It is innovative, using unconventional devices or pedagogical methods, course materials, approach to course content or student-teacher relationships.
It is being tried out on a temporary basis so that its value and effectiveness can be tested before it is added to a department’s permanent curriculum.
It is intended for a limited duration, such as in the case of employing a visiting specialist temporarily available or to satisfy temporary needs and interests of students or to deal with timely issues.
For additional manual language on temporary courses, please see the URI Course Glossary .

passages.heading: How to Propose a New Temporary Course in Kuali
passages.text:
Open your Kuali Dashboard, and click “Courses” in the left-hand menu.
To the right of the search bar, click the “ + New Course ” button.
From here, you will fill in the fields of the proposal form. Most are self-explanatory, but here are a few guidelines for some (not all) of the fields:

passages.heading: Under “General Information”
passages.text:
College & Department
These inputs are the home college/department of the course, not necessarily the college/department of the proposer (though usually, it is).

passages.heading: Under “ Course Information “
passages.text:
Effective Term & Year
See Overview for Final Approvals
General Education
Temporary courses cannot be for General Education credit. Once you select the “no” radio button, you will be able to select a checkbox that indicates that this is a temporary (x) course.

passages.heading: Approval Round Information
passages.text:
Each approval round refers to the workflow sequence that each curricular proposal follows in Kuali. Rounds are structured around key academic dates, working backwards from the Faculty Senate Meetings. There are multiple rounds in an academic year, and as shown in the Approval Calendar, they do overlap.
One full round as shown in the calendar above consists of the following steps:
Temporary & Newly Proposed Course Email
The date which this email is scheduled to be sent
College Curriculum Committee Meetings
The dates provided are recommended . Ideally, the College Curriculum Committees would meet after receiving the Temporary & Newly Proposed Course Email to verify on behalf of their college that the courses listed do not have any content overlap with courses coming from other colleges.
College Dean Approval Deadline
Courses approved by the college deans or delegates by this date will be reviewed by the Faculty Senate Curriculum Committees in the following meeting.

passages.heading: URI Course Glossary
passages.text:
Cross-listed Course A course offered under multiple course codes, meaning students can register for it under different names, but the course content and instruction remain the same. This is not the same as simultaneous courses.
Description Course descriptions are written for students, not faculty, and must communicate clearly and concisely to them. Jargon, acronyms, and technical language should be avoided as much as possible. Anyone should be able to read the description and understand the nature and intent of the course.
An acceptable course description with a maximum of 30 words, begins with a verb, e.g. examines, introduces, explores, investigates. Articles, adjectives and adverbs are seldom necessary. Sentence fragments are acceptable.
General Education Learning Outcomes Courses approved for Gen Ed credit have that designation listed at the end of the description (e.g. (A2) (C1) for a course that fulfills the full A2 and C1 outcomes). Only full outcomes are listed; partial outcomes are not.

passages.heading: Annual Awards
passages.text:
The 2026 Service Award Winners were announced at the May 7, 2026 Faculty Senate meeting. Congratulations to Douglass Reed, winner of the Sheila Black Grubman Award, and to Furong Xu, winner of the Fritz Wenisch Award! Please join us in showing the gratitude of the URI community for their dedication, commitment, and service!
Professor Furong Xu’s record of service to the Curriculum and Academic Standards Committee (CASC) has been outstanding. Colleagues and fellow senators noted her skills in orchestrating a challenging committee workload, bringing disparate faculty members and departments together, providing steady leadership, and ensuring CASC was able to successfully navigate a record number of proposals in Academic Year 2025-26. CASC has been a remarkably productive committee this year, due in large part to Professor Xu’s smooth and skillful handling of ensuring the curriculum approval process operated in a timely and well-organized fashion. Additionally, faculty senators noted Furong’s steadfast collegiality, even-handedness, good humor, and grace. We congratulate Professor Furong Xu on winning the 2026 Fritz Wenisch Award for Exceptional Contributions to the Faculty Senate.

passages.heading: Annual Awards
passages.text: Professor Douglass Reed is the 2026 recipient of The Sheila Black Grubman Faculty Outstanding Service Award. This award recognizes a URI faculty member who has consistently dedicated their time, thought, and energy to make important contributions through service in the Faculty Senate, on committees, task forces, working groups, or other activities that promote the interests of the University and the URI community as a whole. As a Senator, Professor Reed was for many years a member of the Teaching, Advising, and Admissions Committee and was at the center of a major reimagining of academic advising. Many of the committee’s key recommendations are currently being implemented. More recently, Professor Reed has served for three semesters as the Administrator Evaluation Coordinator, adopting a mode of calm industriousness and a goal-oriented approach to this important work. Colleagues admire Professor Reed’s collegiality, work ethic, and practicality and we congratulate him this achievement!

passages.heading: Annual Awards
passages.text:
Since the Faculty Senate’s establishment in 1960 as the agent of the general faculty, elected Senators have served the Institution in matters of teaching, research, curriculum, academic standards and calendars, faculty status, and other systems as they affect the faculty as a whole. Senators value the opportunity to influence the practices and policies through shared governance with the President, University Leadership, and the Board of Trustees. They serve on standing, joint, and special committees as well as attend and participate fully in monthly Senate meetings. Faculty voices are essential to the success of an institution and necessary for academic freedom to flourish. Recognition of exemplary service to URI’s Faculty Senate through active and effective participation in the work of the Senate is made through resolutions, and annual and special awards.
The Sheila Black Grubman Award is an annual award established in 2011 and is awarded jointly by the Faculty Senate and the Office of the Provost to a faculty member who has made important contributions to and dedicated significant time and energy to the Senate.

passages.heading: Annual Awards

passages.heading: URI Internal-Facing Survey Assistance (URI-IFSA)
passages.text: URI Internal-Facing Survey Assistance (URI-IFSA)

passages.heading: URI Internal-Facing Survey Assistance (URI-IFSA)
passages.text:
The Faculty Senate recognizes that not everyone is trained in how to create and execute surveys. Nonetheless, even internal-facing surveys at URI should yield relevant and robust findings, and several URI faculty members have expertise in survey design/development. FSEC is creating a list of URI faculty trained in survey research who will volunteer to assist administrative and departmental offices, centers, institutes, unions, and other groups (henceforth referred to as survey organizers) to construct surveys as professional service to the university.
Where will the IFSA list reside?
The IFSA list will reside on the Faculty Senate website, which is openly accessible.
Who will manage the IFSA list?
Judy A. Van Wyk, Department of Sociology & Anthropology has agreed to construct/manage the IFSA list alongside the Faculty Senate Coordinator and apprise the FSEC Vice President about its status each January.
Who will be on the IFSA list?
The list will contain URI faculty members who volunteer to have their information posted on the list.
What will be on the IFSA list?

passages.heading: URI Internal-Facing Survey Assistance (URI-IFSA)
passages.text:
Every faculty member on the list must be willing to volunteer survey assistance. To volunteer, faculty will complete a short questionnaire .
Responses will be posted on the IFSA website.
Questions on the form include faculty name, contact information, areas of expertise in survey research, and their willingness to be contacted by other URI faculty for contracted or volunteered survey-related activities (which is not a requirement).
How will volunteers be selected to assist with surveys?
Survey organizers will access the IFSA list when assistance is needed, and they will select a faculty member from that list based on their areas of expertise they have listed in the questionnaire.
Survey organizers will contact faculty members directly via email or by phone. (If volunteers or survey organizers need assistance, contact Judy Van Wyk at vanwyk@uri.edu , or Lisa Bourbonnais at lbourbonnais@uri.edu .
Faculty are encouraged to respond to requests in a timely manner.
Do faculty members have to volunteer when they are contacted?
No. All faculty members are incredibly busy and may not be available when contacted.
What are volunteer tasks?

passages.heading: URI Internal-Facing Survey Assistance (URI-IFSA)
passages.text:
Specific tasks will be negotiated between faculty members and the survey organizers. The intention is to help/assist URI offices with professional survey development. Needs may vary, and the availability and expertise of faculty will vary.
Possible Examples
Faculty may meet with organizers before a survey is written to clarify the purpose and intent of the survey.
They may want to review survey drafts written by organizers and provide suggestions for revision, or they may wish to write the survey questions to be reviewed by the organizers.
Additional tasks may be negotiated and should be compensated by survey organizers.
Possible Examples
Faculty might input the survey for electronic administration in survey software or prepare paper formatting.
They may facilitate a focus group to test the survey instrument.
They may compile responses and create a database for the organizers.
They might analyze the data for the organizers and present their findings to them.

passages.heading: URI Internal-Facing Survey Assistance (URI-IFSA)
passages.text: Ethical guidelines : Survey organizers should be reassured, and faculty consultants should undertake, that work on a survey remains confidential and any discussions or draft language (even if not finally adopted) should never be shared, even after the survey period has passed.

passages.heading: Background
passages.text: Background

passages.heading: Background
passages.text:
Through RI General Law §16-32-10 , academic responsibility at URI is delegated to the President and the Faculty Senate. With the President’s concurrence, the Faculty Senate has the authority to formulate policy concerning teaching and research, study, exercise, discipline, and government.
The Faculty Senate has oversight of the University Manual, which contains the rules and regulations that govern faculty and students. Additional oversight functions include curriculum approval, which provides for the establishment, abolition, and merger of programs, departments, courses, and curriculum, including general education.
To facilitate its charge, the Faculty Senate is composed of a six-member Executive Committee, six standing committees, and special committees as needed. Once elected to serve a three-year term, Senators are assigned to a Standing Committee based upon their interests. Senators may also serve on joint committees of the Faculty Senate and the President.

passages.heading: Summer 2026 Kuali System Updates
passages.text: Summer 2026 Kuali System Updates

passages.heading: Summer 2026 Kuali System Updates
passages.text:
During summer 2026 we will be implementing a comprehensive update to the Kuali curriculum management system. This essential update includes revisions to proposal forms and workflow processes to improve usability, reduce errors, and align with recent Faculty Senate Legislation that modified our course approval process.
Because this update affects both forms and workflow functionality, a temporary pause in all proposal submissions (courses, programs, and specializations) is necessary to ensure a smooth transition.

passages.heading: During the submission pause:
passages.text:
Proposals already in workflow will continue to move forward and may still be approved
Draft course, program, and specialization proposals can still be created and edited, but not submitted
On June 2, any proposals that have not advanced beyond the College Dean level will be returned to draft status. This step is necessary to reduce the number of proposals in workflow during system updates and minimize the risk of errors. Faculty will receive an email notification once the updates are complete and Kuali operations have resumed. At that point, they may resubmit any drafted proposals into the workflow.
During this update period, undergraduate curriculum items will be reviewed by the Special Summer Curriculum Committee, and in necessary cases, may be approved during the summer on behalf of the full Senate by the Faculty Senate Executive Committee per UM Appendix C, 4.3. Graduate curriculum items will be held for review by the Graduate Council at their first meeting of AY 2026–2027.

passages.heading: During the submission pause:
passages.text: This temporary pause is an important step to ensure the system can better support our curriculum processes moving forward. This update also establishes a foundation for smaller, annual improvements in future years.

passages.heading: BTS: What this Process Involves
passages.text: This update is a collaborative effort between the Office of the Registrar, Faculty Senate leadership, Kuali technicians, and URI IT staff who support integration between Kuali and eCampus.

passages.heading: Key Partners
passages.text:
University Registrar (Jack Humphrey)
Catalog Coordinator (Taylor Flynn)
Kuali technical team
URI IT staff supporting eCampus integration

passages.heading: Process Overview
passages.text:
1. System Updates in Kuali
We begin by working with Kuali technicians to update existing forms. This may include adding, removing, or modifying form elements (“gadgets”) to improve functionality and alignment with institutional needs.
2. Testing in Sandbox Environment
Updated forms are tested in the Kuali sandbox environment to ensure they function as intended before any live changes are made.
3. Integration Testing with eCampus
In collaboration with URI IT, we test how the updated Kuali workflows interact with eCampus to confirm system compatibility and data integrity.
4. Review and Refinement
Based on testing results, necessary adjustments are made to ensure the workflows and integrations function correctly and efficiently.
5. Production Deployment
Once testing is complete and the system is fully validated, Kuali technicians deploy the updates to the live production environment.
6. Return to Normal Operations
After deployment, standard Kuali operations resume with the updated system in place.

passages.heading: Why are we doing such a major update now rather than incremental changes?
passages.text:
This is the first full system-wide update since Kuali was implemented in AY 21-22.
It addresses accumulated system and workflow issues and aligns Kuali with FSEC Bill 25-26-01.
Going forward, we will make smaller, annual updates so the system can evolve incrementally rather than requiring large-scale overhauls.

passages.heading: How will these updates improve usability for faculty who regularly submit proposals?
passages.text:
Proposal forms will be more intuitive and streamlined, reducing errors during submission.
Workflows will better match updated approval processes, making it easier to track proposals and understand what’s required at each step.

passages.heading: Are there any risks to data or proposals during this update?
passages.text:
There is a risk for proposals currently in the workflow, which is why we are pausing submissions and controlling which proposals remain under review.
This allows us to monitor a smaller, manageable set of proposals and catch errors before they affect final approvals.

passages.heading: Will these updates become the standard for annual summer updates going forward?
passages.text: Yes. The goal is to transition to smaller, regular updates each summer so the system evolves alongside university needs.

passages.heading: What happens if a proposal isn’t approved by the College Dean by the June 1 deadline?
passages.text:
It will remain in draft status in the proposer’s dashboard until the ability to submit proposals to the workflow is resumed, and the proposer can re-submit it to the workflow.
Faculty can continue to edit it but cannot submit it until the system resumes full operations after the update.

passages.heading: Can the deadlines be extended if there are delays in approvals or testing?
passages.text: The deadlines are set to provide a predictable workflow, but if unexpected technical issues arise, we can adjust timelines and communicate changes clearly to faculty.

passages.heading: How strict is the May 15 pause for submissions—what if someone misses it?
passages.text:
After May 15, new submissions cannot enter the workflow.
Drafts can still be created and edited, so nothing is lost, but proposals cannot be submitted until the update is complete.

passages.heading: Can proposals already in the workflow be edited during the update?
passages.text: Yes, drafts can still be edited. Proposals under review remain accessible, but submission of new proposals is temporarily paused to reduce risk.

passages.heading: If my proposal is returned to draft status, will I lose any data or attachments?
passages.text: No. Returning proposals to draft preserves all information; it simply prevents them from moving through the workflow until the system update is complete.

passages.heading: How will faculty know if a proposal encounters an error during the update?
passages.text:
We will monitor all proposals actively and communicate directly with affected proposers if any issues arise.
Support contacts will be provided for troubleshooting.

passages.heading: What about Temporary Courses?
passages.text:
Remember: Temporary Courses require approval by:
A vote of the department faculty
The department chair
The college curriculum committee
And the dean.
They also require a 7-day commenting period by faculty – this is accomplished by the monthly Temporary and New Course Email that is distributed on the last week day of every month.
If any temporary courses in the workflow as of June 2 have a Fall 2026 effective date, I will contact the proposer and the relevant approvers to assess the likelihood that the course can be fully approved before the June Temporary Course email is distributed. Those proposals with a likelihood of being approved by the college dean prior to the June Temp. Course Email will remain in the workflow.

passages.heading: How will proposals approved by the Special Summer Curriculum Committee (SSCC) and have an effective date for Fall 2026 be handled?
passages.text:
The Faculty Senate Executive Committee (FSEC) has authority to approve these on behalf of the Senate over the summer per UM Appendix C, Section 4.3.
These proposals will appear on the September 2026 Senate report for formal acknowledgment.

passages.heading: Will faculty need to resubmit proposals if errors occur during testing?
passages.text:
Our goal is to prevent errors through careful testing.
If any issues occur, faculty will be contacted with clear instructions, but resubmission should be minimal and will likely be handled by the Kuali System Admins.

passages.heading: How does the FSEC’s emergency approval authority work?
passages.text:
It allows curricular items eligible for a Fall effective date to be approved over the summer by FSEC.
This ensures timely implementation without waiting for a full Senate meeting.

passages.heading: Will there be training or guidance on the updated forms and workflows?
passages.text:
Yes. We will provide resources for faculty to navigate the updated forms in the “Curriculum Toolkit” Faculty Senate website.
Additional support will be available during the transition period.

passages.heading: What changes can faculty expect in the proposal forms themselves?
passages.text:
Forms will be more intuitive, with clearer fields and streamlined options to reduce errors.
Some steps are being automated to align with the updated approval workflows.

passages.heading: How will integration with eCampus be tested, and will it affect course registration?
passages.text:
Integration will be tested in a sandbox environment with URI IT and Kuali technicians.
The goal is a seamless transfer into eCampus with no disruption to registration once updates are implemented.

passages.heading: Who should faculty contact if they run into issues after the update?
passages.text: Faculty can continue to contact Genviéve Spitale for Kuali questions, or Enrollment Services for eCampus questions

passages.heading: Will there be a sandbox environment for faculty to practice using the updated forms?
passages.text: No, the sandbox environment is only available to URI IT and Kuali System Administrators

passages.heading: How will feedback from this update cycle be incorporated into future improvements?
passages.text: Feedback from faculty and staff during this summer update will inform subsequent enhancements, keeping Kuali aligned with user experience and workflow needs.

passages.heading: When will my proposal be approved?
passages.text: When will my proposal be approved?

passages.heading: When will my proposal be approved?
passages.text:
Quick Links:
Step-by-Step Guide
TL;DR
Submitting a curricular proposal in Kuali begins a structured, multi-level review process, and we know you’re eager to know when your item will be reviewed and approved. While timelines vary across colleges, this guide will help you understand where your proposal is in the process and when to expect its full approval.

passages.heading: Step 1: Understand the approval path
passages.text:
All curricular proposals move through multiple levels of review. While this can vary slightly, most proposals follow this sequence:
Department-level review(s)
College Curriculum Committee
College Dean
Faculty Senate Curriculum Committees (Graduate Council, Curriculum & Standards, General Education)
Faculty Senate (courses are fully approved at this level)
University President (program modifications and new certificates, minors, and specializations are approved at this level)
Board of Trustees (new major and degree programs are approved at this level)
Each step depends on the successful approval at the previous level.

passages.heading: Step 2: Know the current proposal status
passages.text:
All who have access to Kuali have the ability to check on the status of every proposal currently under review. To find the current workflow status:
Open the proposal in Kuali.
Access it from your dashboard if you are the proposer, or
Search by name in the Proposals section, and use filters to refine results
Review the workflow status. At the top of the proposal page, the workflow status shows:
The current stage of approval
The users in the role of approving that step
Expand for full details. Click the expand option to the right of “ Workflow Status ” to view:
The completed approval steps, and
The remaining steps before final approval.

passages.heading: Step 3: Know the submission deadlines
passages.text:
Department, college, and Faculty Senate committees each have deadlines for including proposals on their meeting agendas. Faculty should consult with their department or college curriculum committees for specific deadlines at those levels of approval.
Each summer, submission deadlines are set for college deans to help ensure proposals are approved by the Faculty Senate on a predictable timeline.
Using the table below as an example: Proposals approved by College Deans by February 9 were scheduled for the late February/early March Faculty Senate Curriculum Committee meetings. If approved there, they were then presented to the Faculty Senate for approval at the March 12 meeting.

passages.heading: Step 4: Factor in Revisions
passages.text:
Many proposals require revisions during the review process. The following meeting results can impact your approval timeline:
Tabled : The committee needs additional information before making a decision. Once the requested information is provided, the proposal will be reviewed again at the next meeting.
Contingently Approved : The proposal is approved pending minor revisions or clarifications. No additional committee review is required. Once the conditions are met, the proposal will move to the next step.
Sent Back : The proposal requires substantial revisions. It must be updated and resubmitted, at which point it will re-enter the workflow from the beginning.

passages.heading: Step 5: Track Your Proposal Status
passages.text:
Proposal statuses can be tracked by logging into Kuali and expanding the workflow, or by searching for items that have been fully approved by the college in the Proposal Tracker.
Please note: The proposal tracker is updated manually by the Faculty Senate Office and is not automated. While every effort is made to ensure accuracy, occasional errors may occur and are typically corrected after each Faculty Senate meeting. For the most up-to-date status, please check Kuali .

passages.heading: Step 6: Final Check
passages.text:
By the Monday prior to each monthly Faculty Senate meeting, the Faculty Senate Office distributes the Senate agenda to all faculty.
This agenda includes reports from the Graduate Council, Curriculum & Standards Committee, and General Education Committee, which are voted on during the meeting.
If your proposal has been approved by a committee but does not appear on the agenda, please contact the committee chair or the Faculty Senate Office. Reports are prepared manually, and with a high volume of proposals each month, occasional errors may occur. These are typically resolved quickly.

passages.heading: Course Proposals after the Senate Meeting
passages.text: The integration between Kuali and PeopleSoft is not immediate, can take several days, and requires review by Enrollment Services to ensure all information migrated accurately. Please allow up to two weeks after the Senate Meeting for new courses and course modifications to appear in eCampus.

passages.heading: Program Proposals after the Senate Meeting
passages.text:
Once curriculum committee reports are approved by the Faculty Senate, they are converted into Bills. Bills are signed by the Faculty Senate President and forwarded to the University President for review and signature. Once the University President signs & approves, the Bills are returned to the Faculty Senate Office and the proposals are approved in Kuali.
Special Case: New Majors and New Degree Programs
After University President approval, these proposals are forwarded to the Board of Trustees. Once the Faculty Senate Office confirms Board approval, the new major or degree is fully approved in Kuali.
The URI Board of Trustees meeting dates can be found here.

passages.heading: Choosing the Right Proposal Type
passages.text: Choosing the Right Proposal Type

passages.heading: Course Proposal Types
passages.text:
There are two types of curricular proposals: modifying an existing curricular item or creating a new one. It is important to select the correct type, as proposals submitted under the wrong category will be denied and must be resubmitted.
Course modifications that are often mistaken for new courses include:
Making a temporary course permanent
Changing the course code of an existing cross-listed, or non-cross-listed course
Adding a new cross-listing to an existing course
New course proposals are appropriate for:
Creating a new permanent course
Creating a new temporary course
Creating a new cross-listed course
Course Proposal Guide

passages.heading: Program Proposal Types
passages.text:
There are two types of curricular proposals: modifying an existing curricular item or creating a new one. It is important to select the correct type, as proposals submitted under the wrong category will be denied and must be resubmitted.
In addition to these proposal types, each program is classified under one of four credential types: Degree, Major, Certificate, or Minor.
Degree: An academic credential awarded by the University upon successful completion of a prescribed program of study. Degrees include bachelor’s, master’s, and doctoral degrees.
In Kuali, “Degree” is selected under credential type when it is the only program offered under that degree. Examples include the MPS (Master of Professional Studies), BIS (Bachelor of Interdisciplinary Studies), Pharm.D. (Doctor of Pharmacy), and DNP (Doctor of Nursing Practice).
Major: A defined field of study within a degree program consisting of a required set of courses and related academic requirements in a specific discipline.
In Kuali, “Major” is selected under credential type when the program is one of multiple options offered under the same degree. These typically include BA, BS, MA, MS, and PhD programs.

passages.heading: Program Proposal Types
passages.text:
Certificate: A formal program of study consisting of a defined set of courses in a focused area. Certificates may be completed independently or in conjunction with a degree program.
Minor: A secondary field of study consisting of a prescribed set of courses in a discipline outside a student’s major. A minor is intended to complement a student’s primary area of study.
Program proposal guide

passages.heading: Specialization Proposal Types
passages.text: There are two types of curricular proposals: modifying an existing curricular item or creating a new one. It is important to select the correct type, as proposals submitted under the wrong category will be denied and must be resubmitted.

passages.heading: 🚨The Difference Between Specializations, Sub-Plans, Options, Tracks, Focus Areas, & Concentrations
passages.text:
Do these terms mean different things? Yes. These terms represent distinct curricular structures. Understanding the differences is essential to ensure that programs and specializations are proposed accurately.
Sub-plans (eCampus), Specializations (Kuali), Options (UM), Tracks
Are coded in eCampus
Represent a formally recognized area of study within the program
Have defined requirements that students must complete
Appear on the student’s transcript
Are formally created and maintained in the Specializations section of Kuali
Concentrations, Focus Areas
Are not coded in eCampus
Represent an optional area of study chosen by the student
May include suggested course sequences for guidance
Do not appear on the student’s transcript
Are described only within the program description to which they belong

passages.heading: What about ABMs?
passages.text:
Accelerated Bachelors to Masters programs (ABMs) are Specializations . ABMs require an identified set of courses that are eligible to be double counted towards the Bachelor degree requirements and the Masters degree requirements.

passages.text: Academic Requirements

passages.heading: Chapter 8 – Academic Regulations
passages.text: 8.20.10 General Education. The foundation of all academic efforts begins with a broad base of knowledge covering all areas of human accomplishment and experience, broadly categorized as the arts, the humanities, the sciences including mathematics, and the social sciences. Therefore, URI students will gain exposure to the theories and practices of these four areas, as well as in their relationships to one another, regardless of each student’s major. Knowledge, by itself, is insufficient for development of well-rounded individuals. URI students will receive focused training and practice in the competencies of writing, oral communication, mathematics, and information literacy and apply all four to a wide variety of projects. Knowledge and competencies, however, are still insufficient. To be a fully functioning citizen, students must develop a sense of their place in society at the local, national, and global levels. URI students will be exposed to the experience and practice of responsibilities in civic engagement, global perspectives, and diversity and inclusion to clearly perceive and engage with the world in which they live. Through a General Education program pursued across a college career and in conjunction with specialized work in one or more majors, the student must clearly demonstrate the ability to synthesize knowledge, competencies, and responsibilities in a coherent and comprehensive display of scholarly or practice-based work. This is the fundamental goal of the URI General Education program — to enable students to develop themselves as scholars and individuals ready to employ and synthesize knowledge, competencies, and responsibilities, to solve problems and to engage confidently with the personal, public, and professional spheres.

passages.heading: Chapter 8 – Academic Regulations
passages.text:
The General Education program will assess student exposure to twelve (12) Student Learning Outcomes in four (4) areas:
A. Build knowledge of diverse peoples and cultures and of the natural and physical world.
Understand and apply theories and methods of the science, technology, engineering, and mathematical (STEM) disciplines .
Understand theories and methods of the social and behavioral sciences .
Understand the context and significance of the humanities using theoretical and historical perspectives.
Understand the context and significance of arts and design using aesthetic and technical perspectives on form, creativity, and performance.
B. Develop intellectual and interdisciplinary competencies for academic and lifelong learning.
Write effective and precise texts that fulfill their communicative purposes and address various audiences.
Communicate effectively via understanding audiences, listening, delivering oral presentations, and actively participating in teams or group work.
Apply the appropriate mathematical , statistical, or computational strategies to problem solving.
Develop information literacy to independently research complex issues.

passages.heading: Chapter 8 – Academic Regulations
passages.text:
C. Exercise individual and social responsibilities .
Develop and engage in civic knowledge and responsibilities .
Develop and exercise global responsibilities
Develop and exercise responsibilities relating to diversity and inclusion
D. Integrate and apply these abilities and capacities, adapting them to new settings, questions, and responsibilities to lay the foundation for lifelong learning.
Demonstrate the ability to synthesize multiple knowledge perspectives, competencies, and responsibilities.
#13-14-21 , #15-16-13 , #15-16-20
8.20.11 All baccalaureate students at the University of Rhode Island shall fulfill the University’s General Education requirements as outlined in paragraphs 8.20.12 through 8.20.14. Students may fulfill their University General Education requirements throughout their undergraduate career. Transfer students may receive General Education credit for courses taught at another institution insofar as such courses are equivalent to courses given General Education credit at the University of Rhode Island. #03-04–29 , #13-14-21 , #15-16-13 , #15-16-33

passages.heading: Chapter 8 – Academic Regulations

Knowledge (Area A) and Competency (Area B)
Knowledge (Area A) and Responsibility (Area C)
