passages.heading: JCODL Annual Report for AY 2022-2023 | Page 1
passages.text: Joint Committee on Distance and Online Learning Final report 2022-2023 Membership Kathleen Torrens, Chair, Interim Director, Office for the Advancement of Teaching and Learning. Anne Veeger, Vice Provost for Academic and Faculty Initiatives. Joannah Portman-Daley, Associate Director, Online Ed/URI Online, Office for the Advancement of Teaching and Learning. Michelle Peach, Clinical Assistant Professor, Department of Natural Resources Science. Amy Correia, Clinical Assistant Professor, College of Education. Farhad Atash, Professor, Landscape Architecture. Nilton Porto, Associate Professor, Human Development & Family Science. Kamilah A’Vant, Assistant Dean DEI, College of Arts & Sciences. Michelle Rogers, Director. ITS Teaching & Learning. Alicia Vaandering, Assistant Professor, URI Libraries Karl Aspelund, Associate Professor, College of Business . Meeting dates The committee met on the follow dates: Tuesday 11/15 Weds 1/25 Weds 2/22 Thurs 3/30 Weds 4/26 Executive Summary: The JCODL, which reconvened in 2022-2023 after a pandemic-related hiatus, considered two key priorities during the current academic year: ● Exam Proctoring Policy for Online Courses ● URI Instructional Modalities and Descriptions The Committee is recommending Faculty Senate action on these two items, including rescission of the 2013 “Exam Proctoring Policy for Online Courses”, and adoption of revised definitions of instructional modalities which clarify course delivery for faculty and students. Committee Recommendations 1. Exam Proctoring Policy for Online Courses.

passages.heading: JCODL Annual Report for AY 2022-2023 | Page 2
passages.text:
Context: In 2013, an “ Exam Proctoring Policy for Online Courses ” was approved by the Faculty Senate, though never included in the manual or any other official venue, concerning exams for online courses.
In short, this policy allowed for online courses to require in-person proctored exams, whether on one of the URI campuses, or at an approved venue elsewhere.
Should the student be unable to travel to a URI campus, it was the student’s responsibility to find an appropriate venue and an approved proctor, AND to shoulder any related fees.
This policy was brought to light in 2022 by a faculty member teaching an online undergraduate course who wished to require a proctored in-person exam on the Kingston campus.
Discussion: The committee discussed this policy and its ramifications at some length, including the fact that it was not in the University Manual, etc.

passages.heading: JCODL Annual Report for AY 2022-2023 | Page 2
passages.text:
Discussion further circulated around the fact that best practices for online instruction recommend against proctored exams due to issues with proctoring services such as lockdown browsers, questions of access and fairness to all learners, privacy concerns, the fact that a key reason that learners enroll in online classes relates to scheduling flexibility, and that most courses can be effectively assessed without the use of high-stakes, in-person exams.
Recommendation: It is the recommendation of the Joint Committee for Online/Distance Learning that the Faculty Senate rescind the 2013 “Exam Proctoring Policy for Online Courses”.
Courses delivered in a fully online modality should assess students through the online modality.
Fully online certificate/degree programs with accreditation requirements related to assessment may implement remote proctoring solutions at no additional cost to students.
The Office of ATL is available to support faculty as they develop assessments for their online courses. 2.
Definitions of learning modalities.

passages.heading: JCODL Annual Report for AY 2022-2023 | Page 2
passages.text:
Context: Several years ago (circa 2013), URI adopted definitions of online and blended learning (Face to face < 25% online, Blended 25-75% online, Online 75-100% online), with the implicit, but unstated, assumption that the online portion was asynchronous.
The COVID era of remote instruction gave rise to additional approaches to remote instruction and the need to reflect all available modality options and to provide clear, comprehensible and accessible definitions and descriptions for the benefit of faculty and students.
The work: The committee spent a large amount of time researching, discussing, evaluating, and compiling a list of instructional modalities in the digital space.
Recommendation: The committee recommends that the Faculty Senate and University adopt, institutionalize, and publicize the following learning modality definitions and descriptions.
The committee further recommends that the Faculty Senate review the approval process for blended and online courses, including the percentage ranges of online delivery.

passages.heading: JCODL Annual Report for AY 2022-2023 | Page 2
passages.text:
URI Instructional Modalities and Descriptions The following recommendations are the result of collaborative effort by the JCDOL membership which includes representation of faculty across the Colleges, URI’s Office for the Advancement of Teaching and Learning, ITS Teaching and Learning, and the Office of the Provost, and.
Past and current practice at URI, best-practices in online education, and a review of online education definitions in use at peer-institutions were used to develop the following overview of the

passages.heading: JCODL Annual Report for AY 2022-2023 | Page 3
passages.text: university’s instructional modalities, a definition of each, and considerations for implementation starting in the Fall 2023 semester. Definitions Modality (location/ meeting arrangement) Description In-person All instruction occurs in a specified physical location and on specified days/times. Blended* I nstruction combines both in person meetings on speciﬁed days/times and online asynchronous instruction. The schedule of instruction and the weekly time commitment to online asynchronous instruction are clear to students in the syllabus on the ﬁrst day of class. Online synchronous* All instruction occurs online at specified days/times. Online mixed* All i nstruction occurs online in a combination of synchronous meetings on speciﬁed days/times and asynchronous instruction. The schedule of instruction and the weekly time commitment to online asynchronous instruction are clear to students in the syllabus. Online asynchronous All instruction occurs online with no specified meeting days/times. The weekly time commitment to online asynchronous instruction is clear to students in the syllabus. Considerations for Implementation Schedule : Regardless of modality, the schedule of all required meetings must be made clear in the syllabus and in eCampus to ensure that students understand the pattern of required meetings. Time Commitment : The approximate weekly time commitment (time on task) for asynchronous instructional activities should be clear in the syllabus so that students can plan their schedules for greatest success. Per 8.31.10 Basis for Credit, “ the student workload for an online class shall be equivalent to the in-class and out-of-class work in its face-to-face equivalent.” For

passages.heading: JCODL Annual Report for AY 2022-2023 | Page 4
passages.text: example, “ For this 3-credit hour in-person semester course, you should expect to spend around three hours in class each week and an average of six hours preparing for class (this includes readings, homework, and other assigned activities),” and for an online class “For this 3-credit hour online class you should expect to spend three hours per week completing online instructional activities, and an additional six hours on related activities, including readings, homework, online discussions, and other assigned activities.” Synchronous Online and Online Mixed Modality options : Asynchronous online delivery of courses and degree programs is designed to increase student access to education by reducing the barriers to attendance presented by conflicts between work-life responsibilities and scheduled in-person classes. This student access lens should therefore be centered in decisions and policies about the use and scheduling of synchronous and mixed online courses. The scheduling of synchronous online classes during standard working/class hours (e.g. M-F 8-5) creates barriers to attendance and should be avoided. We recommend, however, that flexibility be extended to J-Term, summer, evening, and graduate program classes, particularly for the modalities noted above with an asterisk (*). Membership Note for 2023-2024: Dr. Chris Lavan, incoming Associate Vice Provost of Teaching and Learning, will assume leadership of the JCODL in Fall 2023.

passages.text: 1 FACULTY SENATE OFFICE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND FACULTY SENATE September 17, 2020 Faculty Senate Curriculum and Standards Committee Report 2019-2020-12 At the July 28, 2020 special summer meeting of the Curriculum and Standards Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate. SECTION I Informational Matters NEW TEMPORARY (X) COURSES: COLLEGE OF ENGINEERING: EGR 101X, Engineering's Response to COVID-19 (1 cr.) Invited speakers discuss how the engineering profession has and is responding to the coronavirus pandemic. (Seminar 1) S/U only. ELE 446X, Introduction to Power Electronics (3 crs.) Principles of power electronics: switched-mode converters; AC modeling; controller and compensator design; magnetic circuit theory. Examples such as server and network power supplies, grid-connected power systems, and wireless power transfer. (Lec. 3) Pre: ((ELE 212 or 220 or OCE 206) and PHY204 and MTH (244 or 362)) or permission of instructor. Not for graduate credit. COLLEGE OF THE ENVIRONMENT AND LIFE SCIENCES: GEO 101X, Undergraduate Seminar: Hot Topics in Geosciences (1 cr.) Seminar featuring oral presentations of the results of current topical research with individual student investigations. Compressed model yields 1 credit for 4 weeks of work. (Seminar) Pre: Any 100-level course in GEO, NRS, OCG, BIO, CHM, PHY. May be repeated for a maximum of 4 credits with a different topic. COLLEGE OF ARTS AND SCIENCES: AAF 120X, Rewatching The Watchmen: Race and Media (1 cr.) Revisits The Watchmen graphic novel and HBO series to consider African-American history, the intersection of race and gender, the landscape of new media, and pop-culture's role in inspiring social change. (Online) S/U grades only.

passages.heading: #20-21-1A | Page 3
passages.text:
2 AAF 207X, Conversations on Race (1 cr.) Examines American conversations about race.
Students survey current attitudes on race in popular culture, internet, social media and major networks and then host an online forum on race. (Online) S/U grades only.
CCJ 100X, Interrogating Criminal Justice Reform (1 cr.) Overview and analysis of selected topics essential to criminal justice reform agendas.
Topics focus on the criminal justice system’s role as a social institution and mechanism of social stratification. (Online) S/U grades only.
ENG 150X, Tolkien, Wordsworth, and Escapism (1 cr.) Consideration of the political, intellectual, and aesthetic qualities of escapism as a practice of self care and engagement in challenging times, through the work of two master practitioners of the concept: Wordsworth and Tolkien. (Online) S/U grades only.
HIS/APG 392X, The URI Campus: A Walk Through Time (1 cr.) Exploration of the complexities of place and power through time.
URI was founded in 1892, but the history of this space is much older and intertwined with the Narragansett People. (Online) S/U grades only..

passages.heading: #20-21-1A | Page 3
passages.text:
PSC 101X, Workplace Readiness for Social Science Majors (1 cr.) An online career readiness workshop designed for social science majors in the College of Arts and Sciences.
Students create personalized content and discuss various related topics with associated URI alumni. (Online) Pre: sophomore, junior or senior standing; for CCJ, AAF, SOC, APG, ECN, GWS, or PSC majors only.
S/U grades only.
PSC/AAF 301X, Racial Inequality in Government and Politics (1 cr.) Introduction to anti-racist theory and the cultural and societal implications of the manifestation of racism in institutions, culture, and most critically, government policy. (Online) S/U grades only.
SCM 351X, 2020TV: Broadcasting Contemporary Issues (1 cr.) Examination of the realities of 2020 with students producing content responding to current issues and topics concerning contemporary challenges for a weekly web broadcast, shot and captured remotely with Zoom. (Online) S/U grades only.
SOC/APG 140X, Anti-Black Racism and White Supremacy (1 cr.) Examine key causes and consequences of anti-black racism and white supremacy in the United States.
Reflect and engage with a learning community on these issues. (Online) S/U grades only.

RECOMMENDATION FROM THE FACULTY SENATE EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE CHANGES TO 2020-2021 UNIVERSITY MANUAL APPENDIX C: BY-LAWS OF THE FACULTY SENATE: Section 7.
Quorum and Meeting Times. 7.1 A majority of the elected Senate shall constitute a quorum except at special meetings where there shall be no quorum required if actions taken at such special meetings are to be returned to the Senate for final action. 7.2 Regular Senate meetings shall begin at 3:00 p.m. or as soon thereafter as a quorum is determined to be present, and shall be adjourned at 5:00 p.m.
When the Senate fails to complete its agenda within the time limit, the meeting either (1) shall be recessed and reconvened one week thereafter at the usual time, or (2) shall be adjourned and the unfinished business postponed definitely until the next regular meeting of the Senate. 7.3 Regular Faculty Senate Meetings shall be held at least once each month on Thursdays during the academic year. #00-01–28 7.4 At all Senate meetings debate on each main motion, each amendment thereto and discussion subsequent to informational reports shall be limited to fifteen minutes.

passages.heading: #20-21-3 | Page 2
passages.text:
Debate may be extended in any Senate meeting by one-third vote of the members present. 7.5 In the event that Senate meetings are held virtually, Senate meetings may extend past the 5:00 p.m. required adjournment time (see 7.2) for a period of no longer than 30 minutes.
Virtual meetings may not extend past 5:30 p.m.
At 5:00 p.m. a motion to extend the meeting must be called and passed.
If discussion is not completed in fifteen minutes, one more motion to extend the meeting must be called and passed.
When the Senate fails to complete its agenda in the virtual meeting within the time limit, the meeting either (1) shall be recessed and reconvened one week thereafter at the usual time, or (2) shall be adjourned and the unfinished business postponed definitely until the next regular meeting of the Senate. 1

passages.heading: JCODL Annual Report for AY 2024-2025 | Page 1
passages.text:
Chris Lavan, Associate Vice Provost, ATL, JCODL Chair Purpose of the Committee The purpose of the Joint Committee on Online and Distance Learning (JCODL) is to propose, examine, and recommend institutional policies and practices for developing, planning, and evaluating online and distance learning with a focus on quality, sustainability, and connection to the University’s mission, with approval of the Faculty Senate and Provost.
Further, JCODL, considers faculty training, quality in delivery of online offerings, student learning outcomes, and ADA compliance regarding online and distance learning, as well as develops and implements strategic plans for online courses, certificate, and degree programs. (University Manual 5.78.10 - 5.78.11).
Executive Summary The committee discussed several topics internally (listed in the next section) during the 2024-2025 academic year, and brought forth one proposal for consideration and a vote to the university’s Faculty Senate.

passages.heading: JCODL Annual Report for AY 2024-2025 | Page 1
passages.text: Proposal: Updated Adoption of New Course Modalities and Methods of Instruction This proposal had been a priority of this committee for three academic years, and with collaboration between several Faculty Senators, including past Curriculum and Standards 1

passages.heading: JCODL Annual Report for AY 2024-2025 | Page 2
passages.text:
Committee (CASC) Chair and Faculty Senate Executive Committee (FSEC) member Senator Preisser, as well as the Office of the Provost and University Registrar’s Office, the proposal was introduced during the November 2024 Faculty Senate meeting.
At the November Faculty Senate meeting the proposal was tabled, but then brought back to the floor of the Faculty Senate during its January 2025 meeting where it was approved by a vote during that same meeting.
Ultimately, the initial proposal for updated recognized teaching methods evolved to include methods of instruction as well.

passages.heading: JCODL Annual Report for AY 2024-2025 | Page 2
passages.text: A portion of the slides presented during that January 2025 meeting are included within this report under section “Appendix A: Sample presentation slides of proposed course modalities and methods of instruction”, and the official titles of each proposal are listed directly below. ● FSEC Report #2024-2025-02 - Proposal to define the various modalities of instruction within the University Manual ● FSEC Report #2025-2025-03 - Proposal to define the various methods of instruction within the University Manual Internal Topics of Discussion During the 2024-25 Academic Year ● Reviewed Data Related to 2023-2024 Participation and Completion Rates of URI Instructors Engaging the 4 Qualification Pathways to Teach Online at URI ○ Outcome: ■ 83 new faculty qualified to teach online during the 2023-2024 academic year. ● Reviewed New Self-Paced Option for Online Pedagogy Experience ○ Outcomes: ■ Piloted over Summer 2024 and softly launched for the 2024-2025 academic year. ■ Completed by 13 instructors with generally positive feedback from participants. ● Reviewed Online Teaching Recommendation Qualification Survey ○ Outcome ■ This new tool was presented to the committee during the 2024-25 academic year.

passages.text: It’s a resource intended to provide guidance to URI instructors about which of the 4 pathways for qualifying to teach online would be best suited for them based on their level of experience teaching online. ■ Feedback from the committee was received and used to improve this tool. 2

passages.heading: #20-21-4A | Page 2
passages.text:
​ FACULTY ​ ​ SENATE ​ ​ OFFICE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND FACULTY SENATE October 15, 2020 Faculty Senate Curriculum and Standards Committee Report 2020-2021-1 At the October 1, 2020 meeting of the Curriculum and Standards Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate.
SECTION I Informational Matters COLLEGE OF ARTS & SCIENCES: MTH 103, Applied Precalculus Add online section Linear, quadratic, power, exponential, logarithmic and periodic functions - their graphs and properties.
Emphasis on interpretation and real-life applications, examples and modeling.
Not for major credit in mathematics.
Not intended for students planning to take MTH 111 or MTH 141. (Lec. 3) MTH 244, Differential Equations Add online section (3 crs.) Classification and solution of differential equations involving one independent variable.
Applications to the physical sciences.
Basics for further study in applied mathematics and for advanced work in physics and engineering. (Lec. 3) Pre: MTH 142.

passages.heading: #20-21-4A | Page 2
passages.text:
MUS 280, Mid-program Portfolio in Music Delete course (0 crs.) Individual accomplishment of activities and experiences, demonstrating interest and competency in music at the midpoint in the student's program of studies as a music major. (Portfolio) Pre: sophomore standing in music.
MUS 480, Graduation Portfolio Delete course (0-2 crs.) Seminar covering topics and the development of a graduation portfolio appropriate to the student's degree program.
The portfolio shows accomplishments from throughout the degree program and achievement of competencies indicating potential success as a graduate. (Portfolio) Pre: MUS 280 or permission of chairperson and senior standing in music.
For music education majors, concurrent enrollment in EDC 484 required.
To be taken during the last semester of coursework in the major.
May be repeated.
Not for graduate credit. 1

passages.heading: #20-21-4A | Page 3
passages.text:
COLLEGE OF PHARMACY: BPS 334, Pharmacology and Medicinal Chemistry of Cardiovascular and Renal Drugs Delete course (2 crs.) Mechanism of action, adverse effects, and therapeutic applications of drugs affecting cardiovascular and renal function. (Lec. 2) Pre: Doctor of Pharmacy professional student in good standing; or permission of instructor.
SECTION II Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation by the Faculty Senate COURSES CHANGES: COLLEGE OF ARTS & SCIENCES: PRS/JOR 340, Public Relations Strategies Change title, prerequisite (3 crs.) Cross-listed as (PRS), JOR 340.
Principles and procedures in public relations: emphasis on role of the public relations practitioner as a specialist in communication; analysis of publications produced as a part of public relations. (Lec. 3/Online) Pre: Declared PR majors or PR minors, PRS100.
COLLEGE OF PHARMACY: BPS 301, Pharmaceutics I: Biopharmaceutics Change title, description, prerequisites (2 crs.) Application of kinetics to stability, dissolution, absorption, and other biopharmaceutical processes.
Bioavailability and generic equivalence. (Lec. 2) BSPS majors with junior standing and above.
CHE students by permission number only.

passages.heading: #20-21-4A | Page 3

passages.heading: #20-21-5 | Page 2
passages.text: 1 Constitution, By-Laws and University Manual Committee Report # 2020-2021-1 to the Faculty Senate Proposal to Change Titles of Faculty Senate Officers The FSEC proposes to change the titles of the Faculty Senate Officers: Chairperson/Chair to President and Vice Chairperson/Vice Chair to Vice President. Rationale: ● The Student Senate, the Graduate Student Association, and the AAUP use the titles of President and Vice President. The proposed change will make the titles of the officers of the Faculty Senate consistent with other organizations at URI. ● The titles of President and Vice President will distinguish the roles and responsibilities of the Faculty Senate from other chair titles used for committees. ● The change is timely considering the recent establishment of the URI Board of Trustees (a change from Board of Education/Council on Postsecondary Education) and anticipated interaction with the Faculty Senate. ● The titles of President and Vice President will emphasize the significance and stature of the Faculty Senate and its role in shared governance both externally and within URI. ● President Dooley supports this proposed change in titles of Faculty Senate officers. Process: If approved, the Faculty Senate authorizes the Committee on Bylaws and the University Manual to propose appropriate edits in the University Manual and present the proposed changes in the University Manual to the Faculty Senate at the September 2020 meeting.

6 University Manual – Chapters 2, 5, 8 The Administration 2.39.13 The Areas of Responsibility of the Ombudsman are Equity, Critical Review, and Recommendations and Report.
Equity: to help individuals or groups in specific cases to get just and equitable treatment.

passages.heading: #20-21-5 | Page 7
passages.text: In securing equity, the Ombudsman shall: afford full opportunity for presentation in confidence of any complaint or grievance from any student, faculty member, or member of the administrative staff alleging unfairness, discourtesy, undue delay, or other malfunctioning in any and all processes at the University of Rhode Island; investigate, in confidence, to determine the degree of validity of the complaint; and mediate or otherwise resolve the problem, arriving in confidence at what appears to him/her to be a just resolution (in the dismissal of the complaint, or in recommended action based on the verified complaint). (The Ombudsman will not be expected to concern him/herself with the normal operations of established grievance processes or disciplinary procedures contained in the University Manual, except that s/he may, on the basis solely of his/her own judgment, inquire into possible bias or malfunction in any of those proceedings, and make a confidential report thereon to the office of the President and to the PresidentChairperson of the Faculty Senate).

passages.heading: #20-21-5 | Page 7
passages.text:
Critical Review: to help administrative functionaries (whether connected with Student Government or with faculty or administrative offices) to improve their processes, not only correct a particular inequity or injustice but also to prevent its recurrence.
In carrying out this function the Ombudsman shall: be receptive to all suggestions, comments and criticism regarding the general functioning of University processes and procedures (as distinguished from individual grievances or complaints of inequity); make appropriate inquiries; make recommendations in confidence to the administrative officer who heads the particular unit involved; and report to the office of the President and to the PresidentChairperson of the Faculty Senate as to the disposition of the recommendation.

passages.heading: #20-21-5 | Page 8
passages.text:
7 Recommendation and Report: on the basis of inquiry and experience to recommend such changes in procedure and practice as may seem to him/her to be appropriate, and to make a final public report of his/her actions.
In fulfilling this function, the Ombudsman shall: in addition to any recommendations submitted in connection with the foregoing functions, from time to time, make such reports and recommendations as s/he deems wise, directly to the office of the President and to the PresidentChairperson of the Faculty Senate, with such substantiation as may be appropriate and prepare an annual report reviewing and evaluating the activities of his/her office during the year, the report to be distributed to the general faculty, the members of the Student Senate, and deans, directors and department heads.
In addition to the annual report, the Ombudsman shall periodically publish in appropriate campus media information on University regulations and suggestions regarding their application. 2.39.15 Having completed his/her inquiries s/he shall make such disposition of each case as, in his/her sole judgment, is best.
S/he may dismiss the charges as without foundation or merit.

passages.heading: #20-21-5 | Page 8
passages.text:
S/he may recommend corrective action to achieve justice or equity in the particular case.
S/he shall determine the question of equity and fairness not on the basis of opinion or bias or preference, but on the basis of whether or not the rules, guidelines and other governing statutes have been followed honestly and fairly without undue delay.
If s/he finds that a particular rule or regulation or statute is itself unfair or makes for inequity, s/he shall convey that finding to the office of the President and to the PresidentChairperson of the Faculty Senate; but s/he shall not at the same time make a finding against an individual who has faithfully adhered to the guidelines then governing the case.
Should the Ombudsman arrive at conclusions which are critical of the operations and practices of the office of the President, or of the Presidential disposition of cases duly reported by the Ombudsman to the President, s/he shall so inform the President; and if there is no resolution of the problem which is satisfactory to him/her the Ombudsman may take the matter directly to the Chairperson of the Board of Education, informing the President before s/he does so.

(See Appendix B) Natural Resources and the Environment – The Graduate Council approved a Notice of Change to restructure the delivery of the online Graduate Certificate in Natural Resources and the Environment. The new structure will replace 6 two-credit courses with 4 three-credit courses. Content will be redistributed across the four courses to ensure that all program learning outcomes are met. This change will make the certificate consistent with other URI Online offerings and facilitate using this certificate as a pathway to the MESM degree. (See Appendix C) 1

Summary description of proposed program (not to exceed 2 pages).
The Graduate Certificate in Natural Resources and the Environment was first online program proposed in CELS.
Our proposal included the creation of 6 required 2-credit courses (EVS 509, EVS 511, EVS 514, EVS 515, EVS 518 and EVS 519) that all enrolled students would complete to obtain the certificate.
Since the approval of both the courses and the program, URI Online has grown and developed more standard practices, including offering most accelerated online courses for 3 credits.

passages.heading: #20-21-6B | Page 5
passages.text:
In order to be consistent with this format we are proposing to increase the credits for four of the courses from two to three and eliminate two other courses.
The workload in the remaining classes will be increased to reflect the additional credit by a combination of 1) additional readings and/or instructional videos to cover more content, 2) increasing the number of quizzes, discussion forums, and homework assignments, and 3) the addition or expansion of a final project.
Content will be redistributed over the remaining four courses, so all program learning outcomes will still be met.
The total number of required credits will remain the same (12).
The benefits of this restructuring extend to both students in the program as well as URI Online overall.
First, students will be able to complete the certificate in nine months rather than twelve.
This change will make it more competitive with similar programs and will appeal to working professionals and active duty service members who have to balance professional expectations with academic pursuits.

passages.heading: #20-21-6B | Page 5
passages.text:
Students will be able to complete the certificate more quickly, which will both limit their time in the program and allow them to apply the new skills they gain to the workforce more quickly.
Second, the courses

passages.heading: #20-21-6B | Page 6
passages.text:
2 Updated: 9.2018 associated with the NRE certificate will be more consistent with URI Online standard practices.
As a result, it will be easier for courses associated with the NRE program to support other online programs currently under development.
To facilitate this role we are also proposing to adjust the pre-requisite language for each remaining NRE course to include enrollment in the NRE certificate or permission of the instructor.
For example, the new Online GIS and Geospatial Technology Certificate is proposing to use the 3-credit version of EVS 509 as a core course and the Online Masters in Oceanography (currently in development) would allow students to take NRE courses to fulfill elective requirements.
Long-term, we anticipate students being able to fulfill the majority of MESM degree requirements by completing online certificates in related areas; updating the structure of the NRE program and courses will provide students the flexibility they need to use NRE courses for this purpose.
We propose to increase the number of credits from two to three for EVS 509, EVS 514, EVS 518 and EVS 519 while eliminating EVS 511 and EVS 515 (Table 1).

passages.heading: #20-21-6B | Page 6
passages.text:
Content from EVS 511 will be distributed across EVS 509 and EVS 519 while content from EVS 515 will be added to EVS 514 and EVS 518 (Attachment 1).
As a result, EVS 509 will be a required prerequisite for EVS 519 and EVS 514 will be required for EVS 518.
EVS 509 and 511 were going to use different GIS software, so there was a lot of conceptual redundancy teaching students how to complete the same tasks in different programs.
We will use a different software in EVS 509 that retains the initial functionality required for 509 and adds the spatial analysis tools required for EVS 511 thereby retaining all content and eliminating unnecessary redundancy.
We will restructure EVS 514 to integrate the data visualization concepts throughout and shift several EVS 515 topics into the openings.
We will also add EVS 515 topics to EVS 518 to cover methods associated with the scientific papers being read.

1 FACULTY SENATE OFFICE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND FACULTY SENATE September 17, 2020 Faculty Senate Curriculum and Standards Committee Report 2019-2020-12 At the July 28, 2020 special summer meeting of the Curriculum and Standards Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate.
SECTION II Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation by the Faculty Senate ORGANIZATIONAL CHANGES: COLLEGE OF ARTS AND SCIENCES: Africana Studies Program: See Appendix A To make Africana Studies an academic department rather than a program.
Africana Studies has been a program at the University of Rhode Island for more than three decades.
During that time, Africana Studies (referred to as AAF) has always embodied the values of racial and social justice.
AAF has served in many ways as a moral center of the University regarding issues of equity and fairness.
The curriculum provided by AAF is a mainstay of cultural, social and historical understanding and a critical and defining part of the American narrative, a narrative that is wholly American, not just singularly Black American.

passages.heading: #20-21-1B | Page 2
passages.text:
Recent articulation of the transformational goals and mission of the University directly spell out the necessary movement from institutionalized racism to new constructs of diversity (racial and ethnic affirmation for all people) and inclusion.
The proposal for departmental status is not a reactionary idea.
The expectations and goals of AAF have come to far exceed ‘program’ status.
It is critical that AAF be confirmed as a department because AAF needs the designation to create the infrastructure to develop its relevance to our students and build our curriculum.
Departmental status will situate AAF in a more competitive position to attract internal and external funding recruit new faculty, recruit students to the major and minor, and enlarge our capacity to respond nationally and globally, in more informed ways, to an increasing demand for justice.

passages.heading: #20-21-1B | Page 3
passages.text: 2 Gender and Women’s Studies Program: See Appendix B To make Gender and Women’s Studies an academic department rather than a program. In designating Gender and Women’s Studies (GWS) as a “Department,” URI will affirm that GWS is equal in status and importance to all other Departments at URI. Consistent with the goals outlined in the Academic Strategic Plan (2016-2021), this change will demonstrate unequivocally URI’s commitment to student success, diversity, and social justice—all at the core of GWS teaching and scholarship. Except for being accorded equal status as a “Department,” since 1972, GWS has operated just like other departments. GWS has its own budget, “director” who participates in all chair obligations and duties, growing number of majors (45 in FY2021) and minors, TT, full-time, and joint faculty lines, an endowed chair, URI Foundation funds, student scholarships, sponsored events, and a graduate certificate program that has graduated over 30 students. But it is time now to give GWS equal status.

RATIONALE: There should be a demonstrable purpose and documented need for the proposed organizational change. 1.
Explain why the organizational change is being proposed.
Africana Studies has been a program at the University of Rhode Island for more than three decades.
During that time, Africana Studies (referred to as AAF) has always embodied the values of racial and social justice.
AAF has served in many ways as a moral center of the University regarding issues of equity and fairness.
The curriculum provided by AAF is a mainstay of cultural, social and historical understanding and a critical and defining part of the American narrative, a narrative that is wholly American, not just singularly Black American.
Recent articulation of the transformational goals and mission of the University directly spell out the necess ary movement from institutionalized racism to new constructs of diversity (racial and ethnic affirmation for all people) and inclusion.

passages.heading: #20-21-1B | Page 5
passages.text:
Given the recent events of George Floyd's tragic death and other killings of Black men and women at the hands of American police officers, our nation is embroiled in a resurgence of racial conflict.
The urgency of this time in history is to re -think our commitments to racial equity.
It is a time for our institution to review policies and practices and confront long-standing institutional racism.
Specifically, URI has begun to respond to these exigencies by confronting the issues of institutional racism through enacting courses of action that are direct and measurable.
As part of that important response, we propose the explicit endorsement of Africana Studies to departmental status.
The proposal for departmental status is not a reactionary idea.
The expectations and goals of AAF have come to far exceed 'program' status.
It is critical that AAF be confirmed as a department because AAF needs the designation to create the infrastructure to develop its relevance to our students and build our curriculum.

passages.heading: #20-21-1B | Page 5
passages.text:
Departmental status will situate AAF in a more competitive position to attract internal and external funding recruit new faculty, recruit students to the major and minor, and enlarge our capacity to respond nationally and globally, in more informed ways, to an increasing demand for justice.
As the state's flagship public research institution, the University of Rhode Island is a vibrant and dynamic community that is connected by: a common quest for knowledge to transform the way we perceive and understand the world; a sincere desire for innovation to enrich the campus community and the state of Rhode Island; and a real commitment to embrace social justice and to promote civic engage-ment.
These same connecting principles (i.e., knowledge, innovation, social justice, civic engagement, etc.) are the foundations upon which the Department of Africana Studies were established, over thirty years ago.

passages.heading: #20-21-1B | Page 5
passages.text:
More importantly, these same principles have guided the Department in its efforts to coordinate and collaborate, with other public institutions of higher education (i.e., Rhode Island College, the Community College of Rhode Island, etc.), while ensuring an environment designed to enhance college teaching, learning, research, and student development.
Since the inception of Africana Studies, at the University of Rhode Island, affiliated faculty have been consistently recognized as established leaders in their respected academic fields (i.e., African American History and culture, Art and Art History, English and Film Media, Philosophy and African American Literature, Communication Studies, Clinical Psychology, Environmental Sciences, Religion Studies, Sociology, etc.), and have also been acknowledged for providing undergraduate, graduate, and professional students with the

passages.heading: #20-21-1B | Page 6
passages.text:
3 distinctive educational opportunities expected of a major research university, especially opportunities to negotiate the trans-disciplinary nature of Africana Studies.
In recent years the University of Rhode Island has recognized the teaching, research, and scholarship that defines Africana Studies, and the critically important role our faculty has played in preparing a new generation of students, not only with the analytical and theoretical skills necessary to understand the intersections of racial difference and inequality, but with the cultural competencies necessary to provide transformational leadership in every aspect of American society.
Consequently, we sincerely hope that this request for organizational change will enable the university to appoint tenured/tenured -track faculty, in Africana Studies, consistent with other flagship public research universities throughout New England and around the country, including the University of Connecticut, the University of Massachusetts Amherst, Buffalo State: The State University of New York, and The Pennsylvania State University.

passages.heading: #20-21-1B | Page 6
passages.text:
AAF for many years has been treated like a department in the College in the Arts and Sciences with the Director attending all Chair meetings, operating budget allocated, PTF funding allocated and event funding allocated.
Thus, the change to department status will recognize the current status and operations of the AAF program within the College of Arts and Sciences.
In other words, AAF is already functioning like a department and this organizational change will visibly demonstrate this for the campus and for the prospective students and faculty.
More importantly, a more strongly supported and validated Africana Studies Department will help URI students to prepare to face and engage in national and global communities successfully.
Africana Studies can help meet this need not just for Students of Color, but for all students.
Africana Studies affirmed as a Department can also help lead the way for URI to address institutional racism within our own University and the Rhode Island and New England region.

passages.heading: #20-21-1B | Page 6
passages.text:
Because of the nation-wide systemic neglect of Africana programs, taking this initiative positions URI to lead other universities throughout the nation in correcting a lack of institutional support for their Africana Studies programs/ departments.
With departmental status, Africana Studies is poised to contribute to African research.
First, several of our faculty are internationally recognized scholars in the area of African research.
Secondly, URI has developed on-going research relationships through the Biological Sciences and Marine Affairs Departments and both departments have invited Africana Studies to participate in several research projects.
For instance, we are currently working as a consultant with Dr.
Brian Crawford and the US Aid Fisheries Program to establish Covid-19 public health initiatives in the Cape Coast, Ghana area.
In addition, Africana Studies has developed relationships with the Faculty of The University of Ghana at Accra and The University of Cape Coast, Cape Coast, Ghana.
Thirdly, URI through Africana Studies has developed successful Study Abroad programs in Ghana and nearby Cape Verde.

passages.heading: #20-21-1B | Page 6
passages.text:
Africana Studies outreach has taken us to Bermuda, Trinidad and Tobago and we have received invitations to Jamaica and St.
Lucia to explore connections between West Indian cultures, the Caribbean and African Americans.
The opportunities for growth and expansion are plentiful but the ability to attract funding, internal and external grants are stymied by the program status.
Departmental status for Africana Studies would increase URI's visibility and respectability in the scholarly communities within the African Diaspora.
The proposed change of status, from program to department, would be a demonstrable stride toward directly confronting institutional racism at URI.
Initiatives toward diversity have not been strong enough to deinstitutionalize long-standing apathy toward Africana Studies.
Departmental status would be a measurable, clear and strong expression of anti-racism, a proactive dismantling of institutionalized racism and classicism.

passages.heading: #20-21-1B | Page 7
passages.text: 4 C. INSTITUTIONAL ROLE: The organizational change should be clearly related to the published role and mission of the institution and be compatible with the organizational structure of the institution 1. Explain how the organizational change is consistent with published role and mission of institution and how it is related to institutional planning The organizational change of Africana Studies from program to departmental status would be consistent with the published role and mission of URI, specifically as it relates to institutional planning of goals and initiatives for transformational change (diversity, equity and inclusion). As the discipline that focuses primarily on the African and African American presence in the world, Africana Studies is uniquely in sync with the goals for transformational change. Africana Studies as a department could better fulfill the initiatives of The Community, Equity & Diversity Strategic Plan 2017 - 2022 as well as those outlined by Dean Jen Riley, College of Arts & Sciences in her letter of June 11, 2020. Africana Studies will be better positioned as a department to enact the following goals, strategies and actions. Goal #1 of CED Strategic Plan, Recruitment • Encourage undergraduate students from marginalized groups to apply for graduate school at URI. This will provide a valuable service to undergraduate students, with a secondary benefit to URI graduate recruitment. Departmental status will enable Africana Studies to interface with more undergraduate students from marginalized groups and walk with them more comprehensively through graduate school preparation.

passages.heading: #20-21-1B | Page 8
passages.text:
5 • Work with academic units to identify and expand URI's connections with minority-serving institutions (e.g., Asian American and Pacific Islander institutions, historically black colleges and universities, Hispanic-serving institutions, tribal colleges and universities, and women's colleges) to expand URI's network of diverse applicants.
Africana Studies is one such academic unit that can clearly identify and expand URI's connections with institutions that serve Students of Color and marginalized students.
Specifically, Africana Studies interacts with historically Black colleges, Hispanic-serving institutions and Colleges that serve Native American students.
For example, Africana Studies is a major sponsor and host in support of the URI DIVE Student Conference that welcomes Students of Color from all over the New England region; Africana Studies works closely with the Narragansett Native American community in our own state of Rhode Island.
Africana Studies sponsors URI Students of Color as they attend Conferences and special events at historically Black colleges.

passages.heading: #20-21-1B | Page 8
passages.text:
We are currently working to create a Black Student Support Consortium between Black students at historically Black Colleges and State Universities such as URI.
Departmental status for Africana Status will enable us to do this kind of outreach more effectively and strengthen our ability to expand URI's network of diverse applicants.
Goal #2 of CED Strategic Plan, Retention • Offer discussion lunches for all faculty; strongly encourage faculty members from marginalized groups, along with their mentors, to attend.
Departmental status will enable Africana Studies to be substantively encouraging of Faculty of Color and proactively organized in developing mentoring opportunities for Faculty of Color.
Africana Studies fully supports Discussion lunches and would strongly encourage Faculty of Color to attend (along with their mentors).
Department status will also bring more recognition to service contributions and collaborations by faculty in the annual review process. • Acknowledge and publicize accomplishments, contributions, and career milestones for employees.

passages.heading: #20-21-1B | Page 8
passages.text:
Affirming innovation in research, teaching, and service of faculty from marginalized groups is a way to convey the many ways in which people from marginalized groups contribute to the community.
For too long the university has been negligent in recognizing Faculty of Color.
Africana Studies needs Departmental status to be effective in advocating for the recognition of Faculty of Color at the Departmental and University levels.
As noted previously, departmental status can also assist with recruiting new faculty to URI.
Finally, Africana Studies is uniquely aligned to deliver Strategy 3 of the CED Strategic Plan, to address the mental models and assumptions that reflect unconscious bias, taken-for-granted beliefs, perceptions, thoughts, and feelings rooted in the oppression of community members from marginalized groups.
With the affirmation of Departmental Status, Africana Studies can lead the way in modeling, providing guidance, and encouraging equity-mindedness in planning and decision- making processes across the institution.

Description of institutional review and approval process Approval Date Department 7/10/20 College CAC/Graduate Council Faculty Senate President of the University July 23, 2020 July 28, 2020 September 17, 2020 7. Summary description of the proposed organizational change To make Gender and Women's Studies an academic department rather than a program. 8. Signature of the President

passages.heading: #20-21-1B | Page 17
passages.text:
David M.
Dooley 9.
Person to contact during the review Rosaria Pisa, Director of GWS rpisa@uri.edu Tel. 874-2482 Provost Donald DeHayes ddehayes@uri.edu Tel. 401-874-4410 B.
RATIONALE: There should be a demonstrable purpose and documented need for the proposed organizational change.
Rationale for becoming the Department of Gender and Women's Studies instead of the Gender and Women's Studies Program Overview: In designating Gender and Women's Studies (GWS) as a "Department," URI will affirm that GWS is equal in status and importance to all other Departments at URI.
Consistent with the goals outlined in the Academic Strategic Plan (2016-2021), this change will demonstrate unequivocally URI's commitment to student success, diversity, and social justice-all at the core of GWS teaching and scholarship.
Except for being accorded equal status as a "Department," since 1972, GWS has operated just like other departments.

passages.heading: #20-21-1B | Page 17
passages.text:
GWS has its own budget, "director" who participates in all chair obligations and duties, growing number of majors (45 in FY2021) and minors, TT, full-time, and joint faculty lines, an endowed chair, URI Foundation funds, student scholarships, sponsored events, and a graduate certificate program that has graduated over 30 students.
But it is time now to give GWS equal status.
The current and pressing historical issues in our society-#MeToo, #BlackLivesMatter, the 2020 Centennial of the Women's Vote, and the struggle for LGBTQ rights-make it clear that leaders must take action to create equality in their institutions.
This organization change can and will make URI a leader among its peers.
This proposed change to "Department" will be a visible declaration at URI of the equal stature it accords all of its academic units.
Insofar as human rights, equality, and anti- racism teaching and scholarship are also integral to the discipline of Gender and Women's Studies, this proposed change will recognize the crucial work GWS does at URI.
Currently, there are more than 800 GWS departments nationally, but none in RI.

passages.heading: #20-21-1B | Page 17
passages.text:
As the flagship university, URI will lead in establishing the first GWS department in RI, placing URI in the good company of "aspiring to be like" institutions, the University of Delaware https://www.wgs.udel.edu/academics/wgs and the University of Virginia https://wgs.as.virginia.edu/.
Specific Outcomes and rationales: As a "Department," Gender and Women's Studies will be one among equals in the College of Arts & Sciences and at URI, and across the professions, generating the following outcomes: • Affirm the value and place of Gender and Women's Studies in a university that seeks to uphold the values of diversity, equality, antiracism, and social justice.
GWS as a discipline focuses on the teaching of human rights, LGBTQ rights, social justice, Black Lives Matter, and the Me Too Movement.
The intersectional approach central to the discipline of GWS demands and enacts the study of simultaneous oppressions related to race, class, gender, sexuality, ageism, disabilities.
This intersectional approach and pedagogy positions GWS as central to educating students to understand and 2

passages.heading: #20-21-1B | Page 18
passages.text:
3 address current and future national and global historical and political crises.
GWS at URI and in the world is a leader in antiracist teaching.
The designation as Department will recognize and validate GWS's role in impacting the antiracist intellectual and cultural climate and practices at the university and beyond. • Validate and honor the interdisciplinary discipline of GWS in its own right.
URI's Academic Plan places high value on interdisciplinary work.
Gender and Women's Studies is a formal interdisciplinary field unto itself.
Scholarly journals: GWS has about 40 journals worldwide dedicated to its scholarship.
A scan of the list at the end of the Rationale reveals the vast number of interdisciplinary foci that are all considered part of GWS.
Two of the journals coming out of URI are not on the Internet search list but should be: Dignity and Journal of Feminist Scholarship.
Associations and Conferences: GWS has hundreds of gender conferences and organizations worldwide, including the National Women's Studies Association, a global organization founded in 1977 with membership in the thousands and an annual conference attended by thousands.

passages.heading: #20-21-1B | Page 18
passages.text: NWSA's stated goals speak to the interdisciplinary nature inherent to the field of Gender and Women's Studies: "to demonstrate the contributions of feminist scholarship that is comparative, global, intersectional and interdisciplinary to understandings of the arts, humanities, social sciences and sciences; and to promote synergistic relationships between scholarship, teaching and civic engagement in understandings of culture and society." Leadership in the world: UN Women, established in 2010 as a major global working group, also articulates the many disciplines and subjects that come together in GWS: Leadership and political participation; economic empowerment; ending violence against women; peace and security; humanitarian action; youth; governance and national planning; sustainable development; HIV and AIDs.

passages.heading: #20-21-1B | Page 18
passages.text:
While UN Women "focuses on priority areas that are fundamental to women's equality," they also recognize that this equality "unlock[s] progress across the board." As UN Women states: "All human development and human rights issues have gender dimensions." URI is long overdue in recognizing both the rightful position and place of interdisciplinary disciplines as valid and complete in themselves, and the rightful and important role GWS plays in educating students, faculty, staff, and the world on the many ways gender matters.
On the one hand, the creation of an academic department formalizes the role and responsibility of the Chair, faculty, and affiliated faculty, institutionally strengthening the academic major and course of study.
On the other hand, designating GWS as a department validates the interdisciplinary validity of this field in its own right. • Lend more credibility for students looking to major or double major in GWS.
Students will understand their investment in GWS as a single or double major as equally validating as majoring in all other departments.

passages.heading: #20-21-1B | Page 18
passages.text:
In addition, on a transcript, majoring in a "Department" rather than a "Program" may also be perceived by employers and graduate programs as more substantial and equal to majors in other "Departments." As a department, with equal recognition and validation as all other departments, socially justice-minded prospective students and young scholars whose work, teaching, and passion are grounded in gender, equal rights, and social justice work will be all the more drawn to courses and majoring or double majoring in GWS. • Enhance the connections between many URI departments and faculty involved in the study of gender, equality, and social justice.
Department designation will encourage more administrators, faculty, and students to affiliate and collaborate with GWS.
Research indicates that where an organization has status differentials, including between a "Department"' and a "Program," cross- pollination and collaboration are less likely to occur.
As the GWS Department, other departments and administrators will be inclined to take GWS more seriously and reach out more to GWS as equal stakeholders.

passages.heading: #20-21-1B | Page 19
passages.text:
4 • Bring URI in line with colleges and universities around the country, including universities URI aspires to and competes with for students and faculty.
There are approximately 800 universities around the country that have acquired Department status and others, like us, are seeking it.
In RI, no other college or university currently has department designation for their GWS programs.
As a Flagship University, URI should be at least up to par with our peer or "aspiring-to-be-like" institutions. "Thinking Big," URI should strive to be a leader in education and organizational design.
In RI, especially, URI should be the first to accomplish this important goal. • Attract highly competitive and diverse faculty who wish to be part of a fully recognized "Department" rather than "Program." In promotion and tenure decisions, it is also possible that working for a "Department" will be seen as more valuable, permanent, and reputable than working for a "Program." • Create growing interest in GWS leadership.
As a Department with a "Chair" instead of a "Director," faculty might be more interested in taking on the position as "Chair" of Gender and Women's Studies. • Attract external funding.

passages.heading: #20-21-1B | Page 19
passages.text:
As a Department, getting grants for an individual or a department as a whole may have more credibility than getting grants for a "Program." To external funders and reviewers, programs may appear more ad hoc and less permanent than departments.
Those seeking to support research and scholarship are likely to seek more permanent "homes" for resource allocation. • Send a powerful message to all URI alumni and to GWS alumni conveying URI's commitment to the value, teaching, and scholarship of gender and women's studies, including a focus on: LGBTQ rights, black lives matter, the Me Too Movement, and global human rights.
Showing alumni the unequivocal support for a Department of GWS will perhaps catalyze more gift giving, scholarships, and further endowments. • Send a powerful message of support to URI students, faculty, and staff who are women, LGBTQ, nonbinary, and males advocating for equal rights URI's commitment to the value, teaching, and scholarship of gender and women's issues.
C.
INSTITUTIONAL ROLE: The organizational change should be clearly related to the published role and mission of the institution and be compatible with the organizational structure of the institution 1.

passages.heading: #20-21-1B | Page 19
passages.text:
Explain how the organizational change is consistent with published role and mission of institution and how it is related to institutional planning.
GWS strongly aligns with URI's 2016-2021 Academic Strategic Plan GWS upholds Goal 1: Enhance Student Success-Strategies 1, 2, 3 GWS, anchored in interdisciplinary and multidisciplinary methodologies, offers URI students a unique educational experience from which they learn not only the complex root causes of all forms of devaluation of human life and nature, but also how to overcome them through human agency.
Our transformative curriculum comes alive through our students, their actions, and their success at URI and beyond.
GWS gives URI students the education and skills to thrive and lead in a multicultural, diverse, antiracist world and workplace.
Foundational to the GWS program is praxis: theory and action.
We transmit to our students the know-how and skills to create the world they want to live in through timely coursework that includes engaged learning opportunities here and abroad.
Through mentorship, GWS faculty encourage students to strive, lead, and transform their lives and those of

passages.heading: #20-21-1B | Page 20
passages.text:
5 others for the better.
Experiences with action projects, field assignments, on and off campus activism, and public service shape the character and education of our students.
GWS students are visible, active, and inspiring to each other and other students at URI.
More than 90% of our students are double majors.
They integrate what they learn in GWS courses with their other major(s).
Through our majors, GWS contributes to and fortifies the discourse on human rights, anti-racism, dignity, equality, and social justice throughout the curriculum and across the disciplines.
Strongly aligning with Strategy 3, a critical element of the GWS formula of student success is to provide a dynamic and fluid curriculum that combines the traditional classroom, online courses, faculty-supervised internships, field trips (including to Washington DC), study abroad, and participation in topical programs.
GWS also offers a Graduate Certificate Program that has been operational for many years now, with a total of more than 25 graduates, and a history of graduate studies collaborations with English, History, Psychology, and Political Science.

passages.heading: #20-21-1B | Page 20
passages.text:
GWS upholds Goal 2: Expand Research, Scholarship and Creative Work-Strategies 1, 4 GWS sustains interdisciplinary and multidisciplinary research and scholarship through its faculty's research programs, institutional curricular and research collaborations (AAF, LAX, Honors, Nonviolence and Peace Studies, and nearly all A&S departments), academic journals (Dignity and Journal of Feminist Scholarship), and programming (F18 Honors Colloquium on Reimagining Gender, Dana Shugar Colloquium, Feminisms in Action Lectures, Schweer Lecture on Gender and Public Health, the new Gender and Race Lecture, more).
GWS faculty engage in international research (Latin America, Europe, and Asia) and work in areas with policy implications, especially in human and sex trafficking, reproductive rights, sexual violence, and environmental justice.
In line with Strategy 4, our students have exciting opportunities for undergraduate and graduate research.
GWS has a research group in human and sex-trafficking supervised by Dr.
Donna Hughes.
Through their collaboration with Dr.

passages.heading: #20-21-1B | Page 20
passages.text:
Hughes, students have been successful in presenting at conferences, publishing research, and securing coveted graduate school offers and professional positions.
GWS upholds Goal 4: Embrace Diversity and Social Justice-Strategy 2 and 3 GWS' mission as a discipline is to center human rights, equality, dignity, anti-racism, and social justice in all we do.
GWS does this especially well through its transformative and topical curriculum by offering courses that include Black Feminisms, Black Masculinities, Latinx Masculinities, Transgender Lives and Cultures, and other courses in the field of Queer Studies.
Central to this mission, is a yearly program of events that prioritizes diversity, inclusion, and social justice.
GWS actively recruits a variety of students and is one of the most diverse discipline on campus.
We have the highest number of students of color and other minoritized groups among our majors and minors.
Through our scholarship funding, GWS prioritizes need-based decisions and the fair distribution of resources across eligible students.
GWS also has a single-mother Carlson scholarship that offers the student full-tuition for the duration of their matriculation.

passages.heading: #20-21-1B | Page 20
passages.text:
As a Department, GWS is poised to extend anti-racist principles and actions at URI, the RI community, and beyond.
GWS embodies key URI Strategic Goals, in particular in the area of Embrace Diversity and Social Justice.
The designation of GWS as a Department goes hand in hand with the demand for an Africana Studies Department.
GWS joins African Studies in upholding the core values of diversity, inclusion, antiracism, and social justice in all areas of academic life at URI.

GWS becoming a department does not impact other departments and programs.
As discussed above, GWS has operated as a department for many years without impacting other academic units.
Rather, GWS has collaborated closely with other academic units to uphold its interdisciplinary and multidisciplinary discipline.
With department designation, GWS will fortify and broaden collaboration across the disciplines.

URI will lead the way in RI by creating a Department of Gender and Women's Studies.
Regionally, there are several departments that include UMass-Dartmouth, Connecticut College, Wellesley College, and Simmons College.
None of our similar peer institutions has departments in Women's Studies (JMU, UNH, UVM, etc.).
Of our "aspire to be like" peer institutions, the University of Delaware and University of Virginia have departments in Women's Studies, UCONN does not.
This moment offers an ideal opportunity for URI to take a leadership position by designating GWS as a department and rise to the level of two out of three "aspiring to be like" institutions.

passages.heading: #20-21-1B | Page 21
passages.text:
There will be no impacts to other RI institutions in terms of loss of students or revenue.
Nearly 99% of our majors come from within URI and select GWS as a second major in their sophomore year or as a first semester junior.
All major RI public and private institutions offer Women's Studies or similar programs like Gender and Sexuality Studies.
These institutions have successfully recruited students for their programs over the years.
There is no reason to believe that a change in GWS designation as a department will change that pattern. 2.

passages.text: DATE: July 24, 2020 TO: Margaret Benz Coordinator, Faculty Senate FROM: Linda Barrett Director, Budget and Financial Planning SUBJECT: Proposal for an Organizational change in Arts & Sciences - Gender and Women's Studies As requested in an email from Brian Krueger, Associate Dean in the College of Arts & Sciences, dated July 10, 2020, the Budget and Financial Planning Office has reviewed the submitted documents related to the proposal for an Organizational change in the department of Gender and Women's Studies program. The Budget and Financial Planning Office, including communication with Enrollment Services, concurs that the request for an organizational change related to the Gender and Women's Studies program is anticipated to have a small positive net revenue impact on the Fund 100 unrestricted budget as it has been presented. In accordance with the proposal, Gender and Women's Studies will be an official department in the College of Arts and Sciences effective December 2020. Since Gender and Women's Studies is technically set up as a department in the financial, human resources and budget systems, no action is required relative to these systems. 1 FACULTY SENATE OFFICE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND FACULTY SENATE November 19, 2020 Faculty Senate Curriculum and Standards Committee Report 2020-2021-02 At the October 22, 2020 meeting of the Curriculum and Standards Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate.
SECTION I Informational Matters TEMPORARY COURSES: COLLEGE OF ENGINEERING: ELE 420X, Cyber Physical System Security (3 crs.) Fundamental constructions and emerging challenges unique to today’s cyber-physical systems.
Solutions from the perspectives of systems specification, system modeling, network programming, and formal verification (specific focus on electrical power grids). (Lec. 3) Pre: ELE 208 or permission of instructor.
COLLEGE OF THE ENVIRONMENT AND LIFE SCIENCES: AFS 397X, Underwater Photography & Film Laboratory (1 cr.) Students gain experience in underwater photography and film techniques while snorkeling and/or scuba diving.
Additional snorkel or scuba certifications by Scuba Diving International are provided.
Travel course, additional fees. (Lab. 1) Pre: Credit or concurrent enrollment in AFS 395, and permission of instructor, must pass basic swim evaluation.

passages.heading: #20-21-7A | Page 2
passages.text:
CMB 240X, Introduction to Biomedical Research (3 crs.) Provide a comprehensive introduction to biomedical research, and will emphasize best practices in experimental design, data management and analysis, biomedical career preparation, and computational skills development. (Lec., Online, Workshop) Pre: BIO 101 OR BIO 110 or permission of instructor.
COURSES DELETIONS: COLLEGE OF PHARMACY: PHC 327, Interactive Learning Session II Delete course (1 cr.) Small group active learning designed to reinforce progressively the basic science curriculum, promote communication and problem-solving skills, and enhance patient assessment and the delivery

passages.heading: #20-21-7A | Page 3
passages.text:
2 of pharmaceutical care. (Seminar) Pre: first-year Doctor of Pharmacy professional student in good standing; or permission of the instructor.
PHP 332, Pharmacotherapy of Renal and Cardiovascular Disorders Delete course (3 crs.) The appropriate use of medications in the treatment of human disease.
Interpretation of clinical data to design, monitor, and modify drug therapy in renal and cardiovascular disease. (Lec. 3) Pre: first- year Doctor of Pharmacy professional student in good standing or permission of instructor.
PHP 401, Pharmacy Resources for Practice Delete course (3 crs.) Introduces pharmacy management skills to assist students in understanding the effective use of the human, technological, and fiscal resources to manage a positive work environment and maximize their patient interaction time. (Lec. 3) Pre: First year Doctor of Pharmacy student in good standing; or permission of the instructor.
PHP/BPS 310, Foundations of Human Disease: Renal and Cardiovascular Diseases Delete course (2 crs.) Cross-listed as (PHP), BPS 310.

passages.heading: #20-21-7A | Page 3
passages.text:
The etiology, pathogenesis, epidemiology, and symptomatology, and diagnosis of renal and cardiovascular diseases. (Lec. 2) Pre: first-year Doctor of Pharmacy professional student in good standing or permission of instructor.
COLLEGE OF ENGINEERING: OCE 310, Basic Ocean Measurement Delete course (3 crs.) Basic ocean measurement and instrumentation exercises using boats and laboratories.
Includes cruise design, navigation and mapping systems, sonar systems, water quality sensors, wave spectra, computer data acquisition, and signal processing. (Lec. 1, Lab. 2) Pre: OCE 206 or permission of instructor.
COLLEGE OF NURSING: NUR 467, Independent Study in Human Sexuality Delete Course (2-6 crs.) A specifically designed learning experience for the theoretical study of human sexuality and related practice strategies. (Independent Study) Pre: NUR 150 or equivalent; permission of instructor.

passages.heading: #20-21-7A | Page 3
passages.text:

A specifically designed practicum involving the application of theory and development of practice strategies in specific areas within the field of human sexuality. (Practicum) Pre: NUR 150 and 467 or equivalent; permission of instructor.
NUR 485, National Council Licensure Examination (NCLEX) RN Review Delete Course (1 cr.) Comprehensive review of essential nursing knowledge across content areas, according to the NCLEX-RN test plan, in preparation for taking the NCLEX-RN exam. (Lec. 1) Pre: Graduate of an accredited RN nursing program, or permission of instructor.
Not for graduate credit.

FACULTY SENATE OFFICE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND FACULTY SENATE November 19, 2020 Faculty Senate Curriculum and Standards Committee Report 2020-2021-02 At the October 22, 2020 meeting of the Curriculum and Standards Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate.
SECTION II Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation by the Faculty Senate PROGRAM CHANGES: COLLEGE OF HEALTH SCIENCES: Human Development and Family Science-BS See Appendix A In the Spring of 2020, Human Development and Family Science made a number of changes to the structure of the HDF curriculum.
Recently, however, we noticed that the legislation (19-20-28B) that was put forth and approved for the changes to the HDF major were not exactly what the department intended.
Although ecampus accurately reflects what was stated in the legislation, the changes do not line up with our intended changes.
Change Requested: HDF is seeking to reconfigure the subplans so that students in 2020 catalog year and forward will use the new subplans.
Students using the 2019 and earlier catalog year will complete old subplans.

passages.heading: #20-21-7B | Page 2
passages.text:
Both the new and old subplans must be present simultaneously to allow this to happen.
Health Studies-BS See Appendix B We are proposing that HLT312: Intersecting Social Identities and Health be approved as a specialization class for all three specialization areas: global & environmental health, health promotion, and health services.
The 3 credit class examines how social identities, social roles, and social categories (i.e., race, class, gender, sexuality, ability, age, etc.) affect health from an interdisciplinary perspective.
We believe that students in all three specializations who are interested in this topic would benefit from the class.
COLLEGE OF THE ENVIRONMENT AND LIFE SCIENCES: Marine Affairs Department See Appendix C Marine Affairs - BA & BS majors: EGR 213G was recently cross-listed with MAF (Fac Sen #19-20-28A).
The course is co-taught by professors in Ocean Engineering, Marine Affairs, and GSO.
EGR/MAF 213G introduces students to the fundamental concepts of energy with regard to the physical, environmental, and socioeconomic aspects, which prepares them to critically understand global energy challenges and possible solutions 1

passages.heading: #20-21-7B | Page 3
passages.text: for sustainable energy development. We are requesting that MAF 213G be added to the coastal and marine policy and management concentration list for Marine Affairs BS and BA majors. COLLEGE OF BUSINESS: Core Requirements for Majors Listed: See Appendix D The college of business is requesting to remove the language requirement of two semesters that is currently required to complete the BSBA degree for all Accounting, Finance, Marketing, Supply Chain Management, Management, Management Information Systems*, and Innovation & Entrepreneurship majors. The replacement will be two semesters of a Global Cultural Experience requirement. Given the global nature of all of our business courses, the foreign language requirement is no longer necessary to achieve global competency. Management: See Appendix E The Management major requirements are being updated (see attached) to 1) differentiate the major from the new Entrepreneurship and Innovation Major and 2) allow for greater flexibility and customization of the degree for students to study different facets of management (human resources, sustainability, globalization, etc.) and be better prepared for the job market. 2

passages.text: THE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND Revised 8/2016 Notice of Change form Notice of Change for: Human Development and Family Science Date: 9/10/2020 A. PROGRAM INFORMATION 1. Name of institution University of Rhode Island 2. Name of department, division, school or college Department: Human Development and Family Science College: College of Health Sciences 3. Intended initiation date of program change. Include anticipated date for granting first degrees or certificates, if appropriate. Initiation date: 2020 First degree date: 2024 4. Intended location of the program: 2 Lower College Road Transition Center Kingston RI 02891 5. Summary description of proposed program (not to exceed 2 pages). In the Spring of 2020, Human Development and Family Science made a number of changes to the structure of the HDF curriculum. Recently, however, we noticed that the legislation (19-20-28B) that was put forth and approved for the changes to the HDF major were not exactly what the department intended. Although ecampus accurately reflects what was stated in the legislation, the changes do not line up with our intended changes. Issue: The existing subplans were updated to align with our three new content areas (Child and Family Development, Counseling and Social Services, Health and Aging Services). However, the legislation was written such that the new subplans override the old subplans from 2019 and earlier.

passages.heading: #20-21-7B | Page 5
passages.text: Intention: We intended to close existing subplans and change them to the new subplans for the 2020 catalog and forward. We intended to let our current students in the 2019 and earlier catalogs complete their existing subplans. Change Requested: HDF is seeking to reconfigure the subplans so that students in 2020 catalog year and forward will use the new subplans. Students using the 2019 and earlier catalog year will complete old subplans. Both the new and old subplans must be present simultaneously to allow this to happen. Subplans for 2019 and earlier Subplans for 2020 forward Child Settings Child and Family Development Family and Community Settings Counseling and Social Services Family Finance Health and Aging Services Please note that there are no additional resources associated with this change. The courses being offered in all catalog years are the same (only the grouping of courses is different). The temporary time where there are two sets of subplans exist will not result in additional courses needing to be taught or additional resources required. 6. If applicable, please include the existing URI catalog language and proposed catalog changes indicated in Track Changes. N/A 7. Signature of the President David M. Dooley 2
