Twelve (12) credits of free electives must be at the 300 or 400 level.
Students select a specialization in one of the following three areas: Global and Environmental Health.
This specialization prepares students to address health problems and concerns that transcend national boundaries.

passages.heading: #20-21-7B | Page 7
passages.text:
The goals of the curriculum are to foster critical thinking about world health problems and disparities; examine biological, social, economic, political, and environmental factors that influence global health problems; develop practical strategies and sustainable international partnerships to address major global health and environmental challenges; and inspire a commitment to real world change.
Students select six courses from the following list.
At least four courses must be at the 300 or 400 level.
Courses must be selected from at least three different disciplines/departments: APG 319; BIO/ENT 286; BPS 201; COM/SUS 315; COM 361, 460, 461, 462; GCH 104; GWS 325; HLT 312, 320; HPR 319; NRS 100, 411; NRS/CPL 300; NUR 160; PHL 454; PHP 201; PSC 113, 402, 403.
Health Promotion.
This specialization is designed to prepare students for careers in fields whose primary emphasis is on facilitating individual, family, group, worksite, and community behavior change to promote healthy lifestyles and behaviors (e.g., increase exercise, cease smoking, manage stress).

passages.heading: #20-21-7B | Page 7
passages.text:
It also aims to improve life quality via the prevention and improved management of chronic illness and to help increase the length of life by reducing disease and increasing health-promoting behaviors.
Students select six courses from the following list.
At least four courses must be at the 300 or 400 level.
Courses must be selected from at least three different disciplines/departments: BPS 201; COM 361; GWS 350, 351; HDF 200, 201, 357, 440, 450; HLT 312, 320; KIN 275, 325, 401, 425; NFS 207, 276, 360, 394, 395; PHP 201; PSY 255, 381, 460, 479.
Health Services.
This specialization equips students with a range of skills necessary for careers in the health care industry, with an emphasis on preparing students for roles within the health care workforce of tomorrow that do not involve direct patient care.

passages.heading: #20-21-7B | Page 7
passages.text:
Graduates will: 1) possess foundational knowledge of human health and disease; 2) gain an awareness of and appreciation for how the current health systems serve those in need; 3) understand economic principles and forces that influence the efficiency of health care service delivery and administration; and 4) be capable of effectively communicating within organizations and with other stakeholders, orally and in written form.
Students select six courses from the following list.
At least four courses must be at the 300 or 400 level.
Courses must be selected from at least three different disciplines/departments: BPS 2

passages.heading: #20-21-7B | Page 8
passages.text: 201, 202; BUS 341, 342; COM 351, 361, 402, 450, 461; ECN 201, 360; HLT 312, 320; HSA 360; PHP 201; PSC/HDF 405; PSY 255; SOC 224; WRT 306. 7. Signature of the President David M. Dooley 3

Intended location of the program Coastal Institute Kingston 5. Summary description of proposed program (not to exceed 2 pages). EGR 213G was recently cross-listed with MAF (Fac Sen #19-20-28A). The course is co-taught by professors in Ocean Engineering, Marine Affairs, and GSO. EGR/MAF 213G introduces students to the fundamental concepts of energy with regard to the physical, environmental, and socioeconomic aspects, which prepares them to critically understand global energy challenges and possible solutions for sustainable energy development. We are requesting that MAF 213G be added to the coastal and marine policy and management concentration list for Marine Affairs BS and BA majors. 6. passages.heading: #20-21-7B | Page 10
passages.text:
Marine Affairs URI’s Department of Marine Affairs offers the following degrees: B.A., B.S., M.A., M.M.A. (Master of Marine Affairs), and Ph.D.
The B.A. and B.S. in marine affairs focus on coastal and ocean areas and examine environmental resources, human uses, and governance from a variety of perspectives.
Both degrees qualify for New England Regional Tuition.
Topics include conservation, ocean policy and law, climate adaptation and resilience, tourism and recreation, environmental justice, ocean energy resources, coastal and island communities, ports and shipping, fisheries and marine ecosystems, spatial planning and management.
A marine affairs major establishes a background for careers in the public or private sectors in a wide variety of marine-related fields.
Typical areas of employment include positions in government concerned with coastal zone, environmental, or fishery management, and marine transportation.
In the private sectors, students have secured positions in environmental consulting firms, marine insurance, public interest nongovernmental organizations, marinas, ports, and companies involved in shipping.

passages.heading: #20-21-7B | Page 10
passages.text:
The major serves well as an educational background for continued study in law, especially environmental, fishery, coastal zone, admiralty, and ocean law.
Students have also entered graduate and professional programs in environmental management, public administration, community planning, marine affairs, and related fields.
Students in the Department of Marine Affairs who participate in the New England Regional Student Program must maintain a 2.80 G.P.A. and take at least one MAF course per year to retain their New England regional tuition status.
Failure to meet these objectives will result in suspension of the reduced tuition privilege.
Reinstatement may occur if the student meets these requirements for one year after the time of the suspension.

SECTION II Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation by the Faculty Senate NEW PROGRAMS: COLLEGE OF BUSINESS: Creation of a Business Analytics and Intelligence Minor: See Appendix A The Business Analytics and Intelligence program is to provide students with the opportunity to better integrate data insights into their analyses and decision-making process. The program is also designed to strengthen knowledge from their primary major with advanced business analytics skills. Students will be prepared to bring insights from the large amounts of data to their functional areas such as marketing, finance, supply chain management, accounting among others. Students will specialize in one of the functional areas of business to gain additional skills that will prepare them for data-driven and analytics-based decision making. A minimum of six courses (18 credits) with an overall GPA of 2.0. A GPA of 2.0 (includes all attempts) is mandatory for the minor. Half of the credits for the minor (3 courses) must be completed at URI. All the courses for the minor must be taken at an AACSB accredited business school, at the URI Data Science program (CSC 201 or CSC 211) or through an approved study abroad program. 1

Summary description of proposed program (not to exceed 2 pages).
Business Analytics and Intelligence (BAI) is the area of study that deals with skills, technologies, practices for efficient data management, continuous iterative exploration and investigation of business performance to gain insight and drive business planning.
There are an increasing number of BAI tools and methodologies newly introduced to the industry and academia every day.

passages.heading: #20-21-8B | Page 3
passages.text:
These tools and methodologies provide field practitioners with statistical and operations analysis, the formation of predictive models, application of optimization techniques, and the communication of these results to customers, business partners, and college executives.
Business Analytics and Intelligence requires quantitative methods and evidence-based data for business modeling and decision making.
Business Analytics and Intelligence provide the industry with a great deal of benefits.
Data management solutions and analytical software continue to proliferate and provide better decision-making tools.
Businesses are increasingly relying on business analytics to gain a competitive advantage or just to keep up with the competition.
As such, students trained with BAI programs are highly-demanding future employees.
According to the U.S.
Bureau of Labor Statistics, Data scientist salaries in the United

passages.heading: #20-21-8B | Page 4
passages.text:
States: $130,290 (2017), and Data scientist was ranked at #1 among 50 best jobs in America (Glassdoor.com).
Business analysts often specialize in a particular industry, such as medical science, telecommunications and energy.
Or, they may work in a specific area of business, like marketing, human resources or supply chain management.
In particular, those who are working for smaller firms may serve as general practitioners.
In all settings, the job of these professionals is to define a problem, collect and analyze data pertaining to it, evaluate company processes and procedures, and ultimately recommend and deploy strategies designed to solve the issue.
The Business Analytics and Intelligence program is to provide students with the opportunity to better integrate data insights into their analyses and decision-making process.
The program is also designed to strengthen knowledge from their primary major with advanced business analytics skills.
Students will be prepared to bring insights from the large amounts of data to their functional areas such as marketing, finance, supply chain management, accounting among others.

passages.heading: #20-21-8B | Page 4
passages.text:
Students will specialize in one of the functional areas of business to gain additional skills that will prepare them for data-driven and analytics-based decision making.
Many of the courses of the program will be revised to include the important learning goals specific to Business Analytics and Intelligence.
Some courses listed in the COB curriculum will be tailored for BAI students.
The program will offer the courses of business statistics and mathematics, business application programming, data analytics software, e-Commerce, data management and visualization.
These courses were offered for the Management Information Systems (MIS) major in the college of business.
A minimum of six courses (18 credits) with an overall GPA of 2.0.
A GPA of 2.0 (includes all attempts) is mandatory for the minor.
Half of the credits for the minor (3 courses) must be completed at URI.
All the courses for the minor must be taken at an AACSB accredited business school, at the URI Data Science program (CSC 201 or CSC 211) or through an approved study abroad program.

Summary description of proposed program (not to exceed 2 pages) The proposed program for an Online Graduate Certificate in GIS and Geospatial Technologies: will enhance and expand workforce development opportunities to a wider audience, fulfill a need for graduates with proficiency in highly sought-after geospatial technology skills including Geographic Information System (GIS), interactive map and data productions and field data collection. The online program delivery and accelerated online calendar provides flexibility to domestic and international students, working professionals, active and reserve service members to obtain meaningful, well-paid employment. Students completing this certificate will

passages.heading: #20-21-6C | Page 5
passages.text:
2 have the 21st century skills increasingly expected by employers in the private and public sectors.
This program builds on the long-standing reputation of the University of Rhode Island as a national and international leader in the field of geospatial technology, particularly GIS.
The Environmental Data Center, a research lab in the Department of Natural Resource Science is considered the state's center of technical expertise in the field.
The power and timeliness of geospatial technologies is more apparent than ever.
Geospatial tools have driven the delivery of Covid-19 data to the public and decision makers.
Spatial patterns of the magnitude of outbreaks, dashboards (e.g., WHO) summarizing local conditions and visualizations of trends are all the result of geospatial technologies.
GIS Story Maps examining the history of transmission have appeared in the NY Times and other venues.
Geospatial technologies are used extensively across many sectors of the economy and are a critical support tool for resource management, planning, disaster management and mitigation, and community health, among others.

passages.heading: #20-21-6C | Page 5
passages.text:
Increasingly, an expectation exists among employers that graduates will have working knowledge and understanding of geospatial technologies as they seek positions in the private and public sectors.
GIS is considered a high growth field, according to U.S Department of Labor and Statistics.
O- Net Online has compiled the data and found that employment in the GIS field is expected to grow 7 - 10 % faster than average, with 35,700 job openings in the U.S expected between 2018 - 2028.
Internationally, GIS analytical skills are highly sought after, and the certificate should be very attractive to students in developing countries.
Geospatial technology is rapidly evolving, and professionals are interested in expanding or acquiring the necessary skills to employ state-of-the-art techniques for collecting, analyzing, interpreting, managing, and presenting location-based data.

passages.heading: #20-21-6C | Page 5
passages.text:
URI's recent market opportunity scan highlights GIS as a program with potential high student and labor market growth for expansion with recommendations to develop online versions of the GIS certificate (URI's Market Opportunity Scan; Hanover Research pg. 6) This proposed program complements undergraduate and graduate programs at URI in Natural Resources Science, Master of Environmental Science and Management and other related programs of study.
We anticipate significant interest for the program based on enrollment in the existing Graduate Certificate in GIS and Remote Sensing currently available to on-campus students.
An Online Graduate Certificate in GIS and Geospatial Technologies will allow learning opportunities for a wider audience and provide flexibility to accommodate and meet the needs of domestic and international students, working professionals, active and reserve service members and those seeking to acquire a powerful and practical skill set for employment.

passages.heading: #20-21-6C | Page 5
passages.text:
The focus of the Online Graduate Certificate in GIS and Geospatial Technologies is two-fold: 1) to prepare students for opportunities in the expanding field of geospatial technologies and offer a workforce pipeline of graduates to meet the demand for geospatial analysts in the public and private sectors nationally and abroad; and 2) to facilitate enrollment and completion of the URI professional Master of Environmental Science and Management (MESM).
All credits associated with the Online Graduate Certificate in GIS and Geospatial Technologies can be used to satisfy a portion of the requirements of the MESM degree.
The certificate will follow the accelerated online academic calendar and include four 7-week courses (3 credits each) that develop core competencies in geospatial technologies: data creation, data acquisition, spatial analysis, data management and data visualization with maps and interactive applications.
The courses will focus on tools and technologies available within the Esri ArcGIS Desktop & Online platforms, considered to be the cross-industry standard for everything geospatial.

passages.heading: #20-21-6C | Page 5
passages.text:
Course format and learning activities will emphasize critical spatial analysis techniques, data management and creative workflows for data analysis, capture and presentation, critical skills for modern day geospatial analysts and managers at all levels.
Upon completion of the Online Graduate Certificate in GIS and Geospatial Technologies, students will: 1) Will have advanced-level technical skills necessary to use geospatial data to address location-based challenges across disciplines.
We expect 10 - 20 students to enroll in the certificate program each year.
Applicants will be expected to provide 1) college transcripts certifying successful completion of a Bachelor's degree 2) two letters of recommendation from peers, mentors, or colleagues attesting to the student's ability to complete graduate level course work, and 3) a personal written statement explaining why the student is seeking a University of Rhode Island Online Graduate Certificate in GIS and Geospatial Technologies.
Accepted students will complete a sequence of four 3-credit classes for a total of 12 credits.
Since this is an online

passages.heading: #20-21-6C | Page 6
passages.text: 3 program, the expectation is that it will be funded through revenues generated by the program itself and no other revenue will be needed. The Online Graduate Certificate in GIS and Geospatial Technologies will support URI's efforts to recruit and retain students in two ways: as a stand-alone program and as a gateway to the Master of Environmental Science and Management (MESM) professional Master's degree program. The Online Graduate Certificate in GIS and Geospatial Technologies will grow the community of geospatial practitioners and enhance opportunities for graduates. A8. Signature of the President David M. An Online Graduate Certificate in GIS and Geospatial Technologies will make it possible to expand offerings to a wider audience and provide flexibility to accommodate and meet the needs of domestic and international students, working professionals, active and reserve service members and those seeking to acquire a powerful and practical skill set for employment.
This program fits the URI Academic Plan in the following ways: Goal 1: Transform undergraduate and graduate student learning and academic support with a firm commitment to student success and the development of knowledgeable, skilled, and engaged graduates prepared for an everchanging world.
The Online Graduate Certificate in GIS and Geospatial Technologies is designed to provide students with the high demand skills needed to analyze location-based data in a variety fields and settings. "Expanding online course offerings for all students and for targeted populations (adult learners)" is a specific action under Strategy 1 that this Online Graduate Certificate in GIS and Geospatial Technologies would address.

passages.heading: #20-21-6C | Page 8
passages.text:
Goal 2: Achieve high-impact, translational, and innovative research, scholarship, and creative work that addresses state, regional, and world challenges to improve health, environmental sustainability, economic development, and the human experience.
GIS skills are in high demand in a variety of fields including terrestrial and coastal natural resources management, community planning, emergency management, engineering, business, and public health.
Geospatial technology and workflows are rapidly evolving and professionals in many sectors of the economy are interested in updating or acquiring specialized GIS skills to employ state-of- the-art techniques for collecting, analyzing, interpreting, managing, and presenting location-based data.
The certificate also answers Strategy 5, action 3 to create programs to address data science and data analytics.
Geospatial technology is a data science at its heart and the techniques for data analysis and presentations will be a benefit to students across multiple disciplines.

Students who complete the Online Graduate Certificate in GIS and Geospatial Technologies will be able to then apply to the MESM program and earn a Master's degree after just 2 semesters on campus since all 12 of their certificate credits would count toward MESM course requirements.
Students completing the Online Graduate Certificate in GIS and Geospatial Technologies can take additional courses during their MESM program to deepen their geospatial education including hydrologic modeling, remote sensing, and programming languages for advanced

passages.heading: #20-21-6C | Page 9
passages.text:

passages.heading: #20-21-6C | Page 9
passages.text:
Researchers in the Environmental Data Center, a lab in the Department of Natural Resource Science, have a long history of collaboration with local, national, and international agencies to apply modern geospatial techniques in support of research, experiential learning, and extension programming.
The lab is considered the state's center of technical expertise in the field and has extensive contacts in the private and public sectors that will aid in marketing the program.
In addition, several hundred working professionals have taken short courses offered by URI's Geospatial Training Program, taught by the extension educators associated with this proposed certificate, many of these participants express interest in further training.
Given the increasing demand for trained personnel in this field, academic institutions have responded by offering online graduate certificate programs for focused training in geospatial technology.

passages.heading: #20-21-6C | Page 9
passages.text:
The University of Connecticut and University of Maine offer online GIS certificates but, market research shows that there is still unmet student demand for these types of programs (URI's Market Opportunity Scan; Hanover Research pg. 6) In addition, the URI program differs from existing regional options in two important ways.
First, the URI program draws on the strengths of Environmental Data Center to supply an experience grounded in practical applications of geospatial technology.
The courses for this program will be designed and taught by the experienced geospatial technology practitioners of the EDC and the Geospatial Training Program.
The course content reflects workflows and strategies used in real-world application of GIS and geospatial technologies: data acquisition, data manipulation, analysis, visualization, and integration with other data sources.

passages.heading: #20-21-6C | Page 9
passages.text:

passages.text: 1 Updated 7.2016 THE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND Academic Program/Degree: Online Graduate Certificate in GIS and Geospatial Technologies College: College of Environment and Life Sciences Date New Program Assessment Plan Submitted: August 2020 Faculty Member(s) Submitting Plan Proposal: Aimee Mandeville F E E D B A C K Strengths: SLOAA: • The Assessment Plan details the knowledge and skills students will acquire as they earn this graduate online certificate. • The goal is clear and the three learning outcomes define the necessary and measurable knowledge and skills students are expected to gain. • All new courses were developed with 2 courses noted as pre-reqs which helps to ensure a developmental learning path; each course has a final project as well presenting excellent opportunities to check on preparedness and achievement. • Completion of the URI Online Design program supported a strong certificate proposal with attention paid to alignment of assignments, assessments and achievement of course and program/certificate-level learning outcomes.

Suggestions for improvement: SLOAA: LOOC: • "Visualize" in outcome 3 is something that cannot be measured by the Instructor.
As a suggestion, please reword thus, .."create (or document) visualizations.." • Outcomes 1.1 and 1.2 seem to overlap.

Defining specific skills respective to the two outcomes will help to make the outcomes more discreet and less overlapping. • Students' application of skills seems to be more emphasized in 570 than 571; however, the description of 571 infers application.

Faculty Senate: Proposal to Support Student Success Context and Background Implementation of Flex-Mix Plan and Student Success The Faculty Senate Officers and Executive Committee have met throughout the fall 2020 semester with different members of the URI community, including student senator Thomas McGrath, to monitor and discuss the implementation of the “Flex-Mix” plan for maximizing safe instructional delivery during the COVID-19 pandemic, paying close attention to student success.
Throughout these discussions, stakeholders from across the community have agreed that, while the fall 2020 semester is indeed challenging in many ways, it is fundamentally different from the aggressive disruption to access to the most basic campus resources and services, and the abrupt pivot to remote instruction that occurred in spring 2020.
In all of these discussions, there has been strong consensus about the power and importance of extensive measures available to both students and faculty to mitigate the challenges that members of our community face.
Our community is and has been demonstrating our unwavering commitment to work for the common good through effective use of these existing measures.

passages.heading: #20-21-13 | Page 2
passages.text:
Students from across the university have been exercising their own autonomy, agency and academic responsibility to address and advocate for their evolving needs by: ⎯ Selecting courses based on preferred modality ⎯ Obtaining a laptop computer on loan from URI to maximize success in remote learning ⎯ Adjusting course schedule, course modality and course load according to individual needs and preferences during the add/drop period (or beyond that time via petition) ⎯ Requesting pass/fail option according to individual needs and goals ⎯ Communicating openly with faculty about needs and desires ⎯ Taking full advantage of academic and other support services i.
Academic Enhancement Center (e.g., online learning, stem tutoring) ⎯ Communicating with faculty about unique needs and to request accommodations i.

passages.heading: #20-21-13 | Page 2
passages.text: Disability Services for Students (e.g., information, intake form) ⎯ Strategically using the second grade option (first-year students and transfer students) [UM #8.33.32] ⎯ Requesting grade of “Incomplete,” to complete remaining work at a later date or to re-enroll in the course at the next opportunity [UM #8.53.21] ⎯ Discussing with faculty the option of late withdrawal from a course ⎯ Following normal administrative hierarchy regarding unresolved course-related concerns and problems: faculty, department chairperson, college dean, vice president of academic affairs, and provost. [Student Handbook, pp. 80-81] ⎯ Requesting Ombud services [UM #2.39.10, #2.39.16] Faculty from across the university are exercising the rights and responsibilities associated with their academic freedom to adapt teaching, learning and assessment plans in ways that address students’ needs and demonstrate compassion for students’ unique circumstances: ⎯ Course-wide modifications to assignments, assessments, due dates, etc. ⎯ Use of grading curves and /or adjustment of grading scales ⎯ Provision of extensions on due dates and reasonable accommodations for specific individual students facing unique difficulties ⎯ Authorization of late withdrawal or grade of “Incomplete” to specific individual students facing extraordinary hardships

passages.heading: #20-21-13 | Page 3
passages.text:
Faculty Senate: Proposal to Support Student Success The Faculty Senate Executive Committee believes that these existing measures are the most appropriate and effective ways to manage difficulties during this academic year.
Given that current challenges will persist into the future, these measures are the most sustainable strategies, and those that will most effectively prepare our students for long-term success – both during their time at URI and beyond.
Student success and extraordinary measures to alleviate grade pressure At several meetings, the Faculty Senate Executive Committee has carefully considered and discussed the issue of student success and, specifically, whether or not our current circumstances this semester merit extraordinary measures to alleviate grade pressure for students.
Throughout these conversations over the past two months, we have weighed both the benefits and risks associated with different extraordinary measures, as well as the intended and unintended consequences of each measure.
In each case, we have reached the same conclusion: the most effective way to manage challenges during this current academic year is through the existing measures mentioned above.

passages.heading: #20-21-13 | Page 3
passages.text: Meetings during which these matters have been discussed at length: ⎯ September 21, 2020 – Provost DeHayes and Vice Provost Veeger with Senate Chair Echevarría and Senate Vice Chair Cardany ⎯ October 7, 2020 – Faculty Senate Executive Committee ⎯ October 8, 2020 – Senate Chair Echevarría and Senate Vice Chair Cardany with Senator Meyerson ⎯ October 15, 2020 – Thomas McGrath with Senate Chair Echevarría and Senate Vice Chair Cardany ⎯ October 21, 2020 – Faculty Senate Executive Committee ⎯ November 10, 2020 – Provost DeHayes and Vice Provost Veeger with Senate President Echevarría and Vice President Cardany ⎯ November 12, 2020 – Faculty Senate Executive Committee ⎯ November 16, 2020 – Faculty Senate Executive Committee and Senate Standing Committee Chairs ⎯ November 17, 2020 – Faculty Senate Executive Committee and Senate Standing Committee Chairs ⎯ November 18, 2020 – Faculty Senate Executive Committee On Thursday, November 19, 2020, Thomas McGrath, Chair of the Student Senate Academic Affairs Committee forwarded to Senate President Echevarría a Student Senate resolution (passed on November 18, 2020) accompanied by a list of 98 comments retrieved by Student Senate leadership via a student survey.

passages.heading: #20-21-13 | Page 3
passages.text:
He requested to speak to the Faculty Senate about the resolution and his peers’ concerns.
At the Faculty Senate meeting on November 19, 2020, Chair McGrath requested that the Faculty Senate consider instituting a measure to alleviate grade pressure for the fall 2020 semester.
During his presentation he noted that he and his Student Senate peers are cognizant of the fact that the challenges associated with this current fall semester are completely different in nature and scale from the difficulties that our community experienced during the spring 2020 semester.
He further acknowledged that he and his peers know that many students do not feel that extraordinary measures are needed, and he underscored that the Student Senate is certain that many students would not take advantage of such measures.

passages.heading: #20-21-13 | Page 4
passages.text:
Faculty Senate: Proposal to Support Student Success Extraordinary measure The Faculty Senate acknowledges the Student Senate concerns that, for some students facing truly extraordinary hardships, the extensive measures highlighted above may not be sufficient during our current circumstances.
In response to the Student Senate request, the Faculty Senate Executive Committee recommends that the Faculty Senate approve one extraordinary measure to support student success and alleviate grade pressure, while also minimizing negative impacts on learning and academic excellence.
Expansion of access to the second grade option for all undergraduate students The Faculty Senate Executive Committee views expansion of the second grade option as the most appropriate and sustainable response to the Student Senate request for grade pressure relief.
The second grade option is a measure currently open solely to students who have completed fewer than 30 credits, or transfer students for courses taken during their initial semester at URI.
The proposed measure would expand access to this option to all undergraduate students throughout the entire 2020-2021 academic year.

passages.heading: #20-21-13 | Page 4
passages.text:
Motion: In the sole case of the 2020-2021 academic year, temporarily suspend certain parts of section 8.33.32 of the University Manual in order to expand access to the second grade option to all undergraduate students: Amendment to motion to expand second grade option: further expansion of access to graduate students (amendment approved 11/25/20) 8.33.32 Students may exercise a Second Grade Option by repeating a course in which the student earned C-, D+, D, or F.
Only courses that fall within the student’s first 30 credits taken at the University may be selected for this option.
Students must exercise this option no later than the next two semesters for which the student registers after completing thirty credits.
Transfer students may exercise the Second Grade Option for courses taken during their initial semester at the University.
This option must be exercised during the next two semesters for which they register after their initial semester.

passages.heading: #20-21-13 | Page 4
passages.text:
When a student exercises the Second Grade Option, only the grade earned when the course is repeated will be used in the calculation of a student’s QPA and only the credits earned for the repeated course will apply toward the graduation requirements.
All grades earned for a given course shall remain on a student’s permanent academic record.
Students who wish to take advantage of this Second Grade Option must obtain approval from their academic deans and submit the appropriate form to the Office of Enrollment Services prior to midterm of the semester in which the course is being repeated.
The Second Grade Option may be used only once per course. (Motion approved 11/25/20) The Executive Committee proposes this extraordinary measure as a sustainable solution to alleviating pressure as different challenges associated with COVID-19 persist and as students adapt to these new circumstances.
This solution alleviates grade pressure without compromising the institution’s ability to accurately track and respond appropriately to different levels of

passages.heading: #20-21-13 | Page 5
passages.text: Faculty Senate: Proposal to Support Student Success achievement. The measure also safeguards the academic integrity of our students’ degrees, and their competitive access to future professional, research and academic opportunities. Summary of strategic advantages of this extraordinary measure: ⎯ Alleviates grade pressure for students who are struggling, by providing opportunities to re-take courses with robust protection for the overall grade point average ⎯ Safeguards each program’s ability to promote and maximize student success by accurately tracking and responding appropriately to varying levels of achievement of learning outcomes ⎯ Provides support for students while minimizing negative impacts on degree progress and achievement of program-specific critical learning outcomes ⎯ Maintains learning incentives to maximize student motivation and accountability to engage actively in learning ⎯ Limits grade point average inflation ⎯ Maintains the integrity of grades ⎯ Limits risks to the University’s accreditation status and to the accreditation status of our programs ⎯ Safeguards and maximizes competitive student access to future employment and research opportunities, and to graduate programs Because, based on individual circumstances, this extraordinary measure may have consequences that students may not immediately foresee, all students considering this option for any of their courses are strongly encouraged to consult with advisor(s), faculty and department chairs in order to determine their status and to analyze and assess all of the potential unintended impacts of their decision. Similarly, faculty and advisors are strongly encouraged to communicate with students about the potential consequences of planning to use this measure in any courses.

passages.text: THE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND Revised 8/2016 Notice of Change form Notice of Change for: Environmental Science and Management (MESM) Date: 10/27/20 A. PROGRAM INFORMATION 1. Name of institution University of Rhode Island 2. Name of department, division, school or college Department: College: CELS 3. Intended initiation date of program change. Include anticipated date for granting first degrees or certificates, if appropriate. Initiation date: Spring 2021 First degree date: Spring 2021 4. Intended location of the program URI Main Campus 5. Summary description of proposed program (not to exceed 2 pages). We are proposing to correct an error in the name of one specialization in the Master of Environmental Science and Management (MESM) program so that it accurately reflects program offerings and requirements. There is currently a discrepancy between the MESM specializations approved by Faculty Senate Bill 16-17-10B (and, therefore, available in ecampus) and the specializations described in the graduate catalog and the MESM website. Both the graduate catalog and the MESM website currently include a specialization in “Environmental Policy and Management”, while ecampus instead has a specialization called “Environmental Science and Management.”

passages.heading: #20-21-15 | Page 4
passages.text: From the inception of MESM many years ago, Environmental Policy and Management has been one of the core tracks, and many students have chosen this specialization specifically because of its emphasis on integrating social science and policy with natural science expertise. Unfortunately, under the current ecampus settings, their transcripts describe the specialization as “Environmental Science and Management” rather than “Environment Policy and Management.” This language does not accurately reflect the knowledge and skills they gain in that specialization. We would therefore like to correct the approved name of the specialization to match what we are currently advertising and providing students. Specifically, we are proposing to change the “Environmental Science and Management” specialization (Academic Plan: MESMESM) to the “Environmental Policy and Management” specialization (Academic Plan: MESMEPM). At a minimum, we would like to change the specialization name so that “Environmental Policy and Management” will appear on transcripts even if the ecampus code remains the same. 6. If applicable, please include the existing URI catalog language and proposed catalog changes indicated in Track Changes. As noted above, the language in the graduate catalog already describes this specialization as “environmental policy and management,” so no changes are necessary. “Specializations Conservation biology; earth and hydrologic science; environmental communication; environmental planning and design; environmental policy and management; remote sensing and spatial analysis; sustainable systems; and wetland, watershed and ecosystem science.” 7. Signature of the President David M. Dooley 2

passages.heading: #20-21-15 | Page 6
passages.text: Admission requirements: Bachelor’s degree with adequate preparation for the proposed area of study. Program requirements: for thesis option, completion of a minimum of 30 credits, including six credits of thesis research. For nonthesis option, completion of a minimum of 33 credits, half of which must be TMD courses numbered 500 or above, including at least one course that requires a substantial paper or practicum involving significant independent study. Student must present the paper to a committee of three faculty members and archive the paper on Digital Commons. TMD 510 is a requirement for all students. For the textile science specialization, TMD 510; a statistics course. For the specializations focusing on historic textiles and fashion, textile conservation, and cultural analysis, TMD 510, 518, 500 or 524, and a supervised internship (TMD 530, 1-4 credits); half of the remaining elective credits must be from TMD courses numbered 500 or above. A minimum of nine credits is required to achieve a competency level in an allied field such as art history, history, or anthropology; this may result in a program of more than 30 credits. The committee may elect to waive this requirement if the candidate has adequate preparation in the allied field as an undergraduate. Candidates lacking undergraduate courses in textile science and fashion history may be required to make up deficiencies without graduate credit. For the fashion merchandising specialization, TMD 510 and 524; six credits to be selected from TMD 432, 442, or 452; a statistics course. Candidates lacking undergraduate courses in textile science and fashion merchandising may be required to make up deficiencies without graduate credit. 7. Signature of the President David M. Dooley 2

passages.text: THE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND Revised 8/2016 Notice of Change form Notice of Change for: We propose adding Physical Therapy as a specialization to the PhD in Health Sciences program. Current specializations include: Communicative Disorders, Human Development & Family Science, Kinesiology and Nutrition & Food Sciences. Date: Nov. 15, 2020 A. PROGRAM INFORMATION 1. Name of institution University of Rhode Island 2. Name of department, division, school or college Department: College: Health Sciences 3. Intended initiation date of program change. Include anticipated date for granting first degrees or certificates, if appropriate. Initiation date: Jan. 1, 2021 First degree date: May 2024 4. Intended location of the program Kingston Campus 5. Summary description of proposed program (not to exceed 2 pages). Health Sciences is a rapidly changing and evolving discipline, requiring highly trained, critical thinkers to solve some of society’s biggest health-related problems. The Ph.D. in Health Sciences is a college-wide degree with faculty from multiple departments/programs in the College of Health Sciences and focuses on health, wellness, and quality of life across the lifespan. Research brings together faculty and students to solve important health-related problems through a mix of basic, applied and translational science. The program allows students the opportunity to gain experience in the various disciplines that make up health sciences and provides them with the opportunity for advanced content knowledge and in- depth training in one discipline or area of study.

passages.heading: #20-21-22B | Page 4
passages.text: Students are eligible to apply for this program after earning a post-baccalaureate degree in a health-related field. Physical Therapy was not initially included as a specialization because the graduate catalog language (which has now been changed) required a master’s degree to have 30 credits from their post-baccalaureate degree apply to their doctoral program. Physical Therapy does not offer a master's degree. Instead, students in this discipline go on to the

passages.heading: #20-21-22B | Page 5
passages.text:
doctoral of physical therapy (DPT).
Therefore, no credits from the DPT would count toward the PhD.
The graduate council approved language (Nov. 9, 2020) in the graduate manual to let students with a master’s or qualifying graduate degree request up to 30 credits from this degree to be applied to their doctoral program.
This includes the Doctor of Physical Therapy (DPT) degree.
Given this change, we would like to add Physical Therapy as a specialization to the CHS doctoral program.
The sub-plan for DPT would be as follows:  CHS Core o 9 credits in health (CHS 601, 605, 610) o 6 credits in statistics from approved list (above) o 3 credits in research methods from approved list (above)  PHT Sub-Plansubplan Course Work o minimum of 42 credits selected with advisor to ensure disciplinary expertise; 6 of these credits must be in courses related to physical therapy  Doctoral Dissertation Research o PHT 699 (12 18 credits) 6.

Program Director: Allison Tovar, alison_tovar@uri.edu Credit Requirements A minimum of 72 credit hours post-baccalaureate is required for the Ph.D.
Up to 30 credits from a previously-earned master’s degree or other qualifying graduate degree can be applied toward the PhD if related to the discipline (i.e., sub-plan).
A minimum of 42 credits must be taken at the University of Rhode Island.
Required course work, research credits and dissertation credits depend on the preparation and study plan of the individual student.
All degree candidates are required to prepare a Program of Study in consultation with their major professor and doctoral committee.

Curriculum: 42 credits (minimum).
A student’s formal curriculum plan will include an interdisciplinary seminar, course work and research/dissertation credits.
The doctoral degree in Health Sciences is designed to foster excellence in research.
Students will be involved in active research projects throughout their PhD program through completion of a dissertation (minimum of 18 credits) and other research experiences (maximum of 9 credits).

passages.text: FACULTY SENATE OFFICE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND FACULTY SENATE October 15, 2020 Faculty Senate Curriculum and Standards Committee Report 2020-2021-1 At the October 1, 2020 meeting of the Curriculum and Standards Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate. SECTION II Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation by the Faculty Senate NEW PROGRAMS: COLLEGE OF ARTS & SCIENCES: New Interdisciplinary Minor in Social Justice and Civic Responsibilities: We propose an undergraduate interdisciplinary minor in Social Justice & Civic Responsibilities. The United Nations defines social justice in terms of human rights and personal dignity for everyone. Other sources include access and equality. Borrowing from these descriptions, we define social justice broadly as the value of human life, equal access to social capital, personal dignity, and the implementation of human rights for ALL. Summary description of proposed program (not to exceed 2 pages) We propose an undergraduate interdisciplinary minor in Social Justice & Civic Responsibilities.
The United Nations defines social justice in terms of human rights and personal dignity for everyone.
Other sources include access and equality.
Borrowing from these descriptions, we define social justice broadly as the value of human life, equal access to social capital, personal dignity, and the implementation of human rights for ALL.
US Citizenship and Immigration Services identifies core civic responsibilities that include staying informed about issues affecting your community and participating in them.
More importantly they add respecting the rights, beliefs, and opinions of others, and participating in the democratic process.
We adopt these descriptions of civic responsibilities for the minor.
Course options for the minor represent an array of multidisciplinary and interdisciplinary approaches to social justice topics.
Students who complete the

passages.heading: #20-21-4C | Page 5
passages.text: 3 minor will emerge with a nuanced understanding of the world around them, the

passages.heading: #20-21-4C | Page 6
passages.text:
4 reasons why people continue to seek to change that world, and a familiarity with the organizing tools and strategies available to those efforts.
A core intellectual component of the minor is an emphasis on seeing the world through the lens of other people's experiences, especially people and groups who have different social, racial, ethnic, economic, religious, gendered, and geographic backgrounds from one's own.
Developing a critical consciousness of the intersections of one's identities, privileges, and power is another important component.
This can lead to more compassionate and meaningful relationships with others.
Moreover, a deep understanding of one's positionality can help perpetuate or dismantle systems and structures that ultimately impact minoritized communities.
Students will learn about subtle and blatant institutional barriers and the micro-aggressions that systematically oppress people.
Students will have experiential learning opportunities that allow them to see the ways in which the ideas they read about and discuss in class actually play out in the real world.

passages.heading: #20-21-4C | Page 6
passages.text:
Students will engage in civic processes visiting with community leaders, activists, and politicians to influence policies.
They will prepare for and engage in civic processes reflecting on these experiences.
They will learn theories, methods, and skills that they can use in their work and personal lives to improve the human condition.
Courses for the minor are organized into three categories; peoples, social and institutional contexts, and methods and skills, and students are required to take at least one course from each category (and not more than three) and then complete their credit requirements in consultation with advisors.
An ongoing advisory committee of faculty, staff, and peers will meet once per semester to review advising strategies, and tweak the course offerings, making sure that courses are still being offered, that faculty who teach them are informed about the minor, and review new course options that become available to include in the minor.
The committee will also develop and distribute marketing materials for the minor and maintain a Google work site for students who pursue the minor and for faculty and staff who contribute to it.

passages.heading: #20-21-4C | Page 6
passages.text:
This site will also serve to inform the community about experiential learning opportunities that arise in the interest of social justice and civic responsibilities.
Currently, the committee includes several faculty, staff, and undergraduate students.

RATIONALE: There should be a demonstrable need for the program.
B1.
Why is the new program being developed?
The world is experiencing monumental institutional changes that have arisen from centuries of oppression against groups of people by age, gender, socioeconomic status, ability, sexual orientation, regionalism, religion, race, ethnicity and nationality.
As a species, we cannot tolerate or participate in group oppression any longer, but the institutionalized nature of systemic oppression requires that people must enter the work- force, build their families, and engage in their communities with the knowledge and skills necessary for creating change.
This is the responsibility of our educational system.

passages.heading: #20-21-4C | Page 7
passages.text:
Regardless of a student's major course of study, every one of them should graduate being prepared to create positive change that improves the lives of everyone.
A minor in social justice and civic responsibilities, coupled with the student's major course of study provides a path toward creating positive change in the world.
B2.
What is the economic need and workforce data related to the program?
Students who complete the minor will explore their connections to the communities in which they live and work, tackling questions of mutual obligation, social and political change, and human impact on the social, historic, and geographic world.
Grounded in an interdisciplinary approach that includes the humanities, social sciences, the arts, and other fields - this new minor will provide students at URI with a foundation for a life of actively challenging systems of oppression. and decolonizing received wisdom, produced knowledge, and told histories [or public memory].
At the same time, students will gain the critical thinking, reading, writing, and analytical tools that are the foundation of an informed and educated citizenry.

passages.heading: #20-21-4C | Page 7
passages.text:
Our students will enter the workforce with skills in human relations that every industry needs for a diverse world.
It is no longer sufficient to train a select few individuals to expertly advise organizations how to navigate diversity.
Everyone must learn the values of a diverse workforce to ensure that each individual can reach their/her/his best potential.
Regardless of a student's major academic and career interests, pursuing the minor in social justice and civic responsibilities will enrich their lives and bring these ideas and skills into all industries, organizations, and occupations.

passages.heading: #20-21-4C | Page 8
passages.text:
6 a.
Provide information on jobs available as a result of successfully completing the certificate or degree: job titles, job outlook/growth, and salaries.
Since this is a minor and not a major course of study, it is intended to enrich the work and personal lives of everyone, not just those who are in a select few careers.
For example, a student majoring in criminology and criminal justice who pursues a career in policing would be more marketable in that career with a sub-specialty in social justice and civic responsibility, as would a nurse, a teacher, an engineer, or a psychologist, for example.
The skills and information learned in this minor are important for journalists, museum curators, researchers, professors, executive directors of non-profit and social justice organizations, politicians, diplomats, UN officials and advisors, community organizers, community educators (like people at Save the Bay, etc.), entrepreneurs including people piecing together careers through podcasting, and freelance writing.

passages.heading: #20-21-4C | Page 8
passages.text:
According to the Rhode Island Department of Labor and Training (RIDLT), the top 10 occupations requiring a Bachelor's degree include registered nurses, elementary and secondary school teachers, and child, family & school social workers.
All of these occupations are projected to show increases in job openings through 2026, all of them require extensive work with the public, so this minor would make our graduates more marketable in these careers.
Organizational rules are changing to include more diverse and equitable processes and roles are being introduced to ensure these processes are followed.
Most people who currently occupy positions of power, in this particular moment, were not taught the skills that are necessary to achieve these goals.
They will be looking for people who have received the kind of education that specifically leads to social justice in any occupation.
A graduate with a minor in this area would be of interest to a company's corporate responsibility division, and human resources positions dedicated to talent diversification.
The RIDLT projects jobs under the Training and Development Specialists category will see a 12.2% increase in jobs by 2026.
B3.

INSTITUTIONAL ROLE: The program should be clearly related to the published role, scope, and mission of the institution and be compatible with other programs and activities of the institution.
C1.
Explain how the program is consistent with the published role, scope, and mission of the institution and how it is related to the institution's Academic Plan.
The University's mission explicitly highlights these values; "diversity, fairness, and respect," and "civic involvement." URI's "Academic Strategic Plan (2016-2021) sets as Goal 4, "diversity and social justice" that is defined to "Inspire an enlightened community that is characterized by vibrant cultural diversity; that embraces difference; that is built upon a learning environment that fosters respect, understanding, and social justice; and that rejects prejudice and intolerance." The first strategy under this goal is to diversify faculty and staff.
Often, members of the URI community who are from underrepresented groups feel disengaged and unwelcomed.
They may embrace inclusion in the advisory committee for this minor and they would greatly contribute to the committee's goals.

passages.heading: #20-21-4C | Page 9
passages.text:
The second strategy focuses on recruiting a diverse study body.
They may seek institutions to attend that offer educational opportunities that clearly value social justice.
The third strategy is to create opportunities for discourse on social justice

passages.heading: #20-21-4C | Page 10
passages.text:
8 and diversity, which every aspect of this minor addresses, from its creation, to its implementation and maintenance, and beyond.
As an extension of the Academic Strategic Plan, the Community, Equity, and Diversity Strategic Plan specifically encourages faculty to establish an interdisciplinary social justice minor that focuses on general or specific topics within diversity, equity, inclusion, and social justice.
D.
INTER-INSTITUTIONAL CONSIDERATIONS: D1.
What are the similar programs in the state and region?
Regionally, the only other state college or university that offers a minor that is in any way similar to the social justice and civic responsibilities minor is the University of Connecticut with their Human Rights minor.
In the state of Rhode Island, no college or university offers anything similar to the social justice & civic responsibilities minor (Providence College, Brown University, Salve Regina, Rhode Island College, Bryant College, or Roger Williams).
Brown University does offer an undergraduate and four graduate degrees in American Studies, which is interdisciplinary and encompasses American and ethnic studies, and public humanities.

passages.heading: #20-21-4C | Page 10
passages.text:
However, as a state institution, it is unlikely that we will compete with Brown for the same students, and Brown offers no minor.
At URI, three other interdisciplinary minors address related topics in their curriculum, but there is currently no minor in social justice or civic responsibilities. • Justice, Law, and Society - focuses on the official justice system and on social justice as it relates specifically to legal justice. • Special populations - focuses on groups of people who face inequality, similar to the first category of courses offered under the new minor. • Work, Labor, and Social Justice - focuses on social justice issues in the singular institution of work/labor (This minor currently has no coordinator and no students).
At URI, in addition to the other interdepartmental and interdisciplinary minors, those offered by independent departments inherently also integrate some of the content in the proposed interdisciplinary minor, particularly departmental minors that are offered from interdisciplinary programs such as Gender and Women's Studies, and Criminology, Criminal Justice.

passages.heading: #20-21-4C | Page 10
passages.text:
The proposed new minor is only possible because so many URI departments, programs, colleges, and faculty already do address social justice in at least some of their courses. a.
If similar programs exist, how is this program different or why is duplication necessary?
No existing minor at URI is similar to the proposed minor, with caveats explained in the previous section.
The organization of the new minor requires students to take from 1-3 (3+ credit courses) from each of three sections.
This forces students to sample courses in

passages.heading: #20-21-4C | Page 11
passages.text:
9 each of the three main areas of social justice - peoples, institutions and contexts, and methods and skills.
No other minor is organized in the same way with the same course options available, and this requirement ensures that students cannot earn this minor by taking the same courses offered for any other minor, regardless of how they are organized within the other minors.
One of the goals for the proposed minor is to expose students to discussions about social justice across the University instead of just within their own major discipline. b.
Have you communicated with other institutions about the development of this program and have any concerns been raised related to role, scope, and mission or duplication?
We have not communicated with other institutions about the development of this minor.
D2.
How do courses in this program transfer to other schools?
The University offers a comprehensive interinstitutional agreement for transferring courses from one institution to another (http://www.ritransfers.org/program-transfer- plans/).
D3.
How does this program align to academic programs at other institutions?

passages.heading: #20-21-4C | Page 11

Are there pre-requisite courses?
If so, please explain/list?
Students could complete the minor by selecting all of their courses from each section that do not require prerequisites, if they choose.
Most of the prerequisites that are required fulfil General Education credits or are only year-specific, i.e. sophomore, junior, or senior standing.
A URI student's degree is divided between their major credit hours (30-32 hrs.), 40 General Education hours, and approximately 50 elective credit hours for most majors.
URI is on a semester-system and the average credits per course is 3 hours (Political Science and English courses are four-credits each semester).
Students may count up to twelve credits from their major as General Education credits, so they can pursue other majors and minor areas of study.
About half of a student's course credits are open for additional major or minor areas of interest.

Curriculum a.
How many credit hours are required to graduate (include all general education and pre-requisites)?
Students must complete 18 credit hours for the minor by completing one (3+ credits) to three courses from each section -- I (Peoples), II (Institutions and Contexts), and III (Methods and Skills) - students must take at least one course that counts as at least three credits from each of the three sections, and cannot count more than three courses toward the minor from any specific section.
General education requirements may be used for the minor.
A maximum of two courses required in a major program (regardless of course code) may be used to apply to both the major and minor fields of study.
Topics courses, and honors sections for courses in the minor, that fit into the minor's concepts must be approved by the minor advisor in the Department of Sociology & Anthropology to count toward the minor.

passages.heading: #20-21-4C | Page 15
passages.text:
To complete a minor, a minimum grade point average of 2.00 must be earned in the minor courses, and at least 12 of the 18 credits must be at the 200 level or above.
At least eight of the credits required for the minor must be earned at the University of Rhode Island.
Minor courses may not be taken on a pass-fail basis.
The requirements for the minor must be completed prior to graduation, and students must submit the required paperwork, signed by the minor advisor in the Department of Sociology & Anthropology in the student's final year of study.
Upon graduation, successful completion of the minor is noted on the student's official transcript. b.

passages.text:
Judy Van Wyck, Chairperson Africana Studies supports the Department of Sociology in their proposal for a Social Justice and Civic Responsibilities Minor.
The AAF Faculty have several concerns that can be summarized in the following statement.
While we support a minor in social justice, we believe the present state of Africana Studies reflects the results of systematic lack of support, marginalization and institutionalized neglect.
Without the adequate funding, staffing and support that is necessary for any area of study to carry out basic administrative and academic functions, successful and progressive development is impeded.
Complexly, Africana Studies has "partnered" in the past with other departments in well-meaning projects.
Often the result has been that the other departments receive the recognition and subsequent funding while Africana Studies remains perpetually without recognition of its contributions and thereby unable to garner the funding and support necessary for progress.
We have seen this pattern repeated too many times and we are hoping that these kinds of institutional blocks to true equity and social justice can be dismantled.

passages.heading: #20-21-4C | Page 33
passages.text:
We would like our support of the Social Justice and Civic Responsiblities minor to strengthen increased support of Africana Studies, specifically, adequate funding, staffing and departmental status.
Toward that end, we conditionally support Sociology in the effort to establish a very important minor, the Social Justice and Civic Responsibilities minor, and even expect our relationship with Sociology to model social justice by noting the following concerns: A.) This Minor should not be seen as a segue away from the Africana Studies Major/Minor, but rather a field of study that is compatible with the academic goals of Africana Studies.
B.) Africana Studies will be able to "count" involvement in the Social Justice minor as credit in our overall assessment C.) Africana Studies maintains rightful decision -making over hiring of Faculty (especially adjunct Faculty) to teach the courses that are solely designated as AAF.
D.) The Sociology Department will keep Africana Studies informed of decisions about the minor that will impact Africana Studies.

I know you only just got this information from the Dean's office.
Let's replace 210 with 212 as you suggested.
All other courses will be included in the minor thanks to your department's authorization to do so.
Your department asks good questions.
I am a criminologist who has been at URI for over 20 years now.
I teach several courses in the JLS minor.
I do not feel that the new minor in Social Justice and Civic Responsibilities duplicates the JLS minor for many reasons.
First, the focus in that minor is on legal justice, not necessarily social justice.
Of course, many of the included courses do address both issues, but the focus of the minor is what is important.
The new minor includes many courses that are not i n the JLS minor and vice versa for that reason.

passages.heading: #20-21-4C | Page 41
passages.text:
Also, the new minor is designed so that students cannot take 2/3 of their minor in 100 and 200 -level courses.
I feel that that a minor "concentration" doesn't concentrate on much when nearly all of the course s taken to complete it are introductory.
Third, the new minor advisory committee will be advising and directing students to track the courses that they take to suit their career goals and personal interests.
We will meet regularly (once per semester) and we hope to fully engage students with faculty and with each other throughout their college experience - something that almost no other minor does.
We hope to create a community of faculty and students to rally around social justice issues and to engage in civic action.
I envision the two minors as being very different from one another, and it is feasible that a student could pursue both minors, taking completely different courses and having different but related experiences.
Thank you for your endorsement.
Feel free to share this email with others if you think it is helpful.
Also, if anyone from your department is interested in joining our advisory committee for the minor, they are welcome to do so!
Just ask them to contact me.

We have a lot of options in this minor, fortunately.

passages.heading: #20-21-4C | Page 57
passages.text:
I think the biggest incentive for a department to include a course that consists mainly of majors is this gives your majors a chance to take the course and count it toward both the major and the SJCR minor.
Students can now count two courses in both their major and their minor.
Given that, including the oversubscribed course benefits your own majors.
It benefits the minor in that if an HDF major can do that, it might encourage them to complete the minor.
BTW, my daughter majored in HDF from URI and graduated in 2016.
She's always harkening back to things she learned in those courses when she's dealing with her 2 1/2 year old daughter.
Judy Judy Judy A.
Van Wyk, Ph.D.

Vanessa Wynder Quainoo To: Judy Van Wyk <vellosa@uri.edu > Letter of Support for the Social Justice and Civic Reaponsibility Minor in Sociology/ Dr.
Judy Van Wyck, Chairperson Africana Studies supports the Department of Sociology in their proposal for a Social Justice and Civic Responsibilities Minor.
The AAF Faculty have several concerns that can be summarized in the following statement.
While we support a minor in social justi ce, we believe the present state of Africana Studies reflects the results of systematic lack of support, marginalization and institutionalized neglect.

passages.heading: #20-21-4C | Page 72
passages.text:
Without the adequate funding, staffing and support that is necessary for any area of study to carry out basic administrative and academic functions, successful and progressive development is impeded.
Complexly, Africana Studies has "partnered" in the past with other departments in well-meaning projects.
Often the result has been that the other departments receive the recognition and subsequent funding while Africana Studies remains perpetually without recognition of its contributions and thereby unable to garner the funding and support necessary for progress.
We have seen this pattern repeated too many times and we are hoping that these kinds of institutional blocks to true equity and social justice can be dismantled.
We would like our support of the Social Justice and Civic Responsiblities minor to strengthen increased support of Africana Studies, specifically, adequate funding, staffing and departmental status.

passages.heading: #20-21-4C | Page 72
passages.text:
Toward that end, we conditionally support Sociology in the effort to establish a very important minor, the Social Justice and Civic Responsibilities minor, and even expect our relationship with Sociology to model social justice by noting the following concerns: A.) This Minor should not be seen as a segue away from the Africana Studies Major/Minor, but rather a field of study that is compatible with the academic goals of Africana Studies.
B.) Africana Studies will be able to "count" involvement in the Social Justice minor as credit in our overall assessment C.) Africana Studies maintains rightful decision -making over hiring of Faculty (especially adjunct Faculty) to teach the courses that are solely designated as AAF.
D.) The Sociology Department will keep Africana Studies informed of decisions about the minor that will impact Africana Studies.
Sincerely, Dr.
Vanessa Wynder Quainoo On behalf of AAf Faculty https://mail.google .com/mail/u/0?ik=e60 f7df049&view=p t&search=all&pe rmthid=thread-f%3A1677482604128126819%7Cmsg -f%3A1677492341664 6. 1/1

passages.heading: #20-21-4C | Page 73
passages.text: Social Justice & Civic Responsibilities In addition to fulfilling all the basic requirements for a minor (see Minor Fields of Study), students who declare a minor in Social Justice & Civic Responsibilities are required to take at least one course from each of three categories of courses (peoples, social and institutional contexts, and methods and skills) and not more than three from each category for a total of 18 credits. Students are encouraged to meet with someone from the minor advisory committee or the minor director, Dr. Judy A. Van Wyk in the Department of Sociology & Anthropology before they begin to plan which courses best suit their career and academic goals. With at least 68 courses to choose from, students will gain knowledge and skills that are necessary for our diverse and changing world that are applicable to any career. Courses for the minor are available from African American Studies, Business, Criminology & Criminal Justice, Communications, Economics, Education, English, Gender & Women's Studies, Human Development and Family Studies, History, Latin American Studies, Labor Relations and Human Resources, Marine Affairs, Nursing, Music, Philosophy, Political Science, Psychology, Sociology & Anthropology, and Writing. For course selections, and a list of the minor's advisory committee members, visit the Department of Sociology & Anthropology https://web.uri.edu/soc- anth/academics/.

passages.text: THE UNIVERSITY Appendix B OF RHODE ISLAND Revised 8/2016 Notice of Change form Notice of Change for: M.S. in Healthcare Management; Post-Baccalaureate Certificate in Health Leadership and Administration; and Post-Baccalaureate Certificate in Quality Improvement, Process Measurement, and Information Systems Management Date: October 20, 2020 A. PROGRAM INFORMATION 1. Name of institution University of Rhode Island 2. Name of department, division, school or college Department: n/a College: College of Business 3. Intended initiation date of program change. Include anticipated date for granting first degrees or certificates, if appropriate. Initiation date: 1/1/2021 First degree date: 4. Intended location of the program Online via URI Online 5. Summary description of proposed program (not to exceed 2 pages). After several rounds of discussions between the healthcare management program director (Sean Edmund Rogers) and URI Online leadership, as well as analysis of current and prospective student data, we wish to make the following changes to streamline URI’s healthcare management offerings and to enhance their marketability: 1. Ask #1: Offer a single healthcare management graduate certificate instead of the two separate certificates that currently exist, and allow a wider selection of healthcare management (MHM) courses to count towards that single certificate.

passages.heading: #20-21-19B | Page 4
passages.text:
2.
Ask #2: Change the composition of the M.S. degree such that it straightforwardly requires the completion of 30 credits of MHM credits.
Currently, the M.S. degree is structured as the combination of (1) one 12-credit post-baccalaureate certificate, (2) a second post-bac certificate, (3) one MHM elective, and (4) a practicum capstone.
This totals 10 MHM classes and 30 MHM credits.
The certificate portion of this is a so-called stackable certificate approach, with 24 of the 30 credits coming from these two post-bac certificates.
Our desire is to streamline the M.S. in Healthcare Management degree such that it is comprised of 30 MHM credits whether or not a student completes a graduate certificate en passant.
Our primary objective with this entire change proposal is #1 above – to make earning a graduate certificate in healthcare management at URI more accessible.
Per URI Online recruiters and prospectors, there has not been a single expression of interest in the post- bac certificate in quality improvement.

passages.heading: #20-21-19B | Page 4
passages.text:
Students are certainly interested in quality improvement and this is an important topic in healthcare; however, none have expressed a desire to devote an entire program of study to this subject.
Any interest in earning a healthcare grad certificate at URI has been directed toward the other existing certificate in health administration.
Additionally, prospective students have expressed strong interest in being able to earn a certificate by taking courses outside of the strict structure that currently exists (at present, three of the four courses in each certificate are prescribed).
The current structure limits when students can begin and complete a certificate – they must wait until the carousel of courses comes back around for them to hop on, and in some cases that can be a year-long wait.
Creating a single certificate in healthcare management enables URI to alleviate these pain points and reach a wider audience of prospective students.
We have found that most prospective students interested in a grad certificate wish to begin quickly, and URI Online has the structure in place to enable that to happen.
The limiting factor is our current program design.

passages.heading: #20-21-19B | Page 4
passages.text:
A side effect of creating a single graduate certificate in healthcare management is that the “stackable certificate” design of the M.S. would need to go away and be replaced with a straightforward 30-credit MHM approach.
There is no evidence that removing the notion of stackable certificates would do harm.
No prospects in recent memory have expressed interest in earning the stackable certificates as a pathway to the M.S. degree.
In fact, it has created confusion during prospect calls and sessions. 2

passages.heading: #20-21-19B | Page 5
passages.text:
As a final sidenote on the topic of stackable certificates, in my professional opinion (as a scholar of human resources) such a design may even adversely impact URI’s ability to provide accessible healthcare management graduate education to Rhode Islanders and beyond.
As I learned this summer via meetings with enrollment services, financial aid, and URI Online, our healthcare management graduate certificates do not qualify for federal financial aid.
Some graduate certificate programs around the country do qualify for federal aid, but our healthcare management ones were determined not to.
Thus, students must pay for all certificate credits (up to 24 under the current “stackable” model) with non- federal financial aid, such as out of pocket or via private loans.
At current rates, that amounts to $18,792 for two URI certificates.
This has led to more than one prospective student not applying or enrolling at URI this summer and fall.
The streamlining we propose potentially removes barriers to access and may help put URI graduate education within reach for more aspiring healthcare professionals and leaders.

passages.heading: #20-21-19B | Page 5
passages.text:
Summary: In sum, the newly-proposed M.S. degree structure would include all the same courses as before.
We are not changing the curricular offering at all - we are simply proposing that the stackable certificate design be removed.
That’s ask #2 above.
And we are asking for it to be removed because we wish to offer a single grad certificate in healthcare management that offers flexibility and frequency for learners (instead of two separate certificates that are narrowly tailored).
That’s ask #1 above. 6.

The Master of Science in healthcare management is designed for students with a variety of educational backgrounds and professional experience who desire knowledge about business management concepts, skills, and tools to deliver high quality health care efficiently and effectively. The program is aimed at current and potential health professionals, clinicians or administrators, who aspire to upper management positions. The program also provides a pathway for recent bachelor’s degree students to pursue health management careers. The program includes two stackable certificates (12 credits each), and an additional elective course, and practicum course to complete the MS

An applicant with a bachelor’s degree can complete the program of study in two years. Program requirements: minimum of 30 credits, including seven required core courses and three electives. Required core courses include MHM 501 (Health Care in America), MHM 502 (Leadership in Health Administration), MHM 503 (Financial Management of Healthcare Organizations), MHM 505 (Healthcare Information Systems Management), MHM 506 (Healthcare Operations & process Improvement), MHM 507 (Healthcare Quality Science), and MHM 515 (Practicum for Healthcare Management Professionals). Electives include MHM 504, MHM 508, MHM 509, MHM 510, Courses are delivered totally online in 7-week modules in an asynchronous format that follows the URI Online accelerated calendar.
