Summary description of proposed program (not to exceed 2 pages).
Since its founding in the 1970’s, the mission of the Master of Public Administration (MPA) program at the University of Rhode Island is to instill public values, knowledge, and expertise to prepare our graduates to solve problems related to governance, nonprofit management, and policy with integrity, professionalism, and excellence to improve our communities and society.

passages.heading: #20-21-22C | Page 57
passages.text:
To train our students to meet the challenges of the 21st Century, the MPA program is embarking on a series of program revisions and a transition to a fully online program to meet the current and anticipated future needs from employers and various stakeholders across Rhode Island, the region, and nationally.
Although the MPA program will transition to a fully online, accelerated (7-week) format and replace its current blended, 14-week modality, the MPA program will retain many of its successful core features, including the requirement that MPA graduates earn 36 credits.
The accelerated online MPA program also incorporates new curricular innovations that will expand student recruitment and student flexibility.
Additionally, the programmatic and curricular revisions outlined in this proposal are critical for the program to become accredited by the Network of Schools of Public Policy, Affairs, and Administration (NASPAA) – a long-standing goal of the program – in the coming years.

passages.heading: #20-21-22C | Page 58
passages.text:
2 One of the structural revisions and innovations of the online MPA program is the creation of three certificate programs that offer students with both core training in public administration and policy but also specializations mirroring the Public Management and Policy Analysis concentrations in the current program.
The three 12-credit graduate certificates in the online MPA program are: the Professional Certificate in Public Administration and Policy, Public Management, and Policy Analysis.
Students in the online MPA program will need to complete the Professional Certificate in Public Administration and Policy graduate certificate, at least one of the other two MPA graduate certificates, earn at least 36 credits, and complete the capstone course to complete their MPA degree.
The core certificate that forms the basis for the MPA online program is the Professional Certificate in Public Administration and Policy.

passages.heading: #20-21-22C | Page 58
passages.text:
Students completing this certificate program will have an opportunity to learn about the historical and theoretical foundations of public administration and policy (PSC 501), ethical decision-making strategies (PSC 504), diversity and inclusion in the public sector (PSC 502), and an elective course focused on developing core skills or experience for a career in government, non-profit managements, or policy.
All students who want to earn their MPA degree will be required to complete this graduate certificate.
In addition to the certificate in Public Administration and Policy, students choosing to graduate with an MPA degree can choose to complete either one or two additional MPA-offered certificates that form the basis of an added credential or specialization that will make graduates competitive in the job market.
The first is a certificate in Public Management.
The coursework required for this certificate will help students become competitive applicants for positions requiring financial and budgetary expertise (PSC 506 & PSC 507), leadership skills, knowledge of administrative law and procedure (PSC 573), and the management of agency personnel (PSC 503).

passages.heading: #20-21-22C | Page 58
passages.text:
Currently, there is an acute need in many cities and towns for Finance Director positions, which can be a town or city’s highest paid municipal position.
Additionally, these are skills increasingly sought by nonprofit organizations.
By creating a certificate program, we hope to fulfill this workforce need in the state of Rhode Island and beyond by offering incumbent employees and new students the opportunity to develop a competency in Public Management.
Our aim is to have incumbent workers trained so that they will have opportunities for advancement, and their advancement will, in turn, create entry-level opportunities for others pursuing a certificate in Public Management or our students completing the MPA program.
The second of these optional certificates is the Policy Analysis certificate.
The coursework required for this certificate will help students develop research and analytical capabilities (PSC 583 & PSC 510), evaluate public programs (PSC 505), and navigate the public policy process (PSC 524 & PSC 510).
These skills will allow them to become effective at shaping public policy either within public agencies or as part of a broader policymaking process.

passages.heading: #20-21-22C | Page 58
passages.text:
Students pursuing this certificate will develop skills that will allow them to be policy advocates, policy researchers, and/or communication specialists.
The underlying philosophy of the URI MPA online program is that its modular design will guide students along pathways that will allow them to align their graduate study with their career ambitions.
MPA graduates will have earned no less than 36 credits while completing the program.
All students completing the full 36-credit program will:

passages.text: GRADUATE CURRICULAR REPORT #2020-2021-6 GRADUATE COUNCIL APRIL5,2021 FACULTY SENATE APRIL 15, 2021 SECTION 1I Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation by the Faculty Senate Notice of Change Ms in Nutrition - The Graduate Council approved a Notice of Change to (1) replace the "science" requirement with NFS 550 Epidemiology of Nutrition & Chronic Disease and (2) create three tracks to allow students to focus their program of study in preparation for various career pathways. The tracks include Nutrition Communications, Population Health Nutrition, and Nutrition Science. Each track wil! include a minimum of graduate-level 6 credits.

THE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND Revised 8/2016 Notice of Change form Notice of Change for: NFS Masters of Science Program Date: January 11, 2021 A.
PROGRAM INFORMATION 1.
Name of institution: University of Rhode Island 2.
Name of department, division, school or college: Department: Nutrition and Food Sciences (NFS) College: College of Health Sciences (CHS) 3.
Intended initiation date of program change.
Include anticipated date for granting first degrees or certificates, if appropriate.
Initiation date: Fall 2021 First degree date: Spring 2022 4.
Intended location of the program: NFS Department 5.
Summary description of proposed program (not to exceed 2 pages).
The NFS Department aims to make some subtle yet timely changes to its Masters of Science (MS) in Nutrition program, based on feedback from students and alumni, as well as changing needs in the workforce.
The first is to change the somewhat vague 3-credit ³science´ requirement to NFS ª Epidemiology of Nutrition & Chronic Disease (3 credits).
The second is to add tracks, so students can develop skills in related areas that will better prepare them for interprofessional careers.

passages.heading: #20-21-33B | Page 3
passages.text:
The 3-credit science requirement has been in place for decades.
Over the years, it has been inconsistent, and challenging to decide upon at an individual student level.
The recent addition of NFS 550 to the graduate curriculum has resulted in a course option that meets the needs of NFS graduate students.
It covers important concepts such as study design, appropriate data interpretation, and dissemination.
The course also includes hands-on learning with data analyses and understanding the nuances of big data.
With an emphasis on critical thinking, this course also exposes learners to a diverse array of scientific literature.
By including this course in the NFS graduate curriculum, it allows consistent and solid training of our MS students.

passages.heading: #20-21-33B | Page 4
passages.text:
As with many other fields, nutrition has become increasingly multidisciplinary.
Thus, students should gain multidisciplinary learning during their graduate training.
The introduction of tracks within the NFS MS program would allow students to add focus in an area relevant to their career goals.In consultation withthe URl Graduate School,the tracks have been planned toinclude a minimum of six credits from a related discipline.These credits would be included within the minimum of 3o credits towards MS graduation requirements.
After careful consideration of student and workforce needs, as well as thoughtful discussions within and beyond the NFS department, the three proposed tracks would be: 1.
Nutrition Communications: A minimum of six graduate-level credits would be included in courses covering scientific communication in various forms.These courses would befrom URI departments including COM,WRT,NRS,and BES.
The NFS Graduate Program Director(Melanson)has who can communicate evidence-based nutrition recommendations to the public in understandable, meaningful ways.These courses will prepare students to better translate nutrition science to non- nutritionists through multiple genres. 2.

passages.heading: #20-21-33B | Page 4
passages.text:
Population Health Nutrition:A minimum of six graduate-level credits would be included from courses related to nutrition and public health.This trackwill provide students with an understanding of public health, and community nutrition, including a deeper understanding of epidemiology,the impact of food programs, food policy, and other systemic drivers on diet,health, and sustainability in the US and globally.Students in this track will be able to apply this knowledge within community or public health settings. 3.
Nutrition Science:A minimum of six graduate-level credits would be included from NFS courses and related science courses.
These would allow students to gain deeper and broader learning in biological aspects of nutrition, and possibly other related courses at the discretion of the student and major professor.This track prepares students to workin various aspects of food and nutrition research.
It develops readiness for careers in industry, academia, or other health-related workplaces, and may precede doctoral studies. 6.
If applicable, please include the existing URI catalog language and proposed catalog changes indicated in Track Changes.

passages.heading: #20-21-33B | Page 4
passages.text:
Program requirements (30 credits): Thesis (6 credits), 2 credits of NFS 511 or NFS 512; NFS 550; NFS 505, 553, and 554; a minimum of 6 credits from one of the three MS program track options.
The tracks include: Nutrition Communications, Population Health Nutrition, and Nutrition Science. 7.

In accordance with Article VII, 1 and 2 of the Constitution, the amendment was subject to ratification "by an affirmative vote of two-thirds of the General Faculty, excluding abstentions." The results of the referendum are: Affirmative votes 310 Negative votes 48 Abstentions 3 Total votes 361 Total votes, excluding abstentions 358 Excluding abstentions, of the votes cast, 87% were affirmative: the amendment has been ratified. Presently, the School of Professional and Continuing Studies offers four tracks within the Bachelors of Interdisciplinary Studies (BIs) program: Applied Communication, Business Institutions, Health Services Administration, and Human Studies.

passages.heading: #20-21-34C | Page 3
passages.text:
Due to a trifecta of reasons including (a) accreditation issues, (b) courses no longer in existence, and (C) courses no Ionger available at the Feinstein Providence Campus, we propose to integrate the four tracks into a single General Studies program. (Ultimately, if approved, this would enable students at URI to pursue and earn two Bachelors of Interdisciplinary Studies degrees: Learner Designed (Three Minor Major) as well as this re-formulated General Studies degree.
The proposed General Studies program is specifically designed for and tailored to meet the needs of students who transfer or re-admit to the University with a substantial number of credits (i.e., 60 or more credits).
Currently, no program provides these students with an efficient path to graduation.
Our goal with the General Studies program is to maximize their credits and integrate their learning from previously-taken courses.
These students are opting for competitive institutions due to the length of time it would take them to graduate and the ultimate cost of their educational pursuits.
Currently, if they were to attend URl, they would need to study within a traditional program and earn those major-specific credits.

passages.heading: #20-21-34C | Page 3
passages.text:
Many of their previously-earned credits would not be viable ultimately resulting in a lengthy duration, higher educational costs, and earned credits being perceived as "worthless".
We believe this program change to establish a BIS General Studies would be remarkably beneficial to students who are pursuing other institutions with similar programs.
The General Studies program supports students who: Enter URI with substantial (e.g., 60+), yet scattered credits.
These students would be able to fulfill degree requirements in two or three semesters, as compared to four or more semesters in other programs. 02-25-2021 akt

passages.heading: #20-21-34C | Page 4
passages.text:
Are seeking a broad, yet individualized, interdisciplinary degree.
The General Studies program is structured to support students who have limited interest in currently available majors and want to craft a learning experience that resonates with their professional pursuits.
Have a primary focus on earning a degree quickly, regardless of major designation.
Many students who will pursue this degree are seeking a highly flexible program that accepts a high number of credits.
This degree option will meet the demands of students focused on speedy degree completion, evening course options, and the viability of scattered credits Want to complete their degree solely on the Feinstein Providence campus.
As adult-learners, they want to study with other adult-learners in face-to-face classrooms.
More so, This degree can be earned, in full, by taking courses at the Feinstein Providence Campus where we guarantee night-time and weekend courses which align with their work, family, and community obligations.
We believe this General Studies program would be remarkably beneficial to the University of Rhode Island and the College of Education and Professional Studies.

passages.heading: #20-21-34C | Page 4
passages.text:
For example: · We would attract and serve a specific student population who are otherwise enrolling With this additional student population, we could boost enrollments in courses our other School of Professional Studies s majors (e.g, Nonprofit Administration, Professional Leadership Studies) as well as courses offered at the Feinstein Providence Campus by other Colleges, Schools, and Departments.
This major can operate without any additional costs.
Students would be able to fulfill their major and general education requirements by taking courses currently offered.
No new courses will need to be developed and Kingston-based programs would not be obligated to reserve spaces for Interdisciplinary Studies students.

passages.heading: #20-21-34C | Page 4
passages.text: We would be able to maintain the flexibility of the former four Bl S tracks for our adult- learner student population, while ensuring that all classes offered at the Feinstein Providence Campus fulfill requirements towards graduation. By-Laws Section 5.
Election of Officers. 5.1 In February of each academic year, the Senate shall elect for the following academic year a Vice President/President-elect who shall serve one year as Vice President/President-elect and a second, consecutive year as President.
Senators who are elected to serve this two-year leadership position, as described, shall remain full members of the Faculty Senate as representatives of their colleges for the duration of their service even if the two-year position exceeds the three-year term limit as a Senator (Appendix C, section 2.1).
The outgoing President whose term has expired shall continue as an ex officio member of the Executive Committee for a period of one year after expiration of the term as President, and shall be considered ex officio member of the Faculty Senate during the same year.
At its the organizational meeting in May of the newly constituted Senate, the Senate shall elect at least one senator for a one-year term on the Executive Committee.
In order to ensure continuity, the remaining three members of the Executive Committee shall be elected to serve for two years.

passages.heading: #20-21-41 | Page 2
passages.text:
To stagger their terms, two of the 2-year term members shall be elected on even numbered years and the other 2-year term member on odd numbered years. #04-05-25, #10-11-29, #14-15-25, #20-21-5 6.1 Appointing Committee Members and Committee Chairs.
The Executive Committee, with the consent of the Senate, shall appoint for three-year terms faculty members and for two-year terms chairpersons of standing committees and subcommittees to replace those faculty members and chairpersons whose terms are about to expire.
These appointments shall be on a staggered basis so that one-third of the members of each committee are replaced each year and so that the chairpersons of half the committees are replaced each year.
Besides students (see By-laws 4.13), only elected Faculty Senate members shall be eligible to serve on standing Faculty Senate committees.
At Within two weeks of adjournment of the newly elected senators shall submit to the Senate President lists of at least three standing committees and/or subcommittees on which they are willing to serve.
These committees and/or subcommittees may be listed in an order of priority.

passages.heading: #20-21-41 | Page 2
passages.text: A newly elected senator who will have to miss the organizational meeting shall send May organizational Faculty Senate meeting of the newly constituted Senate, all

passages.text:
the list to the Faculty Senate office prior to the organizational meeting, or as soon as possible thereafter.
The Executive Committee shall use these lists to nominate, during the summer, for Faculty Senate approval (see below), new committee and subcommittee members for three-year terms to replace those committee members whose terms are about to expire.
When the term of a committee or subcommittee chair is about to expire, a new chair shall also be nominated for a two-year term (see By-laws 4.13).
Ideally, chairs shall be chosen from those committee and/or subcommittee members whose remaining Senate terms are two years; committee chairs may, however, also be chosen from newly elected senators.
While efforts will be made to nominate senators for a committee and/or subcommittee included in the list a senator submitted, there is no guarantee that this will be possible.
If the only committee slots available for a senator differ from the committees contained in the list the senator has submitted, the Faculty Senate Coordinator shall contact the senator to determine whether he or she is willing to serve on a committee on which a slot is not yet filled.

Intended location of the program Kingston The Than at ology minor (THN) has been very popular at the University since 1998. Over the past two decades there have been major advances in the field, including a shift to living with serious illness as well as end of life care. Current approaches, such as palliative care, expand the scope to address these advances and reflect contemporary practice for healthcare delivery. Thus, the curriculum needs to be updated to reflect these advances. The College of Nursing would like to suspend entry into the THN minor so we can evaluate currently approved classes and their ability to expand into a palliative care lens and develop 1-2 new classes for a minor in Palliative Care. This suspension will not impact students currently enrolled in the minor. 6. passages.text: FACULTY SENATE OFFICE On April 29, 2021, the Faculty Senate adopted the following resolution recommended by the Academic Calendar Subcommittee of the Curriculum and Standards Committee: WHEREAS, the University of Rhode Island Faculty Senate believes that racial justice and diversity are the business of the URI faculty, BE IT RESOLVED: That the Faculty Senate of the University of Rhode Island is in full support of June 19th or Juneteenth being designated an official state holiday in Rhode Island and a federal holiday in the United States.

passages.text: FACULTY SENATE OFFICE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND FACULTY SENATE April 29, 2021 Faculty Senate Curriculum and Standards Committee Report 2020-2021-10 At the April 22, 2021 meeting of the Curriculum and Standards Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate. SECTION I Informational Matters COLLEGE OF BUSINESS: FIN 220, Financial Management Create online version (3 crs.) Study of the basic principles of finance and the applications of these principles. Topics include time value of money, risk and return, valuation, capital budgeting and other corporate financial decisions. (Lec. 3/Online) Pre: ECN 201 or ECN 201H or EEC 105, and ACC (BUS) 201or 201H, and BAI (BUS) 210 or STA 308. FIN 420, Advanced Financial Management Create online version (3 crs.) Intensive research on selected current topics relating to the financial management of the firm. Extensive use of the case method. (Lec. 3/Online) Pre: BAI (BUS) 211, FIN (BUS) 220 or 220H or permission of instructor. Not for M.B.A. credit. FIN 428, International Finance Create online version (3 crs.) International financial background and history. Trade, national income accounting, and balance of payments. Currency markets, multinational firms, and currency risk management. International monetary system, exchange rate determination, parity conditions and exchange rate forecasting, country risk analysis, foreign exchange market, and currency derivatives. Corporate strategy, treasury function, cost of capital, foreign direct investment, international financial reports and capital budgeting for international, multinational, global and transnational companies. (Lec. 3/Online) Pre: FIN (BUS) 220 or 220H or permission of instructor. Not for M.B.A. credit. 1

1 FACULTY SENATE OFFICE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND FACULTY SENATE April 29, 2021 Joint Report of the Faculty Senate Curriculum and Standards Committee and Graduate Council Report 2020-2021-03 At the April 8, 2021 meetings of the Curriculum and Standards Committee and the April 19, 2021 meeting of the Graduate Council, the following matter was considered and is now presented to the Faculty Senate.
SECTION II Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation by the Faculty Senate PROGRAM CHANGE: College of Business: BS Supply Chain Management and Professional Master of Science in Supply Chain and Applied Analytics: The Curriculum and Standards Committee and the Graduate Council approved a proposal to create an Accelerated Bachelor’s to Master’s Degree in Supply Chain and Applied Analytics.
This ABM program is open to students pursuing a BS in Business Administration.
Students will be able to double-count up to 9 credits between the two degrees.

passages.heading: #20-21-43 | Page 2
passages.text:
As the Professional Master’s of Science in Supply Chain and Applied Analytics is in the accelerated online calendar and the BS in Business Administration is on the traditional calendar, all courses eligible for double-counting are at the 400-level and in the traditional calendar.
Any BA/BS and the MS Labor Relations and Human Resources: The Curriculum and Standards Committee and the Graduate Council approved a proposal to create an Accelerated Bachelor’s to Master’s Degree in Labor Relations and Human Resources.
The program is open to students in a bachelor’s degree program.
Majors that have many courses eligible for double counting include, but are not limited to Communication Studies, Human Development and Family Science, Management, Psychology, Sociology, and Statistics.
Students will be able to double-count up to 12 credits between the two degrees.

(Aquaculture and Fisheries Science, Animal Science and Technology, Sustainable Agriculture and Food Systems) and the Masters of Environmental Science and Management (MESM): The Curriculum and Standards Committee and the Graduate Council approved a proposal to create an Accelerated Bachelor’s to Master’s degree in Sustainable Food Systems. This ABM program would create an accelerated pathway to the Masters of Environmental Science and Management (MESM) non-thesis professional degree from the following majors: Aquaculture and Fisheries Science, Animal Science and Technology, and Sustainable Agriculture and Food Systems. Students will be able to double-count up to 12 credits between the two degrees.

Director: Associate Professor Dara Schniederjans Professional Master of Science in Supply Chain Management and Applied Analytics At URI, The Professional Master of Science in Supply Chain Management and Applied Analytics (STEM) is the first online program of its’ kind.
Each course provides training toward world class leadership in developing resilient and flexible supply chains in uncertain environments.
With a committed faculty of academics and practitioners, this program will equip you with the skills needed to succeed in this dynamic industry and provide students with lean six sigma certification.
You will learn to analyze and develop innovative solutions to global supply chain problems.

passages.heading: #20-21-43 | Page 8
passages.text:
The Professional Master of Science in Supply Chain Management and Applied Analytics provides courses in: building resiliency in supply chains, accounting and finance for supply chain mangers, global supply chain management, international transportation, supply chain analytics and data mining, warehousing and distribution systems, procurement and supplier management, customer analytics, supply chain network design and lean six sigma innovation protocols.
The curriculum also prepares students for purchasing certification.
Admission requirements: Applicants are required to submit a statement of purpose, two letters of recommendation, undergraduate transcript and TOEFL or IELTS scores taken within the last two years.

Joint Program: Master of Science in Labor Relations and Human Resources (URI) and Juris Doctorate (Roger Williams University School of Law) A cooperative dual degree program offered at URI and Roger Williams University School of Law permits dual enrollment leading to an M.S. in labor relations and human resources and a J.D.
The integrated program of the two degrees allows a student to complete both programs in four years instead of the five required if both degrees are pursued separately.
Admission requirements: Students must apply and be accepted into each program under the separate admission requirements currently in effect at each school.
Applicants must indicate the M.S./J.D. on the “Degree Sought” section of the URI application form.
Program requirements: At Roger Williams University, the J.D. program requires 90 credits, which can be completed on a full -time basis in three years.
The M.S. degree in labor relations and human resources at URI requires 36 credits, which can be completed on a full -time basis in two years.

passages.heading: #20-21-43 | Page 17

A student matriculated in the joint program will take some credits in one program that will help satisfy the overall credit requirements of the other degree program as well.
Students in the joint program must complete the following core required courses as part of their 30 -credit requirement at URI in addition to 6 credits taken at Roger Williams: LHR 500, 542, 551, and 580.
Students who specialize in human resources must also take LHR/MBA 573 and 578, while students specializing in labor relations must take LHR/PSC 521 and LHR 545.
Students must complete the required law school curriculum at Roger Williams.
For students matriculated in the joint program, Roger Williams will accept the following 15 URI credits to satisfy the requirements for the J.D. degree: LHR 500, 542, and 580; LHR/ECN 526; and LHR/PSC 521.

The students accepted into the ABM in the Sustainable Food Systems program will be able to double count credits towards both degrees up to one-third (12 credits) of the total credits required for the MESM degree (36 credits total).
Only AFS/AVS/SAF 400-level and 500 level courses allowable for graduate credit (Appendix A) are eligible to be double-counted in

passages.heading: #20-21-43 | Page 19
passages.text: the ABM in Sustainable Food Systems program. All credits counted towards the MESM portion of the ABM must be earned at URI. Students must complete all degree requirements for the ABM in Sustainable Food Systems within two years after enrollment and coding as ABM students. As outlined in the Graduate School Manual, one additional year may be allowed, with the permission of the

passages.text:

Failure to complete the ABM in the allotted time effectively ends the ABM, and the students will not be able to double count credits.
Admission requirements Students shall apply for the ABM in Sustainable Food Systems through the URI Graduate School admission system, and are eligible to apply once they have earned at least 75 credits.
Students will be enrolled in the ABM in Sustainable Food Systems within the Department of Fisheries, Animal & Veterinary Science (the department hosts three B.S. degrees: Aquaculture and Fisheries Science, Animal Science and Technology, Sustainable Agriculture and Food Systems) after they have met all Graduate School admission requirements and after completion of their B.S. degree requirements (typically at the end of the Spring semester of their senior year).
The program is open to undergraduates in the Sustainable Food Systems degree program within FAVS who have completed 75 credits with a minimum cumulative GPA of 3.0.
A letter of support for admission from the student’s undergraduate advisor or the student’s future major professor must be included as part of the application process.

6 Appendix B B.S.
Sustainable Food Systems Degree Program and Masters of Environmental Science and Management (M.E.S.M.) Degree Program B.S. in Aquaculture and Fisheries Science Aquaculture and Fisheries play an essential role in the sustainability and health of our planet by providing food and other services.
This major prepares students for professional, technical, academic, or research careers focused on the safe and sustainable production of products and services from aquatic (marine and freshwater) environments.
Core values include an emphasis on the intrinsic value of sustainable food production in the context of other ecosystem processes, heterogeneous scales of production (from small farms and fishers that sell directly to consumers to large scale producers), and preserving local cultures and biodiversity while understanding future demands.

passages.heading: #20-21-43 | Page 24
passages.text:
The major requires 10 credits in introductory professional courses including AFS 105G/106, EEC 105, and NRS 100; and a minimum of 24 credits in basic sciences including BIO 101/103, BIO 102/104, CHM 101/102 or CHM 103/105, one course in mathematics (MTH 103, MTH 111, MTH 131 or MTH 141), one course in the physical sciences, one course in ecology or ecosystem science, and one course in computational sciences or statistics.
In addition, the major requires a minimum of 20 credits in concentration courses at the 300 level or above, and 12 credits of the concentration courses must be selected from courses offered by AFS.
The additional credits of the concentration may be selected from courses offered in BIO, EEC, MAF, NRS, and OCG.
The major also requires a minimum of 3 credits in an internship or special project.
Finally, the program requires a minimum of 25 credits of supporting electives selected from an approved list of courses in AFS, APG, AVS, BIO, EEC, GEO, MAF, NRS, OCG and SAF.
A total of 120 credits is required for graduation.

passages.heading: #20-21-43 | Page 24
passages.text:
B.S. in Animal Science and Technology This major, offered by the Department of Fisheries, Animal and Veterinary Science, is designed for students interested in applied animal science careers.
Animal and veterinary sciences play a vital role in the management and care of livestock, companion animals as well as those animals maintained at zoos, aquariums and laboratory animal facilities.
Options are available to students interested in animal sciences or veterinary medicine.
The major requires the following core courses: AVS 101, 102, 110, 331, 333 (9 credits) plus option-specific courses as indicated below.
Including the core courses, there are 25-46 credits of basic science including BIO 101/103 and BIO 102/104, 21-31 credits of concentration courses and 11-30 credits of supporting courses required for this major.
A total of 120 credits are required for graduation.
Animal Science Option.
This option includes coursework in animal management, nutrition, physiology, behavior, and disease, and provides broad flexibility for students in their choice of animal science courses.

passages.heading: #20-21-43 | Page 24
passages.text: Students have the option to focus their coursework specifically on domestic livestock, exotic animals or animal technology, or be more broadly focused.

passages.heading: #20-21-43 | Page 25
passages.text: 7 Research techniques and procedures for animal care are emphasized along with a strong background in the sciences. Students in this option pursue careers as researchers, veterinary technicians, food animal producers, laboratory animal technicians or high school agricultural education teachers. Additionally, there are career opportunities at zoos or aquariums (educator, researcher and exotic animal manager), within the federal, state and local government as well as with many animal-related businesses.

passages.heading: #20-21-43 | Page 26
passages.text:
8 In addition to the core courses specified of the major, the following courses are required: AVS 212, 332, 343, and 6 additional credits in 400-level courses in AVS; COM 100, CHM 101/102 or 103/105; MTH course which fulfills A1, B3 general education outcomes, WRT 104 or 106, and an additional 300-level or higher WRT course.
The remaining credit requirements will be selected from the concentration courses (9 credits) and supporting electives (26 credits) approved for this option.
Pre-Veterinary Option.
This option requires a demonstrated capability in the basic sciences and prepares students for admission to veterinary schools offering a Doctorate of Veterinary Medicine (DVM) degree.
Students in this option will also be well prepared to pursue graduate programs in animal physiology, nutrition and health.
Because admission requirements among schools are not totally uniform and are subject to change, students should determine specific requirements of the schools in which they are interested.

passages.heading: #20-21-43 | Page 26
passages.text:
In addition to the core courses specified for the major, the following courses are required: AVS 304, 332, 412, 472; BIO 341, BIO/CMB 352; COM 100, CMB 211, 311; BUS or ECN (3 credits); CHM 101/102, 112/114, 227, 228/226; PHY 111/185, 112/186; MTH 131, STA 308, WRT 104 or 106, and WRT 332 or 334.
The remaining credits will be selected from the concentration courses (6 credits) and supporting electives (6 credits) approved for this option.
B.S. in Sustainable Agriculture and Food Systems Students completing this interdisciplinary program will graduate with the skills and knowledge needed to contribute to the sustainable development, production, harvesting, management, and utilization of terrestrial and aquatic microorganisms, plants and animals by society worldwide.
The major will allow participants to explore the food chain, from farm to plate to waste and back, emphasizing sustainability, impacts on human health, and resilience from economic, environmental, and societal viewpoints.

passages.heading: #20-21-43 | Page 26
passages.text:
Core values of this interdisciplinary program that distinguish it from more traditional agriculture programs include an emphasis on the intrinsic value of heterogeneous scales of production (from small farms that sell directly to consumers to large scale producers), preserving local food cultures and biodiversity while understanding the way other cultures produce and use food (from local to global), using an ecosystem-based approach to agriculture (also integrating the contributions of aquaculture and fisheries), and the greening of urban landscapes.
By the time of degree completion students will be uniquely poised to enter the workforce in the growing field of sustainable food systems or pursue management (through governmental and non- governmental agencies) and graduate education/research opportunities addressing the challenges of securing access to safe and affordable food for a growing population.

passages.heading: #20-21-43 | Page 26
passages.text:
SAFS students will pursue a curriculum that combines depth in a specialization area chosen from three options within the program (Sustainable Agriculture, Nutrition and Food, and Food and Society) with breadth across the natural and social sciences, engineering, and the arts and humanities.
The program entails a total of 120 credits including: A common introductory core sequence emphasizing the interdisciplinary and systems- approach to sustainability.
As part of this core sequence, students are required to take a set of interdisciplinary general education courses including AFS/AVS/PLS 132G, COM/SUS 108G,

passages.heading: #20-21-43 | Page 27
passages.text: 9 EEC 105, HSS/PSY 130G, NFS 210 and the basic science courses BIO 101/103, BIO 102/104, and CHM 101/102 or CHM 103/105. Students are also required to take APG/SOC/GWS 308. An intermediate-level framework of courses providing depth in the area of specialization (options) while reinforcing the interdisciplinary, systems-thinking focus of the major. The options are:

passages.heading: #20-21-43 | Page 28
passages.text:
10 Sustainable Agriculture Option: Students in this option will specialize in the harvesting and production of either terrestrial or aquatic plants and animals for human uses.
They will understand the integrated components of fisheries and agriculture/aquaculture systems (soils, microbes, plants, animals), and the impacts of agriculture and food harvesting on the environment.
Students are required to take two introductory food production courses (to choose from AFS 105G/106, AVS 101/102, PLS 150, PLS 255), two agriculture management courses (to choose from AFS 201, AFS 202, AFS 215, AFS 321/322, AVS 304, PLS 311, PLS 312, PLS 321, PLS 324, and PLS 325), and other relevant courses in AFS, AVS, or PLS), two environment-related courses (to choose from AVS/PLS 275, CHE 212, ENT 411, and NRS 212).
They are also required to take two courses from each of the two other options (Nutrition and Food, Food and Society).
Nutrition and Food Option: Students in this option will learn the basic principles of food science and nutrition.
Students are required to take NFS 212G, NFS/CMB 245, 336, 337, 375, 376 and two courses from each of the two other options (Sustainable Agriculture, Food and Society).

passages.heading: #20-21-43 | Page 28
passages.text:
Food and Society Option: Students in this option will specialize in the social, political, economic, and marketing aspects of food production.
Students are required to take two courses on the cultural aspects of food (to choose from APG 203, APG/SOC 329, APG/SOC 415 and other relevant courses in APG, GWS, SOC), two courses on policy (to choose from MAF 100, APG/MAF 413, MAF 330, and other relevant courses in APG, MAF), two courses on economics (to choose from EEC 205, 310, 325, 355, 440), and two courses from each of the two other options (Sustainable Agriculture, Nutrition and Food).
A robust capstone experience in which students will master the ability to address the complex challenges in the area of sustainable agriculture and food systems through experiential learning in interdisciplinary teams.
Students are required to take a total of 13 credits, including 4 credits of internship or special project and an additional 9 credits in courses to choose from NRS 300, PLS 320, PLS 385, AVS/NFS 404, or SAF 400G.

passages.heading: #20-21-43 | Page 28
passages.text:
Masters of Environmental Science and Management The Masters of Environmental Science and Management (M.E.S.M.) is an interdisciplinary, interdepartmental, professional degree program designed for students who seek professional environmental positions in areas other than research.
The M.E.S.M. degree program serves graduate students from six departments within URI’s College of Environment and Life Sciences (CELS): Environmental and Natural Resource Economics; Fisheries, Animal and Veterinary Science; Geosciences; Marine Affairs; Natural Resources Science; and Plant Sciences.
It is administered by a steering committee selected from the graduate faculty.
The M.E.S.M. degree program has the following Specializations: Conservation biology; earth and hydrologic science; environmental communication; environmental planning and design; environmental policy and management; remote sensing and spatial analysis; sustainable systems; and wetland, watershed, and ecosystem science.
A minimum of 36 credits of course work consisting of 21-25 credits of core courses, including

passages.heading: #20-21-43 | Page 29
passages.text: 11 at least nine credits in natural sciences, at least six credits in social sciences, and at least three credits in numerical methods; 6-10 credits of electives. A culminating experience for three credits which consists of one of the following: an internship (EVS 597) with an environmental agency, non-governmental agency, or private firm; an independent research project (EVS 598) that results in a substantial, high-quality, written report; or successful completion of EVS 505 (Environmental Leadership); and at least two credits of graduate seminar (typically EVS 501, 502), including a terminal oral presentation.

passages.text: Appendix F: Transfer Policies POLICY FOR ARTICULATION AND TRANSFER BETWEEN PUBLIC INSTITUTIONS OF HIGHER EDUCATION IN RHODE ISLAND COUNCIL ON POSTSECONDARY EDUCATION IH1. Guiding Principles: B. Each college and university has the responsibility and the authority to determine the requirements and course offering of its programs in accordance with its institutional role, internal shared governance practices, and scope and mission as established by Rhode Island statutes and the policies of the Council on Postsecondary Education. D. Completion Degrees 1. To meet the goal of increased baccalaureate attainment and support of a prepared workforce as stipulated in the Council on Postsecondary Education's strategic plan, the public baccalaureate institutions are encouraged to work with the community college to develop completion degrees for students graduating with an Associate in Applied Science, Associate in Technical Studies and other applied or technical degrees; these applied bachelor's degrees may include a Bachelor of Applied Technology, Bachelor of Technical Studies or other bachelor's degrees. These degrees will build upon the technical skills earned in the associate degree, from industry-certified credentials, technical courses taken in career-technical secondary education, or through prior learning assessment. XII: General Education D. The Community College, as it advances its own general education program and courses, will establish general education courses that both meet the needs of their students and satisfy the general education learning outcomes at both Rhode Island College and the University of Rhode Island. This effort will further enhance the transfer ability of

passages.heading: #20-21-36 | Page 17
passages.text: general education credits across the three institutions. The revised Community College of Rhode Island general education program will be presented to the Council on Postsecondary Education by no later than June 3o, 2018 and implemented no later than September 1, 2019. XIV. Resolution of Equivalency Disputes From time to time there may be inter institutional disagreements among the faculty of subject matter disciplines. These disagreements will normally be resolved at the chairperson level. Conflicts not - resolved by the chairperson will be referred to the appropriate deans for review and determination; conflicts not resolved at this level will be referred to the Academic Vice presidents/Provosts. Disputes that are not resolved at the institutional-level will be referred to the Inter institutional Articulation/Transfer Committee. The committee will resolve the dispute or forward a recommendation to the Commissioner of Postsecondary Education. The Commissioner of Postsecondary Education may accept the recommendation or seek an alternate resolution. XVI. Student Rights and Responsibility F. If a student is not satisfied with the college or university transfer appeals decision, the student may submit a request to the senior. academic officer at the Office of the Postsecondary Commissioner for a systems-level appeal to the Inter institutional Articulation Transfer Committee. 1. The student shall submit a letter of appeal and include the decision from the college/university- level, transcripts and other documentation. 2. The senior academic officer shall convene the Inter institutional Articulation Transfer Committee.

passages.heading: #20-21-36 | Page 18
passages.text: If a member of the Inter institutional Articulation Transfer Committee is directly involved in the dispute, the president of that institution shall appoint an interim member of the committee in consultation with the Commissioner of Postsecondary Education. XVII. Reporting and Assessing Transfer Outcomes A. The Office of the Postsecondary Commissioner will be responsible for establishing monitoring and reporting systems based on uniform data collection and reporting methods to facilitate the assessment of the effectiveness of transfer policies and ensure compliance with statewide articulation and transfer policies. XVIl II. Inter institutional Articulation Transfer Committee A. Composition of the Committee To assure compliance with and the continuing viability of the Articulation/Transfer Policy, a permanent inter institutional committee on articulation/transfer was established. This Articulation/Transfer Committee is comprised of eleven members: three from each of the three public institutions of higher education plus a chairperson and a staff person from the Rhode Island Office of the Postsecondary Commissioner (RIOPC). The institutional representatives are appointed by the president of the respective institutions and are to include the institutional articulation/transfer officer. The chairperson is appointed by the Commissioner of Postsecondary Education. Committee appointments shall be reviewed every.three years.

1 Faculty Senate Meeting, September 30, 2021 Recommendation from the Faculty Senate Executive Committee Changes to University Manual Sections 8.39.11 and 8.51.13 Bereavement Policy The University of Rhode Island at present does not have a bereavement policy for our community.
Each semester, faculty receive student requests for excused absences, similar to those for illness or University Sanctioned events, due to the death of a loved one.
Students are often unsure of how to proceed with requests for make-up work or absences.
FSEC believes that students and faculty would benefit from a clearly articulated policy for bereavement leave as a result of traumatic loss.
Further that the Dean of Students Office can and should provide support of students and faculty in determining a recommended period of absence, notifying faculty on behalf of students of a traumatic loss, and verifying such events.
The policy will be articulated in the University Manual and the policy procedure and explanation will be included in the Student Handbook.
FSEC brings this proposed policy to the Senate for approval.
Motion: That URI establishes a bereavement policy for students.

passages.heading: #21-22-1 | Page 2
passages.text:
That “traumatic loss” and its definition be included along with illness and university sanctioned events in the University Manual 8.39.11 and 8.51.13.
Further that a recommended maximum bereavement leave duration be articulated and the support role of the Dean of Students Office be identified in the University Manual 8.51.13.
Motion: That the policy procedure and explanation be included in the Student Handbook.
Re: Proposed Student Bereavement Policy and Procedure Proposed Policy language Course attendance policies are to be determined by the faculty member(s) responsible for teaching a course.
A student’s absence from class may be excused in the event of a traumatic loss (defined as death of a family member or other significant relationship) as reviewed and recommended by the Dean of Students Office (and/or the Degree Granting Academic College) for up to two consecutive weeks, for courses that run eight weeks or longer.
Absences from courses of shorter duration will be determined on a case-by-case basis with the instructor and Dean of Students Office staff.
Students have the right to request professor notification of these

passages.heading: #21-22-1 | Page 3
passages.text:
2 absences by completing the notification request form.
Dean of Students Office staff will then notify the student’s instructors of the absences once the request has been reviewed and approved.
Consideration for academic assistance and the opportunity to complete the course are at the discretion of your instructor(s) and dependent on the nature of the course.
Disagreements over the seriousness of an illness, accident, personal tragedy, traumatic loss, or other serious matter may need to be mediated by the concerned instructor’s department chair, dean, or eventually the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs.
Either students or their instructors may seek such mediation.
If an agreement cannot be reached, the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs shall decide the matter and his/her decision shall be final.
The student is responsible for fulfilling the course requirements and for working with course instructors on an appropriate timeline to submit any missed assignments/requirements.

passages.heading: #21-22-1 | Page 3
passages.text:
The Office of Student Support and Advocacy Services (Dean of Students Office) is the designated office to help support the student and review all available options, in collaboration with the Degree Granting Academic Colleges, if the traumatic loss has an impact on the student’s academic progress for the term.
Faculty requesting confirmation of the traumatic loss resulting in the requested bereavement leave should consult with the Dean of Students Office.
REQUEST FORM LANGUAGE (Maxient database maintained by the Dean of Students Office) Bereavement Notification Request Process: If a student would like to exercise their right to have a bereavement notification sent out to their faculty by the Office of Student Support and Advocacy Services (Dean of Students Office), they are asked to provide an obituary, memorial service pamphlet, death certificate, or other documentation that identifies the student’s relation to the deceased.

passages.heading: #21-22-1 | Page 3
passages.text:
Such documentation whenever possible will include the date of the traumatic loss, date of funeral/memorial service (in case of deaths), and the city and state the services were held. (NOTE: Documents can be attached to this form.) If a student is having difficulty obtaining documentation that meets these criteria, they should reach out to Student Support and Advocacy Services directly at jacqui_springer@uri.edu.
Once documentation is provided, Student Support and Advocacy Services will send out an email notification on the student’s behalf to faculty, requesting that the student be excused during the fall and spring semesters for up to two weeks.
For classes of shorter duration, this will be discussed directly with the instructor.

passages.heading: #21-22-1 | Page 4
passages.text:
3 Consideration for academic assistance and the opportunity to complete the course through alternate arrangements are at the discretion of the instructor(s) and dependent on the nature of the course.
If you have specific questions regarding absence notification, please contact Student Support and Advocacy Services in the Dean of Students Office by emailing jacqui_springer@uri.edu or calling 401.874.2098 during regular business hours (Monday through Friday, 8:30am to 4:30pm).
If you have an emergency or a matter requiring immediate attention, please contact Campus Police at 401-874-2121.
University Manual Language 8.39.10 Attendance Requirements.
Course attendance policies are to be determined by the faculty member(s) responsible for teaching a course.
Faculty should clearly inform students of these policies at the beginning of the semester.

passages.heading: #21-22-1 | Page 4
passages.text:
Notice that a course will require examinations at times other than regularly scheduled class times and will be utilizing “General Assignment Classroom” shall be forwarded to Enrollment Services for room scheduling (see 8.51.15). 8.39.11 Any deviation from announced attendance policy shall normally be a matter between the instructor(s) and the student(s).
A student who will be or has been unable to fulfill an obligation should discuss with the instructor(s) the possibility of and the conditions for making up the missed work.

passages.heading: #21-22-1 | Page 4
passages.text:
Instructors shall make reasonable efforts to allow students to compensate for work missed due to serious verifiable reasons such as illness, participation in University sanctioned events, traumatic loss, etc. (see 8.51.11 – 8.51.14). 8.51.13 When serious illness, accident, personal tragedy, traumatic loss (death of family member or other significant human relationship), or other serious matters prevent students from attending classes, taking examinations, or meeting deadlines, the instructor(s) concerned shall offer the student one of the following options: a. the same quiz, test, or examination to be administered either before or after the normally scheduled time; b. a comparable alternative quiz, test, or examination to be administered either before or after the scheduled time; c. if neither option a. nor b. is possible, faculty shall develop a fair and equitable alternative after discussion with the student.
In the event of a traumatic loss, absences may be excused for up to two consecutive weeks.
The Dean of Students Office may, at the student’s request, notify instructor(s) of bereavement absences.

If an agreement cannot be reached, the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs shall decide the matter and his/her decision shall be final. #16-17-30 8.51.14 Requests for make-up of examinations or other work, for reasons other than those in 8.51.11 and/or 8.51.13, must be made within 7 calendar days of the absence. SECTION II Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation by the Faculty Senate NEW PROGRAMS: Interdisciplinary Program: Colleges: Pharmacy, Health Sciences, Environment & Life Sciences: Creation of Undergraduate Minor in Interdisciplinary Neuroscience: The Interdisciplinary Neuroscience Program is requesting that undergraduate students be able to declare a minor on Interdisciplinary Neuroscience by completing a minimum of 18 credits from the major. Students must complete an application for the minor that is approved and signed by the INP coordinator and the INP Director. Application for the INP minor must be filed in the INP Director's office no later than the beginning of the student's final semester or term but may be submitted as early as the first semester of the junior year. Filing for a minor earlier than the junior year is subject to approval by the student's degree-granting college. 1

Summary description of proposed program (not to exceed 2 pages) The Interdisciplinary Neuroscience Program is requesting that undergraduate students be able to declare a minor on Interdisciplinary Neuroscience by completing a minimum of 18 credits from the major.
Students must complete an application for the minor that is approved and signed by the INP coordinator and the INP Director.
Application for the INP minor must be filed in the INP Director’s office no later than the beginning of the student’s final semester or term but may be submitted as early as the first semester of the junior year.
Filing for a minor earlier than the junior year is subject to approval by the student’s degree-granting college.
A minimum grade point average of 2.00 must be earned in the minor courses, and a minimum of 12 of the 18 credits must be at the 200 level or above.
At least eight of the credits required for the minor must be earned at the University of Rhode Island.
Courses used to fulfill general education requirements may also be used for the minor.

passages.heading: #21-22-4B | Page 4
passages.text:
Up to two courses required in a major program may be used to apply to both the major and minor fields of study (i.e., students may not obtain a minor if their major is interdisciplinary neuroscience).
Students may not take courses required for the minor on a pass-fail basis.
The requirements for the minor must be completed prior to graduation.
Successful completion of the Interdisciplinary Neuroscience Minor will be reflected on the student’s official transcript upon graduation.
Graduates who have earned an undergraduate degree with a minor from URI and who are then readmitted to the university to pursue an alternate major or degree, may apply for that purpose all credits earned in pursuit of the previous minor field of study.
The specific course requirements for the Interdisciplinary Neuroscience Minor include the following: • NEU 101: Foundations of Neuroscience 3 credits • NEU 110: Neuroscience Seminar 1 credit • NEU 210: Neuroethics and Diversity 3 credits • NEU 230: Neuroscience Professional Development 1 credit • NEU 262: Neuroscience Research Methods 4 credits • NEU 301: Cellular & Molecular Neuroscience 3 credits • NEU 310: Developmental OR NEU 320: Clinical 3 credits

There are no external agreements for needed to create the minor. B. RATIONALE: There should be a demonstrable need for the program. B1. Why is the new program being developed? This proposal is for the creation of a new minor in an existing program. The new minor will allow students interested in neuroscience to further their education in this area. The study of neuroscience is complementary to a number of majors at URI including pharmacy, psychology, communicative disorders, biology, chemistry, nursing, health studies, biomedical engineering, and kinesiology to name a few. B2. What is the economic need and workforce data related to the program? a. Provide information on jobs available as a result of successfully completing the certificate or degree: job titles, job outlook/growth, and salaries. The study of neuroscience has relevance in multiple domains. The creation of an undergraduate minor will add options to undergraduate education that will likely attract undergraduates to URI. Studies by Ramos et al., (2011 and 2016) identified the unprecedented growth of undergraduate neuroscience in the US and the number of institutions offering neuroscience majors has risen from <10 in 1986 to 157 in 2014. Their data extend emerging literature demonstrating growth in undergraduate neuroscience education that prepares students for graduate

The undergraduate minor in Interdisciplinary Neuroscience is consistent with the goals of the University’s academic strategic plan.

Goal 1: Enhance student success ● The neuroscience undergraduate curriculum incorporates interactive learning providing students the opportunity to actively engage in learning techniques. ● The interdisciplinary nature of the program provides the opportunity for students to expand their view of neuroscience across a broad representation of skills and professions available to students who study neuroscience.
Goal 2: Expand research, scholarship, and creative work ● Neuroscience research is at the cutting edge of some of the most significant innovative research that addresses global challenges to improve health and understand degenerative neurological conditions. ● Neuroscience research is not discipline-specific which will encourage students to foster collaborations with scientists in related fields.
URI needs a neuroscience undergraduate minor to be competitive with other universities.

Updated September 2019 ACADEMIC PROGRAM ASSESSMENT PLAN All new programs and certificates must have clearly articulated program goals (Section I) and student learning outcome statements linked to curriculum and course experiences/requirements (Section II).
The Curriculum Map guides programs in to present the extent to which their student learning outcomes are aligned with courses and other program requirements intended to provide students with opportunities to develop and master the learning outcomes by graduation.
Each program (not certificates) will also create an Assessment Timeline (Section III) indicating when and how learning outcomes assessment will take place.
All undergraduate and graduate programs are encouraged to create a six-year (3 rounds) Assessment Plan to guide assessment reporting.
If you have questions or need assistance, please contact the Office of Student Learning, Outcome Assessment, and Accreditation (SLOAA) at assess@uri.edu.

passages.text: Date: May 4, 2021 Re: Interdisciplinary Neuroscience Program Minor Proposal To: Curricular Affairs Committee I am submitting the materials to apply for approval of an undergraduate minor in the Interdisciplinary Neuroscience Program (INP). The INP began accepting undergraduate students in Fall of 2020 and there has been expressed student interest in the creation of a minor in this program. The following forms are included with this proposal: • A Learning Outcomes Assessment Plan approved by the LOOC • A Budget Form • A Budget Approval letter from Linda Barrett • A Proposal Form • A letter of support signed by the Deans Oversight Committee that is responsible for the administration of the program and its resources The proposal of a new minor does not require JCAP review. The new minor will include courses already being offered for the INP undergraduate major. No new courses are being proposed so there is no library impact statement included with these documents. Please let me know if you require any additional information or documentation to evaluate our proposal. I would be happy to attend the CAC meeting where you review our proposal if that would be helpful. Sincerely, Lisa L. passages.text: Change to Adult Education Master’s program A Notice of Change form was submitted in fall of 2021 and approved in January of 2021 to move the program to the online accelerated calendar (URIOnline). The intended date of change was September of 2021. During the process of transition, we determined that implementing the changes would be problematic. In particular, only students who are registered in URIOnline programs can take courses in URIOnline courses. The issues are as follows: • Currently, we have a contract with the Navy and students in the ETMS specialization are required to take 2 courses outside of the School of Education (MBA courses, in particular) to meet the needs of their program. We tried to find substitutions, but these were not acceptable to the Navy. • Students in the joint PhD in Education Program at URI/RIC who choose the Adult Education specialization are required to take some of their specialization courses in the Adult Education Master’s program. • Students in the TESOL, MBA, and other programs take our courses as electives in the summer. • Students in other education specializations take two courses housed in AE (EDC 529 and EDC 575). In order to accommodate these students, the AE program would have to run additional sections of many of these courses which we ultimately deemed to be prohibitive to our human and financial resources.

passages.text: 2020-2021 Online Catalog URI 2020-2021 Online Catalog Film/Media Part of the Harrington School of Communication and Media (uri.edu/harrington), the Film/Media Program offers a Bachelor of Arts (B.A.) degree and a minor. Faculty: Rebecca Romanow, Director. Professors Healey-Jamiel, Mandel, Moore, Sama, Swift, Trimm, and Walton; Associate Professors Chadha, Echevarría, Kealhofer-Kemp, Reyes, and Wyatt; Assistant Professor Jaacks; Adjunct Assistant Professors Bergstrom, and Zorabedian; Teaching Professors Brown and Romanow; Lecturer Corsano. The Major. Film/Media is an interdisciplinary program offering hands-on experience in documentary, experimental, narrative, and new media production, balanced with an emphasis on international cinemas, film/media history, criticism, and theory. Our curriculum reflects the dynamic and diverse nature of this field, approached from a perspective of film history and media theory. Students learn to work with the evolving and overlapping technologies involved in the production of moving images (including film, digital video, 3D animation, game design, and new media), with an understanding of the broadening and globalization of their cultural and aesthetic contexts. A wide range of courses is available to the film/media student—courses that examine the historical, theoretical, and global approaches to the analysis and creation of moving images. The film/media program prepares students for careers in such areas as independent

passages.heading: #21-22-9B | Page 10
passages.text:
filmmaking; animation and media design; film and television industries; advertising, marketing, and public relations; and media criticism.
Graduates of this program are also prepared to continue with graduate studies, either in film and media production for an M.F.A., or in a master’s or doctoral program in film and media studies.
Students majoring in film/media must complete a minimum of 31 credits (maximum 46) in approved courses toward the major.
FLM 101 or FLM 101H is a required prerequisite.
All students must complete the core courses: FLM 110, FLM 203 (or ENG 302), FLM 204 (or FLM 205 or 206), including the senior-level seminar FLM 495; a minimum of 6 credits from the production and technique category and 6 credits from the critical studies category; a minimum of 3 elective credits in courses that count toward the film major (following).
This wide range of choices in film/media courses permits students to design a major that will meet both personal and professional goals.
Students must have a plan of study approved by an academic advisor in the film media program before beginning their coursework in the major.

passages.heading: #21-22-9B | Page 10

Courses in general education may count toward the minor. All courses must be taken for a grade except for the internship (Field Experience). It is well-suited for students whose career goals call for training in more than one discipline or who want a breadth of knowledge in several fields rather than a depth of knowledge in a single discipline.
With this degree, one can be even more directly educated with regard to several, specific, job-relevant studies.
This interdisciplinary “three-minor’ major also may work well for students who do not want to limit their career options by majoring in just one area of study.
For the purposes of this proposal, the word “minor" is used to refer to coursework associated with recognized areas of study (as minors) at the University of Rhode Island.
Specifically, students will complete an application that proposes one thematic or topical concentration made up of three (3) recognized minor areas of study that will not be restricted

Students seeking this program must declare it as their major in the same manner, and at the same time,that other URI students declare a major.
It is important to note that, through the completion of this program, students will not receive minors in the three areas of study, rather the integrated coursework will be used to fulfill the requirements of the interdisciplinary major.
Upon completion of the program, the student's approved interdisciplinary concentration will be noted on the university transcript.
Moreover, the Learner Designed major provides an opportunity to develop and pursue a course of study centered on a unifying theme, problem, or issue.

The capstone experience (BIS 399) provides a structure that enables the student to integrate knowledge and skills from coursework and related experiences with a research project.
The project must be designed so that it allows the student to demonstrate the integration of subject matter, theory, and practice.
Students are required to meet with the Director of School of Professional & Continuing Studies (or designee) to plan a project proposal.
The Learner Designed major will provide students with a well-rounded education in multiple academic disciplines, allowing them to gain skills employers will find desirable, including critical thinking, communication and creative problem-solving.
Employers appreciate applicants with diverse backgrounds and the ability to integrate multiple viewpoints.

The main goal of the Learner Designed major is to foster critical interdisciplinary thinking applicable to a variety of future career and academic opportunities.
This major can cover many academic areas, giving students the opportunity to construct an interdisciplinary “major equivalent" that is not restricted to conventional departmental or unit boundaries.
The program will also provide students with a solid academic foundation for multiple careers and graduate programs.
Students can customize their major with a future career or educational opportunity in mind.
The BIS degree in the Learner Designed major enables students to learn from multiple disciplines that will enhance a student's educational and career goals.

The Learner Designed major aims to provide students with the ability to explore their individual interests and develop the necessary skills to succeed and thrive in the professional workforce.

Regionally, Boston University offers a Bachelor of Liberal Studies/Science in Interdisciplinary Studies, however students must propose an interdisciplinary study topic that includes exposure to the humanities, social sciences, and natural sciences, including mathematics and computer science. Also, a BA in Liberal Arts is offered at Southern Connecticut State University, the University of New Haven, St. Joseph College, the University of Massachusetts-Dartmouth, and Bentley University. In addition, several regional institutions including Harvard, Wesleyan, Goddard, Dartmouth, and SUNY campuses offer an M.A. in Liberal Studies. D5. The Learner Designed major would be attractive to a diverse student population, including: ·Students who want a breadth of knowledge in several fields rather than a depth Of knowledge in a single discipline.
Transfer students with a background in Liberal Arts or General Studies.
Undecided students with interests beyond a specific major.
Students who left college after earning some credits and wish to complete a degree.
In addition, the Learner Designed major is ideal for students enrolled in the School of Professional and Continuing Studies - adult learners, many with years of professional experiences and interests.

This innovative program provides students an opportunity to tailor-craft an interdisciplinary program-of-study that capitalizes on these experiences and interests while propelling them to directly apply their learning to their work and community contexts.
Rather than limit these adult learners with a pre-structured one-pronged curricula, we empower these students to think big, broad, and creatively as they tether together three areas of study to dynamically craft a major that has relevance to the lives they lead.

THE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND ALAN SHAWN FEINSTEIN COLLEGE OF EDUCATION AND PROFESSIONAL STUDIES THINKBIG WEDO" SCHOOL OF PROFESSIONAL AND CONTINUING STUDIES Shepard Building,80Washington Street,Providence,RI2903SA 3/16/21 Dear Chris Kincaid and the Curriculum and Standards Committee, I write as a follow-up to our conversation (3/15/21) regarding the Interdisciplinary Studies Learner Designed (Three- Minor) Major proposal submitted by the School of Professional Studies.
Offered below are reflections and rationale for this innovative program.Thank youfor your review.
Sincerely, Jonathan Kroll Program Rationale: The Schoolof Professional Studies is motivated to provide relevant and resonant programs for S.T.A.R. (Service members, Transfer, Adult, and Returning) students.
The vast majority of these students are working full time while studying, caring for family, and serving their communities.
The Learner Designed Major (also referred to as the Three Minor Major)was crafted so that enrolled students can curate a program-of-study that will enable them to acquire knowledge and advance their professional pursuits.

passages.heading: #20-21-34D | Page 34
passages.text:
Rather than force these students into traditional academic programs, this major degree combines three minors of the students own choosing,integrates their learning through specific interdisciplinary (BIS) courses, and fulfills General Education and elective credits to reinforce URI's commitment to a comprehensive learning experience.
Q1)What are thegoals and the purposes of students selecting the Three Minor Major?
S.T.A.R. students are unique in that their academic pursuits are directly connected to their professional status and objectives.
They are working full-time.
Many have been for years,if not decades.
The Three Minor Major is structured to maximize the connections between their professional stations and academic coursework.Rather than study in a traditional major program, the learner designed program enables students to immerse themselves in three academic areas-of-attention.For example,if one of our students is a Coordinator of a nonprofit community agency that focuses on food injustice for an elderly population, she might combine the Gerontology, Hunger Studies, and Leadership Studies minors to curate a highly specialized and resonant Major.

passages.heading: #20-21-34D | Page 34
passages.text:
No single major degree would be as academically supportive to her current and future professional endeavors as this combination.
Similarly, if a student was the Chef/Owner of a sports bar, he might combine minors in Finance, Marketing, and Sports Mediaand Communication to center his studies on what matters most to him.No singular major can provide an academic course of study that is as preparatory for his particular academic needs and interests than the strategic combination of three minor degrees.
The University of Rhode Island is an equal opportunity employer commited to community equity and diversity and to the principles of a ff rm at ive action.

passages.heading: #20-21-34D | Page 35
passages.text:
Q2) Do the minors need to be related or can a student use any 3 minors that the university offers?
Students enrolled in the Three Minor Major can include any three minors of their choosing.
This is intended to provide maximum flexibility while aiso ensuring the design of their major reflects each student's individualized academic and professional pursuits.
Q3) Is there a requirement of a specific number of 300-level courses?
No.
Students are not required to take a specific number of 300-level courses.
Q4) Can you give a quick summary of the program including how the student will be advised?
When students enroll in the Learner Designed Major, they will meet with both their Academic Advisor as well as the School of Professional Studies’ Director.
These initial conversations are intended to lay a foundation and ensure that the students have both the discipline and a clarity of what is expected as Three Minor Major students.
These students will also enroll in BIS 199, the program's introductory course.
Here, they will explore critical approaches to interdisciplinary thinking and begin reflecting on which minors will support their pursuits.

passages.heading: #20-21-34D | Page 35
passages.text:
As students continue through their program, they will meet regularly with their Academic Advisor to ensure their course selections strategically align with their intended three minors as well as other requisite courses (i.e., General Education).
Following the completion of at least two courses in each minor, they will enroll in BIs 299a two-credit course designed to assist these students in intentionally integrating their learning. (Students’ Advising conversations will illuminate the desire that this program is intended to be interdisciplinary and that each semester they should be registering for courses in multiple disciplines, rather than attempting to complete one minor one before the others.) Similar to the BIS 199, the BIS 299 course will be taught by a core faculty member within the School of Professional Studies.
Further advising by their formal Academic Advisor and faculty members, will enable these students to strategically select courses that fulfill minor, general education, and elective credits-—-rather than random courses that do not lead to degree fulfillment.
The program concludes with BIS 399: Supervised Senior Project.

passages.heading: #20-21-34D | Page 35
passages.text:
With this course, students will be expected to purposefully integrate their multi-discipline learning in a culminating academic project. (This course will also be taught by a core faculty member from the School of Professional Studies.) Similar to all School of Professional Studies students, these Learner Designed Major students will engage in tailored advising conversations throughout their URI experience.
More so, as an intimate community, Academic Advisors, Administrators, and Faculty are constantly engaging with one another as well as in advisory dialogue with students to best be of support, serve as guides, and maximize adult-learner best-practices.
We expect this to continue when the Three Minor Major degree is approved and ultimately launches. 2

passages.text: FACULTY SENATE OCTOBER 21, 2021 REFERENDUM AY 2021-2022 - NOVEMBER 2021 On October 21, 2021, the Faculty Senate voted in favor of adding language to the Constitution of the Faculty Senate to allow for editorial changes.
