The current processes would also be streamlined and efficiently maintain the current Constitution as authorized at the October 21, 2021 Faculty Senate Meeting. The referendum of the General Faculty was conducted on October 28, 2021 until November 10, 2021 via electronic ballots. The results of the referendum are: ● Affirmative votes 118 ● Negative votes 8 ● Abstentations 3 ● Total votes 129 ● Total votes, excluding abstentions 126 Excluding abstentions, of the votes cast, 93.7% were affirmative votes: the amendment has been ratified. The Faculty Senate will now forward this Bill to President Parlange for his approval. Film/Media Part of the Harrington School of Communication and Media (uri.edu/harrington), the Film/Media Program offers a Bachelor of Arts (B.A.) degree and a minor.
Faculty:Rebecca Romanow,Director.Professors Healey-Jamiel, Mandel, Moore,Sama,Swift, Trimm, Walton, and Wood; Associate Professors Chadha, Ec he var ria, Kealhofer-Kemp, and Reyes; Assistant Professor Wyatt; Adjunct Assistant Professors Bergstrom, and Zora be dian; Teaching Professors Brown and Romanow.
The Major.
Film/Media is an interdisciplinary program offering hands-on experience in documentary, experimental,narrative,and new media production,balanced with an emphasis on international cinemas, film/media history, criticism, and theory.

passages.heading: #20-21-28B | Page 5
passages.text:
Our curriculum reflects the dynamic and diverse nature of this evolving and overlapping technologies involved in the production of moving images (including film, digital video, 3D animation, game design, and new media), with an understanding of the broadening and globalization of their cultural and aesthetic contexts.A wide range of coursesis available tothe film/media student courses that examine the historical, theoretical, and global approaches to the analysis and creation of moving images.
The film/media program prepares students for careers in such areas as independent filmmaking;animation and media design;film and television industries; advertising, marketing, and public relations; and media criticism.
Graduates of this program are also prepared to continue with graduate studies, either in film and media production for an M.F.A., or in a master's or doctoral program in film and media studies.
Students majoring in film/media must complete a minimum of 31 credits (maximum 46) in approved courses toward the major.
FLM 101 or FLM 101H is a required prerequisite.

INTER-INSTITUTIONAL CONSIDERATIONS: D1.
What are the similar programs in the state and region?
No other schools of communication and media exist within Rhode Island, though many of the components of the core courses are offered by CCRI, RIC, and schools across the country, the Harrington core will allow seamless transfers into the university and the Harrington School's majors.
The core is designed to coordinate with our current Joint Academic Admissions agreements. a.
If similar programs exist, how is this program different or why is duplication necessary?

passages.heading: #20-21-28B | Page 13
passages.text:
While most schools of communication, and there are a growing number of them across the region, have a core curriculum, the Harrington core reflects the unique strengths, breadth, and combination of the Harrington School's programs in Film Media, Communication Studies, Journalism, and Writing and Rhetoric. b。 Have you communicated with other institutions about the development of this program and have any concerns been raised related to role, scope, and mission or duplication?
The chairs of the various programs and the director of the school are continuously in contact with their colleagues at CCRI and RIC, and are confident that there are no concerns regarding role, scope, mission or duplication.
D2.
How do courses in this program transfer to other schools?
All of the courses transfer to other schools, as they represent the fundamentals of communication and media studies of programs in Film Media, Communication Studies, 4

passages.text: A7. Summary description of proposed program The Harrington School of Communication and Media was established in 2008. The current proposal presents a set of courses that constitute the Harrington core curriculum. The Harrington Core Curriculum: Harrington Core is required for students in each of the six undergraduate majors currently offered in the Harrington School of Communication: Communication Studies, Film/ Media Journalism, Public Relations, Sports Media and Communication, and Writing and Rhetoric. Part I: Introductory Courses in the Core: ● COM 100 (Fundamentals of Communication) WRT 104 (Writing to Inform and Explain) · SCM 105 (Production and Presentation Fundamentals) ·JOR 110 (Introduction to Mass Media) or FLM 101 (Introduction to Film/Media) (emphasis on media institutions, structure and regulation in JOR 110, or emphasis on creative/artistic media products in FLM 101) Note: The core fulfills the following general education outcomes: B2; C1; B1; B4; and A3 or A4, C2. Part I: Capstone Experience: All graduating seniors will participate in a capstone course that will produce a capstone project: ●WRT 495 ·Senior Level Topics: COM 410 ·Practicum: PRS 490 Capstone/Portfolio: JOR 411, FLM 495 Students can petition department chairs to use an alternative education opportunity, such as an. internship, study abroad semester or a directed study, to substitute for the capstone course. The Harrington School of Communication and Media* Introduction Norbert Mundorf,Interim Director Justin Wyatt, Associate Director Ann Salzarulo-Mc Guigan, Coordinator Located in the College of Arts and Sciences, the Harrington School of Communication and Media was established in 2008 to create a forward-thinking school of communication and media that prepares students for the rapidly evolving and increasingly global i zed communication ecosystem.
The Harrington School is a dynamic community of outstanding teachers, world-renowned scholars, and passionate learners committed to scholarly, practical, and professional approaches to the study and practice of communication and media in all its historical, contemporary, and future manifestations.
Our faculty and students are principled professionals skilled in critically evaluating and strategically producing information, messages, and media by employing and enhancing communication theories, multimedia platforms, and traditional and cutting-edge technology.

passages.heading: #20-21-28B | Page 21
passages.text:
In our evolving communication ecosystem, our graduates are equipped with the fundamental skills and abilities needed to adapt to an ever-changing communication and media landscape and possess an intellectual commitment to lifelong learning and service to the world through their communication skills and creative abilities.
The school has undergraduate programs and concentrations in communication studies, film/media, journalism, public relations, sports media and communication, and writing and rhetoric.
The school is also home to graduate programs in library and information studies (MLIS), and an MA and ABM (accelerated bachelors to MA) programs in communication studies.
Communication studies’ offers an Accelerated Degree Completion Online (B.A.) program.
The Harrington Core The Harrington core curriculum was developed to ensure that all Harrington School graduates have a shared set of essential skils from across the contemporary communication and media landscape, and is required for students in cach of the six undergraduate majors.
The core curriculum reflects the unique contributions that each program makes to our understanding of communication and media.

Students selecting this major may pursue studies in public communication and persuasion, organizational and professional communication, intercultural and interpersonal communication, media studies,and science,environmental,andhealth communication.
The program requires a minimum of 36 credits (maximum 51) in the major, including COM 202, 221, 381, 382, and 383.
The remaining credits are distributed as follows: at least two courses (6 credits) of COM 200 level; at least two courses (6 credits) of COM 300 level; and at least three courses (9 credits) of COM 400 level.

A student must maintain a 2.o0 grade point average in her or his major to meet graduation requirements.
Courses of independent study (COM 491, 492) and internships (COM 477) do not fulfill the requirements for the major or minor.
In order to transfer from University College for Academic Success to the College of Arts and Sciences, students must complete a minimum of 24 credits and have a GPA of 2.00 or higher.
They must also achieve a passing grade in COM 100.
Students must also complete the Harrington core requirements: COM 100, WRT 104, SCM 105, and either FLM 101 or JOR 110; and a capstone COM 410, FLM 495, JOR 411, PRS 490, or an alternative by permission of thechair.
A total of 120 credits is required for graduation.At least 42 of these must be in courses numbered300orabove.
Accelerated online degree completion program in Communication Studies The program offers students who have completed45or more credits the opportunity to join the Bachelor of Arts program in Communication Studies and complete the remaining requirements for their undergraduate degree completely online.Students will transfer a minimum of 45 credits to the University of Rhode Island.

passages.heading: #20-21-28B | Page 31
passages.text:
These students may enter the program with up to 15 transfer credits in Communication Studies.
The program is also available to qualified students in the Finish What you Started (FWYS) program at URI.
Prior course work in Communication, Public Relations, Writing, Journalism, Advertising or Film is preferred, but not required.
Courses are offered in 7-week sessions through our accelerated online calendar, with two sessions in each term (Spring, Summer, Fall).

Faculty:Rebecca Romanow,Director.Professors Healey-Jamiel,Mandel,Moore,Sama,Swift, Trimm,and Walton;Associate Professors Chadha,Ec he var ria,Kealhofer-Kemp,Reyes,and Wyatt;Assistant Professor Jaacks;Adjunct Assistant Professors Bergstrom,and Zora be dian; Teaching Professors Brown and Romanow;Lecturer Corsano.
The Major.
Film/Media is an interdisciplinary program offering hands-on experience in documentary, experimental, narrative, and new media production, balanced with an emphasis on international cinemas, film/media history, criticism, and theory.
Our curriculum reflects the dynamic and diverse nature of this field, approached from a perspective of film history and media theory.

passages.heading: #20-21-28B | Page 38
passages.text:
Students learn to work with the evolving and overlapping technologies involved in the production of moving images (including film, digital video, 3D animation, game design, and new media), with an understanding of the broadening and globalization of their cultural and aesthetic contexts.A wide range of courses is available to the film/media student courses that examine the historical, theoretical,and global approaches to the analysis and creation of moving images.
The film/media program prepares students for careers in such areas as independent filmmaking; animation and media design; film and television industries; advertising, marketing, and public relations; and media criticism.
Graduates of this program are also prepared to continue with graduate studies,either infilm and media production for an M.F.A.,or in a master's or doctoral program in film and media studies.
Students majoring in film/media must complete a minimum of 31 credits (maximum 46) in approved courses toward the major.
FLM 101 or FLM 101H is a required prerequisite.

This wide range of choices in film/media courses permits students to design a major that will meet both personal and professional goals.
Students must have a plan of study approved by an academic advisor in the film media program before beginning their coursework in the major.

Journalism Partofthe Harrington School of Communication and Media(harrington.uri.edu),the Department of Journalism offers the Bachelor of Arts(B.A.)degree.
Faculty: Associate Professor Pantalone, chairperson.Professor Moore; Assistant Professor Jaacks; Instructors Corey, Cotter, Coyne, Cyr, Phipps, Schaefer, and Stewart.
The study and practice of journalism require the acquisition and application of a broad base of knowledge, so journalism majors at URI pursue a course of study that is strongly grounded in the liberal arts.Along with general education and elective courses from other disciplines, the major in a diverse society.While studying the social, historical, legal, and ethical contexts of journalism, students also learn how to gather and critically assess factual information and communicate it clearly to a variety of audiences in all forms of media.Journalism“skills courses"-through individual and collaborative assignments-focus on reporting,writing, editing, and producing news for all forms of news media: print, broadcast, and multi-media. "Conceptual courses provide students the intellectual foundation and framework tobe responsible journalists.

passages.text:
Through its general education course offerings, the Department of Journalism provides non-majors a forum for studying the importance of journalism and the role of the mass media in society.
Students majoring in journalism must complete a minimum of 31 credits (maximum 45) in journalism.
All journalism majors must complete JOR 115, 220, 221, 310, 410, and 411.
In addition,students must select nine credits from skills courses:JOR320,321,330,331,340,341, 420, 430, 441 and three credits from conceptual courses: JOR 210, 211, 215, 311, 313, 415.
Any journalism courses maybe chosen for the remaining three credits.Students are encouraged to consult with their advisors about the mix of journalism courses that best meets their goals.
The only journalism courses open to freshmen are JOR 110 (for non-majors), 115 (for majors), and220.
Students must earn a grade of C or better in JOR 220 to enroll in the next-level course.
Only three credits of JOR 220 may be used to satisfy graduation requirements.
Students must also complete the Harrington core requirements: COM 100, WRT 104, SCM 105, an alternative by permission of the chair.
A total of 120 credits are required for graduation.

Writing and Rhetoric Part of the Harrington School of Communication and Media (harrington.uri.edu), the Writing and Rhetoric Department offers the Bachelor of Arts (B.A.) degree.
Faculty: Professors Hobbs, Reynolds, and Schwegler; Associate Professor Dyehouse; Assistant Professors Ledbetter,and West-Puckett;Professor Emerita Shamoon.
The Major.
This major is designed for undergraduate students who seek to expand their repertoire of writing for various public and private audiences.
Graduates will have a strong foundation in rhetorical theory balanced with a wide range of situational practices common to professional writers.
Coursework is balanced between in-class learning and experiential fieldwork in real-world settings.All graduates design their own digital electronic portfolios prior to graduation, demonstrating their ability to work with a range of technologies in producing and distributing their polished writing.

passages.text: 2 This major, offered by the Department of Fisheries, Animal and Veterinary Science, is designed for students interested in applied animal science careers. Animal and veterinary sciences play a vital role in the management and care of livestock, companion animals as well as those animals maintained at zoos, aquariums and laboratory animal facilities. Options are available to students interested in animal sciences or veterinary medicine.

passages.heading: #21-22-3B | Page 7
passages.text:
All students in this The major will take the following core requires the professional concentration coursesfollowing core courses: AVS 101, 102, 110, 304, 331, 332, 333, 343, 472 and AVS 212 or AVS 412 (249 credits) plus option-specific courses as indicated below.
Including the core courses, there are 1825-5046 credits of basic science including BIO 101/103 and BIO 102/104, 21-3130-33 credits of concentration courses and 119- 360 credits of supporting courses required for this major.
A total of 120 credits are required for graduation.
Animal Science Option.
This option includes coursework in animal management, nutrition, physiology, behavior, and disease, and provides broad flexibility for students in their choice of animal science courses.
Students have the option to focus their coursework specifically on domestic livestock, exotic animals or animal technology, or be more broadly focused.
Research techniques and procedures for animal care are emphasized along with a strong background in the sciences.
Students in this option pursue careers as researchers, veterinary technicians, food animal producers, laboratory animal technicians or high school agricultural education teachers.

passages.heading: #21-22-3B | Page 7
passages.text:
Additionally, there are career opportunities at zoos or aquariums (educator, researcher and exotic animal manager), within the federal, state and local government as well as with many animal- related businesses.
In addition to the core courses specified of the major, the following courses are required: AVS 212, 332, 343,6 credits of animal management courses, one 400-level animal science elective, 9 credits of animal science elective credit (one 300+) and at least 3 credits of either AVS 399, 491 or 492 and 6 additional credits in 400-level courses in AVS; COM 100, CHM 101/102 or 103/105; MTH course which fulfills A1, B3 general education outcomes, STA 220, 308 or 409; WRT 104 or 106, and an additional 300-level or higher WRT course.
The remaining credit requirements will be selected from the concentration courses (9 credits) and supporting electives (246 credits) approved for this option.
Pre-Veterinary Option.
This option requires a demonstrated capability in the basic sciences and prepares students for admission to veterinary schools offering a Doctorate of Veterinary Medicine (DVM) degree.

passages.heading: #21-22-3B | Page 7
passages.text:
Students in this option will also be well prepared to pursue graduate programs in animal physiology, nutrition and health.
Because admission requirements among schools are not totally uniform and are subject to change, students should determine specific requirements of the schools in which they are interested.
In addition to the core courses specified for the major, the following courses are required: AVS 304, 332, 412, 472; BIO 341, BIO/CMB 352; COM 100, CMB 211, 311; BUS or ECN (3 credits); CHM 101/102, 112/114, 226, 227, 228/226; PHY 111/185, 112/186; MTH 131, STA 308, WRT 104 or 106, and WRT 332 or 334.
The remaining credits will be selected from the concentration courses (36 credits) and supporting electives (96 credits) approved for this option. 3

Students must select one research methods course from the following: ECN 306, PSC 310, PSY 200, or SOC 440 (301).
If students are double majors with ECN, PSC, PSY, or SOC, this course will be accepted for the CCJ major, but the credits will need to be made up with an additional elective.

SECTION II Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation by the Faculty Senate EXISTING COURSE SEEKING GENERAL EDUCATION: MGT 201, Management Foundations: Building Better Businesses seeking C3, A2-p (3 crs.) Management concepts, processes and practices with an emphasis on inclusion, agility and evidence based decision making: organizational behavior; individual differences and elements of diversity; interpersonal dynamics and communication; work design, motivation and outcomes; social justice and worker voice; structure (including business functions) and culture. (Lec. 3) (C3) EXISTING COURSE SEEKING CHANGES AND GENERAL EDUCATION: AAF/ENG 352, Black Images in Film change credits, description, seeking A3, C3 (4 crs.) Cross-listed as (AAF), ENG 352. Exploration of the cultural, economic, political, and ideological motivations behind the standard representation of people of the African diaspora in cinema in the U.S. and other areas of the world, while examining film as a genre with a vocabulary and idiom of its own. (Lec. 3, Proj. 1) (A3) (C3) COURSE CHANGE AND REMOVAL GENERAL EDUCATION OUTCOMES: GER 215, Language Study Abroad change title, descript., method of instruction, credits, prereq, remove general education outcomes (1-6 crs.) Credit for intermediate language study in a German-speaking country. (Seminar) Pre: Students enrolling in this course should have taken GER 204 or 214 or equivalent.

passages.heading: #21-22-20 | Page 3
passages.text: 2 NEW COURSES SEEKING GENERAL EDUCATION: GEO 210, Landforms: Origin and Evolution seeking B2, A1-p (4 crs.) Development, distribution, and geologic significance of landforms produced by rivers, glaciers, coastal processes, weathering, and other geomorphic agents. Interpretation of landforms through field studies, topographic maps, and aerial photographs. (Lec. 3, Lab. 2) Pre: GEO 103 or permission of instructor. (B2) GWS/HIS/LAX 383, Gender and Sexuality in Latin America seeking A2, C2 (3 crs.) This class examines social movements and state formation in modern Latin America in the 19th and 20th centuries through the lens of gender and sexuality. Through an analysis of Latin American regional case studies, students will consider how gender and sexuality shaped discussions of indigenous rights, race, class, reproduction, revolution, and resistance movements. Using a combination of primary and secondary source materials, including film and popular music, this course challenges students to analyze current debates in Latin America through the perspective of gender and sexuality. Special emphasis will be given to gender and revolution in Latin America. (Lec. 3) Pre: GWS 150 or permission by instructor. (A2) (C2)

Health Studies The interdisciplinary curriculum in health studies leads to a Bachelor of Science degree.
The major is designed to prepare students for non-clinical careers in public health, health promotion, health services management, for-profit companies, not-for-profit organizations, and community health agencies.
Students seeking admission to this program must have completed 24 credits and have a minimum GPA of 2.50.
Students majoring in Health Studies are required to earn a C or higher in HLT 200 and HLT 450.
Students earning less than a C in HLT 200 or HLT 450 will be able to take the class one additional time.
Program Requirements.

passages.heading: #21-22-16B | Page 5
passages.text:
Students are required to complete the following core curriculum (120 credits): 1) At least 40 general education credits. 2) Core courses including BIO 105 110 or 101 and 103; CHM 100 or 103; COM 100 and 202, 208, 210, or 251; HLT 100, 200 (grade of C or higher required), and 450 (grade of C or higher required); KIN 122 and 123; MTH 103, 107, 108, 111, 131 or 141; PHL 101, 103 or 212 and 314; PHP 405; PSY 113; and STA 307, 308, or PSY 200; URI 100; WRT 104 or 106. 3) 18-24 credits (6 courses) from one of the following specializations: global and environmental health; health promotion; or health services. 4) 25-31 credits of free electives.
Twelve (12) credits of free electives must be at the 300 or 400 level.
Students select a specialization in one of the following three areas: Global and Environmental Health.
This specialization prepares students to address health concerns that transcend national boundaries.

passages.heading: #21-22-16B | Page 5
passages.text:
The goals of the curriculum are to foster critical thinking about world health problems and disparities; examine biological, social, economic, political, and environmental factors that influence global health; develop practical strategies and sustainable international partnerships to address major global health and environmental challenges; and inspire a commitment to real world change.
Students select six courses from the following list.
At least four courses must be at the 300 or 400 level.
Courses must be selected from at least three different

passages.heading: #21-22-16B | Page 6

3 disciplines/departments:: APG 319; APG 345; AVS/ENT 390; BIO/ENT 286; BPS 201; COM/SUS 315; COM 361, 460, 461, 462; GCH 104; GWS 325; HLT 312; HLT/COM 320; HPR 319, 375; HPR 412; NFS 524; NRS 100, 411; NRS/CPL 300; NUR 160; PHL 454; PHP 201; PSC 113, 402, 403; WRT 303, 332, 388.
Health Promotion.
This specialization is designed to prepare students for careers in fields whose primary emphasis is on facilitating individual, family, group, worksite, and community/population behavior change to promote healthy lifestyles and behaviors (e.g., increase exercise, cease smoking, manage stress).
It also aims to improve life quality via the prevention and improve management of chronic illness and to help increase the length of life by reducing disease and increasing health-promoting behaviors.
Students select six courses from the following list.
At least four courses must be at the 300 or 400 level.
Courses must be selected from at least three different disciplines/departments: : BPS 201; COM 361; GWS 350, 351; HDF 200, 201, 357, 440, 450; HLT 320; KIN 275, 325, 401, 425; NFS 207, 276G, 360, 394, 395; PHP 201; PSY 255, 381, 460, 479, WRT 303, WRT 332, WRT 388.
Health Services.

passages.heading: #21-22-16B | Page 6
passages.text:
This specialization equips students with a range of skills necessary for careers in the health care industry, with an emphasis on preparing students for roles within the health care workforce of tomorrow that do not involve direct patient care.
Graduates will: 1) possess foundational knowledge of human health and disease; 2) gain an awareness of and appreciation for how the current health systems serve those in need; 3) understand economic principles and forces that influence the efficiency of health care service delivery and administration; and 4) be capable of effectively communicating within organizations and with other stakeholders, orally and in written form.
Students select six courses from the following list.
At least four courses must be at the 300 or 400 level.
Courses must be selected from at least three different disciplines/departments: BPS 201, 202; COM 351, 361, 402, 450, 461; ECN 201, 360; HLT 312; HLT/COM 320; HSA 360; KIN 425; MGT 341, 342; PHP 201; PSC/HDF 405; PSY 255; SOC 224; WRT 303, 306, 332, 388. 7.

All Bachelor of Music students must successfully demonstrate piano proficiency through passing a series of seven examinations or completing MUS 272 with a C or better.
Students complete a diagnostic examination during their audition for placement in piano courses, MUS 171, MUS 172, MUS 271 or MUS 272.

passages.text: Students will need to demonstrate the following seven piano proficiencies by the fall semester of their junior year: 1) Five-finger patterns, playing a vocal warm-up sequence, hands together; 2) scales, playing two-octave major scales up to three sharps and flats, and one- octave minor scales in all three forms up to three sharps and flats, hands together, by memory at a tempo of M.M.=144 per note; 3) transposition, transposing at sight two melodies selected by the examination committee, students will be asked to transpose the melodies up or down by either a half step or whole step; 4) harmonization, reading two melodies taken from any major or minor key chosen by the examination committee, improvising suitable accompaniments for the melodies by using diatonic triads and secondary dominants, and reading from chord symbols; 5) patriotic songs, playing America and The Star-Spangled Banner in a manner suitable for accompanying community or school singing; these accompaniments are to be prepared in advance; 6) sight-reading, playing at sight selections chosen from a simple accompaniment part and/or beginning -level solo scores; and 7) repertoire, playing two prepared piano pieces by contrasting composers; each piece must be approved in advance by a member of the piano faculty or an instructor of class piano (piano majors are exempt from #7).

Medical Laboratory Science This major, offered by the Department of Cell and Molecular Biology, is designed to prepare students for applied careers in the medical laboratory and biomedical sciences, as well as to prepare students for graduate or professional school.
Students are required to take the following courses as part of the curriculum: BIO 101, 102, 103, 104, 220, 221, 222, 223; CHM 101, 102, 112, 114, 124, 126; CMB 201 or 211, 311, 333, 352; MLS 102, 360, 405, 406, 409, 410, 411, 412, 413, 414, 415, 416, 451, 483; MTH 111 or 131 or 141; PHY 111, 185; STA 307 or 308; and two of the following professional electives: BIO 341, CMB 320, 334, 432, 435, 437.
A total of 120 credits is required for graduation.
During the first three years of the program, emphasis is on general education and on basic courses in the biological, chemical, and quantitative sciences.
The courses of the senior year are taught off campus by clinical instructors from the schools of medical technology at affiliated hospitals.
These schools are accredited by the National Accreditation Agency for Clinical Laboratory Sciences.
The senior year is an 11-month clinical internship that begins in mid-June.

passages.heading: #21-22-16B | Page 32
passages.text:
It is taken at one or more of the following clinical agencies: Rhode Island Hospital, Miriam Hospital, Fatima Hospital, and the Rhode Island Blood Center.
The clinical program includes lecture and laboratory instruction in clinical chemistry, clinical microbiology, hematology, immunology, immunohematology, and molecular pathology, and prepares the student for national certification examinations and state licensure.
Applicants to this curriculum should have completed 60 credits and taken most of the required courses by the end of the sophomore year.
Students apply for acceptance into the clinical internship during their junior year and candidates are selected by the departmental curriculum committee and by program officials of the hospital schools.
Since the number of student placements in the clinical internship is limited, interested students should consult with the program director early in their college career, so they will be familiar with the requirements and application procedures.
Flexibility in the curriculum permits students who are not admitted to the program to fulfill

Our interdisciplinary approach will provide studentsyou with knowledge in areas such as nervous system diseases and current therapeutic strategies, the cellular molecular biology of the nervous system, cognition and behavior. Students will You’ll have the opportunity to gain experience with a variety multitude of experimental approaches and techniques used to solve unanswered questions in the field of neuroscience. Three There are three major options are currently available for the B.S. degree: • a major in Clinical Neuroscience from the College of Health Sciences, • a major in Molecular Neuroscience from the College of Environment and Life Sciences, and • a major in Neuropharmacology from the College of Pharmacy. The INP option for different majors is unique and makes URI truly distinct when it comes to undergraduate neuroscience education. The interdisciplinary nature of the program allows students you access to a broad range of faculty with expertise in neuroscience research labs across the campus as well asand the George and Anne Ryan Institute for Neuroscience. Master of Public Administration (M.P.A.) The Master of Public Administration (M.P.A.) Program leads to the M.P.A. degree conferred by the University of Rhode Island.

passages.heading: #21-22-21B | Page 9
passages.text:
This program is offered in an accelerated online format and provides federal, state, city, and nonprofit officials and agencies with flexible access to its instructional programs and research expertise.
In addition to delivering its online degree and certificate programs, internships, and workshops, the M.P.A. faculty conducts research into the formation and implementation of public policy and the administration of public and nonprofit agencies.
Admission requirements: Minimum GPA of 2.5.
Program requirements: a minimum of 36 credits, including completion of the Professional Certificate in Public Administration and Policy, 12 credits through the completion of either the Public Management certificate or the Policy Analysis certificate, and 12 elective credits.
The 3 required core courses of the Professional Certificate in Public Administration and Policy are PSC 501, PSC 502, and PSC 504.
Students completing this certificate can choose an additional 3 credits from either PSC 508, PSC 556, PSC 590, or PSC 592.
For a certificate in Public Management, students must complete 12 credits from the following courses: PSC 503, PSC 506, PSC 507, PSC 508, PSC 556, PSC 573, or PSC 592.

passages.heading: #21-22-21B | Page 9
passages.text:
For a certificate in Policy Analysis, students must complete 12 credits from the following courses: PSC 505, PSC 508, PSC 524, PSC 556, PSC 583, PSC 510, or PSC 592.
Students graduating from the

passages.heading: #21-22-21B | Page 10
passages.text:
4 M.P.A. program are required to complete the PSC 592 capstone course, which can only be applied toward one of the M.P.A. certificate programs.
PSC 508, PSC 555, and PSC 556 can only be applied to one of the M.P.A. certificate programs.
Students in the MPA program taking elective courses at other institutions will be governed by the same regulations effective for courses taken at URI.
Under this rule, grades (including failures) for all graduate courses taken at other institutions will be included in the grade point average and will become part of the student’s record.
The Professional Certificate in Public Administration and Policy, the Public Management certificate, and the Policy Analysis certificate offered by the MPA program can also be completed as independent, standalone certificate programs.
Each certificate program requires at least 12 credits.
Professional Certificate in Public Administration and Policy A 12-credit post-baccalaureate Professional Certificate in Public Administration and Policy is open to current students and college graduates with or without the M.P.A. degree.

passages.heading: #21-22-21B | Page 10

MPA and MLIS Cooperative Program A cooperative program permits joint enrollment in URI’s Master of Public Administration and Master of Library and Information Studies programs.
The integrated pursuit of the two degrees makes it possible for six credits of appropriately selected coursework from one program to serve as electives in the other, and for six credits of such coursework to be applied in the opposite direction.
Thus, when planned and taken jointly, the two programs can be completed with a total of 60 credits.

Summary description of proposed program (not to exceed 2 pages) Background: This proposal is requesting the addition of tracks to an existing degree program, the MS in Dietetics. This is being requested because the program is seeking accreditation by its external credentialing agency. We are requesting that the MS degree now has two tracks – one for students completing the accredited program and one for students who are not completing the accredited program. Currently, the degree does not have any tracks. The MS in Dietetics Program has been in existence since 2015. It was created in partnership with Sodexo Dietetic Internship in anticipation of the 2024 entry level 11/28/2021 12/14/2021

passages.heading: #21-22-21C | Page 4
passages.text:
2 credentialing requirement which states that all students need a master’s degree with experiential learning to become Registered Dietitian Nutritionists (RDNs).
Until 2024, a BS degree and an internship that provides experiential learning are required to become a RDN.
This change prompted free-standing internships to partner with universities to meet this new degree requirement.
The University of Rhode Island has successfully worked with Sodexo to provide a master’s degree to its interns for the past 6 years.
We are now formalizing the existing partnership with Sodexo by becoming an accredited Future Graduate Program to meet the Future Education Model (FEM) Standards as outlined by the Accreditation Council for Education in Nutrition and Dietetics (ACEND).
The FEM requires enhanced integration between the didactic and experiential components as part of the accreditation.
Curriculum changes to meet the new standards were approved in the spring of 2021.
The FEM Program will begin in the fall of 2022.
Students who complete these requirements need to be in a separate track to best manage our accreditation.
In 2018, URI expanded the master’s degree offering to RDNs employed by Sodexo.

passages.heading: #21-22-21C | Page 4
passages.text:
This program was requested by Sodexo to help their current RDNs to remain competitive with new graduates entering the workforce with master’s degrees.
RDNs complete the MS degree in a separate cohort, and complete individualized learning experiences instead of the standard experiential learning rotations.
We are requesting a second non-accredited track in the MS in Dietetics degree to allow us to continue to offer the program to these students and to students who are unable to complete the accredited track.
The MS in Dietetics has graduated 217 students as of December 2021.
Rationale: Tracks need to be added to the MS in Dietetics degree to accommodate students affiliated with Sodexo who will not complete the integrated FEM Program.
Track 1 –Integrated Experiential Track 1.
Students completing the integrated program with alignment between experiential learning and didactic material.
This track will be accredited by an external agency.
Track 2 –Individualized Experiential Track 1.
Students who are RDNs employed by Sodexo who are seeking a master’s degree who have already completed the experiential learning component. 2.
Students with experiential learning timing issues.

passages.heading: #21-22-21C | Page 4
passages.text:
As the new accreditation requirements are phased in nationwide, it is possible that a small number of students with off-sequence experiential learning may be able to complete this track and sit for the Registered Dietitian exam more quickly.
This is likely a very small number of students. 3.
Students who are unable to complete the experiential component of the FEM track and need a path to degree completion.
This is also likely to be a very small number of students.
Program Description: The students in each track complete the program in separate cohorts.
There are a total of 17 courses for 37 credits.
All students complete the same 11 core didactic

passages.heading: #21-22-21C | Page 5
passages.text: 3 courses. Students in FEM track complete 6 credits of experiential learning that is integrated in the program (NFS 571-576). Students in the non-FEM track complete 6 credits of individualized learning experiences (6 credits of NFS 591, or 6 credits from 571-6 and/or 591). The course plan for each track is listed below. Track 1 – Track 2 – The program length for both tracks is being condensed from 14 months to 12 months to allow students to sit for the national registration exam upon program completion. If the 14-month program duration continued, students would complete the program in October and would have to wait for degree conferral at the end of December to be eligible for the exam. A 12-month duration will align program completion with both degree conferral and national exam administration so there is no gap.

passages.heading: #21-22-21C | Page 6

The Program is currently in a revenue share model that was approved by the Provost.
There is a single URI program fee which funds all faculty and operating expenses.
Sodexo will charge its own program fee to cover all expenses related to the experiential component.

RATIONALE: There should be a demonstrable need for the program.
Two tracks are being requested to allow one track to become an accredited program and for the second track to serve students, predominately Sodexo RDNs, not seeking the accredited program.
Sodexo employs 4,000 dietitians worldwide.

passages.heading: #21-22-21C | Page 6
passages.text:
URI has an opportunity to continue to offer master’s degrees to this population of RDNs looking to obtain graduate degrees to remain competitive with master’s educated entry-level RDNs.
The RDNs cannot participate in the new FEM program since it will be an accredited program that includes integrated didactic and experiential learning and they have already completed the experiential component.
Therefore, they need a separate track.
This track will also accommodate other students who do not fit the traditional FEM model (students with experiential learning timing issues who will not be able to complete the integrated model).
B1.
Why is the new program being developed?
The MS in Dietetics program has been in existence since 2015, and has taught both internship students and RDNs in the single program in separate cohorts.
With the change to an accredited program for traditional students, we now need 2 tracks – one for traditional students who want to become RDNs and one for the Sodexo RDNs.
Sodexo has a new initiative to advance RDN’s education to the graduate level and offers tuition reimbursement to incentivize RDNs to obtain graduate degrees.

passages.heading: #21-22-21C | Page 6
passages.text:
To date, we have accommodated Sodexo’s needs to train their RDNs in our online master’s program but they will not be eligible for the FEM track.
As a result, there is a need to create a track for the RDNs to complete the MS.
This is a market that we do not want to lose.
B2.

Registered Dietitian Nutritionists are in high demand as the population faces chronic diseases associated with obesity.
It is estimated that there are 73,000 RDNs employed nationally with a median salary of $63,000 (2020).
The 10-year growth rate is projected at 11% (above than the national average).
B3.

Was an advisory board used to develop the curriculum?
Sodexo Dietetic Internship has partnered with URI to develop this program.

Sodexo Corporation is the largest employer of RDNs worldwide and has one of the largest internship programs in the country, accepting over 100 interns each year.
An internal group of URI faculty originally designed the curriculum and now will revisit the curriculum along with Sodexo’s Dietetic Internship Directors to meet new competencies required by the accrediting body.

What are the new courses and descriptions that will go into the course catalog?
Curriculum changes were approved in the spring of 2021.
These changes will go into effect in the fall of 2022.
Changes include: separating the 4 credit courses (which were previously 3 credits of didactic and 1 credit of practicum) into 3-credit didactic courses and standalone 1 credit practicum courses. d.
Are there specializations and options?
If so, please describe.
We are requesting the two tracks described above.
Once a track is selected, students complete that track in a cohort. e.
Is the program content guided by program-specific accreditation standards or other outside guidance?
The program has submitted a Reorganization Request Document this fall (2021) to become an accredited Future Graduate Program to meet the Accreditation Council for Education in Nutrition and Dietetics 2022 Future Education Model Standards. f.
What are the learning goals (what students are expected to gain, achieve, know, or demonstrate by completion of the program)?

passages.heading: #21-22-21C | Page 10
passages.text: Goal #1- The Future Graduate Program will prepare graduates from diverse backgrounds to become Registered Dietitian Nutritionists who will promote and advance the profession of dietetics. a) At least 80% of program graduates complete program/degree requirements within 2 years (150% of the program length). b) At least 90 percent of program graduates take the CDR credentialing exam for dietitian nutritionists within 12 months of program completion. c) The program’s one-year pass rate (graduates who pass the registration exam within one year of first attempt) on the CDR credentialing exam for dietitian nutritionists is at least 80%. d) Of those who complete a survey one-year post graduation, 25% of graduates will show activities that promote and advance the field of nutrition and dietetics. e) At least 10% of graduates will be from diverse backgrounds.

passages.heading: #21-22-21C | Page 10
passages.text: Goal #2- The Future Graduate Program will prepare graduates will be highly competent practitioners with expertise in medical nutrition therapy, community nutrition, foodservice management, leadership, and research. a) Of those who complete a survey upon program completion, 75% of graduates will rate their knowledge and practice skills as ‘above average’ or ‘excellent’ in medical nutrition therapy, community nutrition, foodservice management, leadership, and research. b) Of graduates who seek employment, 75% percent are employed in nutrition and dietetics or related fields within 12 months of graduation. c) Of those returning surveys, 75% percent of employers will rate graduates ‘above average’ or ‘excellent’ in their knowledge and practice skills in medical nutrition therapy, community nutrition, foodservice management, leadership, and research.

passages.text:

FACULTY AND STAFF: The faculty and support staff for the program should be sufficient in number and demonstrate the knowledge, skills, and other attributes necessary to the success of the program.
F1.
What are the number of each needed?
The Program currently uses NFS faculty members as course designers who create, manage and update course content each year.
Courses are taught by instructors (who may or may not be NFS faculty) with expertise in the subject area who teach the pre- determined course material developed by the course designers.
The number of instructors varies each year by student enrollment and number of sections offered.
Our existing full-time positions include: Jennifer Arts-Salvatore – Program Director Chelsea Warrell – Program Coordinator F2.
Are these new positions or reassignments?
No new positions are required.
Existing instructors will teach the courses and if there is turnover, new instructors will be hired to fill vacancies.
All of this will be funded by tuition revenue so no additional funds are required.
F3.
What are the minimal degree level and academic/technical field requirements and certifications required for teaching in this program?

passages.heading: #21-22-21C | Page 11
passages.text:
Course instructors must hold a minimum of a master’s degree in nutrition, dietetics or a closely related field.
They must be Registered Dietitians and have a minimum of one- year full-time experience in the area of instruction.
Instructors need to have formal training in online teaching.
G.
STUDENTS: G1.
How are students selected for the program?
Students will need to meet admission requirements listed in G2.
Sodexo Experiential Learning Regional Directors and URI’s admission committee consisting of the Program Director, Program Coordinator and 1-2 NFS faculty will score applicants and send them to the Graduate School for the final admission decision.
G2.
Are there admission requirements?
Bachelor’s degree with a minimum of 3.0 GPA A bachelor’s degree must be completed prior to beginning the program.
To be a competitive candidate, an overall 3.0 GPA is required.
Official transcripts from post-secondary institutions Official transcripts of courses completed at the time of application must be submitted.
Final transcripts showing degree completion must be submitted prior to completing the FG Program.

passages.heading: #21-22-21C | Page 11
passages.text:
Verification Statement, Declaration of Intent Form, or Pre-requisite courses A Verification showing DPD completion, a Declaration of Intent Form showing the remaining courses needed for DPD completion, or a list of pre-requisite courses must be submitted.
The pre-requisite courses include: 2 courses in anatomy and physiology including 1 laboratory, general chemistry with a laboratory, organic chemistry with a laboratory, biochemistry, microbiology, statistics, general nutrition, advanced nutrition that requires biochemistry and general nutrition as a pre-requisite, 6 credits in medical

passages.heading: #21-22-21C | Page 12
passages.text:
10 nutrition therapy or nutrition and disease that includes nutrition assessment and the nutrition care process (course must be completed in the past 5 years), community nutrition or lifecycle nutrition, nutrition counseling and education, foods-related course that includes food science and food preparation, and foodservice management.
Applicant’s statement An applicant statement will be submitted that describes why you are a good fit for the FG program.
Include the following in your statement why you want to enter the profession, experiences that have prepared you for your career, your short and long- term goals, and your strengths and weaknesses.
Letters of recommendation Three letters of recommendation are required.
At least one recommendation should be from a professor and at least one from a work supervisor.
The source of the third reference is the applicant's choice.
You should have a recommendation from at least one Registered Dietitian Nutritionist.
We strongly recommend that you not ask a relative or family friend to provide a reference for you, even if they are a Registered Dietitian.
Resume A professional resume is required for admission.

passages.heading: #21-22-21C | Page 12
passages.text:
The resume will provide a description of work experiences and will be evaluated based on how relevant it is to the successful completion of the FG program.
Electronic portfolio Applicants are required to submit an electronic portfolio highlighting your experience, achievements, goals, and commitment to the profession.
Additionally, a well-crafted electronic portfolio demonstrates your computer and technology skills.
G3.
What is the primary source of students?
Students will either be completing their experiential learning through Sodexo or will be currently employed by Sodexo. a.
New students or drawn from other programs?
Students will be new and will not be drawn from existing programs b.
Industry sponsored students/ employees?
Describe.
N/A G4.
What is the estimated number of students in the program?
It is estimated that we will have 3 cohorts of students (one cohort of students in the FEM Track and two cohorts in the non-FEM Track) for the next 3-5 years as the new accreditation requirements are rolled out.
We currently have 44 students enrolled and are expecting an increase in enrollment with the addition of these new tracks.

passages.heading: #21-22-21C | Page 12
passages.text:
It is projected that we will have 72 students enrolled (approximately 24 per cohort), with the majority of students in the FEM track in 5 years.
G5.
What is the estimated number of annual graduates?

passages.heading: #21-22-21C | Page 13
passages.text:
11 Since it is an accelerated 12 month program starting in September and ending in August, annual graduates will be equal to enrollment.
Therefore, it is estimated that we will have 72 graduates per year.

EVALUATION: H1.
How will the program be evaluated? a.
Performance measures to evaluate the program.
Internal and external evaluations will be conducted.
Internal measures will be conducted annually and include: 1.
Enrollment of Students – Values available on eCampus, reviewed by Program Director. 2.
Course Evaluations (IDEA) – Evaluations completed by students enrolled in each course, results reviewed by the NFS Department Chair. 3.
Program Evaluation by Students – Anonymous surveys sent to students upon program completion via SurveyMonkey reviewed by the Program Director. 4.
Outcome Data – Data will be collected on all of our learning outcomes required for accreditation (described under E2f).
External evaluations will be conducted by ACEND to ensure that specific competencies and performance indicators are addressed in the curriculum. b.
Will the program be accredited?
If so, when?
How?
The Program is under review by ACEND for its initial accreditation.

passages.text:
ACEND will perform a site visit for accreditation renewal 2-4 years after the first class is enrolled.

Special instructional resources and services needed? (Clinical space, internships, proctors) The Program is 100% online so no physical resources are needed.
Sodexo is responsible for overseeing all of the supervised experiential learning placements so no resources are needed from URI to administer the internship.

Facilities and capital equipment?
There are no facilities or capital equipment needed to operate the program other than office space for full-time employees.

AFFILIATION AGREEMENT AFFILIATION AGREEMENT BETWEEN: The University of Rhode Island on behalf of its Department of Nutrition and Food Sciences (hereafter referred to as the "University") And Sodexo Operations, LLC (hereafter referred to as “Sodexo").
I.
PURPOSE OF AGREEMENT The parties wish to collaborate for the purpose of enabling the University, with the assistance of Sodexo, to offer a masters-level graduate degree program in dietetics at the University to be known as The University of Rhode Island - Sodexo Future Graduate Dietetics Program (here in after to be referred to as the “Graduate Program'), as described herein and to be delivered in accordance with the terms and obligations of this Agreement and the Scope of Work in Appendix 1 attached hereto.
II.
COMMENCEMENT This Agreement shall commence on August 31, 2022 and shall be automatically renewed each year upon the anniversary of said commencement date (the “Renewal Date') and shall continue for a maximum of ten (1o) years, unless sooner terminated by either party in accordance with the terms herein.
Upon expiration of the Agreement, any additional term extensions shall be mutually agreed upon in writing by the parties.

passages.heading: #21-22-21C | Page 16
passages.text:
Either party may terminate this Agreement by serving upon the other party a written notice, of not less than 90 days, in advance of the Renewal Date.
IH.
INSURANCE, INDEMNIFICATION and LIMITATION OF LIABILITY Insurance Throughout the entire term of the Agreement, each party shall maintain commercial general liability insurance covering their activities under this Agreement, in amounts of at least One Million Dollars ($1,000,000) per incident and Two Million Dollars ($2,000,000) in the coverage via electronic (email) distribution to an address designated by University.
All students participating in the Graduate Program who are enrolled as students at the University will be covered by the University's aforementioned commercial liability insurance.
All students participating in the Graduate Program who are also employed by Sodexo, or obtaining supervised experiential learning in dietetics provided by Sodexo shall likewise be covered by Sodexo's aforementioned commercial liability insurance.

Appendix 1 SCOPE OF WORK Scope of Workfor the University of Rhode Island - Sodexo Future Graduate Dietetics Program (the “Graduate Program") Program Name and Official Address University of Rhode Island - Sodexo Future Graduate Dietetics Program (the “Graduate Program") Department of Nutrition and Food Sciences University of Rhode Island 120 Ranger Hall Kingston, RI 02881 Collaborating Organizations URI and Sodexo will serve as collaborating organizations for the Graduate Program Brief Description of the Graduate Program The Graduate Program will be accredited by the Accreditation Council for Education in Nutrition and Dietetics (ACEND) to provide the education and experiential learning requirements for students to become Registered Dietitians.
URI will provide the didactic requirements culminating in a MS degree in Dietetics, and Sodexo will provide the required minimum of 1,000 hours of supervised experiential learning.

passages.text:

FACULTY SENATE OFFICE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND FACULTY SENATE December 9, 2021 Faculty Senate Curriculum and Standards Committee Report 2021-2022-4 At the December 2, 2021, meeting of the Curriculum and Standards Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate.
SECTION II Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation by the Faculty Senate ORGANIZATIONAL CHANGE: COLLEGE OF ARTS AND SCIENCES: Film/Media Program: CREATE A FILM MEDIA DEPARTMENT: Film/Media (FLM) became a BA degree program in AY 2006, after existing as an interdepartmental minor (Film Studies) since AY 1999.
FLM remains one of the unique interdisciplinary majors (and minors) at URI, with courses that count towards the major spanning 14 different disciplines across the University.
Film/Media has been a unit in the Harrington School of Communication and Media since the inception of the Harrington School in 2008.
Departmental status will situate FLM in a stronger competitive position to attract prospective students to the Harrington School and the future success and commitment to communications and media that the School promises.

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 2
passages.text:
FLM has long been a discipline that attracts potential University applicants, and it is necessary that we present a quality, fully formed department that enhances the entire Harrington School project and URI.
Departmental status will underscore and enhance our national and global reputation: it is essential for our faculty to place FLM in a more competitive position to attract internal and external funding and grant opportunities, as well as encouraging internship and experiential opportunities for our students, and career advancement for our growing number of alumni.
Departmental status for Film/Media will emphasize the University’s commitment to offering our students the necessary tools and technologies that will shape their futures. 1

FLM remains one of the unique interdisciplinary majors (and minors) at URI, with courses that count towards the major

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 4

2 spanning 14 different disciplines across the University.
Film/Media has been a unit in the Harrington School of Communication and Media since the inception of the Harrington School in 2008.
The program offers hands-on, technical experience and professional preparation in documentary, experimental, narrative, commercial, and new and evolving media production, balanced with an emphasis on the study of international cinemas, film and media history, criticism, and theory.
This curriculum has allowed for FLM to be a focal point for delivery of University and Harrington School goals, as reflected in their strategic plans, with an emphasis on enhancing international and diverse cultural awareness and relationships, offering experiential and collaborative learning, preparation for successful professional careers, and exposure to interdisciplinary disciplines that emphasize innovative and integrative critical thinking.
Departmental status will situate FLM in a stronger competitive position to attract prospective students to the Harrington School and the future success and commitment to communications and media that the School promises.

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 4
passages.text:
FLM has long been a discipline that attracts potential University applicants, and it is necessary that we present a quality, fully formed department that enhances the entire Harrington School project and URI.
Departmental status will underscore and enhance our national and global reputation: it is essential for our faculty to place FLM in a more competitive position to attract internal and external funding and grant opportunities, as well as encouraging internship and experiential opportunities for our students, and career advancement for our growing number of alumni.
Departmental status for Film/Media will emphasize the University’s commitment to offering our students the necessary tools and technologies that will shape their futures.
This proposal for departmental status for Film/Media is based on its past growth, the intense relevance and importance of visual culture and its production as a core skill for meeting the future of communications across media and industry, the continued development of curriculum that expands the majors’ goals and outcomes, and which are supported by a solid infrastructure which exceeds what is available with program status.

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 4
passages.text:
FLM must be confirmed as a department because the designation is essential to create this infrastructure to underscore its relevance to our students and to deliver the curriculum that will support not only this major, but the broader inter-departmental goals and core values of the Harrington School and the University.
It should be emphasized that the global Film/TV industry in 2020 was estimated to be valued at $244.4 billion, with Berkshire Hathaway estimating that this will reach $284 billion

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 5
passages.text:
3 by 2023.*1 Our Film/Media major, which is designed to promote student creativity as well as the attainment of essential professional technical skills, prepares our students for the widest variety of jobs in these industries, as well as the jobs of the future which they will be able to successfully negotiate with the skills and flexibility they develop in the Film/Media major.
For our majors to successfully train in and prepare for participation in this complex, lucrative, and essential industry, which sits at the forefront of 21st century media and creative innovation, the recognition and advantages of situating Film/Media equally among departments at URI is necessary and will help to assure that we attract and retain students in this major--as well as securing the importance of FLM to potential external mentors for our majors and potential donors to the Harington School and the University. 8.
