passages.text:
RATIONALE: There should be a demonstrable purpose and documented need for the proposed organizational change. 1.
Explain why the organizational change is being proposed.
Film/Media originally emerged as an outgrowth of URI’s English Department and became a major in the College of Arts and Sciences in the 2006 academic year.
It had existed as an Interdepartmental Minor (Film Studies) since at least 1998, and the smaller number of majors at the time of its inception as a major did not, perhaps, seem to warrant immediate 1 Business Wire, 8 August 2020. https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20200821005370/en/Global-Film-and-Video- Market-Report-2020-to-2030---COVID-19-Impact-and-Recovery---ResearchAndMarkets.com

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 6
passages.text:
4 department status.
As we have reached 15 years of the growth and impact of the Film/Media major, it is now of importance to finally address this issue.
Film/Media has long functioned as a department, without being awarded Departmental status.
FLM operates as a fully-fledged university department and is expected to fulfill the demands, expectations, and duties of an academic unit at that level: Film/Media has its own budget--and in addition to the budget afforded to us from the College of Arts & Sciences and the University, we manage approximately $125,000 in lab fees annually which are used to purchase and repair equipment, hardware and software, and to meet the financial demands that are necessary to adequately deliver courses and classrooms for the major.
Film/Media’s director fulfills all of the obligations and responsibilities of a department chair, and our faculty--tenure-track, full-time, Joint, and PTF--who exemplify dedicated and engaged pedagogical and scholarly rigor-- do not benefit from being identified or recognized as members of a valued academic department and discipline in the University.

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 6
passages.text:
Film/Media recorded 236 majors in Oct. 2020 and is the 5th largest major in Arts & Sciences, and the 2nd largest in the Harrington School.
The major has grown by 43% in the 5 years since 2017.
The program has served as a flagship for the Harrington School and the University in attracting prospective students, and, for the most part, the number of our incoming Freshmen class has grown steadily over the years from 28 in AY 2007 to an entering class of 48 in September 2020.
It should be noted that in the four B.A.-granting undergraduate majors that comprise the Harrington School, all except FLM operate with departmental status, although FLM is larger than two of the other three in the number of our majors, our budget, and the number of incoming freshmen that we attract each year.
The Department of Writing and Rhetoric has 42 majors, while the Department of Journalism has 88 majors [data for Fall 2021 semester].

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 6
passages.text:
Film/Media, serving 224 majors this Fall, is not given parity with these other units, which presents an unclear, confusing, and lopsided picture of the emphasis, resource allocation, and focus of the Harrington School and its aims, goals and the importance of its students within the overall structure.
This inequity sends a message to prospective and current students and their families that Film/Media may be less important and less vital than the rest of the Harrington School, and that it might not be the recipient of the attention and resources that a future major might desire.
The data on Film/Media emphasizes the contribution which is made by the major: FLM delivered 2,954 credit hours/semester (Fall 2019 CDR), a 14% increase over the prior year, and delivers approximately 900 General Education seats for the University each year.

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 7
passages.text:
5 We have participated in delivering a 3-credit version of FLM 101, FLM 100 for Accelerated Online Programs, for the RN-BS program and have been delivering 150 GenEd seats to that program every year since the inception of RN-BS’ in 2016.
We are in the process of adding an additional 3-credit version at the 300-level of FLM 205, History of Film II, as a new GenEd offering to Online Programs, and plan to get this approved in Fall 2021.
FLM has historically had to function with an extremely small faculty (1.5 tenure-track and 3 full-time Lecturers--the most recent only hired in 2020) and has been granted a TT line only once in its history, in 2010.
The lack of departmental status has certainly contributed to the University’s lack of investment in our major, creating a cycle that only allows growth to a certain point before it becomes unsustainable.
Film/Media’s student: teacher ratio was 22.6 in 2019 [CDR] with only 3% of credit hours delivered by tenure-track faculty.

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 7
passages.text:
The message may be inadvertent, but the result is clear: When only 3% of our credit hours are allowing our majors to interact with our tenured faculty, it is, indeed, extremely difficult for FLM to maintain the excellence which is drawing our majors to us and the Harrington School in the first place.
With a major with so much potential to deliver in-demand skills in a time of unprecedented opportunity, innovation, and emphasis on this field, departmental status will help to break this cycle and encourage University interest, support, and the resources required for growth and the continued level of pedagogical and academic excellence necessary for the future of FLM.
It should be noted that even with a small faculty, Film/Media has made constant and consistent contributions to the College and the University that would expand with the recognition that this organizational change would provide.
We have an active Graduate Faculty that sits on numerous PhD Committees for the English Department.

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 7
passages.text:
Importantly, for the Harrington School, it is noteworthy that both Associate Directors of the Harrington School are Film/Media faculty: Justin Wyatt was housed 1/3 in FLM (and is now a member of the FLM Unlimited Joint faculty), and Harrington’s second Associate Director, Nicholas Corsano, is a full-time Lecturer in FLM.
In 2020, URI righty granted department status to both Africana Studies [9 majors] and Gender and Women’s Studies [30 majors], and Film/Media submitted supporting letters for both.
In these cases, there were numerous reasons to make these organizational changes, not least of which is the inherent necessity to clarify and emphasize the crucial importance of diversity, equity, and social justice in our academic community.
The granting of departmental status is also importantly reflected in the words of the GWS proposal stating that it is “a visible declaration at URI of the equal stature it accords all of its academic units.” The shift to departmental status for Film/Media is also a similarly necessary statement of organizational equity in the University and the Harrington School that

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 8
passages.text:
6 supports, celebrates and recognizes the academic, cultural and economic importance of this discipline.
Film/Media is an active and essential participant in the ongoing success, not only for the Harrington School, but for the University as a whole.
FLM remains an essential contributor in attracting students to URI and should serve as a desirable home for a future growing creative, diverse, and globally-oriented faculty.
It should be granted Departmental status-- and the validation, expectations and goals that accompany that change-- to not only reflect our students’ and faculty’s positions in the life of the University, but also the very essential role that Film/Media plays in promoting the unique blend of fostering creativity, advanced training in technical skills, and the career preparation for success for our students that the major is designed to deliver.
C.
INSTITUTIONAL ROLE: The organizational change should be clearly related to the published role and mission of the institution and be compatible with the organizational structure of the institution 1.

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 8
passages.text:
Explain how the organizational change is consistent with published role and mission of institution and how it is related to institutional planning.
The articulation of the transformational and essential goals and mission of the University which are presented in the statement of the Academic Strategic Plan emphasizes the overarching focus on “Innovation with Impact.” These three words could not more clearly also express a description of what the Film/Media major is designed to achieve, and the goals that we have set for the major, our students and our faculty.
These goals can best be reached by this organizational change to department status, to assure the recognition of these “innovations and impacts” that our faculty and students make to be recognized as products of a discipline that is appreciated and fully supported by the University community.
There can be no doubt that the visual moving image is-- and will remain-- at the forefront of communication in the arts, in business, and across emerging and existing social media in the 21st century.
Department Status will ensure that FLM can deliver the promise set out by the goals of our major, the Harrington School, and URI.

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 8
passages.text: This overarching introduction to the University Academic Strategic Plan 2016-2021 emphasizes these three goals: ~~Exciting and relevant collaborations deeply rooted in innovation that push the frontiers of learning, discovery, and problem solving: Film/Media is an interdisciplinary major, encouraging students to seek to explore, examine, and “push the frontiers” of ways of thinking and integrating learning across majors. 45%

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 9
passages.text:
7 of FLM majors are double majors in disciplines across the Harrington School and as varied as Marine Affairs, Global Languages, Wildlife Conservation, and Innovation Management.
Our major is one that inherently defines and executes the General Education goal of “Integrate and Apply,” as our students bring their unique and varied array of wide resources and approaches to learning to our classrooms. ~~New applications of technology that promote innovation, engagement, efficiency and effectiveness: Film/Media is necessarily at the locus of new technologies of communication.

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 9
passages.text: This does not just include cameras and visual recording equipment, but, of course, also emphasizes new software applications and breakthrough programming that will challenge and change the ways in which content for art, media, and business is created and produced in the future. ~~A community that reflects innovation and a commitment to strategic institutional advancement is all areas: Film/Media’s faculty and leadership have consistently been present and active in supporting new and ongoing initiatives at the University: we were among the first majors to create and submit new General Education courses at the inception of the new GenEd program in 2015; we supported the RN-BS program as it became operational with some of its first course offerings; we participated in offering special 1-credit courses for the University as the COVID crisis deepened.

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 9
passages.text:
FLM offers unique education/experiential learning opportunities like our annual trip to the South by Southwest Conference and Festival and JTerm experiences in Cape Verde and Belize; our faculty has developed and run alumni career panels and film screenings; and we connect the University with the community through our Client Media program which pairs FLM majors with local companies and non-profits to produce PSAs or advertisements.
The change to departmental status will afford FLM opportunities to expand these classroom learning and experiential opportunities in several ways: as a fully recognized department of the University--and an equal partner in the structural dynamics of the Harrington School--FLM should more strongly attract internship and mentoring opportunities from members of the Harrington Advisory Board and other corporate contacts; as a department, it is hoped that Film/Media will more easily expand its tenure- track faculty--and attract Joint Faculty from other URI departments-- both of which will increase and open dialogues about new ideas and original, interdisciplinary avenues.

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 9
passages.text:
The faculty of Film/Media sit on a variety of University Committees: the University Joint Steering Classroom Committee, the University Alumni and Family Weekend Committee, the Center for the Humanities, the Service & Community Life Committee, the Executive Committee of URI/AAUP, and have served as moderators for Student Entertainment Committee events.
Of course, the FLM faculty is also active in many areas of the Faculty

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 10
passages.text:
8 Senate.
On the College level, members of our faculty have served on the Arts & Sciences Curriculum Committee, the A&S Committee on Diversity, and a wide range of ongoing committee work for the Harington School.
Film/Media is an integral contributor--and highly visible member--of the academic and service communities at URI, and this should be reflected in granting the major Departmental status.
Most importantly, Film/Media directly addresses 4 of the major goals in the University Academic Strategic Plan 2016-2021: Goal #1: Enhance Student Success: Strategy #2: Significantly expand opportunities for experiential learning within all majors, and restructure academic advising and career advising to better support students in meeting their life goals~~ As mentioned above, Film/Media is consistently offering new and varied travel and experiential learning opportunities for our students.
Because of the nature of our major, we have many requests from national production companies, community organizations, businesses, and other departments across the University for the services of our students.

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 10
passages.text:
Our majors are expected to understand how to behave as professionals from the beginning of their careers with us, as teaching film is teaching a professional skill and a professional experience that encompasses not just the technical and creative aspects of film production, but, importantly, the ways in which our students learn the nature of teamwork and collaboration which is the underpinning of all visual media creation.
Film/Media advising emphasizes the very unique and individual nature of our majors as each of them approaches their interest in film through different avenues.
This is not only reflected in the wide variety of double majors that we see in FLM students, but this is also seen in the ways in which they choose to work, or concentrate, within the broad categories of film production: narrative film, documentary production, commercial/corporate work, and art or experimental cinemas.
We emphasize that each of our majors is on a unique path through our major and URI, and their career choices and goals--because the Film/TV industries offer so many different types of work---will be individualized.

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 10
passages.text:
Recognizing the nature of this means that Film/Media advisors are focused on enhancing the personal success of each student and appreciating the unique goals that we must help them reach.
Strategy #5: Reframe and redefine liberal education at URI in the context of the 21st century~~ The 21st century has “reframed and redefined” liberal education, and this statement of this strategy is reflective of the ways in which the University is committed as an active participant in these changes.
The Harrington School tagline of “Think.
Create.
Communicate” could not more aptly describe the process of filmmaking, the important

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 11
passages.text:
9 nature of collaboration on these projects, and the emphasis on both technical and critical analytical skills that are embodied in the FLM major. “Liberal Education” now often means to our students and their families a grounding in critical reading, critical writing, and critical thinking skills, that must be applied to critical and skillful communication that opens avenues to successful and rewarding careers.
These three tenets of the liberal education project are now, more than ever, being considered in light of hands-on technical and professional skills that our alumni can bring to the jobs they will encounter.
Film/Media is a major with the unique position of offering not only strong communication and analytical skills, but these strengths are added to a wide array of technical job-ready knowledge, aptitude, and experiences that mean that our majors graduate from the University with extremely concrete skills in hand.
Film/Media asks our majors to be flexible, open to new experiences and opportunities--as well as the unexpected--and always to embrace new ways of doing things.

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 11
passages.text:
Film, itself, for over 125 years, has always been at the forefront of cultural, sociological, and technological breakthroughs, and the major, as a department, should be a visible leader at URI in introducing, experimenting with, and solidifying new ways to teach and learn.
Goal #2: Expand Research, Scholarship, and Creative work Strategy #1: Broaden resources and support for significant growth in research opportunities with the state, nation, and world, and demonstrate value and recognition for multiple forms of scholarship~~ The FLM faculty has applied for and been awarded URI Project Completion Grants, Faculty Career Enhancement Grants, and grants from the Rhode Island State Council on the Arts.
Professor Justin Wyatt has just been awarded the Ralph C. and Mary Lynn Heid Research Fellowship, at the University of Michigan for his upcoming sabbatical research.
Professor Keith Brown was designated as a consultant for a Course Development Grant with Kathryn S.
Meier, Associate Director, Institute for Integrated Health and Innovation, Cancer Prevention Research Center and Justin Z.
Laferrier, Assistant Professor, Physical Therapy Department at URI.

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 11
passages.text:
The FLM faculty has participated yearly in proposals for Champlin grants, including awards for the $100,000 Phantom camera, the $1.25 million Broadcast Center renovations, and other innovative equipment proposals.
Because of the nature of their professional work, the film faculty, by definition, demonstrates “the value and recognition of multiple forms of scholarship.” We are critical and analytical scholars of film and television and other forms of visual media, participating in a wide range of scholarship over various topics relevant to the history, theory, and ongoing innovations of the moving image, the cultural and artistic impact of filmic artifacts, and the film, television, and media industries.
The faculty also embodies creative work and research in experimental, documentary, narrative, and corporate/commercial filmmaking.
As noted in Goal #3 below, this faculty research is global in nature and practice, consistently bringing our faculty work into the international arena.
Granting

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 12
passages.text:
10 departmental status for Film/Media is essential in recognizing the many scholarly, pedagogical, and creative contributions of this faculty, and will allow them more opportunity and visibility for their work to be reflected and foregrounded in the overall achievements of the Harrington School and the University.
Strategy #4: Involve undergraduate and graduate students in rich and varied research, creative projects and other opportunities~~ Film/Media continues to offer new and innovative courses and topics.
At the University’s request to create and deliver special 1-credit courses during AY21 to offset the negative impact of learning under COVID, Professor Keith Brown developed a course for the Harrington school, SCM 351X: Broadcasting Contemporary Issues.
This fully remote, online course allowed students to research, prepare and record broadcasting segments on their reflections on the many vital current issues going on during that difficult year.
Every week those segments were edited together to present a television show that was aired online.

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 12
passages.text:
This class was offered in Fall 2020 and Spring 2021 as a special 1-credit course experience and was so successful that it is being offered again for Fall 2021.
Professor Mary Healey Jamiel developed FLM 444: Filmmakers Professional Portfolio.
This course, which may serve as a prototype for the Harrington School, prepares the Film/Media major for entry into their chosen professional fields.
Offered beginning in Fall, 2020, this course asks students to prepare a portfolio reflective of their work at URI, including a PSA to be shot during this course, and to hone the skills necessary to present themselves and their work and launch successfully into professional careers.
Film/Media continues to offer a plethora of special events and opportunities for our students including end-of-the semester student film screenings-- attended by friends and families-- and a wide variety of guest speakers: industry professionals, alumni, and filmmakers with Q&A sessions for our majors.
In Fall 2019, we hosted director Spike Lee’s editor, Hey Mee Na, for an in- person discussion and Q&A for our students.

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 12
passages.text:
Even in the difficult AY21, Film/Media ran a YouTube series “URI Film Presents,” releasing weekly student work, and “Life After Harrington” presented a conversation between Professor Keith Brown and alumna, Ashton Avila about her burgeoning career in Los Angeles.
With the Harrington School, our majors participated in a media production talk with Victoria Coloruno-Caretto and Corrado Caretto.
Film/Media also invited the Hollywood film editor, Joaquin Elizondo, for an online talk and very impactful Q&A.
With great creativity, given COVID protocols, Professor Keith Brown arranged for the year- end film student screening in May, 2021 to be held at the Misquamicut Drive-In Theatre in Westerly, RI.
The event was a huge success and is reflective of the ways in which the FLM faculty constantly strives to offer our students--and the URI community-- new, original, and exciting events and experiences.
The annual trip to the South By Southwest Conference and Festival (SXSW) remains immensely popular to our majors and is fully enrolled every year.
This trip--which is

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 13
passages.text:
11 constructed as a full course--involves weeks of preparation ahead of the festival, participation in a plethora of events and screenings during this important festival, and follow-up work and analysis on the students’ return to campus.
Film/Media also joined forces with Writing and Rhetoric to offer “Careers in Film and Writing Alumni Panel” at the Harrington School Job Fair, and we regularly offer the Client Media Independent Study for 5-10 students to be paired with local businesses and non-profits to produce film and video content.
In the classroom, our topics courses open up ever-changing concentrations on varying aspects of the study of the moving image.
Each of these new topics then encourages students to consider new research and new avenues of thought.

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 13
passages.text:
In AY20 and AY 21, some of these topics included: FLM 220: Making Personal Media, Introduction to Cinematography, Introduction to Directing, and Creative Cloud Workshop; FLM 351: Producing the Short Narrative Film, Analog Cinematography, and Advanced Cinematography; FLM 352: American Independent Cinema, Animated Television, True Crime in Film and TV; FLM 451: International Animated Film, British Comedy Film, and International Long-Form Television; FLM 495: Global Art Cinema.
The recognition of Film/Media as a department will introduce resources and recognition for the major to expand these innovative offerings that so richly supplement the academic careers of students in FLM, the Harrington School and URI, and will attract both internal and external partners to develop new potential curriculum initiatives.

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 13
passages.text:
Goal #3: Grow a Global Presence: Strategy #3: Create opportunities for the internationalization of the curriculum and co- curriculum to ensure that all students are exposed to global perspectives and build global competence~~ Film/Media holds an essentially central focus in delivering global and international content to our students, and we emphasize the importance of global content in our curriculum in many ways.
One of the foundational aspects of our teaching is that all critical studies courses, including FLM 101, should contain at least 50% international or global films on our syllabi.
Teaching film and TV means that we are focused on global media and on instilling in our students a true understanding of different global perspectives, cultural attitudes, and the ways in which lives, people, and places occupy their spaces in the world and how that relates to our students here in Rhode Island.
Film is a global industry, and the viewing and production of film is usually not defined by geopolitical borders or demarcations.

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 13
passages.text: The Film/Media major is one that must--and does-- always forefront the world in which the film artifact moves and exists, the populations that consume and view it, and the essential importance to our students of understanding the global impact and interconnectivity of what they watch and create.

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 14
passages.text:
12 Strategy #4: Create institutional policies and support mechanisms to provide faculty with opportunities to develop global competence to maximize the impact of student global experiences on learning outcomes~~ Film/Media faculty maintain a solid international presence: in the past several years, we have represented the discipline at conferences in London and Scotland.
Films by our faculty have been shown in Germany, India, Lithuania, Dubai, Lebanon, and The Netherlands.
Professor Mary Healey Jamiel’s film, Searchdog , was released on iTunes internationally in the UK, Canada, and Ireland.
Professor Ashish Chadha’s body of work is streaming on MUBI’s platform for art cinema with 10 million subscribers in over 195 territories around the world.
Professor Chadha’s significant accomplishment and presence as a world-renowned filmmaker underlines the ways in which he operates at the highest level of the art of filmmaking, reinventing and reimagining the limits of the form to create and express work in an innovative and provocative manner.

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 14
passages.text:
Film/Media faculty demonstrate a total commitment to the advancement of their craft, with an impressive record of creative work screened/broadcast around the globe.
Faculty work is consistently selected for important festivals, national/international broadcasts, theatrical screenings and college and museum lectures.
Film/Media is dedicated to supporting our faculty in their creative work and research and in assuring that this work is seen and applauded internationally.
Our faculty’s wide and ongoing experiences in engaging with geopolitical spaces around the globe, and the wide scope of Film/Media’s international visibility, warrants Departmental recognition for our faculty’s continued contribution to URI’s and the Harrington School’s global footprint.
Goal #4: Embrace Diversity and Social Justice Strategy #2: Increase the recruitment, retention, and graduation of students from underrepresented groups, and provide support for their inclusion and success in the academic environment~~ The Film/Media major is dedicated to Diversity and Social Justice.

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 14
passages.text:
This is, of course, reflected in our curriculum as we focus on films and filmmakers that we study from every geography and nation, from all ethnicities, gender identities, and sexual orientations.
As a discipline that is enmeshed in inter-and multi-disciplinary studies, the foundation of FLM relies on --and focuses upon--exposure to different voices and different ways of seeing.
Film/Media is defined by the concept that film and filmmaking is universal, humanistic, and that the making and appreciation of art--and its inclusion in our lives-- is, perhaps, one of the foremost common denominators of the shared human experience.
Recruitment: Film/Media--with the support of the Harrington School-- has pursued for several years the possibility of introducing a program of concurrent enrollment between URI and the JM Walsh School for the Visual and Performing Arts in Pawtucket, RI, so that students at JM Walsh will receive college credit while finishing high school.
This successful

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 15
passages.text:
13 proposal allows for the offering of three courses required for the FLM major: FLM 101, 110 and 220 to be taught at JM Walsh to students in their Junior and Senior High School years.
This is an extremely positive step in opening up avenues for diverse students to enter the University with some coursework completed and a foothold into the FLM major.
Beginning in Spring, 2022, our first FLM courses will be held at the JM Walsh school, and we are very much looking forward to working closely with the school to support this curriculum with on-campus events and screenings, and collaborative interactions with our majors.
JM Walsh also offers majors in Art, Music and Theater, and we are hoping that this program will introduce students to the wider Harrington School disciplines and other URI majors as well.
In addition, to aid in recruitment and retention, since 2018, Film/Media has offered FLM 100 and FLM 110 in tandem as part of the summer Talent Development Program (we did not offer this in Summer 2020 because of the difficulties of teaching introductory production remotely during COVID).

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 15
passages.text:
Successful recruitment of diverse students will remain problematic without the organizational change for FLM to department status.
Although it is difficult to quantify, it can be assumed that prospective students and families may well be uncertain about committing to a major that is allocated only as a program, and that concern no doubt stems from questions of resource allocations and available institutional support for the major and its students.
In addition, it is no doubt more difficult for our Admissions Office to advocate on behalf of a discipline that has somehow not seen and named as a department.
It is extremely important for FLM to become a department in order to better attract our major to potential students of all backgrounds.
Department status conferred on Film/Media will also strengthen our ability to engage with the community, as we have with JM Walsh and encourage them to participate in often difficult negotiations to institute new and innovative programs.
Inclusion/Retention: Film/Media is committed to diversity, inclusivity and anti-racist principles.

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 15
passages.text:
Our topics courses focus on an extensive variety of film from differing geopolitical areas, among filmmakers around the globe, and which address difficult and relevant topics concerning race, gender, economic and social disparities, and the history and ongoing reality of oppression, power, and imperial violence.
Filmmaking affords all of our students a voice, and our end-of-semester student film screenings, which are attended by friends and families and other URI students and community members, assure that every student’s work is seen and heard.
We encourage our students to submit their work to film festivals, and, with the support of the Harrington School and the College of Arts & Sciences as well, Film/Media has been able to help students to attend important and prestigious festival screenings of their films.
We also are able to offer our students paid work in the Ranger Hall Media Equipment Center and as Student Assistants to Film/Media.
All available scholarships are awarded based on need.
The ethos of Film/Media is to form a cohesive working, creative and

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 16
passages.text:
14 inquiring community--and the center of that is the foundational practice of the importance, equality, opportunity, and dignity of every member of our community.
Strategy #3: Create an active learning community among students, faculty, staff, and administrators that engages in open discourse and enhance understanding about what it means to be a diverse and socially just community.
As an interdisciplinary major, FLM offers courses from Africana Studies and Gender and Women’s Studies, including the cross-listed ENG/AAF 352, Black Images in Film.
Studies in French, Italian and Spanish cinemas also count towards completion of the major, and have focused on Hispanic, Carribean, LatinX, and Maghreb filmmakers.
In the Fall of 2020, FLM faculty joined in a co-teaching project with Professors from Theatre and Honors to offer a section of AAF 300: Challenging Racism Through Film and Theatre.
This special topic course investigated the relation between race and theatre, and how racial issues have impacted on, or have, in turn, been affected by theatrical/filmic representations of race.
We are certainly hoping to offer this course again in the future.

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 16
passages.text:
Part of the gift of the FLM major is the ways in which our students work collaboratively on each other's films from beginning to end, and learn so much about each other in this process, as well as about the situations and topics around which their films are based.
Our diverse students are often tackling very personal subjects and reflecting on their histories and their lives in ways that intimately open up realities and lived experiences to other students.
Filmmaking--and discussions about the films that we watch and analyze together--is often difficult, as film leaves no topic unopened and ultimately excludes no one from the conversation, and Film/Media assures our commitment to that goal.
Film/Media has a small, but diverse faculty.
Our hope is to maintain equitable representation in not only the films that we include on our syllabi, but in promoting the ways in which the production of the moving image is not only a locus of international and global realities and creative endeavors, but a discipline that must ensure that all voices are heard and that all voices are afforded the opportunity to speak and be seen.

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 16
passages.text:
Our current position request for a potential future hire asks for an Assistant Professor of Production & Post-Production, specifically with a record of work that addresses issues of race, social and/or economic inequity and social justice.
Creating a Department of Film/Media should afford us a stronger chance of having this hire--and future diverse hires-- funded.
It is a goal of FLM to not only forefront the moving image as a reflection and focus of international and global realities and creative endeavors, but to also ensure that we are a part of the project that actively ensures that the film/TV and media industries move constantly towards social justice, equity, and diversity.

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 17
passages.text:
15 2.
Explain how the organizational change impacts other units and programs within the institution.
Have you communicated with the other units and programs and have any concerns been raised relative to the organizational change?
Describe the concerns.
Attached are letters of support for the organizational change of Film/Media to Departmental status from all of the Harrington school majors (COM, JOR, WRT, GSLIS, and SCM), as well as support from English, Modern and Classical Languages, ART, GWS, AAF, THE, HIS and the Honors Program.
There have been no concerns raised about this status change.
As an interdisciplinary major, Film/Media’s history has emphasized--and proven-- its dedication to multi- and inter-disciplinary cooperation and collaboration.
Department status will strengthen Film/Media’s impact and contributions to the academic disciplines and units among whom we have long worked.
Very importantly, the change to Department status for Film/Media will have a highly positive impact on the Harrington School, as it will strengthen its position as a fully formed school of communication with departments of equal value, importance, and strength.

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 17
passages.text:
The appearance that Film/Media is somehow minimized in comparison to the other units in Harrington will be corrected, and this will greatly influence the Harrington School’s ability to recruit, support, and retain students who are eager to major or second major in the very important field of visual media production.
Because the skills in Film/Media so importantly overlap with those of the other Harrington units — and particularly with the new Sports Media major-- it is essential for the Harrington School to present a balanced structure of its majors.
As a department, Film/Media will more confidently plan future contributions to the Harrington School and the University including potential interdisciplinary minors like Television Studies/Production, the development of multi-interdisciplinary General Education courses—especially in Grand Challenge, for example with collaborations with THE on Costuming, Set Design, or Performance in Film-- and investigating opportunities for co-teaching and team teaching of multi- and inter-disciplinary courses.

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 17
passages.text:
As the goals of the Harrington School state, granting Film/Media departmental status will serve to support, “accelerate and extend faculty and student engagement and collaboration in innovative, high-impact, and multidisciplinary teaching and research.” D.

Granting Film/Media departmental status will positively affect our collaboration with the other RI institutions offering similar programs.
There should be no loss of students or revenues at any other Rhode Island institutions as we currently co-exist and work closely with other film programs at CCRI, RIC, RISD, and Brown.
We are ongoing and important collaborators with these other institutions, and meet at least once per year for Transfer Articulation, and communicate regularly about new or changing courses and curriculum.
The director of Film/Media maintains a seat on CCRI’s Advisory Board for their Communication and Film program, which also includes members from all of the RI academic institutions and Emerson College in Boston.
Film/Media accepts many transfers from CCRI and RIC into our major, and the change of status for FLM would not, in any way, change the enrollment dynamics of students who choose to begin their college careers with the Community College experience. 2.

Rebecca Fine Romanow August 10, 2021 Film/Media Program College of Arts & Sciences University of Rhode Island, Kingston, RI 02881 Dear Dr.
Romanow: The Harrington School is pleased to come together to support Film/Media’s proposal to become a department at URI in the College of Arts & Sciences.
As a department, Film/Media (FLM) will be strengthened which will emphasize its crucial importance to our majors in the Harrington School of Communication and Media.
This action implements the clear priorities of the Academic Strategic Plans of both URI and Harrington, and places focus on the importance of Film/Media as we prepare our students to become future global leaders, offering them the necessary tools and technologies that will shape their professional careers.
FLM remains one of the unique interdisciplinary majors (and minors) at URI, with courses that count towards the major spanning 14 different disciplines across the University.

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 28
passages.text:
Departmental status will underscore and enhance the Harrington School’s national and global reputation, while placing FLM in a more competitive position so that our faculty can attract internal and external funding and grant opportunities, as well as encouraging internship and experiential opportunities for our students, and career advancement for our growing number of alumni.
Film/Media, serving 224 majors this Fall, although the second largest organizational unit in the Harrington School, is not given parity with the other units, which presents an unclear, confusing, and lopsided picture of the emphasis, resource allocation, and focus of the Harrington School and its aims, goals and the importance of its students within the overall structure.
This inequity sends a message to prospective and current students and their families that Film/Media may be less important and less vital than the rest of the Harrington School, and that it might not be the recipient of the attention and resources that a future major might desire.

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 28
passages.text:
Departmental status will situate FLM in a stronger competitive position to attract prospective students to the Harrington School and the future success and commitment to communications and media that the School promises.
FLM has long been a discipline that attracts potential University applicants, and it is necessary that we present a quality, fully formed department that enhances the entire Harrington School project and URI.
Film/Media is a central and vital discipline to the Harington School, the College of Arts and Sciences, and the University in assuring their goals, and this field surely requires its own department.
Sincerely, Ammina Kothari Valerie Karno John Pantalone Genoa Shepley Norbert Mundorf Director, Director, Department Chair, Department Chair, Department Chair, Harrington School GSLIS Journalism Writing & Rhetoric Communication Studies

DEPARTMENT OF THEATRE Fine Arts Center, 105 Upper College Road, Suite 3, Kingston, RI 02881 USA p: 401.874.5921 f: 401.874-5618 web.uri.edu/theatre August 13, 2021 Dear President Parlange, Provost DeHayes, and Dean Riley, Please consider this letter to represent my support for the proposal by Dr.
Romanow and the Film program to achieve departmental status within the Harrington School.
It is my belief that a more developed Film department can only strengthen the university and, in turn, the Theatre department.
Film and Theatre both share similar developmental principals, organizational needs for production, and a sense of story telling through collaboration of artists.
The development of the Film program to a full fledged department will give students in both departments the advantage of a stronger working knowledge of the fields upon graduation.
Film and Theatre have been inextricably linked for a hundred years: both converging and connecting as methods and tastes change.
However, the two fields will be forever associated with the structural forms that create art: the process of planning, developing characters, and understanding the visuals that inform the piece.

passages.heading: #21-22-16C | Page 29
passages.text:
Though a great deal of the Film program’s current emphasis is on the technical and pedagogical aspects of the field, I see, with a deepening of programming, an expanded body of artistic course work between Film and Theatre.
With careful planning as to not overburden either of our departments, I can envision a number of courses and work that could be developed within the two fields: Script Analysis and Script Writing, Acting, Directing, and Design.
Not only will the Film Department be able to develop their artistic course work, but I can see benefits for students within the Theatre BFA program, as they have more access to opportunities in recorded media.
We speak of preparing our students for opportunities.
A more robust Film department will support our students with more opportunities in the Entertainment Industry.
Though the Theatre department has integrated techniques required for recorded media in our curriculum, a stronger departmental presence of Film may lead to course work that develops a fuller scope for all students upon graduation.
Thank you very much, and if you have any questions or concerns, please feel free to contact me at dthoward@uri.edu.
Sincerely, David T.

The Film/Media faculty feels strongly that recognizing FLM as a department will not only serve to support and enhance the major’s growth, but is also of vital importance to the departments and joint faculty who participate in our curriculum, as well as the vision, goals, and disciplinary diversity that is presented to prospective and current students of the College of Arts & Sciences and the University.
Equity and parity among URI’s departments tells a compelling story, and granting this discipline —and our faculty —their rightful place in an academic area of study worthy of department status is crucial in underscoring the many combined and co -existing strengths that our major interdisciplinary study have to offer.
The FLM faculty, Nedra Reynolds, as our Associate Dean, Ammina Kothari, as the director of the Harrington School, and all Harrington Departments have all approved this proposal.
We will be following up this request to all interested departments with individual requests to each of Film/Media's Joint faculty members.
We will then be ready to submit this to A&S Curriculum.

passages.text: 1 FACULTY SENATE OFFICE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND FACULTY SENATE February 24, 2022 Faculty Senate Curriculum and Standards Committee Report 2021-2022-6 At the February 10, 2022 meeting of the Curriculum and Standards Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate. SECTION II Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation by the Faculty Senate NAME CHANGE: ALAN SHAWN FEINSTEIN COLLEGE OF EDUCATION & PROFESSIONAL STUDIES: School of Professional and Continuing Education: Proposal to remove ‘Continuing’ Studies from the formal name of the School (School of Professional and Continuing Studies). ‘Continuing’ education is understood as an all-encompassing term to describe formal learning activities that are generally not focused on a college degree outcome. These are considered additional, noncredit-bearing educational and learning opportunities. The term mainly references the process of refreshing knowledge, skills, and current practices. We do not offer these learning activities through the School. Rather, we provide STAR (service-members, transfer, adult, and returning) students with the opportunity to complete a degree that has a high level of resonance for working professionals. We believe this change will be important for internal and external constituencies. Internally, the University community still refers to and references outdated School programming, in part because of the ‘Continuing’ designation. Externally, we will be better able to promote our programs and substantial credit-rooted programs to prospective students without the ‘Continuing’ designation.

passages.text:
2 Department of Music: BM - Music Composition: ● Replacing two portfolio classes MUS 280 and 480 with the newly approved course MUS 367 Integrative Career Studies for Musicians.
This course fulfills 3 credits of general education and serves as a D1 for this major.
The portfolio courses no longer address the needs of the students seeking careers in composition; ● deleting MUS 421 (which is only required of BM Composition majors) ● addressing changes in conducting courses for music education; composition majors will be required to take the conducting series (MUS 239 Music Gesture and Sound) and then select one of the conducting labs (MUS 311 or 312); ● adding the new course MUS 411 Advanced Performance Studies to enhance the studio lessons. ● lowering the number of required participations in ensembles to 6 semesters because of the number of required upper level theory. ● eliminating the requirement for secondary applied credits BM - Music Education: Address the gap in instruction for music education majors seeking a BM degree in music education.

passages.heading: #20-21-29B | Page 3
passages.text:
Currently content addressing teaching exceptional learners and issues of inclusion are embedded in other music education courses, however, a focused course is necessary to prepare music students for a professional career in music education.
The BM degree in music education currently allows for 6 electives in music education.
This course would reduce that number of electives to 3.
The music education faculty agree that this content is essential for future music educators.
This NOC also addresses catalog errors including: ○ identifying the correct number of credits in studies in music as variable, ○ including the Unit Plan Assessment in requirements for clearance for teaching residency, ○ providing the correct EDC 484 course title, ○ providing the full and correct Praxis II test name to avoid student confusion, and ○ reflecting the minimum number of credits possible for graduation as 121.

passages.heading: #20-21-29B | Page 3
passages.text: This last item is important because combined with successfully passing piano proficiency without taking a piano class for credit and counting the possible 9 credits of MUS and 3 credits of EDC toward general education requirements students could graduate with a total of 118 credits; This is unlikely to occur, additional electives in music should be taken were that to occur COLLEGE OF BUSINESS: Management Degree: We are making these changes in a continued reimagining and reinvigoration of the Management Major and in an effort to 1) further rationalize the management major and existing tracks to streamline and support student success 2) transfer administrative ownership for the General Business Major to the Management Area as it currently has no home and 3) reinvigorate the General Business Major (which has not been reviewed or updated in more than 20 years) by combining it with management while maintaining its interdisciplinary structure within the Management major.

The program maintains relationships with state and local agencies serving Rhode Island’s older population.
This affords opportunities for research, internships, and field experiences to students interested in the issues of aging and health.
This minor is designed for students in any major to do a specialized study in the area of aging.

passages.text: 2020-2021 Online Catalog URI 2020-2021 Online Catalog Film/Media Part of the Harrington School of Communication and Media (uri.edu/harrington), the Film/Media Program offers a Bachelor of Arts (B.A.) degree and a minor. Faculty: Rebecca Romanow, Director. Professors Healey-Jamiel, Mandel, Moore, Sama, Swift, Trimm, and Walton; Associate Professors Chadha, Echevarría, Kealhofer-Kemp, Reyes, and Wyatt; Assistant Professor Jaacks; Adjunct Assistant Professors Bergstrom, and Zorabedian; Teaching Professors Brown and Romanow; Lecturer Corsano. The Major. Film/Media is an interdisciplinary program offering hands-on experience in documentary, experimental, narrative, and new media production, balanced with an emphasis on international cinemas, film/media history, criticism, and theory. Our curriculum reflects the dynamic and diverse nature of this field, approached from a perspective of film history and media theory. Students learn to work with the evolving and overlapping technologies involved in the production of moving images (including film, digital video, 3D animation, game design, and new media), with an understanding of the broadening and globalization of their cultural and aesthetic contexts. A wide range of courses is available to the film/media studentȄcourses that examine the historical, theoretical, and global approaches to the analysis and creation of moving images. The film/media program prepares students for careers in such areas as independent

passages.text:
filmmaking; animation and media design; film and television industries; advertising, marketing, and public relations; and media criticism.

FLM 101 or FLM 101H is a required prerequisite.
All students must complete the core courses: FLM 110, FLM 203 (or ENG 302), FLM 204 (or FLM 205 or 206), including the senior-level seminars FLM 495 (or FLM 496); a minimum of 6 credits from the production and technique category and 6 credits from the critical studies category; a minimum of 3 elective credits in courses that count toward the film major (following).
This wide range of choices in film/media courses permits students to design a major that will meet both personal and professional goals.
Students must have a plan of study approved by an academic advisor in the film media program before beginning their coursework in the major.

We are making these changes in a continued reimagining and reinvigoration of the Management Major and in an effort to 1) further rationalize the management major and existing tracks to streamline and support student success 2) transfer administrative ownership for the General Business Major to the Management Area as it currently has no home and 3) reinvigorate the General Business Major (which has not been reviewed or updated in more than 20 years) by combining it with management while maintaining its interdisciplinary structure within the Management major. This will allow students to continue to combine interests across disciplines and colleges as they have done in General Business, but with more intention by following the evidence-based portfolio approach to

NEW MANAGEMENT MAJOR CURRICULUM The College of Business Administration offers a curriculum leading to the Bachelor of Science (B.S.) in Business Administration with a major in Management.
The curriculum is intended to provide the student with the necessary skills to analyze diverse business problems and develop evidence-based solutions in a variety of disciplines across multiple industries.
Students may generalize and design their own cross-disciplinary track (General) or choose to specialize their program of study to focus on human capital/human resources (People Track).
Qualified students can prepare for graduate studies in Labor Relations and Human Resources (ABM) or other degree.

Skye Leedahl and I, affiliated Faculty in Gerontology, have been working to suggest some changes to the interdisciplinary, campus-wide Gerontology minor at URI in an effort to increase enrollment and provide additional opportunities for students across the campus to expand their academic qualifications in the area of aging and health.
Many new courses have been offered at URI since the gerontology minor was last revised, and we wanted to include these new courses to enhance the minor and identify new pathways for students to enter and complete the minor.
We have examined the course catalog and consulted with affiliated faculty from gerontology to identify courses that could be added.
We would like to include the following course(es) in your program/department in the minor as options for students to take: BPS 205G: The Challenged Brain As you know, students may apply two courses in their major to a minor.
As part of advising students for the minor, interested students will be made aware of any prerequisites for these courses, and also that Gerontology minors will have lower enrollment priority than majors.

passages.heading: #20-21-29B | Page 43
passages.text:

Also, please let me know if I have missed any permanent courses in your department that are not listed that may also fit nicely into the minor.

Our intention is to give students more choices and flexibility as they work towards a degree in this interdisciplinary major, and to formalize the acceptance of courses that have been approved as curriculum modifications in the past. Since the inception of the major, new courses have been implemented that can fulfill either the core Health Studies courses, or one of the specialization areas in the major. We are requesting that the following be added as options for the major (as specified below). 1) HPR 375: Honors Seminar in Global Responsibility and Social Sciences - add to Global Health 2) AVS/ENT 390: Plant Sciences and Entomology - – add to Global Health

Health Studies The interdisciplinary curriculum in health studies leads to a Bachelor of Science degree.
The major is designed to prepare students for non-clinical careers in public health, health promotion, health services management, for-profit companies, not-for-profit organizations, and community health agencies.
Students seeking admission to this program must have completed 24 credits and have a minimum GPA of 2.50.
Students majoring in Health Studies are required to earn a C or higher in HLT 200 and HLT 450.
Students earning less than a C in HLT 200 or HLT 450 will be able to take the class one additional time.
Program Requirements.

passages.heading: #20-21-29B | Page 66
passages.text:
Students are required to complete the following core curriculum (120 credits): 1) At least 40 general education credits. 2) Core courses including BIO 105 or 101 and 103; CHM 100 or 103; COM 100 and 202, 208, 210, or 251; HLT 100, 200 (grade of C or higher required), and 450 (grade of C or higher required); KIN 122 and 123; MTH 103, 107, 108, 111, 131 or 141; PHL 101, 103 or 212 and 314; PHP 405; PSY 113; and STA 307, 308, or PSY 200; URI 100; WRT 104 or 106. 3) 18-24 credits (6 courses) from one of the following specializations: global and environmental health; health promotion; or health services. 4) 25-31 credits of free electives.
Twelve (12) credits of free electives must be at the 300 or 400 level.
Students select a specialization in one of the following three areas: Global and Environmental Health.
This specialization prepares students to address health problems and concerns that transcend national boundaries.
The goals of the curriculum are to

passages.heading: #20-21-29B | Page 67
passages.text:
foster critical thinking about world health problems and disparities;examine biological,social, economic, political, and environmental factors that influence global health problems; develop environmental challenges; and inspire a commitment to real world change.Students select six courses from the following list.At leastfour courses must be at the300 or 400level.Courses must be selected from at least three different disciplines/departments: AVS/ENT 390, APG 319; BIO/ENT 319;NFS 212G,524; NRS100,411;NRS/CPL 300; NUR 160;PHL 454; PHP 201;PSC 113,402, 403, WRT303,WRT332,WRT388.
Health Promotion.
This specialization is designed to prepare students for careers in fields whose primary emphasis is on facilitating individual, family, group, worksite, and community behavior change to promote healthy lifestyles and behaviors (e.g., increase exercise, cease smoking, manage stress).

passages.heading: #20-21-29B | Page 67
passages.text: It also aims to improve life quality via the prevention and improved management of chronic illness and to help increase the length of life by reducing disease and increasing health- promoting behaviors.Students select six courses from the following list.At least four courses must beatthe300or400level.Courses must be selected from atleast three different disciplines/departments: BPS 201; COM 361; GWS 350, 351; HDF 200, 201, 357, 440, 450; HLT 320; KIN 275,325, 401, 425; NFS 207, 276, 360,394,395; PHP 201; PSY 255, 381, 460, 479, WRT 303, WRT 332,WRT388. the health care industry, with an emphasis on preparing students for roles within the health care workforce of tomorrow that donot involve direct patient care.Graduates will:1)possess for how the current health systems serve those in need; 3) understand economic principles and forces that influence the efficiency of health care service delivery and administration; and 4) be capableof effectively communicating within organizations and with other stakeholders,orally and in written form.Students selectsix courses from the following list.At least four courses must be at the300or400level.Courses must be selected from atleast three different disciplines/departments: BPS201,202;BUS341,342;COM351,361,402,450,461;ECN201,360;HLT320;HSA360;PHP 201;PSC/HDF 405; PSY255;SOC 224;WRT303,WRT 306,WRT 332, WRT 388. 7.Signature of the President David M.Dooley 3

Requested deletions appear with a strikethrough, and requested additions appear in italic font. The minor in leadership studies is based on a broad cross-disciplinary philosophy of leadership. The goal is to prepare students for leadership roles and responsibilities. The minor will provide students with opportunities to develop and enhance a personal philosophy of leadership that includes understanding of self, others, and community as well as the acceptance of responsibility inherent in community membership. The curriculum is focused on expanding VWXdenWV¶ knoZledge, skills, and understanding of specific leadership theories, concepts, and models in applied settings.

passages.text: THE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND Revised 8/2016 Notice of Change form Notice of Change for: Professional Leadership Studies Date: October 2020 A. PROGRAM INFORMATION 1. Name of institution University of Rhode Island 2. Name of department, division, school or college Department: Professional Studies College: Education and Professional Studies 3. Intended initiation date of program change. Include anticipated date for granting first degrees or certificates, if appropriate. Initiation date: Fall 2021 First degree date: (Already being granted) 4. Intended location of the program Feinstein Providence Campus 5. Summary description of proposed program (not to exceed 2 pages). Each of the individual course changes as well as this overall program change reflects significant student-focused alterations that strategically and systemically support our adult-learner student population. Included with these documents are our Professional Leadership Studies Curriculum Sheet (track-changed) that indicate the positive impact it will have for our students. Ultimately, we will be providing them with (a) a cohort-style experience with other adult learners, (b) flexibility to craft a learning experience that capitalizes on their professional growth, and (c) courses that offer knowledge-acquisition and skills-development that resonate with the needs of professional workplaces. In summation, the Professional Leadership Studies program changes include: • SPC 211 (Professional Communication) o A new course designed to enhance the professional writing and communication of our Professional Studies students. • SPC 221 (Finance and Budgeting for Professional Workplaces) o A shift in course number a title to entice students from across Professional Studies to take it earlier in their academic journey.

passages.heading: #20-21-29B | Page 128
passages.text:
2 • SPC 325 (Socially-Just and Culturally-Relevant Leadership for the Workplace) o A new course that prepares students to effectively lead diverse organizations with a social justice and equity lens. • SPC 335 (Planning and Analysis)—formally SPC 207 o A shift in course number to make it a more advanced course and hopefully attract non-Professional Studies to take it as a 300-level elective. • SPC 490 (Independent Study) o A new course to give both students and faculty an opportunity to craft independent courses that resonate with innovative learning experiences.
For students, they will be able to propose courses not traditionally offered that might propel their growth for work and community engagements, create opportunities for a research project, or explore a specialized interest in professional studies in a deeper, more meaningful way. • SPC 495 (Special Topics) o A new course that provides faculty an outlet to be responsive to learning opportunities that go beyond the traditional curriculum.
The “Special Topics” seminar is devised to be utilized for courses that address contemporary topics, problems, and issues that our professional workplaces face.

passages.heading: #20-21-29B | Page 128
passages.text:
Additionally, course this will enable us to craft new learning experiences in international contexts (e.g., “Comparative Leadership: Taiwan and the USA” or “International NGO and Social Sector Impact in the Dominican Republic”) that are not traditionally offered within the curriculum.
Overall, these changes will install a cohort-style experience by encouraging students from across Professional Studies to take three 200-level courses (i.e., SPC 201, 211, and 221) together at the start of the academic journey.
Similarly, they will take SPC 499 as a Professional Studies-wide culminating educational experience.
These four courses are intended to be required for the Professional Leadership Studies degree.
Students will then have the option of taking other PLS-approved SPC courses to secure their remaining eighteen major credits.
This may include the traditional courses (SPC 215, 325, 335, 401, 420, 450), an internship experience for up to six credits (SPC 480), or an Independent Study / Special Topics for up to six credits (SPC 490, 495). 6.

The courses that comprise this 30-credit major have been designed with current workplace needs in mind, focusing on the top gaps reported by employers, which include data analysis and technology, critical thinking and problem solving, decision making and leadership skills and communication and interpersonal skills. Name of institution University of Rhode Island 2. Name of department, division, school or college Department: Professional Studies College: Education and Professional Studies 3. Intended initiation date of program change. Include anticipated date for granting first degrees or certificates, if appropriate. Initiation date: Fall 2021 First degree date: (Already being granted) 4. Intended location of the program Feinstein Providence Campus 5. Summary description of proposed program (not to exceed 2 pages). Each of the individual course changes as well as this overall program change reflects significant student-focused alterations that strategically and systemically support our adult-learner student population. Included with these documents are our Nonprofit Administration Curriculum Sheet (track-changed) that indicate the positive impact it will have for our students. Ultimately we will be providing them with (a) a cohort-style experience with other adult learners, (b) flexibility to craft a learning experience that capitalizes on their professional growth, and (c) courses that offer knowledge-acquisition and skills-development that resonate with the needs of professional workplaces. In summation, the Nonprofit Administration program includes: • SPC 201 (Intro to Professional Leadership) o A current Professional Studies course that will serve as the foundational and introductory course for the Nonprofit Administration program. • SPC 211 (Professional Communication) o A new course designed to enhance the professional writing and communication of our Professional Studies students.

passages.heading: #20-21-29B | Page 135
passages.text:
2 • SPC 221 (Finance and Budgeting for Professional Workplaces) o A shift in course number a title to entice students from across Professional Studies to take it earlier in their academic journey. • SPC 321 (Nonprofit Governance)—formally SPC 285 o A shift in course number to make it a more advanced course and hopefully attract non-Professional Studies to take it as a 300-level elective. • SPC 490 (Independent Study) o A new course to give both students and faculty an opportunity to craft independent courses that resonate with innovative learning experiences.
For students, they will be able to propose courses not traditionally offered that might propel their growth for work and community engagements, create opportunities for a research project, or explore a specialized interest in professional studies in a deeper, more meaningful way. • SPC 495 (Special Topics) o A new course that provides faculty an outlet to be responsive to learning opportunities that go beyond the traditional curriculum.
The “Special Topics” seminar is devised to be utilized for courses that address contemporary topics, problems, and issues that our professional workplaces face.

passages.heading: #20-21-29B | Page 135
passages.text:
Additionally, course this will enable us to craft new learning experiences in international contexts (e.g., “Comparative Leadership: Taiwan and the USA” or “International NGO and Social Sector Impact in the Dominican Republic”) that are not traditionally offered within the curriculum. • SPC 499 (Senior Seminar: Thesis / Project) o A current Professional Studies course made available to Nonprofit Administration students as the culminating course in their degree.
Overall, these changes will install a cohort-style experience by encouraging students from across Professional Studies to take three 200-level courses (i.e., SPC 201, 211, and 221) together at the start of the academic journey.
Similarly, they will take SPC 499 as a Professional Studies-wide culminating educational experience.
These four courses are intended to be required for the Nonprofit Administration degree.
Students will then have the option of taking other Nonprofit Administration-approved SPC courses to secure their remaining eighteen major credits.

Forms Related to this Policy (Administrative) Policy Template (Administrative) Procedures Template Policy Statement A policy is a high-level statement of guiding principles and standards that articulates an institution’s values, communicates behavioral expectations, standards, and requirements related to a specific topic or area, or that otherwise provides guidance or rules for any component of an institution’s operations.
This policy pertains to the development and approval of policies at the University of Rhode Island (also, “University”) and, as such, provides guidance on both Academic and Administrative policies in order to provide transparency as well as coordination in the policy development process across the University.
Authority Approval of University policies will be: • In the case of Academic Policies, by the Faculty Senate and the President, consistent with RIGL 16-32-10 and Article II of the Constitution of the Faculty Senate, except where approval by the University of Rhode Island Board of Trustees is required or appropriate.

passages.heading: #21-22-24 | Page 4
passages.text: In the case of Administrative Policies, by the Administrative Policy Committee, except where approval by the University of Rhode Island Board of Trustees is required or appropriate.

passages.heading: #21-22-24 | Page 5
passages.text:
Policy on Policies Effective: August 5, 2019 Page 3 of 5 DRAFT Development and Format Policy Owners are charged with overseeing the initial development , regular review, and timely revision of policies related to their area of responsibility.
Policy Owners shall be noted as positions, not named individuals. • Academic Policies shall be developed through processes outlined in the University Manual (see University Manual, Chapter 11).
A ll Academic Policies shall be in the form consistent with the general form of the University Manual, as controlled by the Faculty Senate. • Administrative Policies shall be developed by the particular units that manage the operational area of concern for that policy.
The form and content of Administrative Policies shall be consistent with the p olicy template developed by the Division of Administration and Finance. • All University Policies must be consistent with applicable federal, state, and local law and regulations.

passages.heading: #21-22-24 | Page 5
passages.text:
Review and Approval All new and revised policies require approval. • New Academic Policies or material changes to existing Academic Policies require approval by the Faculty Senate and the President, and by the University of Rhode Island Board of Trustees where approval by the Board is required or appropriate.
Once approved by the President, or the University of Rhode Island Board of Trustees if required, the policy may be incorporated into the University Manual, with the information regarding this new policy or change disseminated to the University community and/or specific stakeholder groups, as appropriate. • New Administrative Policies or material changes to existing Administrative Policies require approval by the Administrative Policy Committee, and by the University of Rhode Island Board of Trustees where approval by the Board is required or appropriate.
Prior to submission for such approval, draft p olicies must be reviewed by any office(s) directly responsible for implementing a substantive aspect of the policy.

passages.heading: #21-22-24 | Page 5
passages.text:
Additionally, to the extent such policy or change in policy is not mandated in law or regulation, stakeholder groups likely to be materially affected by the proposed policy or change in policy sh all be given the opportunity to review and comment on the proposed policy or change to policy .
The development process for new or revised policies shall be managed by the Division of Administration and Finance, which shall maintain a working group responsible for stakeholder review and for recommending policies to the Administrative Policy Committee.
Once approved by the Administrative Policy Committee, or the University of Rhode Island Board of Trustees if required, the new policy or change will be disseminated to the University community and/or specific stakeholder groups, as appropriate.

passages.heading: #21-22-24 | Page 5
passages.text: Training If training on a new policy or revisions to a policy is necessary or advisable, the Policy Owner (or proposing unit) will work with Human Resources Management (for staff), the Vice Provost for Academic Affairs (for faculty), and/or the Vice President of Student Affairs (for students), as applicable, to identify, develop, or otherwise make available appropriate training for the University community or relevant subgroup within the University community.

passages.heading: #21-22-24 | Page 6
passages.text:
Policy on Policies Effective: August 5, 2019 Page 4 of 5 DRAFT Review/Revision Academic Policies shall be reviewed per procedures found in Chapter 11 of the University Manual.
Each Administrative Policy will state on its face a “Next Review Date” by which the policy will be reviewed by the Policy Owner and then by the Administrative Policy Committee should the policy revision include material changes.
Any University policy must be reviewed when there are changes in law, statute, or regulation, as well as changes to any University of Rhode Island Board of Trustees policy, that might affect the provisions of that policy.
Reviewed and revised policies shall be submitted through the same approval process as a new policy.
Repository and Archiving Academic Policies are instituted as elements of the body of the University Manual, with a notification within the University Manual (Appendix G) that Administrative Policies are found at the University’s Adminis trative Policies webpage (www.uri.edu/policies).
Administrative Policies are maintained at a central webpage as the single repository for these policies, with a notification that Academic Policies are found within the University Manual.

passages.heading: #21-22-24 | Page 6
passages.text:
All previous versions of amended or revised Policies must be archived.
If a Policy Owner concludes that a policy within its oversight has no continuing applicability , the Policy Owner may propose retirement of the policy through the same review and approval channels set forth above for approval of policies.
Retired Academic Policies shall be incorporated into archived versions of the University Manual.
Retired Administrative Policies will be archived but accessible from the University Policy Website (www.uri.edu/policies).
Additional Information Nothing in this policy limits the authority of the University to issue, amend, or withdraw a policy.
Exceptions None
