We seek to meet our students’ requests by oﬀeringa minor in cannabis studies.
We believe this will also attract potential new students tothe University of Rhode Island as students inquiring about and/or completing thecertiﬁcate program have been seeking further educational opportunities from theCollege.
B2.
What is the economic need and workforce data related to the program?The cannabis industry is expanding rapidly.
Thirty-seven states and the District ofColumbia now have some level of legal cannabis markets.
Cannabis sales grew 60% in2020 to $19 billion.
With the legalization of adult-use markets in Connecticut, New York,New Jersey, and Virginia, forecasters have increased 2022 sales estimates to $30 billionfrom the previous $28 billion.
The analysis ﬁrm Cowen and Company estimates the 3

passages.heading: #21-22-32E | Page 8
passages.text:
legal cannabis market to grow at a rate of 20-30% year over year reaching $50 billion by2026.
The expanding markets have translated to explosive job growth.
According to Leaﬂyand the Whitney Institute, 2020 saw 77,000 jobs added nationally in the cannabisindustry.
This represents a 32% year over year growth and a 161% growth over theprevious 4 years.
As of January 2021, 321,000 Americans are employed full time in thelegal cannabis industry.
Cannabis job growth continued during the COVID pandemic,demonstrating the industry as recession proof and essential in times of crisis.
Recruitingagencies, including Flowerhire and Vangst, have seen an uptick in hiring in every marketand in jobs across all levels from hourly employees to executives.
Salaries rose onaverage 4% in 2021.
With the emerging cannabis markets in New York, New Jersey,Connecticut, and Virginia, CannaBiz Team estimates 100,000 new jobs will be added in2022.
However, employers are plagued by a shortage of qualiﬁed applicants and expressdiﬃculty in retaining trained employees who are consistently recruited by competingﬁrms. a.

Jobs may include cannabis sales, brandambassador, cannabis laboratory technician, cultivation, qualitycompliance/assurance technician, dispensary managers, and product development.The specialized skills gained through the minor will enable our students to behighly competitive in the cannabis job market.
Knowledge gained during the minorcan also be applied by entrepreneurs, investors, regulators, legislators, andclinicians in their ﬁelds of study to further their own professional development.Salaries in the cannabis sector rose 4% on average, with executive level jobs gaining10% in 2021.

Explain how the program is consistent with the published role, scope, and mission ofthe institution and how it is related to the institution’s Academic Plan.The Minor in Cannabis Studies aligns with the academic vision of the Universityand aids in the achievement of several of the goals of the strategic plan. 4

The program’s use of problem-based learning through the threading of a single projectthrough all four required courses, the promotion of interactions between students/facultyand student/student using highly interactive discussion forms, and the creation ofinformation literacy by evaluating sources for credibility aim to fulﬁll Goal 1, Strategy 1.We believe many students outside of the pharmaceutical sciences will be interested in theprogram.
The interdisciplinary minor will bring together pharmaceutical science, plantscience, and business.
By oﬀering the minor, we aim to realize Goal 1, Strategy 3 to allowfor the exploration of other areas of study.
In whole, the program aspires to enhancestudent success through the use of innovative and engaging pedagogical approaches.
Being on the forefront of cannabis related programs, the University will be leading theway in the scholarship of the growing ﬁeld to improve scientiﬁc rigor and address publichealth and safety concerns.
Much of the current workforce in the cannabis industry isunder skilled which represents a signiﬁcant public health concern.

passages.heading: #21-22-32E | Page 9

The minor programwill expand scholarship with an emphasis in health and sciences and develop theworkforce to enhance public safety which supports Goal 2, Strategies 1 and 3.
The cannabis industry is quickly becoming focused on social equity and justice asstates such as Massachusetts and Illinois have built diversity, equity, and restorativejustice into their regulations.
We believe the program will embrace diversity andsocial justice, the aims of Goal 4, through recruitment eﬀorts and open discourse.

What are the similar programs in the state and region?Within the state, Johnson and Wales University launched a BS in Cannabis Entrepreneurshipin Fall 2021.
The program has a strong focus on business and entrepreneurship with only afew courses in biology of plants and cultivation.
Within the region, the University of Connecticut oﬀers courses in the horticulture of cannabisbut does not have a major or minor in the ﬁeld.

The BS in CannabisEntrepreneurship at Johnson and Wales University focuses on the business side ofthe industry while the proposed minor focuses heavily on the pharmaceuticalscience with some plant science and business aspects.
The online certiﬁcate incannabis studies at URI contains four of the same courses as the proposed minor. 5

passages.text:
Report from Faculty Senate Executive Committee March 24, 2022 Standing Committee Membership Rationale: With changes in apportionment for AY 22-23 the Senate will increase by 10 Senators.
To enable all Senators to serve on a standing committee, as well as provide flexibility in the Committees, the capped number of members per committee should change to identify only the minimum number of members.
Motion: Adjust all membership numbers for standing committees to indicate minimum number of members only.
Appendix C: BYLAWS 4.13 Each committee shall be comprise d of four to six or more faculty members, one of whom shall serve as chairperson, and two students, one undergraduate and one graduate student.
The faculty members of standing committees shall serve for three-year terms on a staggered basis from the time of their approval until the first meeting of the Senate in the fall three years afterwards.
Committee chairs shall serve for two years in that capacity.
Student members shall serve for one year and shall be eligible for appointment to a second term.
Students shall be appointed, respectively, by the Student Senate and by the Graduate Student Association.

passages.heading: #21-22-37 | Page 4
passages.text:
Committee chairs or the Faculty Senate Executive Committee may request that the University administration make available those administrators and/or staff members whose expertise is aligned with the work of the committees to act as liaisons to committees as needed.
Administrator and/or staff liaisons may advise committee members regarding the work of the committee but shall not be considered committee members.
The Executive Committee or committee chairs may also ask faculty who are not Senate members to serve as non-voting advisors to standing committees as needed. #17-18-11, #17-18-17, #20-21-14 4.20 The Curriculum and Standards Committee shall comprise six or more faculty members one of whom serves as the chairperson of the General Education committee.
The chair of the General Education Committee shall be appointed from the members of the committee.
The committee shall consider and make recommendations to the Faculty Senate on the items specifically assigned to it (see By-laws 4.21 to 4.25).
The committee shall meet at least once a month and present reports to the Faculty Senate as often as necessary.

passages.heading: #21-22-37 | Page 4
passages.text: Joint meetings of the Curriculum and Standards and General Education curriculum committees shall occur early fall and late spring to review and calibrate standards for course review. #17-18-12, #20-21-14

passages.heading: #21-22-37 | Page 5
passages.text:
4.27 The General Education Committee shall comprise six or more members, one of whom is the chair of the Curriculum and Standards committee.
The committee shall study and make recommendations on the establishment, modification or abolition of General Education requirements for graduation to be applicable to degree candidates; consider new and existing courses proposed for general education; evaluate the effectiveness of the general education program; maintain liaison with the University administration for effective implementation of approved recommendations; and cooperate closely with the Director of General Education (see University Manual section 8.20.30).
The Curriculum and Standards Committee and the General Education Committee shall maintain consistent standards by which courses are reviewed. #17-18-12, #20-21-14, #21-22-6 4.28 The Academic Calendar Committee shall comprise four or more members.

passages.heading: #21-22-37 | Page 5
passages.text: The committee shall study the University Calendar for fall, winter, spring, and summer session semesters as prepared by Enrollment Services in accordance with University Manual passages 8.70.10 and 8.70.61, respectively, report it to the Faculty Senate by December 1; study the calendar for the fully-online accelerated program developed in accordance with University Manual passage 8.70.72 and present the calendar to the Faculty Senate by March 1 of the year preceding the one during which the calendar is to become effective; carry out all other functions assigned to it by University Manual passages 8.70.10-75; examine, cooperatively with the Graduate Council, such academic matters as may affect jointly the two committees; consider such calendar matters as may be referred to it by the Senate or its Executive Committee, and study, on its own accord, desirable changes in the University Calendar; review any proposed change in the approved calendar originating outside the committee as well as any amendments attached by the Faculty Senate to a calendar proposal prior to Faculty Senate adoption of the calendar in its final form except that, if the Senate Executive Committee declares an emergency situation prior to the Faculty Senate meeting at which calendar proposals are to be considered, a calendar proposal amended on the Senate floor may be approved at the meeting during which the proposal has first been introduced by the full committee. #17-18-12, #19-20-16, #20-21-14, #21-22-6 4.30 The Teaching, Advising, and Assessment Committee shall comprise five or more faculty members, and consider and make recommendations to the Faculty Senate on the items specifically assigned to it (see By-laws 4.31-4.34).

passages.heading: #21-22-37 | Page 5
passages.text:
The Committee shall study and make recommendations to the Faculty Senate (or return the matters unapproved, with comments, to the units from which they originated) on the following matters referred to it by the various colleges, schools, the Faculty Senate or its Executive Committee, the Administration, or from another authoritative source, or taken up by the Committee on its own initiative: 4.40 The Committee for Research and Creative Activities (henceforth referred to as the “full committee”) shall consist of faculty and students active, experienced, or concerned with various aspects of research, creative, and scholarly efforts at URI.
The full committee shall serve as the representative voice of the university community in all matters related to research, creative, and scholarly activities and shall seek to improve the environment for research at URI in all ways possible.
The full committee shall also comprise two subcommittees, the Competitive Grants

passages.heading: #21-22-37 | Page 6
passages.text:
Subcommittee and the Center Review Subcommittee.
Each subcommittee shall comprise three faculty members serving on the full committee and three or more additional faculty Senators members appointed on a staggered basis.
The chairs of the subcommittees shall be appointed from the members of the full committee.

passages.heading: #21-22-37 | Page 6
passages.text: The full committee shall meet at least once a month and present reports to the Faculty Senate in December and April and more often as needed. #17-18-18 4.50 The Committee on Technology and Infrastructure shall comprise five or more faculty members and contribute to the development and maintenance of the strategic plan in collaboration with Information Technology Services and review and make policy recommendations regarding the implications on academic and research planning, standards, services, physical facilities, and allocation of resources on all matters pertaining to information technology, infrastructure, computing, communications, and networking. #17-18-12, #20-21-14 4.60 The Service and Community Life Committee shall comprise five or more faculty members, and aim at supporting the mission of the university by studying and recommending policies to enhance effective faculty governance and oversight; the supportive and diverse nature of the URI community; and URI’s engagement with the broader local, national and international community. #17-18-12, #20-21-14 4.70 Constitution, By-laws, and University Manual Committee shall comprise four or more members.

passages.heading: #21-22-37 | Page 6
passages.text: This committee shall review the operation of University governance and propose changes in the Constitution and By-Laws of the Faculty Senate and in the University Manual; review proposals for changes in University governance from whatever source and make recommendations concerning them to the Faculty Senate and to the other appropriate bodies and individuals; construe the meaning of the Constitution, the By-Laws and the University Manual upon the request of the Senate President or Executive Committee, any senator or member of the General Faculty, or the President; assure that all duly approved changes are incorporated into the Constitution and By-Laws and into the University Manual, and that no unauthorized changes are made in these instruments; and assure that the language of all duly approved changes is consistent with the style, format and arrangement of the Constitution and By-Laws and of the University Manual. #17-18-12 , #20-21-5 , #20-21-14, #20-21-36 4.95 Special Committees shall consider matters referred by the Senate. #21-22-6

Report from Faculty Senate Executive Committee April 5, 2022 Graduate Faculty Status Rationale: In consultation with the Dean of the Graduate School, FSEC proposes changes to language in Chapter 4, “The Faculty” in the University Manual for alignment with the Graduate School Manual.
Motion: Change Manual language pertaining to Graduate Faculty Status as contained in Section 4.70.10 as outlined below.
Chapter 4: The Faculty Current University Manual Language 4.70.10 The Graduate Faculty.
The membership of the Graduate Faculty shall comprise the following President, Provost, Vice President for Research and Economic Development, Dean of the Graduate School, Vice Provosts, deans of graduate professional schools, deans of colleges in which departments offer programs leading to advanced degrees, chairpersons of departments authorized to offer graduate degree programs, the Dean of University Libraries and members of the instructional, research and library faculty who either teach one or more courses on the 500, 600 or 900 level on a continuing basis, serve as major professors sponsoring graduate students, or serve as members of the committees supervising the work of graduate students.

passages.heading: #21-22-39 | Page 4
passages.text:
When faculty members cease to perform the function or functions qualifying them for membership on the Graduate Faculty, they cease to be members.
Reviews of their Graduate Faculty shall be made by Departments or Programs at least once every four years.
Recommendations for removal of a Graduate Faculty member who has ceased to perform the functions required for membership shall come from the Departments or Programs to the Graduate Council through the Dean of the Graduate School.
The Graduate Council may either confirm or deny the recommendation. #21-22-6 Proposed University Manual Language 4.70.10 The Graduate Faculty.
The membership of the Graduate Faculty shall be comprise d the following of the President, Provost, Vice President for Research and Economic Development, Dean of the Graduate School, Vice Provosts, deans of graduate professional schools, deans of colleges in which departments offer programs leading to advanced degrees, chairpersons of departments authorized to offer graduate degree programs, the Dean of University Libraries and members of the instructional, research and library faculty who have been granted Graduate Faculty Status by the Graduate Council.

passages.heading: #21-22-39 | Page 4
passages.text:
Additional Graduate Faculty members from outside the University may be appointed to serve on graduate committees according to the policies of the Graduate Council.
URI faculty maintain Graduate Faculty membership by either teach ing one or more courses on the 500, 600 or 900 level on a continuing basis , serv ing as major professors sponsoring graduate students, or serv ing as members of the committees supervising the work of graduate students.
When faculty members cease to perform the function or functions qualifying them for membership on the Graduate Faculty, they cease to be members.
Reviews

passages.heading: #21-22-39 | Page 5
passages.text: of their Graduate Faculty shall be made by the academic Deans in conjunction with Departments or Programs at least once every four years. Recommendations for removal of a Graduate Faculty member who has ceased to perform the functions required for membership shall come from the Departments or Programs academic Dean to the Graduate Council through the Dean of the Graduate School. The Graduate Council may either confirm or deny the recommendation. #21-22-6

Summary description of proposed program (not to exceed 2 pages) The field of Health Outcomes seeks to identify and measure the relationship between medical treatments and the outcomes achieved in real-world environments. It is applied to help understand what works and what doesn’t work in health care. As a subspecialty, the field of Medication Outcomes endeavors to determine the consequences of prescription drug therapies, including a medication's effectiveness, safety in general use, and its economic impacts on patients and the health system. Contributing disciplines include epidemiology, health economics, statistics, humanistic outcomes assessment and health policy.

passages.heading: #21-22-30E | Page 6
passages.text:
2 As healthcare organizations are increasingly challenged to deliver more effective and efficient care, professionals with expertise evaluating health outcomes will have key roles addressing this challenge.
Because medication is a fundamental aspect of contemporary medical care, skills in medication outcomes assessment are needed to ensure that policies and protocols for using prescription drugs are guided by robust evidence, informed by sound methodologic analyses and based on valid interpretations of scientific and statistical data.
There exists a growing demand for professionals who possess these skills, which are typically not emphasized in clinical training programs.
The URI College of Pharmacy offers a full -time MS/PhD program, with a track specializing in Health Outcomes research.
Yet it is not possible for many working professionals to enroll in a full-time graduate program delivered on campus.
The online graduate certificate program will provide a more feasible option to obtain these skills.
Our market survey revealed a high degree of interest in the program among health care professionals.

passages.heading: #21-22-30E | Page 6
passages.text:
Interest was particularly strong among pharmacists, who view additional training in health outcomes to benefit their career advancement.
Graduates from URI's nationally renowned Doctor of Pharmacy program have strong brand loyalty and rapport with faculty that can be leveraged to recruit students would favor URI over competitors.
Our graduate certificate program will be specifically focused in Medication Outcomes, providing differentiation from competing certificate programs that provide training in Health Outcomes.
It will be delivered online and comprise 12 credits.
It will be administered as four 3-credit courses delivered sequentially, to be completed within a 9-month period spanning September - May.
All courses will emphasize application, with case and project-oriented activities.
The first course will provide an introduction to medication outcomes evaluation, covering basic principles for conceptualizing medication outcomes, and methodologic and statistical approaches for collecting and analyzing data.

passages.heading: #21-22-30E | Page 6
passages.text:
The second and third courses will teach student techniques for conducting pharmacoepidemiologic and pharmacoeconomic evaluations and interpreting and applying evidence in these fields.
The fourth course will extend the skills covered in the prior courses, covering advanced topics and guiding the student through the steps of conducting a chosen medication outcomes project that is relevant to the student's work role and/or interest.
Students completing this certificate program will be able to 1.) Develop and structure a medication outcomes evaluation; 2.) Collect and analyze data using contemporary methods from the fields of pharmacoepidemiology and pharmacoeconomics; and 3.) Translate results of medication outcomes studies to healthcare decision-makers to optimize prescription medication use in the varied work environments.
The online Graduate Certificate in Medication Outcomes meets the Provost's academic priority for active e-learning via technology-enhanced pedagogy and online programs.
Further, it aligns with key goals of URI's Academic Strategic Plan.

passages.heading: #21-22-30E | Page 6
passages.text:
One goal of this Plan is to enhance student success by equipping learners with skills that are in demand in an ever-changing world, which this proposed certificate program aims to achieve.
The Medication Outcomes certificate program also addresses this goal's strategy of facilitating the implementation of new learning pedagogies and the expansion of modes of course delivery and assessment by leveraging space and time in new ways.
This

passages.text: 3 program also addresses the Plan's goal for diversity and social justice, as the Certificate program curriculum will include strategies for reducing racial disparities in medication use, and for optimizing the use of pharmacy resources in programs that serve vulnerable populations. Additionally, this certificate program will augment knowledge in health and sciences, and develop the workforce to enhance public safety, as described in the Plan's goal to expand research, scholarship, and creative work. What is the economic need and workforce data related to the program?
Prescription medications are a top publi c policy concern, and are increasingly impacting the viability of organizations that deliver and finance health care.

passages.heading: #21-22-30E | Page 8
passages.text:
Retail prescription drug expenditure comprises approximately 10% of US national health expenditure.
Many new pharmaceutical innovations have annual prices exceeding six figures, arguably justified by ever-increasing costs of research and development.
To ensure that expensive medications are used judiciously, decision-makers require outcomes data specific to their population to design policies to guide how medications should be used to maximize their benefits in a cost-effective manner.
The US does not set drug coverage policy at the federal level.
Even in Medicare, policy for determining which medications are covered is determined by each private Part D drug benefit sponsor (subject to broad federal guidelines).
Outside of Medicare. policies for medication use are crafted by hospitals, state Medicaid programs, commercial insurers, pharmacy benefit managers, medical group practices, health centers, among other entities.
In each of these settings, personnel with specialized skills are required to evaluate current evidence and generate local data to determine the actual health outcomes experienced by patients.
Medication Outcomes evaluation provides these skills.

passages.heading: #21-22-30E | Page 8
passages.text:
We conducted a needs assessment survey in spring 2021 to ascertain the demand for graduate certificate-level training in Medication Outcomes evaluation.
The results validated the need for this program.
We solicited survey participants using the RI Department of Health’s publicly available email list of licensed pharmacists.
Additionally, we recruited participation through personal requests to contacts at Care

passages.heading: #21-22-30E | Page 9
passages.text:
5 New England, Coastal Medical, Lifespan, RI Medicaid, and the RI Department of Health.
Colleagues from the College of Pharmacy shared the survey link with their contacts, and the survey was also posted on LinkedIn.
There were 114 respondents, among which there were 109 who indicated that the program would have value to themselves or coworkers.
The responses of these 109 participants were analyzed.
Forty percent of respondents were age 25-34 (44/109), while roughly 20% were age 35- 44 years, and 8.3% were under the age of 25, suggesting interest in the program following graduation.
Over 30% of respondents were age 45 or older.
These results indicate interest in the program across age groups.
The majority of respondents (77%) were pharmacists.
Other disciplines represented included MBA (9.2%), MPH (4.6%), Medical Doctor (2.8%), and having a master’s degree in another field (e.g.
MD Ed, MHA).
The most frequent work settings of respondents were hospital (n = 20), community pharmacy (n = 18), primary care (n = 14), pharmaceutical industry (n = 11), and the health insurance industry (n = 8).

Students who successfully complete the certificate will be able to apply their skills to a variety of tasks in organizations where pharmaceutical management is required.
Examples include: • Contributing to coverage policy development by comprehensive analyses of new pharmaceuticals, including determining economic impacts and humanistic benefits (e.g. health-related quality of life).

Hospitals, insurers, pharmacy benefit managers, Medicaid programs, long term care providers, and other entities have a growing need for individuals with such expertise. • Determining the comparative outcomes of medications used in clinical practice in the inpatient, community, ambulatory care and long-term care settings.
Relevant skills include conceptualizing and measuring health outcomes, study designs for medication outcomes evaluation, collecting and managing data, statistical analyses, data interpretation and visualization, and addressing bias. • Engaging in outcomes-based contracts with drug manufacturers, requiring valid and reliable ascertainment of direct, indirect and intangible medication outcomes.
These contracts are an increasingly common method for mitigating the risk associated with covering expensive medications for conditions where health outcomes are uncertain (e.g. cancer, rare disease). • Quality measurement for accreditation and as required by payers for program compliance.

Importantly, the program will extend the expertise of the college's faculty in this specialty area, who have heretofore been involved as instructors for the graduate program track in Health Outcomes research.
The MS/PhD graduate program track in Health Outcomes typically enrolls 12-16 students, many of whom are international students.
Limits in the number of available teaching assistantships has been a barrier to growth.
The graduate certificate program will provide a new avenue for growth, while also attracting a segment who will choose to continue on to the MS degree after completing the certificate.

In addition to gaining insights from the needs assessment, we surveyed existing certificate programs in health or medication outcomes.
The table below lists the salient characteristics of these programs.
No similar programs exist within the state.
Nearby is the Health Economics and Outcomes Research (HEOR) Certificate Program offered Tufts University.
This program's design differs from our model in important ways.
The program's 5-credit curriculum emphasizes regulatory, health technology assessment and policy aspects of outcomes research, which are aligned themes of the Tuft's Center for the Evaluation of Value and Risk in Health.
In contrast, URI's 12 credit certificate program will emphasize methods for evaluating medication outcomes in health care settings through applied examples, exercises and projects.
We aim to make the program practical, relevant and translatable.

passages.heading: #21-22-30E | Page 12
passages.text:
The URI certificate program will be delivered online and asynchronously; while the Tuft's program is a hybrid model that has synchronous components.
Other universities that offer an online certificate program in health or medication outcomes research include Rutgers, Temple, The University of Washington, Johns Hopkins University, Thomas Jefferson University and George Washington University.
While these other programs can be considered competitors, their continuing presence also suggests that there is a continuing demand for this training.
We believe that URI can be competitive recruiting students into our certificate program for several reasons.
The first reason Is familiarity with URI and Its faculty In this area among former students.
The URI PharmD program graduates between 120-145 students each year, and these graduates would likely have loyalty to URI when choosing a program.
We also believe that our focus on medication outcomes (rather than the broader "health outcomes") will differentiate our program.
The online and asynchronous program format accommodates professionals working in any time zone.

We envision that this certificate program will be of interest to pharmacists working in a range of healthcare settings who have responsibility for medication management at the population level.
This includes pharmacists working in managed care environments, and for delivery entities that bear financial risk for health system utilization that can be avoided with optimized medication use.
This certificate program will also be useful to physicians, nurses and other clinicians who are involved with managing medication use for their patient populations.
Additionally, this program will be worthwhile for healthcare administrators who are seeking skills in medication outcomes evaluation, particularly those with non-clinical backgrounds. .

Therefore, the program will not draw student away from existing programs at the University and will instead be targeting a new student population outside of the existing University students.

passages.text: Report from Faculty Senate Executive Committee March 24, 2022 Nominating Committee Rationale: In the interest of providing more time for the Nominating Committee to invite Senators to serve as Vice President and President-elect to the Faculty Senate, and for Senators to consider the service and their workload with their Department Chairs and Deans prior to accepting the nomination, FSEC is proposing that the nominating committee be chosen in the month of December. Motion: Move nominating committee selection for Vice President and Executive Committee to December. Appendix C - By-Laws of the Faculty Senate Section 5. Election of Officers. 5.2 At its regular meeting in January December of each year the Senate shall elect a nominating committee of three members chosen from the members whose terms expire that May. This committee shall present two nominations for the position of Vice President/President-elect in February. The remaining one or two year positions on the Executive Committee shall be elected at the organizational meeting of the newly constituted Senate. In selecting its nominees for terms on the Executive Committee, the nominating committee shall consider the senators newly elected as well as those who have served for one or two years, shall consider continuity of membership, and shall, moreover, seek to maintain a reasonable distribution and rotation of the positions to be filled among the various colleges and schools. #04-05–25 , #10-11–29 , #14-15–25 , #20-21-5, #20-21-41

Report from Faculty Senate Executive Committee April 14, 2022 Alignment with Title IX and Board of Trustees’ Sexual Harrassment Policy Rationale: The University Manual is the primary University Policy document, Federal, State, and Union Contracts notwithstanding, and therefore must reflect accurate and up-to-date policies regarding curriculum and governance as stated in State Statute 16.32.10.
To avoid conflict with Federal legislation regarding Title IX and the Board of Trustees Policy on Sexual Harrassment Manual language must be clear that the University follows procedures and policies in the the BOT Policy on Sexual harrassment in such cases Motion: Delete language addressing sexual harrassment in 5.74.20 in Chapter 5 and add language that clearly states that the cases involving sexual misconduct shall follow procedures accommpanying the Board of Trustees’ Policy on Sexual Misconduct, and change standard of proof to align with University Student Conduct System Standard of Proof.
Chapter 5 5.74.20 Hearing Panels.
For each case to be adjudicated, a hearing panel shall be drawn from the Conduct Board.

passages.heading: #21-22-41 | Page 4
passages.text:
Panel members shall be appointed from the Conduct Board members by the Dean of Students Office, Office of Community Standards.
Faculty or staff who have been Conduct Board members in the past and who are conversant with the current system may be asked to serve on individual hearing panels when a sufficient number of current Conduct Board members are not available.
For non-academic cases, each panel shall comprise one student member, one faculty and one staff member.
In cases where faculty or staff are unavailable, two faculty or two staff members would be sufficient.
For academic cases involving undergraduate students, each panel shall comprise two faculty members and one undergraduate student member.
For academic cases involving graduate students, each panel shall comprise two faculty members and one graduate student member.
For cases involving sexual misconduct and relationship violence involving undergraduate students each panel shall comprise three faculty and/or staff members.
Each hearing panel shall also have an advisor, to be appointed by the Dean of Students.
The role of the advisor, who shall not be considered as a member of the panel, is spelled out in 9.21.10.

passages.heading: #21-22-41 | Page 4
passages.text:
Cases involving sexual misconduct, sexual harassment or relationship violence that meet the applicable definitions of Title IX shall follow the procedures accompanying the Board of Trustees Policy on Sexual Misconduct .
For cases involving sexual misconduct and relationship violence not under the juristiction of Title IX and involving undergraduate students each panel shall comprise three faculty and/or staff members. #04-05–32 #05-06–2E , #18-19-6 Chapter 9 Student Activities

passages.heading: #21-22-41 | Page 5
passages.text: 9.21.21 Presence of Accused, Oaths, Burden of Proof, and Standards of Proof. The accused must be present at the hearing (except as provided in 9.21.26). The accused may present evidence and introduce witnesses. No oaths shall be requested or allowed and the technical rules of evidence applicable to civil and criminal cases shall not apply. The charging official and the chair of the panel will work to eliminate preconduct and irrelevant information. If the charged student feels that this has not been done, the accused may add a written complaint or correction to the materials that are given to the hearing panel or officer. When the charged student denies responsibility, the burden of proof shall rest upon the person(s) bringing the charges. The standard for this proof shall be clear and convincing preponderance of the evidence. #04-05–32, #21-22-6

We now are following up with an update to the section of the Bylaws where this committee's duties are described, as the duties no longer matched with the UM.
In reviewing the changes and in consultation with CBUM, it was noticed that a section of the UM was still vague and needed clarification.
Related changes to Chapter 8 of the Manual were approved at the 3/24/22 Faculty Senate meeting.

passages.heading: #21-22-42 | Page 4

Applications approved by the CRS will be presented to the Faculty Senate for a vote prior to forwarding the application to the Vice President for Research and Economic Development and the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs for final approval.
The CRS will also review applications for continuing authorization of centers and institutes every four years.
The review of the center’s and institute’s activities will be included in the RCAC’s report to the Faculty Senate annually.
Centers and institutes that do not meet the review criteria will be dissolved by being removed from the active list of centers and institutes, following a CRS review and recommendation, notice to the Faculty Senate, and final determination by the Vice President for Research and Economic Development and the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs.
Recommendations by the CRS will be made based on program quality, research, outreach, or educational activities, involvement of undergraduate and graduate students, interdepartmental or intercollege connections, and potential for continued external funding, as appropriate for the mission and goals of the center or institute.

RATIONALE: There should be a demonstrable purpose and documented need for the proposed organizational change. 1.
Explain why the organizational change is being proposed.
The Criminology and Criminal Justice Program requests a change in organizational status from a Program to a Department.
We request this change in organizational status to achieve two goals: 1) align with current disciplinary standards within the College of Arts and Sciences and 2) position the Criminology and Criminal Justice to better achieve a fully actualized and efficient alignment with the University of Rhode Island’s Strategic Plan (2016-2021).

passages.heading: #21-22-32F | Page 6
passages.text:
Background of Criminology and Criminal Justice at URI: In 2006, due to requests from the URI administration to develop programs that would attract incoming students, the Department of Sociology and Anthropology launched a specialized major in Criminology and Criminal Justice (CCJ) under the banner of a specialized “Sociology Bachelor of Science” (Sociology BS) degree.
This major and degree was distinct from both a Bachelor of Arts degree in Sociology and a Bachelor of Arts degree in Anthropology but still under the overarching Sociology and Anthropology Department.
Soon thereafter, the number of students majoring in the specialized Criminology and Criminal Sociology degree surpassed the number of students majoring in both Sociology and Anthropology.
This imbalance in the number of majors understandably generat ed disparate needs within the same umbrella department.
At the same time, URI came to understand that the institution was not fully able to capitalize on the recruitment potential of the Criminology and Criminal Justice major, as students who used the “com mon application” when applying for college would not see that URI offered a specific degree in Criminology and

passages.heading: #21-22-32F | Page 7
passages.text:
3 Criminal Justice if it remained housed in the Department of Sociology and Anthropology.
These concerns helped launch the Criminology and Criminal Justice Program.
In in 2016, as a result of the CCJ major’s success and the continued growth in the number of majors, Jill Doerner spearheaded the effort to successfully propose and implement CCJ as its own self -sustaining Program outside of the Departm ent of Sociology and Anthropology.
At the time the CCJ Program was proposed, the CCJ option in Sociology (BS degree) had roughly 350 majors.
In just a few short years since its launch, the CCJ Program has close to 500 majors and has been able to hire and r etain its own exceptional faculty, unaffiliated with any other discipline at URI.
The CCJ Program at URI was officially launched in 2017.
It was initially designated as a Program, which matched similar interdisciplinary Programs at the time like Gender and Women’s Studies, Africana Studies, and Film/Media.
Since 2019, the CCJ major has boasted the second highest number of majors in the College of Arts and Sciences.

passages.heading: #21-22-32F | Page 7
passages.text:
The Program is staffed by three tenure-track faculty on a 3/3 teaching load, two lecturers on a 4/4 teaching load, and three affiliated faculty contribute approximately 1 course/semester to the CCJ major.
The Program shares an Administrative Assistant with the Department of Sociology and Anthropology, and that assistant splits their time equally between CCJ and Sociology/Anthropology.
Since CCJ’s approval, it has functioned like all other departments on campus, having its own budget, faculty lines (tenure-track, lecturer, per-course and jointly appointed), and Director, who fulfills all of the same obligations and responsibilities of a Department Chair.
Rationale for Change: CCJ is committed to administering rigorous undergraduate education, producing high - quality research in areas of considerable national importance, and innovation in areas t hat will raise the profile of CCJ, the College of Arts and Sciences and URI as a whole.
We contend that a change in status from Program to Department will only better enable us to continue our excellent work in these areas and will remove any unnecessary r oadblocks to our continued success that arise from our current standing as a Program.

passages.heading: #21-22-32F | Page 7
passages.text:
CCJ is currently the only Program in the College of Arts and Sciences —all other academic units are designated as Departments.
In designating CCJ as a Department, URI will acknowledge that CCJ is equal in status and importance to all other Departments within the College of Arts & Sciences and at URI.
Previously, academic majors with interdisciplinary curriculums were designated as Programs rather than Departments.
Now, the College of Arts and Sciences more completely embraces its leadership and innovation with regards to majors with interdisciplinary curriculum.
In 2020, Africana Studies and Gender and Women’s Studies both successfully achieved departmental status, and in 2021 Film/Media become a department as well.
CCJ is delighted that these disciplines are now fully recognized at URI with departmental status.
Our request for departmental status updates our designation to align with new College -wide organizational logics as evidenced by these recent changes.

passages.heading: #21-22-32F | Page 8
passages.text:
4 CCJ strives to be a subject-area leader at URI, and a change in organizational status from Program to Department will only enhance CCJ’s ability to more fully align with URI’s Strategic Goals (2016-2021), especially in terms of enhancing student success (Goal 1), expanding research, scholarship and creative work (Goal 2), and embracing diversity and social justice (Goal 4).
The designation of CCJ as a Program rather than Department does not provide any benefits, only impediments.
Given the background described above, students, faculty, and staff at URI sometimes continue to believe that CCJ is part of the Department of Sociology and Anthropology.
This confusion is exacerbated by the fact that a number of faculty are jointly appointed in CCJ and Sociology/Anthropology and by virtue of the two organizational units sharing an administrative assistant.

passages.heading: #21-22-32F | Page 8
passages.text:
Some examples of inefficiencies presented by this perceived affiliation follow. -In our experiences as faculty, some students report thinking that they couldn’t double major in Criminology and Sociology, or could not pursue a minor in Sociology or Anthropology, because they thought all three disciplines were one in the same. -At times, students, faculty, and staff mistakenly email the Director of Criminology and Criminal Justice with questions that pertain to the Department of Sociology and Anthropology and vice versa.
Achievements of CCJ faculty are sometimes wrongfully attributed to the Department of Sociology and Anthropology and the reverse. -Processing budgetary requests and other financial matters are not infrequently impeded by the relics of CCJ being housed under of Sociology and the distinction between budgetary lines is exacerbated by having a shared administrative assistant.
It is inefficient to still have these bureaucratic processual issues persist.
Changing CCJ to its own department will help ameliorate those inefficiencies.
Moving beyond processual issues, the successes of CCJ should be properly attributed to CCJ.

passages.heading: #21-22-32F | Page 8
passages.text:
The heart and soul of the CCJ major are three junior faculty who were hired at URI starting in 2017.
These faculty should be appropriately credited within their own discipline and organizational unit at URI.
The CCJ faculty should benefit from being identified and recognized as members of a valued academic department and discipline in the University.
In terms of the CCJ faculty’s professional development and growth, this is a particularly opportune moment for CCJ to be granted departmental status and to distinguish itself as an independent academic unit.
For example, two of CCJ’s three tenure -track faculty will be seeking promotion to Associate during the 2022 -2023 academic year.
These faculty are eager to increase their service contributions to the larger University Commun ity after earning tenure, which will increase CCJ’s recognition across the larger URI community.
This increased visibility on campus should clearly signal that CCJ is an independent academic unit with unique skills to offer our community.
In addition, In F all 2022, CCJ will welcome a Distinguished Multicultural Postdoctoral Fellow.

passages.heading: #21-22-32F | Page 8
passages.text:
The CCJ Fellow will join two other Fellows in this inaugural cohort, who will be affiliated with the Sociology and Anthropology Department at URI.
CCJ’s Post-Doctoral Fellow shou ld be able to

passages.heading: #21-22-32F | Page 9
passages.text:
5 benefit from the same benefits that will be afforded to her peers in the cohort who are affiliated with a department rather than a program.
Criminology and Criminal Justice is an active participant in the success of students in the College of Arts and Sciences and the University as a whole.
In addition to serving approximately 500 majors, CCJ also oversees the Justice, Law and Society minor, which provides an important focus in these areas for many more students on campus.
CCJ plays a critical role in attracting students to URI and has a commitment to continued diversification of our faculty and students.
CCJ was fortunate to receive one of three Distinguished Multicultural Postdoctoral Fellow positions which will further support our involvement in diversity and inclusion initiatives on campus.
The granting of department status, and the recognition that comes with it, will only continue to strengthen CCJ’s presence at URI and the ability to recruit and retain the next generation of excellent students and faculty.

passages.heading: #21-22-32F | Page 9
passages.text:
For example, CCJ’s current designation as a Program rather than a Department only raises questions of concern or confusion from prospective students and their parents at Welcome Days.
The designation never elicits questions of excitement.
The move to departmental status is also especially important as CCJ considers expanding its curricular offerings to include online programs at the graduate and undergraduate level.
C.
INSTITUTIONAL ROLE: The organizational change should be clearly related to the published role and mission of the institution and be compatible with the organizational structure of the institution 1.
Explain how the organizational change is consistent with published role and mission of institution and how it is related to institutional planning.
Granting CCJ Departmental status can strengthen our ability to meet URI’s strategic goals, specifically with regards to enhancing student success (Goal 1), expanding research, scholarship and creative work (Goal 2), and embracing diversity and social justice (Goal 4).
As a Program, CCJ actively promotes student success, produces high-impact, innovative scholarship, and embraces diversity and social justice.

passages.heading: #21-22-32F | Page 9
passages.text:
CCJ enhances student success by providing premier, interdisciplinary training to about 465 majors.
Our mission statement reflects our student-centered approach: Our purpose is to empower our graduates to meaningfully consider, contribute to, and reimagine discourses and decisions about crime and justice.
The CCJ program does this by making intentional choices about our work and remaining committed to continual professional growth and community building.
CCJ faculty are productive, energetic scholars whose research tackles some of the most pressing issues in our country.
Our tenure-track, junior faculty are experts in crucial areas of national importance such as police accountability and legitimacy, racial inequality in law enforcement, and the intersection of health and criminal justice.
They have published in high-prestige, high-

passages.heading: #21-22-32F | Page 10
passages.text:
6 quality journals and have a proven track record of securing both internal and external research funding.
The move to departmental status will only enhance the competitiveness of CCJ faculty as they continue to pursue external funding.
Conferring CCJ departmental status will confer its faculty the subject-field expertise that is associated with being in an academic unit that is focused on criminology and criminal rather than in a program, which is perceived as inherently interdisciplinary.
CCJ may embrace interdisciplinarity in its approach to curriculum, but its tenure-track faculty are primarily scholars in the fields of criminology and criminal justice and their primary academic affiliation should clearly reflect that expertise when they pursue funding opportunities.
This is especially important as URI works to pursue R1 status in the coming years.
Our Program prioritizes diversity and inclusion efforts as part of its primary goals.
With approximately 30% of our majors identifying as Black, Latino, Multi-racial, Native, Asian, or non-specified, we strive to be leaders in retaining and supporting our majors from underrepresented racial groups.

passages.heading: #21-22-32F | Page 10
passages.text:
Many of our faculty participate in professional development workshops and trainings around JEDI, serve on committees that specifically promote more diverse and equitable representation in higher education, and teach classes squarely focused on issues of structural inequality.
Granting CCJ Departmental status can only enhance our ability to pursue activities in support of URI’s Strategic Plan with regards to issues of innovative scholarship, student success.
Our current designation as a Program does not bestow any benefits– in fact, at times it is detrimental.
For example, candidates who were interviewed for the Multicultural Postdoctoral Fellowship often asked about our designation as a Program rather than Department, with some specifically stating that our designation as a Program raised questions about the longevity of the position and their potential path towards tenure.
The designation of the CCJ faculty as members of a Department rather than a Program will help their disciplinary colleagues immediately understand their position in academia and increase the perceived legitimacy of the URI CCJ organizational unit.

passages.heading: #21-22-32F | Page 10
passages.text:
Finally, designating CCJ as a Department will help finally and more completely designate CCJ as a distinct and autonomous discipline and unit.
Since the CCJ Program was borne out of the Sociology and Anthropology Department, sometimes people at URI or bureaucratic processes within URI continue to assume that CCJ is a part of the Sociology and Anthropology Department.
This has not only been a problem in terms of CCJ’s ability to assert its own disciplinary identity, it also has resulted in inaccurate record keeping for FTE and mistakes in allocation of resources that required time and energy to correct.
In order to align with URI goals of streamlining processes to improve effectiveness, attract the best students and faculty, and better promote our excellent scholarship and pedagogy, a change in status is needed. 2.
Explain how the organizational change impacts other units and programs within the institution.
Have you communicated with the other units and programs and have any concerns been raised relative to the organizational change?
Describe the concerns.
CCJ becoming a Department does not impact other units at URI.

passages.heading: #21-22-32F | Page 10
passages.text:
As discussed above, CCJ has operated as a self-sustaining unit since it began and has not relied on other units for support or funding.
Given its interdisciplinary nature, CCJ has collaborated closely with other academic units on campus to offer our curriculum and create multidisciplinary experiences for our majors.

passages.heading: #21-22-32F | Page 11
passages.text:
7 If granted Department status, CCJ will continue existing collaborations and seek additional opportunities across campus/disciplines.
Data on the CCJ major demonstrate its sustained success.
Since 2019 (just two years after its launch), the CCJ major has the second highest number of students in the College of Arts and Sciences, with a 3-year average of 465 majors.
We have three tenure-track faculty on a 3/3 load, two lecturers on a 4/4, and three affiliated faculty contribute ~1 course/semester to the CCJ major.
The student to faculty ratio is 17.7:1, which is in line with the College of Arts and Sciences overall student to faculty ratio (17.5:1).
The tenure track credit hour/FTE is 361, which is about 50 hours more than the College overall.
The proposed departmental status can only help CCJ to grow the efficiency of the major.
CCJ has conferred with the various departments that contribute electives to the CCJ curriculum and has received letters of support from all academic units.
There have been no concerns raised by this status change and there are no anticipated impacts on other academic units.
D.

passages.heading: #21-22-32F | Page 11
passages.text:
INTERINSTITUTIONAL CONSIDERATIONS: The organizational change should be consistent with all policies of the Council on Postsecondary Education pertaining to the coordination and collaboration between public institutions of higher education. 1.
Estimate the projected impact of the organizational change on the other public higher education institutions in Rhode Island (e.g., loss of students or revenues), provide a specific rationale of the assumptions make in the projections, and indicate the manner in which the other public institutions were consulted in developing the projections.
Have you communicated with other institutions about the organizational change and have any concerns been raised related to role, scope, and mission or duplication?
As was the case when the CCJ Program was proposed in 2015/16, locally, there are criminal justice programs at CCRI, Johnson & Wales, Rhode Island College, Roger Williams and Salve Regina.
Currently, CCJ receives many transfer students from the two-year program at CCRI so the change in designation is not expected to change that path.

passages.heading: #21-22-32F | Page 11
passages.text:
Overall, the current CCJ Program does not compete with the programs at Johnson & Wales and Salve Regina, as these are more vocationally oriented while our program at URI is a mainstream liberal arts program.
Roger Williams University has a School of Criminal Justice that offers both baccalaureate and master’s degrees in Criminal Justice – to our knowledge, there has not been extensive competition for students.
The program at Rhode Island College is a liberal arts major in Justice Studies.
RIC attracts mainly commuting studies from Rhode Island while approximately one-third of URI students are from out-of-state, and we do not anticipate that the change in designation will impact this trend.
Given that CCJ, and the previous BS in Sociology, has a robust number of majors, we do not believe a change in designation will impact other RI institutions in terms of loss of students or revenue.
The existing programs throughout Rhode Island have successfully recruited students for

passages.heading: #21-22-32F | Page 12
passages.text:
8 their programs over the years.
There is no reason to believe that a change in CCJ designation as a department will change that pattern. 2.
List and describe any cooperative arrangements with other institutions relative to the organizational unit. (Signed copies of any agreements pertaining to the use of faculty, library, equipment, and facilities should be attached.) CCJ does not have any cooperative agreements with neighboring institutions at this time. 3.
If external affiliations are required, identify providing agencies (indicate the status of any arrangements made and append letters of agreement, if appropriate.) No external affiliations are required to deliver the CCJ major or support other activities.
E.

Describe the facilities and capital equipment (e.g., classrooms, office space, laboratories, and telecommunications equipment) and assess the adequacy of these resources relative to the purpose of the unit and to the requirements of the Americans with Disabilities Act and state disability statutes. 2.

[Note: the Council on Postsecondary Education Finance/Facilities Committee will approve lease, purchase or other agreements and ensure that the facility meets all building, fire and health codes and ADA requirements.] CCJ does not require new facilities and capital equipment for this change.
CCJ has been housed on the 5th floor of the Chafee Social Science Center since its inception in 2016, as was the previous BS in Sociology.
Currently, CCJ shares space with the Department of Sociology and Anthropology, as three affiliated faculty are sociologists (one affiliated faculty member is housed in the Honors Program in Lippitt Hall).
CCJ and Sociology and Anthropology also share a conference room, Chafee 501, where program meetings take place.

passages.text:
This space is also available for small classes when necessary.
The majority of the CCJ courses are scheduled in General Assignment classrooms around campus.
All spaces are in compliance with ADA requirements.

In accordance with the proposal, Criminology & Criminal Justice will be an official department in the College of Arts and Sciences effective July 2022. Riley, Dean, College of Arts and Sciences Re: Support for CCJ Unit Reorganization I support this proposal that moves Criminology and Criminal Justice from program status to departmental status within the College of Arts and Sciences. The program has experienced strong growth since it was established in 2017: The program has been treated like a department for many years with the director receiving chair level compensation that includes an academic year chair stipend, course releases, and summer recontracting. The move has no fiscal impact and simply formalizes how the program is viewed within the College of Arts and Sciences. Cc: N. Reynolds C. Robinson A&S Files

passages.text: The University of Rhode Island is an equal opportunity employer committed to community, equity, and diversity and to the principles of affirmative action. 2/1/2022 To the A&S Curricular Committee: On behalf of the URI Philosophy Department, I am writing in support of Criminology and Criminal Justice (CCJ)’s proposed change from program to full department status at URI. With CCJ’s demonstrated work on many of URI’s focus area (i.e., social justice, equity, and ethics), and given CCJ’s growth there could not be a better time for CCJ to make this move. We look forward to CCJ’s continued growth, and offer our support (both here, and generally) to help them see their potential at URI. Thank you, William H. Krieger, Ph.D. Chair: Department of Philosophy

passages.text: January 20, 2022 Re: Support for the Department designation for the Criminology and Criminal Justice Program Dear Christine, As Chair of the Chemistry Department, I fully endorse the proposal to designate the Criminology and Criminal Justice (CCJ) Program as a Department. The Chemistry Department brings many students to the University who initially major in the forensic option of the chemistry major but learn that other aspects of forensic science are more suitable for them. For many of these students, changing majors to CCJ has been an excellent choice for them to pursue a satisfying major and retain enrollment at URI. CCJ deserves full recognition as a Department at URI. Sincerely, William B. Euler Professor & Chair, Chemistry

passages.text: January 28, 2022 To Whom It May Concern: On behalf of the Department of Political Science, I write in enthusiastic support for the proposal by the Criminology and Criminal Justice (CCJ) p rogram to change its designation from a Program to a Department. The Criminology and Criminal Justice program i s already one of the largest majors on campus with several faculty dedicated to its delivery. I strongly encourage the A&S curriculum committee and Faculty Senate to approve this proposal. Sincerely, Marc L. passages.text: Proposed Resolution for Provost Donald DeHayes September 30, 2021 WHEREAS, Donald DeHayes was appointed as Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs at the University of Rhode Island in December 2007, and WHEREAS, Provost DeHayes had come to the University of Rhode Island after earning his Ph.D. at Michigan State University in Population Genetics of Forests, and went on to be a distinguished faculty member in the field o f forest ecology and Dean of the prestigious Rubenstein School of Environment and Natural Resources at The University of Vermont (UVM), and WHEREAS, Provost DeHayes while serving as Provost instituted and institutionalized the practice of campus -community-wide January Academic Summits and creation of the Joint Committee on Academic Planning to develop a ‘grass-roots’ approach for Academic Planning at URI, and WHEREAS, Provost DeHayes developed and instituted the concept of J -term courses at URI that are popular with students, by keeping them on -track with their four-year academic plan and are often conducted in places far-away from Rhode Island’s unpredictable winter weather, and WHEREAS, over the years, Provost DeHayes greatly enhanced the prestige of the University in keeping with its Land Grant, Sea Grant and Urban Grant traditions of instruction, scholarship and community engagement, and promoting the study of health sciences and improved general education with big thinking and grand challenges at the University of Rhode Island, and WHEREAS, after fourteen faithful years of service to the University he has decided to hang up his forestry boots and relinquish his keys to the East Wing of Green Hall in exchange for a fishing pole.

passages.text: THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, The University of Rhode Island Faculty Senate extends its appreciation to Donald DeHayes for his innovation in his role as Provost and Vice President of Academic Affairs, and his dedication to and participation in shared governance with the Faculty Senate, and we wish him all the best in his future endeavors.

1 FACULTY SENATE OFFICE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND FACULTY SENATE April 14, 2022 Faculty Senate Curriculum and Standards Committee Report 2021-2022-8 At the March 31, 2022 meeting of the Curriculum and Standards Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate.
SECTION II Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation by the Faculty Senate PROGRAM CHANGES: COLLEGE OF ARTS AND SCIENCES: Computer Science: BA, BS in Computer Science: Allow BIO 110 as an alternative to BIO 101.
Languages Department BA - Spanish major: Due to an increase in the number of linguistics specialists in the Spanish faculty and the addition of upper level linguistic offerings, the Spanish section wishes to replace SPA 325, "Introduction to Literary Genres", as a universal requirement.
Instead, all SPA majors will be required to take at least one 300- level course in Spanish language and linguistics (SPA 312, 313, or 321) and at least one 300-level course in Spanish or Latin American literature (SPA 305, 306, 307, 308 or 325).

passages.heading: #21-22-32B | Page 4
passages.text:
COLLEGE OF BUSINESS: General Business Minor: The goal is to define the courses that are available to minors to add new course offerings, improve seat management and access to options, and to align upper-level electives with desired learning outcomes. ● Effectively communicate about basic business concepts orally and in writing ● Describe the processes that underlie individual and group behavior in organizations. ● Demonstrate basic financial literacy and the ability to use information from financial reports. ● Execute competitive and industry analyses ● Describe the cultural, social, political, environmental, and ethical issues that impact, and are impacted by, business operations and management decisions in a global society.
Finance Major: We propose to 1) allow students to take FIN412 Introduction to Financial Data Analytics as an alternative to ACC302 Intermediate Accounting II; and 2) allow students to take FIN431 Financial Technologies as an alternative to BAI211 Managerial Decision Support Systems. (See Appendix A) (See Appendix B) (See Appendix C) (See Appendix D)

passages.heading: #21-22-32B | Page 5
passages.text:
2 We are making these changes in a continued reinvigoration of the Finance Major and in an effort to provide more course options for the finance students to choose from and allow students who are interested in financial technologies to learn the topics.
This change may also help the students to obtain a FinTech certificate in the future.
COLLEGE OF EDUCATION AND PROFESSIONAL STUDIES: Early Childhood Education: Since the relocation of the Early Childhood Education (ECE) to the School of Education, there have been many changes in the Human Development and Family Science courses required for the Early Childhood Education.
In addition, some changes made are not accurately presented in eCampus.
Thus, this request is to update courses required for a BS in ECE and a TCP, Pre-K-2 certificate.
We removed four Human development and Family Science courses (HDF 201, 202, 205, and 230) and update the course numbers and titles in the ECE curriculum for both programs (BS & TCP).
Health and Physical Education: We propose to reduce the total credits required for Health and Physical Education (HPE) students from 124 to 120.

passages.heading: #21-22-32B | Page 5
passages.text:
This request is the result of the recently approved (12/9/2021) Anatomy/physiology requirement for HPE students.
Specifically, we are now requiring all HPE students to take KIN122 (3 credits) (Human Anatomy and Physiology) instead of BIO 220/221 (4 credits) and BIO222/223 (4 credits).
That change allows us to reduce the total number of credits for HPE students to 120 which is the minimum number of credits required for graduation as stated in our university manual 8.21.10.
Undergraduate Curricular Requirement.
COLLEGE OF HEALTH SCIENCES: BS Nutrition and BS Dietetics: Currently, NFS offers a 3cr General Nutrition (NFS 207), and a 4cr Applied General Nutrition (NFS 210) course.
BS Nutrition and BS Dietetics students are required to take the four-credit course.
A Course Change Form has been submitted to change NFS 210 to a 1cr lab to be taken concurrently with the NFS 207 lecture.
We are making this change to increase instructional efficiency in the department.
The major requirements must be changed to reflect the change to NFS 207 (3) + NFS 210 (1).

passages.heading: #21-22-32B | Page 5
passages.text:
COLLEGE OF ENGINEERING: BS in Chemical Engineering: (1) Removing the Biology and Pharmaceutical Tracks for a B.S. in Chemical Engineering and moving to a single B.S. curriculum track for all programs.
These tracks are no longer necessary as CHE undergraduate students can receive minors in comparable subjects through established programs and new minors recently approved at URI.
Minors are better understood by potential employers and graduate programs and will be on students’ transcripts and diplomas, which is similar to how the Biology and Pharmaceutical Tracks were presented.

passages.heading: #21-22-32B | Page 5
passages.text:
The coursework and knowledge gained using minors instead of degree tracks will be the same, but will also be more flexible for students. (2) To accommodate students pursuing the Pharmaceutical Manufacturing and Minor and other new minors, we are adding the following course options for professional electives: 300-level or higher in BPS and a clarification of which natural sciences course can be used, including: AFS, AVS, BES, BIO, CHM, CMB, EVS, GEO, NEU, NRS, PLS, PHY, and SAF. (3) Science elective options are being expanded to include BIO 352, 437; BPS 312, 446; CMB 320 (Computational Bio), 341, 437 (Molecular Bio), 482 (Proteins and Enzymes); and PHY 540 (Modern Bio Phys).
PHY 530 is being removed from the list.
This will allow for more flexibility for students in their elective options and in pursuing the various minors CHE students might be interested in pursuing.

passages.text: 3 COLLEGE OF THE ENVIRONMENT AND LIFE SCIENCES: INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT MINOR: Students in the International Development minor are trained to successfully address global challenges associated with international development. Through a combination of coursework, practical experience and study abroad, students gain in-depth knowledge of and experiences associated with the social, cultural, political, and economic challenges in the global South. The International Development minor is an existing program within CELS that, over the last two decades, has been housed in the Natural Resources Science Department. However, with the departure of its key instructor and the minor coordinator, in 2019 the administration of the minor changed from the NRS department to the MAF department, and MAF has hired a coordinator (Assistant Professor, International Development) starting Spring 2021 to further develop the program. The coordinator complements existing teaching and research capacity within Dept of Marine Affairs. The existing structure of the minor is as follows (includes a total of 18 credits with a maximum of six credits at the 100- or 200- level): 3 credits of MAF350/NRS 300 6 credits of language requirement 3-6 credits of electives Approved Internship, research project, or study abroad experience (MAF/NRS 450) We are requesting that the required seminar MAF 496 be reinstated to become a required course for the minor. We are also requesting that the language requirement be waived for students who have grown up multilingual or who have lived in a foreign country. The other requirements will stay the same. (See Appendix J)

The College of Business offers a curriculum leading to the Bachelor of Science in Business Administration (B.S.B.A.) degree with a major in finance. The college also offers the Master of Business Administration (M.B.A.) degree with an opportunity for specialization in finance, and the Doctor of Philosophy (Ph.D.) degree. A finance curriculum is designed to prepare the student to be eligible to pass the Chartered Financial Analyst (CFA) Level 1 exam. This background prepares the student for managerial positions in the private, public, and nonprofit sectors. The curriculum emphasizes both financial decision-making and implementation. Careers in finance are found in financial institutions; security analysis, portfolio, and related investment management; corporate financial management leading to positions as treasurer, controller, and other financial administrative positions; and financial administration tasks in federal and state agencies as well as in the nonprofit sector in hospitals, nursing homes, and educational institutions. passages.text:
Two degrees, B.S. in Dietetics and a B.S. in Nutrition, are available.
The M.S. in Nutrition includes an Accelerated Bachelors to Master of Science (ABM) option for students enrolled in either B.S. degree, described below.
B.S.
Dietetics The Dietetics degree is required of all students planning to become Registered Dietitians.
URI’s Dietetics program is accredited by the Commission on Accreditation Council for Education in Nutrition and Dietetics (ACEND), 120 South Riverside Plaza, Suite 2190, Chicago, IL 60606, 800.877.1600, ext. 5400; https://www.eatrightpro.org/acend/.
Please see the department website for complete program information (https://web.uri.edu/nfs/ ).
The Dietetics major requires 27 credits in sciences (four in general chemistry [CHM 103/105], four in organic chemistry [CHM 124/126], three in biochemistry [CMB 210], 12 in biology [BIO 110/103; 220/221; 222/223], and four in microbiology [CMB 201]), 4 credits in applied general nutrition (NFS 210), 4 credits in introductory professional courses (NFS 110 and 212G); and 41 credits in the concentration including the following courses: NFS 336, 337, 375, 376, 394, 395, 410, 440, 441, 443, 444, 445, and 458 [capstone].

passages.heading: #21-22-32B | Page 39
passages.text:
Additionally, MGT 341 is required and COM 100, MTH 103, PSY 113, SOC 100, STA 220, and WRT 104 are required and may be used to fulfill general education requirements.
There are 16-19 credits of free electives.
Students are encouraged to use supporting elective and free elective courses to study disciplines related to the field.
Students must maintain a 3.00 average in all required courses (NFS courses, science courses, and the remaining degree courses), with no less than a C in any one required class, in order to graduate.
A total of 120 credits is required for graduation.
Students will be admitted to the Dietetics degree program after completing a minimum of 31 credits, including BIO 110/103; CHM 103/105, 124; BIO 220/221; NFS 210 or 212G; WRT 104; COM 100; and STA 220.
Students must have earned a 3.00 average in these classes with no less than a C in any one class to be admitted.Students may repeat NFS courses once.
Transfer students, both internal and external, will be admitted to the major on a space available basis through the Waiting for Dietetics program and there is no guarantee that students in the competitive admissions pool will be admitted to the major.

passages.heading: #21-22-32B | Page 39
passages.text:
Admission is a two-step process: an initial decision made after the completion of two course sequences, and a second decision made after completion of the major admission requirements.
After completing their B.S. requirements, students can qualify for the professional title of Registered Dietitian by completing supervised practice requirements and passing a national exam.
The supervised practice requirement is met by completing an ACEND-accredited dietetic internship program available to students on a competitive basis nationwide.
Admission to internship programs is highly competitive; students are encouraged to review the latest admission information on the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics website (https://www.eatrightpro.org/acend/students-and-advancing-education/information-for-students).
Internships may be combined with graduate programs in universities leading to an advanced degree.
Students who complete the academic and supervised practice requirements are eligible to take the national registration examination.

The Accelerated B.S. to M.S.
Program in Nutrition allows students to complete a Bachelors degree and a masters degree in 5 years.
Students will complete a B.S. in Dietetics or a B.S. in Nutirtion degree by the end of their senior year, and then complete the M.S. degree requirements in the fifth year.
The B.S. degree requirements are the same as for the students completing the degree over 4 years with the exception that they can take NFS 553 (Nutrient Metabolism I) and NFS 554 (Nutrient Metabolism II) in place of NFS 440 (Macronutrient Metabolism) and NFS 441 (Micronutrient Nutrient); the M.S. degree requirements are the same as for students completing the M.S. degree over two years.
Admission Requirements.
B.S. in Dietetics and B.S. in Nutrition students can competitively apply for program admission in the fall semester of the junior year, and will be notified of acceptance in the spring of that year.

passages.heading: #21-22-32B | Page 40
passages.text:

To apply students must have a minimum of a 3.0 GPA in required science courses (BIO, CHM and CMB) and must also have a minimum 3.2 GPA in the required NFS courses.
A letter of support for admission from the identified future major professor must be included as part of the application process.
In addition, students will be admitted to the M.S. degree contingent on meeting the M.S. in Nutrition admission requirements.

Students in the ABM program may double count up to 10 credits for the B.S. and M.S. degrees.
The M.S. program includes a thesis that allows students to gain experience in the research process.
Policies and requirements required of graduate students apply to students enrolled in ABM programs.
