THE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND Revised 10/2021 Notice of Change form Catalog Description The Department of Chemical Engineering (CHE) offers a curriculum leading to the Bachelor of Science (B.S.) degree in chemical engineering.
The chemical engineering program is accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission (EAC) of ABET, Inc. (www.abet.org).
Specializations to the bachelor’s degree are possible by adding a minor.
The department also offers the Master of Science (M.S.) and Doctor of Philosophy (Ph.D.) degrees.
Faculty: Professor Bothun, Chairperson.
Professors Bose, Brown, Gregory, and Lucia; Associate Professors Greenfield and Meenach; Assistant Professors Poling-Skutvik, Roxbury, and Shen; Professors Emeriti Barnett, Crisman, Gray, Knickle, Rivero-Hudec, Rockett, and Rose.
The chemical engineer is concerned with the application and control of processes leading to changes in chemical composition.

passages.heading: #21-22-32B | Page 53
passages.text:
These processes are most frequently associated with the production of useful products (chemicals, fuels, metals, foods, pharmaceuticals, paper, plastics, and the like), but also include processes such as removal of toxic components from the blood by an artificial kidney, environmental cleanup, and semiconductor processing.
The chemical engineer’s domain includes more efficient production and use of energy, processing of wastes, and protection of the environment.
Chemical engineers have a strong foundation in chemistry, physics, mathematics, and basic engineering.
Chemical engineering courses include thermodynamics, transport phenomena, mass transfer operations, materials engineering, process dynamics and control, kinetics, and plant design.
The student has the opportunity to operate small-scale equipment and to visit local industry.
Intensive work is undertaken in the solution of complex problems in which economics and optimization of engineering design are emphasized.
Students who graduate with a degree in chemical engineering work in a variety of fields including pharmaceuticals, biotechnology, environmental engineering, materials science, nanotechnology, etc.

passages.heading: #21-22-32B | Page 53
passages.text:
The URI chemical engineering major provides flexibility for students to pursue a variety of minors, such as cell and molecular biology, pharmaceutical manufacturing and formulation, business, chemistry, engineering entrepreneurship, environmental engineering, nuclear engineering, and neuroscience.
Department Mission Statement.
We are a community in a common quest to create and distribute chemical engineering knowledge in order to prepare our graduates to be successful leaders and practitioners.
Program Educational Objectives.
Three to five years after graduation from the B.S. in chemical engineering, graduates will : 1.
Practice or apply the principles of chemical engineering in a variety of employment areas. 2.
Achieve professional success with an understanding and appreciation of ethical behavior, social responsibility, and diversity, both as individuals and in team environments.

Student Outcomes.
Chemical engineering students demonstrate knowledge in all outcomes required by ABET, Inc. which are listed in the college’s student outcomes section of this catalog.
Program Description.
URI’s chemical engineering program is more than just a collection of courses and credit hours whose content reflects the required criteria.
The program has also been carefully designed to prepare students for the profession of chemical engineering through study, experience, and practice.

passages.heading: #21-22-32B | Page 54
passages.text: Through eight specific program goals, the department of chemical engineering at URI seeks to: 1) provide the necessary background in science, particularly chemistry, physics, and advanced mathematics through the study of differential equations, so that students will be able to continue their education in the engineering sciences, with depth of understanding, and learn to apply these subjects to the formulation and solution of engineering problems; 2) provide a broad cross section of fundamental engineering science courses, including some from other engineering disciplines so that our students will acquire an understanding of the way in which chemistry, physics, and mathematics have been and continue to be used to solve important engineering problems relevant to the general chemical engineering and engineering design; 3) provide students with experience in conducting and planning experiments in the modern engineering laboratory, including interfacing experiments with computers as well as interpreting the significance of resulting data and properly reporting results in well-written technical reports; 4) provide experience in the process of original chemical engineering design in the areas of equipment design, process design, and plant design through the process of formulating a design solution to a perceived need and then executing the design and evaluating its performance, including economic considerations and societal impacts if any, along with other related constraints, culminating in both written and oral presentations of results; 5) provide experience with the multifaceted aspects of using computers to solve problems and present results with word processing, spreadsheet, presentation, and professional-level applications software used for design and analysis; and provide for obtaining and using information on the World Wide Web; 6) provide a familiarity with professional issues in chemical engineering, including ethics, issues related to the global economy and to emerging technologies, and fostering of important job-related skills such as improved oral and written communications and experience in working in teams at a number of levels; 7) encourage students to become actively engaged in the student chapter of the American Institute of Chemical Engineers and other student organizations, and to continue these associations after graduation with an emphasis on the importance of lifelong professional development including the desirability of attending graduate school or otherwise obtaining continuing or advanced education; and

Chemical engineers have a unique opportunity to translate advances in our understanding of biological processes at the molecular and macroscopic levels into useful processes.
Application of the chemical engineering paradigm to biology enables graduates to develop new molecular biology tools; drug delivery systems; artificial skin, organs, and tissues; sensors and alternative fuels; and to integrate new bio-products into existing materials.
Appropriate selection of electives in biochemistry and in cell and molecular biology supports this pathway.

passages.heading: #21-22-32B | Page 56
passages.text:
Specialization with a pharmaceutical manufacturing and formulation minor.
Biopharmaceuticals is one of the fastest growing industrial sectors, both in the United States and worldwide, with a projected growth rate of ten percent per year for the foreseeable future.
Driving this rapid growth are the worldwide increase in average lifespan, major developments in our understanding of key factors behind the development of disease, and important innovations in drug formulations and delivery.
This growth has created a need for graduates who are well-versed in the basic sciences as well as all technological aspects related to the development process for therapeutics agents: production, scale-up and processing, formulation and delivery, and regulatory constraints.
The minor.
Appropriate selection of electives in pharmaceutical sciences supports this pathway.

An Inventor shall meet with the IPMAC IPED Office and disclose the actual or prospective Patent IP at the earliest possible time after its creation.
After consultation with IPMAC IPED Office, the Inventor may be asked to complete and submit an Invention Disclosure describing the Invention.
In the case of Inventions, the Inventor is encouraged to submit an IP Disclosure to the Institution at least ninety (90) days prior to any enabling Public Disclosure.
An Invention Disclosure should be made on a form provided by the IPMAC IPED Office or prepared in conjunction with the IPMAC IPED Office.
If the Invention Disclosure is deemed adequate, the IPMAC IPED Office will assign a unique Institution identifier.
The IPMAC IPED Office will have sole discretion to determine whether the IP Disclosure is sufficient.
If not on file, the Inventor shall assign ownership rights to the URI Board of Trustees and its designee.

This review may entail the commissioning of market, patentability, or similar studies at the sole discretion of the IPMAC IPED Office.
Upon review, the IPMAC IPED Office will advance Invention Disclosure to the IP Committee for review, unless additional research or investigation is required. 10.43.26 Intellectual Property Committee Review.
The IP Committee (IPC) will review the Patent IP with the Inventor and make one of three recommendations.
If necessary, the IPC will prioritize the filing patent applications in the case of an Invention.
The three recommendations are: accept to protect IP; provisional acceptance pending additional work or review of prior art; or return rights to the Inventor. 10.43.27 Notification of the College.
The recommendation of the IPC will be submitted to the Dean of the Inventor College for review.
The Dean may agree with the recommendation or disagree with the recommendation.

passages.heading: #21-22-43 (includes informational items) | Page 11

If the Dean disagrees with returning the IP rights to the Inventor, then the College may be responsible for all IP costs, unless the URIRF agrees to share 50% of the IP costs with the College.
In the case where the College pays all patent costs, it will receive the URIRF Cumulative Net Royalties share. 10.43.28 Final approval by the VP DRED.
Upon determination that the Institution will not pursue protection of IP, and no later than six (6) months after receipt of the Invention Disclosure, all rights in the IP will be returned to the Inventor.
The Institution shall execute one or more assignments to the Inventor to effect this reversion. 10.43.29 Patent IP Application.

Upon the decision to pursue commercialization of Patent IP, the IPMAC IPED Office or URIRF shall outline a commercialization plan in cooperation with the Inventor.
The commercialization may include licensing to a company including licensing to a company started by the Inventor. 10.43.34 The Institution authorizes the IPMAC IPED Office to establish a means of administering and managing the Institution’s Patent IP assets that (1) expedite their commercialization, (2) provide means for the defense of Patent IP, (3) maintain the secrecy of Patent IP when necessary, and (4) provide financial returns to the Inventor and the Institution.

passages.heading: #21-22-43 (includes informational items) | Page 13
passages.text:
Persons in the rank of instructor, assistant professor, associate professor (or their equivalents) who are employed full-time or part-time to carry out specific duties shall be given annual consideration for promotion to a higher rank. #21-22-6 7.21.11 Department chairpersons shall prepare annually a written report in which every member of their departments below the rank of professor (or equivalent) is recommended for retention in rank, promotion to a higher rank or separation from service at the University.
The report shall be submitted to the appropriate dean by December 1.
It shall leave space to accommodate the dean’s remarks. #21-22-6 7.23.10 Promotion of Instructors.
One-year contracts shall be given an instructor (or person of equivalent rank) for a maximum period of four years.
At the end of each contract year, the instructor shall be eligible for reappointment in rank, contract termination or promotion.

passages.heading: #21-22-43 (includes informational items) | Page 13
passages.text:
If the instructor is not to be reappointed, the person must be informed at least three months in advance of termination, except that at the end of the third year, if it is known that the instructor will not or cannot be promoted at the end of the fourth year, the instructor must be informed of this fact before signing the fourth year contract.
Any instructor who remains through the fourth year with the assurance of reappointment at the end of that year, must also be assured of promotion to an assistant professorship effective at the beginning of the fifth year.
Nothing in this paragraph shall be construed to mean that an instructor (or person of equivalent rank) cannot be promoted before the end of four years. #21-22-6 7.23.11 A degree candidate at this institution holding the rank of instructor or equivalent rank (see 6.11.19) shall become eligible for promotion upon (1) completion of degree requirements or (2) waiver of status as a degree candidate, either of which shall be effected within the maximum four-year period as specified in section 7.23.10.

passages.heading: #21-22-43 (includes informational items) | Page 14
passages.text:
6 7.23.12 Promotion of Assistant Professors.
Promotion of assistant professors shall not be automatic.
However, the University shall consider six years as the normal period of time to be spent in the rank of assistant professor (or its equivalent) before advancement to the next rank. 7.23.13 Promotion of Associate Professors.
Promotion of associate professors shall not be automatic.
The University shall not fix limits on the time to be spent as an associate professor (or its equivalent) .
However, 7.20.10 provides that associate professors be given annual consideration for promotion. 7.42.11 For purposes of tenure and promotion, a year of teaching experience shall consist of two semesters or three quarters, except that three semesters or four quarters taught during one fiscal year (twelve-month period) shall not count for more than one year of credit toward tenure.
Teaching in summer session shall not be considered.

passages.heading: #21-22-43 (includes informational items) | Page 14
passages.text:
A year of research or extension experience shall consist of a fiscal year minus the authorized vacation period. 7.42.12 The time to be credited toward tenure for previous experience that cannot be classified as research, extension or teaching of standard college grade, shall be appraised by the dean and department chairperson concerned.
If the experience under consideration is that of a candidate for department chairperson, the appraisal shall be made by the dean and the President of the University and they shall use the formula in 7.43.18. 7.43.10 Eligibility for Tenure.

passages.heading: #21-22-43 (includes informational items) | Page 14
passages.text: Professors (or persons of equivalent rank) who have been advanced to that rank while in full-time service at the University and who have completed a minimum of three years of full-time service shall be granted permanent tenure with the issuance of contract for their fourth year of full-time service. #21-22-6 7.43.11 Professors (or persons of equivalent rank) who begin their service at the University in that rank shall be granted permanent tenure with the issuance of contract for their fourth year or full-time service. #21-22-6 7.43.12 Associate professors (or persons of equivalent rank) who have been advanced to that rank while in full-time service at the University and who have completed a minimum of three years of full-time service at the University shall be granted permanent tenure with the issuance of contract for their fourth year of full-time service. #21-22-6 7.43.13 Associate professors (or persons of equivalent rank) who begin their service at the University in that rank shall be granted permanent tenure with the issuance of contract for their fourth year of full-time service. #21-22-6 7.43.14 Assistant professors (or persons of equivalent rank) who have been advanced to the rank while in full-time service at the University and who have completed seven years of such service including years of service in the rank of instructor (or its equivalent) but excluding any service performed in a rank below that of instructor (or its equivalent) shall be granted permanent tenure with the issuance of contract for their eighth year of full-time service.

passages.heading: #21-22-43 (includes informational items) | Page 14
passages.text:
No credit toward tenure shall be allowed for previous experience in another college or university. #21-22-6 7.43.15 Assistant professors (or persons of equivalent rank) who begin their service at the University in that rank and serve on a full-time basis shall be credited with one year toward tenure for each year of previous service in the rank of assistant professor or above in standard college work, to a maximum of three years of credit.
Whenever such persons, on the basis of credit for previous service and credit for resident service, shall have achieved seven years of total service, they shall be granted permanent tenure with the issuance of contract for the eighth year of weighted service.
The amount of credit to be allowed for previous experience, if any, shall be shown in the first contract to be issued. #21-22-6 7.43.16 An instructor (or person of equivalent rank) shall not be eligible for tenure.

passages.text: FACULTY SENATE OFFICE 224 P ASTORE H ALL , 51 L OWER C OLLEGE R OAD , K INGSTON , R I 02881 U SA , P: 401.874.5176 F ACULTY S ENATE M EETING A PRIL 28, 2022 R ESOLUTION FOR S ENATE P RESIDENT A UDREY C ARDANY Whereas, Audrey Cardany was elected Vice President and President-Elect of the Faculty Senate in early 2020 and served as President from May 2021 through April, 2022, and Whereas, she has consistently supported efforts to increase diversity and equality at URI and beyond, and Whereas, despite being a faculty member in the Music Department, she spared us from singing or musical experiences during senate meetings, and Whereas, she has championed faculty rights, shared governance, and academic freedom, and Whereas, she has maintained the role of the faculty and assured the essentiality of the University Manual in the university's governance, and Whereas, she has managed to provide excellence in leadership in the face of the unpredictabilities of the Covid-19 Pandemic and administrative transitions in both the Offices of the President and the Provost, and Whereas, she worked double-time as both Faculty Senate President and as Coordinator of the Kuali curriculum management system implementation, and Whereas, she has done all of this in a spirit of bonhomie and good cheer, finally Whereas, Audrey Cardany brought a light-heartedness to the Faculty Senate and has given it the best of all possible gifts, a new official mascot, Duncan, the dog, now forever memorialized in the Faculty Senate office, Therefore Be It Resolved, The University of Rhode Island Faculty Senate offers its sincerest congratulations for a job well-done, its deepest appreciation for Audrey’s dedicated service to both the Faculty Senate and the University, and its best of wishes to her in all future endeavors.

(Seminar 3/Project 1) (D1) (B4) NEW COURSE SEEKING GENERAL EDUCATION: HLT 400G, Public Health: Social Justice and Advocacy seeking C3, D1, GC (3 crs.) By emphasizing a broad integrative framework based on social justice, this course will help students to better understand the forces that have widened health inequalities worldwide and within societies. University of Rhode Island Faculty Senate RESOLUTION TO DEFEND ACADEMIC FREEDOM AND REJECT ANY ATTEMPT TO RATIONALE: WHEREAS state legislative proposals have been introduced and enacted across the United States targeting academic discussion of racism (including Critical Race Theory) and related issues in American history in schools, colleges, and universities.
WHEREAS these legislative proposals vary but all seek to prohibit or restrict curricula on what are labeled "divisive concepts” in the teaching and education of students.
WHEREAS the term“divisive”is indeterminate,subjective,and limits the capacity of cducators toexplore a wide variety of topics based on vague criteria incommensurate to the goals of education and the development of essential critical thinking skills. engaged and informed citizens.
WHEREAS the University of Rhode Island (URI) has a stated commitment to diversity, cquity, and inclusion (DEl), and to mitigating inequities related to diverse populations.

passages.heading: Resolution #21-22-2 | Page 2
passages.text:
WHEREAS URI President Marc Parlange has appealed to “all Americans to face the truth about our work that still remains to be done to dismantle systemic racism inour communities andinstitutions,and then tocommit to bc ing part of bringing about that change." WHEREAS in view of the ongoing rcality of violence and discrimination perpetrated against the Black, Indigenous, and People of Color (BIPOC) community, the URI has committed itself to a sincere reconsideration of policies and practices at URI that perpetuate racist patterns.
WHEREAS The American Association of University of Professor(AAUP)and URI's A A UP chapter affirm the importance of academic freedom to the proper functioning of universities, citing the American Association of University Professors1940 statement of Principles on Academic Freedom and Tenure.
WHEREAS the URI's University Manual 6.11.12 and its AAUP contract 7.2 maintain“Academic freedom is essential ... and applies to both teaching and research .. .
Academic freedom in its teaching aspects is fundamental for the protection of the rights of the teacher in teaching and of the student to freedom in learning.

passages.heading: Resolution #21-22-2 | Page 2
passages.text:
WHEREAS approximately150 organizations,including the AAUPand the Association of American Colleges and Universities (AACU), issued the Joint Statcmcnt on Legislative Efforts to Restrict Education about Racism and American History (June 16, 2021) stating their“firm opposition to a spate of legislative proposals being introduced across the country that target academic lessons, presentations, and discussions of under principles of academic freedom that have been widely endorsed, professors are entitled to freedom in the classroom in discussing their subject.
Educators, not politicians, should make decisions about teaching and learning."

passages.heading: Resolution #21-22-2 | Page 3
passages.text:
WHEREASin a nation that hasfor centuriesstruggledwith issues of racialinequity and injustice,many students donothave adequateknowledgeofBIPOCand LGBTQIAhistory and thepoliciesthatcontributed to inequities, the University of Rhode Island has a responsibility and opportunity to help build equity and social justice.
RESOLUTION THEREFOREBEITRESOLVEDthattheFacultySenaterejects any attemptsbybodiesoutsidethe University to restrict or dictate university curriculum on any matter, including matters related to racial and social justice, and will stand firm against encroachment on faculty authority by any organization.
BEITFURTHERRESOLVED that theFacultySenate standswithourK-12colleaguesatpublic and private schools throughout Rhode Island as well as across the country who may be affected by this restrictive legislation.

passages.heading: Resolution #21-22-2 | Page 3
passages.text:
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that the Faculty Senate calls upon the entire community of the University to affirm they reject any attempts by bodies external to the University of Rhode Island to restrict or dictate university curriculum on any matter, including matters related toracial and social justice, and will stand firm against encroachment on faculty authority and university sovereignty.
BEIT FURTHERREVOLVED that theUniversity standsbchinditsfaculty and theprinciple of academic freedom as articulated in the 1940 statement of Principles on Academic Freedom and Tenure.
BEITFURTHERRESOLVEDthat theFacultySenate affirms theJointStatementonEffortstoRestrict Education about Racism, authored by the AAUP, PEN America, the American Historical Association, and the Association of American Colleges and Universities, endorsed by over seventy organizations, and issued on June 16, 2021.

The eleven-ten undergraduate majors in the College of Business allow students to develop competence in special fields of interest and prepare them to meet the changing complexities of life and leadership in the business community.
For the Bachelor of Science in Business Administration, t the majors are Accounting, Finance, Global Business Management, Innovation and Entrepreneurship, Management Tracks (General Business and People), Marketing, and Supply Chain Management.
We also offer a-Bachelor of Science degrees in Textile Marketing; and in Textiles, Fashion Merchandising, and Design.
The College of Business business-curriculum develops the student's professional capabilities through a broad group of business courses with specialization in one area of study.

Emphasis is placed on the total business environment as a part of the national and world economic structure.
Theory, analysis, and decision-making are stressed in all areas of learning.
The College of Business is a professional school with courses in lower and upper divisions.
The lower-division courses constitute those taught in the freshmen and sophomore years; the upper-division courses constitute those taught in the junior and senior years.
Courses taken by transfer students at the lower-division level may be applied to satisfying upper-division requirements only after successful completion of a validating examination.

The Collegeof Nursing is undertaking the process of abolishing the RN-BSOnline Accelerated Program.Ahead of this process we would like to suspend any new admissions to the program asof Summer2022.We Academic Partnerships(AP).Despite a robust launch the admissions numbers have been declining steadily since2018.After careful consideration and in consultation with Vice Provost Anne Veeger,wehave determined the RN-BS Accelerated Online program will not be sustainable for the following reasons: recruitment for the program.Despite a national company with strong purchasing power for web search terms, and an assigned marketing representative, our course enrollment has decreased steadily from the high of624in Spring2018to the current course enrollment of272whichisa56% percent decrease from the peak. 2.
Competition for RN-BS accelerated online programs has increased and dominant programs(Capella, Western Governors,and Southern New Hampshire to name a few)have pulled from our admissions per the annual analysis shared with us by AP.Competitors have robust customer service components,

passages.heading: #21-22-19B | Page 63

Part I Statutes and Rules for the Government of the University Chapter 1 – Chapter 1 – The University of Rhode Island Land Acknowledgement , Board of Trustees and the President of the University Land Acknowledgement 1.10.10 Statement. “The University of Rhode Island occupies the traditional stomping ground of the Narragansett Nation and the Niantic People.
We honor and respect the enduring and continuing relationship between the Indigenous peoples and this land by teaching and learning more about their history and present-day communities, and by becoming stewards of the land we, now too, inhabit.” Board of Trustees 1.10.10 1.20.10 Background .
On May 7, 1981, the Rhode Island General Assembly voted that public higher education in Rhode Island should be regulated by a body called “Board of Governors for Higher Education.” In 2012, the Rhode Island General Assembly voted that, beginning with 2013, the Board of Governors should be replaced by a Board of Education, in charge of all of public education in Rhode Island.

passages.heading: #22-23-2 | Page 2
passages.text:
Subsequently in 2019, the Rhode Island General Assembly enacted Public Law 2019, ch. 88, art. 9, § 5 creating the University of Rhode Island Board of Trustees, later codified as § 16-32-2 of the Rhode Island General Laws, becoming effective February 1, 2020.
Administrative Report January 2017 , Administrative Report February 2021 1.10.11 1.20.11 Composition of the Board Trustees and Quorum Requirements .
The Board of Trustees shall consist of seventeen (17) voting members and four (4) non-voting ex officio members, including one (1) URI faculty member and one (1) URI student to be appointed by the President, and the chair of the Rhode Island Board of Education and the chair of the Rhode Island Council on Postsecondary Education.
The members shall be appointed in accordance with RIGL Section 16-32-2.2, which specifies that the governor will appoint the members with the advice and consent of the senate, and with due consideration to recommendations from the President of the University.

passages.heading: #22-23-2 | Page 2
passages.text:
At least three (3) of the members appointed by the governor shall be residents of the state of Rhode Island, at least one (1) of those members shall be selected from a list of names of at least five (5) individuals submitted by the speaker of the house of representatives, and at least one (1) of those members shall be selected from a list of names of at least five (5) individuals submitted by the president of the senate.
The President of the University of Rhode Island will appoint one (1) faculty member and one (1) student member who shall be a full-time student in good standing at the University, and who shall both serve in non-voting, ex officio capacity for a single two (2) year term.
Six (6) of the members initially appointed pursuant to RIGL Section 16-32-2.2 shall serve terms of three (3) years; seven (7) members initially appointed pursuant to this section shall serve terms of two (2) years, including the member appointed from the list submitted by the speaker of the house of representatives and the member appointed from the list submitted by the president of the senate; and four (4) members initially appointed pursuant to this section shall serve terms of one (1) year.

passages.heading: #22-23-2 | Page 2
passages.text: After the initial terms of appointment have expired, the governor shall appoint nine (9) members with the advice and consent of the senate to serve as members of the board with two (2) members appointed for a term of three (3) years; with two (2) members appointed for a term of two (2) years, including the member appointed from the list submitted by the speaker of the house of representatives and the member appointed from the list submitted by the president of the senate; and with two (2) members appointed for

passages.heading: #22-23-2 | Page 3
passages.text:
a term of one (1) year and shall be eligible to be reappointed for a term of two (2) years.
The remaining eight (8) voting members shall be self-perpetuating members appointed by the Board pursuant to rules adopted by the Board regarding the nomination and appointment of members and shall serve terms as defined by the Board pursuant to the adopted rules and shall be eligible for reappointment.
In making the appointments of self-perpetuating members, the Board shall give due consideration to recommendations from the President of the University.
A quorum shall consist of thirteen (13) voting members of the Board, but less than a quorum may adjourn any meetings.
A majority vote of those present and voting shall be required for action.
A majority of the members of the Board shall elect the chair of the Board in accordance with RIGL Section 16-32-2.2(c) from among the voting members of the Board.
In addition, the members of the Board shall elect a vice chair.
The terms of office shall be three years or until a duly appointed successor is elected.
Administrative Report January 2017 , Administrative Report February 2021 1.10.12 1.20.12 Chief Responsibilities of the Board of Trustees .

passages.heading: #22-23-2 | Page 3
passages.text:
The Board of Trustees (“Board”) is established by act of the Rhode Island General Assembly as the exclusive fiduciary authority for the University of Rhode Island (“University” or “URI”).
In that capacity, the Board is legally entrusted with the institution’s care and has the critical responsibility for protecting the integrity of the institution’s mission as Rhode Island’s premier institution of higher education and overseeing compliance with all provisions of the law.

passages.heading: #22-23-2 | Page 3
passages.text: To meet its statutory mandate as the ultimate governing authority for the University of Rhode Island, the Board of Trustees performs a number of critical functions, including but not limited to: ● Appointment of trustees, consistent with the standards and limitations set forth in the enabling statute; ● Appointment and evaluation of the President of the University; ● Review and approval of the Academic Strategic Plan and the three-year funding plan for the University, which is to be developed and submitted to the Board by the President; ● Upon receipt of the recommendations of the President and appropriate faculty bodies, approval of the awarding of degrees (including honorary degrees, diplomas, certificates and honors to be conferred by the President); ● Approval of recommendations made by the President regarding the awarding of tenure and promotion to qualified members of the University faculty; ● Review of the University’s performance under the institution’s Academic Strategic Plan developed and reported by the President and university community; ● Stewardship of University physical, financial, and human resources consistent with the provisions of all applicable statutes and regulations and policies of the Board of Trustees; ● Promoting and enforcing integrity and effectiveness of all aspects of the University’s budgeting and financial management, including changes in tuition and fees, submission and approval of the University’s annual budget and three-year financial projections; ● Approve the creation or termination of new academic majors and the creation, consolidation or termination of academic departments, schools and colleges based on the recommendations of the President who shall have followed the appropriate University process.

Administrative Report January 2017 , Administrative Report February 2021 The President of the University 1.20.10 1.30.10 Presidential Powers—Shared Governance .
In 2014, the President of the University received authority over certain items that previously needed to be submitted for approval to the super-ordinated state body (Board of Governors, Board of Regents, etc.).
The items over which the President now has authority include: “To create, and consolidate departments, divisions, programs, and courses of study within the university with the assistance of the commissioner of postsecondary education within the approved role and scope adopted by the council on postsecondary education pursuant to § 16-59-4 ” This authority was reaffirmed in 2019 upon passage of legislation forming the University of Rhode Island Board of Trustees (see RI General Law § 16-32-2.1 ).
The law stipulates, however, that this authority is to be exercised “consistent with shared governance practices, [and] in conformity with §

Summary description of proposed program (not to exceed 2 pages) The purpose of the Post Graduate Certificate in School Library Media Teacher Certification is to provide a pathway for people who already have an MLIS degree to complete the requirements of URI’s RI Department of Education state approved educator preparation program for school library media. This post graduate certificate program will be offered in the URI Online format along with the rest of the GSLIS program. There are no new courses

passages.heading: #21-22-21D | Page 4
passages.text:
2 required for the program.
The School Library Media TCP was in existence for many years and then around 2012, when GSLIS made some major program changes, the School Library Media TCP was deleted.
We would like to offer this pathway to students again in the URI Online program.
In the past, we have typically had two-to-three students in the TCP every year and anticipate increased enrollment now that we have transitioned to URI Online.
Therefore, we are submitting this paperwork to officially reinstate the School Library Media TCP.
The SLM TCP program would consist of a minimum of 12 credits Course number Course Title Credits LSC520 School Library Media Services 3 LSC596 School Library Media Internship and Seminar 9 credits total – this course can be taken three times over three seven week sessions Total credits at a minimum 12 The actual number of courses to complete the certificate may be higher depending on a transcript analysis of the student’s MLIS degree program.
It is likely that students may need to take additional coursework that focuses in teaching (LSC527) and youth services (LSC513/530/531) to complete the RIDE requirements.

passages.heading: #21-22-21D | Page 4
passages.text:
Teaching Course number Course Title Credits LSC527 Planning and Delivering Library Instruction 3 Youth Services - Two from the following three Course number Course Title Credits LSC513 Social Justice in Children’s and YA Literature 3 LSC530 Children’s Materials and Services 3 LSC531 Young Adult Materials and Services 3 The total number of credits for each applicant’s TCP Program of Study will be determined on a case by case basis through transcript analysis completed by the School Library Media Program Coordinator.
There is a need for this program because every state in New England and many states across the nation have identified school library media as a shortage area, particularly in urban districts.
This TCP provides a pathway for people who already have MLIS degrees to meet RIDE certification requirements.
Department of Educations throughout New England offer

passages.heading: #21-22-21D | Page 5
passages.text:
3 certification reciprocity for people who have completed our state approved program.
Through the National Association of State Directors of Teacher Education and Certification (NASDTEC), many other states across the country accept RI teaching certificates, making our program attractive to people throughout the U.S. as well as RI.
Since we are now a URI Online program, we hope to grow the program by one new student a year for the next four years.
We can measure success by looking at admissions data and retention rates.
This program is unique to Rhode Island.
No other public higher education institution in Rhode Island offers a master’s degree in library science or a certificate program for School Library Media TCP.
Moreover, the URI MLIS degree with a specialization in school library media is the only RIDE approved educator preparation program for school library media.

RATIONALE: There should be a demonstrable need for the program.
B1.
Explain and quantify the needs addressed by this program, and present evidence that the program fulfills these needs.
The purpose of this School Library Media Teacher Certification certificate program is to provide a pathway for people who already have an MLIS degree to complete the requirements of URI’s RI Department of Education state approved educator preparation program for school library media.
This post graduate certificate program will be offered in the URI Online format along with the rest of the GSLIS program.

passages.heading: #21-22-21D | Page 6
passages.text:
4 B2.
What is the economic need and workforce data related to the program?
Every state in New England and many states across the nation have identified school library media as a high need area.
In Rhode Island specifically, urban districts such as Providence, Woonsocket and Pawtucket, have a hard time filling positions with qualified people.
Oftentimes, RIDE allows districts to hire people without library media certification as “emergency certified” school librarians with the requirement that they complete a state approved program within three years.
Some of these people have MLIS degrees so the School Library Media TCP would be the pathway for them to complete a RI state approved program.
B3.
Provide information on jobs available as a result of successfully completing the certificate or degree: job titles, job outlook/growth, and salaries.
According to the Bureau of Labor and Statistics the median pay of School Library Media Specialists is $60,820 and the job outlook for 2020-2030 is 9% growth.
School Library Media Specialists typically need a master’s degree in library science and a teaching certificate.

passages.heading: #21-22-21D | Page 6
passages.text:
This program would provide students who already have an MLIS with the qualifications for a RI teaching certificate.
The National Association of State Directors of Teacher Education and Certification (NASDTEC), has a directory of jurisdictions that participate in reciprocity agreements and many other states across the country accept RI teaching certificates, making our program attractive to people throughout the U.S. as well as RI.
Students who complete our program could also work as youth services librarians in public libraries and as academic librarians at institutions of higher education.
C.
INSTITUTIONAL ROLE: The program should be clearly related to the published role and mission of the institution and be compatible with other programs and activities of the institution.
C1.
Explain how the program is consistent with the published role and mission of the institution and how it is related to the institution’s academic planning.
The SLM TCP aligns with Goal 1 and Goal 4 of the University plan.
Strategy 2 in goal 1 (Enhanced Student Success) emphasizes the value of experiential learning and the student teaching requirement of the SLM TCP fulfills that expectation.

passages.heading: #21-22-21D | Page 6
passages.text:
Strategy 3 in goal 4 (Embrace Diversity and Social Justice) calls for students to be part of an active learning community that includes open discourse and enhanced understanding of diversity and social justice.
With the majority of K-12 students now comprising minority groups and the current emphasis diversity, equity and inclusion in K-12 schools, the coursework in the SLM TCP emphasized DEI understanding and action steps.
School libraries have a valuable role to play in supporting diverse voices in their book collection and equity of access to technology and digital citizenship instruction – attributes that align with the ideas of civic involvement, diversity, fairness, and intellectual and ethical leadership.

passages.heading: #21-22-21D | Page 7
passages.text:

This program is unique to Rhode Island.
No other public higher education institution in Rhode Island offers a master’s degree in library science or a certificate program for School Library Media TCP.

N/A D4.
How does this program align to academic programs at other institutions?
The goal of the School Library Media Teacher Certification Certificate program is similar to the other school library certification programs at state universities in New England; they provide a pathway for people to complete the requirements of their state’s Department of Education approved program.
Our program has unique advantages because it is the only program offered from an American Library Association accredited Library and Information Studies school.
It is also the only program that offers the in-state tuition rate to all applicants no matter where they live.

passages.heading: #21-22-21D | Page 7
passages.text:
The programs at Salem State and the University of Vermont are not certificate programs.
Our program would be similar to Salem State because we would base the number of credits that would be required on a transcript analysis.
Our program would have a minimum of 12 credits and likely average out to 15 – 18 credits which is lower than all the states except for the University of Vermont but theirs is not a certificate program.

passages.heading: #21-22-21D | Page 8
passages.text:
6 Summary of Similar Regional Public Higher Ed programs Salem State (MA) has a School Library Media Licensure only program for people who have a master’s degree.
It is fully online and 15 – 27 credits based on credential review.
It is not a graduate certificate program.
They have in-state and out-of-state tuition rates.
Southern Connecticut State University has a School Library Media Specialist Graduate Certificate – Cross Endorsement for people who have a teaching certification.
It is a 30 credit online program.
They also have a School Library Media Specialist, Graduate Certificate for Initial Certification.
It is a 45 credit online program.
They have in-state, regional and out-of- state tuition rates.
Plymouth State University (NH) has a K-12 Library Media Specialist Certification Only program for 18 credits (online).
They also have a K-12 Library Media Specialist and K-12 Digital Learning Specialist Dual Certification Only program for 36 credits.
They have tuition rates for NH residents and out-of-state residents.
University of Vermont has a sequence of six courses (18 credits) for School Library Media (online) embedded in their Master of Education Program.

passages.heading: #21-22-21D | Page 8
passages.text:
It is not a certificate program nor does it lead to a degree.
They have in-state and out-of-state tuition rates.
D5.
Are recipients of this credential accepted into programs at the next degree level without issue?
N/A D6.

Existing Catalog Language (Effective Date 2022-2023) The interdisciplinary program in Criminology and Criminal Justice combines courses from six participating departments: sociology and anthropology, political science, psychology, gender and women’s studies, economics, and chemistry, to provide students with a wide range of course options.
Departments will contribute courses in sociology, law and the legal system, behavioral psychology, human trafficking, forensics/criminalistics and more to help students tailor their coursework based on their areas of interest, as well as educational and professional goals.
Faculty: Associate Professor Zozula, Director.
Professor Costell; Associate Professor Doerner; Assistant Professors Farrell, Parry, and Pifer.
The program leads to a Bachelor of Arts (B.A.) degree in Criminology and Criminal Justice.

passages.heading: #22-23-3B | Page 4
passages.text:
The program requires 30-49 credits in the major including CCJ/SOC 230(H) (with a grade of C or better), CCJ/PSC 274(H) (with a grade of C or better), and one of three capstone classes: CCJ 403, CCJ 410 or CCJ/PSC 476.
Students must select one research methods course from the following: ECN 306, PSC 310, PSY 200, or SOC 440 (301).
If students are double majors with ECN, PSC, PSY, or SOC, this research methods course will be accepted for the CCJ major, but the credits will need to be made up with an additional elective.
Students are required to take six elective courses selected from the following two areas: criminology electives – CCJ 200 (approved topics), 370, 400 (approved topics), 403, 410, 450, 476; GWS 365, 370, 401; HIS 366; PHL 318; PSY 254, 466; SOC 420; criminal justice electives – CCJ 200 (approved topics), 280, 330, 331, 332, 333, 480, 400 (approved topics), 403, 410, 476; CHM 391 (must be repeated for a total of 3 credits); HIS 366; PSC 334, 371, 388, 472; PSY 465; SOC 303.
At least two courses must be taken from each elective area and no more than four courses can be taken in either area.
All electives must be a minimum of 3 credits.

Degree Program, EDP track B.L.A. in Landscape Architecture URI’s Bachelor of Landscape Architecture (B.L.A.) degree is a four-year, 126-credit program, fully accredited by the American Society of Landscape Architects. Landscape architecture is a profession that involves the design, planning, preservation, and restoration of the landscape by applying art, science, and technology to achieve the best use of our land and water resources. The program is designed to prepare students for professional careers in public and private practice. Notice_of_Change_Form_LAR_ABM.jb.21 7 Masters of Environmental Science and Management The Masters of Environmental Science and Management (M.E.S.M.) is an interdisciplinary, interdepartmental, professional degree program designed for students who seek professional environmental positions in areas other than research.
The M.E.S.M. degree program serves graduate students from seven departments within URI’s College of Environment and Life Sciences (CELS): Landscape Architecture, Environmental and Natural Resource Economics; Fisheries, Animal and Veterinary Science; Geosciences; Marine Affairs; Natural Resources Science; and Plant Sciences.
It is administered by a steering committee selected from the graduate faculty.
The M.E.S.M. degree program has the following Specializations: Conservation biology; earth and hydrologic science; environmental communication; environmental planning and design; environmental policy and management; remote sensing and spatial analysis; sustainable systems; and wetland, watershed, and ecosystem science.

The Accelerated Bachelor in Landscape Architecture (BLA) to Masters (MS) in Environmental Science and Management (MESM), EDP track, offers qualified students in the Bachelors in Landscape Architecture program the opportunity to complete the requirements for their BLA and the MESM non-thesis professional degree in five years.
MESM is an interdisciplinary, interdepartmental Masters Degree program within URI’s College of the Environment and Life Sciences (CELS) that is focused on building expertise for working professionals.
Students who want to further their careers with private sector firms, governmental agencies, or non-profit organizations should consider this degree.

The MESM degree requirements are the same as for students completing the MESM degree over two years.
The students accepted into the Accelerated BLA to MESM program will be able to double count credits towards both degrees up to one-third (12 credits) of the total credits required for the MESM degree (36 credits total).
Only LAR and CPL 400-level and 500 level courses allowable for graduate credit are eligible to be double-counted in the LAR ABM.
All credits counted towards the MESM portion of the LAR ABM must be earned at URI.
Students must complete all degree requirements for the Accelerated BLA to MESM program within two years after enrollment and coding as LAR ABM students.
As outlined in the Graduate School Manual, one additional year may be allowed, with the permission of the Graduate School, for programs that exceed 30 credits.

passages.heading: #22-23-1B | Page 11

Failure to complete the ABM in the allotted time effectively ends the ABM, and the students will not be able to double count credits.
Admission requirements to the Accelerated Bachelor’s to Masters Program Students shall apply for the Accelerated BLA to MESM program through the URI Graduate School admission system and are eligible to apply once they have earned at least 75 credits in their BLA in LAR with a minimum cumulative GPA of 3.0.
Students will be enrolled in the Accelerated BLA to MESM program after they have met all Graduate School admission requirements and after completion of their BLA degree requirements (typically at the end of the Spring semester of their senior year).
Your application will include the following: 1) A personal statement; 2) Two letters of support (one of these letters of support for admission needs to be from your undergraduate advisor or the MESM Director or Coordinator); 3) Resume/CV; 4) Unofficial URI Transcripts.
Students will be admitted to the MESM degree program contingent on meeting all the admission requirements for the URI Graduate School.
The GRE is not required for the MESM program.

Explores the shockwave mechanics from high-energy sources such as explosives in air and underwater, as well as the fluid-structure interaction during shock events.
Topics covered include shockwave propagation in air, water, and elastic solids, as well as structural deformation and modeling. (Lec. 3) Pre: MCE 354, CVE 220, and graduate standing or permission of instructor.

passages.text: FACULTY SENATE OFFICE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND FACULTY SENATE September 29, 2022 Faculty Senate Curriculum and Standards Committee Report 2022-2023-1 At the September 8, 2022 meeting of the Curriculum and Standards Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate. WRT Summary Description of and Rationale for Proposed Changes to Program Name Change The Department of Writing and Rhetoric’s name does not accurately and fully reflect the research work, course and degree offerings, and trajectory of the department, nor does it resonate with students.
A more representative name for the department is the “Department of Professional and Public Writing.” Furthermore, with national trends favoring professional and technical writing careers, it is imperative that students (current and prospective) and colleagues are aware of our talent and specialty in this area.
This name change is expected to help us recruit students, promote research collaborations (both within and outside the institution), develop online graduate certificate programs, and attract new hires in professional and technical communication.
We anticipate a growing need for departments with this specialization.
The U.S.
Bureau of Labor Statistics projects employment in technical writing occupations to grow 12 percent from 2020 to 2030, which is faster than the average for all occupations.
It documents the median wage for technical writers as $74,650.

passages.heading: #22-23-5B | Page 18
passages.text:
As a faculty, we are well positioned for this change.
WRT faculty hold doctorates in Professional and Technical Writing and are nationally recognized, award-winning researchers in the field.
Areas of expertise include, but are not limited to, technical communication, procedural discourse, user-experience design, civic and community literacy, digital and multimodal writing, cultural rhetorics, information design, accessibility, and science communication.
The department course offerings already reflect this expertise.
The department faculty officially voted to change the department name to the “Department of Professional and Public Writing” on November 22, 2021.
Concentration Areas We are proposing two areas of concentration that capitalize on our strengths as a department and that track with career pathways, at the same time that they fulfill our goal of encouraging civic engagement: Technical Writing and Professional and Civic Writing.
Students may select three courses to fulfill a concentration area.
Note that none of the concentration areas includes the revised core courses (see below).

passages.heading: #22-23-5B | Page 18
passages.text:
Consistent with College strategic plans, concentrations will provide students in the major with an opportunity to customize the major in a way that more effectively coheres with specific career objectives.
Lastly, a nine-credit or three-course sequence constitutes a concentration that will be noted on students’ transcripts.
Revised Core Requirements We are proposing new core requirements in keeping with the latest research in Writing Studies, research into student needs, the Agenda for Change, and the Academic Strategic Plan.
The proposed core reduces the number of requirements to give majors a chance to embark on courses of study best suited to their interests and career paths.
The new requirements represent vertical integration of some of the most exciting and forward-focused of our courses.
In this core, students will find an introduction to the major, an introduction to digital writing, and a capstone that will send students into the world with a professional portfolio.
Moreover, it contains courses that emphasize the Agenda for Change.

passages.heading: #22-23-5B | Page 18
passages.text:
We are retiring courses that, in their current form, are considered outdated and Eurocentric by current scholars and pedagogues in the field (201* and 360).
Instead we will integrate the aspects of these courses that are still useful and relevant into the new core courses.
The new core will contain the following courses: WRT 104: Writing to Inform and Explain.
This course is our flagship first-year writing course that offers some of the most innovative pedagogy available at the university level.
The course offers an introduction to many of the advanced courses in the major.
In particular, it introduces students to digital writing, later reinforced in other courses.
It also forwards the Agenda for Change by promoting a learner-centered classroom in which all students— regardless of preparation—can succeed.
This course also forms part of the Harrington core.
WRT 235: Digital Writing and Rhetoric.
In 235, writers practice the craft of digital writing using a wide array of contemporary digital tools and multiple modes including text, images, videos, and sound, as well as spatial and gestural modes.
We introduce the theory of digital writing and support production by assigning complex digital

passages.heading: #22-23-5B | Page 19
passages.text: genres for diverse digital audiences. This newly revised course also reinforces rhetorical theory and argument in more relevant and culturally inclusive ways. WRT 371G: Write Now: Race, Resistance, and Language Justice. Language is central to racial and cultural identity. Through interdisciplinary perspectives, this course prompts students to consider how language shapes understandings of race and identity and how they can use it as a means to pursue social justice. This course (provisionally approved by the Faculty Senate) speaks directly to the University’s Action Agenda. WRT 495: Advanced Digital Writing and Rhetoric. In this capstone course, students apply cumulative knowledge to create a professional digital portfolio that they can use to secure the career of their choice. In 495, students learn advanced digital writing and rhetorical theory, as well as advanced production skills. *Note: The Public Relations, Data Science, and Computer Science programs currently list 201 as a possible elective in their core. We have spoken with the chairs/directors of these departments, and all support its removal from our course offerings. Film/Media Part of the Harrington School of Communication and Media (uri.edu/harrington), the Film/Media Program offers a Bachelor of Arts (B.A.) degree and a minor.
Faculty: Rebecca Romanow, Director.
Professors Healey-Jamiel, Mandel, Moore, Sama, Swift, Trimm, Walton, and Wood; Associate Professors Chadha, Echevarría, Kealhofer-Kemp, and Reyes; Assistant Professor Wyatt; Adjunct Assistant Professors Bergstrom, and Zorabedian; Teaching Professors Brown and Romanow.
The Major.
Film/Media is an interdisciplinary program offering hands-on experience in documentary, experimental, narrative, and new media production, balanced with an emphasis on international cinemas, film/media history, criticism, and theory.
Our curriculum reflects the dynamic and diverse nature of this field, approached from a perspective of film history and media theory.
Students learn to work with the evolving and overlapping technologies involved in the production of moving images (including film, digital video, 3D animation, game design, and new media), with an understanding of the broadening and globalization of their cultural and aesthetic contexts.

passages.heading: #22-23-4B | Page 4
passages.text:
A wide range of courses is available to the film/media student—courses that examine the historical, theoretical, and global approaches to the analysis and creation of moving images.
The film/media program prepares students for careers in such areas as independent filmmaking; animation and media design; film and television industries; advertising, marketing, and public relations; and media criticism.
Graduates of this program are also prepared to continue with graduate studies, either in film and media production for an M.F.A., or in a master’s or doctoral program in film and media studies.
Students majoring in film/media must complete a minimum of 31 credits (maximum 46) in approved courses toward the major.
FLM 101 or FLM 101H is a required prerequisite.
All students must complete the core courses: FLM 110, FLM 203 (or ENG 302), FLM 204 (or FLM 205 or 206), including the senior-level seminar FLM 495; a minimum of 6 credits from the production and technique category and 6 credits from the critical studies category; a minimum of 3 elective credits in courses that count toward the film major (following).

passages.heading: #22-23-4B | Page 4
passages.text:
This wide range of choices in film/media courses permits students to design a major that will meet both personal and professional goals.
Students must have a plan of study approved by an academic advisor in the film media program before beginning their coursework in the major.
Production and Technique: These courses focus on the different approaches to and practices of film/video production—how moving images are created, designed, and used to serve a variety of functions: ART 204, 213, 214, 215, 304, 306, 314, 315, 316; COM 316B, 341, 342, 344, 445; FLM 110, 220, 344, 351, 445, 477, 491; JOR 221, 331.
Critical Studies: These courses emphasize the important traditions of genre and the literary and aesthetic approaches toward understanding and valuing film/media, and integrates them into their broad historical, cultural, and ideological contexts: AAF 352; ART 374, 376, 377; CLS 451; COM 346, 414; ENG 205 D, 245, 300A, 300B, 302, 303, 304, 305D, 352, 451; FLM 203, 204, 205, 206, 214, 352, 444, 451, 491, 495; FRN 320; GWS 350; HIS 358; HPR 324, 411; ITL 315; JOR 311; SPA 320; THE 182.
FRN 320, ITL 315, and SPA 320 are taught in English.

passages.heading: #22-23-4B | Page 4
passages.text:
Other courses may be used for this category with prior approval of the program director.
The following topics courses have been pre-approved: HPR

passages.heading: #22-23-4B | Page 5
passages.text: 324 Images of Masculinity in Films, HPR 324 Rebel Images in Films, HPR 411 Film and Video Practicum, and GWS 350 Women and Film. Other film-based courses may count toward the major or the minor with the permission of the film/media program director. In order to transfer from University College for Academic Success to the College of Arts and Sciences, students must complete a minimum of 24 credits and have a GPA of 2.00 or higher. A total of 120 credits is required for graduation. At least 42 of these must be in courses numbered 300 or above. The Minor. In addition to fulfilling all the basic requirements for a minor (see Minor Fields of Study), students who declare a minor in film/media must complete 18 credit hours (at least 12 at the 200-level or higher) from those courses currently eligible to count toward the major. Courses in general education may count toward the minor. All courses must be taken for a grade except for the internship (Field Experience). It is strongly suggested that at least one course in the minor be from each of the following two approaches to film and media study: Production. These courses focus on the practices of film/video/media production, the design and creation of moving images. Criticism. These courses address critical and theoretical approaches to film/media and the broader contexts of international film history, genre, and ideology in which they are situated.

passages.text: 2021-2022 Online Catalog URI 2021-2022 Online Catalog About the Harrington School of Communication and Media About the Harrington School of Communication and Media Introduction Ammina Kothari, Director Nicholas Corsano, Associate Director Ann Salzarulo-McGuigan, Coordinator Located in the College of Arts and Sciences, the Harrington School of Communication and Media was established in 2008 to create a forward-thinking school of communication and media that prepares students for the rapidly evolving and increasingly globalized communication ecosystem. The Harrington School is a dynamic community of outstanding teachers, world-renowned scholars, and passionate learners committed to scholarly, practical, and professional approaches to the study and practice of communication and media in all its historical, contemporary, and future manifestations. Our faculty and students are principled professionals skilled in critically evaluating and strategically producing information, messages, and media by employing and enhancing communication theories, multimedia platforms, and traditional and cutting-edge technology. In our evolving communication

passages.heading: #22-23-4B | Page 16
passages.text: ecosystem, our graduates are equipped with the fundamental skills and abilities needed to adapt to an ever-changing communication and media landscape and possess an intellectual commitment to lifelong learning and service to the world through their communication skills and creative abilities. The school has undergraduate programs and concentrations in communication studies, film/media, journalism, public relations, sports media and communication, and writing and rhetoric. The school is also home to graduate programs in library and information studies (M.L.I.S), and an M.A. and ABM (accelerated bachelors to master’s) programs in communication studies. Communication studies also offers an Accelerated Degree Completion Online (B.A.) program. The Harrington Core The Harrington core curriculum was developed to ensure that all Harrington School graduates have a shared set of essential skills from across the contemporary communication and media landscape, and is required for students in each of the six undergraduate majors. The core curriculum reflects the unique contributions that each program makes to our understanding of communication and media. Beyond fulfilling many of the core requirements in general education, the Harrington core provides students with the unique opportunity to develop and enhance their digital media production skills via the Production and Presentation Fundamentals (SCM 105) requirement; competencies that are essential and applicable across a wide variety of industries and careers. Lastly, the core curriculum recognizes the value of interdisciplinary education for all Harrington students. 2 We are proposing a modification of the existing Ph.D. in Computer Science program by adding a Statistics track.
The new name will be Ph.D. in Computer and Statistical Sciences.
The new version of the program will have two tracks.
The track in Computer Science will have only minor modifications compared to the current program and the track in Statistics will be completely new.
The idea behind this proposal is to allow Statistics to have doctoral students, and to foster the collaboration between the two sections of the Department.
Students will be encouraged to design plans of studies that are interdisciplinary.
There will be some cross-requirements.

B1.
Why is the new program being developed?
The new track will address the pressing need for the statistics section of the department to have a Ph.D. program track.
Our MS in Statistics program is rather successful but our faculty need to work with students for longer period of time to complete ambitious research programs.
Given our wide offer of graduate course in statistics, it is very natural to extend the Ph.D. program of the department to have a track in statistics.
Also, the increased level of collaboration between the two sections of the department requires multidisciplinary teams with students specializing from the two different tracks.

Ph.D.
Program in Computer and Statistical Sciences The Ph.D. will have 2 different concentrations: Computer Science, and Statistics.
Some of the prerequisites are common, other are concentration specific.
Ph.D.
Program Prerequisites Admission to this program requires a Bachelors degree in Computer Science, Statistics, Biostatistics, Mathematics, Engineering, or a closely related field.
A Master’s degree is encouraged but not required.
Common requirements include course work covering the material in the following courses: • MTH 141 – Calculus 1 • MTH 142 – Calculus 2 • MTH 215 – Introduction to Linear Algebra • One course in Mathematics or Statistics for which calculus is a prerequisite All applicants will need to take the GRE.
In addition, international applicants will need to report their TOEFL scores.
Waivers can be granted at the discretion of the graduate director.
GRE subject in Mathematics or Computer Science are not required but can be favorably assessed by the admission committee.

passages.heading: #22-23-13C | Page 10
passages.text:
Specific Prerequisites for Computer Science Concentration In addition to the general requirements applicants with a bachelors degree in an unrelated field will be considered provided they have completed course work covering the material in • CSC 211 Object-Oriented Programming • CSC 212 Data Structures and Abstractions • CSC 301 Fundamentals of Programming Languages • CSC 340: Applied Combinatorics • CSC 440 Design and Analysis of Algorithms Specific Prerequisites for Statistics Concentration In addition to the general requirements, following courses or their equivalents (will need approval of the graduate program chair) may be required to be admitted to our program if a student lacks a strong quantitative background.
However, these requirements may be waived based on prior experience in industry or research.

passages.heading: #22-23-13C | Page 11
passages.text:
• MTH 243 – Calculus for Functions of Several Variables • STA 409 – Statistical Methods in Research I • STA 412 – Statistical Methods in Research II • MTH 451 – Intro Probability and Statistics • MTH 452 - Mathematical Statistics Ph.D.
Program Requirements The student must complete a total of at least 72 academic credits beyond the bachelors degree as follows: • At least 52 credits in coursework or 14 classes (3 or 4 credits each) • At least 18 dissertation research credits • At least 2 credit hours in seminar series (1 credit hour per semester).
Attendance strongly encouraged for all full time students.
A student entering the program with an M.S. degree in Computer Science, Statistics or a related area may be granted up to 30 credits toward the Ph.D. in Computer and Statistical Sciences.
A program of study can include at most three courses at the 400-level.
Students who have undergraduate credits for a particular 400-level course (or equivalent) cannot repeat the course for graduate credit.

passages.heading: #22-23-13C | Page 11
passages.text:
Specific Requirements for Computer Science Concentration Students must complete: • Four graduate CSC courses decided after consulting the graduate committee. • Four more CSC courses or equivalent approved by the student’s advisor or major professor. • At least one graduate STA course approved by the student’s advisor or major professor. • Other courses must be selected in order to meet the coursework minimum and will be selected in consultation with the student’s advisor or major professor.
Specific Requirements for Statistics Concentration Students must complete: • Five graduate STA courses decided after consulting the graduate committee. • Four more graduate statistics courses approved by the student’s advisor or major professor. • At least one CSC graduate course approved by the student’s advisor or major professor. • Other courses must be selected in order to meet the coursework minimum and will be selected in consultation with the student’s advisor or major professor.

passages.heading: #22-23-13C | Page 12
passages.text: Milestone 1: Qualifying Exam The qualifying examination will consist of written exams, with the purpose of testing the student’s knowledge of specific core areas for their concentration of studies. A waiver could be granted to a student from taking an exam in one of the areas where the student can demonstrate competence in that area. Waivers could be granted at the time of admission. The qualifying examination should be taken within the first 30 program credits. Core areas for Computer Science Concentration Qualifying Exam The qualifying examination requirements cover the material of CSC 301, 340, 411, 412, 440, and 445. These requirements are checked at the time of admission Core areas for Statistics Concentration Qualifying Exam The qualifying examination requirements cover the material of MTH 451 and 452, STA 502, 542, and 545. These requirements are checked at the time of admission. Milestone 2: Comprehensive Exam Students must take a comprehensive examination, which is composed of a written examination and an oral examination. Typically, a student would be expected to take the comprehensive examination within two years after joining the program. A candidate whose comprehensive exam performance is deemed as failing by the Graduate Committee may, with the recommendation of the committee and the approval of the Graduate School, be permitted one re-examination, to be taken no sooner than four months and no later than one year after the initial examination. Milestone 3: Dissertation Defense Students are expected to write a Ph.D. dissertation, under the supervision of a Major Professor and a graduate committee, according to the rules established by the Graduate School.

Graduate faculty in the CON have been considering curricular changes to the PhD program in the past few years.
In order to be consistent with the American Association of Colleges of Nursing (AACN) recommendations and professional standards as intensive doctoral programs in nursing, Associate Dean Hutchinson and the PhD program committee proposed a revision to the PhD curriculum in AY 2019-2020.

passages.heading: #22-23-13B | Page 6
passages.text:
This is to (a) meet current university standards and AACN standards and recommendations for research-intensive doctoral education in nursing; (b) be comparable to the curricula offered at leading PhD programs in nursing; (c) assist students to qualify for pre-doctoral fellowships and F31 NIH grant funding; (d) provide students with the rigorous research methods courses and experiential training necessary to conduct and disseminate research; and (e) graduate new PhDs with the training, skills and experience in research and scholarship to launch independent research trajectories and to be competitive for post-doctoral fellowships and tenure track faculty positions at research universities.
This change was approved by the university and has applied since August 2020.
As a continued effort to this curricular changes, we are proposing an additional revision to the PhD curriculum.
The proposed revisions were reviewed and approved by the CON PhD program committee (November 3, 2021), the CON curriculum committee (November 24, 2021), and the CON faculty organization (CONFO) (December 15, 2021).

passages.heading: #22-23-13B | Page 6
passages.text:
The speci�c changes proposed for the PhD program include updating the theoretical components of the curriculum and updating and strengthening the statistics training in the program.
A new theory course (NUR 601**) will be added as a replacement of two theory courses (NUR 602 and NUR 603).
A new knowledge synthesis course (NUR 661**) will be added to replace a theory course (NUR 611).
Two statistics courses (NUR 655 and NUR 656) have been added and they will be offered in the NEC.
Dissertation credits were reduced from 18 to 15 credits**, and a new dissertation seminar course (NUR 698**) will be added as a recommended course to take as the �rst three credits of dissertation.
Furthermore, mentored research training** (minimum 150 hours) will be required to complete as a 0 credit requirement.
This is to help PhD students to further develop research skills that will be useful for the conduct of their own research.
The total number of credits required in the PhD program will be reduced to 49 credits**.
A summary of proposed PhD curricula revisions is presented in Appendix A.
Also, newly added courses and a training requirement are marked using ** in this document.

Summary description of proposed program (not to exceed 2 pages) The department of Mathematics and Applied Mathematical Sciences is proposing to add a track in the existing Ph.D.
Mathematics degree.
Currently, there are two tracks, pure mathematics and applied mathematics.
The proposed track, mathematical statistics and probability, does not fit into either current track as it is a unique combination of pure and applied mathematics.
The new track reflects on the recently growing area of applications and theoretical development at the intersection of probability theory and statistics.
This unique blend between pure and applied mathematics, probability theory/applications and

passages.heading: #22-23-13D | Page 4
passages.text:
2 mathematical statistics, makes this combination uniquely deserving a track in the Ph.D. program.
The proposed track targets the same audience as the mathematics department at our aspire to-be-like institution1, University of Connecticut, program, Ph.D. in Mathematics with thesis in Actuarial Science2.
Like, University of Connecticut’s track our proposed track is aimed at attracting students for employment in the financial area to work in industry e.g., brokerage, hedge funds, actuarial science, and insurance companies.
However, unlike University of Connecticut, our track needs to be more broad than focused, since many of our students we do attract are seeking employment in academia and almost all academic settings our students get employed are departments of mathematics and statistics.
Furthermore, we are a much smaller mathematics department than University of Connecticut and cannot create a too focused track.
According to the AMS classification of mathematics departments3, URI’s mathematics department is considered a small public math department.
We currently have 14 tenure-track faculty and 9 Ph.D. students.

passages.heading: #22-23-13D | Page 4
passages.text:
Despite these small numbers, the faculty are highly productive, graduating 2-3 students on average per year4, but the number of graduate students has declined over the years from a high of 17 Ph.D. students in 2011-2012 to the current level of 9 students4.
This declined negatively impacts research.
This track is a much needed track aimed at attracting new graduate students (in line with URI 2016-2021 Academic Strategic Plan Goals 1 and 2 – see C1 Institutional Role) 5 and to further develop our growing area of probability, financial math, and actuarial science.
