RATIONALE: There should be a demonstrable need for the program.
B1.
Why is the new program being developed?
The new track, mathematical statistics and probability, is filling in a gap in the Ph.D. program as a combination of pure mathematics and applied mathematics with additional benefit of application (applied skills) in areas that are highly desirable for employment (see B2a).
The new track focuses on the research area of the mathematical theory underlying statistical methods and their use; including probability theory, stochastic processes, Markov processes, and Banach spaces.
All of these areas are underlying structures in several new program endeavors at URI, actuarial science and data science.
These programs are not mutually exclusive.
URI cannot develop new programs at a research university without providing a research foundation.
The development of undergraduate degrees needs a strong, relevant foundational graduate programs to attract graduate students and researchers so that all programs can be cutting edge and move forward in this ever-changing modern world of mathematics.

passages.heading: #22-23-13D | Page 5
passages.text:
In 2015, the faculty in the department developed a pre-actuarial program in conjunction with the College of Business which followed shortly afterwards with a tenure-track hire in financial mathematics to help foster the growth.
Since 2016, we worked on the development of the data science program and have been participating in research and curricula development and are also participating in the online graduate certificate in Data Science.
In 2018, we were given a position in probability theory to expand our current research program in this area.
Unfortunately, the faculty member resigned in 2020 – however we were reassured by Dean Riley that the position remains in the department and we will be searching in 2021.
By supporting this new track, URI would not only increase its much-needed graduate enrollment in mathematics and generate new revenue, but also establish itself as a provider of researchers in the area mathematical statistics and probability while growing and firmly establishing the building blocks of the actuarial science and data science programs.

passages.heading: #22-23-13D | Page 5
passages.text:
In 1929, famous mathematician, Bertrand Russell stated, “Probability is the most important concept in modern science, especially, as nobody has the slightest notion what it means.” The importance of probability is even more true in this modern age with the need to predict and examine data.
We hope to change the notion that nobody understands what it means.
B2.

People with a Ph.D. in mathematics specializing in mathematical statistics and probability are generally hired for a variety of positions with different titles, for example: Professor/Researcher, Actuary, Mathematician/Statistician, Economist, Market Research Analyst, Operations Researcher, Data Scientist, Business Analyst, Quantitative Scientist (quant), Risk Analyst, and Financial Analyst.

According to the website, in private industry an advanced degree is typically needed like master or doctorate.

The faculty of the Department of Mathematics and Applied Mathematical Sciences is advocating for addition of the mathematical statistics and probability track within the existing Ph.D. program.
The curriculum was initially developed by several faculty members with expertise in the area in the department.

The new track, mathematical statistics and probability, is inherently interdisciplinary and can be viewed as a blend between pure and applied mathematics, probability theory/applications and mathematical statistics with an aim at attracting students interested in employment in the financial sector e.g., brokerage, hedge funds, actuarial science, and insurance companies or academic jobs in departments that are mathematics and statistics.
Therefore, the mathematical statistics and probability track in Ph.D. program directly addresses the following in the URI 2016-2021 Academic Strategic Plan:9 • Academic Plan Goal 1: Enhance student success.

What are the similar programs in the state and region? a.
If similar programs exist, how is this program different or why is duplication necessary?
There are no other similar programs.
The following are mentioned for clarification but are not similar.
As mentioned in A.7.
University of Connecticut has a more targeted program, Ph.D. in Mathematics with thesis in Actuarial Science.
Our program is more broad than focused, allowing students to not only seek employment in industry (financial areas) but also academic settings with departments that are mathematics and statistics.
It should also be noted that University of Connecticut is a lot larger mathematics department (N=40+ faculty) and program comparisons are difficult.

passages.heading: #22-23-13D | Page 7

University of Connecticut has a department of statistics and the program requires some similar courses, mathematical statistics, measure theory and probability, but a statistics department is very different from a mathematics or mathematics and statistics departments with different goals and aims for students – e.g. there are required applied statistics courses – not as many probability courses.
Our program focuses on theoretical development at the intersection of probability theory and statistics.
Regional peer public universities that have comparable math departments are the University of New Hampshire and the University of Vermont.
However, both have departments that are mathematics and statistics.
University of New Hampshire has a Ph.D. in statistics with a clearly defined different aims, i.e., a focus more on applied statistics.
This is more of match with research at URI’s Department of Computer Science and Statistics and lacks the area of probability.
University of Vermont does not have a similar track.
UMass system has UMass Amherst, UMass Boston, UMass Dartmouth, and UMass Lowell.
UMass Lowell, Dartmouth, and Boston do not have similar tracks.

Brown University does have Applied Mathematics and Biostatistics Ph.D. programs, both are not similar.

Entering students are expected to have taken the following courses or their equivalents (17 credits). MTH 435: Mathematical Analysis and Topology I LEC: (4 crs.) (Lec. 3) Pre: MTH 451. Offered spring semesters. MTH 453: Basic Random Processes LEC: (3 crs.) Conditional probability and expectation. Martingales. Topics include Markov chains, Poisson processes, and Brownian motion. Stochastic modeling and applications. If time permits: stochastic calculus, Markov chain Monte Carlo. (Lec. 3) Pre: MTH 451 or equivalent.

Comprehensive Examination.
Shortly before the completion of formal course work, each doctoral candidate shall take the Ph.D. comprehensive examinations.
These consist of a 10-hour written part to be taken over eight days and, on successful completion of the written part, an oral part (normally within four weeks).
The exam is to be taken by the student within the first six semesters of enrollment in the Ph.D. program.
The rules governing the content of the written exam vary depending on which track is being pursued.

passages.heading: #22-23-13D | Page 18
passages.text:
For both pure and applied all tracks, the written exam covers the material corresponding to 10 courses, which are selected by the student’s major professor.
With the permission of the department chair and graduate program director any exams passed as part of the M.S. comprehensive exam may be waived.
The preparation, administration, and evaluation of the written comprehensive examination are the responsibility of the student’s research advisor, the doctoral committee, and other department members assigned by the doctoral committee.
Unanimous approval of all members of the doctoral committee is required for passing.
The oral part of the comprehensive examination is two hours long and is conducted by the oral comprehensive examination committee, which consists of the doctoral committee with two additional members approved by the Graduate School.
This oral exam is in addition to the oral defense of the dissertation (see above).
It is the responsibility of the major professor to request the permission of the dean of the Graduate School to schedule both the written and oral exams and to inform the Graduate School about the results.

CONSTITUTION, BY-LAWS, AND UNIVERSITY MANUAL COMMITTEE Report #2022-2023-5 - SECONDED MOTIONFACULTY SENATE November 17, 2022 RECOMMENDATION TO ADD A NEW SECTION 11.10.17TO UNIVERSITY MANUAL Rationale: To clarify the purview of editorial change to the University Manual and the process bywhich interested parties may request that the Constitution, By-Laws, and University ManualCommittee bring forth such changes to the Faculty Senate.
Seconded Motion: Add a new Section 11.10.17 to Chapter 11, Procedures for Changing the Manual. 11.10.17 Editorial changes to the University Manual are defined as and limited to changes requiredby developments in legal statutes or Collective Bargaining Agreements.
Whenever a determination ismade that editorial changes to a chapter or section of the University Manual are required outside theordinary maintenance schedule established in Section 11.10.16, based on developments in law or aCollective Bargaining Agreement, the interested party shall notify the Faculty Senate President andthe Faculty Senate Coordinator by providing a detailed justification for the request.

passages.heading: #22-23-16 | Page 2
passages.text:
The Faculty SenatePresident will review the request with the Faculty Senate Executive Committee at their next regularlyscheduled meeting or refer the request directly to the Constitution, By-Laws and University ManualCommittee (CBUM).
Upon referral from the Faculty Senate President, CBUM members will review theproposal at their next regularly scheduled meeting or at a special meeting convened sooner than thenext regularly scheduled meeting, formulate a recommendation regarding approval, and present thechange request along with their recommendation in a report at the next regularly scheduled meetingof the Faculty Senate.
Consistent with Section 11.10.10 of the University Manual, changes to the University Manual deemednot editorial by CBUM and/or the Faculty Senate shall be made through legislative action of theFaculty Senate or through Presidential action, and in accordance with the Constitution and By-Laws ofthe Faculty Senate and with Sections 11.10.11, 11.10.12, 11.10.13, and 11.10.14 of the UniversityManual.

Goal 2: Graduates will be competent in intermediate level critical thinking and behavioral data analysis skills.
Goal 3: Graduates will be able to work ethically in settings that emphasize diversity and global thinking.
The BS in Psychology is described to students as a program that focuses on the empirical and methodological aspects of psychology, that emphasizes math, science, and research methods in creating and applying psychological knowledge, and that includes a requirement in hands on research experience.
This program addresses Strategy 1 of the Agenda for Change (Infuse Anti-Racism, Social Justice and DEI Perspectives) in the Curriculum in several ways.
The introductory course (PSY 113) required of all majors, includes sections on anti-racism.

passages.heading: #22-23-14B | Page 8
passages.text:
The lead instructor for this course has published multiple papers on teaching anti-racism and social justice.
Goal 3 of the BS program focuses on teaching students to work ethically in settings that emphasize diversity.
It is in the department's future plan to require a 200-level course titled Do You See What I See: Diversity in Every Day Life for BS majors.
This course is currently approved as GCH 102G: Interdisciplinary Topics in Diversity and Inclusion and will be offered for the first time in Fall 2022 by Assistant Professor Ceren Gunsoy.
The department plans to submit this course for approval as PSY 260G after it has been taught one semester and if approved, submit a program change proposal for the BS in Psychology to require this course.

passages.heading: #22-23-14B | Page 9
passages.text:
According to the website of the American Psychological Association (https://www.apa.org/ed/precollege/psn/2018/01/bachelors-degree), about 25 percent of psychology baccalaureates go to graduate school in psychology, about 18 percent go on for more education but not in psychology, and 57 percent are workforce graduates (Lin, Christidis & Stamm, 2017).
The BS degree prepares graduates especially well to apply to doctoral or other research-oriented advanced degrees in Psychology or other fields.
For those who do not wish to obtain an advanced degree, there are many job opportunities.
The above referenced website lists 70 job titles that students with a BS in Psychology are prepared for.
The BS degree with its focus on methodology, scientific writing, and statistical analysis especially trains graduates for any type of position requiring analytic, scientific writing, or data analytic skills, such as data base design analyst, research assistant, systems analyst, technical writer, information specialist, or data base manager.
A number of these occupations are considered high impact jobs in RI.

passages.heading: #22-23-14B | Page 9

FACULTY SENATE OFFICE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND FACULTY SENATE October 20, 2022 Faculty Senate Curriculum and Standards Committee Report 2022-2023-2 At the October 13, 2022 meeting of the Curriculum and Standards Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate.
SECTION II Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation by the Faculty Senate NEW PROGRAMS: COLLEGE OF EDUCATION AND PROFESSIONAL STUDIES: School of Education: BA in World Language Education (All grades): The School of Education currently offers a Bachelor of Arts degree in Secondary Education, with multiple tracks reflecting various specializations.
Since its inception, the World Language Education Program has been one of these tracks (the other tracks are English, History/Social Studies, Mathematics, and Science).
Upon graduation, students in the Secondary Education Program obtain certification to teach at the High School level (grades 7-12).

passages.heading: #22-23-8B | Page 2
passages.text:
Upon the completion of an additional course and a teaching practicum at a Middle School, students in this existing program also have the option to obtain a Middle School extension, a credential that allows them to teach in grades 5-8 in any Rhode Island elementary, middle, or junior high school.
Recently the Rhode Island Department of Education changed the World Language teacher certification system.
Due to these changes, graduates from our current Secondary Education – World Language program are now certified to teach in Rhode Island at all levels of elementary, middle, and secondary education (grades PK-12).
The new program proposal is intended to address the changes in Rhode Island certification regulations, which will require significant changes (over 25%) to the requirements for our current BA in Secondary Education with a specialization in World Languages, effectively transforming it into a BA in World Language Education-All Grades.

passages.heading: #22-23-8B | Page 2
passages.text:
In the proposed new program, students will take a variety of existing EDC courses in Elementary Education, Early Childhood Education, Secondary Education, and Teaching English as a Second Language / Bilingual Education concentrations so that, upon graduation, they will be more versatile and highly employable educators who are better prepared to teach effectively in a wider variety of educational settings.
The new program will educate our students to become reflective teachers committed to global citizenship, social justice, and multicultural education.
Our program of study, based on current research and best practices, has been carefully crafted to provide our teacher candidates with ample opportunities to learn about different professional contexts and acquire knowledge about learning theory (social, emotional, and academic), and how to address the individualized needs of diverse learners.
Through a 1

passages.heading: #22-23-8B | Page 3
passages.text: variety of hands-on teaching experiences at PK-12 academic settings our candidates will have the opportunity to apply what they learn in URI courses in culturally responsive practices but also to learn to work with and from practicing teachers. The standard program of study that our candidates will follow will allow them to graduate from URI with a double major in Education and in a Foreign Language. Students will develop their teaching skills and acquire knowledge through coursework that focuses on teaching and learning at different developmental levels, and on cutting-edge second language acquisition theories. Our program will help teacher candidates develop the necessary confidence and experience to effectively engage with a diverse group of students in a variety of educational settings. Upon completion of our program and after successfully completing the licensure tests, our well prepared graduates will be ready to apply for the Rhode Island World Language teacher certification in grades K-12. 2

What is the economic need and workforce data related to the program?
One of the purposes of the new program is to attract, retain, and graduate more teachers from multicultural, multilingual, historically marginalized, and under -represented groups in the education profession.
The inclusion of coursework in Bilingual Education and Teaching English as a Second Language aims to attract and harness the unique talents and lived experiences of students from our important local and regional multilingual communities.
In addition to this, the RI

passages.heading: #22-23-8B | Page 8
passages.text:
4 Department of Education, through the work of the Rhode Island Council on Elementary and Secondary Education, is currently in the process of changing the state’s high school graduation requirements.
Among the proposed changes to the system, students will be required to take a minimum of two years of study of the same language in order to successfully graduate from high school.
This change has the potential to strengthen the general pipeline of candidates for our proposed World Language Education-All Grades program.
Finally, given both the regional and national shortage of world language educators, as evidenced by the 100% employment rates of graduates from our existing program and the high percentage of new language teachers who are being hired through an emergency certification process, the demand for well-qualified K-12 world language educators is high and the urgent need for this program is clear.

Embracing Rhode Island ’s heritage of independent thought, we value: As stated in the URI’s mission statement, our institutional values: o Creativity and scholarship o Diversity, fairness, and respect o Engaged learning and civic involvement o Intellectual and ethical leadership The program that we are proposing is not only consistent with those key guiding principles, but it can have a significant impact by strengthening those values in our learning community and RI society.

Our program, based on rigorous scholarship, will help to shape the face of education in the state.
The RI Department of Education is about to approve new high school graduation requirements that include the study of the same World Language for two years.
A new WL Education Program could potentially attract more heritage speakers into the teaching profession.
This will increase the diversity among faculty in our schools and will provide multilingual students with role models with whom they can identify.
We anticipate that our graduates will become

The new proposed program of study will help our graduates develop their intercultural skills and acquire a “glocal” perspective, that is, the capacity to understand how local and global events are interconnected and the effects that they have on each other.

Our program will not create any new competition to attract students that will be detrimental for other RI institutions of higher education, as the intent of the program is to adjust an already existing academic offering to the new certification reality implemented by the RI Department of Education.
The impact of the program will not be noticeable to other WL Education Programs around the state, only to the URI students that would benefit from a curriculum that better adjusts to their future professional needs.

passages.heading: #22-23-8B | Page 9
passages.text:
To the best of my knowledge there are four other higher ed institutions in RI that offer World Language Education programs: Salve Regina, Rhode Island College, Providence College and Roger Williams University.
None of these programs is new: such programs have been in place for at least 10 years.
In all those cases, the original World Language programs were part of the Secondary Education programs, just one of the multiple tracks that students could take.
Two of those institutions have already taken steps to adapt to the new RIDE certification reality.
Recently, in both Salve Regina and RIC the World Language Program has become independent.
According to the information listed on their websites, the World Language Education program is still a track of the Secondary Education Program in the cases of both Providence College (<https://academics.providence.edu/secondary-education/>) and Roger Williams University (<https://www.rwu.edu/undergraduate/academics/programs/secondary-education>).

passages.heading: #22-23-8B | Page 9
passages.text:
The new URI World Language Education program will fill a void that currently exists in the world language teacher preparation programs by focusing on providing more comprehensive preparation to our candidates so they can be effective teachers at the elementary and secondary levels, and it will allow us to continue being the leader in preparing future world language educators in the state of RI.

Upon examination of the program of study of existing academic programs at other institutions, one can say that, in most cases their curriculum still follows very closely the Secondary Education program.

This is true even in the case of Salve Regina, an institution in which the World Language Program has become independent.2 In the case of RIC, our program of study will make a slightly increased emphasis on Second Language Teaching and will include courses that focus on early learners.3 The proposed program will include more offerings (existing courses already taught regularly by the School of Education faculty) that will prepare our students to teach at the PK-5 grades and provide a stronger foundation in theories and methodologies of teaching Second Languages.
Salve Regina currently offers two tracks in their World Language Education program: French and Spanish.
RIC currently offers three tracks in their World Language Education program (French, Portuguese, and Spanish).
Providence Colleges offers three tracks (French, Italian, and Spanish) and Roger Williams University offers five (French, German, Italian, Latin, and Spanish).
URI is the only institution that offers a World Language Education track in Chinese and the only public institution to offer tracks in German, Italian, and Latin.

Students also must complete 40 credits of courses that will count toward URI general education requirements.
There is substantial overlap between the General Education

Students can take elective courses among the multiple courses offered by the School of Education in order to reach the 120 credits required for graduation.
Students would be advised that the following courses will be especially useful for their future careers.
Electives: Course number and title URI’s 2021-22 Catalog description EDC 423: Teaching Comprehension and Response in the Elementary School LEC: (3 crs.) Analysis of narrative and expository text; strategies for teaching literacy in elementary grades using these texts, specifically focusing on vocabulary, comprehension, response, and integrating these literacy practices throughout the curriculum. (Lec. 3) Pre: Acceptance into a teacher preparation program or teacher certification, and prior or concurrent enrollment in EDC 312 or 512; or permission of instructor.

passages.heading: #22-23-8B | Page 15

The RIDE certification requirements for World Language teachers are:4 ● Bachelor’s degree from a regionally accredited institution ● Completion of an approved program or Credential Review Consortium Institution (CRCI) credential review plan for the preparation of All Grades World Language Teachers in a specific language ● Completion of a minimum of 12 weeks of student teaching in this area and a minimum of 60 hours field experience prior to student teaching ● Demonstration of meeting the pedagogical competencies of the Rhode Island Professional Teaching Standards (RIPTS) ● Demonstration of meeting the content competencies as prescribed by the American Council for the Teaching of Foreign Languages (ACTFL) Other requirements: ● Meet all Rhode Island pedagogy and subject matter testing requirements for this certificate area 4 See: <https://www.ride.ri.gov/Portals/0/Uploads/Documents/Teachers-and-Administrators-Excellent- Educators/Educator-Certification/Cert-Requirements/tbd_AG-World%20Languages-Req.pdf?ver=2015-01-22- 123036-823>.
The RIDE has stated that taking the PRAXIS II exam will not be a certification requirement in the near future.

passages.heading: #22-23-8B | Page 16
passages.text:
12 Assessment Requirements: All applicants must meet the following Rhode Island assessment requirements: ● Applicants must achieve a passing score of 160 on the Praxis II Principals of Learning and Teaching – Grades K-6 Test (5622) OR a passing score of 157 on the Praxis II Principals of Learning and Teaching – Grades 7-12 test (5624) AND a passing score of 162 on the French World Language Test (5174), a passing score of 163 on the German World Language Test (5183), a passing score of 161 on the Latin Test (5601), a passing score of 168 on the Spanish World Language Test (5195), or a passing score of Advanced Low on all other world languages – Oral Proficiency Interview. ● Applicants prepared in a program where the language of instruction was not English must achieve a passing core of 64 on the Versant Pro Speaking and Writing English assessments.

The financial cost to the university of this new program will be zero, as our students will be required to take existing courses that are regularly offered in the School of Education.

The World Language Education program will not require the creation of any new faculty positions or the reassignment of existing positions.

Students selected should have the necessary potential and commitment to complete the program successfully.

passages.heading: #22-23-8B | Page 16
passages.text:
We are currently trying to attract more heritage speakers of world languages into the teaching profession.
We are contacting students that have taken SPA 210: Spanish for Heritage Speakers and sharing information with them about the different career paths and employment opportunities that they will have upon graduation if they complete our program.
We are also underlining to them that they could have a direct and significant impact on their communities.
As mentioned above, one of the purposes of the new program is to attract, retain, and graduate more teachers from multicultural, multilingual, historically marginalized, and under-represented groups in the education profession.
The inclusion of coursework in Bilingual Education and Teaching English as a Second Language aims to attract and harness the unique talents and lived experiences of students from our important local and regional multilingual communities.
In addition to this, the RI Department of Education, through the work of the Rhode Island Council on Elementary and Secondary Education, is currently in the process of changing the state’s high school graduation requirements.

passages.heading: #22-23-8B | Page 16
passages.text:
Among the proposed changes to the system, students will be required to take a minimum of two years of study of the same language in order to successfully graduate from high school.
This change has the potential to strengthen the general pipeline of

passages.heading: #22-23-8B | Page 17
passages.text: 13 candidates for our proposed World Language Education-All Grades program. Finally, given both the regional and national shortage of world language educators, as evidenced by the 100% employment rates of graduates from our existing program and the high percentage of new language teachers who are being hired through an emergency certification process, the demand for well-qualified K-12 world language educators is high and the urgent need for this program is clear. Proposer(s): Iñaki Pérez Ibáñez, Assistant Professor in Spanish and Teacher Education Department(s): School of Education College(s): College of Education and Professional Studies Part II.
Briefly provide the following information (not to exceed two pages): The School of Education currently offers a Bachelor of Arts degree in Secondary Education, with multiple tracks reflecting various specializations.
Since its inception, the World Language Education Program has been one of these tracks (the other tracks are English, History/Social Studies, Mathematics, and Science).
Upon graduation, students in the Secondary Education Program obtain certification to teach at the High School level (grades 7-12).

passages.heading: #22-23-8B | Page 28
passages.text:
Upon the completion of an additional course and a teach ing practicum at a Middle School, students in this existing program also have the option to obtain a Middle School extension, a credential that allows them to teach in grades 5-8 in any Rhode Island elementary, middle, or junior high school.
Recently the Rhode Island Department of Education changed the World Language teacher certification system.
Due to these changes, graduates from our current Secondary Education – World Language program are now certified to teach in Rhode Island at all levels of elementary, middle, and secondary education (grades PK-12).
The new program proposal is intended address the changes in Rhode Island certification regulations, which will require significant changes (over 25%) to the requirements for our current BA in Secondary Education with a specialization in World Languages, effectively transforming it into a BA in World Language Education -All Grades.

passages.heading: #22-23-8B | Page 28
passages.text:
In the proposed new program, students will take a variety of existing EDC courses in Elementary Education, Early Childhood Education, Secondary Education, and Teaching English as a Second Language / Bilingual Education concentrations so that, upon graduation, they will be more versatile and highly employable educators who are better prepared to teach effectively in a wider variety of educational settings.
The financial cost to the university of this new program will be zero, as our students will be required to take existing courses that are regularly offered in the School o f Education.
The development of new courses will not be necessary to implement the proposed overhaul of the program.
The new program will not require the hiring of any new faculty (neither full time nor adjunct faculty).

JCAP Pre-Proposal Form Revised 2021 One of the purposes of the new program is to attract, retain, and graduate more teachers from multicultural, multilingual, historically marginalized, and under-represented groups in the education profession.
The inclusion of coursework in Bilingual Education and Teaching English as a Second Language aims to attract and harness the unique talents and lived experiences of students from our important local and regional multilingual communities.
In addition to this, the RI Department of Education, through the work of the Rhode Island Council on Elementary and Secondary Education, is currently in the process of changing the state’s high school graduation requirements.
Among the proposed changes to the system, students will be required to take a minimum of two years of study of the same language in order to successfully graduate from high school.
This change has the potential to strengthen the general pipeline of candidates for our proposed World Langua ge Education-All Grades program.

passages.heading: #22-23-8B | Page 29
passages.text:
Finally, given both the regional and national shortage of world language educators, as evidenced by the 100% employment rates of graduates from our existing program and the high percentage of new language teachers who are being hired through an emergency certification process, the demand for well-qualified K-12 world language educators is high and the urgent need for this program is clear.

FACULTY SENATE OFFICE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND FACULTY SENATE September 29, 2022 Report of the Faculty Senate Special Summer Curriculum Committee Report 2022-2023-03 At the July 7, 2022 meeting of the Special Summer Curriculum Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate.
SECTION II Curricular Matter Which Require Confirmation by the Faculty Senate NEW PROGRAMS: COLLEGE OF EDUCATION AND PROFESSIONAL STUDIES: School of Education: (see Appendix C) B.S. in Early Childhood Education, Pre-K-2 Certificate The Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) program for working professionals in the incumbent workforce comprises two pathways: (1) B.S., Pre-K-2 Certification Pathway and (2) Post Baccalaureate, Pre-K-2 Certification only (proposed separately).
Students in these two pathways will be in the same cohort to complete their undergraduate degree with a Pre-K-2 teaching certification and Post Baccalaureate Certificate only program to be certified as a teacher and advance in their teaching profession.

passages.heading: #22-23-4C | Page 2
passages.text:
At least 30 hours per week of the incumbent workforce candidate’s active teaching are required; other non-traditional work conditions with RIDE approval can be considered.
The ECCE program will be offered fully online through URIOnline with field experience in the candidates’ own PreK-2 teaching setting, running 7-week accelerated sessions, including a summer session, for 2 years.
The Pathway 1 (BS + Pre-K-2 certification) requires an associate's degree from CCRI (or equivalent pre-academic work) to complete the Bachelor's degree.
The ECCE program is designed to meet the needs of the incumbent early childhood care and education workforce to access high-quality teaching certificate programs in order to improve teacher quality and student learning.
Aligned with the URI mission, the SOE & CEPS strategic plans, and the Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) Strategic Plan for Rhode Island, this program is designed to ensure that the incumbent workforce of early childhood educators has accessible, high-quality, and meaningful pathways toward credential attainment, career advancement, and higher compensation.
This program is supported by The RIDE Educator Pathways Planning Grant. 1

passages.text: 4 In the State of Rhode Island, in order to achieve a high-quality rating (4 or 5 stars) on the state’s Quality Rating and Improvement System (BrightStars), child care programs must employ

passages.heading: #22-23-4C | Page 7
passages.text:
5 workers with college credits in Early Childhood Education (ECE) and postsecondary degrees.
In addition, childcare programs that seek to become a Rhode Island Pre-Kindergarten provider must employ Bachelor’s degree and Pre-K-2 certiﬁed teachers in order to achieve Comprehensive Early Childhood Education (CECE) program quality approval (RI Board of Education, 2018).
A lack of a trained workforce prevents child care centers from moving up on the BrightStars continuum, from qualifying to become a State Pre-K provider, and from receiving CECE approval.
Furthermore, with the implementation of tiered reimbursement in 2018, child care programs with higher quality ratings are reimbursed at higher rates by the Child Care Assistance Program.
These higher reimbursement rates will allow programs to increase staﬀ compensation.
More importantly, RI is suﬀering from a severe shortage in staﬃng that consequently aﬀects the quality of early childhood teaching and learning in early childhood education (RI Early Learning Council meeting, RI Kids Count report, 2020, 2021).

These 11 standards are learned and applied early and consistently in the program, beginning in the Methods I course and practicum, to all key assignments, including lesson plans, group presentations, and ﬁeld work.
Speciﬁcally, the 11 standards address the following: 1.
General Knowledge (showing evidence of knowledge, skills, and dispositions); 2.
Content Knowledge (enlisting appropriate instructional materials and resources, multiple means of communication and representation); 3.
Learning and development (activating students’ prior knowledge, preparing developmentally appropriate learning experiences; 4.
Diversity of learners (working with specialists, including appropriate provisions for learners with special needs and Multi-language learners (MLLs), and attending IEP, 504, PLP and PLP meetings, enlisting culturally relevant teaching); 5.
Critical Thinking and Problem solving (applying inquiry, evidence, discovery, and hands–on engagement with learners); 6.
Classroom management (establishing a safe and secure classroom environment; helping students to be self-motivated); 7.

13 General Academic Requirements Students in Pathway 1 for a BS in ECE degree, Pre-K-2 are expected to maintain/earn a minimum overall G.P.A. of 2.50.
Therefore, the ECCE program requires a G.P.A. of 2.50 or better in all transfer credits in Education and in Human Development & Family Studies courses.
All students in both pathways must earn a grade of ‘C’ or above in all ECCE core courses and an ‘S’ in all ﬁeld practicals.
A BS in ECCE requires a minimum of 120 credits (including 39 ECCE program credits).

passages.text: Report of the Academic Calendar Committee (ACC) Abraham Kovoor, Chair February 23, 2023 Faculty Senate Meeting The ACC presented its initial report at the October 20, 2022 Senate meeting and as a result, three bills were approved and signed. This legislation addressed: Juneteenth as a holiday in the summer calendar; the Wednesday before Thanksgiving as a non-standard day; and adjustments to the Columbus Day/Indigenous People’s Day holiday in the long-range calendar. The initial report also addressed a question related to commencement. Given the growing size of the student body and the number of programs offered, the University has space limitations for various graduation-related events. This has led to scheduling such events over the course of a full weekend and this should be reflected in the Calendar. There was no objection to this proposal when originally presented last October but formal approval is now requested. A seconded motion from the ACC now comes to the Faculty Senate: “That the University adopt and the calendar reflect the addition of the Friday immediately previous to the Commencement Weekend (formally just Saturday and Sunday) for Commencement Activities and that the Faculty Senate confirm the change in the calendar for transparency.”

CONSTITUTION, BY-LAWS, AND UNIVERSITY MANUAL COMMITTEEReport #2022-2023-16 -MOTIONFACULTY SENATE, February 23, 2023 Context and rationale: Request from Enrollment Services Advisory Council (ESAC) to the FacultySenate Executive Committee (FSEC), referred directly by FSEC to CBUM to create a policy for resolvinggrades of incomplete within a timely manner and that would trigger the assignment of an automaticpermanent grade when the student or instructor does not meet the grade change deadline.
CBUMreviewed and discussed the ESAC proposal, and considered recommendations from the Curriculumand Standards Committee, the Teaching, Advising and Assessment Committee, the Faculty SenateExecutive Committee, and the Office of the Provost.

passages.heading: #22-23-30 | Page 2
passages.text:
CBUM proposes to the Faculty Senate amendments to our current policy to: ● clarify the temporary nature of the grade of Incomplete and the unique and infrequentcircumstances in which it is appropriate to assign the grade of Incomplete, ● encourage student and faculty accountability in the process of resolving Incompletes, ● promote efficient and just resolution of Incompletes to convert these temporary grades intopermanent grades by the time the student graduates, and ● trigger an automatic grade change to a non-punitive “NC” when the instructor does notsubmit a grade change report prior to the student’s official graduation date.
Current language in Chapter 8 - Academic Regulations: 8.53.20 Incomplete.
A student shall receive a report of “Incomplete” in any course in which the course workhas been passing up until the time of a documented precipitating incident or condition, but has not beencompleted because of illness or another reason which in the opinion of the instructor justifies the report.

passages.heading: #22-23-30 | Page 2
passages.text:
Aninstructor who issues a grade of “Incomplete” may forward a written explanation to the student’s academicdean. #15-16-30 8.53.21 The student receiving an “Incomplete” shall make necessary arrangements with the instructor or, in theinstructor’s absence, with the instructor’s chairperson to remove the deficiency.
This arrangement shall bemade prior to the following mid semester for the undergraduate student and within one calendar year for thegraduate student.
Proposed changes and additions to Chapter 8 - Academic Regulations: 8.53.20 Incomplete.
A student shall receive a temporary grade report of “Incomplete” in any course in whichthe when course work has been passing up until the time of a but is not completed by the end of the semesterdue to documented precipitating incident or condition, but has not been completed because of extenuatingcircumstances beyond the ability of the student to predict and control, such as a serious illness or medicalcondition, or another compelling reason which in the opinion of the instructor justifies the grade.

passages.heading: #22-23-30 | Page 2
passages.text: An instructorwho issues a grade of “Incomplete” may forward a written explanation to the student’s academic dean.Assignment of the temporary grade of Incomplete is made sparingly and presumes both that the studentintends and will be able to complete the coursework in the established time frame, and that the instructorintends and will be able to review the completed work in that established time frame. #15-16-30

passages.heading: #22-23-30 | Page 3
passages.text:
8.53.21 Resolution of Grades of Incomplete.
The student receiving an “Incomplete” shall make necessaryarrangements with the instructor to remove the deficiency. or, iIn the instructor’s absence, with theappropriate administrator shall manage the process of resolving grades of Incomplete (the instructor’schairperson in the case of programs with a chairperson, and in the case of programs without a chairperson, theinstructor’s college dean or the designee of the instructor’s college dean).
This arrangement shall be madeprior to the submission of the temporary grade of Incomplete whenever possible, and not later than prior tothe following mid semester for the undergraduate student and within one calendar year for the graduatestudent.
This arrangement shall not include plans for the student to officially re-enroll in the course during afuture term: official re-enrollment accompanied by a grade reported on a future grade roster shall not resolvethe temporary grade of Incomplete (see 8.53.23).

Our regional competition would be Southern New Hampshire University's Social Media Certificate that focuses heavily on marketing topics and is similar to content offered by Hubspot.

However, despite the numerous advantages of social media use for business and public relations, many organizations are unaware of how they can use social media to maximize the benefits of social media marketing and communication.
Many practitioners are unaware of the need for communication strategies to enhance their sales and reputations.
As the world of social media rapidly changes and grows, having an effective social media communication strategy is imperative.
Using a theory-driven and evidence-based approach, participants will learn how to develop effective social media communication strategies to meet various organizational/business goals, such as product/service sales, campaigns, reputation management, and crisis management.

This course will introduce strategies for developing an effective social media branding campaign.
You will learn how to set measurable campaign goals and use storytelling techniques to create diverse and accessible content for appropriate social media campaigns.
Modes of Creative Content Creation Course Description This course offers an introduction to the modern content creation landscape, with specific focus on best practices for social media applications.
Students will engage in crafting creative briefs, pre-production, production and post production while creating content for campaigns of their own.

Because of the proposed structure of the ABM program, the cost incurred by the student will be substantially less than the traditional path of completing a 4-year bachelor’s degree followed by a 2-year master’s program.

passages.heading: #22-23-26C | Page 6
passages.text:
This program will also provide students with the opportunity to enter the neuroscience workforce with all the benefits of a master’s degree without losing the time and expenses that two years of traditional graduate study would otherwise cost them.
As noted previously, students will complete the same graduate level course work on the INP Master’s, non-thesis or thesis track, thereby becoming knowledgeable about general neuroscience topics as well as research methods, neurobiology, neuroethics, human neuroanatomy and neurology, and much more.
The INP ABM program will also provide students with course instruction and research experience from faculty who are conducting cutting-edge science concerning brain functioning across variety of areas from aging, movement, language processing, medicinal plants, and molecular proteins, to the study of brain-based disorders including Alzheimer’s disease, ALS, ADHD, Fanconia Anemia, Parkinson’s disease, epilepsy, medicinal plants, neuropharmacology and other areas of specialty.
The goal of the program is for students to be able complete an accelerated bachelor to masters program within a five-year period.

passages.heading: #22-23-26C | Page 6
passages.text:
The INP ABM program aligns with the University’s mission and strategic plan by supporting the University’s quest for knowledge and serving and enriching the lives of its students.
The key players in the INP ABM program, namely the students, faculty, staff, will be striving to achieve one common purpose: to learn and lead together.
The ABM program also aligns with the current strategic plan by fostering student success, exposing students to cutting edge research and lab techniques, and by embracing diversity at both the student and faculty level.
It is important to note that the INP is committed to supporting the diversity of the neuroscience students and has a Standing Committee, the Diversity Initiative Committee, devoted to this effort.
Recent research regarding graduation trends in neuroscience supports that greater numbers of females are graduating from neuroscience bachelor’s and graduate degree programs.
White (non-Hispanic) males and females represent the largest group of graduates and Asian/Pacific Islanders represent the largest non-White group of graduates.

CONSTITUTION, BY-LAWS, AND UNIVERSITY MANUAL COMMITTEEReport #2022-2023-15 - SECOND READING OF MOTION TO AMEND THE SENATE BY-LAWSFACULTY SENATE, March 23, 2023 Background and contextIn response to the discussion about preferred modalities of Faculty Senate meetings that arose duringthe Senate meeting on October 20, 2022 and that was included as “Old Business” in the agenda forthe Senate meeting on November 17, 2022, CBUM discussed the issue and with the agenda for theFaculty Senate meeting on December 8, 2022 included for consideration a report with a motion toamend the By-Laws of the Faculty Senate to continue to permit the option of remote participation inFaculty Senate meetings.
During the December 8, 2022 meeting, prior to the presentation of theCBUM report, Senator Preisser moved to eliminate the possibility of remote participation in FacultySenate meetings.
The motion failed.
Subsequently Senate Vice President Nassersharif moved to tablethe CBUM motion to codify the option of remote participation in in-person Senate meetings in theFaculty Senate By-Laws.
A majority of the Senate voted in favor of Vice President Nassersharif’smotion.

passages.heading: #22-23-36 | Page 3
passages.text:
In January 2023 CBUM revised the original motion and submitted a new version to FSEC whorequested that the committee draft specific language changes to the By-Laws for consideration by theFaculty Senate.
RationaleIn recognition of the critical role of meaningful faculty engagement in shared governance, CBUMaffirms that it is essential that Faculty Senators, ex officio members of the Faculty Senate, andmembers of the General Faculty actively participate in Faculty Senate deliberations and meetings.
Thecommittee further urges that all members of the university community participate in Faculty Senatemeetings in-person whenever possible, as a matter of cohesion and of maximizing opportunities tosupport and nurture our sense of community.

passages.heading: #22-23-36 | Page 3
passages.text:
Although the committee urges in-person attendanceand participation whenever possible, in the interests of equity and inclusion and as a means tooptimize our democratic processes by facilitating the broadest level possible of engagement withFaculty Senate business and participation in Faculty Senate deliberations, CBUM invites the FacultySenate to consider amending the By-Laws to codify the option for remote attendance for all in-personFaculty Senate meetings, with community members, Senators, and ex officio members who attendvirtually retaining all rights afforded to people who are able to attend in-person:- All attendees retain the right to speak and to participate in discussions.- All ex officio members of the Faculty Senate retain the right to make and second motions.- All Senators retain the right to make and second motions, and to vote.
Current language in the By-Laws of the Faculty Senate: 7.3 Regular Faculty Senate Meetings shall be held at least once each month on Thursdays during the academic year.
Proposed changes: 7.3 Regular Faculty Senate Meetings shall be held at least once each month on Thursdays during the academic year.

passages.heading: #22-23-36 | Page 3
passages.text: To facilitate the broadest level possible of engagement with Faculty Senate business, all in-person Faculty Senate meetings shall include an option for remote attendance, with community members, Senators, and ex officio members attending remotely retaining the same rights they enjoy when attending in-person and when attending fully virtual meetings.

SECTION II Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation by the Faculty Senate NEW PROGRAMS: COLLEGE OF EDUCATION AND PROFESSIONAL STUDIES: Early Childhood Care and Education TCP Certificate See Appendix B This accelerated online Undergraduate Certificate Pre-K-2 Certification (TCP) program in Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) for working professionals leads to a Pre-K 2 teaching certification only. It provides certificate-required courses and field experiences that improve the professionals' pedagogical knowledge and teaching quality when working with diverse children from birth to Grade 2. This undergraduate certificate program will be offered fully online through URIOnline with a capstone field experience in a Pre-K-2 setting. It will include running seven-week accelerated sessions and a summer session for two consecutive years, and allows working professionals with college degrees to earn their ECCE teaching certification at URI. The program will offer professional support, including manageable time arrangements in curriculum, course format, and the capstone field experience, for the incumbent ECE workforce to advance in their career. It will offer financial opportunities with an affordable tuition rate, T.E.A.C.H. scholarship funding opportunities, and other financial assistance for qualified students.

State the program objectives.
The Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) undergraduate certificate program for Post Baccalaureate, Pre-K-2 Certification is for those who have completed their undergraduate degree to be certified as a teacher and advance in their teaching profession.
At least 30 hours per week of the incumbent workforce candidate’s active teaching are required; other non-traditional work conditions with RIDE approval can be considered.
The ECCE program will be offered fully online through URIOnline with field experience in the candidates’ own PreK-2 teaching setting, running 7-week accelerated sessions, including a summer session, for 2 years.

The Pathway 2: Undergraduate Certificate, Pre-K-2 Certification requires a bachelor's degree in Science or in Art and to complete pre-professional course requirements prior to admission.
The ECCE program is designed to meet the needs of the incumbent early childhood care and education workforce to access high-quality teaching certificate programs in order to improve teacher quality and student learning.
Aligned with the URI mission, the SOE & CEPS strategic plans, and the Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) Strategic Plan for Rhode Island, this program is designed to ensure that the incumbent workforce of early childhood educators has accessible, high-quality, and meaningful pathways toward credential attainment, career advancement, and higher compensation.
This program is supported by The RIDE Educator Pathways Planning Grant.

passages.heading: #22-23-20C | Page 5

In the State of Rhode Island, in order to achieve a high-quality rating (4 or 5 stars) on the state’s Quality Rating and Improvement System (BrightStars), childcare programs must employ workers with college credits in Early Childhood Education (ECE) and postsecondary degrees.
In addition, childcare programs that seek to become a Rhode Island Pre-Kindergarten provider must employ Bachelor’s degree and Pre-K-2 certified teachers in order to achieve Comprehensive Early Childhood Education (CECE) program quality approval (RI Board of Education, 2018).
A lack of

passages.heading: #22-23-20C | Page 6
passages.text:
4 a trained workforce prevents childcare centers from moving up on the BrightStars continuum, from qualifying to become a State Pre-K provider, and from receiving CECE approval.
Furthermore, with the implementation of tiered reimbursement in 2018, childcare programs with higher quality ratings are reimbursed at higher rates by the Child Care Assistance Program.
These higher reimbursement rates will allow programs to increase staff compensation.
More importantly, RI is suffering from a severe shortage in staffing that consequently affects the quality of early childhood teaching and learning in early childhood education (RI Early Learning Council meeting, RI Kids Count report, 2020, 2021).
Our Pathways grant will address this urgent staffing need, thereby enhancing the quality of teaching and learning in early childhood classrooms. b.

A regional university in New England, Arcadia University, PA (Pre-K- 4 certification), offers a program for working professionals in ECCE; however, the age range is different from our program and is not similar to the proposed programs.
Relatively, the state of RI is experiencing a serious shortage of qualified ECE teachers causing staffing problems in early childhood care and education: The state is having a devastating shortage of certified teachers in Pre-K-2.

The ECCE program is also guided by the RI Workforce Knowledge and Competencies and the NAEYC's Professional Content Standards and Professional Educator Preparation Standards.
For the program context-specific contents in connection with teaching and practices, the ECCE program is guided by the Rhode Island Professional Teaching Standards (RI-PTS).
These 11 standards are learned and applied early and consistently in the program, beginning in the Methods I course and practicum, to all key assignments, including lesson plans, group presentations, and field work.

General Knowledge (showing evidence of knowledge, skills, and dispositions); 2.

Critical Thinking and Problem solving (applying inquiry, evidence, discovery, and hands–on engagement with learners); 6.
Classroom management (establishing a safe and secure classroom environment; helping students to be self-motivated); 7.
Working with families (involving families in the school, enlisting their support, keeping continual communication with them); 8.
Communication (using Universal Design for Learning (UDL), tailoring teaching to meet individual needs; 9.
Formal and Informal Assessment (scaffolding students to become reflective practitioners; setting goals based upon student needs and assessment results); 10.

Because early childhood (birth to age 8) is a critically important period for a child’s learning and development, the URI ECCE focuses on the educational, socio-emotional, and developmental needs of young children.
Students will learn a holistic approach to supporting a child’s learning and development.
The ECCE for working professionals at URI will be a fully accredited certification program that leads to an initial teaching certificate for the pre-school and primary grades (Pre-K to 2) in Rhode Island.
Specifically students will: ● Gain high quality field experience through the on-campus child development centers, three field experiences, and two full student teaching sessions during the last spring semester ● Learn developmentally appropriate and culturally relevant care and education ● Promote whole child development and a rich understanding of diverse learners ● Support overarching partnerships among the family, the school, and the community ● Become a passionate and motivated leader in the field of ECE ● Improve knowledge and skills in teaching and learning to advance in their teaching career. b.

ACADEMIC PROGRAM ASSESSMENT PLAN All new programs and certificates must have clearly articulated program goals (Section I) and student learning outcome statements linked to curriculum and course experiences/requirements (Section II).
The Curriculum Map guides programs in to present the extent to which their student learning outcomes are aligned with courses and other program requirements intended to provide students with opportunities to develop and master the learning outcomes by graduation.
Each program (not certificates) will also create an Assessment Timeline (Section III) indicating when and how learning outcomes assessment will take place.
All undergraduate and graduate programs are encouraged to create a six-year (3 rounds) Assessment Plan to guide assessment reporting.
If you have questions or need assistance, please contact the Office of Student Learning, Outcome Assessment, and Accreditation (SLOAA) at assess@uri.edu.

This program provides the academic foundation for alcohol and drug use counseling.
In Rhode Island, the percent of adults reporting alcohol use disorder is higher than the national rate (6.9% vs 5.7% through 2019).
Furthermore, the rate of drug overdose rates in RI exceeds the national rate (37.5 per 100,000 in RI compared to 28.3 per 100,000 in the US through 2019).

passages.heading: #22-23-34C | Page 7
passages.text:
Similarly the age-adjusted opioid overdose death rate in RI exceed the rate in the US overall. https://www.kff.org/statedata/mental-health-and-substance-use-state-fact-sheets/rhode-island/ The overdose death rate is substantially higher in Black or African American Rhode Islanders (57 per 100,000 in Blacks in 2021 compared to 39.1 among Whites). https://preventoverdoseri.org/race-ethnicity-data/ Alcohol and drug counselors are urgently needed in Rhode Island to help all citizens but with a special need among African Americans.
This program is designed to prepare academically well-trained alcohol and drug counselors in the Rhode Island workforce.
As such it aligns with values identified in URI's mission statement including civic involvement, diversity, respect, and ethical leadership.
It is designed to enhance student success as this is one of the few degree/certifications that allow students to perform counseling at the bachelors degree level.
As an interdisciplinary program, it engages students in learning across the curriculum.
Because of the unique focus of this certificate program, it has little overlap with other URI programs.

Substance abuse counselor is also ranked #1 in Best Social Service Jobs and #35 in 100 Best Jobs by U.S.
New and World Report, based upon factors including median salary, unemployment rate, growth and future job prospects.
This is a job that a person can do regardless of where they live, as long as they are licensed or certified to practice in that state.
It also provides an opportunity to work in many different types of treatment settings.
An individual might earn a higher salary on average if they work at a hospital as compared to a local substance abuse clinic.
According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, counselors who work for government agencies and in hospitals tend to earn more money, but the median salary of $47,660 per year in 2020 makes this career path a middle-income career trajectory.

September 2020).
In terms of the workplace alone, per US Drug Test Centers which is supported by SAMSHA, researchers estimated in Oct, 2021, that $81 billion is spent annually on drug abuse in the workplace to cover the costs of absenteeism and accidents.
Perhaps most troubling and tragic is the widely publicized number of overdose deaths in the United States.
In the past year, overdose deaths in the United States have reached an all-time high, as more than 96,000 people died of overdoses during the past year.
That is an increase of almost 30 percent in one year according to the Center for Disease Control and Prevention.
It is also the largest single-year increase in drug overdose deaths ever reported in the United States.
The overall number of overdose deaths nationwide has risen sharply because of the widespread availability of drugs laced with fentanyl, a synthetic opioid that can be up to 100 times more powerful than morphine.

passages.heading: #22-23-34C | Page 14
passages.text:
I've established these minimal estimates using the concept stated in the CADCA guidelines that a 3 credit academic course is equivalent to 45 hours of instruction.
This is what I've determined: 1) Psy 113 (Introduction to Psychology) contains 5 hours specific to substance use / co occurring disorders. 2) HDF 230 (Couple and Family Relationships) contains 10 hours specific to substance use / co occurring disorders. 3) Psy 254 (Abnormal Psychology) contains 20 hours specific to substance use / co occurring disorders. 4) Psy 460 (Substance use: assessment and treatment) is completely 45 hours specific to substance use / co occurring disorders. 5) HDF 450 (Introduction to Counseling) contains 10 hours specific to substance use / co occurring disorders. 5) Psy 255 (Health Psychology) contains 25 hours specific to substance use / co occurring disorders.

Emphasis is given to interdisciplinary team building to solve problems that cannot be solved within a given discipline and to the ethical implications of data on individuals and society.
This program prepares data scientists to excel in machine learning, analysis of large and/or unruly datasets, and visualization through an approach that hones skills in problem solving and collaborative research.
In addition, students analyze problems using advanced theoretical knowledge and skills of data science in statistics, machine learning theory, and mathematical methods to create innovative solutions to complex problems in data science across a variety of domain areas.
This is a 10-course, fully online, asynchronous program that is offered in the accelerated calendar of six 7-week sessions per year.

Students might be looking to upskill in their current position, or change career paths.
Some job advertisements indicate a requirement for a master's degree plus experience.
This program is ideal for students who have experience and want to add the credential they need to be competitive in the job market.
Students from a wide variety of disciplines can enter this program through the Online Graduate Certificate in Data Science.
Approved on FS Bill #21-22-30C Creation of a Master’s Program in Data Science is consistent with the institutional goals stated in the University of Rhode Island Academic Strategic Plan 2016-2021.
In fact, the creation of programs in data science is explicitly mentioned in Goal 2: Expand research, scholarship, and creative work.

The Online Graduate Certificate in Data Science was initiated in Summer 2021.
It has five courses, four of which count toward this online Master’s in Data Science.
The certificate is considered a gateway for students who have little experience in programming, math, and statistics.
Students who complete the certificate are automatically admitted to the master’s degree program.

2/15/23, 12:48 PM Kuali CM | Programs View - Data Science - MS https://uri.kuali.co/cm/#/programs/print/6352f839e1cd0a260f7dccd9 7/8 Data science is a somewhat new discipline and not all universities offer programs in data science.
In Rhode Island, only RIC and URI offer undergraduate programs in data science and Brown offers a face-to-face Masters Program in data science and a certificate in data fluency.
There are no online master’s degree programs in data science offered in the State of Rhode Island.
Although students can take online programs from anywhere in the world, students tend to enroll in online programs near their places of residence.
Within the northeast US, there are several online master’s programs in data science.
With the 30,000 job openings, it appears that there is room in the market for URI’s Online Master’s in Data Science.
The following programs were discovered after a thorough search. 1.
Worcester Polytechnic Institute, Worcester, MA - Master of Science in Data Science Not asynchronous. 2.
Tufts University Online, Medford MA - Master of Science in Data Science 3.
Syracuse University, Syracuse, NY - Masters in Applied Data Science 4.

CUNY School of Professional Studies, New York, NY - Master of Science in Data Science 10.
Drexel University, Philadelphia, PA - Master of Science in Data Science The above programs offer an array of courses that have some in common with URI’s, but each is unique with emphasis that align with faculty expertise at the institution.
Students who complete the Online Graduate Certificate in Data Science will automatically be accepted into the Online Master’s in Data Science.
For the Online Graduate Certificate in Data Science, the admission criteria is that prior courses in calculus, linear algebra, probability and statistics, and programming in Python are recommended, but not required.

passages.heading: #22-23-26B | Page 9

For the Online Master’s in Data Science, the requirement for admission is - prior coursework or demonstrated equivalent experience in: a. programming in R and Python, b. calculus (similar to URI’s MTH 131 or MTH 141), c. linear algebra (similar to URI’s MTH 215), and d. introductory statistics (similar to URI’s STA 308 or STA 409).
Students must have a bachelor’s degree to be admitted to this program, as determined by the URI Graduate Schools admission requirements.
Data science is a somewhat new discipline and not all universities offer undergraduate degrees in data science, but students with undergraduate degrees in data science, mathematics, computer science, or statistics are prime candidates for this certificate.
It is designed to accommodate students from other majors, as well, if they have some experience and/or coursework in the relevant subjects.

The University of Rhode Island’s graduate Interdisciplinary Neuroscience Program (INP) provides students with course instruction and research experience from faculty who are conducting cutting-edge science concerning brain functioning across variety of areas from aging, movement, language processing, medicinal plants, and molecular proteins, to the study of brain based disorders including Alzheimer’s disease, ALS, ADHD, Fanconia Anemia, Parkinson’s disease, epilepsy and more.
The INP graduate program offers three options: a Master of Science (M.S.), Doctor of Philosophy (Ph.D.) degree, or a Certificate in Neuroscience.
Please note that the Master of Science offers a thesis or a non-thesis option.
The thesis program requires students to match with a mentor and conduct research (resulting in a thesis), while the non-thesis program does not require a mentor match or thesis, consequently the acceptance rate tends to be higher in the non-thesis program.
Specializations Students can choose to work with INP faculty across a variety of colleges and departments such as the College of Environment and Life Sciences, Engineering, Health Sciences, Pharmacy, Physical Therapy and more.

passages.heading: #22-23-26B | Page 30
passages.text:
Program requirements: The Ph.D. program requires successful completion of a qualifying exam or an earned M.S. with thesis in an appropriate discipline, a comprehensive examination, and dissertation defense.
As the qualifying exam is meant to be equivalent to the M.S. degree, the exam must be taken no later than the first semester following the completion of eighteen credits of coursework.
A minimum of 72 credits is required.
Of these, 30 credits must be earned through required coursework, 18 to 28 of which may be earned through dissertation and research credits (NEU 591 and NEU 699).
No more than 28 credits can be earned between NEU 591 and 699.
Up to 30 transfer credits will be accepted for students who have already earned an M.S. degree. (Depending on your previous training and experience, certain requirements may be waived at the discretion of your dissertation committee and the Graduate School.) Required courses include: - NEU 502: Introduction to Neurobiology (4 cr) - NEU 503: Introduction to the Neurosciences (3 cr)

passages.heading: #22-23-26B | Page 31
passages.text: - NEU 504: Neuroethics (1 cr) - NEU 511: Human Neuroscience and Neurology (5 cr) - PSY/STA 532: Experimental Design (3 cr) - NEU 581 and 582: Neurosciences Colloquium (Seminar – 1 cr each) - one additional statistics or computational analysis course (e.g. STA 502, 536, 541, 542, 545) Other requirements: - Two semesters of NEU 591: Special Projects in Neurosciences (Independent Study), one in your primary area of research, and one in a related discipline. - Enrollment in journal club (NEU 587: Seminar in Neurobiology or equivalent with permission) for a minimum of 3 credits - A dissertation proposal and successful defense of dissertation - In the final semester, a formal presentation of thesis research is recommended in 581/582

2/15/23, 3:34 PM Kuali CM | Programs View - Physical Therapy - DPT https://uri.kuali.co/cm/#/programs/print/63920b939fcb6d57fd3c2123 4/13 Changes Program Description URI’s Physical Therapy Program is an entry-level Doctor of Physical Therapy program that prepares students for the professional licensure examination and future practice.
There is an emphasis on the development of clinical skill and research capability through the three-year graduate study plan.
The Physical Therapy Program is located in the Independence Square II facility and has a clinical service and research unit that includes a simulated hospital room with an interactive mannequin, computerized anatomical study center, point of service ultrasound imaging and KINCOM muscle performance dynamometry, postural analysis, electromyography, Gait Rite computerized gait analysis system, Balance and vestibular analysis systems, and kinetic and kinematic human motion analysis systems.
Research is currently conducted in the treatment and prevention of: dysfunction of neuromuscular control mechanisms; polytrauma; balance disorders; and concussion.

passages.heading: #22-23-26B | Page 35
passages.text:
Current research areas also include adaptive sport participation, clinical education, interprofessional education, and return to work following injury.
Specializations Research activities are focused on biomechanics, neuromuscular control, muscle performance, neuromuscular rehabilitation, disability, geriatrics and falls prevention, musculoskeletal injury prevention, and patient satisfaction.
Clinical specialty skills are enhanced through faculty clinical practice and internships.

Admission requirements: a bachelor’s degree with 8 credits of biological sciences (introductory and second level biology course (not botany); exercise physiology or neuroscience course can serve as second biology course); eight credits of human anatomy and human physiology courses (both must contain labs; can be separate anatomy and physiology courses, or A&P I and A&P II); physical sciences (16 credits, eight in chemistry and eight in physics, both must include a lab) six credits of social science, including general psychology and a second level psychology course, e.g. development, child adolescent, abnormal, etc.; three credits in mathematics (precalculus or higher) three credits in writing; three credits in statistics.
Courses in pre-calculus, computer science, exercise physiology and research design are recommended but not required.
A clinical experience with a physical therapist is required.
The experience should include observing and aiding a physical therapist in treatment or evaluation procedures.
The minimum number of hours recommended for the clinical experience is 30 hours of voluntary or paid time.

The program would allow students currently receiving a Bachelor’s of Science in Textiles, Fashion Merchandising and Design; or a Bachelor’s of Science in Textile Marketing; or Bachelor’s degree in any other major combined with a TMD minor to also complete an MS as part-time or full-time students.
Under certain circumstances, students enrolled in programs leading to degrees in related areas may be considered for admission into the TMD program, for example Business, Chemistry, History, Art History, or Psychology.
In such cases, half of the total credits must be in TMD.

passages.heading: #22-23-26B | Page 47
passages.text:
To apply for the ABMTMD program, students must have earned a minimum of 75 credits and have a 3.03 GPA.
Students still need to meet the admission requirements for the TMD graduate program; they are allowed to double count up to 11 credits from their B.S. program.
Students will be enrolled in the ABMTMD only after they have met the Graduate School admission requirements and have completed 90 undergraduate credits.
Currently, the MS program has two options: thesis option of 30 credits with six credits of thesis research, and non-thesis option of 33 credits.
The total number of credits required for a BS is 120 credits.
Only the non-thesis option requiring 33 credits will be open to ABMTMD students.
The proposed program will allow up to 11 credits of 400/500 level courses to count for both undergraduate and graduate credit.
These courses include those 400-level courses in other disciplines that count for graduate credit.

THE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND F22-S23 Classical Guitar Performance The BOM degree is the first-level professional degree in music.
Its focus is on the development of skills and concepts essential to the success of the professional musician.
Three options include: Performance - with a focus in either jazz studies or classical performance; Music Education - for those who plan to teach music in elementary or secondary schools; and Composition - with a concentration on the study of the materials and structure of music.

Data science is the study of complex data or big data, while health outcomes research involves using these data to determine the clinical, humanistic, economic, and equity outcomes of healthcare interventions.
This requires developing methods to collect, record, store, analyze, and interpret data to effectively extract useful information and detect patterns, trends, and relationships in data to inform healthcare decision- making.
The �elds of health outcomes and science are interdisciplinary, drawing upon the �elds of computer science, epidemiology, ethics, mathematics, quality improvement, pharmacy and statistics.

Students will be able to prepare, analyze, and interpret the increasing amount and complexity of data across the medical and related fields.
In addition to improving planning and reducing costs in health care, the ethical use of analytics can examine gaps in outcomes based on social determinants, with the aim of reducing inequities in the health care system.
This interdisciplinary program capture the spirit of creativity and scholarship in the URI mission, bringing together two areas of scholarly strength at URI to create a synergy of new knowledge and perspectives.
By centering ethics, the program is taking a leadership position within the online space for this emerging area.

This program targets working professionals in, and related to, the healthcare industry in roles involving medication use and data analytics.
Furthermore, the University aims to "grow URI Online to increase access for all students at every life stage." This innovative masters program through URI Online will advance big data analyses and applications across the health and pharmacology disciplines.
By offering this program fully online, we are able to reach a larger audience, grow our presence in other regions, and foster a 21st century, 24/7 learning environment that is accessible to students across the globe.
College of Pharmacy offers an on-ground Health Outcomes masters degree that does not include the data analytics component.
The focus of this degree on integrating data into health outcomes creates a different program.
