4/13/23, 2:30 PM Kuali CM | Programs View - Health Outcomes and Data Analytics https://uri.kuali.co/cm/#/programs/print/62ebe3abbd5d7acb6e57a1d1 6/13 The rapid growth of health data utilization (e.g., deployment of electronic health records and ehealth) has resulted in an increased demand for a skilled workforce in pharmaceutical data analytics.
Healthcare companies are hiring for data analytics positions at a higher rate compared to all companies hiring for these positions.
Additionally, there was a 15% increase in the number of pharmaceutical companies hiring for data analytic-type jobs as of June 2022 compared to last year (Pharmaceutical Technology, 2022).
The Master of Science in Health Outcomes and Data Analytics aims to meet that market demand by training individuals who possess pharmaceutical-based health knowledge and analytic-skills training to ethically retrieve, analyze, interpret and use a wide-range of data to inform decision-making and improve health outcomes.
Currently, there are only a few online master’s degree programs throughout the Northeast region in related fields.

We envision that this program will be of interest to professionals working in a range of healthcare settings who have responsibility for medication management at the population level.
This includes pharmacists working in managed care environments, and within delivery entities that bear financial risk for health system utilization.
This program will also be useful to physicians, nurses and other clinicians who are involved with using data to manage medication use for their patient populations.
Additionally, this program will be worthwhile for healthcare administrators who are seeking skills in health outcomes evaluation, particularly those with non-clinical backgrounds.
Since the program will be offered in the accelerated 7-week online delivery model, the program will be unavailable to students currently enrolled in degree granting programs on campus.
Therefore, the program will not draw student away from existing programs at the University and will instead be targeting a new student population outside of the existing University students.
This degree will provide students in the online Medication Outcomes and the Data Science certificates a path towards a masters degree.

However, we were unable to meet our enrollment target and delayed the start of the program to fall 2023.
We surmised that several factors contributed to the low level of enrollment.

passages.text:
Other universities that offer an online certificate program in health or medication outcomes research include Rutgers, Temple, The University of Washington, Johns Hopkins University, Thomas Jefferson University and George Washington University.
While these other programs can be considered competitors, their presence also suggests that there is a continuing demand for this training.
We believe that URI can be competitive recruiting students into our program for several reasons.
The first reason is familiarity with URI and Its faculty in this area among former students.
The URI PharmD program graduates between 120- 145 students each year, and these graduates would likely have loyalty to URI when choosing a program.
The online and asynchronous program format accommodates professionals working in any time zone.
Lastly, URI's tuition compares favorably to the tuition costs of competing programs.

Upon completion of the Coastal Resilience Graduate Certi�cate Program, students will be able to: (1) apply knowledge in a variety of disciplines and have practical skills to address real-world problems in coastal resilience; and (2) �nd employment in agencies and businesses involved in research, scholarly, and problem-solving endeavors in the �eld of coastal resilience. 4/13/23, 2:27 PM Kuali CM | Programs View - Coastal Resilience Graduate Certiﬁcate https://uri.kuali.co/cm/#/programs/print/6374daaba2b39d258566a642 4/11 This certificate program will coalesce the world class URI faculty to address one of the most challenging issues of the 21st century: reducing the impacts of coastal hazards and disasters on coastal communities and those that depend upon them.
The study of coastal resilience and translating findings into practice is important for coastal communities, as well as the natural and economic systems that depend upon them.
As climate change impacts become more and more evident, disaster losses will continue to rise in the United States and across the world.
Hazards of concern in these regions include storm surge and wind impacts from tropical storms, wildfires, extreme heat, and inundation of low-lying lands during regular tidal cycles.
With more than 50% of the United States population and a majority of global population living in coastal areas, natural disasters along the coast are particularly devastating.

passages.heading: #22-23-38C | Page 7
passages.text:
The next generation must face these challenges head on and the need to educate tomorrow’s decision makers about coastal resilience will only become more pressing.
Numerous national reports suggest that there is a critical need for multi- disciplinary research, teaching directed specifically at resilience-related issues, and an overall gap in translating resilience research into practice (1-3).
Natural hazards, disasters, and climate change are intricately connected and new learning programs are required to train practioners and researchers about these complex issues.
This program will build on 50+ years of success in the Department of Marine Affairs and draw on URI’s significant expertise in oceanography, ocean engineering, geology, and natural resources sciences.
Certificate programs in natural hazards and disasters are offered at other universities, although most are discipline-specific rather than multi-disciplinary.
Few have the demonstrated track record of URI in coastal and ocean research, nor have they focused on coastal regions and effectively addressed climate change in communities where the design of human settlements reflect past, rather than future, environmental conditions.

passages.heading: #22-23-38C | Page 7
passages.text:
This certificate program will link between climate change adaptation and coastal resilience and draw on the expertise of URI faculty from the physical and social sciences to educate students about policy-relevant research that can be applied in the work force.
As an interdisciplinary program designed to foster the development of future leaders in coastal resilience, this Graduate Certificate program meets.
University of Rhode Island’s mission to learn and lead together.
In particular, the program is consistent with the following goals of the URI Academic Plan: Goal 1: Enhance student success.
This Graduate Certificate program helps to reframe liberal learning at URI by increasing collaboration among departments across the university in an innovative interdisciplinary program that addresses a critical societal issue, coastal resilience.

In 2016, the first US offshore wind farm with a capacity of 30 MW was constructed off Block Island, Rhode Island.
Following the success of this project, several offshore wind farms have been planned by Rhode Island, Massachusetts, New Jersey, and other states in this region.
Due to recent advances in wind energy technology and state- level supports/commitments, offshore wind projects have become highly cost competitive.

The URI Graduate Certificate in Offshore Wind will prepare students in this developing and growing field by capitalizing on existing faculty expertise, educational coursework, and facilities/laboratories.
The proposed certificate program does not require any new classes or FTEs.

The INP graduate program offers three options: a Master of Science (M.S.), Doctor of Philosophy (Ph.D.) degree, or a Certi�cate in Neuroscience.
Please note that the Master of Science offers a thesis or a non-thesis option.
The thesis program requires students to match with a mentor and conduct research (resulting in a thesis), while the non-thesis program does not require a mentor match or thesis, consequently the acceptance rate tends to be higher in the non-thesis program.

As the qualifying exam is meant to be equivalent to the M.S. degree, the exam must be taken no later than the �rst semester following the completion of eighteen credits of coursework.

4/13/23, 2:26 PM Kuali CM | Specializations View - Dietetics Future Education Model Graduate Program https://uri.kuali.co/cm/#/specializations/print/6409f1f2e357b66140efb508 4/11 Program Proposal: Addition of Master of Science in Nutrition Specialization: Dietetics Future Education Model Graduate Program (FG Program) This program is a non-thesis Master’s Program including a minimum of 1,000 supervised practice hours in healthcare and community facilities integrated with supportive didactic coursework.
The program has been approved by the accrediting body for dietetics education, the Accreditation Council for Education in Nutrition and Dietetics (ACEND).
Experiential learning will be based on satisfactory demonstration of Future Educational Model (FEM) Standards competencies and will include both formative and summative evaluation.
At the conclusion of this accredited program, graduates will receive a MS degree and will be eligible to take the Dietetics Registration Examination to become a Registered Dietitian Nutritionist and apply for licensure as a Dietitian Nutritionist in Rhode Island.

FACULTY SENATE OFFICE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND FACULTY SENATE APRIL 20, 2023 Faculty Senate Curriculum and Standards Committee Report 2022-2023-8 At the March 30, 2023 meeting of the Curriculum and Standards Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate.
SECTION II Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation by the Faculty Senate PROGRAM CHANGES: Natural Resource Science (Appendix A) Environmental Science and Management – BS The faculty of the NRS department is proposing changes to the Environmental Science and Management major curriculum in order to better serve the students enrolled in our major by giving them more choices.
There are three types of changes proposed: 1.
Reducing the number of categories in the concentration requirement from five to three (note that the number of credits required in the concentration will remain the same, 24 credits total.

Additional existing courses currently offered in other URI departments (i.e, BIO, GEO, WRT, please see attachments, courses highlighted in yellow) will be included as offerings in concentration requirements to provide students with more choices in the major.

Editorial changes to program description Interdisciplinary Neuroscience Program (Appendix D) Interdisciplinary Neuroscience – Minor Per suggestion of an Assistant Dean from a degree-granting college, we are changing the signature requirements for students.
They now only need the INP Coordinator's signature (to start the minor), and then the degree-granting college Assistant Dean's signature.
The Assistant Dean will be the one to sign off that the student has completed all requirements.
This is typical with most URI minors.
We are also adding a non-NEU course elective option to the curriculum for this minor.
Students will now be able to choose between taking NEU 262- Neuroscience Research Methods lab or the combination of NEU 460- Neuroscience Journal Club (one credit) and then one three credit course in place of NEU 262- six course options total for students to choose from.
These options all come from courses in the three tracks for the Revisions and updates to the description and requirements for the minor. 2

We are offering this option because we believe that students who are pursuing this minor should have the opportunity to choose if they want to take this very intensive lab (NEU 262) or choose a course that better suits their interests.
Education (Appendix E) Early Childhood Education (BS) Early Childhood Education (Birth to grade 2).
This major provides the knowledge, skills, and experiences required to be a successful preschool through grade two teacher and prepares teacher candidates to be eligible for licensure as an early childhood teacher.
Required courses meet the curricular requirements for the Early Childhood Education Teacher Certificate (Preschool through Grade 2) for beginning teachers set by Rhode Island's Department of Education.

passages.heading: #22-23-39B | Page 5
passages.text:
Early childhood education teacher candidates are required to take one required licensure test from the state department of education where they are planning to get certified to teach prior to program completion and are required to submit the score report to the Office of Teacher Education so that faculty and staff can assist students in making a plan for successful teacher licensure after URI program completion.
The courses required include the following: Human Development Setting Contents: HDF 200, 201, 202, 205, and 230; Professional Contents: EDC 102, 250, 312; HDF 203, 208, and 305; Early Childhood Education Core Courses: HDF 420; EDC 301, 303, 402, 424, 426/350, and 461; practical teaching residency: EDC 484 and 485.
To be eligible for the practical teaching residency, students must maintain a grade point average of 2.50 overall; 2.50 in the major; and attain a grade of at least C in HDF 203, 305, and 420; EDC 102, 250, 301, 303, 312, 402, 424, 426/350, 461, 484, and 485. 120 credits required for graduation.

Secondary Education curriculum leads to Bachelor of Arts (B.A.) and eligibility for grades 7-12 teacher certification from a state department of education after program completion.

4/10/23, 5:58 PM Kuali CM | Programs View - Environmental Science and Management - BS https://uri.kuali.co/cm/#/programs/print/63e1635dfc17a1caeefbcc74 3/7 Changes Program Description Environmental Science and Management The major in environmental science and management, offered by the Department of Natural Resources Science, prepares undergraduate students for professional careers in the public and private sectors of natural resources management.
Environmental Science and Management incorporates course work in water resources, geospatial technologies, wetland ecology, wildlife biology, soil science, forestry, and land use/environmental quality relationships.
Coursework emphasizes the �eld techniques that underpin environmental assessment and restoration.
This is a comprehensive major that includes a solid background in the basic sciences and exposure to a broad array of subject matter relating to environmental science and management.
This major provides solid preparation for more specialized study at the graduate level and prepares undergraduate students for professional careers in the public and private sectors of natural resources management.

passages.heading: #22-23-39B | Page 11
passages.text:
Flexible course requirements allow students to develop individual areas of concentration and prepare for a variety of positions in environmental science and management after graduation.
This major is also suitable for students who wish to become certi�ed as teachers of environmental science and natural resources at the secondary level.
With proper course selection environmental science majors can meet the educational requirements for certi�cations by professional and governmental agencies as biologists, soil scientists, natural resource specialists, geospatial specialists, hydrologists, and other classi�cations.
The major requires 1923 credits of professional courses, which include ecology ( Bio 262; 4 credits), introduction to resource economics (EEC 105; 3 credits), physical geology (GEO 103; 4 credits), natural resource conservation (NRS 100; 3 credits), seminar in natural resources (NRS 200; 1 credit), introductory soil science (NRS 212; 4 credits), and conservation biology (NRS 223; 4 credits).

passages.heading: #22-23-39B | Page 11
passages.text:

At least 24 credits of concentration courses must be taken.

The �eld of medicine is facing a signi�cant shortage of well-trained and quali�ed clinical medical physicists, due to the increasing use of complex technology in the �eld of radiation oncology and medical imaging.
Consequently there is a growing demand for the training of professionals in medical physics.
Only specially created programs can accomplish this mission, since among other things medical physics requires a multidisciplinary effort.
This degree program provides students with rigorous training in essential undergraduate and graduate physics courses, as well as in medical physics courses.
Students are introduced to both research and clinical aspects of modern medical physics through the Rhode Island Hospital state-of-the-art medical imaging and therapy facilities.
The program is based on the B.S. and M.S. programs in physics with the introduction of additional courses in photo medicine, nanotechnology, radiation physics and dosimetry, radiation oncology, radio-biology, and a clinical practicum.
These courses are taught by the URI Physics Department, the Rhode Island Hospital-Brown University Medical School Faculty, and the staff at the RI Nuclear Science Center at the Bay Campus.

RATIONALE: There should be a demonstrable purpose and documented need for the proposed organizational change. 1.
Explain why the organizational change is being proposed.
The current College of Education and Professional Studies (CEPS) is composed of three units: the School of Education (SOE), The School of Professional Studies (SPC), and The Office of Strategic Initiatives (OSI).
Ultimately, the proposed change is a change in name based on the dissolution of the two schools with OSI remaining as part of the new College of Education.
This proposal aligns with the new URI strategic plan.
A strong K-12 and higher education system is essential to meeting the strategic vision to “be a leading global research university that drives positive social, economic, and environmental change by contributing and instilling new knowledge to address the world’s greatest challenges.” Excellence and equity in education are among the world's greatest challenges and opportunities.

passages.heading: #22-23-40D | Page 5
passages.text:
A recent Hanover Research report (2023) benchmarked the differences between standalone Colleges of Education and Education departments within interdisciplinary colleges and found that standalone colleges have an enrollment growth rate of 3.8% while education programs in interdisciplinary colleges have a declining growth rate of -6.8%.
Further, standalone Colleges of Education are more likely to employ faculty on the tenure track, while programs in interdisciplinary colleges hire an abundance of instructors with no academic rank.
The proposed shift positions URI as the only institution in the state with a standalone College of Education.
The School of Professional Studies (SPC) has very low enrollment in the current degree granting undergraduate programs.
When SPC was created, the university shifted the model of serving adult learners in Providence to serving adult learners better in all programs at URI.
That shift has left four under-enrolled degree programs in SPC.
The CEPS Dean currently has management responsibilities for the Providence campus.
However, the College (CEPS) and campus (Shepard Building) are two separate entities.

passages.heading: #22-23-40D | Page 5
passages.text:
This proposal addresses the proposed change to the college unit, not the Providence Campus.
Decisions about the Providence campus building are beyond the scope of this academic unit proposal.
On January 26, 2023, the URI Faculty Senate voted to close two of the four SPC programs (Non-Profit Administration; Professional leadership Studies).
Proposals to move the remaining two programs (BIS-General Studies; BIS-Learner Designed) to Arts and Sciences are currently moving though the faculty senate approval process.
With these closures and moves, there are no remaining academic programs in the School of Professional Studies.
This proposal includes keeping the Office of Strategic Initiatives in the College of Education.
The work that OSI does is in line with educational work in K-12 (e.g., concurrent/dual enrollment) and adult education (e.g., grant work, professional development) systems and thus, makes sense to remain with the new College of Education.
As the college moves forward with a more streamlined emphasis, there will be even more opportunities for synergies within the College of Education.

1/20/23, 11:15 AM Kuali CM | Experiences View - Education PhD https://uri.kuali.co/cm/#/experiences/print/63c6a0ba39d1dff86d496521 3/6 In the summer of 2022, the Deans of the URI Alan Shawn Feinstein College of Education and Professional Studies (Dennis) and RIC Feinstein College of Education and Human Development (Dingus-Eason) agreed to discontinue the current Joint Program.
Faculty and students have been notified of this decision and a teach out plan has been developed.
The agreement between URI and RIC states that “The continuation of this program depends on the continued agreement, support, and participation of both institutions.
Termination or withdrawal of support of the program at either institution will result in termination of the program” (p. 86).
As such, the faculty in the school of education have spent 8 months re-designing a stand-alone Ph.D. program in Education at the University of Rhode Island.
Faculty have used the “best of” current courses to design a scholarly doctoral program that is more research intensive than the current joint program–which was initially designed to prepare educational practitioners.

passages.heading: #22-23-33C | Page 19
passages.text:
The proposed program builds on current strengths (courses, faculty, ongoing research) to produce educational scholars who can solve the most intractable contemporary education problems.
The new program will allow students to develop focused expertise in an area of PreK-20 or adult education settings that aligns with our current graduate program offerings and faculty expertise.
How is this program redesigned?
The proposed curriculum keeps selected existing core courses that introduce students to educational research and inquiry as well as academic reading and writing.
The “new” program increases the number of required research methods courses from 9 to 21 credits to foster in-depth educational research knowledge and skill building.
The new program offers flexible options for students to develop focused expertise (18 credits) in an area whereas the current program limits expertise to three “strand” areas.
Finally, the program requires 12 credits of dissertation research.
The new program will draw from pre-existing courses with only two new proposed courses simultaneously submitted with the new program proposal.
The first course is truly new.

passages.heading: #22-23-33C | Page 19
passages.text:
This course tentatively titled “Engaged Research Apprenticeship” will provide a structured opportunity for students to actively engage in research projects that make a difference locally and globally.
We are also in the process of converting a pre-existing special topics course to be a permanent course (EDC 586 – Generalized Linear Models, 3cr).
This proposal aligns with many aspects of the URI mission and new strategic plan.
First, this research-focused program will help URI achieve its vision of becoming a “leading global research university that drives positive social, economic, and environmental change by contributing and instilling new knowledge to address the world’s greatest challenges.” Without an excellent and inclusive PreK-20 educational system, no society can thrive.
SOE faculty study educational systems (locally and globally) and are well-poised to train the next generation of education scholars.
The proposal will offer numerous opportunities for students to collaborate with URI faculty experts to achieve URI Strategic Priorities.

passages.text: College of Education and Professional Studies Proposed PhD Program Curriculum Total Number of Required Credits= 60 Credits (post-Master’s Degree) Curricular Overview Core sequence (12 credits) Research methods (21 credits) Dissertation Preparation and Credits (12 credits) Advanced Electives/Focused Expertise (15 credits) CORE/Foundational Courses (12 Credits total) ● EDP 600 Academic Reading & Writing for Doctoral Studies (3 cr)- Fall ● EDP 610 Contemporary Issues in Educational Inquiry (3 cr)- Fall ● EDP 611 Issues and Problems in Educational Inquiry (3 cr)- Spring ● EDP 622 Societal Perspectives of Education (3 cr)-Spring Research methods courses (21 credits total) ● EDP 623 Research Design (3 cr)- Fall ● EDP 612 Qualitative Research Methods in Education (3 cr)- Fall ● EDC 684 The Analysis of Data: A Hands-On [Qualitative] Approach (3 cr)- Spring ● EDP 613 Introduction to Quantitative Research (3 cr)-Fall ● EDC 624 Applied Educational Quantitative Data Analysis (3 cr)-Fall or Spring TBA ● EDC 625 [New] Engaged Research Apprenticeship in Education (3 cr)-Fall or Spring TBA ● Plus one additional advanced methods course.

passages.heading: #22-23-33C | Page 23
passages.text:
Options include but are not limited to: ○ EDC 685 - Survey Design (3 cr) ○ EDC 682 - Discourse Analysis in Education Research (3 cr) ○ Any other advanced methods course at URI Dissertation Preparation and Research (12 credits minimum) ● EDP 641 Doctoral Dissertation Research Seminar (3 cr) - Fall and Spring ● EDP 699 Doctoral Dissertation Research (minimum 9 cr) - Fall and Spring Focused Expertise (15 credits minimum) Students have the opportunity to use 15 credits to delve deeply into a focus area that aligns with their career goals.
With support from their faculty mentor, students will select 15 credits of courses that best align with their scholarly trajectory.
With the goal of flexibility, students can design a program following any of the following paths: ● Courses selected from an area of education where we already have graduate programming (e.g., Elementary, Secondary, Higher Education/CSP, Adult Education, TESOL/BDL, Reading, Health and Physical Education (HPE).

passages.heading: #22-23-33C | Page 24
passages.text:
● Courses that focus on topic areas that cut across current programs to illuminate complex, cross-cutting issues.
For instance, students could focus on Language, Literacy, and Culture where they could combine courses to develop expertise across areas such as: TESOL and bilingual education, digital and arts-based literacies, reading, and dyslexia.
A second option would be to focus on “postsecondary education leadership, learning and development” and combine pre-existing courses in education policy, college student personnel, and adult education. ● Courses combined with independent study to focus on a particular educational niche.
Like many other fields students, can opt to work with a SOE scholar to develop a narrowly tailored focus that aligns with one or more faculty experts in the college (e.g., STEM education, Social Justice Education, etc.).
URI CATALOG DESCRIPTIONS EDP 600 Academic Reading & Writing for Doctoral Studies (3 crs.) Students develop and practice academic reading, writing, and thinking skills involved in professional practices of educational research and publishing communities.

passages.heading: #22-23-33C | Page 24
passages.text:
Course emphasizes scholarly identity and writing cogent literature reviews. (Lec. 2, Sem 1) EDP 610 Contemporary Issues in Educational Inquiry (3 crs.) Examination of issues and problems related to philosophical and historical aspects of educational thought and the role of society.
Empirical analysis of classroom settings is emphasized. (Seminar) EDP 611 Issues and Problems in Educational Inquiry (3 crs.) Examination of issues and problems related to philosophical and historical aspects of educational thought and the role of society.
Empirical analysis of classroom setting is emphasized. (Seminar) EDP 612 Qualitative Research Methods in Education (3 crs.) Survey of qualitative methods of educational research: terminology, historical development, assumptions, and models of inquiry.
EDP 613 Introduction to Quantitative Research (4 crs.) Educational research data are collected, quantitatively analyzed and interpreted.
Applications of the general linear model to a variety of research designs and analytic strategies are emphasized. (Lec. 3, Rec. 1) EDP 622 Societal Perspectives of Education (3 crs.) Application of theory to the intersection of community service, academic

passages.heading: #22-23-33C | Page 25
passages.text:
EDP 623 Research Design (3 crs.) Research design process including developing problem statements, research questions, hypotheses and appropriate methods (i.e., qualitative, quantitative, or mixed).
Course considers philosophical worldviews, literature reviews, theory use, and research ethics. (Lec. 3) EDP 641 Doctoral Dissertation Research Seminar (1 cr.) Bi-weekly forums present evolving research questions and empirical designs.
Discussion and feedback refine individuals' research plan, enhancing the methodological perspectives and tools of all participants. (Seminar) EDC 682 - Discourse Analysis in Education Research (3 crs.) The analysis of discourse in educational research is examined and practiced in this course.

passages.heading: #22-23-33C | Page 25
passages.text:
Students conduct various analyses of discourse samples and explore a variety of analytic research frameworks. (Seminar 3) EDC 684 - The Analysis of Data: A Hands-On Approach (3 crs.) Students will practice data analysis using three specific qualitative methodologies, noting that each of these methodologies offers a unique lens on phenomena. (Seminar 3) EDC685 - Survey Design (3 crs.) Principles, theories, techniques, and applications for developing survey questionnaires and conducting survey research in education; developing questions; constructing instruments; implementing surveys; reducing coverage and sampling errors. (Seminar 3) EDP 699 Doctoral Dissertation Research (1-12 crs.) Number of credits is determined each semester in consultation with the major professor or program committee. (Independent Study) S/U only.

Faculty and students have been notified of this decision and a teach out plan has been developed.
The agreement between URI and RIC states that “The continuation of this program depends on the continued agreement, support, and participation of both institutions.
Termination or withdrawal of support of the program at either institution will result in termination of the program” (p. 86).
As such, the faculty in the school of education have spent 8 months re-designing a stand-alone Ph.D. program in Education at the University of Rhode Island.
Faculty have used the “best of” current courses to design a scholarly doctoral program that is more research intensive than the current joint program–which was initially designed to prepare educational practitioners.

passages.heading: #22-23-33C | Page 53
passages.text:
The proposed program builds on current strengths (courses, faculty, ongoing research) to produce educational scholars who can solve the most intractable contemporary education problems.
The new program will allow students to develop focused expertise in an area of PreK-20 or adult education settings that aligns with our current graduate program offerings and faculty expertise.
How is this program redesigned?
The proposed curriculum keeps selected existing core courses that introduce students to educational research and inquiry as well as academic reading and writing.
The “new” program increases the number of required research methods courses from 9 to 21 credits to foster in-depth educational research knowledge and skill building.
The new program offers flexible options for students to develop focused expertise (18 credits) in an area whereas the current program limits expertise to three “strand” areas.
Finally, the program requires 12 credits of dissertation research.
The new program will draw from pre-existing courses with only two new proposed courses simultaneously submitted with the new program proposal.
The first course is truly new.

passages.heading: #22-23-33C | Page 53
passages.text:
This course tentatively titled “Engaged Research Apprenticeship” will provide a structured opportunity for students to actively engage in research projects that make a difference locally and globally.
We are also in the process of converting a pre-existing special topics course to be a permanent course (EDC 586 – Generalized Linear Models, 3cr).
This proposal aligns with many aspects of the URI mission and new strategic plan.
First, this research-focused program will help URI achieve its vision of becoming a “leading global research university that drives positive social, economic, and environmental change by contributing and instilling new knowledge to address the world’s greatest challenges.” Without an excellent and inclusive PreK-20 educational system, no society can thrive.
SOE faculty study educational systems (locally and globally) and are well-poised to train the next generation of education scholars.
The proposal will offer numerous opportunities for students to collaborate with URI faculty experts to achieve URI Strategic Priorities.

Options include but are not limited to: ○ EDC 685 - Survey Design (3 cr) ○ EDC 682 - Discourse Analysis in Education Research (3 cr) ○ Any other advanced methods course at URI Dissertation Preparation and Research (12 credits minimum) ● EDP 641 Doctoral Dissertation Research Seminar (3 cr) - Fall and Spring ● EDP 699 Doctoral Dissertation Research (minimum 9 cr) - Fall and Spring Focused Expertise (15 credits minimum) Students have the opportunity to use 15 credits to delve deeply into a focus area that aligns with their career goals.
With support from their faculty mentor, students will select 15 credits of courses that best align with their scholarly trajectory.
With the goal of flexibility, students can design a program following any of the following paths: ● Courses selected from an area of education where we already have graduate programming (e.g., Elementary, Secondary, Higher Education/CSP, Adult Education, TESOL/BDL, Reading, Health and Physical Education (HPE).

passages.heading: #22-23-33C | Page 58
passages.text:
● Courses that focus on topic areas that cut across current programs to illuminate complex, cross-cutting issues.
For instance, students could focus on Language, Literacy, and Culture where they could combine courses to develop expertise across areas such as: TESOL and bilingual education, digital and arts-based literacies, reading, and dyslexia.
A second option would be to focus on “postsecondary education leadership, learning and development” and combine pre-existing courses in education policy, college student personnel, and adult education. ● Courses combined with independent study to focus on a particular educational niche.
Like many other fields students, can opt to work with a SOE scholar to develop a narrowly tailored focus that aligns with one or more faculty experts in the college (e.g., STEM education, Social Justice Education, etc.).
URI CATALOG DESCRIPTIONS EDP 600 Academic Reading & Writing for Doctoral Studies (3 crs.) Students develop and practice academic reading, writing, and thinking skills involved in professional practices of educational research and publishing communities.

passages.heading: #22-23-33C | Page 58
passages.text:
Course emphasizes scholarly identity and writing cogent literature reviews. (Lec. 2, Sem 1) EDP 610 Contemporary Issues in Educational Inquiry (3 crs.) Examination of issues and problems related to philosophical and historical aspects of educational thought and the role of society.
Empirical analysis of classroom settings is emphasized. (Seminar) EDP 611 Issues and Problems in Educational Inquiry (3 crs.) Examination of issues and problems related to philosophical and historical aspects of educational thought and the role of society.
Empirical analysis of classroom setting is emphasized. (Seminar) EDP 612 Qualitative Research Methods in Education (3 crs.) Survey of qualitative methods of educational research: terminology, historical development, assumptions, and models of inquiry.
EDP 613 Introduction to Quantitative Research (4 crs.) Educational research data are collected, quantitatively analyzed and interpreted.
Applications of the general linear model to a variety of research designs and analytic strategies are emphasized. (Lec. 3, Rec. 1) EDP 622 Societal Perspectives of Education (3 crs.) Application of theory to the intersection of community service, academic

passages.heading: #22-23-33C | Page 59
passages.text:
EDP 623 Research Design (3 crs.) Research design process including developing problem statements, research questions, hypotheses and appropriate methods (i.e., qualitative, quantitative, or mixed).
Course considers philosophical worldviews, literature reviews, theory use, and research ethics. (Lec. 3) EDP 641 Doctoral Dissertation Research Seminar (1 cr.) Bi-weekly forums present evolving research questions and empirical designs.
Discussion and feedback refine individuals' research plan, enhancing the methodological perspectives and tools of all participants. (Seminar) EDC 682 - Discourse Analysis in Education Research (3 crs.) The analysis of discourse in educational research is examined and practiced in this course.

passages.heading: #22-23-33C | Page 59
passages.text:
Students conduct various analyses of discourse samples and explore a variety of analytic research frameworks. (Seminar 3) EDC 684 - The Analysis of Data: A Hands-On Approach (3 crs.) Students will practice data analysis using three specific qualitative methodologies, noting that each of these methodologies offers a unique lens on phenomena. (Seminar 3) EDC685 - Survey Design (3 crs.) Principles, theories, techniques, and applications for developing survey questionnaires and conducting survey research in education; developing questions; constructing instruments; implementing surveys; reducing coverage and sampling errors. (Seminar 3) EDP 699 Doctoral Dissertation Research (1-12 crs.) Number of credits is determined each semester in consultation with the major professor or program committee. (Independent Study) S/U only.
NOTES: Some of the pre-requisites on these pre-existing courses may need to be revised.
CEPS will make those minor changes in 2024/2025 to allow the current Joint PhD program students to enroll seamlessly during the teach out of that program.

International Studies is a cross-disciplinary major that requires 33-48 credits.
To become an international studies major students must first become one of the approved ISD language majors.
No student may have International Studies as a single major.
No more than 50% of international studies required credits can come from any one course code.
To graduate with an international studies major, students must remain in the ISD program, which requires students to successfully concurrently complete a major in an approved language, meet the ISD language proficiency benchmark, meet minimum GPA requirements and study abroad at an ISD approved setting for at least one semester.

passages.heading: #22-23-46 | Page 11
passages.text:
International Studies has three Core areas with the following requirements: 1) In the International Relations Core, students must take PSC 116G and PSC 211 and at least one of the following: PSC 300, 312*, 320, 321, 322, 325, 350, 360, 377, 408, 415, 416, 417, 419, 421G, 422, 431, 434, 435, 482*, 492. *Topic must be approved by the ISD director 2) In the International Economics Core, students must take ECN 201, 202, 358 (online study abroad course) and at least one of the following ECN 338, 344, 363. 3) In the History, Culture, and Society Core, students must take APG 203.
In addition to the above Core options, any of the following courses may be taken as major electives that count towards the 33 credits: AAF 410; APG 200, 315, 329, 415, 465; COM 361; ECN 305, 306, 381, 390, 445, FLM 451; GWS 401, 430; HIS 311, 333, 353G, 354, 373, 374, 375, 376, 377, 379, 382, 384, 385, 388; LAN 220; RLS 221. *Topic must be approved by the ISD director Students must take at least one 400-level course from any of the Core or major elective courses.

passages.heading: #22-23-46 | Page 11
passages.text:
In order to transfer from University College for Academic Success to the College of Arts and Sciences, ISD students must have completed a minimum of 30 credits with a cumulative GPA of 2.50 or higher.
Once they have met these requirements and been transferred to the College of Arts and Sciences, students will be advised by three faculty coordinators (one from political Science - who also serves as M.A .director, one from economics, and one from languages).
A total of 120 credits and a cumulative GPA of 2.5 or higher is required for graduation.
At least 42 of these credits must be in courses numbered 300 or above.
Language (B.A.) Students in the ISD program must major in an approved language from the following existing majors: French, Chinese, Spanish, German, Italian, and Global Language Area Studies.
Each of the approved languages attached to the ISD program requires 30 credit hours.
ISD students must achieve B2-level (CEFR) or Advanced-Low (ACTFL) language proficiency in their target language to graduate from the ISD program.
These are the minimum required language proficiency levels for graduate or professional work in that language.

passages.heading: #22-23-46 | Page 11
passages.text: It is recommended that students take LAN 220 during their first or second year.

passages.heading: #22-23-46 | Page 12
passages.text:
Study Abroad Required Study abroad at an approved international institutional setting is a key requirement for the ISD program.
ISD students are required to study abroad for at least one semester but a full academic year abroad is recommended.
Students must meet the intermediate mid (B1.1) language proficiency level or above prior to study abroad.
Upon return from study abroad students must should meet the intermediate high (B1.2) language proficiency level or above to remain in the ISD Program.
Admission, Retention and Graduation Requirements To obtain admission into the ISD Program from high school, students should have a cumulative GPA of 3.2 or above.
For existing URI students to obtain entry into the standard ISD program, they must apply by the end of the first semester of their second year, have an overall GPA 3.0 or above and have earned a C+ or above in PSC 116G.
Students must also obtain formal consultation and approval from the section head of the target language or department chair of Languages to ensure that the student is at the appropriate proficiency benchmark in order to achieve advanced low (B2) language proficiency upon completion of the program.

Rationale for closing program: In 1993, the University of Rhode Island entered into a partnership with Rhode Island College to offer a Joint PhD program in Education.
Although the intention was for the universities to share the responsibility (budget, staffing, etc.), Rhode Island College has not, in recent years, been in a position to support half of the program responsibilities.
As such, the program has largely been supported by URI (teaching faculty, graduate assistants, travel funding, etc.).
Yet, most of the tuition revenue has flowed to Rhode Island College.
In the summer of 2022, the Deans of the URI Alan Shawn Feinstein College of Education and Professional Studies (Dennis) and RIC Feinstein College of Education and Human Development (Dingus-Eason) agreed to discontinue the current Joint Program.
Faculty and students have been notified of the decision to discontinue the joint program and a teach out plan has been developed.

passages.heading: #22-23-45C | Page 5
passages.text:
Dean Dennis has also been working with URI OGC to ensure that the process aligns with the agreements between URI and RIC.
The agreement between URI and RIC states that “The continuation of this program depends on the continued agreement, support, and participation of both institutions.
Termination or withdrawal of support of the program at either institution will result in termination of the program” (p. 86).
As such, the faculty in the school of education have re-designed a stand-alone Ph.D. program in Education at the University of Rhode Island.
The program proposal for that “new” program is being submitted concurrently with this closure paperwork. (See Kuali) URI Faculty have used the “best of” current courses to design a scholarly doctoral program that is more research intensive than the current joint program–which was initially designed to prepare educational practitioners.
The proposed new URI program builds on current strengths (courses, faculty, ongoing research) to produce educational scholars who can solve the most intractable contemporary education problems.

passages.heading: #22-23-45C | Page 5
passages.text:
The new program will allow students to develop focused expertise in an area of PreK-20 or adult education settings that aligns with current graduate program offerings and faculty expertise in the School of Education. 13.

NASustainable Agriculture and Food Systems is a relatively new program.
Since the program's inception, we have found that the curriculum needs to be more �exible to accommodate the needs of students transferring into the program from outside URI or changing majors within the university.
For greater �exibility, we have expanded students' options for ful�lling the the economics and sustainability course requirements for the introduction to SAFS sequence.
In addition, students in both the Sustainable Agriculture and Nutrition and Food specializations now have the option of taking either APG/GW S/SOC 308 Sustainable Agriculture and Food Cultures or SAF 383 Food Justice to ful�ll the food and society requirement of the pre-professional sequence.
We have also revised the interdisciplinary component requirement at the program level for greater �exibility.

passages.heading: #22-23-34B | Page 22
passages.text:
Instead of being required to take two courses from each of the other two specializations, students can now take a total of four courses (12 credits minimum) from the other specializations with a minimum of one course from each specialization.
We have also found that the program's biology and chemistry requirements discourage otherwise interested students from enrolling in the Food and Society specialization.
In consultation with outside experts in food policy and other relevant areas, we determined that these courses are not required for the specialization or for food policy and related work.
Consequently, we removed biology and chemistry from the pre-professional program requirements for the Food and Society specialization but retained them as requirements for the Sustainable Agriculture and Nutrition and Food Systems specializations.

passages.heading: #22-23-34B | Page 22
passages.text:
We otherwise strengthened the pre-professional requirements for the Food and Society specialization and now require that students take APG/GWS/SOC 308 Sustainable Agriculture and Food Cultures, SAF 383 Food Justice, and APG 203 Cultural Anthropology. (Formerly, only APG/GWS/SOC 308 was required.) NRS 212 Introduction to Soil Science has been added to the pre-professional requirements for the Sustainable Agriculture specialization because we deem a basic knowledge of soil science to be essential to the practice of agriculture.

The electrical engineering program is accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission (EAC) of ABET, Inc. (www.abet.org).
The department also offers the Master of Science (M.S.) and Doctor of Philosophy (Ph.D.) degrees.

Program Educational Objectives.

passages.heading: #22-23-34B | Page 55
passages.text:
Three to �ve years after graduation from the B.S. in electrical engineering, graduates will: 1) Successfully practice electrical engineering to serve state and regional industries, government agencies, or national and international industries. 2) Work professionally in one or more of the following areas: analog electronics, digital electronics, communication systems, signal processing, control systems, and computer-based systems. 3) Achieve personal and professional success with awareness and commitment to their ethical and social responsibilities, both as individuals and in team environments. 4) Maintain and improve their technical competence through lifelong learning, including entering and succeeding in an advanced degree program in a �eld such as engineering, science, or business.
Student Outcomes.
Electrical engineering students demonstrate knowledge in all outcomes required by ABET, Inc. which are listed in the college’s student outcomes section of this catalog.
Program Description.

passages.heading: #22-23-34B | Page 55
passages.text:
Since instrumentation is at the heart of modern science and technology, electrical engineers are employed not only in the computer, electronics, communications, and power industries, but also in diverse enterprises such as transportation, the chemical industry, large hospitals, and government laboratories.
The curriculum emphasizes the scienti�c basis of electrical engineering and the application of mathematical analysis to engineering problems.
Work is required in linear systems and signals, analog and digital circuits, electromagnetic theory, and electronics.
Creative use of scienti�c principles in problems of engineering design is stressed, particularly in the senior year.
The development of computer hardware and software is a part of many electrical engineering courses.
Extensive laboratory work serves to bridge the gap between mathematical analysis and the real world of “hardware.” Separate undergraduate laboratories are available for electrical measurements, analog electronics, digital electronics, microprocessors, hardware description languages, embedded systems, electromagnetics, control systems, and communications.

3/20/23, 1:29 PM Kuali CM | Programs View - Ocean Engineering - BS https://uri.kuali.co/cm/#/programs/print/634eef48a49f53d7f5651438 4/11 Changes Program Description Ocean Engineering The Department of Ocean Engineering offers a curriculum leading to the Bachelor of Science (B.S.) degree in ocean engineering.
The Ocean Engineering Program is accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission of ABET, Inc. (www.abet.org).
URI’s Department of Ocean Engineering is nationally and internationally recognized as one of the leaders in ocean engineering, and also offers Master of Science (M.S.) and Doctor of Philosophy (Ph.D.) degrees.
As it is a unique program in New England and throughout the country, quali�ed students can apply under the New England Regional Student Program (RSP).
Department Mission Statement.

passages.heading: #22-23-34B | Page 63
passages.text:
The Department of Ocean Engineering’s mission is to provide high-quality undergraduate and graduate degree programs that prepare our students for professional careers in ocean engineering in industry, academia, and government; to develop and maintain internationally recognized research programs in selected areas of ocean engineering; to actively serve the profession and community in our areas of expertise; and to provide a challenging work and learning environment where diversity, community, scholarship, professional development, and excellence are valued and rewarded.
The program is designed to provide students with a strong base in fundamental sciences, mathematics, and engineering; a broad base in ocean engineering; opportunities for the integration of theory, experimentation, and design; appreciation of ethical, social, and environmental issues in the practice of the profession; and strong oral and written communication skills.
Program Educational Objectives.

passages.heading: #22-23-34B | Page 63
passages.text:
Three to �ve years after graduation, our graduates will be: 1) Gainfully employed with private or government organizations and advancing to positions of increased responsibility, or pursuing an advanced degree in an engineering program. 2) Working in one of the specialty areas within the broad �eld of ocean engineering including ocean instrumentation, ocean robotics and vehicles, ocean waves and coastal engineering, underwater acoustics, marine structures, marine geomechanics, ocean renewable energy, and ocean engineering design. 3) Behaving ethically, contributing to society, participating in strengthening a diverse engineering professional environment, and succeeding in diverse workplaces, nationally and internationally.
Student Outcomes.
Ocean engineering students demonstrate knowledge in all outcomes required by ABET, Inc. which are listed in the college’s student outcomes section of this catalog.
Program Description.
URI’s curriculum provides an ocean engineering program that gives students a �rm base in engineering fundamentals and prepares them for direct entry into a professional career or continued study toward a graduate degree.

passages.heading: #22-23-34B | Page 63
passages.text:
The required ocean engineering courses begin at the freshman level and include laboratory, data analysis, and design courses.
A strong emphasis is on the application of scienti�c principles in the ocean environment gained through laboratory courses.
Experiments covering several basic areas are used to provide an integrated approach to investigations into ocean phenomena and processes.
Students are involved in the planning and execution of experiments, including data collection and analysis and the reporting of results.
This hands-on experience provides graduates with an understanding of ocean engineering activities in scienti�c and industrial �elds.
The broad-based program exposes students to the following topics: offshore renewable energy, ocean instrumentation and data analysis, ocean robotics and vehicles, underwater and sub-bottom acoustics, wave and marine hydrodynamics, coastal processes, marine geomechanics, and coastal and offshore structures.

passages.heading: #22-23-34B | Page 63
passages.text: Students have the option to concentrate in one of the ocean engineering disciplines by following one of the academic tracks, which are faculty selected course sequences in Acoustics, Coastal Engineering, Hydrodynamics (Naval Architecture or Waves/Coastal), Ocean Renewable Energy, Offshore Structures, and Robotics.

3/20/23, 1:29 PM Kuali CM | Programs View - Ocean Engineering - BS https://uri.kuali.co/cm/#/programs/print/634eef48a49f53d7f5651438 5/11 A highlight of the ocean engineering undergraduate experience is a two-semester Senior Capstone Ocean Engineering Design Project, which integrates previously obtained knowledge into a comprehensive team design project.
Each year diverse projects are offered as small sections, many of them with industry participation/funding and typically advised by multiple faculty advisors.
Students work as teams on integrated sub-tasks, prepare substantial reports and give oral presentations.
The Department of Ocean Engineering is located at URI’s Narragansett Bay Campus.
The facilities include a 30 x 3.6 x 1.8 m (length, width, depth) tow and wave tank, a wave-current interaction �ume, a large and deep (4.2 m) acoustics tank, an electronics shop, machine shop, rapid prototyping equipment including 3D printers and a laser cutter, and the Marine Geomechanics Laboratory.
These facilities are available to undergraduate and graduate students for course work, research, and independent study.

passages.heading: #22-23-34B | Page 64
passages.text:
The department has access to a 42-foot research vessel equipped with a fully integrated side-scan sonar and sub-bottom mapping system, and vibracoring and gravity coring systems.
This vessel is used for both lab courses and research.
Also available in the department are a Seaglider Autonomous Underwater Vehicle, several inspection-class Remotely Operated Vehicles (ROVs), aerial drones, and a deep-sea oceanographic winch system.
The ocean engineering major requires 126 credits.

Three to �ve years after graduation from the B.S. in mechanical engineering program, graduates will: 1) Successfully practice mechanical engineering to serve state, local, national, and international industries and government agencies. 2) Work professionally in one of the two major stems of mechanical engineering: mechanical and/or thermal systems or related �elds. 3) Achieve personal and professional success with an understanding and appreciation of ethical behavior, social responsibility and diversity, both as individuals and in team environments. 4) Pursue continued life-long learning through further graduate education, short courses or other training programs in engineering or related �elds.
Student Outcomes.
Mechanical engineering students demonstrate knowledge in all outcomes required by ABET, Inc. which are listed in the college’s student outcomes section of this catalog.
Program Description.

passages.heading: #22-23-34B | Page 74
passages.text:
The curriculum provides a thorough and well-rounded foundation in basic science, mathematics, engineering science, and general education to prepare the graduate for a professional engineering career.
The curriculum is also excellent preparation for graduate school.
The program is strong in providing a background in design, solid and �uid mechanics, systems engineering, and the thermal sciences, including energy and energy transfer.
Computer applications are stressed throughout the curriculum.
All undergraduates are invited and encouraged to join the student section of the American Society of Mechanical Engineers, which sponsors industrial plant visits, special lectures, and other activities.
Students may also join chapters of the Society of Automotive Engineers (SAE) and the American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME).
The work in the �rst two years consists of basic courses in science (math, physics, chemistry), applied science (mechanics, electricity and magnetism, basic computer literacy and computer-aided problem solving), manufacturing processes, and general education requirements (humanities, social sciences, English communication).

passages.heading: #22-23-34B | Page 74
passages.text:
Two introductory engineering courses are included in the freshman year.
The junior year concentrates on fundamental mechanical engineering courses (thermodynamics, �uid mechanics, systems engineering, engineering analysis, heat transfer), materials sciences, and design of machines.
Further general education studies are also covered.
The senior year includes the capstone design sequence, mechanical engineering experimentation, and a wide variety of professional electives such as mechanical control systems, advanced �uid mechanics, advanced mechanics of materials, mechatronics, internal combustion engines, applied energy conversion, tribology, product design for manufacture, air conditioning, heating and ventilation, vibrations, �nite element method, and experimental stress analysis.
The program also includes two laboratory courses in the junior and senior years.
Further general education studies are also covered.
Computer techniques are integrated throughout the curriculum.
Computational facilities including PCs and workstations are available in the College of Engineering’s Engineering Computer Center (ECC) and the University’s O�ce of Information Technology Services (ITS).

Interdisciplinary Studies–Learner Designed Program (Three-Minor Major) The Interdisciplinary Studies Learner Designed degree is an innovative bachelor’s program designed for students whose career goals call for training in more than one discipline or who want a breadth of knowledge in several �elds rather than a depth of knowledge in a single discipline.
This interdisciplinary “three-minor” major provides an opportunity for students to develop and pursue a course of study centered on a self-selected unifying theme, problem, or issue.
Students earning this learner designed major will (a) possess an interdisciplinary perspective by focusing on three areas of study, (b) apply critical thinking skills integrating theory and practice to creatively solve problems across disciplines, and (c) communicate effectively across disciplinary boundaries.
The Bachelor of Interdisciplinary Studies Learner Designed Program consists of the following required sections: 1) Degree Requirements 2) General Education, 3) BIS Courses, 4) Major Curriculum, and 5) General Electives.

The Bachelor of Interdisciplinary Studies Learner Designed major consists of (a) URI General Education Requirements (40 credits); (b) Minor Area of Study I (18 credits), Minor Area of Study II (18 credits) and Minor Area of Study III (18 credits); (c) BIS 199, BIS 299, BIS 399, and WRT 227, and (d) elective courses totaling 120 credit hours. Students are required to meet with the Director of School of Professional & Continuing Studies (or designee) to plan a project proposal. General Education Requirements. Students accepted to URI are initially placed in University College for Academic Success (UCAS). Once students have completed a minimum of 24 credits and have met the basic competencies for internal transfer, they can request to be moved to their degree granting college, the Alan Shawn Feinstein College of Education and Professional Studies. General education consists of 40 credits. For more details regarding General Education, please go to the Academic Requirements and Policies section of this catalog. BIS Courses (8 credits). Three BIS courses serve to launch the program, integrate learner, and synthesize learning with a capstone experience. These courses consist of BIS 199, BIS 299, and BIS 399. Major Curriculum (57 credits). BIS Learner Designed students will select three distinct minor degrees (eighteen credits each) offered from throughout the University of Rhode Island and take WRT 227. Electives (15 credits). Electives permit students to complete the BIS degree in a number of creative ways through course work, internships, or previous but relevant educational experience.

CONSTITUTION, BY-LAWS, AND UNIVERSITY MANUAL COMMITTEE Report #2022-2023-3 - INFORMATIONALFACULTY SENATE Editorial Changes: Faculty Senate legislation (Bill #21-22-10; Bill #21-22-11; Bill #21-22-12)enables the Constitution, By-Laws and University Manual (CBUM) Committee to make necessaryeditorial changes to the University Manual and its Appendices and to report those changes to theFaculty Senate.
Following the report, any Faculty Senator may move that a proposed change shouldbe considered substantive.
This motion, when seconded, will then be considered for a vote, andif passed, the matter shall be handled as a substantive change and will follow University Manuallegislative procedures.
Rationale for changes: The University Manual (UM) is the living written record of the duly approvedrights, statutes, regulations, policies, and procedures by which the University is governedcollaboratively, providing community members with access to information that is vital to ourinstitution’s mission and functioning.
The CBUM Committee is charged with ensuring that allinformation contained in the UM is accurate and current.
Part 1.

passages.heading: IFSR 2022-2023-3 | Page 2
passages.text:
Ensuring clarity and accurate representation of the University's governing body 4.30.10 The Faculty Senate.
The General Faculty, through legislative act on May 12, 1960, authorized the establishment of a Faculty Senate as its agent to conduct in a responsible and efficient manner the business assigned to faculty jurisdiction by law, the President, or by the Rhode Island Board of Trustees (now by the URI Board of Governors Trustees ).
It was the intent that the faculty delegate to the Senate all powers of the faculty, with the exception of those stipulated in this chapter, that are specifically delegated elsewhere, so long as the Senate shall represent the will of the faculty.
Approval of the Senate Constitution and By-Laws was granted by the former Rhode Island Board of Trustees on November 1, 1961. #21-22-6 8.10.30 Residency.
Regulations defining resident and non-resident student status and the appeal process at all public institutions of higher education the University of Rhode Island are under the governance of the URI Board of Education Trustees .
The President of the University shall designate an officer or officers to determine the residency status of students.
Part 2.

passages.text:

The committee is precluded from involvement in any aspect of individual conduct cases or in the daily operation of the Office of Student Life. #02-03–33 5.74.10 The University Conduct Board shall, through hearing panels drawn from it, hear and adjudicate cases of alleged violations of community standards of behavior or university policies as referred to it by the Office of Student Life .
Dean of Students Office .
Procedures to be followed are found in sections 9.18.10-9.25.10 . #05-06–2E #January 27, 2022 Informational Report 5.74.12 New student members shall be selected by the existing board.
In selecting new members, the Board shall make every effort to provide Board representation for each of the following groups: Fraternities/sororities, residence hall students, and commuters.
Care shall also be taken that the interests of minority groups be considered in the selection process.
Only full-time students who do not have current conduct sanctions shall be allowed to serve.
The Office of Student Life .

Dean of Students Office shall appoint a Conduct Board Advisor, who shall not be considered a member of the Board, but who shall be present at board meetings. #07-08–34 #January 27, 2022 Informational Report 5.75.11 The Appeals Board shall comprise one full-time student (who does not have a current conduct sanction) appointed by the President of the Student Senate and one member of the teaching faculty appointed by the President of the Faculty Senate, and a chairperson holding the rank of assistant professor or above appointed by the President of the University.
For a graduate student’s appeal, the Graduate Student Association shall appoint a graduate student member to the Board.
Alternates for each position shall be appointed by the appointing authorities.
A quorum shall require the presence of all three Board members; however, when duly appointed members or alternates cannot be convened quickly, former members of the Appeals Board may be called upon to serve, providing proper Board composition is maintained.

The instructor shall have the right to fail a student on the assignment on which the instructor has determined that a student has cheated or plagiarized.
The circumstances of this failure shall be reported to the student’s academic dean, the instructor’s dean, and the Office of Student Life .

Dean of Students Office.
A cumulative file will be maintained in that office.
The Dean of Students shall notify the student’s dean of subsequent infractions and may initiate conduct action against the student. #04-05–32 9.20.10 Disciplinary Action may be implemented only through referral of violations to the Office of Student Life Dean of Students Office , the Office of Campus Life, or the Office of Housing and

passages.heading: IFSR 2022-2023-3 | Page 4
passages.text:
Residential Life.
Infractions of community standards and University policies shall be reported in a timely manner to the appropriate office by the campus police or by local police departments, by other students, or by faculty or staff.
In all cases, the available facts shall be gathered from the accuser (the reporting agency or complainant), and a careful evaluation of these facts, as well as of the dependability and character of the person(s) reporting them, shall be made.
If corroboration of the information presented is deemed necessary, further inquiry and investigation shall be undertaken.

passages.heading: IFSR 2022-2023-3 | Page 4
passages.text:
If, at this point, in the judgment of the investigating authority, there is insufficient evidence of a violation, or the case lacks merit, a decision not to refer the matter to the conduct system may be made. #05-06–2E 9.21.15 Administrative Hearings shall be conducted (1) if a charged student fails to respond to a charge letter within two working days; (2) if the hearing concerns the sanctions only; (3) if a student requests an administrative hearing; and (4) if in the judgment of the Office of Student Life Dean of Students Office , scheduling it is necessary to ensure that a hearing occurs in a timely fashion, to insure the health and safety of any of the participants or to insure an unbiased hearing. #04-05–32 9.21.16 Panel Hearings shall take place if an accused student denies responsibility for the alleged violation, requests a panel hearing, and none of the conditions making an administrative hearing necessary and/or appropriate (see 9.21.15) apply.
Panel hearings shall normally take place before panels drawn from the University Judicial Board (s ee 5.74.10 – 5.74.21 ).

passages.heading: IFSR 2022-2023-3 | Page 4
passages.text:
When the situation warrants it, however, the Office of Student Life Dean of Students Office shall have the authority to establish special hearing panels. 9.21.17 Procedures for Panel Hearings.
If the accused student requests a panel hearing, and the Office of Student Life Dean of Students Office concurs with this request, every effort shall be made to hold a hearing before the appropriate panel within 20 class days from the date the student furnishes a written response to the charge letter.
The accused student shall receive written notification of the place and time of the hearing at least 72 hours in advance of the hearing.
The notification shall also identify the panel members.
A staff member from the Office of Student Life Dean of Students Office shall be available prior to the hearing at the request of the student to advise regarding the alleged violation and procedural matters.
The student may challenge the participation of (a) panel member(s) for good cause, provided this is done at least 48 hours in advance of the hearing.
Hearings shall be closed. #21-22-6 9.21.20 Panel Advisor.

passages.heading: IFSR 2022-2023-3 | Page 4
passages.text:
All panels shall have an advisor appointed by the Office of Student Life Dean of Students Office who shall be present during all stages of the conduct process, including hearings and deliberations, except during the closed panel session determining whether or not the accused student is responsible for the alleged conduct.
Responsibilities of the panel advisor shall include: (1) advising the panel regarding the requirements and provisions of substantive and procedural due process; (2) serving as a resource person concerning an accused student’s past history of involvement in the discipline system if any; (3) providing continuity in panel operations and procedures; (4) facilitating the implementation of conduct procedures at all levels of the conduct system; (5) acting as a liaison between panels and the University community; (6) assisting the panel in fulfilling its educational responsibility; and (7) preparing a written record of each hearing which is to include a summary of the testimony and evidence presented, and a statement of the decision reached.

passages.heading: IFSR 2022-2023-3 | Page 4
passages.text: The individual who serves as panel advisor shall not be the person who conducted the original investigation as described in 9.20.10 and 9.21.10.

passages.heading: IFSR 2022-2023-3 | Page 5
passages.text:
9.21.28 Deferral of Proceedings.
The staff of the Office of Student Life Dean of Students Office may defer conduct action at any stage of the process for a period not to exceed ninety calendar days when school is in session.
Pending charges may be discontinued thereafter depending upon the good conduct of the accused student. #04-05–32 9.21.31 Conduct Records.
All conduct records, such as complaint letters, correspondence, charge letters, decision letters, and hearing summaries, shall be considered confidential, and be maintained by the Office of Student Life Dean of Students Office for six years after the date of the action.
Records of unresolved incidents shall be reviewed annually starting with the 6-year anniversary.
The Dean of Students shall decide whether or not to destroy such a record or keep it for another year.
Records of permanent dismissal shall be retained permanently.
Access to such records is governed by the University Policies for the Release and Disclosure of Information from Student Records (see section 6.12.21). #04-05–32 9.24.11 Appeal on the Issue of Off-Campus Jurisdiction.

passages.heading: IFSR 2022-2023-3 | Page 5
passages.text:
If a student is accused of an off-campus offense under subsection 2 of Section 9.24.10, and if the representative of the Office of Student Life Dean of Students Office determines that there is cause for presenting the matter to the Student Discipline System, the student shall have the right to dispute the jurisdiction of the Student Discipline System.
Such an appeal must be filed in writing with the Office of Student Life not later than three days after notice of the Office of Student Life Dean of Students Office decision that the student has been charged.
The appeal shall be presented to the Vice President for Student Affairs for disposition of the issue of jurisdiction.
The decision on jurisdiction arrived at by the Vice President for Student Affairs shall be final.
When an affirmative judgment on jurisdiction has been reached through this procedure, the student shall still have the right to accept or deny responsibility for the conduct in question. 9.25.10 Mediation.

passages.heading: IFSR 2022-2023-3 | Page 5
passages.text:
When there is an apparent violation of community standards or University policies for students, the incident may be adjudicated through a formal mediation process if formal mediation is acceptable to all of the following parties: (1) the individual(s) allegedly responsible for the violation; (2) the complainant (student, staff or department reporting the violation), and (3) the Office of Student Life Dean of Students Office .
Mediation shall be conducted by a trained University staff member approved by the Office of Student Life Dean of Students Office .
Mediation requires the cooperation of all parties to resolve a problem.
The process is to result in a written document agreed to by all parties.
The written agreement shall be kept on file in the Office of Student Life Dean of Students Office .
Should Mediation fail to result in an agreement, or should a party fail to abide by an agreement, formal disciplinary proceedings shall then be initiated.

If the accused student requests a panel hearing, and the Office of Student Life Dean of Students Office concurs with this request, every effort shall be made to hold a hearing before the appropriate panel within 20 class days from the date the student furnishes a written response to the charge letter.
The accused student shall receive written notification of the place and time of the hearing at least 72 hours in advance of the hearing.
The notification shall also identify the panel members.
A staff member from the Office of Student Life Dean of Students Office shall be available prior to the hearing at the request of the student to advise regarding the alleged violation and procedural matters.
The student may challenge the participation of (a) panel member(s) for good cause, provided this is done at least 48 hours in advance of the hearing.

passages.text:
All panels shall have an advisor appointed by the Office of Student Life Dean of Students Office who shall be present during all stages of the conduct process, including hearings and deliberations, except during the closed panel session determining whether or not the accused student is responsible for the alleged conduct.
Responsibilities of the panel advisor shall include: (1) advising the panel regarding the requirements and provisions of substantive and procedural due process; (2) serving as a resource person concerning an accused student’s past history of involvement in the discipline system if any; (3) providing continuity in panel operations and procedures; (4) facilitating the implementation of conduct procedures at all levels of the conduct system; (5) acting as a liaison between panels and the University community; (6) assisting the panel in fulfilling its educational responsibility; and (7) preparing a written record of each hearing which is to include a summary of the testimony and evidence presented, and a statement of the decision reached.

passages.heading: IFSR 2022-2023-3 | Page 9

Records of unresolved incidents shall be reviewed annually starting with the 6-year anniversary.

Such an appeal must be filed in writing with the Office of Student Life not later than three days after notice of the Office of Student Life Dean of Students Office decision that the student has been charged.
The appeal shall be presented to the Vice President for Student Affairs for disposition of the issue of jurisdiction.
