CONSTITUTION, BY-LAWS, AND UNIVERSITY MANUAL COMMITTEEReport #2022-2023-20 - Report on Certificates and MinorsFACULTY SENATE - May 4, 2023 Context: Policies relating to Undergraduate Certificates and Minors A disagreement in the interpretation of UM language about minors between representatives of adegree-granting college and representatives from Enrollment Services was referred to FSEC andCBUM.
FSEC charged CBUM with examining the policies relating to minor fields of study andUndergraduate Certificate Programs, as they are codified in the UM, and to bring forthrecommendations to the Faculty Senate.
This report includes proposed editorial changes to the UMand aims to: 1) resolve the ambiguity in current UM language and clarify policies governingUndergraduate Certificate Programs, 2) increase clarity and comprehensibility in the current UMlanguage about Minor fields of study, and 3) report on the need to resolve confusion and conflictinginterpretations of language in UM 8.20.52.

passages.heading: IFSR 2022-2023-10 | Page 2
passages.text: The disagreement stemmed from confusion in UM 8.20.52 about the total number of courses andcredits that students may apply to different degree requirements, including the major field of studyand the minor field of study: - “A maximum of two courses required in a major program may be used to apply to both the major and minor fields of study.” - “Courses from other curricula that are recommended or required for the major may apply to the minor.” - “Courses in General Education may be used for the minor.” The members of CBUM examined and discussed this language that has been interpreted in differentways and agree that, while there are no limits on the number of General Education courses thatstudents may also apply to the minor, the maximum number of courses that may be applied to boththe major and minor fields of study is two, and this limit applies to all courses that students apply tothe major field of study, regardless of course code and including “courses from other curricula thatare recommended or required for the major.” CBUM understands that some faculty and department chairs have interpreted this confusing UMlanguage on minors more broadly and believed that it was permissible to apply to both the major andminor fields of study 1) a maximum of two courses from the major program (courses carrying thecourse code of the major program of study), and 2) an unlimited number of courses from othercurricula (different course codes).

passages.heading: IFSR 2022-2023-10 | Page 2
passages.text:
Upon further investigation and deliberation, CBUM discovered thatone of the fundamental differences between Undergraduate Certificates and Minors revolves aroundthe precise issue of the level of flexibility in applying credits to both the major field of study and theother area of inquiry: Undergraduate Certificate Programs have no limits, minors have limits.
In addition to the following three (3) proposals for editorial changes to the UM, CBUM refers to theCurriculum and Standards Committee the broader issue of establishing clarity in the curricularstandards for Minor programs, and determining if it would be advisable to bring forth additionallanguage to clarify the distinctions between Undergraduate Certificates and Minors.

passages.heading: IFSR 2022-2023-10 | Page 3
passages.text:
Proposal 1: Editorial changes to clarify UM language on Undergraduate Certificates Rationale: Editorial clarifications to UM language on the nature of Undergraduate CertificatePrograms and on the policies governing the process by which students earn an UndergraduateCertificate.
Existing language: 8.20.73 Courses completed in pursuit of an Undergraduate Certificate may be used to apply toward undergraduate degree requirements.
Undergraduate Certificate courses may not be taken under the pass-fail grading option.
Applicants may not transfer courses into an undergraduate Certificate Program that have been taken at institutions other than URI.
Credits earned at URI and applied to the Undergraduate Certificate Program must have been taken within eight years of matriculating into the Undergraduate Certificate Program and cannot total more than two-fifths of the total number of credits required for the Undergraduate Certificate Program. #16-17-22 Proposed changes: 8.20.73 All Cc ourses completed in pursuit of an Undergraduate Certificate may be used to apply toward undergraduate degree requirements.

passages.heading: IFSR 2022-2023-10 | Page 3
passages.text:
Some degree programs consist of multiple certificate programs that, when combined or stacked, comprise many or all of the program’s degree requirements .
Undergraduate Certificate courses may not be taken under the pass-fail grading option.
Applicants may not transfer courses into an Undergraduate Certificate Program that have been taken at institutions other than URI.
Credits earned at URI prior to officially matriculating into the Undergraduate Certificate Program and applied to the Undergraduate Certificate that Program must have been taken within eight years of matriculating into the that Undergraduate Certificate Program and cannot total more than two-fifths of the total number of credits required for the Undergraduate Certificate that Program. #16-17-22

Summary description of proposed program: The College of Pharmacy currently has two departments: Biomedical & PharmaceuticalSciences and Pharmacy Practice.
The College previously was comprised of multipledepartments: Medicinal Chemistry, Pharmacognosy, Pharmacology & Toxicology,Pharmaceutics, and Pharmacy Practice.
In 1996, multiple departments merged resulting inthree departments: Biomedical Sciences, Applied Pharmaceutical Sciences, and PharmacyPractice.
When the College adopted the Doctor of Pharmacy degree as the entry level degreeas part of a national movement to the all-PharmD degree in the early 2000s, AppliedPharmaceutical Sciences was dissolved with Pharmacoepidemiology andPharmacoeconomics (now, Health Outcomes) moving into Pharmacy Practice andPharmaceutics moving into Biomedical Sciences, resulting in the two current departments.
The Department of Pharmacy Practice delivers MS and PhD degree in the Health Outcomestrack of our graduate Pharmaceutical Sciences degrees, supported by six faculty (5tenure/tenure-track, one assistant teaching professor) in Health Outcomes, with twoadditional lines held (Dean Larrat and Associate Dean Quilliam).

passages.heading: #22-23-40B | Page 13
passages.text:
Of those faculty, three arepharmacist scientists (RPh/PhD) while the remaining are MS or PhD trained.
During the 2021-2022 academic year, discussion about a possible name change for thedepartment was discussed in an eﬀort to make the departmental name more inclusive of allfaculty represented in our department.
Numerous potential names were identiﬁed anddebated.
In Fall 2023, the Department, after much discussion and deliberation, voted tochange the department name to Pharmacy Practice and Clinical Research.
The new namenot only acknowledges the multiple faculty from diﬀerent academic specialties, but alsoemphasizes our departmental value for clinical research performed by all our faculty.
Whilethe departmental name would change, our course codes for all courses oﬀered would remainunchanged (PHP) to limit impact on University record-keeping. 2

Departmental websites and departmental curricular and course materials are maintainedindependently and do not necessarily reﬂect University-approved curricular and course information.
Admission Requirements Each admission candidate is given individual consideration.
However, a minimum of 18 units of college(secondary school) preparatory work are expected: ● 4 in English ● 3 in algebra and plane geometry ● 2 in a physical or natural science ● 2 in history or social science ● 2 in the same foreign language ● 5 additional units to total 18 3

passages.heading: #22-23-40B | Page 15

Successful candidates typically have high grades in science and mathematics, do well in SATs or ACTs, andoften have earned advanced placement or college credit while in high school.
Readmission Requirements Students who have been dismissed, have withdrawn, or taken a Leave of Absence for longer than 2consecutive semesters from the College of Pharmacy can seek readmission following University policies andprocedures (web.uri.edu/enrollment/readmission/).
All students requests for readmission will be evaluatedby the Dean of the College of Pharmacy whose decision shall be ﬁnal.
The Dean may consult with theScholastic Standing committee when students were dismissed for academic reasons and/or theProfessionalism Committee when dismissal is related to misconduct.
All students seeking readmission will berequired to provide an application, all academic transcripts from other institutions since last enrollment atURI, and a personal statement outlining the reason for requesting readmission.
The personal statement shouldaddress changes made to address previous academic performance and/or the resolution of disciplinaryactions since dismissal/withdrawal from the College.

passages.text:

Non-native English speakers mustre-sit for the TOEFL or IELTS before applying (within 90 days) for readmission and meet program speciﬁcminimum requirements.
International students who do not meet this requirement at the time of readmissionwill be denied.
Readmission is not guaranteed.
Students readmitted may be conditionally readmitted andmay be placed on probation for at least two consecutive semesters.
General Education Requirements General education consists of 40 credits.
For more details regarding General Education, please go to theAcademic Policies section of this catalog.
Study Abroad and International Experiences The College of Pharmacy encourages students to take advantage of academic related experiences that allowfor international travel and exposure to global opportunities.
These opportunities can occur during the J-term,summer sessions or during the regular academic year (fall or spring semesters).

passages.heading: #22-23-40B | Page 15
passages.text:
Study abroad opportunitieswill be limited to one semester and require careful planning by students in conjunction with academicadvisors.
Students may need to take summer coursework to allow for a study abroad opportunity during theacademic year.
In the Pharm.D. program, study abroad during the regular academic year is restricted to the pre-professionalcurriculum and requires all pre-requisite coursework to be successfully completed prior to the experience.J-term course experiences provide more ﬂexibility and the 1-term limit does not apply to these courseopportunities.
Students requesting longer study abroad experiences (e.g. 1 year) must submit a writtenrequest to the Dean of the College of Pharmacy requesting an exemption from the 1 semester limit; waiversare not guaranteed.
Further, all students wishing to study abroad or participate in a J-term experience must comply with allUniversity policies and secure the necessary approvals before participating in such experiences.
Non-nativeEnglish speakers who study abroad for more than 1 semester must re-sit for the TOEFL or IELTS (within 90days of the semester of return) and meet program speciﬁc minimum requirements. 4

The Master of Environmental Management (MEM) degree program is in direct support of the current 2022-2032 Academic Strategic Plan.
The plan highlights the importance of creating new professional masters degrees that respond to labor market trends and ensure flexible learning pathways that meet both student interests and career trends (Strategic Priority 2; Goal 1; Action 1).

passages.heading: #22-23-45B | Page 6

Additionally, this program is offered completely online and asynchronously (Strategic Priority 2; Goal 1; Action 1 and 2) in order to target working professionals who wish to obtain their credentials while continuing to work full- time.
By offering this program fully online, we are able to reach a larger audience, grow our presence in other regions, and foster a 21st century, 24/7 learning environment that is accessible to students across the globe.
Furthermore, the appeal of the in-state competitive tuition speaks to the accessibility of the program nationwide and internationally.
The College of Environmental Life Sciences currently offers a traditional, on-campus Master of Environmental Science and Management (MESM) degree, however, this accelerated, online program targets a different population.
This program meets the needs of working professionals seeking a professional masters degree in order to become more competitive in the workforce, yet who are often challenged due to accessibility.
This program provides intellectual development for a diverse community of students, including international students, looking to upgrade their skills.

No We propose a flexible master’s program that offers an attractive path to an interdisciplinary graduate degree to current students in the URI online certificate programs and post-graduate professionals looking to bolster their skill sets and attain higher leadership positions and salaries.
The program would require students to successfully complete a graduate certificate program offered through URI Online, two elective courses, and four professional skills courses.
The mix of professional and discipline-specific skills and knowledge aims to prepare professionals for a broad range of careers across private industry, local, state, federal agencies, and community organizations.

The program integrates online certificate programs offered.
Students completing the certificates are accounted for within their respective programs, so it would not be considered an overlap but rather more of an inclusion.
This proposal describes a PSM framework under which focused tracks will be developed.
There are other master's degree programs that incorporate certificates into the masters (Master's of Public Administration, Masters of Science in Healthcare Management, and proposed Masters of Science in Health Outcomes and Data Analytics).
They are very specific in their focus and audience.
For example, students entering the public administration realm will likely prefer an MPA over this program.

passages.text: FACULTY SENATE OFFICE 224 P ASTORE H ALL , 51 L OWER C OLLEGE R OAD , K INGSTON , R I 02881 U SA , P: 401.874.5176 URI Faculty Senate Resolution May 4, 2023 Whereas Michael Rice has served the University of Rhode Island’s Faculty Senate with distinction and dedication as Senate President; Whereas Michael Rice has displayed exceptional leadership qualities, including his ability to delegate tasks effectively and champion academic freedom, thereby fostering a supportive and collaborative environment; Whereas a Jesuit education is a terrible thing to waste, and President Rice has demonstrated time and again that he has taken full advantage of his Jesuit education for the benefit of the URI Faculty Senate and community, Whereas without thorough and nuanced understanding and appreciation for our past, it is impossible to comprehend our present or progress to a brighter future, and President Rice has been a valuable and inexhaustible font of historical institutional knowledge and insights, Whereas Michael Rice's passion for Star Trek and Captain Jean-Luc Picard has infused our meetings with a sense of adventure and fun, while his catchphrase "Make it so" has inspired us to take decisive action; Whereas Michael's frequent use of the phrase "sounds unanimous" has brought levity to our proceedings and demonstrated his commitment to consensus-building; Whereas Michael's leadership has guided us through many meetings, always concluding with his signature motion to adjourn, reminding us to "vote with our feet"; Whereas Michael Rice's term as Senate President will conclude on May 21, followed by a well-deserved sabbatical leave in pursuit of clams, oysters, mussels, and scallops in the Far East; Be it resolved that: 1.

passages.text:

passages.text: FACULTY SENATE OFFICE 224 P ASTORE H ALL , 51 L OWER C OLLEGE R OAD , K INGSTON , R I 02881 U SA , P: 401.874.5176 URI Faculty Senate Resolution in Honor of the Retirement of Joanne Lawrence May 4, 2023 Whereas, Joanne Lawrence has been a dedicated employee of the University of Rhode Island for 40 years, and Whereas, Joanne has been a valued member of the Faculty Senate for nine years, and Whereas, Joanne has demonstrated unwavering commitment to her work and has been a kind and patient person, and Whereas, Joanne has been the soul of the Curriculum and Standards Committee and the keeper of our catalog, and Whereas, Joanne has become a master of the Kuali software, and Whereas, Joanne's contributions to the Faculty Senate and the University of Rhode Island have been immeasurable, and Whereas, Joanne will retire in May and will be greatly missed by all who have had the privilege of working with her, now, therefore, be it Resolved , that the Faculty Senate of the University of Rhode Island expresses its heartfelt appreciation and gratitude to Joanne Lawrence for her many years of service to the University, and Resolved , that the Faculty Senate recognizes Joanne's dedication to her work and her unwavering commitment to the University of Rhode Island, and Resolved , that the Faculty Senate expresses its deep admiration for Joanne's kindness, patience, and professionalism, and Resolved , that the Faculty Senate acknowledges Joanne's important role as the soul of the Curriculum and Standards Committee and the keeper of our catalog, and Resolved , that the Faculty Senate commends Joanne for her mastery of the Kuali software, and Resolved , that the Faculty Senate extends its best wishes to Joanne for a much-deserved and enjoyable retirement, and

passages.text: Call Joanne to the Front: All the Faculty Senators, and indeed all Rhode Islanders know that we are in the Ocean State. This is the state's Land Grant and Sea Grant University so this is the land of the meeting of the Land and Sea ---just like an estuary! The Faculty Senate Executive Committee wrestled with just the perfect gift symbolizing her long tenure at the University now that this is her very last Faculty Senate meeting. I believe we found it! Invite Joanne to Open Gift Joanne's most challenging task at which she was most successful in calming and taming very crabby faculty members and department chairpersons impatient about their course proposals and whether or not they will be able to offer new courses that they want, and when they want them! This blue crab, Callinectes sapidus, is showing up in Rhode Island estuarine waters more frequently these days as time goes on deeper into the 21st Century, but we hope that this one will help her remember her skill at handling all us crabby people!

Describe the mission and vision for the Center or Institute.
The University of Rhode Island’s Digital Forensics and Cyber Security Center (DFCSC) delivers URI’s academic programs in Digital Forensics and Cybersecurity, which include undergraduate minors, graduate certificates, and a masters degree in those fields.
The DFCSC coordinates Digital Forensics and Cybersecurity academic programs and courses with other related programs on campus including those in Criminal Justice within the College of Arts and Sciences (A&S).
DFCSC programs have been recognized by the National Security Agency (NSA) as being a national Center of Academic Excellence (CAE) in Cyber Defense, the premier academic designation in the nation. 2.
Where will the Center/Institute be located physically - or will it be organized virtually?
What physical, hardware, or soft assets will the C/I aim to provide to faculty and students?
The DFCSC is physically located in Rooms 101 and 103 Tyler Hall, Kingston; rooms that have been dedicated to the Center for over 10 years.
The DFCSC provides Digital Forensics and Cybersecurity degree programs for the university.

What role will it play in providing graduate or undergraduate training vs. research support?
The DFCSC’s focus is exclusively teaching – delivering URI’s programs in Digital Forensics and Cybersecurity.
As a smaller part of its mission, the DFCSC has performed training in digital forensics and cybersecurity for organizations.
Some faculty members associated with the DFCSC do research, but those research projects are not conducted through this Center.
Similarly, some faculty and staff associated with the DFCSC perform services in digital forensics and cybersecurity, but those services are not conducted through this Center. 4.

The DFCSC does not seek any internal funding.

The current external funding directly associated with the DFCSC is a $3.8M National Science Foundation CyberCorps Scholarship For Service five-year grant, with Victor Fay-Wolfe as the PI.
This grant provides scholarships for students doing URI’s Professional Science Master’s Degree in Cybersecurity (which is run in the DFCSC).
The DFCSC performs self-assessment in accordance with the guidelines set forth by the NSA CAE designation.
A copy of the goals and assessment plan is attached.
Other goals include graduating at least 30 minors per year from the undergraduate programs and at least 25 students per year from its graduate programs. 5.

Which ones?

The DFCSC is a subsidiary of the URI Computer Science and Statistics Department (CS&S) and thus reports to the Chair of CS&S, and to the Dean of the College of Arts and Sciences (A&S).
The DFCSC has two faculty co-Director’s, Dr.
Lisa DiPippo and Dr.
Victor Fay-Wolfe, and a staff Director, Jacob Fonseca.
This team manages the Center, and makes leadership decisions. 6.

(Note that, for the establishment of an Institute, the potential for achieving international prominence as well as substantial external grant funding is required.) The University Manual section 8.90.10 states that “Centers are formally structured units chartered to provide interdisciplinary coordination within a college directed at an issue beyond the scope of a single discipline”.
The DFCSC coordinates all Digital Forensics and Cybersecurity education at URI including interdisciplinary arrangements with Criminal Justice within A&S, and coordination with other programs in Business and Engineering that involve digital forensics and/or cybersecurity.
The DFCSC has already achieved national recognition with its designation as a NSA CAE, being a recipient of the NSF CyberCorps grant, and its long-time acknowledgment as a national leader in Digital Forensics and Cybersecurity education.

Describe any “competition” from similar Centers or Institutes, both regionally and nationally.
Why is a new (or continuing) C/I singularly important for the University to support?
There are over 100 similar Centers at other universities because the NSA CAE designation, which is the most prominent designation for Cybersecurity academic programs in the nation, requires a dedicated Center for Cybersecurity education at the institution.

passages.heading: #22-23-44 | Page 6
passages.text:
URI maintaining the DFCSC as its designated Center is crucial in keeping this essential CAE designation.
Without the CAE designation, URI would lose the NSF grant and would not be able to compete in the rapidly growing Cybersecurity education field, one in which URI has been a national leader for almost 20 years.
Please see the attached 2021 support letter from the Provost stating the university’s support for the DFCSC as a Center dedicated to Cybersecurity education. 9.

The DFCSC will not make a request for overhead generated from external funds.
It has not done this with its sole external funding source (the NSF CyberCorp grant).
The DFCSC is self-sustaining on the internal revenue generated from its academic programs.
These internal funds are tracked and reviewed by each of the following: DFCSC staff, CS&S Chair and Fiscal Clerk, A&S Financial Manager, and the OIS Financial Manager. 10.

The DFCSC was originally formed in 2004 from an NSF CyberCorps capacity building grant, with no internal URI resources.
The DFCSC has grown based almost solely on revenue that it has generated from the Digital Forensics and Cybersecurity academic programs.
A&S provided support from 2012-2018 for 25% FTE for the DFCSC Director position, but no longer provides that support.

passages.text:
NSF Grant Proposal Pathways To Cybersecurity Careers Submitted April 2022 The U.S.
Bureau of Labor Statistics predicts the growth in cybersecurity employment demand will be 34% in the near future.
This is projected to cause over 700,000 unfilled cybersecurity jobs in the U.S., costing the U.S. economy billions of dollars.
While there exists this dramatic shortage in the cybersecurity workforce, there is a parallel phenomenon that only 4% of entry level cybersecurity positions currently go to people classified as from low-income backgrounds.
This Track 2 S-STEM project, called Pathways To A Cybersecurity Career (P2CC), will support low-income students to graduate with a Master’s degree in Cybersecurity from the University of Rhode Island (URI), and enter the cybersecurity workforce.
The P2CC project will provide yearly scholarships of 1-3 year durations to at least 42 unique recipients over 6 years, with expected retention and graduation rates being at least 90%.
The scholars will be domestic low-income students with academic ability, talent/potential, and with demonstrated unmet financial need.

passages.heading: #22-23-44 | Page 24
passages.text:
They will be recruited by a campaign that targets traditionally under-represented groups in the cybersecurity field including women, rational/ethnic minorities, and differently-abled people.
Selection of scholars will be by a panel that has been trained in potential selection biases when evaluating low-income applicants, using a rubric that is designed for equity.
In addition to providing scholarships, the P2CC project will implement curricular and co-curricular interventions for the scholars that will target cognitive and non-cognitive aspects of low-income students’ experiences and success that focus on academic supports, and on increasing the students’ professional identity through exposure to the cybersecurity workforce and professional skills, professional role modeling, participation in student cohorts, faculty mentoring, and building self efficacy.
Intellectual Merit.
The interventions of the P2CC project will adapt, implement, and study the application to cybersecurity education of evidence-based curricular and co-curricular interventions that have been shown to be effective supporting low-income student recruitment, retention, and success in STEM education.

passages.heading: #22-23-44 | Page 24
passages.text:
The P2CC project’s primary intervention uses Fitzgerald’s definition of “professional identity” as: “containing the attributes: skills and functions; knowledge values and ethics; personal identity; group identity in the profession; and the influence of the context of the field”.
It applies to cybersecurity education specific professional identity enhancement techniques that Peters has classified as “high impact” for low-income STEM student success, and that have been demonstrated on similar S-STEM projects in Math, Science, and Computer Science.
The project includes a robust evaluation of its primary objectives: 1) produce at least 42 graduates who enter the cybersecurity workforce, 2) evaluate the effectiveness of the support interventions in supporting the success of low-income cybersecurity students, and 3) disseminate the results to assist degree programs at other institutions in supporting the success of low-income students in their cybersecurity education.
The evaluation uses data sources including pre and post surveys of scholars, exit tickets following specific activities, exit interviews, demographic data, academic assessments, and career placement data.

passages.heading: #22-23-44 | Page 24
passages.text: The evaluation performs formative evaluation of the objectives using a formal Plan-Do-Study-Act continuous improvement process, and summative evaluation to facilitate reporting and academic publication.

passages.heading: #22-23-44 | Page 25
passages.text: Broader Impacts. This project impacts the scholars themselves, all of which will be low-income students, by providing them access to a high-quality graduate education in cybersecurity - something that is unattainable by many due to economic hardship, and the lack of available financial aid at the graduate level. The professional identity and academic enhancement interventions will help ensure the success of these scholars. The broader impact will be on both the U.S. cybersecurity workforce, which lacks numbers and diversity of workers , and on the U.S. economy as a whole. By producing more qualified cybersecurity workers from low-income background, the P2CC project will serve as an initial step in starting to tap a woefully untapped talent pool that will help address a U.S. cybersecurity workforce deficit crisis that is costing billions of dollars in losses to the nation’s economy, and affecting international competitiveness of U.S. companies.

Excerpt From NSF Grant Proposal For the CyberCorps Scholarship For Service in URI’s Cybersecurity Program NSF grant award made January 2021 Under-Represented Groups.
The need to attract more underrepresented groups (URG), including women and racial/ethnic minorities, into the cybersecurity field is well-documented [48,49,50,51].
The goal of this SFS program is at least 40% women and at least 1 of each 5-student cohort being from other URGs.
The URI CS Department has a Broadening Participation in Computing (BPC) Committee and several initiatives in place, and the CS Department Chair and others are attending the 2020 NSF-sponsored CRA workshop series on establishing BPC plans for CS departments [XX].
The PI will have an Individual NSF CISE-format BPC plan, and the CS Department will have a BPC plan, in place in 2020 (see attached letter of commitment).
Included in these efforts, the URI CS Department recently hired a staff member dedicated to BPC initiatives.
This CS BPC Coordinator will work with the PIs and partner organizations at URI (see attached letters of collaboration) to implement an aggressive recruiting plan to recruit SFS candidates from URGs.

passages.heading: #22-23-44 | Page 26
passages.text:
Aspects of this recruitment plan include: ● Recruitment material.
We will work with URI chapters of the National Society for Black Engineers and Women in Computer Science (see letters of collaboration) to ensure that our SFS program recruiting material (web sites, flyers, messages in classes and events) is effective for a diverse audience of students.
The National Center for Women in Technology’s [52] (NCWIT) Recruit Strategically resources [53] will be employed.
These include techniques to deliver effective messaging strategies to target audiences such as URI women undergraduates and regional high school students.
NCWITs template strategic recruitment plans [54] and Roadshow In a Box [55] will be adapted to SFS candidate recruitment using their techniques for effective messaging to women [53]. ● Recruitment opportunities.
There are populations of URG students on which we will focus recruitment.
Some of them are: ○ The Community College of Rhode Island.
As described above, CCRI has high populations of racial minorities and first-generation college students in its cyber program.

passages.heading: #22-23-44 | Page 26
passages.text:
We will present the SFS opportunity in CCRI cybersecurity classes, train advisors on it, provide flyers, post posters, and have an SFS information session on CCRI’s campus each year (see attached letter of collaboration). ○ URI Talent Development (TD) [56] .
This program recruits and serves Rhode Island high school graduates with college potential who come to URI from historically disadvantaged backgrounds, a majority of whom are students of color.
They come to campus the summer before their Freshman year to participate in a college-preparation program that includes taking college courses.
PI Fay-Wolfe coordinates a CS course in the TD program every summer with 40 TD students.
The course has a module on cybersecurity during which the SFS opportunity will be showcased. ○ URI Chapter of the National Society For Black Engineers (NSBE-URI).
NSBE-URI runs several programs to motivate and encourage youth of color to pursue an interest in CS and engineering majors.
These include events such as development workshops, where students and corporate representatives share their experiences in areas such as resume writing and interviewing techniques.

passages.heading: #22-23-44 | Page 26
passages.text: NSBE-URI also has academic and corporate representatives speak to its undergraduates about research and work opportunities.

passages.heading: #22-23-44 | Page 27
passages.text: NSBE-URI has committed to including cybersecurity, and the SFS program in particular, in its workshops for the duration of this SFS project (see attached letter of collaboration). ○ URI Women in Computer Science. URI’s Society For Women in Computing (SWiC) is an undergraduate organization where women in the CS Department regularly meet to explore Computer Science. The URI SWiC group has committed to helping us recruit undergraduate women for the SFS opportunity including hosting an SFS information session at one of their meetings each year of the project (see attached letter of collaboration). The SFS scholarship selection process will be conducted such that when we have a pool of qualified candidates, addressing increased participation by URG students will be a primary consideration in making SFS scholarship offers within that pool.

CONSTITUTION, BY-LAWS, AND UNIVERSITY MANUAL COMMITTEEReport #2022-2023-19 - EDITORIALFACULTY SENATE, March 23, 2023 Rationale: Update sections of Chapter 8 to reflect the new policy, approved by Faculty Senate onFebruary 23, 2023, for resolving grades of Incomplete.
Proposed changes: 8.53.10 Grades.

passages.heading: IFSR 2022-2023-8 | Page 2
passages.text:
Student grades are defined as follows: A – Superior B – Good C – Fair D – Low grade, passing F – Failure I – Incomplete S – Satisfactory, course taught on S-U basis S* – Satisfactory, course taken by a graduate student under the Pass-Fail grading option U – Unsatisfactory, course taught on S-U basis U* – Unsatisfactory, course taken by a graduate student under the Pass-Fail grading option, not calculated into graduate GPA #13-14-2 P – Passing, course taken under the Pass-Fail option NW – Enrolled – No work submitted NR – Enrolled – No grade reported #06-07–22 NC – Enrolled - Not completed, not calculated in GPA 8.53.11 Grades shall be given quality point values as follows: A = 4.00 points A- = 3.70 points B+ = 3.30 points B = 3.00 points B- = 2.70 points C+ = 2.30 points C = 2.00 points C- = 1.70 points D+ = 1.30 points D = 1.00 points F = 0 points U = 0 points U* = not calculated in GPA #13-14-2 NC = not calculated in GPA 8.53.12 Enrolled – No Work Submitted.
In those instances when a student enrolls in a course through the registration process and (1) never attends the course, or (2) stops attending early in the semester, the instructor may record a grade of NW, no work submitted.

passages.heading: IFSR 2022-2023-8 | Page 2
passages.text:
The grade will not affect the student’s attempted or earned credits and will have no effect on a student’s QPA. 8.53.13 Enrolled – No Grade Reported.
Assigned by Enrollment Services when the instructor does not submit grade (see 8.54.12). #06-07–22, #21-22-6 8.53.14 Enrolled – Not Completed.
Assigned by Enrollment Services when the instructor does not submit a Change of Grade report to resolve a grade of Incomplete (see sections 8.53.20-8.53-24).

passages.heading: IFSR 2022-2023-8 | Page 3
passages.text: 8.56.10 Changes in Records. No grade (including that of NW) shall be changed after it has been reported to and recorded by the Office of Enrollment Services except in the following circumstances. First, a grade may be changed upon written request by the instructor. Second, following an appeals case an instructor’s department chairperson or immediate administrative supervisor shall act on the advice of the appeals committee ( see 8.26.13 ) and change a grade over the instructor’s objection. Third, in the event that the original instructor can no longer be consulted (e.g., having died or moved to an unknown address), the instructor’s chairperson/supervisor can act in the missing person’s stead and initiate a grade change, including the removal of inappropriate NW grades. This shall only happen, however, if an appeals committee has recommended such action in writing. All grade changes must be authorized by the appropriate dean. Entries to a student’s academic record shall not be changed after two years for the undergraduate student and after three years for the graduate student ( s S ee sections 8.26.10 through 8.26.13 for appeals procedures ) . Grade changes for grades received before graduation will not be permitted after graduation unless the change is based on clerical or procedural errors and the change is received and posted to the student’s record by the last day of classes of the semester following the term in which the student graduates (see 8.56.12). #05-06–31

passages.text: CONSTITUTION, BY-LAWS, AND UNIVERSITY MANUAL COMMITTEEReport #2023-2024-03 - Proposed changes to Chapter 5 of the University ManualFACULTY SENATE - October 19, 2023AS AMENDED Context: Proposed updates to language in Chapter 5 of the University Manual, specifically the sections pertaining to the Learning Outcomes Oversight Committee (LOOC; 5.84.10 - 5.84.13) and the Academic Program Review Committee (APRC; 5.86.10 - 5.86.11 ) based on collaborative process last academic year to combine APRC and LOOC into a joint committee. The new joint committee was approved by the Faculty Senate and Faculty Senate Executive Committee. Existing language: 5.84.10. The Learning Outcomes Oversight Committee (LOOC) shall create policies for URI student learning outcomes assessment, data distribution and frequency of measurement at the university-wide level, with the approval of the Faculty Senate and the Provost. Such policies would include but not be limited to external reporting and the release of assessment data, setting of standards for outcomes assessment, identification of strengths and limitations of existing assessment practices and recommendations for resource allocation to enhance assessment practices. #06-07–25 5.84.11. The committee shall provide advice and guidance to the Office of Student Learning, Outcomes Assessment, and Accreditation relevant to faculty learning of best practices of student learning outcomes and assessment and oversee implementation and facilitation of approved policies by the Office of Student Learning, Outcomes Assessment and Accreditation. #06-07–25 5.84.12. The committee shall also develop an ongoing review of the learning outcomes assessment process, interpret external expectations for university-wide learning outcomes

passages.heading: #23-24-08 | Page 3
passages.text:
assessment, including those of accreditation bodies and facilitate internal communication across units regarding ways of meeting those expectations. #06-07–25 5.84.13.

TO: Service and Community Life Committee, URI Faculty Senate FROM: Professors Marc Hutchison, Skip Mark, Karen Sweeting, Cheryl Foster Department of Political Science DATE: February 20, 2023 RE: Resolution for statement of solidarity and support We hereby submit the attached Resolution containing a statement of solidarity and support for our colleagues and associated communities in Florida.
In addition, we urge our Faculty Senate representatives to adopt such a statement as soon as possible given the escalating intrusion of Florida's state government into public education at all levels as well as that government's unwarranted attacks on both legitimate academic inquiry and the building of equitable communities that are inclusive of diverse identities and perspectives.
As the United Faculty of Florida (UFF) have indicated their desire for Faculty Senates and other affiliated members of the higher education community to offer statements of support, we hereby submit such a statement for your consideration and adoption.

passages.text: University of Rhode Island Faculty Senate RESOLUTION: To offer a formal statement of solidarity and support to our fellow colleagues and associated communities in Florida RATIONALE: WHEREAS The Manhattan Institute is now issuing templates for dismantling DEI educational initiatives in every state across the country WHEREAS Florida is at the forefront of a nationwide campaign to silence Black voices and erase the full and accurate history and contemporary experiences of Black people WHEREAS Florida College System presidents issued a collective statement affirming their view that some diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives are harmful to higher education WHEREAS Governor DeSantis has explicitly stated his aim to defund and dismantle DEI initiatives as well as the governing body and administrative leadership of The New College, a public institution WHEREAS Governor DeSantis and the Florida House of Representatives made demands in January for information regarding the funding of programs related to diversity, equity, inclusion, and critical race theory at colleges and universities, now intending to bar funding for these programs across the higher education system WHEREAS under Florida's Stop WOKE Act— which has been temporarily enjoined by a federal court from being enforced in higher education settings— endorsement of theories that criticize systemic racism is forbidden, disparagement of these theories is openly allowed and transgressions can be penalized through revoking millions of dollars in state funding WHEREAS public universities and colleges in Florida must nevertheless administer ideological surveys to all higher ed students, faculty and staff, the results of which may be used to drive budgetary decisions WHEREAS students in Florida are nevertheless permitted to seek permission for recording lectures, which may be used in disciplinary or legal actions against faculty WHEREAS all syllabi and reading lists must nevertheless be posted in publicly accessible locations at least 45 days before the start of classes WHEREAS faculty speech in Florida is nevertheless unconstitutionally compelled in some quarters to expose students to ideas they may find “uncomfortable, unwelcome, disagreeable, or offensive,” through syllabi, reading selection and class discussion WHEREAS Governor DeSantis rejected the AP course in African American History, demanding that The College Board excise specific subject areas from the curriculum WHEREAS The College Board stripped down and altered the AP exam for African American History, followed by a statement of regret for failing to immediately denounce the Florida Department of Education and Governor DeSantis's administration, the latter of which commented that African American Studies “lacks educational value.” WHEREAS Governor DeSantis is considering barring all Advanced Placement Exams in Florida

passages.heading: Resolution #22-23-2 | Page 4
passages.text: WHEREAS investigations target trans students and employees by demanding information that could potentially compromise patient privacy and discourage individuals from seeking medically appropriate care WHEREAS Black leaders, alarmed by Governor DeSantis, have begun to protest and prepare for 2024 WHEREAS higher education workers are organizing around the country, through growing unions like the United Faculty of Florida (UFF) and new coalitions like Higher Education Labor United, to defend our freedoms and throw a much-needed lifeline to the sinking discussions about higher education in Florida and elsewhere WHEREAS the United Faculty of Florida are welcoming statements of support for their fellow colleagues and associated communities in Florida WHEREAS it is vital that students, faculty, staff, and administrators outside of Florida band together in this moment of crisis to defend the public good of higher education ____________________________________________________________________________________________________________ THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that the Faculty Senate of URI extends this statement of solidarity and support to our fellow colleagues and associated communities in Florida.

passages.heading: Resolution #22-23-2 | Page 4
passages.text:
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that this statement confirms URI's current statement of Foundational Values in espousing a commitment to freedom to learn, teach, create, and conduct research with integrity in the pursuit and dissemination of new knowledge aimed at contributing to the public good, as well as an inclusive, accessible, equitable and diverse community whereby we respect the rights and dignity of all.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that in issuing this statement of support, the University of Rhode Island aspires to serve as a national model for the role a flagship public research university can play in driving transformative change for the betterment of its state and the global human condition.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that this statement applauds the URI Board of Trustees' affirmation of the university's determination to embrace Rhode Island ’s heritage of independent thought, valuing creativity and scholarship, diversity, fairness, and respect, engaged learning and civic involvement, and intellectual and ethical leadership.

passages.heading: Resolution #22-23-2 | Page 4
passages.text:
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that this statement affirms our commitment to the ideals of the URI Office of Community, Equity and Diversity and its core values of advancing equity, inclusion, and diversity in the global community and modeling honesty, integrity, and social justice.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that this statement explicitly stands by the URI Cornerstones, acknowledging the University of Rhode Island as a principled community guided by values, including the principles of independent choice, intellectual curiosity, open-mindedness, free expression, the rights and dignity of each individual and group, working to understand and respect differences, and the rejection of prejudice, discrimination, and intolerance.

FACULTY SENATE OFFICE FACULTY SENATE LEGISLATION OCTOBER 19, 2023 Constitution, By-Laws, and University Manual Committee Proposed changes to Chapter 8 of the University Manual Report 2023-2024-06 Context: Proposed updates to language in Chapter 8 of the University Manual, specifically the sections discussing the Learning Outcomes Oversight Committee (LOOC) and the Academic Program Review Committee (APRC) to update terminology to reflect the new Joint Committee on Academic Program Review and Outcomes Assessment (see CBUM Report #2023-2024-03).
Existing Language 8.59.10 Assessment of student learning outcomes shall be coordinated by the Learning Outcomes Oversight Committee (LOOC; see 5.84.10 – 5.84.13) in cooperation with the Assistant Director of Student Learning, Outcomes Assessment and Accreditation (see 2.22.21).
The following policies shall apply to this process: 8.59.11 Academic Program Engagement.

passages.heading: #23-24-07 | Page 3
passages.text:
All undergraduate, professional, and graduate academic programs, including General Education, shall be actively engaged in student learning outcomes assessment as evidenced by, but not limited to: a) Published student learning outcomes that are clear statements of what students are expected to gain, achieve, demonstrate, or know at the completion of the academic program.
These student learning outcomes shall be published on the program’s website as well as on the website for the Office of Student Learning, Outcomes Assessment, and Accreditation (SLOAA).
These student learning outcomes shall be periodically reviewed by the academic program for ongoing relevance. b) A plan of student learning outcomes assessment that is endorsed by the program’s faculty.
Plans should include a regular and predictable cycle for collecting and analyzing assessment data, for discussing curricular and programmatic changes, for implementing interventions, and for re-assessing the impact of implemented changes.

passages.heading: #23-24-07 | Page 3
passages.text:
Outcomes assessment plans will be published on each program’s website as well as on the SLOAA website. c) Reports of student learning outcomes assessment that are provided to SLOAA using staggered cycles of no more than 3 years.
Cycles for accredited programs will be adjusted to decrease redundancy of effort. #09- 10–29 8.59.12 SLOAA Guidance for Academic Programs.
Guidelines and schedules for preparation of outcomes assessment plans and reports shall be provided by SLOAA with the assistance and approval of the Learning Outcomes Oversight Committee (LOOC).
SLOAA shall offer advice on the logistics of collecting assessment data, support for analyzing the results, and feedback on designing curricular and programmatic changes.
Rubrics for evaluating the plans and reports shall be generated by SLOAA and posted on its website. #09-10–29 8.59.13 Evaluation of Plans and Reports.
Student learning outcomes assessment plans and reports shall be submitted through SLOAA for evaluation and recommendations by LOOC.
Programs shall be notified directly of the Bill #23-24-7

passages.heading: #23-24-07 | Page 4
passages.text:
results of the evaluation and whether modification is needed.
Summary reports shall be published on the SLOAA website.
LOOC shall provide a general summary of outcomes assessment in its annual report. #09-10–29 8.59.14 University-Wide Student Learning Outcomes Assessment.
With guidance from LOOC, SLOAA shall work with the Office of Institutional Research and other university offices to collect, maintain, analyze, and distribute student learning outcomes assessment findings, derived from a variety of local and national sources.
SLOAA shall identify patterns of student performance to inform ongoing program and institutional improvement. #09-10–29 Other Related Sections: 8.85.14 A proposal submitted to the coordinating and review committee (section 8.85.11) shall have included the following steps: Step 1: Prior to developing a complete proposal for a new academic program, a brief pre-proposal form describing the program and its likelihood of success, centrality to the mission of the university and consistency with the Academic Plan, shall be completed by the proposer(s).

passages.heading: #23-24-07 | Page 4
passages.text:
It will be provided by the proposer(s), department chair(s) (if applicable) and academic dean(s) to the Joint Committee on Academic Planning (JCAP) for review.
If the program is not consistent with the Academic Plan, the proposer(s) will be urged to reconsider the idea and may submit a revised pre-proposal.
All communications between JCAP and proposer(s) will be copied to the appropriate coordinating and review committee.
While JCAP endorsement is not required for the proposer(s) to continue development of the complete proposal, it is strongly recommended.
Step 2: While the complete proposal is being developed within the college, the proposer(s) shall seek consultation with the Office of Student Learning Outcomes Assessment and Accreditation (SLOAA) in preparation of its plan for student learning assessment and thereafter obtain approval by the Learning Outcomes Oversight Committee (LOOC) of its plan.
The proposer(s) shall also obtain a library impact statement following proper review by the University Libraries and seek written comment from other university departments and programs perceived impacted by the proposal.

passages.heading: #23-24-07 | Page 4

FACULTY SENATE OFFICE FACULTY SENATE LEGISLATION AUGUST 16, 2023 Faculty Senate Special Summer Curriculum Committee Report 2023-2024-1B At the June 20, 2023 meeting of the Special Summer Curriculum Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate Executive Committee on August 16, 2023 for emergency summer 2023 approval.
SECTION I Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation by The Faculty Senate PROGRAM CHANGES COLLEGE OF ARTS & SCIENCES BA Data Science, see Appendix A Updating electives and required courses • We are changing the elective BAI 210 to BAI 211, due to changes in the courses by the COB. • CSC 211 has been added as an alternative to CSC 201 because the material in CSC 211 covers what is in CSC 201. • We are breaking This requirement "CSC/DSP 310 or STA 305 or ART/DSP 404 or BIO 230G (3-4 credits)" into two requirements because they actually have to take either DSP 310 or STA 305 in order to complete the other requirements.

passages.heading: #23-24-02 | Page 2
passages.text:
We are changing it to "(CSC/DSP 310 or STA 305) and (ART/DSP 404 or BIO 230G)" It makes sense to group ART/DSP 404 and BIO 230G as they both cover data visualization. • The requirement of "DSP 477 or 499 or STA/DSP 490 or STA 491 (4 credits)" is moved to the domain area options, to make up for the additional course - see (4) above and keep the number of credits the same. • An option for AMS/DSP 393G is added to the required list "STA/DSP 441 or CSC/DSP 461" because unless a student chooses calculus as their math, they will not be able to take CSC/DSP 461, so we are giving another pathway.] • The list of domain area courses is updated due to some courses having too many pre -requisites, some courses no longer offered, and some additions of appropriate applied data science courses • WRT 201 is removed as an option because the course is being phased out.
We also removed WRT 332.
We replaced them with WRT 235 and 303.
The replacements are more suitable for the kind of writing data scientists do. • The name of LTI/DSP 110 has been changed to DSP 110. • With these changes, the minimum number of credits a student needs for this degree decreased by 1, from 30 to 29.

BA Sociology, see Appendix B Revising requirements The Sociology Department is revamping its curriculum: • to add a bridge course required for majors to help them transition from lower-division courses to upper division ones • to change the methods course from 440 to 301 so that students are better prepared to address research in 400 level courses • to change the statistics course from 460 to 360 so that students are better prepared to address research in 400 level courses • to insure that sociology majors take the sociology statistics course and not another one outside of the department • to streamline the curriculum by changing a few course numbers and adding more logical prerequisites to courses so that students will progress more logically/understandably from 100/200 level course to 300 level, then on to 400 level courses COLLEGE OF NURSING BS Nursing, see Appendix C Rectifying error NUR 208 and NUR 412 were approved as new courses in 2019 and NUR 363 was deleted in 2019.
A notice of change was never processed to officially change the curriculum.

passages.heading: #23-24-02 | Page 3
passages.text:

COLLEGE OF EDUCATION & PROFESSIONAL STUDIES Specialization | Youth Health & Physical Activity, see Appendix D Updating name, GPA requirement, and removing Praxis requirement Changes to this Specialization Description: • Update the specialization description under Health and Physical Education (HPE) in catalog to make it Youth Health and Physical Activity Studies Specialization specific. • Change minimum GPA requirement from 2.5 to 2.0 which is the academic requirement stated in University Manual. • Changes to the Youth Health and Physical Activity Studies curriculum worksheet: o Replace one credit courses EDC 118, EDC322, and EDC 324 with newly approved course EDC 220.
EDC 220 was the combination of those previous one credit courses (EDC 118 + EDC 322 + EDC 324) on our HPE curriculum worksheet. o Replace one credit courses EDC 116 and 117 with newly approved course EDC 230.

passages.heading: #23-24-02 | Page 3
passages.text:
EDC 230 was the combination of those previous one credit courses (EDC 116 + EDC 117) on our HPE curriculum worksheet. o Since EDC 220, 230 have been approved by Faculty Senate in fall 2021 and started to run in fall 2022, we request the change to be effective retroactively as of the beginning of the Fall 2022 semester regardless of when it goes through the curricular channels and is eventually approved. o Lastly, we propose to have the minimum 2.0 GPA requirement for EDC483 instead of minimum 2.5 GPA to align with the overall GPA requirement for Youth Health and Physical Activity Studies Specialization, so it is consistent throughout.
Again, this change will align with the academic requirement stated in University Manual.

Changes Describe the potential students and primary source of students.
Students who thrive in the data science major, are those who are willing to complete the analytical core of mathematics, computing, and statistics classes.
They will also need the “soft” or “essential” skills of communication, team work, management, and ethics.
For the BS, those with stronger interest in applied mathematics will choose the MTH-AMS track, while those who are more interested in using computational statistics and computer science skills will choose the CSC- STA track.
Students who have a strong interest in a domain area will be mainly interested in applying data science techniques to a subject (domain).
We will strongly urge students to double major in order to accomplish this goal.
Examples include: cybersecurity, history, political science, communication studies, journalism, health science, health, humanities, library science, and so on.
In addition, the minor is available for students who would like some skills but have less time to spend on a major.
We expect the number of data science majors to continue to grow over time.
As of August 2021, there are 18 BA and 35 BS Data Science majors.

We expect new students to come to URI seeking to major in data science because URI is one of few universities in the region that has a data science major.

Changes Program Description Nursing (4-year B.S.) URI’s baccalaureate nursing program is designed to prepare students academically and personally to become professional nurses.
It aims to develop knowledgeable, compassionate, and insightful graduates who are poised to become leaders in healthcare delivery.
As future clinicians and scholars, the URI Baccalaureate nursing student will be vested in foundational theory and contemporary practice while being given the opportunity for clinical experiences with individuals, families, and communities, across populations, both locally and globally.
Nursing is the largest discipline in healthcare delivery and our program prepares students for collaborative, interdisciplinary, practice.
Working with faculty who are expert clinicians, scholars, and innovators, students will be challenged to have a deep appreciation of factors that impact patient wellbeing and forward creative, contemporary approaches in patient-centered care.
Prelicensure graduates are eligible for examination for professional licensure as a registered nurse (R.N.).

passages.heading: #23-24-02 | Page 27
passages.text:
First-Year Students, with no previous college study, are admitted to University College for Academic Success with a major in nursing.
After completion of the pre-requisite courses (BIO 220, 221, 222, 223, CHM 103, 124, NUR 100, WRT 104 or 106) with a minimum grade of C or higher in each course and 3.00 overall grade point average, students will be considered for transfer into the College of Nursing and the clinical course sequence.
Seats are limited and competitively granted based on GPA.
Please see the College of Nursing Student Handbook for a full description of the entry process: uri.edu/nursing.
Progression and Graduation Requirements Students are required to achieve a C or higher in all NUR courses and all prerequisite courses.
In addition, students must maintain a minimum GPA of 2.2 to progress through and graduate from the College of Nursing.
Students who achieve less than a grade of C must repeat the course, obtaining a C grade or higher, before progressing in the nursing curriculum.
Permission to retake the course will be granted on a space-available basis only.
Even if successfully repeated, the initial grade remains on record as the �rst unsuccessful attempt.

passages.heading: #23-24-02 | Page 27
passages.text:
There are no further allowances for repeating a NUR course, and any subsequent NUR coursework of C- or below will result in dismissal.
If the student should achieve a C- or less in two NUR courses in a single semester, he or she will be immediately dismissed from the College of Nursing.
Refer to the College of Nursing Student Handbook for detailed policies.
A total of 120 credits is required to earn a B.S. in Nursing.
This includes program speci�c courses as well as general education requirements.
Curriculum Requirements Required Nursing Courses.
The following 64 credits are required: NUR 100, 203, 208, 213, 233, 234, 243, 253, 313, 314, 333, 334, 353, 354, 412, 413, 415, 417, 443 and 444.
A grade of C or higher is required in each of these courses.
Other Required Courses: CMB 201 (4); NFSNUT 207 (3); STA 220 (3) are required for future nursing courses.
A grade of C or higher is required in each course.
General expenses are approximately the same as for other University students.
On-campus Nursing students pay a professional fee which covers special items such as academic achievement testing, and lab fees for each clinical course.

Changes Program Description The six-year Doctor of Pharmacy curriculum is patterned on accepted programs of study recommended by the American Association of Colleges of Pharmacy, the Accreditation Council for Pharmacy Education, and other interested organizations.
The Doctor of Pharmacy is fully accredited by the Accreditation Council for Pharmacy Education (135 S.
LaSalle Street, Suite 4100, Chicago, Illinois, 60603; https://acpe-accredit.org/).
Medication therapy management is the responsible provision of drug therapy to achieve speci�c outcomes that improve a patient’s quality of life.
A pharmacist, in cooperation with a patient and other health care professionals, designs, implements, and monitors a plan of care that will produce desired patient outcomes.
A key element in medication therapy management is that the pharmacist accepts personal responsibility in achieving the desired outcomes.
In learning to provide medication therapy management, pharmacy students must exhibit the highest level of ethical behavior and moral values in all of their decision-making, as well as in their actions both in and outside of the college.

passages.heading: #23-24-02 | Page 42
passages.text:
Furthermore, students must acknowledge that the profession and medication therapy management are based foremost on caring, trust, and communication for the bene�t of patients and society in general.
All students must be committed to maintaining these standards, to fostering the professional development of other pharmacy students, and to responding appropriately when the ethical and moral standards of the profession have been breached.
Graduates of our program have a strong record of passing the national licensing examination (NAPLEX).
Over the past 5 years, the annual (January through December) passage rates have ranged from 8991-9594% for graduates who are taking the NAPLEX exam for the �rst time.
National annual passage rates for the past 5 years were 8583-9487%.
The Pharm.D. program provides preparation for community, institutional and other areas of pharmacy practice.
Students have the opportunity to take professional electives that will advance their knowledge in different areas of pharmacy, including hospital, clinical, manufacturing, managed care, natural products, drug analysis, special populations (e.g. geriatrics), administration, and research.

passages.heading: #23-24-02 | Page 42
passages.text:
A recent survey of graduates of the Class of 20202021 (AACP) indicates that 2342% work in a community practice setting, while 3544% work in hospitals.
Other areas of pharmacy employment included managed care, clinics, industry, long-term care, government, and academics.
Forty percent of graduates in the class of 20202021 were pursuing advanced training in residencies and fellowships.
Job responsibilities vary from staff pharmacists, manager, clinical specialist, consultant, executive, to professor.
Ninety-sevenfour percent of graduates indicate that they would select the URI College of Pharmacy if they were starting their pharmacy programs over again.
Technical Standards In addition to the academic requirements for admission, applicants must also meet the technical standards that the college deems essential for training and practice in the profession of pharmacy.
Upon admission, students in the Pharm.D. program will a�rm that they have reviewed the technical standards and further acknowledge that they are capable of meeting the program’s technical standards with or without accommodations.

passages.heading: #23-24-02 | Page 42
passages.text:
Students who have concerns about their ability to meet these standards should contact the associate dean of the college.
When requested, the college will provide reasonable accommodation to otherwise quali�ed students with disabilities.
Disabled students must work with and be approved by URI’s Disability Services for Students.
These functions include, but are not limited to: Observation: A candidate with or without accommodations must be able to observe demonstrations and experiments in the basic sciences.
A candidate must be able to observe a patient accurately at a distance and close at hand.
The candidate must be able to visually observe and interpret presented information.
This will necessitate the functional use of vision, hearing, and somatic senses.
Communication: A candidate with or without accommodations must be able to communicate effectively and sensitively with patients, caregivers, faculty/staff, and all members of the healthcare team.
The focus of this communication is to elicit SSCC Report 2023-2024-2B Appendix A | PHARM-D, Doctor of Pharmacy Page 3 of 12 Bill #23-24-2 Bill #23-24-2

information, describe changes in mood, activity, and posture, and perceive nonverbal communication.
An applicant must be able to communicate effectively and e�ciently in oral and written English.
Sensory/Motor: The candidate with or without accommodations must have su�cient motor function and skills necessary to perform basic tasks in the practice of pharmacy.
Examples of such tasks may include the compounding of medicinals, physical assessment, the administration of drugs, and the provision of basic cardiac life support.
Such actions require the coordination of both gross and �ne muscular movements, equilibrium, and functional use of the senses.
Intellectual: A candidate must have the ability to measure, calculate, reason, analyze, synthesize, and integrate information that is essential to fully develop these skills.
A candidate must be fully alert and attentive at all times in clinical settings.
Behavioral/Social: A candidate must be of su�cient emotional health to utilize fully his or her intellectual abilities, the exercise of good judgment, and the prompt completion of all patient care responsibilities.

passages.heading: #23-24-02 | Page 43
passages.text:
A candidate must possess the ability to develop mature, sensitive, and effective relationships with patients.
A candidate must be able to tolerate physically and emotionally taxing workloads and to function effectively under stress.
A candidate must be able to adapt to changing environments, to display �exibility and learn to function in the face of uncertainties inherent in the clinical problems of many patients.
A candidate must possess compassion, integrity, interpersonal skills, and motivation to excel in pharmacy practice.
Health: Certain illnesses impair a student’s performance.
These include, but are not limited to, active drug and/or alcohol addiction, severe depression, and other psychiatric illnesses.
It is not permissible for students to interact with patients while impaired by these conditions.
It is the policy of the College of Pharmacy to encourage recognition of these conditions and to support treatment so that the student may resume his or her studies in the college.
The term “candidate” means candidates for admission into the Pharm.D. program and students enrolled in the Pharm.D. program who are candidates for promotion and graduation.

Selection Factors Due to the large number of applications received for a limited number of spaces, admission to URI’s College of Pharmacy is highly selective.
The Admission O�ce carefully evaluates each candidate’s strength in the following areas: High School Transcript including the rigor of the high school curriculum and academic performance.
Standardized Test Scores (only SAT or ACT results are reviewed).
Personal Essay (including an additional paragraph required of all Pharmacy applicants—details are available on the application).
Letters of Recommendation (two letters are required: one from a science or math teacher and one from a guidance counselor or a teacher from another subject area).
These letters of recommendation should comment on your personal motivation, initiative and interpersonal skills.
Extracurricular Activities (including employment experiences) and unique talents.
Doctor of Pharmacy applicants are strongly encouraged to submit all of their application materials by the Early Action deadline.
Professional Standards of Behavior The College of Pharmacy demands that its students adhere to the highest standards of professional behavior.

Pharmacy students are expected to adhere to the highest standard of academic integrity in both the pre-professional and professional programs.
Any evidence of cheating or plagiarism may be grounds for dismissal from the program (see URI Student Handbook for de�nitions of cheating and plagiarism).
Ethical Values: Students must demonstrate the highest level of professional demeanor and behavior, and must perform in an ethical manner in all dealings with peers, faculty, staff, preceptors, and patients.
Alleged violations of professional standards of behavior will be evaluated by the college’s Professionalism Committee in coordination with the O�ce of Student and Academic Affairs.
Students who violate these standards of behavior may be given a reprimand, placed on probation, suspended for a period of time, required to acquire professional evaluation and counseling or other medical care, required to complete community service, or dismissed from the program.

Requirements for Progression to the Professional Program Pharm.D. students must request transfer from University College for Academic Success to the College of Pharmacy at the end of three semesters.
There are three requirements for successful progression. 1) During their sophomore year, all students are required to have a formal interview.
The student’s progression to the professional program will be contingent upon a successful interview.
The interview is designed to assess students’ commitment to the profession of pharmacy, knowledge of the profession, and ability to communicate with patients.
Interviews will follow University policies for excused absences (University Manual Sections 8.51.11-8.51-13).

passages.heading: #23-24-02 | Page 44
passages.text:
If a student fails to attend the scheduled interview for reasons outside of Sections 8.51.11-8.51.13, the student will receive an automatic failure for their �rst interview and be allowed only one other opportunity to successfully interview.
Otherwise, all students will be allowed a maximum of two interviews to successfully complete this program requirement.
Students unsuccessful in completing the interview by the second attempt will be dismissed from the Pharm.D. program. 2) After three semesters, only those pharmacy students having a 2.70 grade point average or better in 13 of the 17 required preprofessional courses (CMB 201 and 311; BIO 101110, 103, 220, 221, 222, and 223; CHM 101, 102, 112, 114, 226, 227, and 228; MTH 131; and STA 307) with no grade less than C- in any of these courses. 3) An overall grade point average of 3.00 Pharmacy students who have met the three criteria above must maintain a grade point average of 2.70 in the remaining four prerequisite courses with no grade less than C-.

Applicants with a grade point average of less than 2.70 for the designated preprofessional courses will not be considered for admission to the college.
For purposes of admission among transfer students (both internal and external), all of the preprofessional courses listed above (or equivalent courses) must be completed.

Retention and Graduation Requirements Starting with the �rst professional year (P1), the College of Pharmacy calculates its own grade point average (GPA), an average which differs from the GPA calculated by the University.
The grade point average calculated by the College includes only required didactic pharmacy courses and is called the quality point average (QPA).
Good academic standing requires a QPA of 2.3 or higher, a semester QPA of 2.30 or higher, and a grade of at least C- in each required pharmacy course.
A student will automatically be placed on probation when they do not meet one or more of the good standing requirements.

passages.heading: #23-24-02 | Page 45
passages.text:
Furthermore, a student whose cumulative QPA falls below a 2.20 at the end of any semester will be dismissed from the program.
A student on probation for two consecutive semesters without returning to good standing also will be dismissed from the program.
A student who receives a grade below C- in any required pharmacy course or whose QPA falls between 2.20 and 2.30 at the end of a semester will be reviewed by the Scholastic Standing Committee and presented with a remediation plan that must be successfully completed in order to progress in the curriculum.
Remediation plans will be designed to meet program standards (QPA and minimum grade requirements) and may include repeating courses, additional self study and or faculty assessment of pro�ciency through assignments and examinations.
Remediation plans will be developed by the Scholastic Standing Committee taking into account the student’s QPA, length of time enrolled in the program(i.e., P1, P2, or P3 status), the number and types of de�ciencies, and trends in academic performance.
A student who is not successful in completing the remediation plan developed by the Scholastic Standing Committee will be dismissed from the Pharm.D. program.

passages.text:
The assessment of successful completion of remediation plans by the Scholastic Standing Committee shall be �nal.
Repeating courses to improve academic standing: A student who is not meeting the required pharmacy QPA of 2.30 may repeat those courses in which they received a C or less, up to 6 credits a semester, and up to a total of 15 credits.
A speci�c course may be repeated only one time.
If the 15 credit maximum of repeat credits is reached without achieving the 2.30 QPA and minimally acceptable grades (at least a C- or demonstrated pro�ciency) in each required course, the student will be dismissed from the program.
A student noti�ed of dismissal for failing to remain in good standing and not meeting retention requirements shall have the right to appeal.
The appeal must be made in writing and received by the Associate Dean of Student and Academic Affairs of the College of Pharmacy within �ve days of the date of dismissal notice.
The appeal will be reviewed by the Scholastic Standing Committee of the College of Pharmacy.
The Committee’s decision to con�rm the dismissal or continue the student on probation shall be �nal.

P3 students must take the Pharmacy Curriculum Outcomes Assessment (PCOA) examination prior to beginning APPE rotations.
Students must earn a C- or better in every APPE rotation.
Graduation requirements: Earn a minimum quality point average of 2.30, a grade of at least a C- (or demonstrated pro�ciency through remediation) in all required professional courses, successfully complete all other required courses, professional elective courses, Introductory and Advanced Pharmacy Practice Experiences, and earn at least 209 credits.

Introductory and advanced pharmacy practice experiential rotations may be scheduled at a distance from the Kingston campus.
These rotations contribute importantly to the depth and breadth of the experiential program.
While the college makes every effort to accommodate student requests regarding rotations, students should anticipate having some rotations assigned at a distance.

Criminal Background Checks.
All students must undergo a criminal background check annually during the professional (P1 to P4) years of the program using the College’s approved vendor.
The criminal background check must be completed prior to the fall semester of each professional year and before any Introductory Pharmacy Practice Experience (IPPE) is initiated.

Many hospitals, clinical facilities, and other professional sites that participate in both the IPPE and advanced pharmacy practice experience (APPE) programs require certi�cation that students have a clear criminal record (or a criminal record which, due to the timing or nature of the criminal behavior, or the relevant circumstances, does not, in the judgment of the site preclude the student’s participation in the practicum experience at their site) prior to initiating pharmacy practice experiences.
Students with criminal records, therefore, should be aware that their criminal record may preclude their participation in clinical experiences at some sites, and as a result, their progression to meet the degree requirements may be impeded.
Drug Testing.
Many hospitals, clinical facilities, and other professional sites that participate in both the introductory practice experiences (IPPE) and advanced practice experiences (APPE) require students to undergo a drug test.
Students who test positive for an illegal drug will be denied positions at these sites.
As a result, their progression to meet the degree requirements will be impeded.

passages.text:
Registration as an intern pharmacist is a requirement of the program; therefore all students in the professional Pharm.D. program must hold a valid Rhode Island intern license when they enter the fall semester of their �rst professional year and before any Introductory Pharmacy Practice Experience (IPPE) is initiated.
The Rhode Island intern license must be maintained throughout the professional program (P1 to P4 years).
Students completing IPPE or APPE experiences in other states must obtain an intern license through the board of pharmacy of the state(s) in which they have those practice experiences.
Intern licensure in Massachusetts is recommended for all students, but not required.
To be eligible for an intern license, students must be currently enrolled in a pharmacy program.
Intern licenses must be returned to the board if a student withdraws or takes a leave of absence from the college.
