University of Rhode Island Exam Proctoring Policy for Online Courses Online courses can and should use a wide variety of assessment methods, which should be designed to promote academic integrity.
In some disciplines proctored exams provide a useful tool for assessment of student learning in online courses.
When designing an online course, faculty should carefully balance the potential difficulties and costs for students who are unable to come to campus at a specific time for testing (i.e. working adults, students who live out of state, Faculty must provide clear guidance to students if they require a proctored exam.
The faculty member must state in their syllabus the beginning of the semester, if a proctored exam is required for the course.
They must note that the exam will be offered during one of the common exam times.
They must alert students as soon as possible: · The date, time, and place that the exam will be offered at the Kingston and/or Providence campuses.
The scheduled window period in which the exam is to be completed by those students who cannot come to campus and should include a link to the URI resources concerning proctored exams.

passages.heading: #23-24-18 | Page 29
passages.text:
Scheduling Proctored Exams for Online Classes: ·Proctored final exams for online classes must be scheduled according to the appropriate policies of the campus where the course is offered (Kingston or Providence).
As soon as the exam is scheduled, faculty should make students aware of the time and date, and place It is the instructor's responsibility to ensure proper proctoring of the on campus exam.
Acceptable Exam Proctors outside of URI Students who cannot come to campus are responsible for making alternative arrangements for taking an exam by locating an acceptable proctor and location.
Proctors may not be friends or family members.
Acceptable proctors include: · Dean, academic department head, or official testing administrator of an accredited college or university Head librarian at a public library or a librarian with faculty status at an academic library ·Personnel at an exam testing center (such as ETS) Commanding officer at a military learning center Organizations that proctor have their own policies and exam takers need to be aware of these policies before taking the exam.

University of Rhode Island Recommended Proctored Exam Procedure for Students If your instructor requires a proctored exam for your online course, it will be clearly noted in your syllabus on the first day of class.
You should carefully read your syllabus to understand the instructor's policy on arranging and completing a proctored exam.
Because online exams are offered in a "common exam space," the syllabus may not inclnde the exact day and time.
The instructor will provide that information to you at least four weeks before the exam is scheduled, sooner if possible.
As soon as possible, the instructor will inform you of: The date, time, and place that the exam will be offered, and which campus (Kingston or Providence).

COLLEGE OF THE ENVIRONMENT & LIFE SCIENCES: MAF 570 | Introduction to Ocean Governance (3 crs.) This class covers the ‘ocean governance regime’ – the principles, norms, rules, and procedures that govern human activity in the ocean.
Students will read, discuss, think, and write about contemporary issues in ocean governance, and form evidence -based opinions about the causes of and solutions to ocean problems. (Accelerated Online Program) Pre: Enrollment in Ocean Science & Policy Graduate Certificate Program.
COLLEGE OF HEALTH SCIENCE: KIN 596 | Kinesiology Research Experience (1-3 crs.) Graduate student research experience to include literature reviews, laboratory research work, and/or other types of research experiences in Kinesiology under the direction of a Kinesiology faculty member. The following 14 c ourses were tabled at the Faculty Senate meeting due to the halt of the newly proposed program titled, “Transitional Doctor of Physical Therapy (tDPT).” The courses will be modified to fit the current Doctor of Physical Therapy Program and return to the senate for approval at a later date.
TDP 601 | Health Promotion, Policy, and Models of Delivery (3 crs.) Addresses theories and research on health promotion, public policy, and health delivery models at the population, organizational and individual levels.
Upon completion of this course, students will be able to evaluate, interpret and critically ana lyze literature related to health behaviors, health education, behavior modification, patient advocacy, compliance, and disease prevention.
Pre: Post-professional tDPT student, or permission from the instructor. (Accelerated Online Program) Pre: Enrollment in tDPT program, or by permission of instructor.
TDP 602 | Research and Evidence-Based Practice in Physical Therapy (3 crs.) Prepare practicing physical therapists for evidence-based practice (EBP) and clinical research.

passages.heading: #23-24-21 | Page 13
passages.text:
Topics will include principles of EBP, research methods, study design, data analysis and interpretation, and research study designs for clinical resear ch.
Upon completion of this course, participants will be able to critically analyze and apply evidence for clinical practice and research. (Accelerated Online Program) Pre: Enrollment in tDPT program, or by permission of instructor.
TDP 603 | Diagnostic Imaging for Physical Therapists (3 crs.) Prepares physical therapists to compare and contrasts medical imaging techniques including X -Ray, CT scan, MRI, and ultrasound imaging.
Radiologic anatomy, normal variants, and pathological and traumatic conditions are reviewed.
Upon completion of this course, students will be able to recognize images from various modalities, recognize normal and abnormal anatomy, make decisions on whether to refer patients for imaging, and understand the scope of physical therapy practice in relation to imaging. (Accelerated Online Program) Pre: Enrollment in tDPT program, or by permission of instructor.

passages.heading: #23-24-21 | Page 13
passages.text:
TDP 604 | Pharmacology for Physical Therapists (3 crs.) Introduces physical therapists to basic principles of pharmacology, pharmacokinetics, and drug receptor function for medications that are encountered by physical therapists.
Topics include analysis of common classes of pharmacological agents, and their potential effects on a physical therapy assessment and plan of care.
Basic principles of pharmacology, pharmacokinetics, and drug receptor function are covered for GC Report 2023-2024-11A Page 5 of 8 Bill #23-24-21

passages.heading: #23-24-21 | Page 14
passages.text:
medications frequently encountered by Physical Therapists; including anti -inflammatory agents, and medications used to treat cardiac, pulmonary, musculoskeletal, endocrine and neurological system dysfunction. (Accelerated Online Program) Pre: Enrollment in tDPT program, or by permission of instructor.
TDP 605 | Medical Screening & Differential Diagnosis: Physical Therapy (3 crs.) Prepares practicing physical therapists to screen patients for non -neuromusculoskeletal conditions, interpret clinical findings, and make sound clinical decisions.
This course explores the role of the physical therapist as an interdependent practitioner working within a collaborative medical model.
Emphasis is placed on examination and recognition of hallmark signs and symptoms of pathology that indicate the need for referral other healthcare providers.
This included the review of practices for ref erral to the appropriate healthcare providers when the patient’s presentation is outside the scope of physical therapy practice. (Accelerated Online Program) Pre: Enrollment in tDPT program, or by permission of instructor.

passages.heading: #23-24-21 | Page 14
passages.text:
TDP 606 | Musculoskeletal Advanced PT Evidence-based Practice (2 crs.) Prepares physical therapists for advanced practice in orthopedics and sports rehabilitation through analysis of current evidence and clinical practice guidelines (CPGs).
Upon completion of this course, students will be able to apply current eviden ce and advanced clinical reasoning to practice within orthopedic and sports rehab environments. (Accelerated Online Program) Pre: Post -professional tDPT student, or by permission of instructor.
TDP 607 | Neurological Advanced PT Evidence-based Practice (2 crs.) Prepares physical therapists for advanced practice in neurological rehabilitation through analysis of current evidence and clinical practice guidelines (CPGs).
Learners integrate rehabilitation and biopsychosocial models to explore factors that influence motor control, motor learning and neuroplasticity.
Upon completion of this course, students will be able to develop evaluation and treatment plans for individuals with neurological conditions through the application of current models, evidence, and CPGs. (Accelerated Online Program) Pre: Enrollment in tDPT program, or by permission of instructor.

passages.heading: #23-24-21 | Page 14
passages.text:
TDP 608 | Cardiopulmonary & Acute PT Evidence-based Practice (2 crs.) Prepares physical therapists for advanced practice in cardiopulmonary and acute care rehabilitation through analysis of current models, evidence, and clinical practice guidelines (CPGs).
Upon completion of this course, students will be able to develop comprehensive physical therapy evaluation and treatment plans for patients with cardiovascular, pulmonary, and acute medical -surgical conditions. (Accelerated Online Program) Pre: Enrollment in tDPT program, or by permission of instructor.
TDP 609 | Motor Control & Motor Learning Applications to PT Practice (2 crs.) Explore theories of motor control and learning applied to rehabilitation approaches, including behavioral, neural, cognitive, and physical components.
Recent advances in neuroscience and technology will be highlighted.
Upon completion of this cour se, students will be able to apply current theories of motor control and learning to strategies for rehabilitation interventions. (Accelerated Online Program) Pre: Enrollment in tDPT program, or by permission of instructor.

passages.heading: #23-24-21 | Page 14
passages.text:
TDP 610 | Pediatric Advanced PT Evidence-based Practice (2 crs.) Prepares physical therapists for advanced practice in pediatric care and rehabilitation through analysis of current models, evidence, and clinical practice guidelines (CPGs).
Upon completion of this course, students will be able to develop evaluation and treatment plans for individuals with pediatric conditions through the application of current models and evidence. (Accelerated Online Program) Pre: Enrollment in tDPT program, or by permission of instructor.
GC Report 2023-2024-11A Page 6 of 8 Bill #23-24-21

passages.text:
TDP 611 | Geriatrics Advanced PT Evidence-based Practice (2 crs.) Prepares physical therapists for advanced practice in geriatric care through the analysis of current models, evidence, and clinical practice guidelines (CPGs) for the care of older adults.
Upon completion of this course, students will be able to develop comprehensive physical therapy evaluation and treatment plans for patients with older adults with complex medical histories and/or risk for disability. (Accelerated Online Program) Pre: Enrollment in tDPT program, or by permission of instructor.
TDP 612 | Virtual Seminar: Research Translation to Clinical Practice (2 crs.) Prepares physical therapists to translate research findings on relevant areas of rehabilitation (e.g., Brain Health, Concussion, Vestibular, Rehabilitation Technology).
Upon completion of this course, students will be able to discuss best practices for translation and implementation of effective interventions clinical practice. (Accelerated Online Program) Pre: Enrollment in tDPT program, or by permission of instructor.
TDP 613 | Leadership & Business in Physical Therapy Practice (2 crs.) Introduces physical therapists to leadership and business models.

passages.heading: #23-24-21 | Page 15
passages.text:
Emphasis is on best practices for clinical administration that are essential for leaders within contemporary healthcare settings.
Upon completion of this course, students will be able apply principles of leadership and business for planning and analyzing healthcare practices. (Accelerated Online Program) Pre: Enrollment in tDPT program, or by permission of instructor.
TDP 614 | Comprehensive Case Study Capstone (3 crs.) This capstone project offers physical therapists an opportunity to write a comprehensive case report that integrates a patient’s history, physical examination, literature review, implementation plan, and outcome analysis.
This case study project integrates learning from all courses taken within the program and culminates as a tDPT program capstone paper and oral presentation.
With assistance from the project advisor, each student will develop a timeline for timely completion of the project. (Accele rated Online Program) Pre: Enrollment in tDPT program, or by permission of instructor.
S/U Credit.

passages.heading: #23-24-21 | Page 15
passages.text:
PHT 543 | Health Promotion and Policy for Physical Therapy (2 crs.) Addresses theories and research on health promotion, public policy, and health delivery models and the role of physical therapists at the population, organizational and individual levels.
Content includes health behavior and health education. (Onl ine) Pre: DPT student in good standing or by permission of the chairperson.
PHT 539 | Management and Administration in Physical Therapy (3 crs.) Practical managerial and supervisory techniques with emphasis on their application in a variety of settings.
Topics covered include: health policy development, third party reimbursement and billing, strategic planning, performance improvement, pro fessional development planning, resumes and interviews, human resource management and performance appraisal, budgeting, measuring productivity, measuring outcomes, and patient satisfaction. (Lec. 3) Pre: Enrollment in DPT program, or by permission of instructor.
PSY 507 | Lifestyle and Career Development (3 crs.) Introduces career development theories and interventions to help clients navigate decision -making.

passages.heading: #23-24-21 | Page 15
passages.text:
Examines practical application in culturally responsive career interventions tailored to clients’ unique life/work circumstances. (Seminar) Pre: Enrollment in the master's program in Mental and Behavioral Health Counseling program or by permission of instructor.

Focuses on transdiagnostic and principle-based psychotherapy skills, understanding client dynamics, cultural and ethical considerations, and integrating theory with practice for effective mental health intervention. (Seminar) Pre: Enrollment in the Mental and Behavioral Health Counseling Master's Program or the Clinical Psychology Doctoral Program, or by permission of instructor.
PSY 644 | Theory and Practice in Group Counseling (3 crs.) Provides in -depth study of group therapy principles and practices in mental and behavioral health counseling.
Emphases on experiential learning and application of group therapy techniques in counseling settings. (Seminar) Pre: Enrollment in the Me ntal and Behavioral Health Counseling Master's Program, or enrollment in the Clinical Psychology Doctoral Program, or by permission of instructor.

An introduction to fundamental oceanographic processes that uses ocean phenomena to explore four primary sub-disciplines of oceanography (geology, chemistry, physics, and biology) and global change events through an interdisciplinary lens. (Accelerated Online Program) OCG 551 | Estuarine Ecology (3 crs.) Examines the complex nature of estuaries through an interdisciplinary lens.
This course is an introduction to the specifics of estuarine science and provides a coherent view of estuaries as ecosystems. (Lec. 3) Pre: Permission of instructor.

passages.text: FACULTY SENATE OFFICE FACULTY SENATE INFORMATIONAL REPORT OCTOBER 19, 2023 Faculty Senate Academic Calendar Committee Report 2023-2024-1 Abraham Kovoor, Chair The University of Rhode Island has not had a December Commencement Ceremony in the past but will begin to do so this year. The official Academic Calendar should be amended to reflect these dates. It is the position of Enrollment Services, supported by the Calendar Committee, that this alteration is an informational item and thus does not require a formal Faculty Senate vote. Dates to be added are ceremonial and do not affect the academic program. The Calendar Committee has discussed the request and unanimously supports alteration of the Academic Calendar to reflect the new date/s of the December Commencement Ceremony. We ask that the Faculty Senate accept this informational report and consider the described calendar change authorized.

Faculty Senate Executive Committee Report 2023-2024-03 - Proposed Creation of a Special Committee Faculty Senate - May 2, 2024 RATIONALE: According to Article II, Section 4 of Appendix B of the University Manual (Constitution of theFaculty Senate), the Senate shall establish such standing and special committees as it deems necessaryto carry out its functions.
During AY 2023-2024, the University community faced operational changes,including various administrative policy initiatives and the planned transition to a new budget model, thatstressed the ability of the Faculty Senate Executive Committee to respond appropriately and react in atimely fashion.
The FSEC has agreed that creating a special committee to advise the FSEC in these andrelated matters would improve the efficiency and effectiveness of the Faculty Senate.
This new groupcould assist in analyzing and making recommendations regarding any major operational changesemerging under the university strategic plan or under independent leadership of the President, VicePresidents, or Deans; including new budget models and their implementations; and any other specificoperational expenditures relevant to faculty.

passages.heading: #23-24-23 | Page 3
passages.text:
Motion: to approve the creation of a Special Budget and Administration Committee to remain in effectuntil the end of Academic Year 2025-2026.
The Committee shall provide reports on their activities to theFaculty Senate at least annually and more often as directed by the FSEC or the Senate.
Any specificproposals for action will flow from the Special Committee to the FSEC and then to the Senate.
Activitiesof the Special Committee will include but not be limited to: review and if necessary develop measuresfor tracking major or incremental expenditures, with the aim of ensuring balanced support of facultyinterests; request information on the university’s performance toward any new goals set up under thenew incentive-based budget model (IBB) and raise questions about the correspondence of theseallocations against performance metrics (KPIs); monitor directions of administrative policies with the aimof supporting academic freedom and faculty efforts.

passages.heading: #23-24-23 | Page 3
passages.text:
The new Special Committee shall makerecommendations to the executive committee and the senate about formal responses to: any plans orproposals by the committees and individuals tasked with the implementation and functioning of theincentive-based budget model; any positions or policy initiatives of the institutional research office,administrative policy groups, purchasing, capital projects, and similar groups as they may be identified orarise.
They may also engage in advocacy on behalf of the faculty for support of research, instruction,professional development, travel, course caps, and service time, so that faculty thrive in their workunder their contractual roles.
Membership will be three senators and 2 non senators, and the chair will be elected by the committeefollowing input from the senate executive committee.

passages.heading: #23-24-23 | Page 4
passages.text:
Faculty Senate Executive Committee Report 2023-2024-04 - Proposed Creation of a Special Committee Faculty Senate - May 2, 2024 RATIONALE: According to Article II, Section 4 of Appendix B of the University Manual(Constitution of the Faculty Senate), the Senate shall establish such standing and specialcommittees as it deems necessary to carry out its functions.
The Executive Committee wasapproached by the Provost’s office regarding the need for more robust ongoing assessment andcontinuous improvement of the General Education Program.
They suggested the formation of a“steering committee” to recommend best practices for assessing the overall program and to helpdetermine if the current program is achieving the goals and outcomes envisioned in the enablinglegislation.
The FSEC and the General Education Committee (GEC) have worked on thisextensively this year and considered a variety of alternatives, including reconstituting theexisting standing committee and creating a new permanent joint committee.

passages.heading: #23-24-23 | Page 4
passages.text:
FSEC ultimatelyagreed that creating a time-limited, special committee would be most effective at this stage.Other recommendations for future action can flow from this working group depending on theiranalysis and findings.
MOTION: to approve the creation of a Special Committee to serve in an advisory capacity to theGEC in the fulfillment of its duties related to the evaluation of the General Education Program:the Special Advisory Committee on General Education Program Evaluation.
GEC shall be responsible for designing specific tasks for the special committee to address overthe course of the 2024-2025 academic year and for making decisions relating to the membershipof the committee and securing commitments from faculty (and any other stakeholders deemedappropriate and advisable) to serve on the special committee by September 12, 2024 (Senateorientation meeting).
GEC shall report to the FS on the membership and planned tasks for the Special AdvisoryCommittee on General Education Program Evaluation at the September 19, 2024 meeting of theFaculty Senate.

passages.heading: #23-24-23 | Page 4
passages.text: GEC shall make recommendations to the FS regarding the advisability ofcontinuing the Special Advisory Committee on General Education Program Evaluation orconstituting a permanent committee at the April 2025 Faculty Senate meeting.

This companion change to Report #2023-2024-07 provides clarification for this conflict.
Existing language: 8.53.20 Incomplete.
A student shall receive a temporary grade of “Incomplete” when course work has been passing but is not completed by the end of the semester due to documented extenuating circumstances beyond the ability of the student to predict and control, such as a serious illness or medical condition, or another compelling reason which justifies the grade.

Describe the change you are proposing.
This organization change will bring the Public Relations B.A. program, which is currently housed in the Communication Studies department, and the Journalism B.A. program together in a new Journalism and Public Relations department. 2.
Give the rationale for your proposed change.
In 1997, the B.A. in Public Relations was approved as an interdepartmental program jointly run by the Communication Studies department and the Journalism department.

passages.heading: #23-24-14 | Page 17
passages.text:
The original legislation (Bill #96- 97-26) called for the program to be administered on a “three-year rotating basis by the Chairs of Journalism and Communication Studies” with an “advisory/admissions committee” comprised of both chairs from the respective departments and the faculty who taught in the program.
Somewhere in the twenty-five plus years that have elapsed since the original proposal, the Public Relations program was effectively subsumed by Communication Studies and the interdepartmental structure of the original vision was lost.
During the academic program review of Journalism this past year, external reviewers suggested the Journalism curriculum would benefit from a “rethinking of [Harrington’s] overall department structure.” While it was originally proposed that the department might merge with the program in Sports Media Communication, subsequent conversations with faculty suggested that public relations would be a better fit as this pairing is common in institutions across the country and presents additional opportunities for collaboration due to the curricular overlap between the two programs.

passages.heading: #23-24-14 | Page 17
passages.text: Interestingly, the original proposal to create the public relations program also emphasized the importance of this relationship: “Because the existing Public Relations courses are Journalism courses, CASC Report 2023-2024-04B Page 2 of 7

passages.heading: #23-24-14 | Page 18
passages.text: V. 23.09.29 because the existing minor has been administered by the chair of Journalism, and because of the extent of the chair’s involvement in the existing internship program, the chair of Journalism will serve as the initial administrator of the program.” Following the guidance of the reviewers and in the spirit of the original vision for this program, the proposed organizational change will restore the interdisciplinary vision for the Public Relations program. It will allow for resource sharing and interdisciplinary collaboration between programs and will also help to rectify a primary issue addressed in the Journalism academic program review, namely, the absence of a Chair. In order to address this leadership gap and ensure a successful start to this new department, a search for a Full Professor who will Chair this new department is currently underway. 3. List all programs/courses/departments/schools, etc. that this change affects. This change will affect the Public Relations BA program (currently housed in Communication Studies department) and Journalism BA program and Journalism department. These units are housed in the Harrington School of Communication and Media in the College of Arts and Sciences. 4. Include any necessary letters of support. Letters of support are included from the faculty of the public relations program , the department of Journalism, the Director of the Harrington School of Communication and Media, and the Dean of Arts and Sciences. passages.text: 29 October 2023 Support for new Department of Journalism and Public Relations As Dean of Arts and Sciences, I fully support the proposed integration of Public Relations with the Journalism Department to create a new Department of Journalism and Public Relations. This merger does not impact the academic programs in any way. Nationally, many institutions have journalism and public relations programs in the same department. Students and faculty both benefit from the synergies between the two disciplines. The merger will also enable more effective use of resources, while also freeing the Department of Communication Studies to focus more fully on their major, as well as continue to provide a home for the rapidly expanding sports communication and media major. The Journalism and Public Relations faculty have all discussed and confirmed their agreement to merge. A full professor line has been allocated for this initiative, and the individual hired will serve as chair; a search committee composed of faculty from both majors has been established. Further, I am committed to providing faculty lines to move fully resource both majors given their import and student interest. This is an exciting move for both programs and for the Harrington School, and I fully support the transition. Jeannette E. Riley Dean, Arts and Sciences CASC Report 2023-2024-04B Page 4 of 7

passages.text:
We are at a unique moment in our history where long-standing struggles of racism, gender inequality, LGBTQ+, socio-economic status, ability, and religious differences are intensified and up for debate in the public and private spheres.
Knowing more about the root causes of the struggles LGBTQ+ individuals experience in the areas of employment, housing, politics, immigration controls, and legal institutions, to name a few, creates an opening for students to engage in systemic change and re-think their lived experiences.
The purpose of this minor is to expose students to histories, theories, concepts, and methods that have contested historical and ongoing harm and oppression.
Students are encouraged to examine their social location, lived experiences, collaborative engagement, and organizing capacity to transform our world by learning how societal structures keep inequality and oppression alive.
The QTS Minor will offer students, especially younger generations, an opportunity to read, discuss, and engage with transnational issues that affect the lives of queer and transgender communities.

passages.heading: #23-24-16 | Page 7
passages.text:
Since we live in a transnational world, the QTS minor will allow students to read, think, and analyze social justice issues through an interdisciplinary and intersectional framework.
While the QTS is complementary and overlaps with courses in the GWS, this minor offers an advanced level of proficiency in Queer and Transgender studies, politics, and culture, with a social justice commitment to scholarship, community engagement, and global citizenship.
From participating in interdisciplinary and innovative research, to social activism, to policy work in housing, wage gap, mental and medical services, media coverage, and decriminalization, these are some of the issues in which students will gain exposure, knowledge, and practical experiences to the problems affecting queer and transgender communities.
By broadening the scope of the QTS minor through an interdisciplinary and intersectional framework, students will be able to expand their prospects in the job market.
URI is “one of the top 50 LGBTQ-friendly universities in the nation.” A minor in Queer and Transgender Studies will add to the university’s local and international reputation as a leader for LGBTQ+ students.

passages.heading: #23-24-16 | Page 7
passages.text:
While the university and the center for Gender and Sexuality pride themselves on education, support, and engagement for LGBTQ+, no sustained intellectual program caters to students’ needs to study queer and transgender histories.
This minor will fill this educational gap and change the campus community’s climate.
For instance, studies have shown that an increasing number of U.S. adults consider themselves LGBTQ+, with Gen Z representing the large segment of LGBTQ+.
Gallup Poll, Social Services report indicated that at least 54.6% of LGBT Americans identify as bisexual, with Generation Z (1997-2002) representing 15.9% of the U.S. population. [1] The University of Rhode Island Climate Survey indicates that 730 students identify as LGBTQ+, roughly 18.3% of the 4,555 students surveyed.
The minor will attract not only this demographic but offer existing students at URI an intellectual space to explore their lived experiences.

passages.heading: #23-24-16 | Page 7
passages.text:
While a growing younger American population identifies or has some experience with same-sex attractions, in 2022, more than 200 anti-LGBT bills were introduced in several states across the U.S. [2] These contradictions reveal a discord between public needs and opponents who continue to push anti-LGBTQ+ legislation.
However, this is not only a U.S.-based issue; similar trends of backlash against LGBTQ+ minorities are occurring in Brazil, Ghana, Russia, and Hungary.
For instance, the Florida "Don't Say Gay" bill was modeled after Hungarian anti-LGBTQ+ bills. [3] There is a global shift towards authoritarianism which seeks to threaten years of marginal gains made by minorities across race, class, gender, sexual, ability, and ethnicity.
The social, political, and economic gains and rights acquired over the last 60 years are subjected to state and national interventions, with growing concerns that minority rights will be rescinded.
Despite the LGBTQ+ population being more visible than ever, there is still systematic discrimination and oppression across post-secondary institutions, civil services, the military, employment, and health care, to name a few.

passages.text:

Students will be required to complete six courses to receive the minor.
The gateway course 210G: Introduction to Queer and Transgender Studies fulfills the general education requirements of A2, C3, and the grand challenge.
The QTS minor is a unique curriculum, allowing students to develop the knowledge and skills necessary to create positive change.

The minor aims to strengthen students’ understanding of how queer and trans identities, activism, movements, and social relations interact with race, class, gender, age, etc., to increase students’ thinking about diversity, social justice, and equity issues.
The skills learned from this minor are essential for teachers, researchers, journalists, policy analysts, health-care workers, psychologists, counselors, LGBTQ+ directors and coordinators at centers, social workers, directors of nonprofits, community organizers, crisis hotlines, or content creators like podcasts.
Over the last few years, the cultural and political landscape has changed drastically, with industries overhauling organizational policies to create more diverse and equitable processes.

passages.heading: #23-24-16 | Page 8

Employers will be looking for candidates with the skills and education necessary to engage with a growing diverse population in Rhode Island and nationwide.
A graduate with this minor will be of interest to several occupations, who can play a critical role in developing and implementing change in their job.
Students who minor in QTS are eligible for scholarships offered by GWS: the Carlson Single Mother, Carlson Trust, Dorothy Donnelly, and Mother Jones.
Rhode Island College is the only institution in the state that offers a dedicated Queer Studies minor for undergraduates from their Gender & Women’s Studies Program.
Regionally, there are two minor programs in Massachusetts and one in New Hampshire: Brandeis University’s minor in Sexuality and Queer Studies through the Women’s, Gender, and Sexuality Studies program; Bridgewater State University’s GLBT Studies minor, through the College of Humanities and Social Sciences; and University of New Hampshire’s Queer Studies minor.
Hampshire College offers a Queer, Trans, and Sexuality Studies certificate.

passages.heading: #23-24-16 | Page 8
passages.text:
Non-degree and non-certificate granting institutions regionally are Yale University, which has a committee on Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, and Transgender Studies primarily overseeing programming, and Wesleyan University, which promotes, each semester, a course cluster in Queer Studies.
The proposed minor in Queer and Transgender Studies is similar in ethos to the minor offered at RIC.
However, in execution, the proposed minor in Queer and Transgender Studies is more focused and rigorous.
Therefore, we do not anticipate that a minor in Queer and Transgender Studies at URI will compete with the minor offered by RIC.

Compared to students at Rhode Island College, the URI student body draws from a broader population of out-of-state students.
As such, we expect that offering a minor in Queer and Transgender Studies will only add to the attractive programs available at URI for prospective and incoming students choosing among colleges and universities in the region.
A minor in Queer and Transgender Studies, as an interdisciplinary focus not only on LGBTQ lives and communities but also on the social, cultural production, and regulation of gender and sexuality, will complement every major on offer at URI.
Because of its interdisciplinary, intersectional, and transnational understanding of sexual and sexualized desires, identities, communities, and cultures in the US and globally, a minor in Queer and Transgender Studies at URI would be a close complement to existing majors in the humanities, social sciences, and sciences such as Communications, Writing & Rhetoric, English, Sociology, Anthropology, Africana Studies, Film Media, Theatre, Biology, Human Development, and Family Studies, Journalism, Economics, History, and more.

Transgender Activism: This course will introduce the emerging �eld of transgender studies through a look at the history of transgender movements in the United States, focusing on their theoretical analysis and their activist praxis.
We will approach transgender identity through an intersectional framework, emphasizing gender as a social construction that is always enmeshed in larger systems of domination.
Students will gain pro�ciency in contemporary transgender thought and the critical thinking skills needed to understand transgender politics and productively participate in transgender movements. (offered every year, 3 credits) GWS 350.
Queer and Trans Disability Studies: This seminar introduces the key concepts and contentions of disability studies and the disability justice movement through its queer and trans activists and thinkers.

passages.heading: #23-24-16 | Page 10
passages.text:
Through theoretical texts, novels, personal narratives, and art created by queer and trans disabled people, we will explore the ways that disabled people are challenging systemic ableism: the devaluing of disabled lives and experiences, disabling structures and systems, and the privileging of normative ways of being.
We will examine the ways that disabled activists and scholars have theorized disability as a part of larger systems of domination, including sexism, capitalism, colonization, and slavery. (offered every year, 3 credits) GWS 350.
Queer Intimacies in the Global South This upper-level seminar takes an interdisciplinary approach to examining “queer intimacies” in the Global South.
Using “queer intimacy” as a heuristic analytic device, we will explore how feelings, emotions, affects, and textures allow us to position intimacy in relation to broader intersectional categories of race, gender, sexuality, nation, and class. ‘Queer Intimacy’ attends to practices that spill out, over, and beyond �xed subjective identities and social, political, and economic structures.

passages.heading: #23-24-16 | Page 10
passages.text:
Engaging in course readings through thematic ideas (e.g., domestic home and labor, kinship, migration, etc.,) we will look at queer intimacies in the Global South that became subject to government intervention, colonial reforms, and post-colonial and decolonial movements. (offered every year, 3 credits) GWS 350.
LGBTQ Movements in the United States: This course investigates the theory and praxis of LGBTQ movements in the United States from 1940 to the present using historical methods.
By putting LGBTQ manifestos and oral histories alongside historical scholarship, we will analyze how LGBTQ people de�ned and rede�ned themselves over time.
Together, we will compare diverging approaches to LGBTQ politics, analyzing how gender, race, ability, and class shaped the strategies of LGBTQ leaders. (offered every year) Appendix A | Queer & Transgender Studies Minor Page 6 of 9 CASC Report 2023-2024-05B Bill #23-24-16

Queer and Feminist Methods: Research methodologies and methods are foundational in advancing our knowledge of the world.
Yet, theories and methods are also domination, power, and control tools.
This interdisciplinary seminar examines non-normative research methodologies as a lens to disrupt dominant knowledge production in the West, centering theories, ideas, and methods from alternative perspectives.

Changes Program Description The Department of Psychology offers a Bachelor of Arts (B.A.) degree, a Bachelor of Science (B.S.) degree, and a minor in psychology.
The department also offers the Master of Science Degree in School Psychology (M.S.)* and provides three doctoral programs in Behavioral Science, Clinical Psychology, and School Psychology* (Ph.D. degrees).
For details on these programs of study, see the Graduate School section of this catalog. *As of Fall 2018, admission to the M.S.
School Psychology Specialization and the Ph.D.
School Psychology Specialization has been suspended.
Students majoring in psychology typically go on either to pursue a career at the bachelor’s level or study for an advanced degree.
In both cases, students should consult the department’s web site (uri.edu/psychology) and their academic advisor to select the appropriate degree option and the appropriate courses for their interests and goals.
Program Requirements.
Students who must repeat a course to meet the minimum grade requirements may use only three credits of that particular course toward graduation.
For the B.A. degree, a total of 120 credits is required for graduation.

passages.heading: #23-24-16 | Page 42
passages.text:
The B.A. degree in Psychology provides students with a solid academic preparation through an overview of the current areas in the �eld of Psychology.
Students gain a better understanding of human behavior and an enhanced awareness of themselves and society, as well as skills for analyzing and evaluating information and data.
Students in this program must complete a minimum of 32 credits (maximum 47) in Psychology.
In order to transfer from University College for Academic Success to Health Sciences as a psychology major (or to be coded as such in the College of Health Sciences), a student must have completed 24 credits, have a C or better in PSY 113; a C average in two of the following courses: PSY 232, 235, and 254; and a C in PSY 200.

passages.heading: #23-24-16 | Page 42
passages.text:
Psychology majors are required to complete a minimum of 32 (maximum 47) credits in psychology courses to be distributed as follows: PSY 113 (with a grade of C or better); a minimum of two courses from PSY 232, 235, and 254 (with a C average); both PSY 200 (300) and PSY 301 (with a grade of C or better in each); a minimum of three topics courses (9 credits) from PSY 255, 310, 324, 335, 361, 381, 384, 385, 399, 425, 432, 434, 436, 442, 460, 464, 470, 479, and 480 (the average in the three courses must be C or better); a minimum of one course (3 credits) in the applied knowledge area to be selected from PSY 103, 261, 275, 324, 334, 340, 399, 465, 466, 471, and 478 (with a C or better); a minimum of one course (at least three credits) from the experiential practice and/or internships area selected from PSY 305, 473, 488, 489, 499; EDC 484; ITR 301, 302; CSV 302, with a C or better in graded courses or a satisfactory in S/U courses.
A particular course can only be used to satisfy one required program area (topics courses or the applied knowledge area).
A minimum of 32 graded psychology (PSY) credits (not S/U) are required for the psychology major.

passages.heading: #23-24-16 | Page 42
passages.text:
Once 47 credits in psychology courses are taken, additional psychology credits will not count toward the 120 total credits required for graduation.
Students pursuing the B.A. degree must complete 4230 of the 120 credits required for graduation at the 300-level or higher.

GENERAL INFORMATION 1. Name of institution University of Rhode Island 2. Name of administrative unit Department: Health Studies College: College of Health Sciences 3. Title of proposed organizational unit Change the name of the department to the Department of Public Health. Current name: Department of Health Studies 4. Intended date of change Initiation date: Fall 2024 5. Intended location of organizational unit Independence Square 6. Description of institutional review and approval process Approval Date Department: 9/12/2023 at Departmental Faculty Meeting College 11/16/2023 at CHS Curriculum Committee CAC/Graduate Council Faculty Senate President of the University 7. Summary description of the proposed organizational change Change program name from Department of Health Studies to Department of Public Health. This change has been proposed as part of the Strategic Investment Initiative and has the support of the provost and president. The department was initially developed as an interdisciplinary approach to studying non-clinical health. The current research and teaching within the department align with the values and learning outcomes associated with Public Health, and it is important for the name of the department to reflect the research and teaching being carried out. There is often confusion between the department name (Health Studies) and the college (Health Sciences) and we want to clarify the area of focus for the department and to provide clarity for the students. SECTION I Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation By The Faculty Senate PROGRAM CHANGES COLLEGE OF ARTS & SCIENCES: Specialization in Libraries, Leadership, & Transforming Communities (MLIS) Revisions to prerequisites see Appendix A Ever since the inception of the Libraries, Leadership, and Transforming Communities Track (LLTC) in the Masters of Library and Information Studies degree (MLIS), there has only been one course for students to “choose” from in the Public Relations and Advocacy category.
But there has also always been the intention of creating a course that would be added to that category to give students a choice.

passages.heading: #23-24-16 | Page 72
passages.text:
LSC 519: Advocacy for Libraries was added to the catalog in AY 2021 -22, so this Notice of Change is to add that course as an option in the Public Relations and Advocacy Category so that students can choose from LSC 517: Co mmunity Relations for Libraries and LSC 519: Advocacy for Libraries.
We are also seeking to add the optional courses LSC 511 and LSC 512 in one of the categories (Communities and Contexts) since those classes would fulfill the underlying theme of that category in the LLTC track.
Since the MLIS has become an Accelerated Online Program, we also need to remove the COM classes from the track as options because those courses are not available in accelerated online format.
COLLEGE OF THE ENVIRONMENT & LIFE SCIENCES: MS Environmental and Natural Resource Economics Remove GRE requirement, add course alternatives see Appendix B 1.
Removing the GRE requirement for admission: Taking the GRE can be an impediment for some potential applicants to apply, given its cost and locations where the exam is held -- these problems can be especially acute for international students.
Removing the GRE requirement will allow more applicants to apply to our program.

passages.heading: #23-24-16 | Page 72
passages.text:
We aim for this change will be effective for the 2023 -24 admission cycle (for students who would enroll Fall 2024).
GC Report 2023-2024-08B Bill #23-24-16

passages.text:

Adding alternative course to for EEC 502: EEC 502 is a required (core) course.
Because it is offered every other year, for some students, especially the ABM students, taking this course in a timely manner can be nearly impossible.
We are adding WRT 533 (Seminar in Graduate Writing in Life Sciences) and BES 521 (Rhetorical Field Methods for Science Communication) as alternative courses in place of EEC 502 on its off-year.
We aim for this change will be effective immediately for students who enrolled Fall 2023.

We aim for this change to be implemented in the 2023-24 admissions cycle.
COLLEGE OF ENGINEERING: PhD Chemical Engineering Removing course requirement see Appendix D The department voted to remove CHE 570: Research Methods in Engineering as a required course for our PhD program.

passages.heading: #23-24-16 | Page 73
passages.text:
CHE 570 is cross -listed with EGR 570.
We intend to continue offering CHE/EGR 570 as a professional elective course for graduate and undergraduate students.
There is college-wide interest in this course and we will be discussing possible options to deliver this course more widely with contributions from other engineering departments.
This could include co -teaching.
Removing CHE 570 as a required course was motivated by three factors.
First, CHE graduate students are gaining much of the knowledge and skills through their research projects with their mentors, through our seminar courses CHE 501 and 502 (required each semester whether for credit or not), and through the university's responsible conduct of research series.
Second, removing this required course is one step we will be taking to reduce our PhD credits from 72 to 64.
In the meantime, the requirement for CHE 570 is replaced in the program of study by an elective.
Third, this course is only required for our PhD program, and consequently it has been under enrolled in comparison to the desired URI course size.

passages.heading: #23-24-16 | Page 73
passages.text:
The last time it was offered, for example, there were six students enrolled in the course and the students ranged from first year to fourth year in their PhD programs.
Teaching "research methods" provides less value to students who are already in their fourth Ph.D. year of conducting research.
We do not have a recurring critical mass of new, incoming PhD students to enroll in this course regularly.
PhD Industrial and Systems Engineering Reducing credit requirement see Appendix E Reduce the total of number of credits for the PhD degree from 72 to 64.
This is consistent with the new requirements set by the Graduate School.
PhD Mechanical Engineering and Applied Mechanics Reducing credit requirement see Appendix F Reduce the total of number of credits for the PhD degree from 72 to 64.
This is consistent with the new requirements set by the Graduate School.

NEW PROGRAMS COLLEGE OF ARTS & SCIENCES: User Interface (UI) Design Certificate see Appendix G The UI User Interface Design Certificate is a four -course accelerated program focused on the user’ s visual experiences.
The program provides students with the crucial knowledge, and the technical and practical skills to become proficient UI designers.
Students will create interface projects integrating branding, animation, pattern - making, and front-end visualizations to depict intuitive user experiences.
The certificate prepares graduates to enter professional design careers that are currently in high demand.
Students are required to take 12 credits: Core Courses in the Certificate: - ART 505 - UI Design: Styling and Prototyping - ART 506 - UI Motion Design - ART 507 - UI Icon Design - ART 508 - UI Information Visualization Design COLLEGE OF ENGINEERING: ABM in Chemical Engineering (MS) see Appendix H The Accelerated Bachelor’s/Master’s program in Chemical Engineering at URI satisfies both the B.S. and M.S. requirements in full and allows for undergraduate courses to be applied and count for up to one -third of the total credits required in the master’s program.

passages.heading: #23-24-16 | Page 74
passages.text:
Students may also transfer up to one-fifth of the required master’s credits of advanced standing credits not counted towards the B.S.
For example, in a 30 -credit program, 10 credits can be counted from the B.S. degree requirements and an additional 6 advanced standing credits can be transferred.
Only 500 and 600 -level courses, as well as 400 -level courses designated for graduate credit, can be applied towards a M.S. degree.
Students must complete the requirements for their M.S. by the end of their additional year – failure to do so will negate the option to apply one -third of the credits taken during a B.S.
The URI Chemical Engineering ABM program is governed by “Appendix K” of the URI Graduate School Manual.
The M.S. program component requires 30 credits, which are detailed on the department website for Thesis and Non-Thesis options.
GC Report 2023-2024-08B Bill #23-24-16

Changes Summary description and rationale of proposed changes to program.
If applicable, list any new courses or added existing courses to program.
The department voted to remove CHE 570: Research Methods in Engineering as a required course for our PhD program.
CHE 570 is cross-listed with EGR 570.
We intend to continue offering CHE/EGR 570 as a professional elective course for graduate and undergraduate students.
There is college-wide interest in this course and we will be discussing possible options to deliver this course more widely with contributions from other engineering departments.
This could include co-teaching.
Removing CHE 570 as a required course was motivated by three factors.
First, CHE graduate students are gaining much of the knowledge and skills through their research projects with their mentors, through our seminar courses CHE 501 and 502 (required each semester whether for credit or not), and through the university's responsible conduct of research series.
Second, removing this required course is one step we will be taking to reduce our PhD credits from 72 to 64.
In the meantime, the requirement for CHE 570 is replaced in the program of study by an elective.

passages.heading: #23-24-16 | Page 100
passages.text:
Third, this course is only required for our PhD program, and consequently it has been under enrolled in comparison to the desired URI course size.
The last time it was offered, for example, there were six students enrolled in the course and the students ranged from �rst year to fourth year in their PhD programs.
Teaching "research methods" provides less value to students who are already in their fourth Ph.D. year of conducting research.
We do not have a recurring critical mass of new, incoming PhD students to enroll in this course regularly.

The courses included in this certificate are consistent with URI's strategy in the Agenda for Change to develop opportunities for students to engage in global exploration and activities that provide valuable real-world experience, and to evolve into a world-class hub for innovation, entrepreneurship, and public-private partnerships.
Strategy 1 in the Agenda for Change is present in the program goals and the learning outcomes considered in each course offered in the certificate.
Students will dive into creative design experiences developing visual, ethical, diverse, and inclusive solutions, that are accessible to the broad audience needs.
The courses' content is consistent with the core values of URI – diversity, fairness, and respect.
The proposed online UI User Interface Design certificate aligns with the URI's mission as a learner-centered research university.
Graduates will have an engaging learning experience in designing and optimizing user interfaces, as well as knowledge of best design practices on user interface research and testing.

passages.heading: #23-24-16 | Page 120
passages.text:
Graduates will engage in the creative process of designing user interfaces and distill complex concepts into simple ideas with creative thinking and strong problem-solving skills.
An important aspect of being a successful UI designer is the capacity to take design decisions that are primarily based on their strong concept development and research.
Students will learn how to visually communicate and share their designs to a variety of stakeholders, in multiple platforms, and to a specific target audience.
When completing the Certificate in User Interface Design, graduates will be proficient to enter the marketplace as UI Design professionals.
They will have the necessary knowledge and skills to design solutions that make complex information easier to understand and to use by a specific audience.They will be able to think divergently using strong concept development processes before deciding on a product idea that would bring value to the society.
This certificate, is part of a stackable Master's in UX/UI Design , and was approved by the President's Strategic Investment Program.

This course introduces students to the theory and practice of user interface design, focusing on visual communication tools and skills to facilitate prototyping.
Students will acquire knowledge of the UI design thinking process centering on the user's visual experience, while creating interfaces for websites and apps, their look and feel, responsiveness, and interactivity of their visual components, considering and recognizing the multiple human factors, audiences and contexts that govern their design decisions.
ART 506 - UI Motion Design Course Description This course introduces motion design in user experience within the principles of communication, orientation, and correlation.
Students will learn how motion design can provide users with more meaningful experiences and interactions.
It explores motion design as a sequence of movements that affects the user’s perception of any interface a user interacts with.
ART 507 - UI Icon Design Course Description This course introduces and develops the skills needed to conceptualize and design icons for user interfaces.

passages.heading: #23-24-16 | Page 123
passages.text:
Students will learn to generate UI icon sets through a process that explores visual rhetoric and shape form creation through a logical visual process.
It provides an overview of the nature and purpose of icons in user interfaces, their key characteristics, and aesthetic rules commonly used in websites and apps.
ART 508 - UI Information Visualization Design Course Description This course focuses on the design, creation, application, and evaluation of information visualization for user interfaces.
Students will learn to organize, visualize, and communicate information visualizations and implement on multiple platforms.
Students will understand the importance of the interface focusing on users and the graphical depictions of complex information for more efficient and effective processing, leading to faster and more accurate results.

NEW CERTIFICATES, MINORS, or SPECIALIZATIONS COLLEGE OF EDUCATION: Minor in Global Education Studies, see Appendix H Global Education Studies (GES) minor allows students to explore globalization and internationalization of education and educational policies using the critical lens of equity and social justice, human rights and global citizenship.
The minor will prepare students with a diversity of backgrounds with the skill sets to become change agents and leaders in education in today’s globalized world.
This minor is part of the College of Education, as K-16 education are important components of the program.
However, students from all majors are welcome to participate or take courses in the minor.
Students interested in pursuing careers in and outside of the U.S. in the field of K-16 education, governmental and non-governmental organizations, international agencies, further their studies of international issues are especially encouraged to pursue this minor.
The curriculum is focused on expanding students’ knowledge, skills, and understanding of specific comparative and international theories, concepts, and practices in education.

passages.heading: #23-24-12 | Page 5
passages.text:
The minor includes a requirement for participation in a faculty-led program in one of the College of Education’s study abroad programs in education or equivalent international experience such as COIL.
To declare a minor in Global Studies in Education a student must contact their major academic advisor at their College.
A program advisor at the College of Education will facilitate the students’ progress toward the minor and help assure that all requirements will be met for completion of the minor.
Minor Requirements: Global Education Studies (GES) minors must complete 18 or more credits related to global, comparative, and international education offered by different departments.
Requirements include a core of nine credits at the College of Education as follows: 1) EDC441-Comparative and International Education; 2) EDC330-Introduction to MLL Education; 3) Participation in a Faculty led study abroad program or an internship that is equivalent (i.e.
COIL (Collaborative Online International Learning, transfer course from another study abroad program).
We have a partnership with BridgeTEFL, students can transfer credits from this program, toward certification to teach English abroad.

passages.heading: #23-24-12 | Page 5
passages.text:
Students will also choose a minimum of one language course from the Languages department or proficiency in another language that may not be offered in the languages department.
This can be waived for a student who has grown up in a multilingual household, or who has lived and studied at least three years or more in a foreign country including grades 1-12 (or equivalent).
For those students, these three credits can be replaced with electives.
Finally, students will take two electives from the approved courses.
Non-Education majors must also take EDC103 G in place of one of their electives.
Other international/global courses may be used as electives if approved by advisor.
CASC Report 2023-2024-3B

Changes Program Description The Major.
Film/Media is an interdisciplinary major offering hands-on experience in documentary, experimental, narrative, and new media production, balanced with an emphasis on international cinemas, �lm/media history, criticism, and theory.
Our curriculum re�ects the dynamic and diverse nature of this �eld, approached from a perspective of �lm history and media theory.
Students learn to work with the evolving and overlapping technologies involved in the production of moving images (including �lm, digital video, 3D animation, game design, and new media), with an understanding of the broadening and globalization of their cultural and aesthetic contexts.
A wide range of courses is available to the �lm/media student—courses that examine the historical, theoretical, and global approaches to the analysis and creation of moving images.
The �lm/media program prepares students for careers in such areas as independent �lmmaking; animation and media design; �lm and television industries; advertising, marketing, and public relations; and media criticism.

passages.heading: #23-24-12 | Page 8
passages.text:
Graduates of this program are also prepared to continue with graduate studies, either in �lm and media production for an M.F.A., or in a master’s or doctoral program in �lm and media studies.
Students majoring in �lm/media must complete a minimum of 31 credits (maximum 46) in approved courses toward the major.
FLM 101 or FLM 101H is a required prerequisite.
All students must complete the core courses: FLM 110, FLM 203 (or ENG 302), FLM 204 (or FLM 205 or 206), including the senior-level seminar FLM 495 (or FLM 496); a minimum of 6 credits from the production and technique category and 6 credits from the critical studies category; a minimum of 3 elective credits in courses that count toward the �lm major from the Production and Technique and Critical Studies categories (see below).
This wide range of choices in �lm/media courses permits students to design a major that will meet both personal and professional goals.
Students must have a plan of study approved by an academic advisor in the �lm media program before beginning their coursework in the major.

passages.heading: #23-24-12 | Page 8
passages.text:
Production and Technique: These courses focus on the different approaches to and practices of �lm/video production—how moving images are created, designed, and used to serve a variety of functions: ART 105, 204, 213, 214, 215, 304, 306, 314, 315, 316; COM 306, 307, 316B, 341, 342, 406, 410, 417, 445; FLM 110, 220, 225, 230, 306, 316, 330, 351, 406, 417, 445, 477, 491, 496; JOR 221, 331; SCM 201.
Critical Studies: These courses emphasize the important traditions of genre and the literary and aesthetic approaches toward understanding and valuing �lm/media, and integrates them into their broad historical, cultural, and ideological contexts: AAF 352; ART 374, 376, 377; CLS 451; COM 346, 414; ENG 205 D, 245, 302, 303, 304, 305D, 352, 451; FLM 203, 204, 205, 206, 214, 352, 444, 451, 491, 495; FRN 320; GWS 350; HIS 358; HPR 344, 411; ITL 315; JOR 311; SPA 320; THE 182.
FRN 320, ITL 315, and SPA 320 are taught in English.
Other courses may be used for this category with prior approval of the program director.

passages.heading: #23-24-12 | Page 8
passages.text:
The following topics courses have been pre-approved: HPR 344 Images of Masculinity in Films, HPR 344 Politics and Protest in Film, HPR 344 Rebel Images in Films, HPR 411 Film and Video Practicum, and GWS 350 Women and Film.
Other �lm-based courses may count toward the major or the minor with the permission of the �lm/media program director.
The Harrington School of Communication and Media requires students in each of the six undergraduate majors to also complete the Harrington core requirements.
In order to transfer from University College for Academic Success to the College of Arts and Sciences, students must complete a minimum of 24 credits and have a GPA of 2.00 or higher.
A total of 120 credits is required for graduation.
At least 42 of these must be in courses numbered 300 or above.

Changes Program Description Sports Media and Communication This interdisciplinary minor in Sports Media and Communication exposes students to historical, critical, analytical, practical, and professional approaches to sports media and communication.
Students who complete the program understand how to critically and effectively evaluate, analyze, and produce sports media and communication products using a variety of technologies and media, from their voice for broadcasting to social media platforms for advertising.
With a focus on the interdisciplinary nature of the sports media and communication industry, students will complete a wide variety of courses that will all develop and harness their skills and help launch their sports media and communication career.
In order to bridge academic instruction with the professional world, students are expected to complete an internship or experiential learning opportunity on or off campus.
Many of these internships can be had on campus and have already been developed.

Kingston Fall 2024 Spring 2026 Global Education Studies (GES) minor allows students to explore globalization and internationalization of education and educational policies using the critical lens of equity and social justice, human rights and global citizenship.
The minor will prepare students with a diversity of backgrounds with the skill sets to become change agents and leaders in education in today’s globalized world.
This minor is part of the College of Education, as K-16 education are important components of the program.
However, students from all majors are welcome to participate or take courses in the minor.
Students interested in pursuing careers in and outside of the U.S. in the �eld of K-16 education, governmental and non-governmental organizations, international agencies, further their studies of international issues are especially encouraged to pursue this minor.
The curriculum is focused on expanding students’ knowledge, skills, and understanding of speci�c comparative and international theories, concepts, and practices in education.

Minor Requirements: Global Education Studies (GES) minors must complete 18 or more credits related to global, comparative, and international education offered by different departments.

The goals of the program are to: 1.
Increase the number of students who have a foundation in global teaching competencies. 2.
Investigate global and national educational issues from different perspectives and engage with real-world issues. 3.
Examine many of the most critical concerns of today’s societies; to wit: poverty, inequity, race, class, gender, human rights, the role of the countries and the international community, NGOs and civil society in policy development and implementation; the role of culture, history and its relation to schooling, society, and economy. 4.
Propose solutions and engage in advocacy to meet the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
The minor in Global Education Studies aligns with the University’s mission and 2023-2033 Strategic Plan Priority 1, Goal 2, Action 1: Become a destination for companies across the globe that seek to collaborate with faculty and students in research and research translation.
Action 3: Develop opportunities for students to engage in global exploration and activities that provide valuable real-world experience.

Students can also apply for the Demers language fellowship to continue their language studies abroad.
It is estimated that by the year 2025, 25% of all students in U.S. public schools will be multilingual learners (MLLs) (Wright et al., 2017).
Rhode Island schools, like those in many other parts of our country., have had an increase in the number of MLLs attending schools.
During the 2020-2021 school year, there were 15,107 MLL students in Rhode Island, representing 11% of all students enrolled in public school.
MLLs face a significant performance gap in standardized content area assessments as compared to their non-MLL peers (RIDE, 2022).
Challenges include student factors, such as linguistic diversity and a broad range of academic skills and needs.
Challenges also include school, district, and state-level factors, such as teacher certification requirements, local-level graduation requirements, schedule restrictions, and segregation of course tracks between MLLs and non-MLLs (Callahan & Shifrer, 2016).
Staffing with appropriately qualified teachers is of significant concern as effective teachers can increase MLL test performance (Apthorp et al., 2012; Yoon et al., 2007).

passages.heading: #23-24-12 | Page 52
passages.text:

Rhode Island’s MLLs are culturally and linguistically diverse: during the 2021-2022 school year, MLL students spoke 92 different languages (Rhode Island Kids Count, 2022).
While the student population especially in urban schools in RI is highly diverse, in Rhode Island and around the country, the teacher workforce is largely White and monolingual (Garcia & Cook, 2017; U.S.

We propose to reduce the length of time from start to finish of the DPT program.
The DPT program is currently on a 3 years/9 semesters schedule.
We propose to change the time it takes for students to complete the program from 3 years (9 semesters) to 2.5 years (8 semesters).

We will add a “Term B” to the summer session of year 2 and move the only course in summer of year 3 (2 credits) to summer of year 2. 2.

Experience design is an integrative approach to design, using research to enhance the quality of human experience in specific situations.
User experience design (UX) is guided by an understanding of human objectives, requirements, and aspirations.
Upon completion of the Graduate Certificate in User Experience Design, graduates will be able to tackle complex design challenges, create inclusive and accessible solutions, and drive positive change through design.
Students will learn how to conduct user research ethically, gathering valuable insights that inform the design process.
They will then gain hands-on experience with industry-standard tools; develop strong writing abilities to enhance their user experiences and create meaningful interactions that guide users through digital interfaces seamlessly; and explore new methodologies, technologies, and design approaches, ensuring they stay at the forefront of UX design advancements.
Strategy 1 in the Agenda for Change is deeply embedded in the goals of this program and the learning outcomes of each course.

passages.heading: #23-24-12 | Page 67
passages.text:
This certificate program emphasizes the application of ethical, collaborative design practices to solve real-world problems, focusing on inclusive design, design justice, person-first design, and designing for the social good.
Students will learn to engage in design processes that prioritize the needs and perspectives of diverse user populations.
By understanding the principles of inclusive design, they will acquire the ability to create solutions that cater to a wide range of users, ensuring accessibility and usability for all.
This certificate, as part of a stackable master's in UX/UI, was approved by the President's Strategic Investment Program.
It aligns with Priority 2, Goal 1, Actions 1 and 2 of the Strategic Plan as follows: Action 1: Create and ensure �exible academic pathways, curricula, global and experiential learning opportunities, and career advising that meets student interests and career trends.
Action 2: Grow URI Online to increase access for all students at every life stage.

passages.text:
In December 2022, Forbes notes "User experience (UX) design, and the closely related field of user interface (UI) design, will become increasingly valuable skills due to the extent to which digital transformation is effectively turning every company into a tech company and every job into a tech job." News of layoffs in tech is misleading for a variety of reasons (including temporary pandemic-related expansions and post-pandemic contractions).
When examining the UX job market potential, The New York Times states that “a majority of tech jobs are at companies outside the tech sector in industries like banking, retail, health care, and manufacturing.” Along these lines, UX professionals are also essential to nonprofit organizations, and our program uniquely positions students to work in the service and civic design fields.
UX is an in-demand facet of web development and digital design, which, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics is growing at a rate of 23 percent.
Websiterating.com records a minimum of 1.97 billion websites in existence as of January 2023 with more than 4 million apps.

passages.heading: #23-24-12 | Page 68
passages.text:
Demand for UX specialists to contribute to the creation and continual revision of these websites and apps is high.
A recent search of Indeed Indeed.com, Glassdoor, Ziprecruiter, and other industry analysis and job listing sites offer average salaries for these positions as follows: Information Architect $146,582 UX researcher $120,465 Usability Specialist $112,181 UX writer $110,000 UX designer $103,136 None Regional Demand While UX/UI is applicable to nearly all industries, it is worth noting that Rhode Island boasts a strong information technology sector, now making up more than $1.5 billion of the state's GDP .
Nearly 9 percent of the state’s total workforce is employed in the tech sector.
Rhode Island is also home to major employers who hire UX/UI professionals in droves, including Hasbro, CVS Health, Textron Aviation, Citizens Financial, and others.
Our graduate certificate will offer recent college graduates living in the New England area high-paying career paths; it will also provide working professionals with much-needed skills for today's job market, greatly expanded job opportunities, and higher salaries in the private, public, and nonprofit sectors in the region.

passages.heading: #23-24-12 | Page 68
passages.text:
The market analysis supporting this certificate has identified significant regional shifts toward UX/UI in numerous industries and fields, including professional/technical writing, communications, design, marketing, healthcare, finance, and technology—to name a few.
A recent job search on Indeed turned up 866 UX jobs within 100 miles of New York, 322 jobs within 100 miles of Boston, and 333 jobs within 100 miles of Providence County.
Competition There is no other academic institution in Rhode Island offering a graduate certificate in User Experience Design.
Institutions in neighboring Massachusetts offer programs appear on the surface to have some overlap with our program, but a close examination reveals key differences in content, credit requirements, flexibility, and cost.
Northeastern University offers an online certificate in Usability.
Housed in the College of Professional Studies, this 20-credit program offers courses that focus more on theory than practice and omits key areas of UX, in favor of human-computer interaction.

passages.heading: #23-24-12 | Page 68
passages.text:
For example, unlike our program, it does not cover UX writing and the ethical issues of user experience design, such as social justice, sustainability, and equity considerations .
Moreover, our certificate pairs with our UI certificate and can build toward a master's in UX/UI, while Northeastern's Usability certificate does not provide complementary graduate education opportunities.
Students must have a GPA of 3.0 to enter the program, which excludes students who may not have performed well in college for a variety of reasons, including financial hardship, but have found their stride in the workplace.
Time to completion of the certificate: 6 to 12 months (we are at two semesters) List any available assistantships, scholarships and fellowships.

WRT 501: Ethical Foundations of UX explores the ethical considerations and responsibilities involved in designing digital experiences for users.
Through a combination of theoretical concepts, case studies, and practical exercises, students will gain an understanding of the ethical challenges faced by user experience designers and develop strategies to create user-centered and ethically sound designs.
Students will explore UX as a research and development method, especially as it relates to inclusive design and design justice.
Students will learn about foundational concepts in UX design, including terminology, history, and evolution of the field.
Using a critical lens, students will investigate issues of social justice, equity, sustainability, accessibility, and inclusion.
WRT 502: UX Research and Methods is an introduction to methods, research design, and data analysis in user experience projects, and aims to prepare professionals for designing, conducting, analyzing, and reporting their own user research studies.
This course will train students in how to determine the best methods and metrics for their projects, as well as design studies for effective data collection.

passages.heading: #23-24-12 | Page 70
passages.text:
This course will also teach students how to communicate research results for decision-making purposes to a variety of stakeholders.
Students in this course will gain hands-on practice at every phase of the user research process, from identifying design problems or questions to developing their own test protocols, recruiting users, conducting user tests, and analyzing their results.
WRT 503: UX and Microcopy Writing is designed to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of the role and impact of effective writing in user-centered design.
Through a combination of theoretical concepts and practical applications, students will develop the skills necessary to create clear, concise, and engaging microcopy for digital interfaces and interactions.
WRT 504: Interaction Design focuses on the process of rapid, iterative design that keeps real people at the heart of creating content—a philosophy and design approach known as human-centered design.
Students in this course will learn agile design workflows, conduct rapid prototyping and wireframing, and share reflections on the process and results of user research meaningfully for public and industry audiences.

passages.heading: #23-24-12 | Page 70
passages.text:
Students will gain hands-on, applied knowledge of the human-centered design process by creating their own design and refining it based on user feedback.
