The prevention sciences graduate certificate combines skills with methods to understand how to reduce risk and promote health and healthy development.
There is an emphasis on examining social determinants of health with the aim of enhancing equity and decreasing disparities.
Additionally, this program provides intellectual development and training to a diverse community of students who can benefit from foundational and applied skills in health promotion and disease prevention but require flexible academic pathways (Strategic priority 2; Goal 1; Action 1).
This certificate can be completed to meet requirements in the Master's of Professional Studies program and the Master's of Public Administration program.
For the Master's of Professional Studies (30 credits total), students complete two certificates, and six additional credits of coursework.
The Prevention Science certificate can be included as one of the certificates toward completion of the degree.
For the Master's of Public Administration (36 credits total), students complete three certificates to complete the degree.

passages.heading: #23-24-12 | Page 76
passages.text:
The Prevention Science certificate can be included as the third certificate the students complete towards their degree.
The certificate could also be taken as a stand-alone certificate for any interested students.
One of the key elements of prevention science is the partnership with key community stakeholders (both public and private) who can work together to develop and implement appropriate interventions that address today’s health-related challenges.
Using evidence-based practices, applied learning, and real-world scenarios, students will be able to explore a range of issues through the lens of promoting and protecting health (e.g., social justice, family trauma, substance abuse and/or other addictions).
Therefore, the interdisciplinary nature of the program aims to foster meaningful interactions amongst students who bring expertise from a variety of health backgrounds.

passages.heading: #23-24-12 | Page 76
passages.text:
This program aligns with the URI strategic plan priorities and goals in several ways to include: 1) Strategic Priority 1 (Broaden Our Impact), Goal 1: Contribute to broad and deep impacts on the social, cultural, and economic ecosystems across Rhode Island, the nation, and beyond. 2) Strategic Priority 2 (Enhance Student Achievement), Goal 2: Increase graduate student enrollment and degree completion. 3) Strategic Priority 4 (Power the University of the Future), Goal 4: Expand research and new academic programs and services through an increased focus on revenue generation.
Offered completely online and asynchronously, this program targets working professionals across a myriad of health sectors who wish to advance within the workforce while still holding full-time jobs.
This will be attractive to students while meeting employers’ needs.
Additionally, the stackable design of this program highlights the intersection of specialties that employers look for while offering a flexible path for students.
Furthermore, the appeal of the in-state competitive tuition speaks to the accessibility of the program nationwide and beyond.

With 38 states allowing medical cannabis and 23 states now having adult use markets, legal cannabis has become the fastest growing industry in the United States.
The legal cannabis workforce has tripled over the past five years, outpacing the height of the technology sector's job growth.
Cannabis retail sales are estimated to reach $33.6 billion in 2023 with an additional economic impact of $100.8 billion.
These estimates do not include the hemp nor cannabidiol (CBD) markets that have grown out of the federal legalization of cannabis containing less than 0.3% tetrahydrocannabinol (THC).
The rapid job growth represents a problem for employers and has created public health concerns due to the lack of qualified employees.
The graduate certificate in cannabis sciences aims to address these concerns by providing students with the current knowledge in cannabis pharmacology and skills in cannabis formulation, manufacturing, and analysis.
Graduates of the certificate will have the knowledge to evaluate, develop, and research cannabis products in terms of safety and function.

passages.heading: #23-24-12 | Page 83
passages.text:
Specifically, graduates will be able to 1) relate concepts of pharmacology and pharmaceutics to the development and therapeutic use of cannabis products, 2) propose strategies for the development of safe, stable, and functional cannabis products that meet or exceed current regulatory frameworks, and 3) apply analytical and bioanalytical techniques to assess the quality of cannabis products and the presence of cannabis metabolites in biological matrices for pharmacological studies.
The certificate program aligns with the University's mission and Strategic Plan by aiming to be an innovator in cannabis science education.
Specifically, the certificate addressed Priority 1: Broaden our Impact by providing students with the skill and knowledge necessary to make meaningful impacts and drive innovation in the cannabis field by adding to the scientific understanding of cannabis, solving challenges with product safety and stability, and addressing the stigma of cannabis through rigorous scientific inquiries (Goal 1 Action 2).

passages.heading: #23-24-12 | Page 83
passages.text:
This will be accomplished by exploring current evidence-based literature and immersing students in the real world techniques and processes of cannabis and related industries (Goal 2 Action 3).
Priority 2: Enhance Student Achievement will be meet by the program through the use of interactive teaching technologies, the design of active learning discussions and assignments, and the implementation of andragogical strategies (Goal 1 Action 1).
The certificate is being offered in the accelerated 7 week format through URIOnline making it accessible to working professionals, those seeking career advancement or change, and other nontraditional graduate students (Goal 1 Action 2).
The program is designed as a stand alone certificate, but also has the potential to form the technical component of a new professional science master's (PSM) degree (Goal 2 Action1).
The certificate will enable the RI workforce to meet the challenges of the expanding medical and recreational cannabis market in RI and provide an opportunity for alumni to gain expertise in the evolving field aligning with Priority 3: Foster an Inclusive Culture (Goal 1 Action 3).

passages.heading: #23-24-12 | Page 83

Finally, for Priority 4: Power the University of the Future , the certificate will generate new revenue streams in three ways: as a new academic program, by creating four new online courses, and as the technical component of a new PSM degree to be proposed in the future (Goal 4 Action 1).

The science of pharmaceutical development is essential to the process of bringing a therapeutic entity from compound discovery to treatment in humans.
Most importantly, it seeks to create dosage forms for the compound that are safely consumed by humans (and animals), are stable until ingested, release the active drug product efficiently, avoid detrimental biologic interactions, have a consistent response, and have a known and controllable safety profile.
Advances in the knowledge and uses of injectable, biotech products have added a significant complexity to the drug development process.
In comparison to small molecule drug products, biological molecules have four levels of structure considerations making the development process much more complex and challenging.
Currently, over 70% of the compounds in the bio/pharmaceutical insudstry's drug development pipeline are large biological molecules.
This is a rapidly evolving area mandating continued education for those holding entry level degrees.
Graduates will have the knowledge to design and articulate a whole team approach to the product life cycle of a candidate drug molecule from initial identification through commercial launch.

passages.heading: #23-24-12 | Page 92
passages.text:
Specifically, students completing this on-line certificate program will be able to 1) Describe the design and challenges of the pharmaceutical product development process from initial concept to market as well as the roles and responsibilities of each operational group; 2) Implement cGMP regulations for pharmaceutical drug substance and drug product manufacture; and 3) Develop product development strategies to optimize the creation of novel pharmaceuticals in industrial settings.
The online Graduate Certificate in Pharmaceutical Development meets the Provost's academic priority for active e-learning via technology-enhanced pedagogy and online programs.
Further, italigns with key goals of URI's 2022-32 Strategic Plan.
One goal of this Plan is to enhance studentsuccess by equipping learners with skills that are in demand in an ever-changing world, which this proposed certificate program aims to achieve.
The Pharmaceutical Development certificate program also addresses this goal's strategy of facilitating the implementation of new learningpedagogies and the expansion of modes of course delivery and assessment by leveragingspace and time in new ways.

passages.text:
The Curriculum and Standards Committee (CASC) Procedures CASC examines course and program proposals to ensure they are comprehensible and user-friendly for undergraduate students.
Within the Kuali proposal, we examine all ﬁelds to conﬁrm clear details vital to student success, such as prerequisites, course rationale and description, the number of seats and sections offered per year, and syllabi.
Syllabi should accompany all major course proposals (new classes, signiﬁcant modiﬁcations to a course).
To ensure proposal syllabi will be clear to students, we look for: ● straight-forward course information (class description & objectives, method of instruction); ● clear course policies, structures, and methods of teaching; ● clarity regarding grade scale & methods, assignments, and how coursework connects to credit hours; ● current information about accessible technological resources and apps necessary for the class; Further, students are best served by having up-to-date information on support services such as DAI; illness policies; and procedures reﬂecting current University standards.
Where these items are overlooked or out-of-date, CASC may provide friendly feedback.

passages.heading: CASC Procedures | Page 1
passages.text:
Also, ATL has resources and templates for syllabi ( https://web.uri.edu/atl/design/syllabus/ ).
New courses should provide supporting documentation uploaded by the chair of the department/academic unit into the proper Kuali ﬁeld, indicating the date that their department/program voted to approve the course.
Program-level proposals should include all materials relevant to the new program/proposed changes, including supporting documentation from other academic units impacted by these changes.
All program and applicable accreditation requirements should be listed .
The Kuali ﬁelds for program proposals should include courses impacted by changes.
Course and Program Overlap Overlap is when a newly proposed or modiﬁed course/program intersects with the content of an existing course or program.
The amount of overlap might range from small (the topics of a single class) to approaching virtual duplication.
Proposers and curriculum approval committees can use search features within Kuali to compare other current and proposed courses/programs for potential overlap.

passages.heading: CASC Procedures | Page 1
passages.text:
When CASC recognizes potential overlap, they will ask the course proposer and department/instructor to consult regarding the degree and signiﬁcance of overlap.
Even with substantial replication in content, there might be key differences in approach.
As CASC cannot be experts in all disciplines, we request that the proposer and faculty for the existing course/program work together.
This collaboration can be documented in a statement communicating the resolution to CASC.
If this collaboration cannot occur, CASC exercises its best judgment regarding student beneﬁt.
Note: overlap issues can also be addressed on the Faculty Senate ﬂoor or even at ﬁnal approval with the President.
We also encourage colleges to check for overlap themselves.
Starting in Fall 2025, CASC’s ‘Proposed Temporary and Permanent Courses/Programs’ email will be distributed at the end of the last full week of each month.
We encourage each college’s curriculum committee to meet during the ﬁrst full week of each month and, as part of their deliberations, carefully consider all newly proposed offerings in that CASC newsletter for potential overlap.

passages.heading: CASC Procedures | Page 1
passages.text: Any overlapping courses/programs should be reported to Genviéve Spitale ( genvieve.spitale@uri.edu ); the course/program will not be reviewed until the originating and overlapping colleges agree in writing that either the original proposal or a revised version can move forward for CASC/Gen Ed/Grad Council consideration.

Objective: The Accelerated Bachelor’s/Master’s (ABM) program in Electrical Engineering has been introduced with the dual aim of enhancing the graduate student population and addressing the pressing need to match student enrollment with the availability of Research Assistantship (RA) funds.
This initiative is especially crucial for faculty members engaged in projects funded by the Naval Undersea Warfare Center (NIUVT) and other Department of Defense (DOD) entities, which stipulate U.S.
Citizenship for participants.
By encouraging our undergraduates to pursue a Master's degree within a condensed timeframe, we aim to navigate these challenges effectively.
Program Options: The ABM program offers two distinct pathways for completion: Thesis Option: Under this track, students are urged to initiate research as early as their junior or senior year.
The goal is to facilitate the timely completion of a Master's thesis by the end of the 5th year.
Non-Thesis Option: Details for this pathway will cater to students seeking to complete their Master's degree without the requirement of a thesis.

passages.heading: #23-24-24 | Page 31
passages.text:
Strategy for Growth: Recruiting from our existing undergraduate talent pool and offering the incentive of achieving a Master's degree in the 5th year is a strategic response to the aforementioned challenges.
This approach not only augments our graduate student numbers but also aligns with the funding prerequisites of critical research projects requiring U.S.
Citizenship.
Through this structured program, we aim to foster a robust pipeline of skilled electrical engineers ready to contribute to advanced research and meet the demands of significant funding bodies.
No User Selected Application Timeline: Students aiming to join the Accelerated Bachelor’s/Master’s (ABM) program must submit their application to the graduate school by October 15th during their senior year.
Application Criteria: Academic Performance: Applicants are required to have maintained a minimum GPA of 3.3 throughout their Bachelor of Science (B.S.) studies.
Letters of Recommendation: The application must be accompanied by three letters of recommendation, with at least one from a faculty member within the department who agrees to provide graduate advisement.

Educational need - Based on inquiries about and applications to the online Master of Oceanography (MO) program there is a strong interest in ocean science and policy knowledge among those who do not have majors or substantial background in the natural sciences, technology, engineering, or math (STEM).
A strong STEM backgrounds is necessary for the existing classes in the online MO and Ocean Science Graduate Certificate, thus, these potential students do not qualify for our existing online programs.
Applicants without STEM backgrounds are likely to be interested in Ocean Science specifically as it applies to law, policy, and management.
MAF has a slate of relevant in-person courses, which will be adapted into a new class (Introduction to Ocean Governance) that will be a required in this program.
This new class will complement the Ocean Science courses in the certificate, providing students with a strong understanding of the multiple sites of science/policy interface.

passages.text:
This program aims to grow a workforce of professionals interested in various economic sectors of the Blue Economy such as: offshore wind energy, marine aquaculture, marine business services, State and Federal personnel serving institutions such as Rhode Island Department of Environmental Management (RI-DEM), Coastal Resources Management Council (CRMC), National Oceanic Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), and Unites States Coast Guard (USCG).
The proposed program aligns with the URI Strategic Plan in numerous ways.
Below is a list of the specific actions in the Strategic Plan with which the proposed program aligns.

If this proposed certificate is approved, we will work with Dean Rogers to do this.
The goal is to simplify the existing Blue MBA program which we view as requiring too many credits (it is presently a combination of the MBA and MO).
Priority 2 Enhance student achievement by cultivating an engaged and inclusive learning environment Goal 1 Continuously invigorate the learning environment to reflect active learning; student agency; and contemporary, high-impact learning pedagogies.
Action 1: Create and ensure flexible academic pathways, curricula, global and experiential learning opportunities, and career advising that meets student interests and career trends.
Action 2: Grow URI Online to increase access for all students at every life stage.
This program is designed and ideally suited for working professionals who want to advance in their present careers or those that seek career change.

passages.heading: #23-24-24 | Page 54
passages.text:
As stated above, based on inquiries about our Online MO program there are many students interested in the type of certificate program we are proposing.
We have discussed this certificate option with some present MPA students and several of them would like to pursue this certificate.
Goal 2 Increase graduate student enrollment and degree completion.
Action 1: Develop new professional master’s degree programs that respond to labor market trends, as well as student interests and needs.
As stated above, we anticipate that this new certificate will be accepted as part of the Online MPA program and potentially the MBA.

passages.heading: Chapter 5 – Committees of the University
passages.text: (Chapter 5 was reorganized in accordance with #03-04–9 . Identified changes are linked to other legislation)

passages.heading: Preamble
passages.text: 5.10.10 Committees, Boards, Councils and other such entities which have a university-wide function are described in this chapter. With few exceptions, committees with a narrower scope are not included here. For information on them, consult policy documents of various campus units, such as college by-laws, where available, and the Graduate Student Manual. Standing committees of the Faculty Senate, although having university-wide function, can be found in the by-laws of the Faculty Senate.

passages.heading: Preamble
passages.text: 5.10.11 The committees included here are organized according to the jurisdictional rubric under which they fall, and are divided into (1) committees falling under presidential jurisdiction; (2) committees falling under direct jurisdiction of the general faculty or of the Graduate Faculty; and (3) committees falling under the joint purview of the Faculty Senate and the President. The division into the various jurisdictional rubrics has been proposed by a Faculty Senate Constitution, By-Laws, and University Manual (CBUM) subcommittee on the basis of research conducted during the 2001-02 academic year. This research primarily took into consideration the jurisdictional divide between the President (administration) and the Faculty Senate resulting from Article II of the Senate Constitution; when this was not conclusive, the historic understanding of who had jurisdiction at the time of the establishment of a committee or its predecessor was taken into account. In most cases, these criteria allowed a clear determination of a committee’s jurisdictional rubric. To limit future disputes about jurisdiction, the subcommittee proposed that the Faculty Senate endorse and accept the jurisdictional division resulting from the subcommittee’s research, the senate did so at its meeting on November 11, 2003, and the President endorsed the senate legislation on December 5, 2003.

passages.heading: Preamble
passages.text: 5.10.12 Faculty, administrators, and staff members are expected to serve on committees, if designated. Each standing committee of the University shall make an annual report for the academic year to its appointing authority.

passages.heading: Committees falling under Presidential jurisdiction
passages.text:
5.11.10 University Committees listed under this heading can be formed, abolished, or altered by presidential action, preceded by consultation with relevant groups and/or individuals as appropriate. Committees the President appoints under this authority are not to duplicate or interfere with the work of committees established by the Faculty Senate. Unless otherwise specified, members shall be appointed from the University community with an attempt to ensure administration, faculty, and student representation; in addition, staff members shall be appointed in accordance with collective bargaining agreements. Members shall serve two-year terms, one-half of the appointments to be made each year, and which may be renewable; the President shall designate the chairperson. (# October 21, 2021 Informational Report)
5.12.10 The Deans’ Council shall comprise the deans and vice provosts and the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs, who shall be chairperson.
5.12.11 This council shall provide opportunity for the academic deans to discuss common problems and to review administrative procedures among the several colleges.

passages.heading: Committees falling under Presidential jurisdiction
passages.text: 5.14.10 The Athletics Advisory Board shall serve as a policy review board for all athletic programs for men and women, including intercollegiate, club, intramural, and recreational sports and the management of facilities and equipment. The Board shall make its recommendations to the President. In performing its functions, the Athletics Advisory Board shall advise and review, on a continuing basis, all fiscal, educational and social policy affecting all athletic programs, make recommendations regarding level of competition, and the nature of intercollegiate schedules. For the role of the Athletics Advisory Board on issues regarding championships and special tournaments during the final examination period see section 8.51.31 . #10-11–24

passages.heading: Committees falling under Presidential jurisdiction
passages.text: 5.14.11 The Board shall be comprised of nine voting members: four faculty members, one undergraduate student, one graduate student, two alumni; the President shall appoint one additional faculty member to serve as the ninth member and chairperson. The faculty membership shall be appointed in consultation with the Faculty Senate; the student membership shall be appointed in consultation with the Student Senate and the Graduate Student Association; the Alumni representatives shall be appointed in consultation with the Alumni Association. For each appointment made to the Board, each constituency shall nominate two persons. The President shall make appointments from among these nominations. Terms of appointment for faculty and representatives of the Alumni Association shall be for three years, renewable once at the end of the first term. Terms of appointment for students shall be for one year, renewable at the end of the first term. The Director of Athletics, the Associate Director/Senior Woman Administrator, the Assistant Director of Recreational Services, the Vice Provost for Faculty Affairs, the Chief NCAA Compliance Officer, the Enrollment Services Assistant Director of Compliance, and a delegate from the Student-Athlete Advisory Committee shall be ex officio non-voting members of the Board #07-08–35 #10-11–24 #IFSR–AAB

passages.heading: Committees falling under Presidential jurisdiction
passages.text: 5.23.10 The Institutional Biosafety Committee (IBC) shall review and approve the use of recombinant DNA, synthetic DNA, infectious microorganisms, certain biological toxins, and human or nonhuman blood, unfixed tissues or cells in all research projects and educational activities under the jurisdiction or control of the University. The use of these materials shall be in accordance with the National Institutes of Health (NIH) Guidelines for Research Involving Recombinant or Synthetic Nucleic Acid Molecules and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Biosafety in Microbiological and Biomedical Laboratories as well as any other applicable federal, state and local law. Administrative Report September 2015

passages.heading: Committees falling under Presidential jurisdiction
passages.text: 5.23.11 The membership shall comprise at least five members appointed by the Vice President of Research and Economic Development selected so that they collectively have experience and expertise in recombinant or synthetic nucleic acid molecule technology and the capability to assess the safety of recombinant or synthetic nucleic acid molecule research and to identify any potential risk to public health or the environment. At least two members shall not be affiliated with the institution (apart from their membership on the Institutional Biosafety Committee) and who represent the interest of the surrounding community with respect to health and protection of the environment. The Vice President for Research and Economic Development or the Vice President’s designee shall serve ex officio , as a non-voting member. An effort will be made to appoint members to the IBC that will have the qualifications of experience and expertise needed to provide guidance and counsel to researchers.

passages.text:
5.24.10 The Conflict of Interest Management Committee (CIMC) is responsible for the review and assessment of all financial disclosures related to research projects at URI and for determining any actions required to ensure that real or perceived financial conflicts of interest are managed or eliminated as required by the RI Public Private Partnership Act as well as any other applicable federal law or policy. Administrative Report September 2015
5.24.11 The membership shall be appointed by the Vice President of Research and Economic Development and shall at a minimum include a public member and a faculty member from an institution of higher education outside the system of public higher education in Rhode Island. The Vice President for Research and Economic Development or the Vice President’s designee shall serve ex officio , as a voting member.

passages.heading: Committees falling under Presidential jurisdiction
passages.text: 5.25.10 The Institutional Review Board (IRB) shall review and approve all biomedical and behavioral research involving human subjects which is conducted or sponsored by the University. The Code of Federal Regulations, 45 CFR 46, revised in 2005, requires the existence of this committee in order to protect the rights and welfare of the human subjects of such research. See Appendix G for the University’s policy and procedures concerning the protection of human subjects.

passages.heading: Committees falling under Presidential jurisdiction
passages.text: 5.25.11 The IRB shall comprise at least five members appointed by the President. The chairperson shall be recommended by the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs to the President, to be appointed for one three-year term. Other IRB members shall be appointed for two-year, renewable terms. The IRB shall not consist entirely of men, entirely of women, or entirely of members of one profession. At least one member shall be a person whose primary training and research concerns are in nonscientific areas; for example, lawyers or members of the clergy. At least one member shall be a person who is not otherwise affiliated with the institution or part of the immediate family of a person who is affiliated with the institution. One member shall be a person whose primary training and research concerns are in the scientific area, for example a physician, a biologist, or a psychologist. When research is reviewed involving a category of vulnerable subjects (e.g., prisoners, children, individuals institutionalized as mentally disabled), the IRB shall include at least one member who has as a primary concern the welfare of these subjects. The Vice President for Research and Economic Development or the Vice President’s designee shall serve ex officio , as a non-voting member. An effort will be made to appoint members so that the IRB will be sufficiently qualified through the experience and expertise of its members, the diversity of their racial and cultural backgrounds, and their sensitivity to community attitudes, to be respected for its advice and counsel in safeguarding the rights and welfare of human subjects.

passages.heading: Committees falling under Presidential jurisdiction
passages.text:
5.25.12 To avoid conflict of interest, an IRB member shall not participate in the IRB’s review of any project in which the member is involved as a researcher or subject.
5.26.10 The Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) shall review and approve the use of vertebrate animals in all research projects, educational or outreach activities under the jurisdiction or control of the University. The procurement, care, and use of animals shall be in accordance with the regulations and terms of the federal Animal Welfare Act as well as any other applicable federal, state and local law.

passages.heading: Committees falling under Presidential jurisdiction
passages.text: 5.26.11 The IACUC shall be comprised of at least five members appointed by the President including the University of Rhode Island Attending Veterinarian, a scientist experienced in laboratory animal research, a non-scientist and an individual who has no other affiliation with the University besides membership in the IACUC. The Vice President for Research and Economic Development or the Vice President’s designee shall serve ex officio, as a non-voting member. An effort will be made to appoint members to the IACUC that will have the qualifications of experience and expertise needed to provide guidance and counsel to animal researchers.

passages.heading: Committees falling under Presidential jurisdiction
passages.text: 5.27.10 The Diving Control Board (DCB) has authority over all scientific diving operations at the University of Rhode Island. The DCB sets rules and regulations in compliance with the American Academy of Underwater Sciences standards and in conformance to University policy. All research diving involving equipment or personnel from the University of Rhode Island shall adhere to the rules and regulations which are included in the Research Diving Manual. The Diving Control Board also serves as a search committee for the Diving Safety Officer and provides advice and counsel to the Vice President for Research and Economic Development who makes the appointment.

The new program proposal is intended to address the changes in Rhode Island certification regulations, which will require significant changes (over 25%) to the requirements for our current BA in Secondary Education with a specialization in World Languages, effectively transforming it into a BA in World Language Education-All Grades.
In the proposed new program, students will take a variety of existing EDC courses in Elementary Education, Early Childhood Education, Secondary Education, and Teaching English as a Second Language / Bilingual Education concentrations so that, upon graduation, they will be more versatile and highly employable educators who are better prepared to teach effectively in a wider variety of educational settings.
The new program will educate our students to become reflective teachers committed to global citizenship, social justice, and multicultural education.

passages.heading: IFSR #2023-2024-1 | Page 5
passages.text:
Our program of study, based on current research and best practices, has been carefully crafted to provide our teacher candidates with ample opportunities to learn about different professional contexts and acquire knowledge about learning theory (social, emotional, and academic), and how to address the individualized needs of diverse learners.
Through a variety of hands-on teaching experiences at PK-12 academic settings our candidates will have the opportunity to apply what they learn in URI courses in culturally responsive practices but also to learn to work with and from practicing teachers.
The standard program of study that our candidates will follow will allow them to graduate from URI with a double major in Education and in a Foreign Language.1 Students will develop their teaching skills and acquire knowledge through coursework that focuses on teaching and learning at different developmental levels, and on cutting-edge second language acquisition theories.
Our program will help teacher candidates develop the necessary confidence and experience to effectively engage with a diverse group of students in a variety of educational settings.

passages.heading: IFSR #2023-2024-1 | Page 5
passages.text:
Upon completion of our program and after successfully completing the licensure tests, our well- prepared graduates will be ready to apply for the Rhode Island World Language teacher certification in grades K-12.

Since its inception, the World Language Education Program has been one of these tracks (the other tracks are English, History/Social Studies, Mathematics, and Science).
Upon graduation, students in the Secondary Education Program obtain certification to teach at the High School level (grades 7-12).

Due to these changes, graduates from our current Secondary Education – World Language program are now certified to teach in Rhode Island at all levels of elementary, middle, and secondary education (grades PK-12).

To the best of my knowledge there are four other higher ed institutions in RI that offer World Language Education programs: Salve Regina, Rhode Island College, Providence College and Roger Williams University.
None of these programs is new: such programs have been in place for at least 10 years.
In all those cases, the original World Language programs were part of the Secondary Education programs, just one of the multiple tracks that students could take.
Two of those institutions have already taken steps to adapt to the new RIDE certification reality.
Recently, in both Salve Regina and RIC the World Language Program has become independent.
According to the information listed on their websites, the World Language Education program is still a track of the Secondary Education Program in the cases of both Providence College (<https://academics.providence.edu/secondary-education/>) and Roger Williams University (<https://www.rwu.edu/undergraduate/academics/programs/secondary-education>).

The RIDE certification requirements for World Language teachers are:4 ● Bachelor’s degree from a regionally accredited institution ● Completion of an approved program or Credential Review Consortium Institution (CRCI) credential review plan for the preparation of All Grades World Language Teachers in a specific language ● Completion of a minimum of 12 weeks of student teaching in this area and a minimum of 60 hours field experience prior to student teaching ● Demonstration of meeting the pedagogical competencies of the Rhode Island Professional Teaching Standards (RIPTS) ● Demonstration of meeting the content competencies as prescribed by the American Council for the Teaching of Foreign Languages (ACTFL) Other requirements: ● Meet all Rhode Island pedagogy and subject matter testing requirements for this certificate area 4 See: <https://www.ride.ri.gov/Portals/0/Uploads/Documents/Teachers-and-Administrators-Excellent- Educators/Educator-Certification/Cert-Requirements/tbd_AG-World%20Languages-Req.pdf?ver=2015-01-22- 123036-823>.
The RIDE has stated that taking the PRAXIS II exam will not be a certification requirement in the near future.

passages.heading: IFSR #2023-2024-1 | Page 15

12 Assessment Requirements: All applicants must meet the following Rhode Island assessment requirements: ● Applicants must achieve a passing score of 160 on the Praxis II Principals of Learning and Teaching – Grades K-6 Test (5622) OR a passing score of 157 on the Praxis II Principals of Learning and Teaching – Grades 7-12 test (5624) AND a passing score of 162 on the French World Language Test (5174), a passing score of 163 on the German World Language Test (5183), a passing score of 161 on the Latin Test (5601), a passing score of 168 on the Spanish World Language Test (5195), or a passing score of Advanced Low on all other world languages – Oral Proficiency Interview. ● Applicants prepared in a program where the language of instruction was not English must achieve a passing core of 64 on the Versant Pro Speaking and Writing English assessments.

JCAP Pre-Proposal Form Revised 2021 Joint Committee on Academic Planning Pre-Proposal for New Programs Part I: Title and affiliation(s) of proposed program: Program Title: World Language Education Program Degree Type: B.A.
Proposer(s): Iñaki Pérez Ibáñez, Assistant Professor in Spanish and Teacher Education Department(s): School of Education College(s): College of Education and Professional Studies Part II.
Briefly provide the following information (not to exceed two pages): The School of Education currently offers a Bachelor of Arts degree in Secondary Education, with multiple tracks reflecting various specializations.
Since its inception, the World Language Education Program has been one of these tracks (the other tracks are English, History/Social Studies, Mathematics, and Science).
Upon graduation, students in the Secondary Education Program obtain certification to teach at the High School level (grades 7-12).

passages.heading: IFSR #2023-2024-1 | Page 27
passages.text:
Upon the completion of an additional course and a teach ing practicum at a Middle School, students in this existing program also have the option to obtain a Middle School extension, a credential that allows them to teach in grades 5-8 in any Rhode Island elementary, middle, or junior high school.
Recently the Rhode Island Department of Education changed the World Language teacher certification system.
Due to these changes, graduates from our current Secondary Education – World Language program are now certified to teach in Rhode Island at all levels of elementary, middle, and secondary education (grades PK-12).
The new program proposal is intended address the changes in Rhode Island certification regulations, which will require significant changes (over 25%) to the requirements for our current BA in Secondary Education with a specialization in World Languages, effectively transforming it into a BA in World Language Education -All Grades.

passages.heading: IFSR #2023-2024-1 | Page 27
passages.text:
In the proposed new program, students will take a variety of existing EDC courses in Elementary Education, Early Childhood Education, Secondary Education, and Teaching English as a Second Language / Bilingual Education concentrations so that, upon graduation, they will be more versatile and highly employable educators who are better prepared to teach effectively in a wider variety of educational settings.
The financial cost to the university of this new program will be zero, as our students will be required to take existing courses that are regularly offered in the School o f Education.
The development of new courses will not be necessary to implement the proposed overhaul of the program.
The new program will not require the hiring of any new faculty (neither full time nor adjunct faculty).

passages.heading: IFSR #2023-2024-1 | Page 28
passages.text:
JCAP Pre-Proposal Form Revised 2021 One of the purposes of the new program is to attract, retain, and graduate more teachers from multicultural, multilingual, historically marginalized, and under-represented groups in the education profession.
The inclusion of coursework in Bilingual Education and Teaching English as a Second Language aims to attract and harness the unique talents and lived experiences of students from our important local and regional multilingual communities.
In addition to this, the RI Department of Education, through the work of the Rhode Island Council on Elementary and Secondary Education, is currently in the process of changing the state’s high school graduation requirements.
Among the proposed changes to the system, students will be required to take a minimum of two years of study of the same language in order to successfully graduate from high school.
This change has the potential to strengthen the general pipeline of candidates for our proposed World Langua ge Education-All Grades program.

passages.heading: IFSR #2023-2024-1 | Page 28
passages.text:
Finally, given both the regional and national shortage of world language educators, as evidenced by the 100% employment rates of graduates from our existing program and the high percentage of new language teachers who are being hired through an emergency certification process, the demand for well-qualified K-12 world language educators is high and the urgent need for this program is clear.

passages.heading: Course Approval Process | Page 1
passages.text:
The Course/Program Approval Process at URI 1.
Initial Submission on Kuali.
Faculty members submit course (for both new and modified classes) and program proposals within Kuali Curriculum Management.
Kuali provides workflow at URI for curricular changes and is in the university’s Microsoft 365 suite; further information and login link can be found here: https://web.uri.edu/facsen/kuali/.
A library impact statement will be generated for new courses within one week of submission to Kuali.
Crosslisted classes, courses/programs that might overlap with existing offerings, and classes/programs assuming prerequisites from other departments need to provide documentation regarding approval from those other relevant academic units.
New programs need to allow two weeks for a Budget Impact Statement to be completed by the Budget Office.
Note: new programs must also complete the New Program Assessment Plan (https://web.uri.edu/atl/assessment/newprograms/) and submit it to the Assessment Team at assess@uri.edu. 2.
Approval Requirements.

passages.heading: Course Approval Process | Page 1
passages.text:
Once a faculty member submits a new course proposal, either the department’s curriculum committee or the department chair/program head must approve it based on the governance structure of the department.
This approval requires a vote of the faculty of the originating department.
Courses not originating within a specific department or college must be approved by the governing committee responsible for administering the program.
As part of their approval, the departmental curriculum committee or chairs/program heads must submit an official statement confirming departmental approval via faculty vote for the proposal. 3.
College-level Review.
After approval by the department, the proposal is reviewed for approval by the college curriculum committee(s), and then approved by the college dean or delegate.
Colleges assess course proposals for issues such as staffing, intra-college departmental and interdepartmental overlap, and collegewide programmatic needs and requirements. 4.
Senate Committee Review.
After college-level approval, proposals go to the Faculty Senate Specialist who formats and prepares them for the following month’s curriculum committee meetings.

passages.heading: Course Approval Process | Page 1
passages.text:
Course/program proposals are directed to the appropriate Senate Committee(s): undergraduate General Education courses to the General Education Committee (GEC); all other undergraduate courses/programs to the Curriculum and Standards Committee (CASC); graduate courses/programs to the Graduate Council (GC).
These committees examine proposals with an eye to legibility and benefit to students. 5.
Full Senate Review.
The GEC, CASC, and the GC each make monthly reports to the entire Faculty Senate.
During these reports, they bring forward all new course/program proposals approved at the committee-level for a vote by the entire Senate.
Courses approved by this vote are then added to a bill for signature by the Faculty Senate President.
The President/Provost then provides final signature approval.
Concerns covered at this level typically include unexpected impacts on other programs or lack of resources.
Please note: 400 level courses proposed for graduate credit need to be approved by both the undergraduate and graduate committees within the department and college; at the Faculty Senate level, these proposals go before both the GC and CASC.

passages.heading: Course Approval Process | Page 1
passages.text:
Please also note: courses are not approved for an immediate change; after completion of the approval process, they only become active in the term and year indicated in the proposal.
A complete proposal approved by each of the necessary levels might move through the process in 2-3 months.
Faculty submitting course proposals should carefully consult the meeting schedules for their college-level curriculum committee(s); the GEC, CASC, and GC; and the Faculty Senate itself.
They should also watch for notifications from Kuali if one of these bodies needs more information.

Informational Report on Changes to the University Manual, Appendix F Submitted on behalf of President Parlange by John Rooney, Assistant Director, University College/ Transfer Resource Center, and Dean Libutti, Associate Vice President for Enrollment and Student Success Date: March 28, 2023 RATIONALE: The University Manual currently includes a copy of the 2017 Office of the Postsecondary Commissioner's policy for A,ticulation and Transfer Between Public Institutions of Higher Education in Rhode Island.
This policy does not address the University of Rhode Island's shift to governance under the University of Rhode Island Board of Trustees.
With this governance change, the University of Rhode Island must update portions of the policy to align with our current transfer policies and practices.
These updates do not change the University's specific commitment to articulation and transfer but rather simply further clarify our policies and practices for faculty, students, staff, and families.
The language below will replace the current language of Appendix Fi n its entirety.
