passages.text: General Education Advisory Committee Final Report 2024-2025-1 Committee Membership The committee’s roster for the 2024-2025 school year was: ● Joëlle Rollo-Koster, A&S Chair ● Sen. Jay Fogleman (2027), COE ● Rachel DiCioccio, OIGE ● Elaine Finan, ATL ● Christian Gonzales, A&S ● Shane Tutwiler, COE ● Amanda Missimer, CHS ● Prasasti Pandit, A&S ● Daniel Carpenter, A&S ● Robert Widel, A&S Purpose of Committee In May of 2024, the Faculty Senate approved a proposal to create a Special General Education Advisory Committee (GEAC) to assist the General Education Committee (GEC) in fulfilling its duties related to the evaluation of the General Education Program. The GEAC was to receive specific guidance from the GEC, and present its recommendation regarding the need for a similar committee beyond the 2024-2025 year. Executive Summary The GEAC was formed in response to a proposal in the Faculty Senate for a special committee to assist the GEC in evaluating the General Education program (GEP). The committee reviewed three sets of General Education Learning Outcomes Assessment Data Runs for the 2021, 2022, 2023 assessment efforts and contributed to the corresponding Outcomes Assessment Reports. The committee met monthly to discuss these results and recommendations. The committee’s findings point to encouraging signs of student competency in most areas, but also highlight critical challenges, particularly in low faculty participation and alignment of assessment practices. The GEAC strongly affirms that sustained improvement in GEP will hinge on a more engaged and better-supported faculty, clearer alignment between assignments and assessment tools, and a commitment to equity in the evaluation process. 1

passages.heading: Special Advisory Committee Final Report | Page 2
passages.text:
Based on its work, the GEAC recommends that a standing advisory body similar to this committee be continued beyond the 2024–2025 academic year to ensure ongoing reflection, responsiveness, and renewal of the GEP.
Constitute a Committee of General Education Stakeholders The GEAC was formed in August 2024 for the purpose of reviewing General Education Outcome Data and making recommendations for enhancing the GEP.
The committee was convened by the GEC Chair, Jay Fogleman.
Invited committee members included a variety of GE stakeholders, a representative of the ATL Assessment Office, the Director of the Office of Innovation in General Education, an assessment methodologist, as well as several faculty recognized as effective and experienced General Education instructors.
The GEAC met monthly in the fall to review and discuss existing outcomes evaluation data.
Joëlle Rollo-Koster, A&S, was appointed as committee Chair by the committee in the first meeting.
The process of convening and charging the GEAC was presented to the FSEC in mid September of 2024.

passages.heading: Special Advisory Committee Final Report | Page 2
passages.text:
Review Existing General Education Outcome Evaluation Data and Make Recommendations The committee summarized the data and made recommendations for program improvement.
Committee members were charged with reviewing outcome data provided by the Outcomes Office and providing recommendations.
Committee feedback was collected and organized around broad areas of improvement.
The committee chair used this feedback and meeting discussions to complete the results and recommendation sections on the outcomes reports for the four of the six outcomes based on committee discussions and feedback (2021, 2022).
The GEC chair completed similar work for the last two outcomes for the 2023 report.
The GEC chair consolidated the GEAC feedback and kept the GEC informed of the progress of the GEAC and integrated their concerns into GEAC discussions.
Outcomes Assessment Results Year (Spring) Outcomes Examined Number of Artifacts Collected Number of Artifacts Scored Faculty Participation (Act/Poss) * 100 Overall Average Competency Notes 2021 B2 - Communicate Effectively 661 36 22/71 31% 1.63/3 (Approaching) 2021 B4 - Information Literacy 1454 139 56/179 31% 1.92/3 (Approaching) 2

passages.heading: Special Advisory Committee Final Report | Page 3
passages.text:
2022 B1 - Write Effectively 639 60 39/169 23% 2.49/3 (Competent) 2022 C1 - Civic Knowledge and Responsibility 827 84 59/108 54% 2.10 (competent) 2023 B3 - Math, Stat, Comp Literacy 451 144 32/85 38% 2.43 (competent) 2023 C3 - Diversity and Inclusion 649 52 14/89 16% 2.27 (competent) Key Findings ● Faculty participation rates for all of the outcome assessments were low, ranging from 16% to 51%.
Despite the low response rate, results from samples for all outcome assessments were deemed generalizable. ● Generally, students are competent with four of the outcomes, approaching competency on the remaining two outcomes. ● A significant number of submitted student artifacts were not accessible, mainly due to not being de-identifiable.
Recommendations The GEAC reviewed evaluation data for six of the General Education outcomes and has identified several key areas to enhance faculty participation in and assessment of the General Education program.
To increase faculty participation in the evaluation process, the committee emphasizes the need for structured support systems, regular professional development, and alignment of assignments with rubrics.

passages.heading: Special Advisory Committee Final Report | Page 3
passages.text:
Additionally, it highlights the importance of incentivizing faculty through recognition in tenure and promotion processes.
The committee also recommends periodic review of outcomes and targeted training for all faculty involved in General Education courses.
Evaluation processes should be refined to ensure assessments prioritize questions that can inform program improvement, document student growth over time, and include student voice in the process to better understand how students value their general education.
These recommendations aim to foster a more engaged and committed faculty, improve the quality of General Education courses, and ensure meaningful and equitable assessment practices.
Increase Faculty Awareness, Engagement and Participation ● Implement resources to support faculty involvement in the General Education program. 3

passages.heading: Special Advisory Committee Final Report | Page 4
passages.text:
● Strengthen faculty identity and engagement through regular training and professional development. ● Recognize participation in the assessment process in tenure and promotion processes. ● Support faculty understanding and buy-in of outcomes targeted for assessment: ● Communicate early with instructors of outcomes to be evaluated to determine potential assessments. ● Conduct virtual open forums to align rubrics and assignments for assessed outcomes. ● Review and align assignment templates with rubrics to facilitate faculty participation.
Refine Assessment Practices: ● Use the initial round of assessments as a baseline and support faculty in developing a plan to prioritize, support, and measure improvements in coming years. ● Periodically review outcomes, rubrics, and assessment tools for potential improvements. ● Ensure sufficient assessment of marginalized students to determine their standing relative to outcomes. ● Focus on realistic expectations of student competency and lifelong learning.

passages.heading: Special Advisory Committee Final Report | Page 4
passages.text:
Conclusion and Plans for 2025-2026 The General Education Advisory Committee (GEAC) has fulfilled its charge for the 2024–2025 academic year by providing a detailed review of outcome evaluation data and offering concrete recommendations to strengthen the assessment and delivery of General Education.
The committee’s findings point to encouraging signs of student competency in most areas, but also highlight critical challenges, particularly in faculty participation and alignment of assessment practices.
Faculty needs to be more engaged.
On the other hand, in this current climate it is difficult considering that general education is taking a hit at most institutions.
The GEAC strongly affirms that sustained improvement in the GEP will hinge on a more engaged and better-supported faculty, clearer alignment between assignments and assessment tools, and a commitment to equity in the evaluation process.
Closer collaboration between the GEC and the Office of Innovation in General Education would strengthen the faculty’s voice and ownership in the development of the GEP over time.

passages.heading: Special Advisory Committee Final Report | Page 4
passages.text:
Based on its work, the GEAC recommends that a standing advisory body of this nature be continued beyond the 2024–2025 academic year.
Such a committee can serve as a vital bridge between faculty, administration, and the GEC, ensuring ongoing reflection, responsiveness, and renewal of the GEP. 4

Faculty Senate Executive Committee Report #2024-2025-13 Introduction: April 10, 2025 Faculty Senate Meeting Amends the Faculty Senate By-Laws to Restructure The Center Review Subcommittee RATIONALE: The Faculty Senate Executive Committee, in conjunction with the existing Center Review Subcommittee, and representatives from the Office of the Provost, have been working all year to update the University’s definitions and classification system for all center and institute (C/I) types.
This comprehensive update initiative has clarified and expanded requirements around budgeting, reporting, application and renewal for all C/I’s.
This major change is expected to increase the workload of the Center Review Subcommittee and the working group agreed that the subcommittee should thus become a full, permanent standing committee as part of this shift.
A By-laws amendment to Section 4 of Appendix C is therefore proposed.
According to Section 12.1 of the By-Laws, amendments require two meetings and a two-thirds majority vote of senators present to pass.

passages.heading: Initial Report Presentation, September, 2023 | Page 2
passages.text: The CTI’s Goals and Objectives for AY 23-24: Overall Goal: Continue collaboration with Information Technology Services and review and make policy recommendations regarding the implications on academic and research planning, standards, services, physical facilities, and allocation of resources on all matters pertaining to information technology, infrastructure, computing, communications, and networking. Primary objectives for AY 23-24: • Ensure protection of academic freedom in all matters related to IT. • Advocate for all faculty’s teaching and research needs to be met in all matters related to IT.

passages.heading: Initial Report Presentation, September, 2023 | Page 3
passages.text: Challenges and Issues the CTI hopes to address during AY 23-24: • URI Secure wifi difficulties from Linux (affecting students and faculty) • Proofpoint blocking emails from AAUP (faculty union); gets into larger issue of academic freedom and URL rewriting (the latter affects the readability of URLs in recipient’s inboxes, which presents issues for instruction) • eCampus replacement (tentatively Workday for the HR, financial, and administrative components, particularly the need for demos, faculty input); we don't want a repeat of Brightspace • Although we may have no input into the Workday transition for HR, Financials, etc., we may have influence on the student module

passages.heading: Initial Report Presentation, September, 2023 | Page 4
passages.text: Challenges and Issues the CTI hopes to address during AY 23-24 (continued): • Draft a letter to CIO about IT security mandates: specifically the user policy that may have conflicts with how University policies are enacted - may overlap with CBUM. At some institutions, one can opt out of the standard configuration. At others, this is not an option: • How does this affect academic freedom? • Letter would need to strike the right balance • National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has the draft of a cybersecurity policy available ( NSPM 33) and, if implemented, may affect University faculty and students. Apparently, this has not been shared with the faculty. Understanding how it will be implemented and affect research is essential.

passages.heading: Initial Report Presentation, September, 2023 | Page 5
passages.text: Challenges and Issues the CTI hopes to address during AY 23-24 (continued): • How does ITS’s budget allow them to handle unforeseen expenditures that may arise mid-year, such as the need to respond to a critical systems vulnerability? • How does the university (e.g. facilities, police, etc.) handle both faculty and teaching staff (TAs) getting access to labs or classrooms as needed; at the same time, how are security concerns (such as being able to lock a classroom from the inside in the case of a lockdown) addressed?

passages.text: PROPOSALS SUBMITTED AND AWARDS Summary of 2026 proposals Type of proposal # Submissions # Awards # Assistant Professor awardees # New awardees Career Enhancement 10 7 2 5 Proposal development 26 7 5 5 Collaborative proposal development 15 4 3 3 Total 51 18 10 13 The total number of proposals submitted (51) was significantly higher than the past three years: 2024-5 (35), 2023-4 (41), 2022-3 (31). The number of awards made (18) was higher than previous years last years (14 each in the past two years). The success rate for both proposal development and collaborative proposal development was about 27% and that for career enhancement was about 70%. Out of the 18 awardees this year, 10 were assistant professors and 13 were new awardees. These awards continue to serve as a mechanism for new PIs to develop extramural proposals. Summary of funding Type of proposal $ Requested $ Awarded Career Enhancement $90,282 $63,098 Proposal development $746,553 $199,450 Collaborative proposal development $683,377 $178,539 Total $1,520,212 $441,087 The VPR was able to invest $441,087 this year, almost doubled the amount from last year ($226,610). COMMITTEE REVIEW PROCESS The committee were able to continue the practice established by the 2022-3 committee of seeking three reviews per proposal for the Career Enhancement proposals. However, due to the significant increase of proposals in Proposal Development and Collaborative Proposal

passages.heading: Competititve Grants Subcommittee Annual Report | Page 4
passages.text:
Development, the committee must reduce to two reviews per proposal for these two categories.
This year’s committee only has 4 members, much smaller than previous years (7 members in 2024-5 and 10 members in 2023-4).
For that reason, the committee relied on 6 other members of the Committee for Research and Creative Activities as well as 25 previous awardees to contribute reviews.
Each committee member (10 total) reviewed 5-6 proposals, and each external reviewer reviewed 2-3 proposals.
Proposals were assigned so that at least one committee member reviewed each proposal.
The committee attempted to assign knowledgeable reviewers to each proposal while avoiding conflicts of interest.
The nature of the competition, however, means that most proposals were reviewed by faculty outside their discipline.
The committee created rankings of the proposals in each funding category based on the reviewer scores and comments, but the committee discussed the merits of each proposal, focusing particularly on proposals with variable scores and on proposals close to the funding threshold.
In situations where ratings were very similar, the committee gave preference to junior faculty.

passages.heading: Competititve Grants Subcommittee Annual Report | Page 4
passages.text:
The committee created a written summary of the deliberation for each proposal in the Career Enhancement category and most proposals in the Collaborative Proposal Development category.
We acknowledge that reviewers are likely to differ in the range of scores assigned and checked the possibility that a reviewer might give consistently “high” or “low” scores respectively.
Because the number of proposals reviewed per reviewer is low, our ability to correct for reviewer “leniency” was limited.
RECOMMENDATIONS FOR 2027 Be prepared to handle more proposals The number of proposals increased substantially in both Proposal Development and Collaborative Proposal Development, while remaining relatively stable in Career Enhancement.
This growth has made it challenging for the subcommittee to manage the workload and secure enough qualified reviewers.
We anticipate that proposal volume will remain at this level or continue to rise next year.
To address this, we may need to (1) expand the size of the committee and (2) seek additional review support from colleagues who are not previous awardees.

passages.heading: Competititve Grants Subcommittee Annual Report | Page 4
passages.text:
Emphasize the expectations in more detail The RFP states that this is a campus-wide competition and that proposals will be reviewed by non-experts.
While most PIs appeared to understand and appreciate this, some submissions seemed to be revised versions of proposals originally prepared for specific agencies and therefore included a level of technical detail that may not be accessible to a generalist audience.
Regarding plans for future external submissions, reviewers expected applicants to identify not only a specific target agency or program but also a realistic timeline.
Several proposals did not include a timeline and were consequently scored lower.
Placing additional emphasis on this requirement in future RFPs would help applicants avoid unnecessary point deductions.

passages.heading: Competititve Grants Subcommittee Annual Report | Page 5
passages.text: Communicate expectations from reviewers Reviewers may benefit from more explicit guidance on both the criteria and process for evaluating proposals. For example, using prior external funding as an example some reviewers assigned lower scores to applicants with extensive previous awards, while others scored them more favorably. Similarly, for the Career Enhancement category, some reviewers assumed that awards are primarily intended for assistant professors, which is not the case. Providing more detailed and standardized review criteria would help improve consistency across evaluations. Peer reviewers The committee sought the assistance of other members of the CRCA committee and previous awardees to provide proposal reviews. The success of the program is contingent on their willingness to provide thorough and thoughtful reviews. passages.heading: Faculty Senate Executive Committee
passages.text:
Through RI General Law §16-32-10, academic responsibility at URI is delegated to the President and the Faculty Senate. The Faculty Senate Executive Committee (FSEC) serves as the steering committee of the Senate. It represents the Senate in meetings with other University bodies and with the Provost, the President, and the URI Board of Trustees. Meetings of the FSEC are held weekly to coordinate the Senate’s business and its committees and address concerns within its jurisdiction.
For the description of the powers and duties of the Executive Committee, please see University Manual Appendix C: By-laws of the Faculty Senate, Section 4.1 – 4.9.

REPORT OF THE PRESIDENT a.
Report: Responding to the question previously raised, President Parlange explained his generaldesire to free up faculty time for greater research endeavors.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 2

The President offered a brief slide presentation that highlighted several recent events aroundcampus and the community.
He then addressed a Senate-approved bill from the Novembermeeting that he has opted not to sign.
The rationale was related to his foregoing comments as henoted that the university has long been and continues to be in something of a budgetarypredicament.
While the faculty control the curriculum, the financial metrics of the curriculum areultimately his responsibility.
Over time, he hopes to expand the community’s understanding of thebudget choices that are continuously being made and empower department heads and deans toundertake more robust budgetary assessments of curricular proposals before they reach theFaculty Senate.
In the case of the specific unsigned proposal, which called for a new track withinthe Mathematics Ph.D., the President’s understanding is that the program is not large and the newtracks appear to require the teaching of additional classes, the enrollments for which arereasonably expected to be very small.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 2

It was speculated that the full details and rationale may not have come through in thewritten proposal, in which case the current setting is likely not the place to debate its merits.

Administrative Report January 2017, Administrative Report February 2021 1.20.11 Composition of the Board Trustees and Quorum Requirements.
The Board of Trustees shall consist of seventeen (17) voting members and four (4) non-voting ex officio members, including one (1) URI faculty member and one (1) URI student to be appointed by the President, and the chair of the Rhode Island Board of Education and the chair of the Rhode Island Council on Postsecondary Education.
The members shall be appointed in accordance with RIGL Section 16-32-2.2, which specifies that the governor will appoint the members with the advice and consent of the senate, and with due consideration to recommendations from the President of the University.

passages.heading: Informational Report, March, 2024 | Page 2
passages.text:
At least three (3) of the members appointed by the governor shall be residents of the state of Rhode Island, at least one (1) of those members shall be selected from a list of names of at least five (5) individuals submitted by the speaker of the house of representatives, and at least one (1) of those members shall be selected from a list of names of at least five (5) individuals submitted by the president of the senate.
The President of the University of Rhode Island will appoint one (1) faculty member and one (1) student member who shall be a full-time student in good standing at the University, and who shall both serve in non-voting, ex officio capacity for a single two (2) year term.
Six (6) of the members initially appointed pursuant to RIGL Section 16-32-2.2 shall serve terms of three (3) years; seven (7) members initially appointed pursuant to this section shall serve terms of two (2) years, including the member appointed from the list submitted by the speaker of the house of representatives and the member appointed from the list submitted by the president of the senate; and four (4) members initially appointed pursuant to this section shall serve terms of one (1) year.

passages.heading: Informational Report, March, 2024 | Page 2
passages.text:
After the initial terms of appointment have expired, the governor shall appoint nine (9) members with the advice and consent of the senate to serve as members of the board with two (2) members appointed for a term of three (3) years; with two (2) members appointed for a term of two (2) years, including the member appointed from the list submitted by the speaker of the house of representatives and the member appointed from the list submitted by the president of the senate; and with two (2) members appointed for a term of one (1) year and shall be eligible to be reappointed for a term of two (2) years.
The remaining eight (8) voting members shall be self-perpetuating members appointed by the Board pursuant to rules adopted by the Board regarding the nomination and appointment of members and shall serve terms as defined by the Board pursuant to the adopted rules and shall be eligible for reappointment.
In making the appointments of self-perpetuating members, the

passages.heading: Informational Report, March, 2024 | Page 3
passages.text:
Board shall give due consideration to recommendations from the President of the University.
A quorum shall consist of thirteen (13) voting members of the Board, but less than a quorum may adjourn any meetings.
A majority vote of those present and voting shall be required for action.
A majority of the members of the Board shall elect the chair of the Board in accordance with RIGL Section 16-32-2.2(c) from among the voting members of the Board.
In addition, the members of the Board shall elect a vice chair.
The terms of office shall be three years or until a duly appointed successor is elected.
Administrative Report January 2017, Administrative Report February 2021 1.20.12 Chief Responsibilities of the Board of Trustees.
The Board of Trustees (“Board”) is established by act of the Rhode Island General Assembly as the exclusive fiduciary authority for the University of Rhode Island (“University” or “URI”).
In that capacity, the Board is legally entrusted with the institution’s care and has the critical responsibility for protecting the integrity of the institution’s mission as Rhode Island’s premier institution of higher education and overseeing compliance with all provisions of the law.

passages.heading: Informational Report, March, 2024 | Page 3
passages.text: To meet its statutory mandate as the ultimate governing authority for the University of Rhode Island, the Board of Trustees performs a number of critical functions, including but not limited to: ● Appointment of trustees, consistent with the standards and limitations set forth in the enabling statute; ● Appointment and evaluation of the President of the University; ● Review and approval of the Academic Strategic Plan and the three-year funding plan for the University, which is to be developed and submitted to the Board by the President; ● Upon receipt of the recommendations of the President and appropriate faculty bodies, approval of the awarding of degrees (including honorary degrees, diplomas, certificates and honors to be conferred by the President); ● Approval of recommendations made by the President regarding the awarding of tenure and promotion to qualified members of the University faculty; ● Review of the University’s performance under the institution’s Academic Strategic Plan developed and reported by the President and university community; ● Stewardship of University physical, financial, and human resources consistent with the provisions of all applicable statutes and regulations and policies of the Board of Trustees; ● Promoting and enforcing integrity and effectiveness of all aspects of the University’s budgeting and financial management, including changes in tuition and fees, submission and approval of the University’s annual budget and three-year financial projections;

passages.heading: Informational Report, March, 2024 | Page 4
passages.text:
● Approve the creation or termination of new academic majors and the creation, consolidation or termination of academic departments, schools and colleges based on the recommendations of the President who shall have followed the appropriate University process.
Administrative Report January 2017, Administrative Report February 2021 The President of the University 1.30.10 Presidential Powers—Shared Governance.
In 2014, the President of the University received authority over certain items that previously needed to be submitted for approval to the super-ordinated state body (Board of Governors, Board of Regents, etc.).
The items over which the President now has authority include: “To create, and consolidate departments, divisions, programs, and courses of study within the university with the assistance of the commissioner of postsecondary education within the approved role and scope adopted by the council on postsecondary education pursuant to § 16-59-4” This authority was reaffirmed in 2019 upon passage of legislation forming the University of Rhode Island Board of Trustees (see RI General Law § 16-32-2.1).

passages.heading: Informational Report, March, 2024 | Page 4
passages.text:
The law stipulates, however, that this authority is to be exercised “consistent with shared governance practices, [and] in conformity with § 16-32-10,” which states that it “shall also be the duty of the president and a committee of the faculty, . . . to arrange courses of study conforming to all acts of Congress, and prescribe any qualifications for the admission of students and any rules of study, exercise, discipline, and government as the president and committee may deem proper.” Since 1960, the committee of the faculty mentioned in this legislation has been understood to be the URI Faculty Senate.

Chapter 1 – The University of Rhode Island Land Acknowledgement, Mission, Board of Trustees andthe President of the University #22-23-2 StatementThe University of Rhode Island 1.10.10 Statement Land Acknowledgement Statement. “The University of Rhode Island occupies the traditional stomping ground of the Narragansett Nation and the Niantic People.
We honor and respect the enduring and continuing relationship between the Indigenous peoples and this land by teaching and learning more about their history and present-day communities, and by becoming stewards of the land we, now too, inhabit.” #22-23-2 1.10.20 Background.
The University of Rhode Island, the state’s land and sea grant research institution began as the state of Rhode Island’s Agricultural Experiment Station and agricultural school chartered in 1888.
In 1892, the institution’s name was changed to the Rhode Island College of Agriculture and the Mechanic Arts.
This name was subsequently changed to Rhode Island State College in 1909.
The current name- the University of Rhode Island— was adopted in 1951 by an act of the State of Rhode Island’s General Assembly.

passages.heading: Informational Report, March, 2024 | Page 5
passages.text:
For a complete history of the University, refer to https://www.uri.edu/about/history/. 1.10.30 Mission.
The University of Rhode Island is the state’s flagship land and sea grant research institution, with a commitment to urban initiatives.
A student-centered research institution, URI actively partners with other organizations globally and locally to advance knowledge and to develop informed residents and leaders.
URI is committed to high-quality education, community engagement, and solving the world’s most important challenges.
Situated on the traditional land and territories of the Narragansett Nation and the Niantic People, URI strives to create a diverse and inclusive environment for researchers, teachers, learners, and community members. 1.10.40 Values.
The University of Rhode Island is committed to the following foundational values: ● Freedom to learn, teach, create, and conduct research with integrity in the pursuit and dissemination of new knowledge aimed at contributing to the public good. ● An inclusive, accessible, equitable and diverse community whereby we respect the rights and

passages.heading: Informational Report, March, 2024 | Page 6

dignity of all. ● Intellectual curiosity, lifelong learning, leadership, and scholarship in creating a thriving URI community in service to Rhode Island and the world. ● Sustainability and care of our environment conducive to the physical and mental health of our community. ● Self- and institutional reflection of our values in our work, scholarship and interactions, holding ourselves, each other, and the institution accountable to uphold them to a high standard.

Administrative Report January 2017, Administrative Report February 2021 1.20.12 Chief Responsibilities of the Board of Trustees.
The Board of Trustees (“Board”) is established by act of the Rhode Island General Assembly as the exclusive fiduciary authority for the University of Rhode Island (“University” or “URI”).
In that capacity, the Board is legally entrusted with the institution’s care and has the critical responsibility for protecting the integrity of the institution’s mission as Rhode Island’s premier institution of higher education and overseeing compliance with all provisions of the law.
To meet its statutory mandate as the ultimate governing authority for the University of Rhode Island, the Board of Trustees performs a number of critical functions, including but not limited to: ● Appointment of trustees, consistent with the standards and limitations set forth in the enabling statute;

passages.heading: Informational Report, March, 2024 | Page 9
passages.text: ● Appointment of the President of the University of the President and evaluation of the Presidentof the University on an annual basis; ● Review and approval of the Academic Strategic Plan and the three-year funding plan for the University, which is to be developed and submitted to the Board by the President; ● Upon receipt of the recommendations of the President and appropriate faculty bodies, approval of the awarding of degrees (including honorary degrees, diplomas, certificates and honors to be conferred by the President); ● Approval of recommendations made by the President regarding the awarding of tenure and promotion to qualified members of the University faculty; ● Review of the University’s performance under the institution’s Academic Strategic Plan developed and reported by the President and university community; ● Stewardship of University physical, financial, and human resources consistent with the provisions of all applicable statutes and regulations and policies of the Board of Trustees; ● Promoting and enforcing integrity and effectiveness of all aspects of the University’s budgeting and financial management, including changes in tuition and fees, submission and approval of the University’s annual budget and three-year financial projections; ● Approve the creation or termination of new academic majors and the creation, consolidation or termination of academic departments, schools and colleges based on the recommendations of the President who shall have followed the appropriate University process.

FSEC (Faculty Senate Executive Committee) Meeting Minutes Date: Wednesday, June 3, 2026 - Time: 12:30 pm – 2:30 pm Pastore Hall Room 224 -Remote option via ZOOM Find the Acronym Glossary here Action Items: Pres.
Preisser will reach out to potential committee chairs to determine their ability and willingness to serve.
Staff will provide live links, where available, in the project tracker to enhance usability and will adjust settings in the Advance Agendas template so FSEC members can make edits.
Sen.
Chen is asked to write up her faculty advocacy initiative by providing a brief rationale/problem statement, relevant data, and proposed action steps for in-depth discussion next time.
Staff will complete the proposed “Bill Template” so it can be shared for feedback from FSEC members.
Staff will continue to work with the FS Pres. and VP on committee assignments for all senators based on survey results.
A draft should be ready for presentation at the next meeting. 1.
Call to Order - Pres.
Preisser called the meeting to order at 12:33 pm.
VP Trimm and Senators Van Wyk, Daniels, Chen, and Meyerson were present. 2.
Minutes for approval - The following minutes were approved as edited. 2.1.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 1
passages.text:
Minutes of the 5/8/26 FSEC meeting. 2.2.
Minutes of the 5/7/26 Faculty Senate meeting. 3.
Priority Items 3.1.
Development of 2026-2027 Faculty Senate Work Plan 3.3.1 Current Project Tracker - Pres.
Preisser briefly described the 15 or so initiatives that are enumerated in the tracker.
Some are operational items to be implemented by individual committees or as part of monthly senate meetings, and others will require formal legislation.
A couple of items are carry-overs from AY 25-26 and several others are new priorities.
FSEC members volunteered or suggested names of other faculty who might be able to lead some of these initiatives.
Top legislative priorities to be introduced early in the year will include wrapping up the JCODL restructuring project, working with the CRCA to update their committee’s charge and membership, and assigning specific timely topics as part of some other standing committees’ work programs.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 1
passages.text:
On-going projects which might take a little longer to complete will include addressing college liaisons as a vehicle for enhancing college-level governance (as discussed last year), and updating the guidelines for committee creation to include a trial period as a special committee before any new standing committee is finalized.
Staff was asked to provide live links within the spreadsheet, where available, for ease of use and convenience. 3.3.2 Advance Agenda Setting - Staff had compiled a spreadsheet showing all reporting requirements for each of the nine Faculty Senate meeting , per the University Manual, and also showing additional informational reports and action items that have either become customary or have been suggested as useful going forward.
The goal is to pre-set the AY 26-27 faculty senate agendas over the summer and be able to push information to committee chairs and other presenters well in advance, so that the burden of actual month to month agenda setting and the compiling of reports, attachments and other back-up is reduced.
The “advance agendas template” will be regularly linked to FSEC meeting agendas for efficient and effective meeting management. 1

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 2
passages.text:
3.2 Committee Assignment Process—Member List 3.2.1 Standing Committees - Preference survey results are still coming in but a draft member list is starting to take shape.
Returning senators who have not expressed a desire to switch committees will remain in their AY 25-26 roles.
Only a handful of newly elected senators have not responded to the poll and staff and/or Pres.
Preisser will reach out to them individually.
The final committees list must be ratified by the senate at the September meeting. i.
Committee Chairs - Suggestions for chairpersons for each standing committee were made.
Some Chairs from AY 25 - 26 will remain in place.
Pres.
Preisser will reach out to nominated individuals to determine their willingness and ability to serve as Chairs and the list will be finalized at the next meeting. ii.
FSEC Committee Liaison Role - The role of FSEC liaison to the various standing committees was briefly discussed and the following assignments were agreed to: Sen.
Chen - ACC and Grants Subcommittee Sen.
Meyerson - CBUM and BAC Sen.
Daniels - CTI and CRCA Sen.
Van Wyk - SCLC and TAAC VP Trimm - CASC and GEC Pres.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 2
passages.text:
Preisser - CIRC 3.2.2 Joint Committees and other Appointments (AEC, Parliamentarian, etc.) - Joint Committee memberships will be discussed in detail once all standing committee appointments have been made.
It was noted that approved legislation at the end of AY 25-26 resulted in creation of a new joint committee (The Ombuds Committee) which will need to be “stood up” jointly by the FSEC and university administrators and initial appointments will need to be made. 4.
Continued Items 4.1.
Faculty Concerns submitted through the FS Webpage - No new concerns via the form, but a faculty concern had been posed to the FS President and VP.
It concerned the ability of teaching professors to pursue research.
Specifically, a teaching professor was denied a stipend to attend a research proposal workshop and subsequently suggested that, while teaching professors are not required by contract to conduct research if they are interested in doing so on their own, it would seem to be in the interest of the University to encourage it.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 2
passages.text:
The matter was discussed at some length and a variety of considerations and variables were deliberated, including the fact that stipends are in short supply and priority consideration should probably go to those faculty members who are contractually obligated to research and publish.
The FS President has looped the VP RED into the discussion and will continue to discuss the appropriateness of the policy with that office. 5.
Updates/Ongoing Items 5.1.
Updates i.
Meetings with Administrators, Committees, or Others - No new meetings were reported but there are meetings of both the Administrative Policy Committee and the Stewardship Council next week and Pres.
Preisser is resuming regular meetings with Vice Provost Adams. 2

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 3
passages.text:
6.
Report of the Coordinator - Staff noted that current priorities include archiving the University Manual for AY 25-26, sorting results of the Committee Preference Survey so that senators can be appropriately placed on committees, and updating the FS webpage to reflect all approved legislation, etc.
Staff is also hoping to roll out a Proposed Legislation Form that any person or committee could use to draft a bill.
It will include sections for: rationale, input from relevant offices and committees, and draft language for the Manual or other documents.
A draft is in progress and it will be ready for the start of the legislative year.
Staff also suggested that, as the FSEC considers rolling out a new College Liaisons role, it might be useful to conduct a forum early in the fall semester to share information with faculty about the need, disparate practices across colleges, and benefits of improved two-way communications between faculty and the senate via the respective colleges.
FSEC will consider this further over the summer. 7.
New Business – Open for additional items not listed in the agenda. 7.1.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 3
passages.text:
Copyright Policy - VP Trimm noted he had shared the current draft with all FSEC members and had circled back with past President Williams about the status of the document.
The policy is designed as “opt-in” guidance and FS leadership as well as administrators believe the current document should be ready for presentation to the faculty senate in September. 8.
Closing Remarks – Recap of decisions made, action items, and plans for the next meeting.
Sen.
Chen explained that she ran for an FSEC seat because she sought an opportunity to effectively advocate for Associate Professors.
She has already met with the President, Provost and VIce Provost about the challenges facing these faculty members and hopes the senate will give her an additional platform to raise awareness.
She explained that the University’s lack of leadership and communications training, internal networking opportunities and absence of effective mentorship programs seems to be harming Assoc.
Professors’ further advancement.
She has data that bears this out and also has qualitative feedback from female full professors about the unique challenges faced by female faculty members.
Sen.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 3
passages.text:
Chen added that some mitigation measures are low or now cost and would be easy to implement and she is hopeful that they will gain traction among faculty.
Sen.
Chen was asked to write up a brief explanation of her proposed initiative and the problems it seeks to address so that it can be discussed in detail at the next FSEC meeting.
In other announcements, Pres.
Preisser encouraged FSEC members to consider the proposal to restructure the standing curriculum committees as means to more evenly distribute workload as to ensure expertise in the area of program development and review is brought to bear.
The hope is that during AY 26-27, the CASC and GEC will be reformed as two committees: one focused on courses and one focused on programs.
The new “program committee” would be a joint committee so that it might effectively include non-faculty members who have relevant experience.
VP Trimm will be working with staff and the Summer Curriculum Chair to advance this initiative over the summer.
Thoughts and input on logistics, possible language, etc., are welcome. 9.
Adjournment - The meeting adjourned at 2:30 pm. 3

FSEC (Faculty Senate Executive Committee) Meeting Minutes Date: Monday, August 17, 2026 - Time: 1:00 pm – 3:00 pm Pastore Hall Room 224 - Remote option via ZOOM Find the Acronym Glossary here Action Items: The FS President, VP, and staff will refine the draft legislation related to creating new standing committees from special committees for final FSEC review and assignment to other review committees at the 8/31 meeting.
Staff shall add a “problem statement or rationale” section to the proposed Bill Cover sheet.
Additional nominees to the Joint Classroom Steering Committee are requested so the committee might be maximally helpful in the effort to create a mapped classroom database.
Staff will finalize Chapter 3 updated language with affected parties and prepare an informational report for presentation at the September 17 FS meeting.
The FS President will work with the VP RED’s office to round out membership in the CRCA. 1.
Call to Order - Pres.
Preisser called the meeting to order at 1:03 pm.
VP Trimm and Senators Van Wyk, and Chen were present. 2.
Minutes for approval 2.1 Minutes of the 7/27/26 FSEC meeting.
The minutes were approved. 3.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 1
passages.text:
Presentation - Catalog Descriptions Standardization Project - Certificates Demonstration Special Guests: Indrani Mandal and Liam McKenzie from the URI Lab, along with Faculty Senate Specialist Genvieve Spitale, provided an overview of the initiative to standardize descriptions to make for a more user-friendly database, as well as improve the readability and searchability of the catalog.
The project will have the added benefit of greatly reducing the amount of staff time spent manually correcting new proposals in Kuali.
The ultimate goal is to expand the initiative to all programs and specializations, but this initial attempt has focused on Certificates as a sort of pilot project to test the programming.
A summary of the need and rationale for this project was provided.
It was noted that the need for a ‘program description template’ has been called for by Enrollment Services for a long time, as there is considerable variability in the way that descriptions are written, which has implications not only for consistency of appearance, but also for coding in Ecampus.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 1
passages.text:
The guests explained that the AI Lab will run an Auto Check (analogous to ‘spell-check’) on new draft proposals to look for missing data fields, typos, formatting problems, etc. and alert proposers of the need to make corrections before formally submitting their proposals.
The Lab generates an email with suggestions, but it will be up to the proposers to make the changes; the AI will not make corrections independently.
Details of the methodology were discussed in some detail (programming language, turn-around times, privacy and transparency considerations, as well as any academic freedom implications for faculty members).
FSEC also discussed implementation of the model and the best way to get the word out to faculty.
Faculty will need to be advised ahead of time that their proposals will initially be assessed by the AI Lab, before being processed through the normal curricular approval channels.
Ideally, a training would be run for faculty members, but at a minimum, clear instructions will need to be provided.
The hope is that the Certificates project can be finished over the next couple of weeks, at which point they will move 1

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 2
passages.text:
on to Minors.
Majors and Specializations will be more complicated (and greater in number) and will be addressed later. 4.
Priority Items 4.1.
Curricular Approvals - 4.1.1 FSEC approval of curriculum proposals on behalf of the full Senate over the summer for matters deemed urgent or essential, Per Scn. 4.3 of the By-Laws, specifically Reports SSCC-01A (Courses) and SSCC-01B (Program modifications).
The reports were deemed essential as they need to take effect fall semester, 2026.
Both reports were approved and will be presented to the full senate on 9/17 as informational items. 4.2.
Reintroduction of JCODL Legislation - Bill #25-26-FSEC-09 was tabled last May.
Discussion of proposed changes to last year’s Bill in preparation for reintroduction at the 9/17/26 senate meeting.
Pres.
Preisser offered a recap of the substance of the original bill, the proposed amendments that led to tabling of the bill at the May 7 senate meeting, and the version that he now proposes be offered for adoption.
He has been working with the bill co-sponsors over the summer and they have reached an agreement on UM Sections 5.78.11 and 5.78.12.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 2
passages.text:
While amendments to Section 5.78.10 had been part of the original Bill #25-26-09, it is now recommended that the bill presented for action on 9/17 address only Sections 5.78.11 and 5.78.12; updates to Section 5.78.10 may be forthcoming later in the academic year.
The Bill Title and Indexing Number will not change. 4.3.
Current Project Tracker and Advance Agenda Setting updates.
Staff noted that a new category for completed items has been added to the Tracker, and the FSEC discussed several specific items, some of which are addressed elsewhere in these minutes.
Regarding the restructuring of Curriculum committees to better grapple with Program proposals, the FS President and VP have been discussing the idea of a special programs subcommittee with the college deans.
It was agreed that any such special committee should work under CASC, with its recommendations folded into CASC reports, should CASC see fit.
The special committee’s function would be to assist CASC in the job of proposal review, but that its recommendations shall be advisory in nature, with CASC retaining the authority to accept, modify, or reject its suggestions.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 2
passages.text:
The Senate will hold a forum on this restructuring in the fall in hopes of gathering additional input before a formal bill and charge are written.
Proposed fora are now reflected and color-coded in the advance agenda setting spreadsheet. 4.3.1 Orientation (specifically - duties of FSEC members/committee chairs) - Staff has started pulling together the slide presentation and a script for the FS President.
FSEC members will be asked to assist with committee chair presentations.
A slide template (committee charge, highlights of last year’s accomplishments, priorities for AY 26- 27) is being prepared for each standing committee and the liaisons and chairs are asked to work together to finalize the slide info and related comments.
Slide templates will be shared in the coming days so that liaison and chair work can begin. 4.4.
Committee Assignment Updates 4.4.1 Standing Committee Members - Standing committee membership are fully set except for one Chairship which has not been confirmed.
One senator resigned recently, 2

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 3
passages.text:
but that member’s committee already had an extra member, so no new appointments are needed at this time. 4.4.2 Joint Committees - For Action - Several joint committee appointments have occurred since the last meeting and several others are in progress.
Staff is still waiting to hear back from some of the nominees.
Committees that still need confirmed faculty members include the SAC, JAPROA, and the non-senator members of the CRCA.
One faculty member nominee was approved unanimously as a member of the JCSC.
Staff and the FS President will continue to refine the list. 5.
Continued Items 5.1.
Faculty Concerns submitted through the FS Webpage - no new concerns, but the previously reported concern about the appropriateness of assigned classroom spaces was further discussed.
It was noted that while the Facilities and Campus Planning offices are doing a great job with outreach and instructional space mapping, without significant faculty input, any resulting database may not be optimally searchable and may not include the most relevant criteria.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 3
passages.text:
It was noted that the Joint Classroom Steering Committee is likely best positioned to advise these efforts and the UM provides that it can have as many faculty appointees as the Faculty Senate sees fit.
Additional nominees to the committee were suggested and staff will keep following up with interested parties. 5.2.
Chapter 3 Revisions needed - update - Staff has reached out to all colleges about the sections of Chapter 3 (mostly 3.21.XX, although CoED and GSO are addressed elsewhere), that mention their colleges and related programs and departments.
Two colleges indicated no updates to their sections were needed.
All but two other colleges provided updates in writing.
Staff will finalize all relevant language with affected parties and prepare an informational report on Chapter 3 for presentation at the September 17 FS meeting. 5.3.
Continued Discussion - Creation of College Liaisons (evolution of draft: 2025 to 2026) The FS President and VP have met with most of the college deans and Liaisons have been/will be discussed with all of them.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 3
passages.text:
There seems to be full support for Liaisons (1 per college) that would perform three functions: provide a customized news digest to faculty after each senate meeting; be invited to speak at any all-college meetings to brief faculty about relevant issues and solicit feedback on initiatives; meet together as a group twice per semester to discuss college-level governance writ large and share best practices.
FSEC has agreed to hold a forum on Liaisons early in the year and schedule a vote on legislation to formally create the special committee during spring semester.
In the meantime, there will be a call for volunteers to see if any sitting senators would be willing to serve informally as liaisons this year as a sort of ‘soft launch’ of the initiative and also gain experience that might inform the drafting of better legislation. 5.4.
Continued Discussion - Transitioning Special Committees to Standing Committees - Draft legislation was reviewed.
The FS President, VP, and staff will refine it for final FSEC review and assignment to committees at the 8/31 meeting. 5.5.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 3
passages.text:
Update: Transition of UCAS to Fannon Institute - UM updates may be complete but CMS and Catalog (Program Descriptions/Admission Requirements) still refer to ‘UCAS.’ It was discovered that 112 programs include language that still references UCAS currently.
The 3

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 4
passages.text: FS Office’s graduate student worker is attempting to reconcile the language with current program requirements, while reflecting the transition to ‘Fannon Institute.’ It is hoped the changes can be made by the start of classes. 6. Updates/Ongoing Items 6.1. Updates i. Meetings with Administrators, Committees, or Others a) APC Meeting of 08/11/26 and additional Travel policy concern - A senator has prepared and submitted a well-reasoned objection to certain travel policies that the administration agreed had merit. The current policy will be reviewed/updated with an eye toward those concerns. ii. Status of the URI FY 26-27 Budget - The FS Pres. and VP met with the Provost and Vice Provost to discuss the budget and other matters. It was noted that while faculty have received a cumulative 43% increase in pay since 2011, service compensation for senators has not increased at all. (Some additional assigned work, for example, during summer, is associated with additional compensation, but baseline provisions are unchanged). Specifically regarding the AY 26-27 budget, the totals for faculty service compensation represents a cut compared to last year, which FSEC leaders find objectionable. It is hoped that the administration will be able to fill this gap as the year goes on. 7. Report of the Coordinator 7.1. Development of a Bill Proposal Form and cover sheet - The draft cover sheet was shared and FSEC members asked that a section addressing the ‘problem statement’ or ‘rationale’ be added. 8. New Business – Open for additional items not listed in the agenda. None 9. Closing Remarks – Recap of decisions made, action items, and plans for the next meeting. None. 10. Adjournment - The meeting adjourned at 2:55 pm. 4

Preisser will: Follow up on the earlier inquiry regarding teaching faculty being excluded from research grant opportunities; follow up with East Farm about a Faculty Senate apple-picking/family day in the fall; reach out RFA/OLLI representatives about offering a presentation to the full senate in November; check the status of the course withdrawals draft bill; continue outreach with enrollment services about the mapped classroom database and how best to interface with faculty about their spaces needs as related to their pedagogical style.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 1
passages.text:
Staff will: create a ‘microphone duty roster’ so that comments from the floor in senate meetings can be optimally accommodated.

Call to Order - Pres.
Preisser called the meeting to order at 1:03 pm.

Minutes for approval 2.1.
Minutes of the 7/13/26 FSEC meeting.
The minutes were approved as edited. 3.
Priority Items 3.1.
Current Project Tracker - FSEC’s top nine priorities were discussed.
The conversation centered around the College Liaisons initiative.
The Senate President and VP have started meetings with college deans to gather feedback on this idea and other initiatives and areas of potential collaboration.
Restructuring of the undergraduate curriculum committees was also discussed.
A meeting was held earlier today to work on the logistics of creating a joint committee or subcommittee that would be focused on program review.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 1
passages.text:
Project priorities include keeping By-laws amendments to a minimum, and following the newly conceived protocol of running a 3-year trial period for new committees before they gain permanent status.
It was agreed that both the College Liaisons and the Curriculum Committee Restructuring ideas would be good topics for a special Forum within early fall senate meetings to get senator feedback that could be incorporated into formal proposals for action.
Other FSEC priorities were also discussed briefly.
This included legislation to require new senate committees and joint committees to be initially formed as temporary Special Committees so that informed decisions about permanent status can be made (as relates to committee charge, appropriate membership, etc.). 3.2.
Advance Agenda Setting (broadly) FSEC members agreed the first half of legislative year 26-27 looks well organized.
The Orientation event set for 9/10 was discussed in some detail in terms of logistics and assigned roles.
Staff will share last year’s slides, which 1

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 2
passages.text:
should make an effective template for this year’s presentations, as well as talking points for each topic.
It was agreed that a series of fall forums should be scheduled for the OCt. - Dec. meetings on the topics of: Curriculum Committee reorganization; College Liaisons; and the senate budget.
The fora would be a great opportunity to present the need for each of these initiatives and gather early input from senators so that effective formal legislation can be drafted, or other actions taken. 3.3.
Committee Assignment Process 3.3.i.
Standing Committees - Updates 3.3.i.1.
Committee Members - The Committees are 99% set: one Chair needs to be confirmed and one member has been reassigned.
Appointment letters are currently being drafted. 3.3.ii.
Joint Committees - For Action - Joint Committees fall into three categories: those to which the Senate or Executive Committee can only nominate faculty members and the University President makes the appointments; those to which the full faculty senate has appointment authority; and those to which the FSEC or the Senate President can make appointments independently.
A recruitment effort has been underway to fill several vacancies on the joint committees.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 2
passages.text:
Several seats seem ready for action, to the extent that the FSEC can take it.
These include nominations or appointments to: the SAC, HDC, Conduct Board, new Ombuds Committee, the Public Safety Advisory Committee, and JAPROA. 4.
Continued Items 4.1.

Last year, the senate conducted some outreach with the space allocation and classroom steering committees and their respective staff and worked on restoring a classroom database that would help faculty in identifying spaces appropriate to their teaching styles.
Pres Preisser will continue to liaise with Enrollment Services regarding optimizing the map/database of classroom types and amenities.
Sen.
Daniels will work with the CTI Chair in developing a plan that would help ES better understand the variables that go into a faculty member’s classroom preference and to optimize a survey instrument or other information gathering tool that might lead to more appropriate placements.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 2

Chapter 3 Revisions needed - update - Staff created a contact group for Assoc.
Deans or other administrators in each college who would have up-to-date information on all programs, departments and schools within the colleges so that editorial updates to Chapter 3 can be made.
An email has gone to relevant parties and about a third have responded.
Once new language (or other ‘sign-off’) has been received from each of the nine degree granting colleges, Chapter 3 (specifically sections starting at 3.21.11) will be updated. 4.3.
Continued Discussion - Creation of College Liaisons - discussed as part of 3.1 above. 4.4.
Continued Discussion - Transitioning Special Committees to Standing Committees - discussed as part of 3.1 above. 2

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 3
passages.text:
4.5.
Continued Discussion: Transition of UCAS to Fannon Institute - UM updates may be complete but CMS and Catalog (Program Descriptions/Admission Requirements) still refer to ‘UCAS.’ Progress on catalog corrections to be reported next time. 5.
Updates/Ongoing Items 5.1.
Updates i.
Meetings with Administrators, Committees, or Others - The Senate President and VP have started their annual visits with the Deans and have 7 of 9 meetings either completed or on the books.
Feedback is expected to be useful in development of draft legislation for senate consideration. ii.
Status of the URI FY 26-27 Budget - The initial budget release for the senate office and senate activities may be insufficient to support faculty service given that the customary supplement for summer work does not appear to have been awarded.
Dialog with the Provost’s office about the need for such support continues. iii.
Other Updates 6.
Report of the Coordinator 6.1.
Development of a Bill Proposal Form - Staff considered feedback on the draft form and noted that it seemed several questions included in the draft would be most appropriately by staff or FSEC.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 3

The form is being reconsidered as a much more basic template with perhaps a standard ‘cover sheet’ addressing the staff/FSEC issues as an attachment.
Staff will continue to refine the draft. 7.
New Business – Open for additional items not listed in the agenda.
At the last meeting, it was noted that an informal social event for senators and their families seemed like a good idea.
Specifically an apple picking event at East Farm was suggested, which has multiple benefits, including being a family-friendly event, it provides support for the farm operation, expands awareness and appreciation of the activities carried out there, and also provides food for the RI Food Bank.
Pres.
Preisser volunteered to coordinate with farm managers to set a date and time so the event can be publicized. 8.
Closing Remarks – Recap of decisions made, action items, and plans for the next meeting.
The next meeting will be held on 8/17 and the focus will be on the agenda for the 9/10 Orientation. 9.
Adjournment - The meeting adjourned at 2:25 pm. 3

FSEC (Faculty Senate Executive Committee) Meeting Minutes Date: Monday, July 13, 2026 - Time: 1:00 pm – 3:00 pm Pastore Hall Room 224 Remote option via ZOOM - Meeting ID: 929 8712 9868 - Passcode: 508143 Find the Acronym Glossary here Action Items : Pres.
Preisser will coordinate with the University President’s office regarding the new Land Acknowledgement format at meetings, which is especially relevant in the months that the Senate meetings are preceded by a General Faculty meeting.
Staff will work toward finalizing a draft agenda for the 9/10 Senate Orientation.
Establishing a ‘mic duty’ rotation will be added to the FSEC priorities tracker and FSEC members will plan to play that active role in senate meetings.
Group photos will be added to the end of the 9/17 FS agenda.
The FS Pres. will remind the University President’s office that the new Ombuds Committee needs to be populated and convened.
Staff will double check the term end dates for all senate-appointed joint committee members, especially the PSAC.
Staff will set a standing reminder to notify all colleges each Summer that attention to Chapter 3 of the University Manual is required.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 1
passages.text:
Staff will continue to refine the new “Bill Proposal” form based on feedback received from FSEC members in hopes it will be ready for use in September. 1.
Call to Order - Pres.
Preisser called the meeting to order at 1:02 pm.
VP Trimm and Senators Van Wyk, Daniels, Chen, and Meyerson were present. 2.
Minutes for approval 2.1.
Minutes of the 6/29/26 FSEC meeting.
The minutes were approved as edited. 3.
Priority Items 3.1.
Current Project Tracker - A few top priorities were briefly discussed and one new operational item was added to the tracker.
The logistics of changing the land acknowledgement protocol are being worked out, but additional coordination with the University President’s office will be required.
Pres.
Preisser will follow up. 3.2.
Advance Agenda Setting - The general legislative arc of the academic year was briefly discussed.
It was noted that the FS President should not be in the position of “wearing two hats” during meetings.
This means that when Pres.
Preisser must present and advocate for FSEC legislation, the administrative duties of running the meeting need to be formally handed off to the Vice President.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 1
passages.text:
It was also noted that while not all legislation currently anticipated will formally require two meetings for formal action, this is a model that works well and should be expected for most bills. 3.2.i Orientation - A template agenda based on last year’s event was provided in advance.
It was agreed that specific topics and duties would be assigned to FSEC members based on the committees for which they serve as liaison.
The balance of the presentations will be handled by the Officers and the Parliamentarian.
Some changes since last year (like introduction of a bill proposal template) will need special emphasis and will also need to be recapped at the regular 09/17 senate meeting.
Staff will work with Pres.
Preisser to finalize the agenda. 3.2.ii September 17 meeting - Draft - The agenda was reviewed as it stands.
The JCODL bill will be reintroduced to the legislative body as comprised for AY 26-27.
The bill regarding course withdrawals will likely not be ready in September.
Staff will arrange for 1

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 2
passages.text:
a Senate photo to be taken at the end of the meeting.
The draft agenda will be refined over the coming month. 3.3.
Committee Assignment Process 3.3.i.
Standing Committees - Updates - All but one committee chair is finalized and the committee memberships are set except for one Senator.
Staff will start to formalize appointment letters pending ratification by the senate. 3.3.ii Joint Committees - The joint committee appointment list was presented as it stands.
The list only includes vacancies currently requiring attention.
Terms on other joint committees that will expire mid-year or in the spring will be addressed separately.
Some of the nominees that have been contacted have not responded.
Staff and FS Pres. will follow up.
Of particular concern is the Ombuds Committee which is new and the initial convening of that group will occur through the University President’s office.
Pres.
Preisser will remind appropriate administrators of the need to set up operations for this committee. 3.4.
BS - Interdisciplinary & Applied AI Proposal - The proposal as revised was approved with the condition that the final Kuali version be reviewed and signed off on by Sen.
Van Wyk.
Sen.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 2
passages.text:
Van Wyk has had an ongoing dialog with the proposers about concerns coming from FSEC and her department.
These pertain to things like discipline encroachment and lack of robust content around the ethics and writing intensive components.
The dialog has been both positive and productive and Sen.
Van Wyk described the building of a collegial relationship with the COB and CAS (Computer Science and Statistics) faculty involved in the proposal and the opportunity for her department (SOC) to contribute courses in the new program in the future. 4.
Continued Items 4.1.
Faculty Concerns submitted through the FS Webpage - It was discovered last week that the “Faculty Concerns” link was not working, but that has now been corrected.
In the meantime, a new concern was submitted to the FS Pres. regarding the confusion that has persisted around there being two “Coastal Institutes” (one in Kingston and one at the bay campus).
This issue is already well known to the administration, however, and there don’t appear to be any actions the Senate can take that would lead to a solution. 4.2.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 2
passages.text:
Chapter 3 Revisions needed - Staff is working on a list of contacts in each college to press into service on updates needed this year.
In addition, a process or protocol needs to be put in place to ensure that the Chapter remains up to date on an ongoing basis.
Staff had discussed adding a Kuali field indicating that any changes to department, program, etc would also require appropriate modification in the UM, It was noted, however, that because the personnel involved in updating degrees and programs in Kuali are different from the people charged with keeping the UM up to date, and because every such action would likely produce companion bills that could clutter a legislative session, this may not be the most efficient solution.
It was agreed that the Faculty Senate office should serve as the institutional memory on this issue, and should send a reminder to all colleges every summer that attention to Chapter 3 is required.
Changes would then be implemented as Editorial updates. 4.3.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 2
passages.text:
Continued Discussion - Creation of College Liaisons (evolution of draft: 2025 v. 2026) - It was noted that the draft from last year leaned heavily toward Liaisons playing a meaningful role in college-level governance.
The current version refocuses on setting 2

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 3
passages.text:
expectations for Liaisons centered around things the senate itself can control.
The FS President and VP considered feedback from the college deans received last year and advocated for the current version based on the level of support they think it will garner.
They have not yet circled back to the deans with the current draft, but will.
That activity will only happen over the summer if there is money in the budget for a new round of meetings; otherwise, it will have to wait.
FSEC also discussed how to move forward operationally.
While any legislation to create a new committee (By-Laws amendment) would take effect in fall 2027, the idea of informally convening volunteer liaisons during AY 26-27 was suggested.
This would provide an opportunity for the actual legislation to benefit from people performing liaison duties and providing input.
There were questions about the level of specificity that should be included in the bill (selection process, timeline and member criteria like faculty rank).
FSEC members agreed to consider these questions and continue the discussion at the next meeting. 4.4.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 3
passages.text:
Continued Discussion - Transitioning Special Committees to Standing Committees - Draft legislation would create a process by which any newly created special committee would become eligible for standing committee status.
It would involve a review after three years and affirmative action by the senate.
There is currently no language in the Manual that addresses such a process or any other details of special committees, like their ability to modify their charge or alter the composition of their membership.
The burden would be on the special committee to understand its timeline and the window for appealing to the senate for standing committee status.
The current plan would be to introduce this legislation at the 9/17 meeting and vote on it in October. 4.5.
Continued Discussion: Transition of UCAS to Fannon Institute - UM updates may be complete but CMS and Catalog (Program Descriptions/Admission Requirements) still refer to ‘UCAS.’ Pres.
Preisser discussed this issue with VP Adams who looped in Enrollment Services.
There may be a way to provide template language for admission requirements that simplifies the process of updating all the program descriptions.
Pres.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 3
passages.text:
Preisser will work with staff and Jack Humphrey on a solution. 5.
Updates/Ongoing Items 5.1.
Updates i.
Meetings with Administrators, Committees, or Others - Pres.
Preisser met with VP Adams today and has a follow up with her and AVP Mello on Wednesday regarding the budget specifically.
Other matters discussed in the meeting with Sue Adams included Sen.
Chen’s proposal regarding mid-career faculty support.
The current plan is to assign the SCLC the task during AY 26-27 of reviewing Sen.
Chen’s research and recommendations and reporting out to the senate about steps the university should take. ii.
Status of the URI FY 26-27 Budget - While initial budget numbers have been released, the administration is now asking departments to prepare for the possibility of additional cuts.
FSEC members had comments that touched on both the impacts of cuts as well as the actual factors that give rise to their need.
Pres.
Preisser hopes to learn more in his meeting on Wednesday and will report back. iii.
Other Updates - None 3

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 4
passages.text:
6.
Report of the Coordinator 6.1.
Development of a Bill Proposal Form - Comments were offered about the draft, notably that there are questions that proposers should probably skip and leave for staff to complete (examples: expected senate action date, relevant review committee, etc.).
A process for ‘triaging’ all proposals was briefly discussed and while legislative proposals have traditionally flowed through FSEC, there may be some advantage to letting the CBUM take a first pass at them.
Staff will make modifications to the form and FSEC will continue to discuss.
It was noted that not all community members routinely use Microsoft forms so a fillable pdf would be a useful alternative.
It was suggested the draft bill currently being developed regarding standing/special committees be used as an initial test of the form. 6.2.
Digital Archive update - Staff has been working this summer on entering senate records, including legislation, into the Digital Commons.
As bills and other documents get moved off of local drives and into the Commons, links in the UM and on the webpage are broken.
Once the batch uploads are complete, links will be redirected to the new home of the source material.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 4
passages.text:
The problem may appear worse before it gets better.
If FSEC members have trouble locating past records, or knows anyone else who is having trouble, please reach out to staff for help.
This project is on track to be complete by the time classes resume. 7.

Pres.

It was agreed that inviting the faculty senate to an apple picking event in the fall might be an opportunity to mingle with colleagues in an informal setting. 9.

Preisser will share the description of the College Liaison role which FSEC is considering creating to inform future discussions.

FS Pres.
Preisser will discuss Sen.
Chen’s proposal regarding advocacy and support for mid-career faculty with Vice Provost Adams in his next meeting with her.

FS Pres.

passages.text:
