Pres.
Preisser will ask for support from the Provost’s office in hopes that a student worker there or in Enrollment Services - or some other staffer- might be able to help with this task. 1.
Call to Order - Pres.
Preisser called the meeting to order at 1:03 pm.
VP Trimm and Senators Van Wyk, Daniels, Chen, and Meyerson were present. 2.
Minutes for approval 2.1.
Minutes of the 6/3/26 FSEC meeting.
The minutes were approved as edited. 3.
Priority Items 3.1.
Development of 2026-2027 Faculty Senate Work Plan - The work program is summarized in the Project and Priority Tracker (see 3.2 below), which has now been organized to show FSEC priorities (initiatives that FSEC members or the committee itself are expected to advance) separate from broader senate goals and priorities (expected to advance procedurally through other committees, offices, or administrators).
FSEC priorities will be addressed in weekly meetings.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 1
passages.text:
Broader senate priorities will be discussed as needed and as updates from the committees become available.
Communication through Committee liaisons to the FS Pres. will be important for agenda-setting. 3.2.
Current Project Tracker - FSEC will focus on its own priorities, some of which are purely operational matters while others involve major updates to the University Manual and/or FS By-Laws.
There are currently eight priorities listed.
One of the more substantive initiatives will be the creation of College Liaisons.
It was noted that if each standing senate committee were populated with the minimum number of members called for in its charge, 55 senators would be assigned.
Given that there are 66 senators per the current apportionment formula, there are enough senators to create a ‘Liaisons Committee’ (one from each degree-granting college without reapportioning or requiring senators to do ‘double duty.’ FSEC would like to roll out a trial of this group during AY26-27, in which case senators involved would be volunteers and would be serving on other committees concurrent with their service in the Liaisons.
But once relevant 1

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 2
passages.text:
legislation is approved and the new Liaisons are formalized in the By-Laws, the new service model would take effect (expected Fall 2027).
Pres.
Preisser has a written ‘job description’ of a College Liaison which he will share with FSEC members.
This description actually includes two visions for liaisons, one more robust than the other.
In their most basic iteration, Liaisons would be assigned to bring concerns from their colleges to the senate and conversely, take information back from the senate meetings to their constituents in the colleges via a brief monthly ‘digest.’ With adequate support from deans, however, liaisons become a real partner in college governance and are given the floor at all college meetings to share information and gather feedback.
They also meet as a committee of all Liaisons to share information about how their colleges are governed with the goal of identifying disparate practices and inequities, and standardizing certain best practices where possible.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 2
passages.text:
Other priorities discussed included: 1) Transitioning away from the standard reading of the Land Acknowledgement and moving toward a more meaningful presentation regarding the cultural heritage and practices of local tribes.
Sen.
Van Wyk is taking the lead on this initiative and will provide details for each month’s agenda in advance. 2) VP Trimm noted that the curricular committee restructuring might involve moving from a ‘CASC & GEC’ approach to a Courses versus Programs structure.
He will have more to report after a meeting with Summer Curriculum Committee members and staff later this month. 3) VP Trimm also reported on the draft copyright statement which appears ready for a Fall 2026 roll-out as an opt-in policy for faculty. 4) Chapter 3 of the University Manual is out of date.
This chapter addresses all schools, colleges, departments, and degree programs.
There has been a lot of dynamic change in departments, programs and degrees the last few years but this chapter has not been kept current.
Staff was assigned to draft a communication to go to all colleges advising them of this problem and asking that they submit updated and corrected information.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 2
passages.text:
They will be advised that the more specific the information is, the more attention will need to be paid in the long run to keep it up-to-date.
The choice of approach (more versus less specificity) will be theirs, however. 3.3.
Advance Agenda Setting - A spreadsheet shows all reports required either by the University Manual, other policies, or by custom and tradition, across the academic year.
Committee Chairs and Liaisons can use this tool to visualize where their initiatives might best fit for introduction and debate.
In cases where specific reports are required to be delivered in a specific month, the Chairs or relevant administrators will know well in advance.
In addition to this tool, staff is hopeful that the agendas for all fall semester senate meetings will be drafted by the time classes start in September.
Templated agendas already exist in the FSEC’s shared drive and members are encouraged to add items that they know are upcoming. 3.4.
Committee Assignment Process—Member List 3.4.i.
Standing Committees 3.4.i.1.
Committee Chairs - Chair for all standing committees except one are firmed up and the draft list was presented. 3.4.i.2.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 2
passages.text:
Committee Members - In a unanimous vote, standing committee assignments were approved.
All standing committees have been 2

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 3
passages.text:
populated with members.
The approval is provisional, pending ratification at the 9/17/26 FS meeting. 3.4.ii.
Joint Committees and other Appointments - Joint Committee needs were discussed and some ideas were offered.
The FS Pres. will continue to work with staff on these placements and they expect to present a draft list at the next meeting. 3.5.
BS - Interdisciplinary & Applied AI Proposal - There was substantive discussion on both the merits of the proposal and on the process that has been followed in advancing it toward an approval decision.
It was noted that the proposal had been tabled by the senate at the end of the legislative season and FSEC’s summer work on this issue has been aimed at resolving the issues brought up by the senate.
The proposers have made a good-faith effort toward that end.
It seemed unfair to some FSEC members that new issues/objections could now be raised.
Others countered, however, that the issues now being raised by FSEC members, who are charged with acting on behalf of the full senate, are not out of bounds, as they might equally be raised on the floor of the full senate, should the proposal be revisited there.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 3
passages.text:
It was agreed that the subject proposal has been subjected to a level of scrutiny by FSEC that is very unusual, and the members should be mindful of fairness and equitable treatment.
It was also noted that, should the FSEC opt not to approve the proposal on behalf of the senate, the proposal is not dead in the water: it simply must go back to the floor in the fall.
FSEC voted to table the proposal.
Pres.
Preisser will reach out to concerned FSEC members to compile a list of specific concerns that can be passed along to the proposers.
If they are able to address these in a timely way, the proposal may still be actionable by FSEC over the summer. 4.
Continued Items 4.1.
Faculty Concerns submitted through the FS Webpage - None 4.2.
Chapter 3 Inquiry from A&S - Discussed as part of Item 3 above. 4.3.
Discussion: Transition of UCAS to Fannon Institute - UM updates may be complete but CMS and Catalog (Program Descriptions/Admission Requirements) still refer to UCAS.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 3
passages.text:

Preisser will ask for suggestions/support from the Provost’s office in hopes that a student worker there or in Enrollment Services - or some other staffer- might be able to help with these corrections.
The other option would be to distribute the workload to the colleges and have them update their respective sections. 5.
Updates/Ongoing Items 5.1.
Updates i.
Kuali Update and 9/1/26 Curriculum Meeting - Specialist Spitale provided an update on the progress made in mapping courses and creating an optimal workflow.
The goal is to make the proposal process more intuitive and compliant with recent changes to Appendix E of the University Manual.
A request was made for ‘beta testers’ who might volunteer to create some courses to test the new workflows.
Once the course workflows are finalized, staff will move on to programs and specializations, which should go quicker. 3

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 4
passages.text:
6.
Report of the Coordinator - Tabled. 6.1.
Development of a Bill Proposal Form - Draft fillable Microsoft Form available for review 7.
New Business – Open for additional items not listed in the agenda. 7.1.
Sen.
Chen’s Faculty Advocacy Initiative Please review the one-page summary and the detailed report for discussion - Sen.
Chen summarized her research, noting that the work was performed with the help of a Career Enhancement Grant.
Her findings have led her to conclude that the associate professor stage is a critical leverage point for retention, research productivity, faculty morale, and equity.
Interviews with female full professors and other campus leaders show that many faculty lose structure, mentoring, resources, and research momentum after tenure, while service and caregiving demands increase.
URI can address this with practical, low cost, scalable support.
Sen.
Chen pointed out that implementing solutions would be a win-win, as the associate professors will benefit alongside the university, which has already made a significant investment in them but is at risk of losing them if that support does not continue.
FSEC members agreed that Sen.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 4
passages.text:
Chen’s research is important and should be shared widely to build support for mid-career faculty development.
Several discussion points followed, like the need for “post-tenure workshops,” the non-standardized criteria used for promotion and tenure that vary widely across colleges, the need to explore partnerships as the community considers action steps (like with the AAUP and perhaps outside funding sources).
Pres.
Preisser suggested that this would be an ideal topic to bring to the Service and Community Life Committee (SCLC).
He is meeting with the Vice Provost this week and will mention the findings to her.
He asked for and received FSEC consent to approach the SCLC Chair about rolling this into their AY 26-27 work program. 8.
Closing Remarks – Recap of decisions made, action items, and plans for the next meeting.
None 9.
Adjournment - The meeting adjourned at 2:58 pm. 4

passages.text: Academic Calendar CommitteeInformational Report #2024-2025-ADecember 12, 2024 Context: The Office of Community, Equity and Diversity has promulgated an annual calendar of“Cultural Heritage Celebrations”. The 2024-2025 calendar was presented to the FS President ata meeting of the President’s Stewardship Council and was then passed on to the CalendarCommittee to determine if there were any impacts on the Academic Calendar and to decidehow the Faculty Senate or the ACC could help to distribute/raise awareness of the calendar. Conclusions and Suggestions: The Committee concluded that there were no new impacts on theAcademic Calendar. To help raise awareness and make the calendar easily accessible to allmembers of the URI community, the ACC recommends that a link to the calendar be added tothe Enrollment Services webpage that currently houses the Academic Calendar plus links to theAccelerated Online Program Calendars and Final Exam Schedule(https://web.uri.edu/academic-calendars/).

TAAC Report to Faculty Senate
1-23-2025
Mid-year Report
TAAC - Teaching, Advising, and Assessment Committee
* Link for general information
* Doug Reed - Philosophy – 3rd year on committee
* Penny Steen - Kinesiology – 3rd year on committee
* Mikong Kim - Communicative Disorders – 2nd year on committee
* Leon Thiem - Civil and Environmental Engineering – 2nd year on committee
* Justin Wyatt – Communication Studies - 1st year on committee
* Ingrid Lofgren - Nutrition – 3rd year on committee and past chair
* Rebecca Romanow – Film/Media - 1st year on committee and chair
* Ted Walls - FSEC liaison
Priorities for TAAC
Advising
* Penny Steen (KIN) and Doug Reed (PHIL) are TAAC members who are attending the meetings of the Reimagining Advising Committee chaired by Dean Libutti
* Dean Libutti visited with the committee in November with updates from the RAC
* Since last January the Re-Imagining Advising Committee, in consultation with the deans of each college, has begun sketching a new advising model which would be a hybrid model that gives the colleges more control over how advising is done in their units

passages.heading: here
passages.text:
* This model is not fully decentralized, however, because there would still be standards across campus and other shared advising resources
* No timeline for when the model would go into effect--the committee is exploring the feasibility of implementation
* URI’s goals:
* more advisors to improve advising ratios and the potential for a mixed advising model, where colleges could decide their own advising approach raise retention rates
* model would involve the rebranding of University College into an exploration center, with advisors moving to the colleges
* need for advisors with mental health and social work skills
* importance of maintaining a 12-month advising system
* investing in technology to enhance advising, such as AI tools for better student support.
* Committee has reviewed national reports and best practices, gathering information from different Colleges across URI about advising
Honors Program
* Ingrid Lofgren [NUT] and Leon Thiem – Engineering
* Proposal for implementation of Honors “Institute” and Honors Contracts has consumed much of the committee’s time this Fall

passages.heading: here
passages.text:
* In November, TAAC voted down both the Honors Contract Proposal and the Honor Program becoming an institute. The Honors Institute proposal has been sent back to the Honors Program, but with more direction provided by other Faculty Senators during the open discussion at the 12/12 meeting. The proposal may well come back to TAAC with more needed details and protocol.
* Proposal from the Honors Program to create “Honors Contracts” as an alternative to having specified Honors Courses: at the 12/12 Faculty Senate meeting, the Faculty Senate voted to allow Honors to have trial contracts for the Spring 2025 semester [Resolution to extend this through Fall 2025 will be presented at the 1/23/25 Faculty Senate meeting]. This may assist Honors in providing a new/modified proposal for the Honors Contracts.
Teaching
* Mikyong Kim (CMD) and Jusitn Wyatt (COM)
* Committee to discuss examining how ATL supports faculty teaching through their various offerings and ATL’s future plans
* Committee may also take up consideration of IDEA scores, metric, and rankings
Assessment
* Rebecca Romanow (FLM) [to possibly be moved to JAPROA]
Admissions

passages.heading: here
passages.text:
* Last year LOOC [Learning Outcome Oversight Committee] and APRC [Academic Program Review] were consolidated into JAPROA, and the addition of accreditation related work and assessment moved to the charge of that committee.
* Faculty Senate does not have a group focused on Admissions data, standards, and goals. RI law affords the Faculty Senate shared governance authority with the president over admission, as in all the other academic functions. Currently, Faculty Senate has no committee overseeing admission data, standards, and goals, and this best fits as a charge for TAAC.
TAAC shall study and make recommendations to the Faculty Senate on the following matters:
* good teaching, advising, and assessment at the University by conducting and reporting to the Faculty Senate an annual audit of programs, activities, policies, etc.,
* assess university-wide advising and make policy recommendations to the Faculty Senate on all advising matters pertaining to the University College for Academic Success,
* in collaboration with the Director of the Honors Program, shall oversee the Honors Program and bring distinguished scholars to the campus for general lectures and/or other public programs

The Committee shall study and make recommendations to the Faculty Senate (or return the matters unapproved, with comments, to the units from which they originated) on the following matters referred to it by the various colleges, schools, the Faculty Senate or its Executive Committee, the Administration, or from another authoritative source, or taken up by the Committee on its own initiative: #21-22-37

passages.text:
FSEC (Faculty Senate Executive Committee) Meeting Minutes Date: Monday, August 31, 2026 - Time: 1:00 pm – 3:00 pm Pastore Hall Room 224 - Remote option via ZOOM Find the Acronym Glossary here Action Items - Staff will reach out to the six individuals that VP DeBoef suggested for membership in the CRCA to gauge their interest.
Staff will finalize the slides for Orientation and recruit helpers who might play a role in the “motions demonstration” and elsewhere.
Sens.
Chen and Van Wyk will work with the SCLC and Chair Kusz to develop actionable items for the senate related to the proposal to expand support for mid-career faculty. 1.
Call to Order - Pres.
Preisser called the meeting to order at 1:03 pm.
VP Trimm and Senators Van Wyk, Daniels, Meyerson, and Chen were present. 2.
Minutes for approval (5 minutes) 2.1 Minutes of the 8/17/26 FSEC meeting.
The minutes were approved. 3.
Priority Items and New Business (50 minutes) 3.1.
Orientation - Planning for the 9/10 meeting - Staff and the FS Pres. will meet separately to refine the scripts and slides for the meeting, but the agenda is set.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 1
passages.text:
A special meeting will take place next Wednesday to refine roles, plan logistics, and essentially ‘rehearse’ scripts.
A new resource being rolled out this year is a “quick guide to parliamentary procedure” that staff plans to make available via the website and with each monthly agenda.
The goal is not to have senators memorize all the ins and outs of meeting management, but to reinforce that some baseline knowledge of procedures (like when certain motions or inquiries are actually in order) by all members always improves meeting efficiency while maximizing meaningful participation. 3.2.
Reintroduction of JCODL Legislation - Bill #25-26-FSEC-09 was tabled last May.
FSEC has reviewed proposed changes to last year’s Bill in preparation for reintroduction at the 9/17/26 senate meeting.
Action requested on the current draft.
Related: Consideration of the JCODL’s annual report.
FSEC agreed the JCODL annual report should be delivered by the URI Online Director at the September meeting, separately and before the presentation of the bill.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 1
passages.text:
The bill was discussed at length, covering the travel of the legislation over the last year, potential concerns or objections that could arise during the meeting, and the logistics of Pres.
Preisser presenting the bill substantively while VP Trimm takes over as presiding officer for that portion of the meeting.
The bill text was approved unanimously. 3.3.
Course Withdrawals Legislation and back-up - The bill language was reviewed in detail with several questions raised.
These pertained to things like the faculty “sign-off” of a later-semester withdrawal and whether that should more appropriately be an actual approval versus an acknowledgment, the impacts on student workload for those involved in group work when there are late semester withdrawals, and whether or not there might be impacts to the academic calendar or to Ecampus coding.
Questions about to what degree students are aware of the effect withdrawals could have on scholarships, 1

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 2
passages.text:
financial aid, graduation timelines, etc. were raised.
It was noted that Enrollment Services representatives have been involved in drafting the bill and are not concerned about Ecampus.
FSEC can and should send the bill to the ACC for a recommendation.
Regarding other consequences for students, Pres.
Preisser noted that peer institutions universally have later withdrawal deadlines than URI and they are not reporting disastrous results for affected students.
The bill text was approved unanimously by FSEC with the condition that it gain CBUM and ACC review prior to action being taken at the October FS meeting. 3.4.
Current Project Tracker and Advance Agenda Setting updates - FSEC discussed the status of current priorities, especially those that don’t involve legislation.
A ‘mic rotation’ schedule was briefly reviewed, to help ensure FSEC members are involved in securing feedback from the floor during senate meetings.
An outline for the Land Acknowledgment to be presented at the September FS meeting was reviewed, and FSEC members had only positive comments concerning the new model. 3.5.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 2
passages.text:
Committee Assignment Updates 3.5.1 Standing Committee Members - The list was finalized for presentation/ratification at the 9/17 FS meeting.
The only names still needed are the VPRED’s appointees to the CRCA.
Staff will reach out to those that VP DeBoef suggested to gauge their interest. 3.5.2 Joint Committees - For Action - Additional appointees to the BAC and JCSC were approved but the full list of joint committee appointees will likely not be available until October as staff is still waiting for confirmations from several nominees regarding their willingness and ability to serve. 3.6 Agenda Setting - 9/17/26 Faculty Senate Meeting - The agenda was discussed in detail and it was agreed that in terms of legislation, the JCODL will be docketed for action and the course withdrawals and ‘special committees’ bills will be introduced with votes planned in October.
The editorial report on Chapter 3 will likely be held until October as staff is still awaiting proofreading by the affected colleges. 4.
Continued Items (25 minutes) 4.1.
Faculty Concerns submitted through the FS Webpage - No new concerns but Pres.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 2
passages.text:
Preisser offered an update on a past concern related to appropriateness of classroom assignments and the importance of a searchable classroom database.
Names of faculty members who would be willing to provide guidance to the Facilities team as they develop the database are requested. 4.2.
Chapter 3 Revisions needed - update - As noted elsewhere, staff has completed a draft of editorial updates to Chapter 3 and distributed it to the colleges for review. 4.3.
Continued Discussion - Creation of College Liaisons (evolution of draft: 2025 - 2026) The current draft serves as a conceptual framework for creation of these roles.
Because Liaisons would initially be formed as a special committee (not requiring By-laws language), the ‘bill’ will not actually be introduced as legislation this year.
As the special committee operates over the next couple of years, their experience and input will inform future legislation, likely aimed at formalizing the roles and making them permanent.
Thus far, the college deans have only voiced support for the idea.
The hope is that, during AY 26-27, a volunteer from each college will agree to serve in the volunteer 2

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 3
passages.text:
position of Liaison, with a duly authorized Special Committee being seated fall, 2027.
It was noted that staff will need to remember, when annual “Notices to Elect” go out in March, that the colleges must be informed of the requirement to name a Liaison. 4.4.
Continued Discussion - Transitioning Special Committees to Standing Committees - The bill text was reviewed and approved.
It will be introduced on 9/17 and docketed for action on 10/15.
It will require CBUM review prior to 10/15. 4.5.
Continued Discussion - Creation of a Programs Subcommittee (current draft) - It was agreed that for purposes of hosting a forum this fall on this theme, a more basic “ask” of the senators is likely in order.
A draft of a simple problem statement and proposed solution was presented by VP Trimm and FSEC concurred this was the right approach.
The actual legislation can be crafted following the forum and an early draft does not necessarily need to be part of the forum presentation.
There were questions about potential membership in the proposed subcommittee and FSEC members sought assurance that the four administrators involved will be from different colleges. 5.
Updates/Ongoing Items (10 minutes) 5.1.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 3
passages.text:
Updates i.
Meetings with Administrators, Committees, or Others - VP Trimm noted that his and Pres.
Preisser’s meetings with the college Deans have wrapped up, and for the most part, they have been both productive and enjoyable.
Deans are supportive of initiatives like the creation of Liaisons, and the exercise of conducting meetings every summer has proven valuable, and is a tradition that should continue. ii.
The scheduled meeting with curriculum committee chairs and college deans/delegates to go over Kuali and proposal/approval procedures is scheduled for tomorrow.
A message from Vice Provost Adams to concerned parties should bolster attendance over last year.
In other news, the FS Pres. and VP met with administrators about the FS budget, and noted that additional funds will be needed to complete all objectives this year.
A formal response has not yet been forthcoming. 6.
Report of the Coordinator (5 minutes) 6.1.
Special Meeting reminder - 9/9 at 10 AM to prepare for orientation.
The regular fall weekly meeting schedule will begin on Wednesday 9/16. 7.
New Business – Open for additional items not listed in the agenda.
Sen.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 3
passages.text:
Chen asked about next steps in her initiative to expand support for mid-career faculty.
A path forward was briefly described wherein she presents the details to the SCLC and the committee assesses steps the senate could perhaps take, versus those that would require administration participation (for example, any action items that require funding).
The likely result is expected to be a resolution put forward by the Committee to the senate calling for specific items to be implemented.
Sen.
Chen and Van Wyk will continue to work together with the Service Committee to develop something for senate action in the coming months. 8.
Closing Remarks – Recap of decisions made, action items, and plans for the next meeting.
None 9.
Adjournment - The meeting adjourned at 2:53 pm. 3

Methods of Instruction The CAC has adopted the following definitions of methods of instruction: Definitions for Methods of Instruction Revision of definitions in the CAC's Three Hundred and Seventh Report (October 13, 1993) Lecture: A course in which the primary method is presentation and students are expected to participate in a variety of ways, such as small- group discussions, questions and answers, writing-exercises, etc.
Laboratory: In-class applied course work, generally involving experimentation or observation, typically using special equipment (including computers and specialized software).
Recitation: Separate sections of a lecture course regularly scheduled for discussion.
Studio: In-class, supervised work with an emphasis on performance and creativity in which facuity instruct, assist, and critique. 2

passages.heading: Four Hundred Fifty-First Report of the Curricular Affairs Committee (April 3, 2007) | Page 5
passages.text:
Seminar: Course offered to a small group (usually no more than 20* students) where participants actively exchange ideas and findings based on readings or research.
Independent Study: One-on-one instruction in which the student enters into an agreement with the instructor that defines the focus of inquiry and nature of activities.
Includes tutorials, directed readings, special projects.
Practicum: Structured experiences where the primary aim is to connect theory with practice.
Includes clinics, internships, ex tern ships, student teaching, field experiences.
May include regular class meetings.
Workshop: Similar to a seminar, with emphasis on applied rather than theoretical learning, but not offered for degree-program credit.
Online: A course that is delivered entirely online. (CAC policy includes possibility of a required organizational session, etc.) SECTIONI Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation by the Facuity Senate A.

passages.text: Priorities for TAAC AY 2026 • Admissions • Collaboration, transparency and openness remain essential, with the focus for TAAC on understanding the admissions process rather than oversight. • Ongoing goal would be of having the Faculty Senate informed and involved so we help to support URI to be fair, competitive and successful. • With that in mind, TAAC is organizing a walkthrough with Dean Libutti to begin to learn more about the technical details of admissions processes. • Admissions team will report to the committee, providing updates and addressing concerns when/if they arise. • TAAC will input to the Faculty Senate on Admissions/Enrollment Management issues around maintaining high admissions standards, and topics like yielding high- achieving students. • An annual verbal summary will be delivered to the committee, detailing the admissions process and addressing any concerns.

passages.heading: Committee Report, December, 2025 | Page 7
passages.text: Priorities for TAAC AY 2026 Advising • TAAC members have been attending the meetings of the Reimagining Advising Committee chaired by Dean Libutti • Since last January, the Re-Imagining Advising Committee, in consultation with the deans of each college, has begun sketching a new advising model which would be a hybrid model that gives the colleges more control over how advising is done in their units. This model is not fully decentralized, however, because there would still be standards across campus and other shared advising resources. No timeline for when the model would go into effect--the committee is exploring the feasibility of implementation • URI’s goals: • more advisors to improve advising ratios and the potential for a mixed advising model, where colleges could decide their own advising approach raise retention rates • model would involve the rebranding of University College into an exploration center, with advisors moving to the colleges • need for advisors with mental health and social work skills • importance of maintaining a 12-month advising system • investing in technology to enhance advising, such as AI tools for better student support.

passages.heading: Appendix B: Constitution of the Faculty Senate – University Manual
passages.text: Appendix B: Constitution of the Faculty Senate – University Manual

passages.heading: Preamble
passages.text: The Faculty Senate was authorized by an act of the General Faculty on May 12, 1960, and approved by the former Board of Trustees on June 1, 1960, as an agent to conduct the business of the Faculty responsibly and efficiently. It was the intent of the Faculty to create a smaller legislative body to which the powers of the Faculty should be delegated so long as it should represent the will of the Faculty. The Faculty intended that the Senate should act in the best interests of the University as a whole and of all its parts, in the pursuit of its aims and in the performance of the service for which the University exists. To the extent permitted by the laws of the state of Rhode Island and the laws of the United States, the authority of the Constitution and By-Laws of the Senate derives from approval by the General Faculty and by the former Board of Trustees. This document was first approved by the General Faculty on April 19, 1961; amendments were proposed by the Attorney General on October 3, 1961; the former Board of Trustees approved the Constitution and By-Laws with these amendments on November 1, 1961; and the General Faculty subsequently approved the amendments in May, 1962.

passages.heading: Article I – Name
passages.text: 1. The name of this deliberative body shall be the Faculty Senate of the University of Rhode Island, referred to hereafter in this document as the Senate.

passages.heading: Article II – Powers
passages.text: 1. The Senate, subject to the provisions of state and federal law, subject to consistency with the general objectives established by its governing Board, and subject to the referendum power of the General Faculty, has ultimate legislative power on educational policies. It shall, with the concurrence of the President, formulate policy concerning teaching and research, study, exercise, discipline and government: for example, and without excluding others not listed, academic standards (scholastic standing, admission and dismissal policy, class attendance, grading systems, etc.), the University calendar, University-wide curriculum matters both graduate and undergraduate, and research and patent policy as they may affect the faculty as a whole. Nothing in this article should be construed to interfere with the authority or responsibility of the appropriate administrative officers in the carrying out of established policy, or in proposing, through the President, such changes in policy as they deem desirable.

passages.heading: Article II – Powers
passages.text:
2. The Senate, with the concurrence of the President, shall formulate such policies regarding student activities as it may deem appropriate to advance the educational purposes of the University and to promote satisfactory discipline and behavior.
3. The Senate may make recommendations to the President and/or the URI Board of Trustees through the President in regard to policies affecting faculty status and welfare, including such subjects as promotion, tenure, rank, leaves of absence, salaries, grants and contracts. This section shall not be construed to conflict with the rights delegated to an exclusive collective bargaining agent duly authorized to represent the faculty in conformity with public laws. #20-21-36
4. The Senate shall establish such standing and special committees as it deems necessary to carry out its functions: for example, Academic Standards, Curriculum, Faculty Welfare and Research and Patent Policy.

passages.heading: Article II – Powers
passages.text: 5. The Senate shall exercise all authority delegated to the General Faculty by law and all authority lawfully delegated to it by the URI Board of Trustees, except that the General Faculty shall act upon the recommendations made by the various college faculties and by the Graduate Faculty for granting of degrees in course to those recipients who have fulfilled the requirements for the appropriate degrees. #20-21-36 #January 27, 2022 Informational Report

passages.heading: Article II – Powers
passages.text: 6. The General Faculty may review decisions made by the Senate. Upon petition to the President of the University signed by 10 percent of the members of the General Faculty, and notice to the President of the Senate, any vote of the Senate shall be submitted to the General Faculty at a meeting that shall be called for that purpose within five (5) weeks after the time of the Senate vote. The President or, in the absence of the President, the Vice President for Academic Affairs will preside. In computation of elapsed time, as provided for in this article, days during the Christmas recess, spring recess, and days between commencement and the first day of registration in the fall semester shall not be counted. (Approved by referendum October 2020) #20-21-5, #21-22-6 (Approved by referendum September 2021)

passages.heading: Article II – Powers
passages.text: The faculty member who originates the objecting petition shall act as chairperson of a committee of the opposition, and shall select at least two other signers of the petition to form a committee of three or more to prepare and lead the presentation of the case for the opposition. The names of this committee shall be published to the General Faculty in the call to the meeting. The meeting shall be conducted according to the same parliamentary authority that governs meetings of the Senate and its committees. Amendments to the Senate act may be adopted at this meeting. No final vote on the decision of the Senate or the version of this decision as amended by the General Faculty shall be taken at this meeting, but voting on this referendum shall be conducted by a secret mail ballot, as prescribed in the By-Laws. A majority of the legal votes cast shall be conclusive, provided that a majority of the General Faculty participates in the referendum. If a majority of the General Faculty do not cast valid votes, the Senate action shall stand as voted.

passages.heading: Article III – Membership
passages.text: 1. The Senate shall consist of designated ex officio members and of elected members of the General faculty, chosen in the approximate ratio of one senator for each 12 full-time faculty members, or a minimum of two senators. In the case of colleges with five or fewer senators, at least half of the senators shall be tenure-track faculty. In the case of colleges with six or more senators, at least two-thirds of the senators shall be tenure-track faculty. Any member of the tenure-track faculty with the rank of professor, associate professor, assistant professor, or instructor may be elected a member of the Senate. Any member of the General Faculty with the rank or title of clinical professor, associate clinical professor, research professor, associate research professor, teaching professor, or associate teaching professor and who has had a full-time academic appointment at the University for a minimum of five continuous years may be elected a member of the Senate. The Senate will provide means by which all eligible faculty members not in a college or the library have the opportunity to vote and to be candidates for election.

passages.heading: Article III – Membership
passages.text: The President, the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs, the Vice Provosts, the Vice Presidents, the deans of the colleges and schools, the Dean of Admissions, the person who served as Senate President during the previous academic year, t he current Retired Faculty Association President or, in the absence of that person, a designee member of the Retired Faculty Association, the current Student Senate President or, in the absence of that person, a designee member of the Student Senate, and the President of the Graduate Student Association or, in the absence of that person, the Vice President of the Graduate Student Association shall be members of the Senate ex officio without the right to vote, but with the right to make and second motions. Other officers of administration, including personnel deans and the directors and assistant directors of the University administrative divisions, shall not be eligible for election to the Senate. #01-02–8 ; #01-02–12 (Approved by referendum, May 2002) #03-04–10 ; #06-07–1 (Approved by referendum, April 2007) ( Approved by referendum March 2015 ) ( Approved by referendum March 2016 ) #17-18-34 (Approved by referendum October 2020) #20-21-5, #20-21-39, #21-22-6 (Approved by referendum September 2021) Administrative Editorial Report 22-23-2 #24-25-17 (Approved by referendum May 2025)

passages.heading: Article IV – Officers
passages.text: 1. The officers of the Senate shall be a Vice President/President-elect and a President. Any tenured member of the Senate may serve as an officer of the Senate. The duties of these officers are those usually associated with the titles of Vice President and President, except as modified or added to in the By-Laws. In the absence of the President, the Vice President/President-elect shall exercise the full powers of the President. These officers shall be elected in accordance with 5.1 of the Senate By-laws. #01-02–12 (Approved by referendum, May 2002) ( Approved by referendum March 2015 ) (Approved by referendum October 2020) #20-21-5, #20-21-39

passages.heading: Article IV – Officers
passages.text: 2. The faculty members serving as Vice President/President-elect and as President of the Faculty Senate shall be entitled to reductions of at least one-third and one-half, respectively, of their normal duties. Normal duties include teaching, assigned research, advisement, committee work, thesis direction and other assigned responsibilities. For this reason, faculty members should consult with their appropriate administrative officers prior to acceptance of nomination for these offices. Entitlement should follow automatically upon election, and no further negotiation would be required except for consultation within the department and college to determine how the reduction might best be accomplished. ( Approved by referendum March 2015 ) (Approved by referendum October 2020) #20-21-5

passages.heading: Article V – Executive Committee
passages.text: 1. The Vice President/President-elect, the President, and four senators elected from the elected membership of the Senate in accordance with 5.1 of the Senate By-laws shall constitute the regular members of an Executive Committee. The person who served as President during the preceding year shall serve as an ex officio Executive Committee member. The President of the Senate shall be President of the Executive Committee. This Committee shall meet on call of the President, or on request of any two of its members. It shall serve as the steering committee of the Senate and shall represent, or designate persons to represent, the Senate in meetings with the President, Board of Trustees, and other University bodies. ( Approved by referendum March 2015 ) (Approved by referendum October 2020) #20-21-5, #20-21-39

passages.heading: Article VI – Meetings
passages.text:
1. Regular meetings of the Senate shall be held at least once a month during the academic year, unless otherwise voted by the Senate.
2. Special meetings may be called upon due notice at any time during the academic year (1) by the President of Senate, (2) upon request by a majority of the Executive Committee, (3) by vote of the Senate at any regular or special meeting, (4) by petition to the President of at least 25 percent of the senators, or (5) by a petition to the President of at least 10 percent of the members of the General Faculty. (Approved by referendum October 2020) #20-21-5
3. Within two weeks after the meeting of the Senate at which the results of elections of new members are announced, a meeting of the newly constituted Senate shall be held. If a date has not already been set for this meeting in the yearly calendar of Senate meetings, the time and place shall be set by the out-going President and Executive Committee. The out-going President shall preside at this meeting. Newly elected officers shall assume their duties at the close of this meeting. Out-going senators shall have no vote. ( Approved by referendum March 2015 ) (Approved by referendum October 2020) #20-21-5

passages.heading: Article VI – Meetings
passages.text: 4. Prior to each meeting the agenda of the business to be conducted must be sent to all members of the General Faculty. Senate meetings shall be open to all members of the faculty, the student body, and the administration. Non-Senate members may address the Senate upon invitation of the presiding officer of the Senate. Procedure is outlined in the By-Laws.

passages.heading: Article VII – Amendment of the Constitution
passages.text:
1. Except as provided in VII/3 and VII/6, amendments shall be proposed to the General Faculty by a majority of the total voting membership of the Senate, and ratified by an affirmative vote of two-thirds of the General Faculty voting on the question, excluding abstentions, as determined by a mail ballot conducted by the Executive Committee and by three tellers appointed by the President of the University. #01-02–21 (Approved by referendum, May 2002) #21-22-11 (Approved by referendum, October, 2021)
2. Balloting shall be conducted in accordance with the By-Laws governing secret balloting. #IFSR 24-25-03

passages.heading: Article VII – Amendment of the Constitution
passages.text: 3. Proposals for changing titles of ex officio members of the Faculty Senate shall be submitted to the Faculty Senate Executive Committee. If in the judgment of the Committee, a title change is of a nature such that incorporating it into the Membership Article (III) of this Constitution does not require a referendum, the Committee shall report this finding to the Faculty Senate, together with a recommendation for an appropriate change of the Membership Article. Unless specified otherwise in the recommendation, the change shall become effective upon a two-thirds majority vote of the senators present and eligible to vote. The recommendation may not be voted upon at the meeting at which it is first moved. #01-02–21 (Approved by referendum, May 2002)

passages.heading: Article VII – Amendment of the Constitution
passages.text:
4. Any member of the Senate may challenge a finding of the Faculty Senate Executive Committee that a change of the title of an ex officio member of the Faculty Senate can be incorporated into the Faculty Senate Constitution without a referendum. Such a challenge may be presented only prior to the actual vote on the change. If the challenge is upheld by a majority of the senators present and eligible to vote, the title change shall be submitted to the referendum process as outlined in Article VII, 1 and 2, of this Constitution. #01-02–21 (Approved by referendum, May, 2002)
5. Changes to the provisions determining Faculty Senate membership can be made only in accordance with the referendum process as outlined in Article VII, 1 and 2, of this Constitution. #01-02–21 (Approved by referendum, May 2002); #06-07–1 (Approved by referendum, April 2007)

passages.heading: Article VII – Amendment of the Constitution
passages.text: 6. Proposed changes to the Constitution deemed editorial by the Constitution, By-Laws and University Manual Committee will be provided as an informational report to the Faculty Senate and will require no action. Following the report, any Faculty Senator may move that a proposed change should be considered substantive. This motion, when seconded, shall then be considered for a vote, and if passed, the matter will be handled as a substantive change, and will follow formal Constitution amendment procedures as provided in VII/1 and VII/2. #21-22-11 (Approved by referendum, October, 2021)

passages.text: Informational Report of the Academic Calendar Committee (ACC) Abraham Kovoor, Chair October 19, 2023 Faculty Senate Meeting The University of Rhode Island has not had a December Commencement Ceremony in the past but will begin to do so this year. The official Academic Calendar should be amended to reflect these dates. It is the position of Enrollment Services, supported by the Calendar Committee, that this alteration is an informational item and thus does not require a formal Faculty Senate vote. Dates to be added are ceremonial and do not affect the academic program. The Calendar Committee has discussed the request and unanimously supports alteration of the Academic Calendar to reflect the new date/s of the December Commencement Ceremony. We ask that the Faculty Senate accept this informational report and consider the described calendar change authorized.

The charge of the Committee shall be to advise the Faculty Senate and the Provost on myriad matters related to Online and Distance Learning from instructional best practices and student learning outcomes to EdTech platforms and faculty professional development.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 4

There was some faculty concern that the new budget model holds the potential to incentivize competition between departments and a ‘race to be first’ in new areas like AI, which could thwart attempts to take a more productive interdisciplinary approach.

Discussion of Advising Day, fall 2027.
Pres.
Williams noted that the approved Fall, 2027 Calendar lists Columbus/Indigenous People’s Day as an 4

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 5
passages.text:
instructional day.
This was done because there had not been a way to accommodate an advising day without using the holiday as a class day.
Nicole King, faculty member in the College of Education noted, joined by several of her colleagues, that the calendar is a values statement and if the university states that its mission is to provide an inclusive and diverse experience for its students, it should honor the holiday.
Senate Vice President Preisser noted that there was precedent for using the holiday as an instructional day when the calendar does not otherwise provide enough instructional days during the fall semester.
Senator Xu (representing COEdu rather than CASC, where she serves as Chair) suggested that legislation could be prepared that would address the use of holidays in priority order (addressing C/IP Day, Veteran’s Day, Wednesday before Thanksgiving) that could be employed as needed.
She volunteered to help draft a bill that could be introduced in April.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 5
passages.text:
ACC Chair Donnelly explained that such legislation would be welcome, but the preparers should bear in mind that in some years, there simply are not enough days between Labor Day and the end of the term, and a holiday will need to be sacrificed in order to secure an adequate number of class meetings. ii.
Discussion of spring 2026 late semester adjustments - Pres.
Williams explained that the four snow days experienced so far this year mean that the university must consider adding a day of instruction (make-up day for Monday classes).
He outlined four options that included such possibilities as using a Saturday for instruction or exams, asynchronous instruction on Reading Day, and starting and ending exams a day later than the published calendar currently reflects.
There was considerable debate and it was noted that some disciplines and modalities are more impacted than others.
It was further noted that doing nothing (leaving the calendar as-is) is also an option.
Faculty were invited to share their preferences and rationals with Faculty Senate leaders and the Provost’s office.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 5
passages.text:
Any change to the calendar at this point would be subject to a vote by the senate, either at the April meeting or before that via special called session (virtual), with confirmation by the full Senate to follow. g.

The affected language was introduced.
In brief, the Ombuds office provides independent, impartial, informal, and confidential resources for faculty, staff, and students; to address concerns, conflicts, and systemic issues.
Ombuds are guided by the International Ombuds Association Standards of Practice and their office would be structurally housed under the office of the University President. 5

FACULTY SENATE OFFICE 224 P ASTORE H ALL , 51 L OWER C OLLEGE R OAD , K INGSTON , R I 02881 U SA , P: 401.874.2616 MINUTES FACULTY SENATE MEETING Thursday, April 16, 2026 3:00 p.m. - 5:00 p.m.
In Person Hope Room - Higgins Welcome Center Remote option via ZOOM 1.
Call to order of the General Faculty - Graduate Faculty meeting by President Parlange at 3:02 pm. 2.
Call to order of the Faculty Senate Meeting immediately following the General Faculty - Graduate Faculty Meeting by Faculty Senate President Williams.
All Senators were on hand except Senators Burns, Deng, Ghonem, Liu, Lundy, Martin, Matson, Porto,Thomas, Zhang, and Yuan (sabbatical).
Ex officio members and others in attendance included: President Parlange, Vice Provost Adams, Vice Provost Johnson, VP’s Reynolds, Jenkins, Benson, Mello, Associate VP’s Libutti and Lavan, Deans Dennis, VanderGheynst, Meyerand, LaPlante, and DeBoef, Past President Walls, and RFA Representative Honhart. a.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 1
passages.text:
SPECIAL REMEMBRANCE of Faculty Member, Faculty Senator, and General Education Committee Chair Kathy Quick - Faculty Senate President Travis Williams paid tribute to former GEC Chair and A&S faculty member Kathy Quick, and he read a statement from her Department of Art and Art History colleagues who could not be present.
The statements emphasized the jolt and collective sorrow experienced by the community with the loss of a colleague in the prime of their career.
Chair Quick’s strong work ethic, willingness to serve and to lead, and her thoughtfulness and good nature will be missed by all, students, faculty, and staff alike. 3.
REPORT OF THE UNIVERSITY PRESIDENT/OTHER ADMINISTRATORS a.
Updates and Announcements - President Parlange thanked all faculty who participated in URI Day at the Statehouse, as well as other recent events, like World Quantum Day.
Faculty were reminded that Budget Model Town Halls are ongoing in the Colleges, and other notable events, like the Excellence Awards and the annual Day of Giving, are also coming up this month.
The spring commencement ceremonies are set for May 15 - 17 and all faculty are strongly encouraged to participate.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 1
passages.text:
President Parlange provided a brief update on the proposed Medical School, noting the initiative has moved into ‘Phase 2 of exploration,’ which involves detailed financial feasibility investigations, analysis of existing gaps in service provision and training pipelines, and other studies and assessments.
He also provided a brief update on his and VP Abby Benson’s efforts to ‘undo’ the state-imposed cap on FTE’s at URI, which has been in place for far too long. 1

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 2
passages.text:
b.
Administrative Report on UM Chapter 5 - amends Sec. 5.41.11 to update the Space Allocation Committee for alignment with current practice - The report was tabled pending possible revisions. c.
Report on results of College of Education Dean Dennis’ evaluation, consistent with Chapter 10 of the University Manual. (Sec. 10.90.15) A point of order was raised about the senate’s authority to hear the report but it was overruled.
Vice Provost Adams, filling in for Provost Wolfe, provided a summary of the evaluation, noting results were generally favorable across all metrics. d.
Presidential Administrative Report on Chapter 2 with related additions to Chapter 9 of the University Manual.
Vice Provost Adams presented the report, noting it had been introduced and discussed at the January 22, 2026 meeting.
The legislation was moved, seconded, and approved. e.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 2
passages.text:
Status of Actions Forwarded to the President: ● The following Bills were signed by President Parlange on 3/18/26 ○ Curriculum & Standards Committee Bill #25-26-6B ○ Graduate Council (GC) Bill #25-26-5B ○ FSEC Bills #25-26-10 and#25-26-11 ○ Administrator Bill #25-26-02 ○ CASC Bill #25-26-6C and GC Bill #25-26-5C, which require final approval by the Board of Trustees. 4.
REPORTS OF OFFICERS AND THE EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE a.
Announcements - Faculty Senate President Williams i.
Today’s reception is being sponsored by the College of Pharmacy - Thank you Dean LaPlante! ii.
Call for Nominations: At the October Faculty Senate meeting, Sens.
Kendall Moore, William Krieger, and Alison Roberts were chosen as this year’s Nominating Committee.
Per Section 5.2 of the Senate By-Laws, the Nominating Committee shall prepare a slate of candidates for one (1) one-year and two (2) two-year vacancies on the Executive Committee.
The Executive Committee Election shall be held May 7, 2026 .
Please reach out to a member of the Nominating Committee if you are interested in this role. iii.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 2
passages.text:
Announcement regarding making rooms available to rent to grad students - VP Preisser offered a reminder about concerns recently shared by the Graduate Student Association related to the temporary closure of Graduate Village.
Dozens of students remain on a waitlist for housing.
In an effort to ensure that all enrolled students have access to appropriate housing, FSEC encourages faculty and staff, especially those who live in close proximity to campus, to consider offering a room to rent.
VP Preisser encouraged faculty to spread the word, and suggested that they explore relevant housing webpages or reach out to him directly for more information. iv. ‘All-hands’ curriculum meeting prior to the start of fall semester 2026 - VP Preisser announced that the Faculty Senate and Vice Provost Adams are co-hosting a mandatory meeting on September 1, at 1 pm, aimed at improving curriculum proposal quality and review process consistency in Kuali.
The meeting would be required for Deans and Associate Deans who have approval roles in the CMS and it is strongly recommended that the faculty chairs of college-level curriculum 2

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 3
passages.text:
committees also attend.
More information will be forthcoming but affected parties need to make sure this meeting is in their calendars. b.
Disposition of the Minutes - Faculty Senate President Williams i.
Minutes of the Faculty Senate Meeting of 3/12/26 were approved. c.
Activities of the Executive Committee - Senate Vice President Preisser noted the important work of FSEC reflected in the following minutes.
There were no questions. i.
Executive Committee Meetings of March 6, March 13, and March 27, 2026 meetings. (No meeting on 3/20 due to Spring Break.) d.
Recommendations of the Faculty Senate Executive Committee: FSEC recommends the following bills: i.
Approval of Faculty Senate Meeting Calendar for AY 2026-2027.
Pres.
Williams noted that FSEC has recommended a meeting calendar that prioritizes ‘third Thursdays’ for consistency, while avoiding holidays, breaks, and cultural or religious celebrations that preclude work.
The calendar was approved. ii.
Bill 2025-2026-FSEC-09: Amendments to UM 5.78.10 - 5.78.12 regarding the Joint Committee on Online and Distance Learning - Continued from the 2/19/26 And 3/12/26 meetings.
Pres.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 3
passages.text:
Williams noted the proposal had been discussed by the faculty senate at previous meetings and is now offered for approval.
It was moved to the senate docket for action by FSEC and was seconded.
Questions were raised from the floor about some particulars of the bill and FSEC members responded.
Comments were also offered from the floor noting one senator’s outstanding concerns about the bill as written.
A motion was made to table the bill in its entirety.
Pres.
Williams noted a motion to table is not debatable or amendable and requires a ⅔ majority for approval.
The motion to table passed. iii.
Ratification of appointment to the Space Allocation Committee: Leon Thiem , representing the College of Engineering.
A motion to ratify was approved. iv.
FSEC Bill 2025-2026-12 regarding precluding use of the Veteran’s Day holiday as an instructional day - VP Preisser noted that while State and Federal calendars list Veteran’s Day as a holiday, language in the University Manual does not preclude its use as an instructional day.
FSEC sought to clear up any confusion via the proposed amendment, which was moved for action by FSEC and seconded from the floor.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 3
passages.text:
College of Education senators inquired whether or not the current proposal was the result of their petition last month to amend the University Manual to preclude the use of Indigenous People’sDay/Columbus (IP/C) Day as an instructional day.
VP Preisser answered affirmatively, explaining that the detailed review of UM Sec. 8.70.25 that occurred with their proposal marked the first time the ACC, CBUM and FSEC had all taken an in-depth look at the relevant language in quite some time, and the question of Veteran’s Day seemed to warrant clarification independent of what happens with the IP/C Day legislation, which is still under consideration.
In response to further questions, VP Preisser confirmed 3

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 4
passages.text:
that approval of the subject bill does not preclude approval of the IP/C Day bill, but he acknowledged that the constrained number of available instructional days in certain fall semesters certainly makes the Calendar Committee’s work more challenging. 5.
SPECIAL REPORTS : a.
Bill 2025-2026-Joint-01, a joint proposal of the University Administration, FSEC, and the SCLC regarding reorganization of the Office of the University Ombuds.
Faculty Senate President Williams explained that the proposal was the result of work done by multiple committees and individuals over the course of more than a year.
Also, the plan to professionalize the Office of the Ombuds had been discussed at previous senate meetings, including, most recently, the March 12 meeting.
With no further questions or discussion, there was a motion and second to approve the proposal.
The motion was approved. b.
Student Senate Resolution on Accessible Education Material, as approved by the Student Senate on March 25, 2026.
Tabled. c.
Kuali pause for proposal submissions, summer 2026 - Faculty Senate Specialist Spitale, FSEC member Trimm, and Enrollment Services Assoc.
Director Humphrey.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 4
passages.text:
Specialist Spitale explained that a pause in new Kuali submissions is planned for the summer months to allow system administrators the opportunity to make much-needed updates to workflows and user experience features.
All proposals entered by 5/15 will still advance through the approval process to the Dean-level of review.
Any proposal not approved by the relevant dean by 6/1 will revert to draft form.
Such drafts will remain in the system and will still be viewable, but will need to be resubmitted at a later date to advance toward approval.
Normal proposal submission procedures and workflows will resume on 8/15.
Additional information is available via the Curriculum Toolkit on the Faculty Senate’s webpage.
Questions from the floor were offered, including inquiries about the degree to which suggestions from the various college curriculum committees factor into the update.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 4
passages.text:
It was noted that the current effort is focused more on compliance with the curricular streamlining initiative approved by the faculty senate earlier this year, but it is hoped that this year’s initiative will lay the groundwork for future short pauses wherein incremental process improvements like those that would be suggested by the curriculum committees might be made. 6.
REPORTS OF STANDING AND SPECIAL COMMITTEES a.
Curriculum and Standards Committee - Chair Furong Xu was on hand to field questions about the reports.
The following were advanced by the Committee, seconded from the floor, and approved. i.
Bill No. 2025-2026-07A, Courses, covering one new temporary course and fifteen new permanent courses, as well as numerous course modifications across five colleges. ii.

passages.text:
iii.

Bill 2025-2026-06A, Courses, covering multiple course modifications across seven colleges, along with several new courses in the the Colleges of Arts and Sciences, Business, Education, Engineering, Pharmacy, and the College of the Environment and Life Sciences. ii.

Tabled to the May 7 meeting. d.
Teaching, Advising, and Admissions Committee Annual Report- Chair Romanow praised her fellow committee members and noted they have had a very busy and productive year.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 5
passages.text:
The TAAC was involved in the review and approval of several key pieces of legislation this year, including the creation of a President’s List and modernizing the Second Grade Option.
They were also involved in the curricular streamlining initiative and the reconfiguration of the Honors Program.
As a result of legislation approved last year, the Committee now has a role to play in Admissions and is still determining, with AVP Libutti’s help, how that new charge will be implemented.
In terms of future priorities, the Committee has been tasked with looking at UM provisions related to academic dishonesty, especially where it intersects with grade disputes.
The Committee hopes to craft relevant amendments for consideration next year. e.
Budget and Administration Committee Annual Report - Chair Triki explained that his committee’s primary task this year has been to try to measure faculty sentiment toward the new budget mode via a survey distributed broadly to the community.
As of now, the Committee intends, according to Chair Triki, to share their results with the Financial Strategy and Planning Office so that a conversation about improving messaging might be had.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 5
passages.text:
It has not yet been decided how the data collected might otherwise be shared or disseminated.
Based on the survey results, the Committee had concluded that there seems to be a serious disconnect between the actual outcomes of the budget model roll-out and the faculty’s perception of those outcomes.
As examples, a majority of those surveyed did not see the new model as improving transparency or ensuring a more fair allocation of resources across colleges.
Chair Triki suggested that expanding dissemination of information about the details and mechanics of the budget might result in more positive perceptions.
VP Jenkins asked if current sentiment around higher education generally might have colored the survey results.
She enumerated several recent and ongoing concerns and challenges facing universities around the country (constrained research funding, various Federal actions, outside influence and interference in curricular matters, etc.) and suggested that the current landscape likely has a negative ‘baseline mood’ undercurrent that would be hard to measure.
Chair Triki agreed that the survey probably did roll out at an unfortunate time for measuring faculty understanding and satisfaction.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 5
passages.text: He noted that one positive takeaway from the results 5

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 6
passages.text: was the degree to which faculty are engaged and paying attention, and he praised their resilience in the face of unrelenting bad news. f. Committee on Technology and Infrastructure Annual Report - Chair Wallace noted the many projects his committee tackled this year, including providing input to improve Brightspace and EdTech operations, helping to recreate a searchable classroom database, and suggesting strategies for improving the IT contracts/software approval process. They also provided important outreach to faculty about their roles in website editing, and helped raise awareness about current IT Policies. Priorities for next year will include understanding faculty needs and habits around responsible AI use in research, and aiding in Brightspace file recovery and migration, among other things. 7. Assessment reports are evaluated during an intensive 3-day summer retreat, following a 3-day trainingand norming session for faculty peer reviewers using faculty teams and a third level of oversight toreview reports.
Ten faculty served on peer review teams (2023) for the first round of review (Level 1);each reviewer then served as an independent reviewer (Level 2) for all reports providing oversight toensure consistency in the review and scoring process.
Scoring rubrics guide report review of assessmentreport templates (accredited, non-accredited, interim).

passages.heading: LOOC Annual Report, December, 2023 | Page 5
passages.text:
To meet expectations in reporting, allnon-accredited and accredited program reports are expected to achieve a score of “Satisfactory”.
Programs exceeding expectations are recognized for their excellence in assessment practice.
It isimportant to note that rubric scores assigned by peer reviewers reflect neither a judgment of instructorsnor the student learning results revealed during the assessment process, but rather, all scores reflect thelevel of achievement of programs in their effort to use best practices and processes to conductassessment in order to yield valuable results.
The results of outcomes assessment are intended strictlyfor use by academic programs for curricular or assessment process improvement.
The use of a peer review process and a rubric scoring tool provides the opportunity to identify facultyand programs undertaking best practices in learning outcomes assessment.
The recognition of excellencein reporting is currently available for non-accredited undergraduate and graduate programs.

passages.heading: LOOC Annual Report, December, 2023 | Page 5
passages.text:
This doesnot diminish the content nor effort of accredited programs to report, but reflects the streamlinedaccredited report template which requires summary content and metrics that are typically readilyavailable, rather than the reporting on a program of the authentic assessment of student learning.

Annual Report (2024-25) Joint Committee for Academic Program Review and Outcomes Assessment (JCAPROA) Members: Mehdi Hossain (Chair), Kathy Peno, Roberta King, Disa Hatfield, Jung Eun Lee, Christopher Kincaid, Shane Tutwiler, Jennifer Jones, Theodore Walls, Sen.
Sumanta Das, Angela Google, Ashley Buchanan, Christopher Lavan, Elaine Finan, John Stringer, Rachel DiCioccio This report provides highlights of the committee’s work through the 2024-25 academic year.
JCAPROA was formed in late Spring 2024.
The committee combines the previous Academic Program Review Committee and the Learning Outcomes Assessment Committee.

passages.heading: Committee Report, May, 2025 | Page 1
passages.text:
The charges to the committee are as follows: According to the University Manual at sections 5.84.10 – 5.84.14, this committee is responsible for: (1) developing policies for URI student learning outcomes assessment, data distribution, and measurement frequency at the university-wide level, with the Faculty Senate’s and the Provost’s approval; (2) developing an ongoing review of the learning outcomes assessment process, interpreting external expectations for university-wide learning outcomes assessment, including those of accreditation bodies, and facilitating internal communication across units regarding way of meeting those expectations, and (3) guiding the implementation and revision of the Academic Program Review process (sections 8.86.10 – 8.86.14) and serving as a resource to departments and programs being reviewed.
The committee shall also develop an ongoing review of the learning outcomes assessment process, interpret external expectations for university-wide learning outcomes assessment, including those of accreditation bodies and facilitate internal communication across units regarding ways of meeting those expectations.

passages.heading: Committee Report, May, 2025 | Page 1
passages.text:
In the beginning 3 months of the committees work which involves April-May, and September 2024, the committee deliberated on the scopes of the work and developing clarity around the charges.
Through such deliberations the committee developed the following goals and subsequent objectives to be pursued over a period of three years.
GOAL 1: SEAMLESS INTEGRATION OF THE ACADEMIC PROGRAM REVIEW AND THE LEARNING OUTCOMES ASSESSMENT PROCESS.
Objective 1: Revision of the learning outcome assessment process.
Action point 1: Reflection on the design of an ideal assessment process.
Action point 2: Determine appropriate revision of the process towards an ideal process.
Action point 3: Conduct appropriate revision of the process for its integration with APR.

passages.heading: Committee Report, May, 2025 | Page 2
passages.text:
Objective 2: Revision of the academic program review process for necessary integration of the learning outcomes assessment.
Action point 1: Reflect on the current program review process and identify scopes for improvements.
Action point 2: Reflect on ways to facilitate the integration of the learning outcomes assessment with academic program review.
Action point 3: Implement changes to the APR process for the integration of learning outcomes assessment.
GOAL 2: INCREASE TRANSPARENCY AND ACCESSIBILITY IN THE ACADEMIC PROGRAM REVIEW AND THE LEARNING OUTCOMES ASSESSMENT PROCESSES.
Objective 1: Increasing faculty, staff and student participation in APR and LOO processes.
Action point 1: Reflect on maximizing faculty, staff, and student participation in academic program review and outcomes assessment.
Action point 2: Implement the above in consultation with teams 1 and 2.
Objective 2: Content development and management (Notifications regarding program review/ JAPROA website management/FAQ document/Creating templates) Action point 1: Timely notification to relevant departments and programs for self-study.
Action point 2: Curate and update contents on JCAPROA website periodically.

passages.heading: Committee Report, May, 2025 | Page 2
passages.text:
Action point 3: Develop a FAQ document for program review and outcomes assessment.
Action point 4: Develop evaluation rubric for academic program review reports.
In fall 2024, the committee identified that the departments who were supposed to be notified for their APR in Spring 2024 were not in fact notified.
The committee deliberated to create an off-cycle timeline for the department who were disadvantaged.
The timeline was adopted unanimously by the committee.
Also, the committee offered a training/information session to respective department chairs on the APR process in December 2024.
In early Spring 2025, the committee sent out notifications to the departments who are going up for APR review.
The committee also offered training/information session on the APR process to the departments going up for review.

passages.heading: Committee Report, May, 2025 | Page 3
passages.text: In Spring 2025, the major focus of the committee has been to develop a comprehensive handbook for the APR process. This is motivated by the fact that in the past departments who were going up for review struggled to find all the information about the process and the timeline in one place. In this effort, the committee reviewed APR handbooks from other esteemed institutions and decided to model URIs handbook after that of The Ohio State University. This handbook is being developed to compile all the process documents in one place and make necessary additions to the processes. In this effort, the committee adopted a division of labor approach and divided the entire committee into 4 sub-groups. A team leader was assigned to each team who led the effort for specific sections of the team. We are happy to report that we now have a good preliminary draft of the handbook that will soon be posted on a Brightspace repository and be made accessible to the departments going up for review. During fall 2024, the committee also updated the APR schedule that keeps track of the cycles of review for specific departments and programs. It has been a tremendous team effort and a functional joint committee with voluntary and enthusiastic participation from all.

Daniels and Meyerson were elected by electronic ballot.
Sen.

Recommendations of the Faculty Senate Executive Committee i.
