passages.text:
Bill 2025-2026-FSEC-09: Amendments to UM 5.78.10 - 5.78.12 regarding the Joint Committee on Online and Distance Learning - Continued from the 2/19/26, 3/12/26, and 4/16/26 meetings.
A motion to approve the bill was seconded and debate was managed by VP Preisser.
Senate President Williams offered an overview of the bill and its travel to the senate floor.
A question was raised from the floor by a senator from Engineering who noted he had provided a memo outlining seven specific concerns with the bill that he would like addressed individually.
Not all voting senators had seen the memo, which was very detailed, however.
Vice Provost Adams spoke in favor of the proposal as drafted, noting that a committee had worked collaboratively for almost two 2

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 3
passages.text:
years on the draft, with a special eye toward accreditation standards and best practices in online education.
The first of the seven proposed amendments was discussed in detail and a motion was made to make the language change that it recommended, but it was not approved.
A subsequent motion was made to table the proposal, along with the six remaining suggested amendments.
As part of the motion, it was noted that the areas of concern addressed by the memo deserved serious consideration.
The motion to table was approved. ii.
Bill 2025-2026-FSEC-13: Amendments to UM 8.60.10 - 8.65.12 regarding the Honors Program.
Senate President Williams explained the proposal, noting that the legislation is designed to bring the University Manual into alignment with the the restructuring of Honors that was approved by the Faculty Senate back on January 22, 2026 (Bill #2025-2026-TAAC-01).
The FSEC and Honors Program Directors worked on the bill together and it had been reviewed by TAAC and CBUM.
The bill was moved by the FSEC, seconded from the floor and approved. 4.
REPORT OF THE PRESIDENT and OTHER ADMINISTRATORS a.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 3
passages.text:
President’s Remarks - President Parlange noted several recent events, including the April 30 Academic Excellence Awards Ceremony and the success of the URI Day of Giving, during which the overall fundraising goal was exceeded.
It was also announced that the university had set a new record in terms of new applications for enrollment and the overall economic impact of the university on the state of RI is currently estimated at over $2 billion.
The President reminded all faculty that they are strongly encouraged to participate in commencement ceremonies coming up May 15 - 17 and he made a special point of thanking outgoing Faculty Senate President Travis Williams, whom he praised as a strong, diplomatic, and effective leader. b.
Status of Actions Forward to the President: i.
The following bills were signed by the President on 05/06/26. ● Curriculum & Standards Committee Bill #25-26-07B and 7C ● Graduate Council Bill #25-26-06B ● Joint Bill #25-26-01, Reorganization of the Office of the Ombuds ● Faculty Senate Executive Committee Bill #25-26-12, regarding use of Veteran’s Day as an instructional day. ● Administrative Report on UM Chapter 2 and related Chapter 9 amendments. c.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 3
passages.text:
Administrative Report on UM Chapter 5 - amends Secs 5.41.10 and 5.41.11 to update the Space Allocation Committee for alignment with current practice.
Senate President Williams explained the bill, noting that it was administrative in nature, designed to bring Manual language into comportment with current practices in terms of the committee’s charge and composition, and it will also update or correct various titles and roles.
Vice President Benson was on hand to support the bill.
There was a motion 3

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 4
passages.text:
and second to accept the report and update the University Manual accordingly.
The motion was unanimously supported. d.
Annual Athletics Presentation - Vice President and Director of Athletics Pat Lyons introduced his co-presenters, including student athletes and Associate Athletics Directors.
The presentation began with a snapshot of the academic performance of the student athletes and it was noted that the 2025 cumulative gpa for URI athletes was the highest ever achieved.
Several teams were highlighted for their strong conference finishes, especially the women’s basketball, men’s football, and track and field teams.
Updates were provided on various facilities upgrades, including to the track and field complex and Meade Stadium, along with a summary of NCAA compliance issues, ongoing fundraising initiatives, and athlete development issues like mental health, financial literacy, and sports gambling training. 5.

Faculty Senate Awards i.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 4
passages.text:
Presentation of the Fritz Wenisch Award for Exceptional Contribution to the Faculty Senate - President Williams announced that this year’s winner is Furong Xu (College of Education), who served as this year’s Curriculum and Standards Committee (CASC) Chair.
The presentation included details about CASC’s record number of proposals processed this year.
The task would have been made immensely more challenging but for Chair Xu’s ability to keep atop myriad details, organize information and meetings so as to come to good decisions, and communicate well with colleagues.
As a result, CASC was a remarkably productive committee this year, due in large part to Sen.
Xu’s smooth and skillful handling of the process, during which her good humor and collegiality never waned. ii.
Presentation of the Sheila Black Grubman Faculty Outstanding Service Award - President Williams presented the award to Douglass Reed (Arts and Sciences, Philosophy), who served as Administrator Evaluation Coordinator (AEC) for the past two years.
Pres.
Williams highlighted Dr.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 4
passages.text:
Reed’s spirit of ‘calm industriousness’ that he brought to the AEC role and noted that he received praise from his colleagues for his diplomacy, tact, and resourcefulness.
Pres.
Williams further noted that before being appointed as AEC, Dr.
Reed had served in the Faculty Senate on the Teaching, Advising and Assessment Committee (TAAC) and had brought the same ambitious and proactive energy to that role.
Concluding his remarks, Pres.
Williams noted that in addition to today’s award, Dr.
Reed is a 2022 Arts and Sciences Teaching Excellence Winner and also winner of the URI Excellence in General Education Award for 2026. 6.

Announcement of Election Results - See item 3c above. b.
Curriculum and Standards Committee - Chair Xu was on hand to field questions about the reports.

Bill No. 2025-2026-08C, covering the new BS in Interdisciplinary Artificial Intelligence proposed by the College of Business.
An objection was raised by a Senator from the Department of Computer Science and Statistics, who asserted that their department had not been given an opportunity to comment on possible overlap.
A second question was raised about the extent to which ethics will be addressed by the new program and it was suggested that ethical use of AI should be integrated.
CASC Chair Xu noted that her committee has a duty to address overlap, but typically, by the time a proposal reaches CASC, overlap should have been addressed or resolved at the level of the department and college curriculum committees.
In the subject case, appropriate documentation from the affected colleges was included. c.

The following were advanced by the Committee, seconded from the floor, and approved. i.
Bill 2025-2026-07A, Courses, covering several course changes across multiple colleges, and new courses in the Colleges of Arts and Sciences, Engineering, and the Environment and Life Sciences. ii.

Centers and Institutes Review Committee Report - The CIRC is required to present annually on any new Centers and Institutes and on the rechartering status of other C/I’s reviewed.
Committee member Julia Lovett presented the report, thanking her fellow committee members and highlighting their key accomplishments.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 5
passages.text:
In addition to reviewing three existing centers for renewal and authorizing creation of a new Institute, the Committee also worked to revise their forms in light of recent legislation, provided feedback on proposed University Manual language in Chapter 8, Section 90, and continued their tracking and oversight functions per their charge, among other things.
A motion to accept the report was made, seconded and approved. 5

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 6
passages.text:
f.
Research and Creative Activities Committee (CRCA) and SubCommittee Reports – Chair D’Agata thanked the members of her committee and reviewed the committee’s charge.
Highlights of AY 25-26 activities included providing support to faculty during an era of rapid change in the research environment.
The Committee had also prioritized supporting graduate students who faced unique and exacerbating housing and other financial challenges this year.
The Committee has outlined proposed changes to its scope, structure, and strategic alignment with institutional governance over research functions which they hope to formalize during AY 26-27.
Subcommittee Chair Wei also thanked fellow committee members, as well as the volunteer reviewers who assisted in reading and ranking applications for Career Enhancement, Proposal Development, and Collaborative Research Development grants.
Proposals were due in January and awards were announced on April 6.
A total of 51 submissions were received (significantly higher than in recent years) and 18 were awarded.
In looking ahead to next year, the Committee noted a need for more reviewers if the number of applications exceeds expectations again.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 6
passages.text:
They also noted a need for more explicit guidance to be provided to both proposers and reviewers, which would help to streamline and improve consistency across submissions and evaluations.
The reports were accepted. g.
General Education Committee (GEC) Report - GEC Acting Chair Stark explained that the Committee was focused on assessing the C2 (Global Responsibilities) and D1 (Integrate and Apply) outcomes this year.
An ongoing challenge with outcomes assessment for the committee continues to be participation in the process, with only between 13 and 37 percent of relevant courses participating this year.
The low level of participation constrains the degree to which conclusions about findings can be drawn.
The results seemed stronger for the D1 outcome than the C2, as students more often approach competency in the D1 areas.
Students assessed for C2 outcomes consistently struggle with communicating in a language other than English, considering multiple perspectives, and examining global responsibilities.
Questions from the floor centered around C2 findings and whether they represent a structural weakness in foreign language proficiency within the current GenEd framework.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 6
passages.text:
Chair Stark, Associate Teaching Professor in Languages, suggested that it appears to be so.
He advocated for treating language proficiency as a central pathway to achieving the university’s goals, rather than as optional enrichment for students.
The report was accepted. 7.
NEW BUSINESS - A Senator from the College of Business moved that Bill CASC 8c, introduced and tabled earlier in the agenda, be revisited.
The motion was seconded.
Several senators spoke from the floor before the question was called.
Points made included the fact that practices differ from department to department in terms of how engaged faculty are on curricular proposals from outside their own college or department, and the degree to which they actually get a voice in advancing those proposals.
It was also noted that the community is likely ripe for a forum or larger conversation with faculty about how best to integrate AI across the curriculum at the university.
Pres.
Williams called for a vote on whether or not to lay the issue back on the table for substantive consideration.
The motion to reconsider was defeated. 6

Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation By The Faculty Senate NEW CERTIFICATES OR SPECIALIZATIONS COLLEGE OF HEALTH SCIENCE Human Development and Family Science ABM, Effective Fall 2025 Appendix A An accelerated Bachelor’s to Master of Science Program is available through a competitive admissions process for students enrolled as a major or minor in Human Development and Family Science.
Students who are admitted and complete the ABM-HDF Program will earn a Bachelor's degree and a Master's of Science in Human Development and Family Science with a Prevention Science emphasis by adding one additional year to their academic plan.
Nine credits of approved HDF undergraduate courses will be counted towards students’ Bachelor’s degree and their HDF Master’s degree.

Overview.
There is renewed interest in ocean acoustics due to undersea defense applications as well as concerns about the effects of anthropogenic noise (e.g., from offshore wind farms) on marine animals.
The US Navy recently began a five-year, $2.4 billion investment in industrial base and workforce development support, including nearly $750 million in FY23 for the submarine industrial base.
In the realm of offshore renewable energy, the US has a goal of installing 30 gigawatts of offshore wind farms by 2030, or enough to power more than 10 million homes for a year.
One of the major objectives of the graduate certificate is to provide an option for students from engineering, oceanography, or other fields who would like to have graduate preparation in ocean acoustics.
Many of the courses below are already offered in a hybrid mode indicated by the asterisks.
We propose that an adequate number of hybrid courses be available for this certificate.
A concern for the public and environmentalists is the ocean noise impact of wind farm construction on marine mammals and fish.
Both the defense and offshore wind industries need people with expertise in ocean acoustics.

INFORMATIONAL MATTERS TEMPORARY COURSE COLLEGE OF ARTS & SCIENCES: THE262X | Introduction to Theatre Production Technologies, Spring 2026 (3 crs.) Introduces to technologies utilized within theatrical production, including processes, equipment, system configurations, and basic operations of lighting, audio, and video systems. Base CAD fundamentals are also covered. (Lec. 2/Lab. 2) FOR CONFIRMATION BY THE FACULTY SENATE COURSE MODIFICATIONS COLLEGE OF ARTS & SCIENCES: ART364 | American Art, Spring 2026 Change course description (3 crs.) Emphasis placed on the construction of US -American mythologies, identities, and the legacies of colonialism, slavery, oppression, abolition, and resistance. (Lec. 3)

passages.heading: 2025-2026-SSCC-02A | Page 3
passages.text:
BIS325 | Leadership, Power, and Opression, Spring 2026 Change home college, modality, academic career, prerequisites (3 crs.) Explore the culturally relevant leadership learning (CRLL) model.

(Accelerated Online Program) COLLEGE OF HEALTH SCIENCES: HLT201 | Contemporary Public Health Challenges in the US, Spring 2026 Change title, prerequisites (3 crs.) This course is designed to introduce students to current and controversial public health challenges.
Students will be required to explore the implications of numerous current topics from a public health perspective. (Lec. 3) Pre: HLT101G, for Public Health majors only.
COLLEGE OF PHARMACY: PHP201 | Introduction to the U.S.
Healthcare Systems, Fall 2026 Change description, add general education outcomes A2 and C1 (3 crs.) This course introduces the student to the U.S. health care system, and explores how cost, quality and access dynamics impact patients and other stakeholders.

(Accelerated Online Program) Pre: Credit in one PHL course. (B2) (C3)

FOR CONFIRMATION BY THE FACULTY SENATE PROGRAM MODIFICATIONS COLLEGE OF ARTS & SCIENCES: BIS – Bachelor of Interdisciplinary Studies, Spring 2026 Appendix A Students coming in with 24 credits will be able to complete their degree (120 credits) with courses available in the accelerated online degree completion programs, credit for prior learning, and general education. COLLEGE OF NURSING: BS – Accelerated Online R.N. to B.S., Spring 2026 Appendix B - Accelerated online version of existing in-person RN to BS degree program. The University of Rhode Island College of Nursing’s Accelerated Online R.N. to B.S. program is dedicated to providing an education that will broaden your view of the world and create opportunities to transform healthcare in your own community. Building upon your clinical experience, the R.N. to B.S. program expands your scientific knowledge base, giving you a set of skills that allows you to integrate clinical practice, scientific inquiry and critical, creative thinking. You’ll graduate fully prepared for a whole new world of healthcare opportunities. Progression and Graduation Requirements Students are expected to achieve a C or higher in all required courses. In addition, students must maintain a minimum GPA of 2.2 to progress through and graduate from the College of Nursing.

passages.text: Students who achieve less than a grade of C must repeat the course, obtaining a C grade or higher, before progressing in the nursing curriculum. Permission to retake the course will be granted on a space-available basis only. Even if successfully repeated, the initial grade remains on record as the first unsuccessful attempt. There are no further allowances for repeating a NUR course, and any subsequent NUR coursework of C- or below will result in dismissal. If the student should achieve a C- or less in two NUR courses in a single session or semester, he or she will be immediately dismissed from the College of Nursing. A total of 120 credits is required to earn a B.S. in Nursing. This includes program specific courses as well as general education requirements. R.N. to B.S. A grade of C or higher is required in each of these courses. General Education. All College of Nursing Students must meet the University's General Education requirements. General education consists of 40 credits. For more details regarding General Education, please go to the Academic Requirements and Policies section of this catalog.

passages.text: PROGRAM REPORT SPECIAL SUMMER CURRICULUM COMMITTEE Report 2025-2026-01B At the June 17, 2025 meeting of the Special Summer Curriculum Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate for approval. FOR CONFIRMATION BY THE FACULTY SENATE PROGRAM MODIFICATIONS COLLEGE OF ARTS & SCIENCES: Specialization – Creative Writing (English BA), Fall 2025 Appendix A Adding course options Specialization – Literature (English BA), Fall 2025 Appendix B Adding course options NEW PROGRAMS COLLEGE OF HEALTH SCIENCES: Minor – Communicative Disorders, Fall 2025 Appendix C The CMD Minor is designed for students in related programs (e.g., communications, education, psychology, human development and family sciences, health sciences) who are interested in learning more about the typical development and use of speech, language, hearing, and other communicative processes across the lifespan. Students completing the minor will have completed most of the prerequisites required for graduate study in speech-language pathology.

passages.text: In addition to fulfilling all the basic requirements for a minor (see Minor Fields of Study), students who declare a minor in CMD must complete the following courses: CMD160, CMD272, CMD273, CMD276, CMD375, and one of the following: CMD460, CMD493G, CMD494. Minor – Public Health, Fall 2025 Appendix D In addition to fulfilling all the basic requirements for a minor (see Minor Fields of Study), students who declare a minor in public health must complete the following requirements: Requirements include 20 credits. All courses must be taken for a grade, and an average grade of 2.00, unless otherwise specified (e.g., HLT 201, 300, and 450 require a grade of "C" or better, in line with the minimum grade requirements for the major). To declare this minor, a student must have the approval of a program advisor and an academic advisor. Core courses (4 courses): HLT101, HLT201, HLT300 (4 credits), and PHP405 (4 credits). Electives: Select two courses from the following: HLT312, HLT313, HLT320, HLT350, HLT360, HLT400, HLT401, HLT450; PHP201; NUT212G (prerequisite NUT207). Other public health-related courses, such as courses in the MPH program, may be used to fulfill minor r equirements with approval from the Department Chair.

***Agenda for Change link is broken*** We have noticed an increase in the demand for a CMD minor (which can currently be completed by taking 18 credits in CMD).
The goal of this specified minor is to outline a consistent set of courses for those students interested in supplementing their education with a deeper understanding of human communication processes, or those preparing to proceed to graduate study of communicative disorders (speech-language pathology or audiology).
Because the coursework in CMD is largely sequential, we also want to maximize student success by ensuring that they are taking the foundational coursework in the field. ***Strategic Plan link is broken*** Communication is an essential but complex human function.
The CMD minor helps broaden impact by raising the profile of careers (speech-language pathology and audiology) which are very much in demand in Rhode Island.
For students in related majors, the CMD minor option enhances interdisciplinarity and provides opportunities for increased flexibility in students' academic pathways.

This elective course aims to enhance students' knowledge of adjunctive therapies for dermatological conditions. Beginning with an introduction to adjunctive therapies, skincare ingredients, and skin types, the course will focus on non -prescription treatments for common dermatological conditions such as acne vulgaris, atopic dermatitis, seborrheic dermatitis, hyperpigmentation, rosacea, and xerosis. Non-prescription approaches to anti-aging modalities and oncodermatology will also be explored. Students will utilize primary literature and guidelines to develop treatment plans, compare and contrast available products, and identify and respond to medical misinformation regarding various dermatological concerns. (Online) Pre: Second/third year PHARM-D students in good standing, or third/fourth year Pharmaceutical Science BS students in good standing. Or by permission of instructor.

INFORMATIONAL MATTERS GCH101G | Topics in Civic Knowledge Newly Approved Topics for General Education Outcome C1-Full & GC In Data We Trust: Truth in Public Health This course explores how health information impacts individual health choices and public health, with an emphasis on critically evaluating data and evidence from credible sources. Students will also reflect on their civic responsibility to engage ethically and collaboratively in strengthening trust and validity in health communication. Health and Disease: Teetering on Disaster Many countries have undergone a shift from acute infectious to chronic diseases and this transformation is often fostered by changes in social norms, the economic climate, and political infrastructure, often generating issues of public importance and concern. Epidemiological methods, grounded in overarching ethical theories, provide a useful approach to evaluate these changes. This course will introduce students to relevant theories of population health and ethics, and then apply these frameworks to modern case studies. Students will gain an understanding of how social, environmental, economic, and political forces influence public health and identify opportunities and responsibilities for positively impacting the health of communities in the US and globally. This class is designed to provide students with a view of health and disease as a member of local and global community and stimulate their thinking about ways they can impact the health of their communities as a member of those communities, not necessarily as a public health professional.

Program Description Marine Affairs URl's Department of Marine Affairs offers the following degrees: B.A., B.S., M.A., M.M.A. (Master of Marine Affairs), and Ph.D.
The B.A.and B.S.in marine affairs focus on coastal and ocean areas and examine environmental resources, human uses, conservation, ocean policy and law, climate adaptation and resilience, tourism and recreation, environmental communication, ocean and coastal justice, ocean energy resources, coastal and island communities, ports and shipping, fisheries and marine ecosystems, spatial planning and management, and international development.
A marine affairs major establishes a background for careers in the public or private sectors in a wide variety of marine-related fields.
Typical areas of employment include positions in government concerned with coastal zone, environmental, or fishery management, and marine transportation.
In the private sectors, students have secured positions in environmental consulting shipping.
The major serves well as an educational background for continued study in law, especially environmental, fishery. coastal zone, admiralty, and ocean law.

The Graduate Council Part3.Approval Process A.Course Changes/Modifications:University statutes require that both new courses and changes to existing offerings be reviewed and approved prior to implementation.
All proposals originate with a faculty member; non-faculty members who wish to propose adding/modifying a course must work with a faculty member to do so.
Submitted proposals move to the Departmental Undergraduate or Graduate Committee for review (if applicable) and signature by the Department Chair or equivalent.
In addition to approving the proposal, the department chair or equivalent must add a document to the proposal confirming that department/section faculty voted in favor and giving the date on which the vote was conducted.
Department- approved proposals move to the pertinent College Curriculum Committee for review.
College-approved proposals move to the Faculty Senate for action.Proposals classified as“Major Changes"(see below for definitions) are reviewed by one or more of the three university-level curriculum committees (Curriculum and Standards, General Education, or the Graduate Council).

passages.heading: 2025-2026-FSEC-01 | Page 5
passages.text:
Upon approval by each committee responsible for its review, the proposal becomes part of a Bill subject to review and passage by the full Faculty Senate.
Proposals classified as “Minor Changes" (see belowfor definitions),after being checked by Faculty Senate staff for completeness. are automatically become part of a Bill approved by the pertinent Senate Committee and included in a bill from said committee subject to review and approval by the full Faculty Senate.
For more information on the approval process, refer to Chapter 8 of the University Manual, Part III.
Changes to an existing course fall into two categories: Minor Change and Major Change.
Questions regarding whether a proposed change is major or minor shall be directed to the Faculty Senate Specialist/Staff, who will review it with the chair of the

passages.heading: 2025-2026-FSEC-01 | Page 6
passages.text:
pertinent committee (CASC, GEC, or GC).
The chair will communicate the decision regarding major or minor status to the proposer; their word is final.
A course change proposal that contains both ‘minor' and *major' elements will be reviewed according to the major change review and approval process. i.I Minor change to existing course.: Minor course changes involve one or more small alterations that do not substantive ly alter course content.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-FSEC-01 | Page 6
passages.text:
These include removing graduate credit from a 400-level course; deleting a course or modifying a course code; changing a title; changing a course from variable- to fixed-credit(aslong as thefixed number is within the previously established range); modifying a credit range inside of the current range (e.g. from 3-6 credits to 3-4 credits); adding, removing or modifying a cross-listing (assuming that approval from any affected units is provided) or prerequisite: adding, removing or modifying a grading method for any courses not carrying a General Education outcome; removing a General Education Outcome: modifying the home department or college for a course; removing a modality: adding, removing or modifying the 'repeat for credit² provision; changing an open-ended topics course into a permanent topics course; changing an X- course into a permanent course;or changing course numbers within a hundred-level (e.g., from 201 to 202).
Course syllabi are not generally required for minor change proposals.
At any point in the review process, however, a syllabus may be requested from the proposing faculty member to facilitate effective review of the proposal.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-FSEC-01 | Page 6
passages.text:
Minor course change proposals undergo review at the department and college level.
Following approval at the college level, minor change proposals are checked by Faculty Senate staff for completeness and then become part of a Bill subject to review and passage by the full Faculty Senate.If objections are raised to a minor course change proposal prior to the Faculty Senate vote, the proposal shall be returned to the college-level committee for revision.
NOTE REGARDING MINOR COURSE CHANGES: The minor course change procedure exists to provide flexibility in and development of the curriculum as disciplines, methodologies, and knowledge evolve.
It is intended to streamline the approval process to help ensure the curriculum remains current.It is not intended to allow circumvention of the normal processes for proposing new courses or making major changes.
A college-level committee can, at their discretion, require that a minor course change proposal also be reviewed by the pertinent University Curriculum Committee(s).
Proposals selected for such review must include a syllabus, or be amended to include one, before being reviewed at the university level. i.

completeness and accuracy of curricular proposals.
Accurate information is critical to the catalog, course scheduling, advising, and admissions/marketing materials.
Signatures of approval verify that the information provided on a proposal is factually accurate and that all possible curricular impacts both within and outside of the originating department have been considered.
General Principles.
The Curriculum and Standards Committee (CASC) reviews undergraduate curriculum matters, including proposals for courses at the 100-, 200-, 300-, and 40o-levels, except in cases of General Education courses, for which the General Education Committee (GEC) performs the review.
The Graduate Council (GC) processes graduate curriculum matters, including proposals for courses at the 400- (for graduate credit), 500-, 600-, and 900-levels.
If a proposal for a 400-level course indicates that it is to be offered for graduate credit as well as undergraduate credit, it is processed by both the respective undergraduate curriculum committee and the Graduate Council.
These review committees meet monthly and submit approved proposals to the Faculty Senate for action (approval at a Faculty Senate meeting).
Part 2.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-FSEC-01 | Page 8
passages.text:
Deadlines and Timeline.
In planning for the first offering of 1) a newly proposed course, or 2) the implementation of major changes to an existing course or academic program, please be aware that the review and approval of a proposal is a multi-step process that can take several months and is not complete until the course/course change is officially listed in e-Campus or, with regard to new programs, until approval has been received from the URI Board of Trustees.
All faculty have access to the Kuali Curriculum Management System for submitting a new proposal, checking the status of an existing proposal, or viewing an approved proposal.
Questions regarding Kuali access and use should be directed to the Faculty Senate office.
It is advisable to think 'a year ahead,' i.e., proposals for a fall-semester course should be submitted early in the previous fall semester.
This suggested timeline reflects the fact that courses submitted at the end of the year-1 fall semester may not be listed in e-Campus before student enrollment for the year-2 fall semester begins in the middle of the year-1 spring semester (see below).

passages.heading: 2025-2026-FSEC-01 | Page 8
passages.text:
There may not be sufficient time for proposals submitted in the spring to be fully approved before the end of the academic year (consult the Faculty Senate website for important academic-year deadlines).
Fully approved course changes will be made in e-Campus for the subsequent semester up to, but not after, the start of pre-registration for that semester (on or about mid- semester).
Pre-registration for the Spring semester starts in mid-October; pre-registration for the Fall semester starts in early March.
Contact Enrollment Services for exact dates.
Fully approved course changes to Learning Community courses for the subsequent academic year will be made in e-Campus only up to the second week of February.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-FSEC-01 | Page 9
passages.text:
Fully approved new courses and temporary courses may be added to the Course Schedule (classroom space and available meeting times permitting) up to the start of the semester in which they are to be first offered and will appear in the subsequent catalog only if officially listed in e-Campus before July 1.
Projected effective dates for proposals will be implemented as requested if the curricular approval process has been fully completed within the appropriate time to meet that deadline.
Part 3.
Approval Process A.
Course Changes/Modifications: University statutes require that both new courses and changes to existing offerings be reviewed and approved prior to implementation.
All proposals originate with a faculty member; non-faculty members who wish to propose adding/modifying a course must work with a faculty member to do so.
Submitted proposals move to the Departmental Undergraduate or Graduate Committee for review and signature by the Department Chair or equivalent.
Department-approved proposals move to the pertinent College Curriculum Committee for review.
College-approved proposals move to the Faculty Senate for action.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-FSEC-01 | Page 9
passages.text:
Proposals classified as "Major Changes" (see below for definitions) are reviewed by one or more of the three university-level cur ric u lun committees (Curriculum and Standards, General Education, or the Graduate Council).
Upon approval by each committee responsible for its review, the proposal becomes part of a Bill subject to review and passage by the full Faculty Senate.
Proposals classified as "Minor Changes" (see below for definitions), after being checked by Faculty Senate staff for completeness, automatically become part of a Bill subject to review and approval by the full Faculty Senate.
For more information on the approval process, refer to Chapter 8 of the University Manual, Part III.
Changes to an existing course fall into two categories: Minor Change and Major Change.
Questions regarding whether a proposed change is major or minor shall be directed to the Faculty Senate Specialist/Staff, who will review it with the chair of the pertinent committee (CASC, GEC, or GC).
The chair will communicate the decision proposal that contains both "minor' and 'major' elements will be reviewed according to the major change review and approval process. i.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-FSEC-01 | Page 9
passages.text:
Minor change to existing course: Minor course changes involve one or more small alterations that do not substantive ly alter course content.
These include removing graduate credit from a 400-level course; deleting a course or modifying a course code; changing a title; changing a course from variable- to fixed-credit (as long as the fixed number is within the previously established range); modifying a credit range inside of the current range (e.g. from 3-6 credits to 3-4 credits); adding, removing or modifying a cross-listing (assuming that approval from any affected units is provided) or prerequisite; adding, removing or modifying a grading method for any courses not carrying

passages.heading: 2025-2026-FSEC-01 | Page 10
passages.text:
a General Education outcome; removing a General Education Outcome; modifying the home department or college for a course; removing a modality; adding, removing or modifying the *repeat for credit' provision; changing an open-ended topics course into a permanent topics course; changing an X- course into a permanent course; or changing course numbers within a hundred-level (e.g., from 201 to 202).
Course syllabi are not generally required for minor change proposals.
At any point in the review process, however, a syllabus may be requested from the proposing faculty member to facilitate effective review of the proposal.
Minor course change proposals undergo review at the depart i ment and college level.
Following approval at the college level, minor change proposals are checked by Faculty Senate staff for completeness and then become part of a Bill subject to review and passage by the full Faculty Senate.
If objections are raised to a minor course change proposal prior to the Faculty Senate vote, the proposal shall be returned to the college-level committee for revision.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-FSEC-01 | Page 10
passages.text:
A college-level committee can, at their discretion, require that a minor course change proposal also be reviewed by the pertinent University Curriculum Committee(s).
Proposals selected for such review must include a syllabus, or be amended to include one, before being reviewed at the university level.
NOTE REGARDING MINOR COURSE CHANGES: The minor course change procedure cxists to provide flexibility in and development of the curriculum as disciplines, methodologies, and knowledge evolve.
It is intended to streamline the approval process to help ensure the curriculum remains current.
It is not intended to allow circumvention of the normal processes for proposing new courses or making major changes. i.
Major change to existing course: Major course changes involve significant alterations of substantive content.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-FSEC-01 | Page 10
passages.text:
These include modifying the course description; modifying the number of credits; modifying a credit range outside graduate credit' to a 400-level course; modifying the grading method of a General Education course; adding or modifying General Education Outcomes; adding, modifying, or removing a method of instruction; or changing course numbers to a new hundred-level (e.g., from 100-level to 200-level).
Course syllabi are required for new courses and major change proposals.
Major course change proposals undergo review at the department and college level.
Following approval at the college level, minor change proposals are checked by Faculty Senate staff for completeness before being submitted to the pertinent University Curriculum Committee for review.
Upon approval by the pertinent university-level committee(s), the proposal becomes part of a

Faith in the fundamental importance of freedom forms a major theme in the history, government and tradition of the State of Rhode Island and Providence Plantations and of the United States of America.
Freedom is also recognized on practical grounds as vital to scholars in their search for and dissemination of truth.
Although academic freedom is not written into law, it is well established in custom and grounded in traditions of long standing in the colleges and universities of the Western world, protecting professional scholars and teachers from interference with their obligation to pursue truth.

passages.text: FACULTY SENATE OFFICE 224 P ASTORE H ALL , 51 L OWER C OLLEGE R OAD , K INGSTON , R I 02881 U SA , P: 401.874.2616 Faculty Senate Resolution 2025-2026-01 Resolution of Appreciation and Gratitude Honoring Kent and Diane Fannon WHEREAS , Kent and Diane Fannon, distinguished alumni of the University of Rhode Island, Class of 1974, have made a profound and lasting impact on the University through their longtime support of the University of Rhode Island; and WHEREAS , the Fannon’s previous gifts, including direct scholarships for students, endowed support for the College of Business, and establishment of the Diane and Kent Fannon Education Research Endowment, have already made a significant impact on the University and its students; and WHEREAS , the University College for Academic Success has evolved into a dynamic center for student community and support under the visionary leadership of founding Dean Emerita Jayne Richmond and current Executive Director Kim Stack; and WHEREAS , the Fannon’s commitment to student achievement, career readiness, and holistic support have now propelled the launch of the Fannon Institute for Student Success, which will transform the University College for Academic Success with revitalized and modernized programming; and WHEREAS , the new Fannon Institute for Student Success will bring together, under one administrative umbrella, five key areas of student support: Career and Experiential Education, Academic Enhancement, Retention, Exploratory Advising, and Student-Athlete Support Services; and WHEREAS , creation of the Fannon Institute for Student Success will transform the student experience, ensuring that every student has access to the tools, mentorship, and resources to succeed; and, finally, WHEREAS , Kent and Diane Fannon’s extraordinary generosity is a testament to their unwavering belief in the power of education and their desire to leave a legacy that will inspire future generations; NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED , that the Faculty Senate of the University of Rhode Island, on behalf of the entire General Faculty, expresses its profound appreciation and heartfelt gratitude to the Fannon Family for their visionary generosity, their enduring legacy of support for URI students, and their commitment to ensuring that generations of students will have the tools and resources they need to achieve their highest ambitions; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED , that this resolution be entered into the official minutes of the Faculty Senate and that a copy be sent to Kent and Diane Fannon as a token of our deep appreciation.

Online -Academic Year No Initiation Date First Degree Date Spring 2026 Fall 2027 Program Description @ The Graduate Certificate in the Foundations of Science Communication is designed for individuals who seek to deepen their understanding of the principles and conceptual frameworks underpinning effective science communication. This program explores the interdisciplinary theories that inform how scientific knowledge is disseminated, perceived, and used by diverse audiences. Students will engage with topics such as message framing, perception, and persuasion; political ideologies, identity politics, and policymaking; disability studies and accessible design; health communication; and the ethics of public engagement with science. Students will develop a critical lens to analyze the impact of communication strategies on societal trust in science and policy decision-making. This certificate will prepare students to excel as science and health communicators, advocates, and policy advisors. This certificate complements the Graduate Certificate in thePractices of Science Communication, serving as a pathway to the stackable Master of Arts in Applied Science Communication, Program requirements: - WRT534(NRS540) -COM525(MAF525) -WRT565 - One of the following: C0M460, COM455, COM523, COM522(MAF522), NRS509, PHL533, HLT504, HLT505, HLT506

This senior capstone course builds on Advanced Studio Seminar I. Students will finish their art portfolio and prepare to professionally exhibit it while further developing their professional skills. BS - Biotechnology, effective Fall 2026 Appendix D Biotechnology education relies heavily on inquiry-based, experiential learning.
The Biotechnology program at the University of Rhode Island provides students with lecture- and laboratory-based opportunities to engage in active learning, apply scientific concepts, and develop analytical, critical- thinking, and problem-solving skills.
Students additionally gain real-world experience through experiential learning projects, undergraduate research, and internships that prepare them for employment in biotechnology and pharmaceutical industries as well as academic and clinical research settings.
Beginning in Fall 2026, the Biotechnology program will implement a program fee to ensure that students continue to receive high-quality, modern laboratory experiences.
Current introductory laboratory courses (BTC 111 and BTC 195) require costly consumables and instrumentation that cannot be adequately supported by the existing course-specific fees.
The program fee will allow for modernization of curriculum and laboratory offerings, the purchase and maintenance of updated equipment, and the development of new laboratory exercises.

The ECCE program will be offered fully online through URl Online with field experience in the candidates' own Pre K-23 teaching setting, running 7-week accelerated sessions, including a-summer session sessions, for 2 years.
The Pathway 1 (BS + Pre-K-23 certification) requires an associate's degree from CCRl (or equivalent pre-acadermic work) to complete the Bachelor's degree.

UR's baccalaureate nursing program is designed to prepare students academically and personally to become professional nurses. Nursing is the largest discipline In healthcare delivery and our program prepares students for collaborative, interdisciplinary. practice. Working with faculty who are expert clinicians, scholars, and innovators, students will be challenged to have a deep appreciation of factors that impact patient wellbeing and forward creative, contemporary approaches in patient-centered care. Constitution, By-Laws and University Manual Committee CBUM Informational/Editorial Report #2025-2026-02 February 19, 2026 Faculty Senate Meeting Approved by CBUM 1/15/26 Approved by FSEC 1/23/26 Editorial change: Bachelor of Interdisciplinary Studies (BIS) has moved from Feinstein College of Education to the College of Arts and Sciences and the following University Manual sections that reference the BIS are to be removed: 3 .40.16, 4.80.10, 5.80.10, 5.80.12-13, 5.81.10-11 and section 8.15.11 is to be revised in reference to the BIS.
Changes shall take effect immediately upon acceptance by the Faculty Senate.
Bill reference for BIS: Bill #24-25-02 Bill reference for Alan Shawn Feinstein College of education: Bill #22-23-40D Remove: 3.40.16 The Dean of the Alan Shawn Feinstein College of Education and Professional Studies shall appoint General Faculty members as instructors for special BIS courses with the approval of the appropriate department chairperson and college dean.

The Dean of the Alan Shawn Feinstein College of Education and Professional Studies (or designee) shall serve as an advisor to the committee.

The BIS Special Faculty Committee shall review the professional qualifications of persons other than tenure-track URI faculty members who wish to teach BIS courses as temporary lecturers.
Persons who have once been appointed as temporary lecturers for the BIS Pro-Seminar may be reappointed in that capacity by the Dean of the Alan Shawn Feinstein College of Education and Professional Studies without a second review by the BIS Special Faculty Committee.

(Lec. 3/Online) Pre: Senior or Graduate standing or permission of instructor.
EDC 507 | Translanguaging Pedagogy, Effective Summer 2026 Change course number, change in modality (3 crs.) (Lec).

(Lec/Online) Pre: Senior or Graduate standing or permission of instructor.

EDC 563 | Culturally and Linguistically Responsive Pedagogy, Effective Spring 2027 Change course title and/or course description (3 crs.) This course uses the Culturally and Historically Responsive Curriculum and Instruction framework to guide teacher candidates to center multilingual students’ identities, skills, intellect, criticality, and joy in lesson and unit planning, implementation, and assessment. (Lec/Online) Pre: Senior or Graduate standing, or permission of instructor.
MPS 598 | Integrated and Applied Capstone, Effective Summer 2026 Change college (3 crs.) In this course, students integrate knowledge and concepts acquired during two different certiﬁcate programs offered by URI Online through development of a project related to a problem of practice.

(Accelerated Online Program) Pre: Admission is required to the Master of Professional Studies; completion of the requirements for two URI online graduate certiﬁcate programs; completion of MPS Applied Leadership and Ethics.
COLLEGE OF THE ENVIRONMENT AND LIFE SCIENCES: BIO 416 | Intertidal Ecology, Effective Fall 2026 Change prerequisites (4 crs.) The ecology of intertidal shores within New England, with a focus on common marine macroalgae.
Includes field surveys, specimen identification, and an emphasis on research planning and hypothesis testing. (Lec. 3, Lab. 1) Pre: BIO260 or BIO360 or BIO262 or permission of instructor BIO 422 | Biology of Sharks and Their Relatives, Effective Fall 2026 Change prerequisites (3 crs.) (Lec. 3) Pre: BIOBIO260 360or BIO360, and junior standing, or permission of the instructor.

passages.text:

(Lec. 3) Pre: BIO201 or BIO220 or BIO272 or BIO352. (A1) (B2) (GC) BIO 455 | Marine Ecology, Effective Fall 2026 Change prerequisites (3 crs.) Investigation of the structure and dynamics of various marine ecosystems.
Includes mineral cycling, energy ﬂow, community and population organization, and behavioral ecology in selected marine environments. (Lec. 3) Pre: BIO260 or BIO360 or BIO262 or permission of instructor.

passages.text:

Emphasis on examples from Bermuda's marine environment.
Laboratory includes ﬁeld collections, identiﬁcation, and preparatory techniques for taxonomic studies. (Practicum, Lab. 8) Taught in Bermuda.
Pre: BIO260 or BIO360 or BIO272, and junior standing, and permission of instructor.
BIO 475 | Ecology of Coral Reefs in Bermuda, Effective Fall 2026 Change prerequisites (5 crs.) Structure and function of coral reef ecosystems with emphasis on the biology of corals.

Pre: BIO260 or BIO360, and BIO262, and junior standing; SCUBA certiﬁcation required.
CPL 523 | Theory and History of Planning, Effective Fall 2026 Change course title and/or course description, modality, prerequisites, method of instruction (3 crs.) Explores the history and key theories of urban and regional planning.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-GC-04A | Page 5
passages.text:

CPL 525 | Introduction To Planning Methods, Effective Fall 2026 Change course title and/or course description, change method of instruction, change course credits (3 crs.) Application of basic quantitative methods in planning: collection, analysis, and presentation of demographic, housing, and economic data.
Introductory survey techniques.
Introduction to computer applications in planning. (Lec/Accelerated Online Program).
GEO 562 (BIO562, BES562) | Biogeochemical Cycles, Effective Fall 2027 Change course title and/or course description, change method of instruction (4 crs.) Cross-listed as (GEO) BIO562, BES562.

(Lec. 3, Lab 2) Pre: Graduate standing or permission of instructor.

Focuses on problems of marine resources development and management at the local, state, national and international policy levels. (Lec. 3) S/U only.

Rationale: URI's‘Second Grade Option'(UM S8.33.32; SGO hereafter) allows students at the beginning of their URI career toretake courses inwhich they received a C-orbelow.
When they do so, the original grade remains on their transcript but is not used in QPA calculations.The only exception to this rule occurs when determining whether students are eligible to graduate with distinction(≥3.3cumlaude,≥3.5magna cumlaude,≥3.7summa cum laude).The QPA to determine eligibility for this honoris calculated using ALL courses taken at the university, including any repeated using the SGO, rather than the QPA printed on the student's transcript.This results in some students who exercised the S GO being ineligible for honors despite having a suitable QPAon their transcript.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-FSEC-04 Amended | Page 2
passages.text: The argument for the current approach is comparing two students with the same QPA, one of whom exercised their rights to a SGOand the other who did not,the latter student is more deserving of graduation with distinction than theformer.Put another way,students wishing to courses attempted at the University dates back to the7o's.There was a concern that by not counting all attempts,academic honors could be awarded on an unequal basis(thosethat utilized the2nd grade option could be given the academic honors as students that did not have any courses that qualified for the2nd grade option).In addition,sincethe2nd grade option is not mandatory,it could disenfranchise students who chose to not exercise the2nd grade option who would have otherwise qualified for academic honors had they chosen to use the2ndgrade option at the start of their undergraduate academic career.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-FSEC-04 Amended | Page 2
passages.text:
My concern if we were to eliminate calculating distinction without taking into account all course attempts would be that distinction at commencement would become less meaningful." Therewas also concern that changing the current policy might affect students who, although initially dismissed from URI for poor grades, significantly improved their academic performance after being readmitted under the ^conditional read mission’ program (UM $8.25.13 - 8.25.16).
Their poor initial performance makes these students functionally ineligible for honors; changing the policy might increase their chances of earning this distinction.
There are two arguments against the current approach.
First, both the SGO and conditional read mission program provide a measure of forgiveness for mistakes made early in a student's career; the same principle should apply to students’ability to graduate with distinction.
Second, many students logically assume that the transcript-listed QPA determines eligibility - the fact that it does not is confusing and engenders hard feelings in soon-to-be-alumni.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-FSEC-04 Amended | Page 2
passages.text:
We ask the Faculty Senate to consider eliminating the sentence in s8.22.40‘Distinction' that specifies the QPA for graduating with distinction is calculated using all courses attempted at URI.
Its deletion would mean that student eligibility for graduating cum/ magna/summa laude would by default be determined using the transcript-listed QPA.Thiswould eliminate student confusion over their eligibility and ensure that the forgiveness embodied in the SGOand conditional read mission policies applies throughout a student's time at the university.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-FSEC-04 Amended | Page 3

All but 10 of the 369 were prevented from graduating with honors because they employed the second-grade option; the remaining 10 students were prevented because they participated in the conditional read mission program.

passages.text: FACULTY SENATE INFORMATIONAL REPORT CENTERS & INSTITUTES REVIEW COMMITTEE Report 2025-2026-01 On January 21, 2026, the CIRC notified the Vice President for Research Jenkins and Provost Wolfe of their recommendation to approve the CHILD (Child Health, Innovation, Learning, and Development) Institute.

passages.heading: IFSR-2025-2026-CIRC-01 | Page 3
passages.text:
Lisa Bourbonnais <lbourbonnais@uri.edu> CHILD Institute 3 messages Nilton Porto <nilton_porto@uri.edu> Wed, Jan 21, 2026 at 1:49 PM To: Bethany Jenkins <bdjenkins@uri.edu>, Barbara Wolfe <bwolfe@uri.edu> Cc: Lisa Bourbonnais <lbourbonnais@uri.edu>, Travis Williams <tdwilliams@uri.edu>, Samantha Meenach <smeenach@uri.edu>, Justin Parent <justin.parent@uri.edu> Dear Vice President for Research Jenkins and Provost Wolfe, The Centers and Institute Review Committee has completed its review of the proposal submitted by Dr.
Justin Parent, Director of the proposed Child Health, Innovation, Learning, and Development (CHILD) Institute.
The committee recommended approval and rated the overall quality of the proposed institute as high value to the University of Rhode Island.
Committee Comments The proposal is well organized and comprehensive, with a clear articulation of collaborators, planned activities, and strong potential for impactful research.
The institute has presented a thoughtful and feasible plan for securing external funding, including philanthropic support.
Notably, Dr.
Parente has a demonstrated record of obtaining external funding.

passages.heading: IFSR-2025-2026-CIRC-01 | Page 3
passages.text:
The proposal was accompanied by a highly enthusiastic and supportive letter from College of Health Sciences Dean Patrick Vivier.
Committee Considerations While the proposed CHILD Institute aligns more closely with the University’s current definition of a “Center” rather than an “Institute,” the committee voted to recommend approval based on its strong potential for cross-college collaboration, including sustained and meaningful collaboration with the College of Nursing.
Recommendation Approve as proposed.

8.45.10 Policy on Non-Credit Course Offerings.
Public notice shall be given for all non-credit offerings to be conducted under the auspices of the University.
Notification to the University community in the form of a brief public announcement shall be provided at least six months in advance of planned non-credit offerings.
Such offerings would include, inter alia, non-credit seminars, meetings, short-courses, workshops or conferences.
Notification shall be given according to the following steps: a.
The Alan Shawn Feinstein College of Education and Professional Studies (ASFCEPS) shall serve as the coordinator for all non-credit offerings.
Course organizers, including ASFCEPS staff, shall notify ASFCEPS of the proposed course at least six months in advance of the offering date(s). #21-22-6 b.
Notification shall be in the form of a memorandum filed with ASFCEPS which includes the following elements: course title, course topic(s), identification of course contact person, proposed course presenter(s), proposed date(s), time(s), location, and intended audience. c.
ASFCEPS shall publish a formal, public notification for all proposed non-credit course offerings in a university-wide publication. d.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CBUM-03 | Page 14
passages.text:
Interested persons shall first communicate their concerns and suggestions to the designated course contact person.
If questions remain, they should be directed to the Dean of the Alan Shawn Feinstein College of Education and Professional Studies who will assist in responding to issues raised. e.
ASFCEPS shall receive comments and suggestions and work with the course organizers to insure that the proposed offering meets the terms of this policy and that course content and instructor’s qualifications are consistent with continuing education standards.
Grant or contracted training, workshops, or similar activities are not to be a part of the review and notification procedure outlined above but ASFCEPS should be informed as soon as possible.
Exempted from this policy are staff development programs limited to University personnel.

passages.text: C/l proposed language Senate 20260219 LEFT COLUMN: PROPOSED RIGHT COLUMN: CURRENT 8.90.25 Governance. A proposal for an Academic Center or Institute that includes more than one college or school in its activities and governance shall articulate the structure, membership, and function of a governing body of personnel drawn from among the participating units, and from external units/institutions in appropriate cases. The governing body shall be empowered to propose changes to the Academic Center or Institute's charter, with support for the proposed changes indicated in letters from every participating unit. Proposals for change shall seek approval in turn by CIRC, the Faculty Senate, the Vice President for Research and Economic Development (for research centers and institutes), and the Provost and Executive Vice President for Academic Affairs. In cases where a governing body cannot reach consensus on its own, the Provost shall mediate. No participating unit shall be prevented from departing from an Academic Center or Institute after notice to CIRC, the Faculty Senate, the Vice President for Research, and the Provost, and after suitable provision has been made to account for the departing unit's existing obligations to the Academic Center or Institute.

passages.text: FOR CONFIRMATION BY THE FACULTY SENATE COURSES GEC Bill 2025-2026-06A At the March 4, 2026 meeting of the General Education Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate for approval. NEW COURSES COLLEGE OF ARTS & SCIENCES: ART102 | Drawing as Thinking, effective Fall 2026 (4 crs.) Students develop foundational drawing and visual research skills as tools for ideation, communication, and problem-solving in art and design. Assignments emphasize experimentation, process- oriented learning, and building a visual language. (Studio) (A4) SMC203 (SOC203) | Sports, Media and Culture, effective Fall 2026 (3 crs.) Cross-listed as (SMC) SOC203. Using different theoretical perspectives, students explore how sport intersects with society and consider how sport can contribute to and, at times, disrupt social inequalities and the operation of power. (Lec. 3/Online) Pre: SMC100 and SMC101, or sophomore status and permission of the instructor. (C3) COLLEGE OF THE ENVIRONMENT & LIFE SCIENCES: AVS222 (AFS222) | Science and Ethics of Animal Welfare, effective Spring 2027 (4 crs.) Cross-listed as (AVS) AFS222. Introduces the science of animal welfare and the study of animal ethics. Focus on domestic, companion and laboratory species. (Lec. 3) Pre: Completed or concurrently enrolled in AVS101 and AVS102. (A1) (GC)

passages.heading: 2025-2026-GEC-06A | Page 3
passages.text: COLLEGE OF PHARMACY: PHP208 | Clinical Fluency: Introduction to Health Communication, effective Fall 2026 (3 crs.) Introduction to clinical communication in a health setting. Students will learn various communication modalities in which they are used in a health setting. This course will introduce students to accepted conventions and best practices in relation to the creation and delivery of effective clinical communication as well as how to recognize and mitigate communication-based errors. (Lec. 3) Pre: BIO220, or by permission of instructor. (B2) COURSE MODIFICATIONS COLLEGE OF BUSINESS: TMD326G | What is Good Design, effective Fall 2026 (3 crs.) Understanding the concept 'good design,' from philosophical, cultural and historical viewpoints. Consideration of aesthetics, practicality, creativity, and human needs. Multiple cultural and historical perspectives in critiquing a variety of design contexts. (Lec. 3/Online) Pre: TMD126 or ARH120. (A3) (C2) (GC) COLLEGE OF THE ENVIRONMENT & LIFE SCIENCES: SAF400G | Urban Agriculture: Policy, Planning, and Design, effective Fall 2026 (3 crs.) Explores urban agriculture through lectures, readings, field trips, and hands -on learning. Culminates in an assessment of a local food system and a proposal for increasing its resilience, sustainability, and equity. (Lec. 3) Pre: junior standing. Not for graduate credit. (D1) (GC)

passages.text: FACULTY SENATE LEGISLATION March 12, 2026 Graduate Council Report 2025-2026-5A At the March 2, 2026 meeting of the Graduate Council, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate for approval. Informational Matters COLLEGE OF BUSINESS BUS 580X | Special Topics in Sports Management, Effective Summer 2026 (3 crs.) Provides an in-depth exploration of emerging and timely issues in the sports industry through case studies, guest lectures, and applied research. Topics vary by semester to reflect current developments in the field. (Lec. 3/Online) Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation By The Faculty Senate COURSE CHANGES COLLEGE OF ARTS & SCIENCES PHL 452G | Philosophy Of Science, Effective Fall 2026 Change 400-level course to qualify for graduate credit (3 crs.) Analysis of the nature and structure of scientific thought. Consideration of issues such as structure and types of scientific explanation, verification and falsification, and unity of the sciences. (Seminar) Pre: PHLPHL101 101,or 215,PHL215 or 451PHL451, and one 300-level PHL course, and 6 credits of natural science; or permission of instructor. (D1) (C2) (GC) PSC 542 | Labor Relations And Collective Bargaining, Effective Fall 2026 Change course title and/or course description, change method of instruction, change modality, change College (3 crs.) Collective bargaining literature, theories, and practice. Emphasis on the institutional features of public service-related bargaining, sectors as well as techniques, and dynamics of the bargaining process. (Lec. 3/Accelerated Online Program) Pre:Graduate standing, or by permission of instructor. COLLEGE OF ENGINEERING

passages.heading: 2025-2026-GC-05A | Page 3
passages.text:
MCE 569 | Shockwaves & Structures, Effective Fall 2026 Change course title and/or course description, change course number (3 crs.) Explores the shockwave mechanics from high-energy sources such as explosives and supersonic flight, as well as the fluid-structure interaction during shock events.
Topics covered include shockwave propagation in air, water, and elastic solids, as well as structural deformation and modeling. (Lec. 3) Pre: MCE354 and CVE220 or permission of instructor.
COLLEGE OF ENVIRONMENT AND LIFE SCIENCES BIO 425G | Marine Biodiversity: A Larval Perspective, Effective Fall 2026 Change prerequisites (3 crs.) Almost all marine life has a biphasic life cycle.
This course explores the diversity of marine reproduction and larval forms, and how humans interact with species from a larval perspective. (Lec. 3) Pre: BIO260 or BIO360, and BIO262 or BIO272. (D1) (B2) (GC) BIO 437 (CMB437) | Fundamentals of Molecular Biology, Effective Fall 2027 Change prerequisites (3 crs.) Cross-listed as (BIO), CMB437.
Biochemical basis of heredity as seen through the structure and function of nucleic acids.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-GC-05A | Page 3
passages.text:
Includes DNA replication, transcription, translation, gene regulation, and gene organization in prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
Current methods emphasized. (Lec. 3) Pre: CMB211 and CMB311, and BIO232 or BIO 352, or permission of instructor.
BIO 465 | Coral Reef Ecology, Effective Fall 2026 Change prerequisites (3 crs.) An introduction to coral reefs, the processes generating their exuberant biodiversity, the effects of human activities on them and the promising ways to restore and preserve these unique ecosystems. (Lec. 3) Pre: BIO260 or BIO360 or BIO262 or permission of instructor.
BIO 467 | Animal Behavior, Effective Fall 2026 Change prerequisites, change method of instruction (3 crs.) Roles of natural selection, individual learning, and cultural transmission in shaping animal behavior. (Lec. 3) Pre: BIO262 or BIO272 CPL 510 | Community Revitalization, Effective Spring 2027 Change course title and/or course description, change method of instruction (3 crs.) Introduction to systems and central theories of determinants for social and planned change in urban and urbanizing communities.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-GC-05A | Page 3
passages.text:
Focus on methodologies for political and social assessments in 3 spatial typologies: coastal, post-industrial and urban communities. (Accelerated Online Program/Lec.) Pre: CPL523 or permission of instructor.
CPL 522 | Planning Law, Effective Spring 2027 Change course title and/or course description, change method of instruction, change modality (3 crs.) Overview of the legal foundations of community planning practice in the United States.
Examines the historical development of land use planning law, the constitutional and statutory basis for local planning authority, and the role of planners within evolving legal frameworks governing land regulation and development.
Emphasis is placed on zoning, subdivision control, eminent domain, regulatory takings, due process, equal protection, exclusionary zoning, and growth management.
Students analyze significant court decisions shaping contemporary planning practice and apply legal precedent to real-world planning scenarios. (Lec. 3/Online/Accelerated Online Program) EEC 440 | Benefit-Cost Analysis, Effective Fall 2026 Change general education requirements (3 crs.) Basic concepts in benefit-cost analysis.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-GC-05A | Page 3
passages.text:
Measurement, comparison of benefits and costs over time, and criteria for evaluation of projects and public policies.
Problems and case studies in evaluation of current natural resources issues. (Lec. 3) Pre: EEC105 or permission of instructor. (B2) (D1)

passages.heading: 2025-2026-GC-05A | Page 4
passages.text:
COLLEGE OF HEALTH SCIENCE CMD 504 Evidence-Based Practice in Communicative Disorders, Effective Spring 2027 Change course title and/or course description, change prerequisites, change method of instruction (3 crs.) Examination of different types of research underlying evidence-based practice in speech-language pathology, audiology, and communication sciences; promotion of critical analysis of research and the application of scientific thinking to clinical practice. (Lec. 3) Pre: Graduate standing in CMD or permission of instructor.
NEW COURSES COLLEGE OF ARTS & SCIENCES COM 443 | Politicized Health Communication, Effective Fall 2026 (3 crs.) This course examines how health communication is shaped by political context and dynamics, how various health issues have been politicized, and how these forces affect both individuals and society. (Seminar) Pre: COM100 and COM320 and junior standing, or by permission of instructor.
ISD 458 | Capstone in International Studies & Diplomacy, Effective Fall 2026 (4 crs.) Capstone course for the International Studies & Diplomacy program where students develop a research project focused on international affairs.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-GC-05A | Page 4
passages.text:
Analysis of research related to global politics, international economics, and diplomacy. (Seminar) Pre: PSC211 or PSC310 or ECN201, junior standing, or by permission of instructor. (D1).
COLLEGE OF BUSINESS BAI 512 | Applied Artificial Intelligence for Business Decision-Making, Effective Fall 2026 (3 crs.) A practical, hands-on introduction to AI for business students, focusing on applications of LLMs, prompt engineering, workflow automation, and data-driven decision-making through real-world applications and an AI-enhanced final project. (Online/Lec. 3) BAI 557 | Visualizing Data for Business Intelligence, Effective Fall 2026 (3 crs.) Concepts, methods and techniques in creating business intelligence through descriptive analytics and data visualization techniques, as defined in business settings, used to develop business insights from real-world dataset. (Lec. 3/Online) BAI 576 | Machine Learning for Business Intelligence, Effective Fall 2026 (3 crs.) This course provides a hands-on introduction to machine learning for business applications.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-GC-05A | Page 4
passages.text:
Students learn Python-based implementation of core models, explore case studies in predictive analytics, HR, marketing, and finance, and develop skills to interpret results and make data-driven managerial decisions. (Lec. 3/Online) Pre: BAI210 or STA308; and MBA500 or one of the following: CSC310(DSP310), BAI356, BAI312 BUS 570 | Sports Marketing , Effective Summer 2026 (3 crs.) Examines strategic marketing principles as applied within the sports industry, spanning sport properties, teams, athletes, sponsors, and fans.
Emphasizes digital platforms, analytics, brand management, sponsorships, consumer behavior, and strategic planning. (Online/Lec. 3) BUS 577 | Sports Analytics, Effective Fall 2026 (3 crs.) Explore fundamental principles, key methodologies, and analyses relevant to sports analytics problems.
Quantify relationships present in data and utilize analytics as an entrepreneurial tool.
The use of data-driven decision making for managers is an essential component of the sports industry's future.
During this course, students will examine the use of analytical techniques and quantitative methods in the areas of marketing, ticket sales, and business operations.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-GC-05A | Page 4
passages.text:
Skills such as critical thinking, mathematical modeling, statistical analysis, predictive analytics, and optimization are crucial skills needed by sport managers.
The

passages.heading: 2025-2026-GC-05A | Page 5
passages.text:
course seeks to develop and refine these skills in the business application area of sport management. (Lec. 3/Online) Pre: Graduate standing or by permission of instructor.
COLLEGE OF PHARMACY PHP 571 | Methods in Epidemiology, Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis, Effective Fall 2026 (3 crs.) Introduction to epidemiology, the study of health and disease in populations.
It emphasizes epidemiologic methods and research design for conducting and interpreting health research.
Additionally, the course details the systematic review process, discusses the strengths and limitations of the method, and provides step-by-step guidance on how to perform a systematic review and meta-analysis using statistical software. (Lec. 3) Pre: 2nd or 3rd year PharmD student in good standing, or undergraduate student with credit in PHP308 or PHP405, or Graduate student status.
Or by permission of instructor.
PHP 572 | Measuring Outcomes and Identifying Causal Effects, Effective Spring 2027 (3 crs.) Introduction to the foundations of health outcomes measurement and causal inference.
We will examine how clinical, humanistic, and patient-reported outcomes are defined, measured, and validated.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-GC-05A | Page 5
passages.text:
Students will also learn the potential outcomes framework for assessing whether interventions cause changes in health outcomes in both randomized trials and observational studies.
Examples from epidemiology and medical research will illustrate how accurate outcome measurement and rigorous causal reasoning support evidence-based decision-making in health care. (Lec. 3) Pre: PHP405, STA411, STA412, or equivalent; permission of the instructor.
A basic knowledge of statistics and familiarity with linear and logistic regression is required.
PHP 670 | Advanced Epidemiologic/Economic Methods in Health Sciences, Effective Spring 2027 (3 crs.) Advanced training in pharmacoepidemiologic and pharmacoeconomic research methods and statistical analyses for evaluating health and cost outcomes, with emphasis on applied exercises utilizing contemporary approaches in the field.
Key aspects of the course include multivariable methods for common study designs, addressing bias, deriving and interpreting measures of effect, and economic modeling for assessing cost effectiveness.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-GC-05A | Page 5
passages.text:
Course exercises utilize SAS and MS Excel to provide students with hands-on experience with various statistical models. (Lec. 3) Pre: STA411 or STA412, and PHP550 and PHP580.
Or by permission of instructor.
COLLEGE OF ENGINEERING MCE 539 | Chemical Rocket Propulsion, Effective Fall 2026 (3 crs.) Explores the application of thermodynamics and fluid mechanics to chemical rocket engines, including thrust, propellants, combustion, and basic liquid, solid, and hybrid designs for space missions. (Lec. 3) Pre: MCE341 and MCE354, or permission of instructor.
