passages.heading: IFSR-2025-2026-FSEC-01 | Page 2
passages.text:
FSEC Editorial Report 2025-2026-01 March 12, 2026 Faculty Senate Meeting Name change of University College for Academic Success (UCAS) change its name to Fannon Institute for Student Success (FISS) the following manual sections need to be updated: 2.35.10, 3.21.20 - 3.21.23, 5.76.11, 5.76.12, 8.10.10, 8.13.10, 8.15.21, 8.16.10 - 8.16.14, 8.16.16, 8.19.10, 8.19.11, 8.20.40, 8.20.72, 8.33.12, 8.65.10, 10.90.11, Appendix C- 4.22, Appendix C- 4.22, 4.25, 4.32 Faculty Senate Resolution 2025-2026-01 2.35.10 The Dean of the University College for Academic Executive Director of the Fannon Institute for Student Success #2013-14-12B ( see 3.21.21 – 3.21.23 for duties) 3.21.20 The University College for Academic Fannon Institute for Student Success .
All undergraduate students who have not successfully completed at least 24 credits, except those licensed, registered-nurse students enrolled to obtain the BS degree in Nursing, shall be enrolled in this college the Fannon Institute .

passages.heading: IFSR-2025-2026-FSEC-01 | Page 2
passages.text: Students who have indicated a preference for a particular professional college before the completion of 24 credits shall be considered to be enrolled in the college as well as in the University College Fannon Institute if professional licensing or financial support requirements make this desirable . #2013-14-12B 3.21.21 The Dean of University College for Academic Executive Director of the Fannon Institute for Student Success shall have administrative responsibility for the University College Fannon Institute (including New Student Programs and the Academic Advising program for Athletes), for non-matriculating undergraduate students on the Kingston campus ( see 8.19.11 ) and for the following special academic programs: the Office of Internships and Experiential Education, the Learning Assistance Center, the National Student Exchange and the Office of International Education. #2013-14-12B 3.21.22 In carrying out these responsibilities, the Dean Executive Director shall have appropriate administrative assistance including an Associate Dean and an advising staff composed of faculty members from the various URI colleges who shall serve part-time as special area advisers and an advising staff composed of faculty members from the various URI colleges who shall serve part-time as special area advisers.

passages.heading: IFSR-2025-2026-FSEC-01 | Page 2
passages.text:
Nine hours a week shall normally be considered a part-time advising load.
Advisers shall be assigned to this activity by the dean of their permanent college after approval by the Dean of the University College for Academic Executive Director of the Fannon Institute for Student Success.
No faculty members shall be required to act as adviser

passages.heading: IFSR-2025-2026-FSEC-01 | Page 3
passages.text:
either as part of their regular load or as an overload without their consent.
Appropriate adjustments in the individual’s University responsibilities shall be made to permit effective performance of the advising function.
The dean of each undergraduate college in consultation with the department chairperson shall provide the University College Fannon Institute with sufficient advisers to cover all areas of undergraduate concentration offered by that college. #2013-14-12B, #21-22-6 3.21.23 The advising staff as described in 3.21.22 shall comprise the voting faculty of the University College for Academic Fannon Institute for Student Success. #2013-14-12B This is the updated version approved at the Feb. 19 faculty senate meeting to update Alan Shawn Feinstein College of Education and Professional Studies to Feinstein College of Education. 5.76.11 Each administrator evaluation committee shall consist of 5 members of the tenure-track faculty.
Three members shall be selected from a slate of nominees or volunteers by the Faculty Senate Executive Committee.
The administrator shall choose one member of the committee.

passages.heading: IFSR-2025-2026-FSEC-01 | Page 3
passages.text:
In addition, the President or Provost as appropriate shall choose one member of the committee.
All members of the committee shall usually come from the constituent group.

passages.heading: IFSR-2025-2026-FSEC-01 | Page 3
passages.text: Committee members shall be selected from the following groups: a) for the academic deans of: the Feinstein College of Education, the College of Arts and Sciences, the College of Business, the College of Engineering, the College of the Environment and Life Sciences, the College of Health Sciences, the College of Nursing, the Graduate School of Oceanography, the College of Pharmacy, and the University Libraries: all tenure-track faculty within the academic or administrative unit; b) for the Dean of University College for Academic Executive Director of the Fannon Institute for Student Success, the Dean of the Graduate School, the President, Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs, Vice President for Research and Economic Development, the Chief Information Officer, and the Vice Provost for Faculty Affairs: all university tenure-track faculty. #07-08–4 #13-14–26 , #18-19-33 This is the updated version approved at the Feb. 19 faculty senate meeting to update Alan Shawn Feinstein College of Education and Professional Studies to Feinstein College of Education. 5.76.12 The constituent groups shall be defined as the following: a) for academic deans of: the Feinstein College of Education, the College of Arts and Sciences, the College of Business, the College of Engineering, the College of the Environment and Life Sciences, the College of Health Sciences, the College of Nursing, the Graduate School of Oceanography, and the College of Pharmacy: all college faculty (tenure-track, research, clinical and teaching); b) for the President, Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs, the Chief Information Officer, the Vice Provost for Faculty Affairs, the Dean of University College for Academic Executive Director of the Fannon Institute for Student Success, the Dean of University Libraries: all faculty (tenure track,

passages.heading: IFSR-2025-2026-FSEC-01 | Page 4
passages.text:
research, clinical and teaching); c) for the Vice President for Research and Economic Development: all faculty (tenure track, research, and clinical); d) for the Dean of the Graduate School: all graduate faculty (tenure track, research, clinical, and teaching). #07-08–4 #13-14–26 #15-16-15D #16-15-21 , #18-19-33 #October 20, 2022 Informational Report. 8.10.10 Matriculating Students.
A matriculating student is a student who has been formally admitted to University College for Academic Fannon Institute for Student Success or to a degree-granting program by the Dean of Admissions or the Dean of the Graduate School.
A matriculating student may be either full or part-time and is entitled to full privileges as a student at the University of Rhode Island. 8.13.10 Undergraduate Transfer Candidates.
A student who has earned at least 24 transferable credits, and has met all of the requirements for admission to a specific degree-granting college at the University of Rhode Island, may be admitted directly to that college.
However, some students may be admitted to the University College for Academic Fannon Institute for Student Success provided not more than 60 transferable credits are presented.

passages.heading: IFSR-2025-2026-FSEC-01 | Page 4
passages.text:
Students with more than 60 earned credits must be admitted into a major and should not apply as undeclared. #17-18-29A 8.15.21 Departments may alter their standards for CLEP Subject Examinations or may withdraw their approval of an exam with the consent of the college dean.
College deans will inform the Dean of the University College for Academic Executive Director of the Fannon Institute for Student Success, the Dean of Admissions, and the catalog coordinators of all changes in CLEP policies of the departments of their colleges. #17-18-29A 8.16.10 The University College for Academic Fannon Institute for Student Success.
All qualified freshman students who plan to pursue a curriculum leading ultimately to a baccalaureate degree shall be admitted to the University College for Academic Fannon Institute for Student Success ( see 3.21.20 ) (see 8.13.10 for admission of transfer students). #17-18-29A 8.16.11 The University College for Academic Fannon Institute for Student Success shall make it possible for students to acquire education and skills basic to several baccalaureate programs at the University.

passages.heading: IFSR-2025-2026-FSEC-01 | Page 4
passages.text:
Some baccalaureate programs require admission at the point of matriculation to the University, thus may not be available options to continuing students. #17-18-29A 8.16.12 Students who have a clear educational or professional objective when they enter the University shall be encouraged to pursue this objective as directly and rapidly as possible, subject to the educational requirements established by the various college faculties and approved by the Senate.
They shall be assigned to the appropriate adviser and shall have access to advisers drawn from all University curriculums.
Entering freshmen who do not know which curriculum

passages.heading: IFSR-2025-2026-FSEC-01 | Page 5
passages.text:
they want to select shall be encouraged to experiment and “sample” courses in several fields of study.
Such students shall also have access to an effective advising system ( see 3.21.21 ) and shall select at an appropriate time the courses of study which will satisfy entrance requirements to one or more University colleges and curriculums.
They shall be assigned to advisers by the Dean of University College for Academic Executive Director of Fannon Institute for Student Success. 8.16.13 A student may transfer from the University College for Academic Fannon Institute for Student Success to a degree-granting college of the University after completion of at least 24 credit hours (including transfer credits) provided that the requirements for admission to that college and major have been met.
A student who has earned more than 75 credits may not be registered as a University College Fannon Institute student.
Students who have a 2.00 average or better will transfer to a degree-granting college.

passages.heading: IFSR-2025-2026-FSEC-01 | Page 5
passages.text:
Students with less than a 2.00 average and who do not meet the criteria for academic dismissal ( see 8.23.12 ), may petition the Scholastic Standing Committee of the degree-granting college for an exception to the 2.00 requirement for transfer.
If the petition is denied, the student will be blocked from matriculating status by the Director of Enrollment Services on recommendation of the dean and will be allowed to take courses only as a non-matriculating student (see 8.19.10 ff.). #17-18-29A, #21-22-6 8.16.14 A student who has transferred from University College for Academic Fannon Institute for Student Success but has earned no more than 75 credits may change colleges through the mechanisms provided by University College Fannon Institute .

passages.heading: IFSR-2025-2026-FSEC-01 | Page 5
passages.text:
After earning 75 credits, the student will transfer directly from degree-granting college to degree-granting college. 8.16.16 In cases where there may be more students seeking access to a program or college than can be accommodated, because of limited faculty and/or facilities and/or rapidly shifting student preferences and needs, this situation shall be reported to the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs by the dean of the college impacted by excess enrollment applications.
The Provost must declare the impacted program officially “oversubscribed” in order to allow restricted admissions.
When a program has been declared officially oversubscribed by the Provost, only those students considered to have demonstrated the highest promise for academic success will be admitted to the oversubscribed program.
The Provost, in consultation with the department chairperson and dean of the college concerned, shall determine the number of students to be admitted.
Oversubscribed programs shall be reviewed at least once a year.

passages.heading: IFSR-2025-2026-FSEC-01 | Page 5
passages.text:
Students not being admitted shall have the choice of either entering any other college or program for which they have satisfied entrance requirements or devoting up to one year of additional study within the University College for Academic Fannon Institute for Student Success to satisfy entrance requirements of another program. 8.19.10 Non-matriculating Students.
A non-matriculating student is one who is enrolled for courses at the University but has not been admitted to University College for Academic Fannon Institute for Student Success or a degree-granting program by the Dean of Admissions or the

passages.heading: IFSR-2025-2026-FSEC-01 | Page 6
passages.text:
Dean of the Graduate School or one who has been academically dismissed from a college of the University (see 8.25.10 – 8.25.18 for regulations pertaining to academically dismissed students).
Although visiting students, including those on exchange programs, are considered as non-matriculating for reporting purposes, they are otherwise excluded from regulations applying to non-matriculating students (see 8.14.10). 8.19.11 With the exception of students dismissed for academic reasons, all undergraduate, non-matriculating students (i.e., those who have not earned a baccalaureate degree) enrolling for courses on the Kingston campus shall be the administrative responsibility of the Dean of University College for Academic Executive Director of Fannon Institute for Student Success; all undergraduate, non-matriculating students registering only for continuing education courses or educational opportunities through the Office of Strategic Initiatives shall be the administrative responsibility of the Dean of the College of Education. and Professional Studies . #17-18-29A 8.20.40 Major Fields of Study.

passages.heading: IFSR-2025-2026-FSEC-01 | Page 6
passages.text:
An undergraduate student’s concentrated field of study in a degree-granting college shall be the student’s “major”; University College Fannon Institute students may have a “preferred major.” The major field of study for graduate students shall be the student’s “program.” Curricular requirements for majors and programs are defined in the University Catalog.
At least half of the credits required in an undergraduate student’s major field of study must be earned at The University of Rhode Island, with exception for an approved articulation agreement in Nursing.
A student’s major(s) or program(s) and option(s) will be listed on the student’s permanent academic record after graduation. #00-01–2 #13-14–2 #16-17-22 8.20.72 Students pursuing an Undergraduate Certificate must be admitted through the Office of Admissions or the Alan Shawn Feinstein College of Education and Professional Studies , Office of Strategic Initiatives upon the recommendation of the appropriate admissions officer.
Such admissions shall be limited to completion only of the Undergraduate Certificate Program.
Students admitted under this regulation are subject to the same regulations as students admitted in the usual way.

passages.heading: IFSR-2025-2026-FSEC-01 | Page 6
passages.text:
Undergraduate Certificate-only students seeking admission to any undergraduate major at the University shall be considered transfer students and are subject to all transfer admission criteria outlined in 8.13.10 – 8.13.13.
A student accepted directly into an Undergraduate Certificate program is one who is enrolled for appropriate courses to complete the Undergraduate Certificate at the University but who has not been admitted to University College for Academic Fannon Institute for Student Success nor to a degree-granting program by the Dean of Admissions or the Dean of the Graduate School nor one who has been academically dismissed from a college of the University (see 8.25.10 – 8.25.18 for regulations pertaining to academically dismissed students). #16-17-22, #19-20-34

passages.heading: IFSR-2025-2026-FSEC-01 | Page 7
passages.text:
8.33.12 The Director of Enrollment Services shall not register in University College for Academic Fannon Institute for Student Success a student with more than seventy-five (75) credit hours and at least a 2.00 quality point average (QPA). 8.65.10 Department and College Responsibilities.
University College Fannon Institute advisors and upper division advisors shall inform eligible students about the Honors Program. #16-17-15 8.81.30 Temporary Course.
A Temporary Course shall have approval of the department(s) or committee proposing it, the dean(s) of the college(s) involved, and the Curriculum and Standards Committee and/or the Graduate Council, except that a temporary University College Fannon Institute mini-course (a one-credit lower-level undergraduate course taught during the fall or spring semester) does not require the approval of the Curriculum and Standards Committee.
The Curriculum and Standards Committee shall, however, receive information about any temporary University College Fannon Institute mini-course after it has been approved by the college dean.

passages.heading: IFSR-2025-2026-FSEC-01 | Page 7
passages.text:
The Graduate Council may refuse to grant or may attach conditions to the granting of graduate program credit for a temporary course.
Each college may require internal channels of approval in addition to those specified here. #17-18-23 10.90.11 The President, the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs, the Vice President for Research and Economic Development, the Chief Information Office, the Vice Provost for Faculty Affairs, the Deans of: the Alan Shawn Feinstein College of Education and Professional Studies, the College of Arts and Sciences, the College of Business, the College of Engineering, the College of the Environment and Life Sciences, the College of Health Sciences, the College of Nursing, the College of Pharmacy, the University College for Academic Fannon Institute for Student Success, the Graduate School, the Graduate School of Oceanography, and of the Library are subject to faculty evaluation.
The evaluation shall be scheduled during the academic year immediately preceding the consideration of reappointment of each administrator.

passages.heading: IFSR-2025-2026-FSEC-01 | Page 7
passages.text: Administrators must be reviewed through this process prior to their reappointment. #07-08-4 , #13-14-26 , #18-19-33 Appendix C - 4.22 Academic Standards: The full committee shall study all matters pertinent to the establishment and maintenance of high academic standards that may be referred to it by the Senate, the Senate Executive Committee, or other agencies; propose improved regulations and practices related to academic standards; observe the effects of rules for dismissal of students for academic reasons; review periodically the academic standards, rules, and procedures in the University Manual and make recommendations concerning them to the Faculty Senate; make policy recommendations to the Faculty Senate on all matters pertaining to the University College for Academic Fannon Institute for Student Success other than advising; and review and evaluate standards and policies concerning recruitment, admissions, and yield, except for the

passages.heading: IFSR-2025-2026-FSEC-01 | Page 8
passages.text: establishment of annual admissions targets which is the responsibility of the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs. #17-18-12 Appendix C - 4.25 Liaison: The committee shall maintain liaison with administration offices such as the U niversity College for Academic Fannon Institute for Student Success, the School of Professional Studies, and the Online Education division of the Office for the Advancement of Teaching and Learning. #17-18-12, #20-21-14 . Appendix C - 4.32 Further, the Committee shall assess university-wide advising and make policy recommendations to the Faculty Senate on all advising matters pertaining to the University College for Academic Fannon Institute for Student Success. #17-18-12

Members of the administration with the title dean, provost, vice president, and president who have served the University ten years in that capacity immediately prior to retirement, and are in good standing shall be granted emeritus status. Individuals who otherwise meet the conditions of this section , and who have served the University with exceptional contributions may be granted emeritus status regardless of length of service. Emeritus status may be revoked for cause by the Board of Trustees upon recommendation of the President, or by the Board of Trustees of its own accord in the case of the a President. #20-21-26

Rationale Summary description and rationale of proposed specialization.
Program Context: The TESOL/BDL program allowed undergraduates to earn their ESOL or BDL certification as part of their undergraduate experience between 2018-2024.
In 2023-2024,the State added certification requirements to undergraduate programs, such as Right to Read Legislation and a year-long teaching residency, making it too difficult for students to add a full certification (21 credits) to their undergraduate program.
As a result, TESOl/BDL faculty have been encouraging undergraduates to it did not allow for double counting of credits and it required students to pay a Graduate School application fee.
Adding an ABM would formalize a pathway for undergraduate students to complete two certification and earn two degrees in five years.
Out of state undergraduate students would benefit from the ABM pathway because many states (excluding Rl) require educators to earn a masters degree within five years of employment (e.g., Connecticut, Massachusetts, New York).

passages.heading: 2025-2026-GC-04B | Page 73
passages.text:
Additional State-wide Context: the Regulations specifies that educators in Rhode Island schools must demonstrate"proficiency or awareness" in Multilingual Learner (MLL) education.
Proficiency and awareness were defined by The Rhode Island Department of Education in September 2025, with the release of their MLL Competencies.
These regulatory changes have reduced the demand for educators to earn their full teaching certification through UR's M.A. in TESOL/BDL program.
As a result, TESOL/BDL faculty are proposing changes to the existing courses and program to meet the State's"proficiency" requirements and retain enrollment through a variety of pathways:Graduate Certificate,Accelerated Bachelors to Certificate (ABC), and Accelerated Bachelors to Masters (ABM).

The Master of Arts in Applied Science Communication provides a comprehensive foundation in the principles and practices of science communication, focusing on effectively conveying scientific knowledge to diverse audiences.
This interdisciplinary program examines key topics such as message framing, perception, and persuasion; political ideologies and communicating with policymakers; disability studies and accessible design; health and/or environmental communication; and the ethics of public engagement with science.
The program emphasizes the social dimensions ofscience and the importance of fostering meaningful connections among scientists, communities, and the public to address issues of social justice and equity.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-GC-05C | Page 6
passages.text:
Students develop skills in inclusive science communication, including storytelling methods, rhetorical techniques, and digital tools, enabling them to create accessible and engaging science communication materials.
Coursework, projects, and internships provide opportunities to Graduates of the MA in Applied Science Communication are prepared for a wide range of positions across diverse fields.
These include roles in science communication and outreach for research institutions, museums, and nonprofit organizations; public information or media relations for government agencies, environmental organizations, or healthcare entities; and policy advising for advocacy groups and legislative offices.
With an ability to craft inclusive, ethical, and audience-tajlored strategies, students can address the communication challenges in fields such as climate change, biotechnology, and artificial intelligence, ensuring informed decision-making and engagement across industries.

Three to five years after graduation from the B.s. in environmental engineering, graduates will: 1) Practice and actively contribute to the environmental engineering profession in one or more of the technical areas of water and wastewater treatment, air polution control, environmental chemistry, sustainability, and related environmental systems. 2) Practice environmental engineering with an awareness of and commitment to ethics and social responsibility, sustainability, and diversity both as individuals and in team environments. 3) Pursue life-long learning through graduate education, professional licensure, or advanced training in environmental engineering or related fields.

Environmental engineers apply scientific and engineering principles to protect designing, and managing systems that provide clean water, treat wastewater, control air pollution, remediate contaminated sites, and promote sustainable infrastructure.

The curriculum provides students with an excellent background to pursue graduate study or to enter directly into professional practice in industry or government after graduation.
The first year is devoted largely to courses in mathematics, chemistry, physics, and engineering science common to all engineering curriculums.
During the sophomore year, students take foundational courses in environmental engineering including fluid mechanics and environmental chemistry.
In their last two years, students develop proficiency in water and wastewater treatment, air pollution control, and sustainable design.

However, these overlaps are limited, and the EVE curriculum quickly diverges into a set of courses and competencies that are not present in either existing program.
In the case of CHE, some upper level CHE courses may be taken as electives by EVE BS-seeking students (and vice-versa).
The CHE and EVE programs share a few core courses, including CHE 212 - Chemical Process Calculations and CHE 213 - Thermodynamics I.
These shared courses reflect efficient use of instructional resources in overlapping technical domains.
However, the CHE curriculum contains more broad application of engineering principles to chemicals, biochemical and bio molecular systems, and materials, with advanced coursework in reactor design (CHE 364), transport operations (CHE 347, 348, 449), process control (CHE 425), and plant design and economics (CHE 451/452)-areas not covered to the same extent in EVE, which focuses on water and air.

These EVE courses are aligned with the professional practice of environmental engineers, particularly in the municipal and consulting sectors.
Overlap with Environmental Science and Management (ESMG) is limited to the introductory science sequence, including BIO 101/102, CHM 101/112 (note that CHM 101 is not adequate for C0E admission), GE0 103, and MTH 131/141.
Beyond that, Coursework includes NRS 212 - Soil Science, NRS 223 - Conservation Biology, STA 308 - Introductory Statistics, and a suite of electives in Gl S, wildlife ecology, and wetland management.
These courses provide broad scientific literacy and field training but do not offer the design-oriented, quantitative curriculum needed for engineering licensure.

7.Summary description of the proposed organizational change The College of Engineering proposes establishing a standalone Department of Biomedical Engineering Electrical,Computer,and Biomedical Engineering(ECBE).A standalone B ME department will elevate program visibility,strengthen student recruitment and enrollment,support faculty recruitment and retention,and promote stronger research collaborations and industry partnerships.
B.RATIONALE There should be a demonstrable purpose and documented need for the proposed organizational change. 1.
Explain why the organizational change is being proposed.
Biomedical engineering is a rapidly expanding interdisciplinary field bridging engineering, biology, and medicine.URl's B ME program has strong undergraduate enrollment,successful graduates,and faculty conducting nationally funded research in areassuch as wearable bio sensing,brain- machine interfaces,and neural robotics.Despite these successes,the program's administrative integration with EC BE limits its visibility,ability to tailor curricula,and competitiveness in recruiting faculty and students.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-05C | Page 4
passages.text:
Establishing a standalone department will address these limitations, align with industry and workforce needs,and strengthen URl's role in biomedical research and education.
Theneed fora standalone Department of Biomedical Engineering at URl is reinforced by direct feedback from our key stakeholders and comparisons with peer institutions.Our graduates consistently emphasize the value of a clear,independent B ME identity,noting that it would strengthen their professional preparation,enhance visibility for research opportunities,and better position them inthe competitive job market.Similarly,members of research partners have recommended the establishment of an independent department as away to foster stronger industry and academic collaborations, attract high-caliber faculty, and provide a more focused administrative and organizational structure to support growth.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-05C | Page 4
passages.text:
In addition,a review of peer and aspirational institutions shows that independent BME departments are the norm.Remaining administratively within EC BE places URl at a competitive disadvantage in student recruitment,faculty hiring,and research prominence.Creatinga standalone department addresses these gaps, aligning URl with national standards and ensuring the program can continue to thrive as a leader in biomedical engineering education and research.
C.INSTITUTIONAL ROLE The organizational change should be clearly related to the published role and mission of the institution and be compatible with the organizational structure of the institution. 1.Explain how the organizational change is consistent with the published role and mission of the institution and how it is related to institutional planning.
The creation of a standalone Department of Biomedical Engineering directly supports URl's mission to foster innovation, advance interdisciplinary research, and prepare graduates to meet the needs of aglobal society.It builds on existing strengths in engineering,health sciences,and statewide biomedical initiatives,aligning with institutional planning priorities and strategic goals.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-05C | Page 5
passages.text:
2.Explain how the organizational change impacts other units and programs within the institution.
How have you communicated with the other units and programs about this proposed change, and what were the concerns raised relative to the organizational change?
The proposed organizational change to establish a standalone Department of Biomedical Engineering will have minimal impact on other units and programs within URl.The B ME program already exists aspart of Ec BE, and this transition does not reduce resources or capacity for other departments.Instead,it provides greater clarity in administrative structure and enhances opportunities for interdisciplinary collaboration acrossthe Collegeof Engineering and the broader university.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-05C | Page 5
passages.text:
It will enhance interdisciplinary engagement through joint faculty appointments with units such as Kin es i ology,the Interdisciplinary Neuroscience Program(INP),and the Health Sciences,supporting shared teaching,co-advised students,and collaborative research across bio mechanics,neuroscience,rehabilitation,and translational health technologies.The department will also promote shared use of core facilities and research infrastructure,maximizing institutional resources and fostering cross-unit innovation.
Communication regarding the proposed organizational change has been ongoing and multi-level.
Discussions have taken place with faculty and leadership within ECBE,aswell as with other engineering departments,including Mechanical Engineering and Industrial Engineering.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-05C | Page 5
passages.text:
Engagement has also occurred with the INP, Kin es i ology, and relevant health-related units through faculty meetings,individual consultations,advisory input,and regulars take holder updates.These conversations have helped shape the proposed structure and identify opportunities for collaboration and alignment.As a result of these discussions,wehave received support from ECBE,Kin es i ology,Mathematics and Mathematical Sciences,Interdisciplinary Neuroscience Program, and the Dean of the College of Engineering.
Overall,the proposed organizational change is designed to strengthen—not compete with—other expanding shared research opportunities,and creatinga transparent framework for resource planning.The establishment of a standalone B ME department is expected to enhance institutional cohesion and advance URl's broader goals in health,biomedical science, and interdisciplinary education.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-05C | Page 5
passages.text:
D.INTER INSTITUTIONAL CONSIDERATIONS The organizational change should be consistent with all policies of the Boardof Trustees and the Rhode Island Department of Education pertaining to the coordination and collaboration between public institutions of higher education. 1.Estimate the projected impact of the organizational change on the other public higher education institutions in Rhode Island(e.g.,loss of students or revenues),provide a specific rationale of the assumptions made in the projections,and indicate the manner in which the other public institutions were consulted in developing the projections.Have you communicated with other institutions about the organizational change and have any concerns been raised related to role, scope,and mission or duplication?
The change is not expected to negatively impact other public higher education institutions in Rhode Island,as URl isthe only public institution in the state offering engineering degrees and has an established BME program.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-05C | Page 5

the proposed curriculum and departmental structure and reinforced that the change is consistent with the expected scope and mission of a standalone B ME department.
The primary assumption underlying the projected impact is that establishing an independent BME department will primarily retain and attract students who might otherwise pursue biomedical engineering programs outside of Rhode Island,rather than drawing students away from other in- state public institutions.
By improving program visibility, curricular alignment, and degree pathways,the proposed change is expected to strengthen URl's competitive position regionally and nationally.
Communication regarding the organizational change has occurred through internal institutional channels and faculty discussions,and no concerns have been raised related torole,scope,mission, or unnecessary duplication.

On September 8, 2025, the Department of Electrical, Computer, and Biomedical Engineering (ECBE) convened a faculty meeting.
A total of 22 faculty members participated in the vote.
Of these, 20 were present in person, while two faculty members, who were unable to attend due to scheduling conflicts, cast their votes remotely during the meeting time.
In addition, you and Professor Emeritus Ramada Kumaresan attended the meeting as non-voting participants.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-05C | Page 18

The faculty unanimously supported the following actions: (a) Initiating the process to seek approval for the Biomedical Engineering program to become the Department of Biomedical Engineering (BME). (b) Renaming the current ECBE department as the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering (ECE), contingent upon the establishment of BME as a separate department.
This decision was based on the vision for the future Biomedical Engineering department and the department-level resource allocation plan presented during the meeting.
Thank you for your continued leadership and support as we take this important step toward advancing the college's long-term vision.
This collective faculty decision reflects our readiness to support the next stages of the process under your guidance.

Mission.
The Office 18 of the Ombud (The Office) provides 19 independent, impartial, informal, and 20 confidential resources for faculty, staff, and 21 students to address concerns, conflicts, and 22 systemic issues.
Engagement with The 23 Office can serve as an initial step in the 24 process for community members who seek 25 support with regard to complaints, 26 concerns, and problems.

Ombuds are 27 trained conflict mediators who can offer 28 guidance through listening, fact-finding, 29 identifying options with resources, 30 providing information about University 31 policies and resources, and facilitating 32 informal conflict mediation when 33 appropriate.
All cases are handled with 34 respect, the highest standard of 35 confidentiality, and fairness, without 36 Ombuds taking sides or having formal 37 authority.
The Office is not intended to 38 replace other channels on campus 39 specifically designated to handle certain 40 issues or problems, such as the Offices of 41 Title IX or Equal Opportunity.
The Office 42 will not conduct formal investigations, 43 make binding decisions, or replace existing 44 grievance, compliance, or disciplinary 45 processes, or collective bargaining 46 agreements.
Except when explicitly stated 47 otherwise in this section, the Office shall be 48 guided by the current International Ombuds 49 Association’s Standards of Practice which 50 are based on the fundamental principles of 51 Independence, Confidentiality, Neutrality, 52 and Informality. #21-22-6; Informational 53 Report 2022-2023-4 54

passages.text: 6 5.88.13 The Areas of Responsibility of 190 Ombuds are Equity, Critical Review, and 191 Recommendations and Report. #21-22-6; 192 Informational Report 2022-2023-4 193 Equity: to help individuals or groups in 194 specific cases to get just and equitable 195 treatment.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-Joint-01 | Page 7
passages.text: In securing equity, Ombuds 196 shall: afford full opportunity for 197 presentation in confidence of any complaint 198 or grievance from any student, faculty 199 member, or member of the administrative 200 staff alleging unfairness, discourtesy, undue 201 delay, or other malfunctioning in any and 202 all processes at the University of Rhode 203 Island; investigate, in confidence, to 204 determine the degree of validity of the 205 complaint; and mediate or otherwise 206 resolve the problem, arriving in confidence 207 at what appears to the Ombuds to be a just 208 resolution (in the dismissal of the 209 complaint, or in recommended action based 210 on the verified complaint). (The Ombuds 211 will not be expected to be concerned with 212 the normal operations of established 213 grievance processes or disciplinary 214 procedures contained in the University 215 Manual, except that they may, on the basis 216 solely of their own judgment, inquire into 217 possible bias or malfunction in any of those 218 proceedings, and make a confidential report 219 thereon to the office of the President and to 220 the President of the Faculty Senate). #20-221 21-5, #21-22-6 222 223 5.88.13 On Cases Concerning the 224 Conduct of the President of the 225 University.

Program Description Ocean Engineering The Department of Ocean Engineering offers a curriculum leading to the Bachelor of Science (B.s.) degree in ocean (www.abet.org) under the commission's General Criteria and Program Criteria for Naval Architecture, Marine Engineering, Ocean Engineering, and Similarly Named Engineering Programs.
URl's Department of Ocean Engineering Is nationally and internationally recognized as one of the leaders in ocean engineering, and also offers Master of Science (M.S.) and Doctor of Philosophy (Ph.D.) degrees.
As it is a unique program in New England and thro ui gh out the country, qualified students can apply under the New England Regional Student Program (RSP). graduate degree programs that prepare our students for professional careers in ocean engineering in industry, academia, and actively serve the profession and community in our areas of expertise; and to provide a challenging work and learning environment where diversity, community, scholarship, professional development, and excellence are valued and rewarded.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-06B | Page 97
passages.text:
The program is designed to provide students with a strong base in fundamental sciences, mathematics, and engineering; a broad base in ocean engineering; opportunities for the integration of theory experimentation, and design; appreciation of ethical, social, and environmental issues in the practice of the profession; and strong oral and written communication skills.
Program Educational Objectives.
Three to five years after graduation,our graduates will be: pursuing an advanced degree in an engineering program. 2) Working in one of the specialty areas within the broad field of ocean engineering including ocean instrumentation, ocean ocean renewable energy,andocean engineering design. and succeeding in diverse workplaces, nationally and internationally.
Student Outcomes.
Ocean engineering students demonstrate knowledge in all outcomes required by ABET, Inc. which are listed in the college's student outcomes section of this catalog. fundamentals and prepares them for direct entry into a professional career or continued study toward a graduate degree.
The strong emphasis is on the application of scientific principles in the ocean environment gained through laboratory courses.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-06B | Page 97
passages.text:
Experiments covering several basic areas are used to provide an integrated approach to investigations into ocean phenomena and processes.
Students are involved in the planning and execution of experiments, including data coli ect ion and engineering activities in scientific and industrial fields.
The broad-based program exposes students to the following topics: offshore renewable energy ocean instrumentation and data analysis, ocean robotics and vehicles,underwater and sub-bottom acoustics,wave and marine hydrodynamics,coastal processes, marine geo mechanics, and coastal and offshore structures.
Students have the option to concentrate in one of the ocean engineering disciplines by following one of the academic tracks, which are faculty selected course sequences in Structures, and Robotics.
A highlight of the ocean engineering undergraduate experience is a two-semester Senior Capstone Ocean Engineering Design

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-06B | Page 98
passages.text:
projects are offered as small sections, many of them with industry participation/funding and typically advised by multiple faculty advisors.
Students work as teams on integrated sub-tasks; prepare substantial reports and give oral presentations.
The Department of Ocean Engineering is located at URl's Narragansett Bay Campus.
The facilities include a 30 x 3.6 x 1.8 m (length, width, depth) tow and wave tank, a wave-current interaction flume, a large and deep (4.2 m) acoustics tank, an electronics shop, machine shop, rapid prototyping equipment including 3D printers and a laser cutter, and the Marine Geo mechanics Laboratory.
These facilities are available to undergraduate and graduate students for course work, research, and independent study.
The department has access to a 42-foot research vessel equipped with a fully integrated side-scan sonar and sub-bottom available in the department are a Seaglider Autonomous Underwater Vehicle, several inspection-class Remotely Operated Vehicles (Rovs), aerial drones, and a deep-sea oceanographic winch systemt.

Animal and veterinary sciences play a vital role in the management and care of livestock,

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-06B | Page 108
passages.text:
companion animals as well as those animals maintained at zoos, aquariums and laboratory animal facilities.
Options are available to students interested in animal sciences or veterinary medicine.
Graduates of this program will be prepared to use professional concentration courses: AVs 101, 102, 110, 304, 331, 332, 333, 343, 472 plus additional option-specific courses as indicated below.
Including the core courses, across options, there are 30-33 credits of professional concentration; 9 credits of basic non-science (C0M 100; WRT 104 or 106 and w RT 300+); 18-50 credits of basic science including Bl0 101/103 and Bl0 102/104; and 9-36 credits of supporting electives required for this major.
A maximum of 12 credits total of experiential learning courses such as Avs 399, 491, 492 and 498 can be counted towards the degree.
A total of 120 credits are required for graduation.
Animal Science Option.
This option includes lecture and lab-based coursework in animal management, nutrition, physiology. behavior, and disease, and provides broad flexibility for students in their choice of animal science courses.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-06B | Page 108
passages.text:
Students have the option to focus their coursework specifically on domestic livestock, exotic animals or animal technology, or be more broadly focused.
Research techniques and procedures for animal care are emphasized along with a strong background in the local government agencies focused on animal care, welfare, and regulation.
Many work directly with animals as veterinary as high school agricultural teachers, conduct animal-based research in academic settings and private industry, or help bridge the gap between research and practical application as extension agents.
The option also provides strong entrepreneurial opportunities for graduates interested in establishing their own businesses, whether in food animal production, pet care and domestic or wildlife species.
In addition to the core courses specifed of the major, the following professional courses are required: AVS 212-or412; one 300+ (3 cr) animal management course; one 400-level animal science elective, one 300+ additional concentration course.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-06B | Page 108
passages.text:
Supporting electives requirements for the Animal Science option include one Av S management course (3 cr), 6 credits of Av S elective courses and 3 credits minimum of experiential learning courses (maximum 12 credits)plus an additional 24 credits of supporting electives.
The following 18 credits of Basic Science courses are required:BIO 101/103 and 102/104; CHM 101/102 or 103/105; MTH 103 or 111 or 131 or 141; STA 220,308 or 409.
Pre-Veterinary Option.
This option requires a demonstrated competency in the basic sciences and prepares students to pursue a Doctor of Veterinary Medicine degree through rigorous coursework in the basic sciences in addition to specialized animal science courses.
Students in this option will also be well prepared to pursue graduate programs in animal physiology. nutrition and health.
Because admission requirements among schools are not totally uniform and are subject to change, students should determine specific requirements of the schools in which they are interested.
In addition to the 21 credits of AVS 412, Bl0 341 and a 300+ concentration course are required as well as 9 credits of Supporting Electives.

passages.heading: R-2025-2026-FS-03 | Page 1
passages.text: Williams May 7, 2026 Whereas, Travis Williams was elected Vice President and President-Elect of the Faculty Senate in spring 2024 and served as President from May 2025 to May 2026; and Whereas, he has served the University of Rhode Island Faculty Senate with distinction and dedication as Senate President; and Whereas, he has championed a collaborative approach to shared governance; and Whereas, he has brought a scripted – but not stilted – structure to the monthly meetings of the Faculty Senate; and Whereas, his written scripts for each meeting maintain order and are squirrelled away for use by future Officers; Whereas, he has prioritized outreach to deans and brought their voices and expertise into our discussions; and Whereas, his efforts to address concerns and build consensus before Faculty Senate meetings have facilitated the passage of important legislation; and Whereas, he has superbly navigated the Scylla and Charybdis of policy advocacy versus his role as neutral arbiter of Senate discussions and votes; and Whereas, he has kept an opinionated Executive Committee on task and been a truly superb mentor to his Vice President; and, finally, Whereas, he has often done all of this in less than two full hours; now Therefore, be it Resolved, that the University of Rhode Island Faculty Senate expresses its profound gratitude and congratulations to Travis Williams for his truly exceptional service and leadership as Senate President; and Be it further Resolved, that a copy of this resolution shall be presented to Travis Williams as a token of the Senate’s appreciation.

Film/Media is an interdisciplinary major offering hands-on experience in documentary, experimental, narrative, and new media production, balanced with an emphasis on international cinemas, film/media history, criticism, and theory.

Rationale for Proposed Changes per The 23Theatre BA is currently suspended and only open to those students who are pursuing a degree in Elementary.
Education.We propose reinstating the BA for all eligible students in order to serve the shifting demographic of our student body as well as refine our BFA program to introduce more rigorous standards appropriate to a pre-24professional training. program.
The Rhode Island Promise Act has increased the number of transfer students considerably, making it highly difficult for those students to complete a BFA in 4 years.Additionally, the number of double majors/minors has increased making it equally difficult for those students to complete the very narrow BFA curriculum without impact to their other majors (particularly those, such as Nursing, who also have to meet clinical requirements that tend to conflict with our required courses).
A BA offers more flexibility for order of courses, thus making it more feasible for our transfer students and those completing more than one major.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-08B | Page 53
passages.text:
URI Theatre completed an External Review in Spring of 2024.Among their recommendations was to standardize evaluation tools across our curriculum and instate more rigorous standards for degree completion,including capstone performances and projects.
Many BFA programs also involve standards that, if not met, result in dismissal from the program, lt has never been the policy of UR! theatre to dismiss students from our program except in very rare cases of academic failure.
Introducing this type of standardization is.possible if we have the option to invite students to our BA program in the event that the BFA curriculum is not a good fit.
Bifurcating our program in this way allows URl Theatre to serve the widest number of students while also introducing more clear standards for our BFA students.
The reinstatement of the BA does not require any new courses or staffing.
Students in the BAprogram will be taking courses already offered in our existing curriculum but have more choice in terms of when and what they take.
Because our program has undergone some changes to course codes since the suspension of the BA, we include here the courses we propose for completion of the BA in Theatre.

Optional electives within the major include THE112, THE200, THE300, THE400.
For many students, this would include participating in our.production season for which they receive course credit(THE200/300/400).

This proposed change allows URI Theatre to serve the broadest number of students, in particular, those students for whom completing a BFA in four years may be less feasible due to their status as transfer students or students who need to work or provide critical care to their families.
The BFA is a credit-heavy degree that requires students to take coursework at nights and on weekends.
This can be a major barrier to students who work, commute, and/or have families to care for.
By offering the BA, we diversify our student body to include those types of students who would otherwise be math, business, and other disciplines not typically associated with the performing arts.

The undergraduate program offers three major options (tracks): a B.s. degree with a major in Clinical Neuroscience from the College of Health Sciences, a B.S. degree with a major in Molecular Neuroscience from the College of Environment and Life Sciences, and a B.s. degree with a major in Medicinal Neuroscience from the College of Pharrmacy.

THE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND FACULTY SENATE NEW PROGRAM REPORT CURRICULUM & STANDARDS COMMITTEE REPORT 2025-2026-07C At the April 2, 2026 meeting of the Curriculum & Standards Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate for approval.
FOR CONFIRMATION BY THE FACULTY SENATE NEW PROGRAMS COLLEGE OF ARTS & SCIENCES BFA-Film, effective Fall 2026 Appendix A The Major.
The BFA in Film/Media is an intensive, experiential degree that integrates advanced creative practice with critical and historical study.
The curriculum emphasizes sequential training in film and media production alongside rigorous engagement with theory, research, and analysis.
Students develop technical and conceptual proficiency through sustained coursework, collaborative projects, and advanced culminating work that reflects professional standards and disciplined artistic inquiry.
FLM 496 (Capstone Seminar in Film/Media) and FLM 397 (1 Credit) BFA portfolio are required in the junior year; and FLM 497 (BFA Capstone) is required in the senior year.
Students learn to work with the evolving and overlapping technologies involved in the production of moving images.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-07C | Page 2
passages.text:
A wide range of courses is available to the Film/Media student-courses that examine the historical, theoretical, and global approaches to the analysis and creation of moving images.
The Film/Media program prepares students for careers in such areas as independent filmmaking; animation and media design; film and television industries, advertising, marketing, public relations, and media criticism.
Graduates of this program are also prepared to continue with graduate studies in film and media production for an M.F.A.
Students majoring in the Film BFA must complete a minimum of 52 credits (maximum 67) in approved courses toward the major.
FLM 101 or FLM 101 H is a required prerequisite.
We recommend that students take at least one film production course per semester beginning with FLM 110 in their

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-07C | Page 3
passages.text:
freshman year, establishing a regular and consistent creative process.
The wide range of choices in Film/Media courses permits students to design a major that will meet both personal and professional goals.
Students must have a plan of study approved by an academic advisor in the Film/Media program before beginning their coursework in the major.

COLLEGE OF THE ENVIRONMENT & LIFE SCIENCES BA -Sustainable Food Systems, effective Fall 2026 Appendix B A BA in Sustainable Food Systems is ideal for students who wish to pursue a degree in food systems in the context of a liberal arts education.
Because the study and practice of food systems intersects with a wide range of other disciplines, the major is also ideal for those who wish to combine interdisciplinary training in food systems with a complementary major.
Students completing the program will graduate with the skills and knowledge needed to contribute to the development of sustainable, equitable, and resilient food systems from local to global scales.
The major allows participants to explore diverse aspects of the food supply chain from production to processing/distribution to consumption to waste management and recovery, with an emphasis on systems thinking, food system policy, and social, cultural, and political context.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-07C | Page 4
passages.text:
By the time of degree completion, students will be uniquely positioned to enter the workforce in the growing field of sustainable food systems or to pursue opportunities in graduate education or research addressing the challenges of securing access to safe and affordable food for a growing population.
SFS BA students will pursue a curriculum offering breadth across the natural and social sciences and the arts and humanities.
The program entails a total of 120 credits, 30 credits of which must be in courses at the 300 level or above, including: A core sequence emphasizing an interdisciplinary and systems-approach to sustainable food systems.
Required courses include AFS/AVS/PLS 132G, an economics course (to choose from ECN 201, EEC 105, or INE 149), HSS/PSY 130G, NUT 207, one course in sustainability (3 credits minimum, to choose from SUS 102, SAF 305, COM/SUS 108G, COM/SUS 315, COM/SUS 460, and other relevant courses), APG/GWS/SOC 308, SAF 383, and one course in sustainable production (3 credits minimum, to choose from AFS 105G/106, AVS 101/102, or PLS 150).
A minimum of two electives related to food systems at the 300 level or above (6 credits minimum).

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-07C | Page 4
passages.text:
A robust capstone experience in which students master the ability to address the complex challenges in the area of sustainable food systems through experiential learning in interdisciplinary teams.
Students are required to take a total of six credits, including three credits of internship or special project and an additional three credits in another capstone course.
Current examples of capstone courses include AFS 440, PLS 385, and SAF 400G.
Compared to the BS in SFS, the BA allows students greater flexibility in selecting courses relevant to their specific interests.
In addition, students may have more flexibility in combining this major with a complementary major in another subject to gain greater breadth of experience they can apply to their future careers.

The BFA in Film/Media is an intensive, experiential degree that integrates advanced creative practice with critical and historical study.
The curriculum emphasizes sequential training in film and media production alongside rigorous engagement with theory, research, and analysis.
Students develop technical and conceptual proficiency through sustained coursework, collaborative projects, and advanced culminating work that refiects professional standards and disciplined artistic inquiry.
FLM 496 (Capstone Seminar in Film/Media) and FLM 397 (1 Credit) BFA portfolio are required in the junior year; and FLM 497 (BFA Capstone) is required in the senior year.
Students learn to work with the evolving and overlapping technologies involved in the production of moving images.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-07C | Page 9
passages.text:
A wide range of courses is available to the Film/Media student-courses that examine the historical, theoretical, and global approaches to the analysis and creation of moving images.
The Film/Media program prepares students for careers in such areas as independent filmmaking; animation and media design; film and television industries, advertising, marketing, public relations, and media criticism.
Graduates of this program are also prepared to continue with graduate studies in film and media production for an M.F.A.
Students majoring in the Film BFA must complete a minimum of 52 credits (maximum 67) in approved courses toward the major.
FLM 101 or FLM 101 H is a required prerequisite.
We recommend that students take at least one film production course per semester beginning with FLM 110 in their freshman year, establishing a regular and consistent creative process.
The wide range of choices in Film/Media courses permits students to design a major that will meet both personal and professional goals.
Students must have a plan of study approved by an academic advisor in the Film/Media program before beginning their coursework in the major.

What is the demand and regional competition for this program?
Students in the program demonstrate strong interest in advanced media production, and an evaluation of the current population indicates that approximately 25% of our annual graduates would pursue a BFA in film/media if available.
This reflects a clear demand for a rigorous, production-focused degree within Rhode Island, where no large public university currently offers such a pathway.
Regional competition includes private institutions like RISD, which emphasizes artistic and experimental film, and Emerson College in Boston, which offers a highly regarded, production-intensive BFA in media arts.
A public BFA program in Rhode Island would provide accessible, hands-on professional training, prepare graduates for careers in the growing media industry, and retain local talent that might otherwise leave the state for comparable programs.

Kingston No Initiation Date Fall 2026 Program Description 9 First Degree Date Fall 2026 A BA in Sustainable Food Systems is ideal for students who wish to pursue a degree in food systems in the context of a liberal arts education.
Because the study and practice of food systems intersects with a wide range of other disciplines, the major is also ideal for those who wish to combine interdisciplinary training in food systems with a complementary major.
Students completing the program will graduate with the skills and knowledge needed to contribute to the development of sustainable, equitable, and resilient food systems from local to global scales.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-07C | Page 27
passages.text:
The major allows participants to explore diverse aspects of the food supply chain from production to processing/distribution to consumption to waste management and recovery, with an emphasis on systems thinking, food system policy, and social, cultural, and political context.
By the time of degree completion, students will be uniquely positioned to enter the workforce in the growing field of sustainable food systems or to pursue opportunities in graduate education or research addressing the challenges of securing access to safe and affordable food for a growing population.
SFS BA students will pursue a curriculum offering breadth across the natural and social sciences and the arts and humanities.
The program entails a total of 120 credits, 30 credits of which must be in courses at the 300 level or above, including: A core sequence emphasizing an interdisciplinary and systems-approach to sustainable food systems.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-07C | Page 27
passages.text:
Required courses include AFS/ AVS/PLS 132G, an economics course (to choose from ECN 201, EEC 105, or INE 149), HSS/PSY 130G, NUT 207, one course in sustainability (3 credits minimum, to choose from SUS 102, SAF 305, COM/SUS 108G, COM/SUS 315, COM/SUS 460, and other relevant courses), APG/GWS/SOC 308, SAF 383, and one course in sustainable production (3 credits minimum, to choose from AFS 1058/106, AVS 101/102, or PLS 150).
A minimum of two electives related to food systems at the 300 level or above (6 credits minimum).
A robust capstone experience in which students master the ability to address the complex challenges in the area of sustainable food systems through experiential learning in interdisciplinary teams.
Students are required to take a total of six credits, including three credits of internship or special project and an additional three credits in another capstone course.
Current examples of capstone courses include AFS 440, PLS 385, and SAF 400G.
Compared to the BS in SFS, the BA allows students greater fiexibility in selecting courses relevant to their specific interests.

What opportunities does this program provide for graduates?
Cultivating sustainable and resilient food systems is a state, regional, and national priority.
The New England Feeding New England initiative, for example, has established the goal of producing 30 percent of the food consumed in New England within the region by 2030.
With a liberal education in food systems that incorporates interdisciplinary systems thinking, graduates of the BA program will be uniquely positioned to enter the workforce in this exciting and growing field or to pursue opportunities in graduate education or research addressing the challenges of securing access to safe and affordable food for a growing population.
Potential career paths include food systems management and entrepreneurship, policymaking, food journalism, research, and education.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-07C | Page 29
passages.text:
Because the majority of programs in sustainable food systems at regional public universities offer BS rather than BA degrees, URl's BA program will fill a unique niche in the New England ecosystem in postsecondary education and attract regional students wishing to pursue a BA rather than a BS in food systems.
The only similar program at a regional land grant university is the BA in Agriculture and Food Systems at the University of New Hampshire.
URl's more flexible program will differentiate it from UNH's, allowing students enrolling at URI to combine their passion for food systems with their other passions, whether those be in the natural sciences, social sciences, humanities, arts, engineering, or business.

FACULTY SENATE OFFICE FACULTY SENATE LEGISLATION JUNE 18, 2024 Curriculum & Standards Committee Report 2023-2024-09 At the April 4, 2024 meeting of the Curriculum & Standards Committee, the following program was considered and is now presented to the Faculty Senate Executive Committee on June 18, 2024 for emergency summer 2024 approval.
SECTION I Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation by The Faculty Senate COLLEGE OF ARTS & SCIENCES Bachelor of Independent Studies (BIS) in General Studies Move program to URIO Summary of proposed changes Given the nature of the population we seek to serve (adult learners, working students, returning veterans, for example) working through URI Online and its accelerated online format is the most reasonable way to facilitate degree completion.
Existing courses that will be added to the program include: WRT 227 Professional Writing; THE338G Ethical Dilemmas in Contemporary Theater; PHL101 Critical Thinking; as well as offerings in Gender and Women's Studies, and Sociology.

passages.heading: Curriculum & Standards Committee Report #2023-2024-09 | Page 1
passages.text:
Arts and Sciences has also requested, with the support of the College of Education, to move courses designated BIS and SPC to A&S, with 8 of those courses designated for inclusion in the BIS curriculum.
Those courses will include: · SPC 325 Leadership, Power, and Oppression · SPC 420 Facilitating Leadership Development · SPC 450 Leading through Change · SPC 305 Learning and Career Principles for Adult Students · BIS 350 Directed Study · SPC 201 Intro to Professional Leadership Studies · SPC 319G Negotiating Difference: Diversity and Inclusion in America's Narrative At this time, the program is interdisciplinary.
Over time, the goal is to support the development and offering of interdisciplinary courses as well.
In collaboration with URI Online and the Strategic Communication program, offerings of General Education courses are sufficient for students to complete those requirements.
We also anticipate working closely with UCAS to monitor and evaluate potential Credit for Prior Learning credits.
As these additions are approved, changes will be made to future catalog years for accuracy.
It should be noted that this degree is a Bachelor of Interdisciplinary Studies, not a Bachelor of Arts.

The Executive Committee shall have the power to act for the Senate during the interim between the last Senate meeting in the spring and the first meeting in the fall on matters requiring urgent action. (UM Appendix C, 4.3) SECTION I Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation By The Faculty Senate NON-STANDARD PROPOSAL COLLEGE OF ARTS & SCIENCES: Department name change from “Department of English” to “Department of English and Creative Writing” see Appendix A The English Department voted unanimously to change our name to reflect the curriculum we already teach. The department name “English and Creative Writing” is an accurate representation of who we are and what we do. We have long offered undergraduate and graduate courses in both Literature and Creative Writing, but in 2020, we began offering a two-tracked major for anyone majoring in English: the Literature Track and the Creative Writing Track. We also offer a Creative Writing minor, as well as a Creative Writing option for the Masters portfolio and the PhD dissertation. We also wish to disambiguate Creative Writing from other kinds of writing specializations offered by the Department of Professional Writing. As matters stand currently, students arriving at URI are often confused. SSCC Report 2024-2025-02B Page 1 of 4

passages.text: FACULTY SENATE OFFICE FACULTY SENATE LEGISLATION AUGUST 13, 2024 Faculty Senate Special Summer Curriculum Committee Report 2024-2025-02B At the July 31, 2024 meeting of the Special Summer Curriculum Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate Executive Committee for summer 2024 approval . The Executive Committee shall have the power to act for the Senate during the interim between the last Senate meeting in the spring and the first meeting in the fall on matters requiring urgent action. (UM Appendix C, 4.3) SECTION I Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation By The Faculty Senate NON-STANDARD PROPOSAL COLLEGE OF ARTS & SCIENCES: Department name change from “Department of English” to “Department of English and Creative Writing” see Appendix A The English Department voted unanimously to change our name to reflect the curriculum we already teach. The department name “English and Creative Writing” is an accurate representation of who we are and what we do. We have long offered undergraduate and graduate courses in both Literature and Creative Writing, but in 2020, we began offering a two-tracked major for anyone majoring in English: the Literature Track and the Creative Writing Track. We also offer a Creative Writing minor, as well as a Creative Writing option for the Masters portfolio and the PhD dissertation. We also wish to disambiguate Creative Writing from other kinds of writing specializations offered by the Department of Professional Writing. As matters stand currently, students arriving at URI are often confused. SSCC Report 2024-2025-02B Page 1 of 4

FSEC Report #2024-2025-01October 10, 2024 Context: The Faculty Senate Executive Committee (FSEC) has identified the need for achange in Chapter 2 of the University Manual.
Chapter 2, “The Administration,” is typicallyreviewed for routine updates by administrators led by the Provost’s office.
The Chapteraddresses the Administrative Offices of the University, the Channel of Authority, and theappointment of Administrative Officers.
At Section 2.14.10 of the University Manual, theprocess for filling vacant administrator positions is described.
This Section requires thatthe Faculty Senate appoint two members to these search committees.
The FSEC finds thisto be a logistical and operational challenge given that typically, there are time constraintsassociated with commencing a search process and convening a search committee.
Becausethe Faculty Senate only meets monthly during the academic year and not at all over thesummer, the FSEC believes the process would be made more efficient by allowing the FSECto play this appointing role rather than the full Senate.
Existing Language 2.14.10 Appointment of Administrative Officers.

CASC Report #2024-2025-02October 10, 2024 Faculty Senate Meeting Context: URI awards graduating students academic honors according to the languagelocated at Section 8.22.40 (Academic Regulations) of the University Manual.
Last spring, asituation arose which made clear the language has some vagaries and was due for anupdate.
The following proposed amendment was approved unanimously by CASC on4/4/24 and referred to the Constitution, By-Laws, and University Manual Committee(CBUM).
The two committees now agree the matter is ripe for introduction to the fullFaculty Senate.
In the specific instance that brought the issue to light, a stellar studentserved as an Undergraduate Teaching Assistant and received 5 credits for an S/U course inreturn.
This student was deemed to have completed fewer than 60 required graded creditsand was not afforded the opportunity to graduate with honors.
The proposed languagewould provide much-needed clarity around the minimum number of graded creditsrequired.

passages.heading: Curriculum & Standards Committee Report #2024-2025-02 | Page 1
passages.text:
It would allow transfer students to take at least one S/U course, or exercise a‘Second Grade Option’ for a course taken in their first semester at URI, without costingthem the opportunity to graduate with honors.
Existing Language: 8.22.40 Distinction.
Students who complete at least sixty (60) credits of their work at theUniversity are eligible to graduate with honors.
Grades in all courses attempted at theUniversity shall be included in the calculation of the quality point average.
On therecommendation of the student’s dean, an exception may be made for students who havebeen readmitted but have not used any of the prior work to satisfy the degreerequirements.
Those who attain a cumulative quality point average at the time ofgraduation of at least 3.30 shall be recognized as graduating “cum laude.” Those whoachieve a quality point average of 3.50 shall graduate “magna cum laude,” and those whoattain a quality point average of at least 3.70 “summa cum laude.” Participation in an honorsprogram shall not be a condition for graduating “cum laude,” “magna cum laude” or “summacum laude.” #00-01-29 Proposed Language: 8.22.40 Distinction.

SECTION I Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation by The Faculty Senate PROGRAM MODIFICATIONS COLLEGE OF ARTS & SCIENCES: BS Mathematics, Effective Winter 2025 Appendix A There are three main modifications: 1. Change in Transfer from UC: Completion of MTH 141 with grade C or better is added in order to ensure students are prepared for the major. MTH 141 is also the first course that counts toward each of the tracks in BS. 2. Change in BS - General and Applied Tracks: MTH 362 is now allowed to count toward the elective credits, but not in conjunction with MTH 244. The rationale behind counting only of these courses is that the y cover similar topics. (Please see accompanying specialization proposals) 3. Change in BS Applied Option: EGR 106 has been added as an additional option (out of many) to satisfy a computational requirement in Applied Math BS. EGR 106 is a very popular course among our major and covers necessary topics. Specialization, Music Composition (BM Music), Effective Winter 2025 Appendix D Music composition lessons are a bit different than other lessons, and the work typically done in MUS 411 is already done in the lessons.
MUS 411 is enrichment through repertoire, therefore MUS 411 is superfluous for composition students, considering they already engage in rigorous score analysis as part of their composition curriculum.

passages.heading: Special Summer Curriculum Committee Report #2024-2025-03B | Page 2
passages.text:
Composition students typically undergo a curriculum that already includes regular analysis of scores relevant to their lessons, in addition to taking Counterpoint, Form and A nalysis, and Orchestration.
This means they are already exposed to a variety of Western Music styles, techniques, and structures through their coursework.
Composition lessons often involve in -depth discussions and analyses of specific compositional techniques, styles, and works.
These discussions are tailored to the individual needs and interests of the composition students, providing a more targeted and personalized learning experience.
Students not only listen and analyze scores but also actively apply what they learn to their own compositions.
This hands -on approach allows them to directly experiment with techniques and styles discussed in their lessons, r einforcing their understanding and skills development.
Composition students integrate the techniques learned from studying scores (Saariaho, Boulez, Webern, Harvey, Risset, Grisey, Ravel, Berio, Ligeti, Higdon, Aberdam, Revueltas) and sometimes innovate upon these techniques in their own compositions.
MUS 411 is definitely redundant for composition students.

The result is an additional 2 credits in required courses (MUS 235, and MUS 311 OR 312).
To balance the loss of 4 credits from 411, students will have the opportunity to take 7 cr. of electives instead of 5.

Changes Summary description and rationale of proposed specialization.
Music composition lessons are a bit different than other lessons, and the work typically done in MUS 411 is already done in the lessons.
MUS 411 is enrichment through repertoire, therefore MUS 411 is superfluous for composition students, considering they already engage in rigorous score analysis as part of their composition curriculum.
Composition students typically undergo a curriculum that already includes regular analysis of scores relevant to their lessons, in addition to taking Counterpoint, Form and Analysis, and Orchestration.
This means they are already exposed to a variety of Western Music styles, techniques, and structures through their coursework.
Composition lessons often involve in-depth discussions and analyses of specific compositional techniques, styles, and works.
These discussions are tailored to the individual needs and interests of the composition students, providing a more targeted and personalized learning experience.
Students not only listen and analyze scores but also actively apply what they learn to their own compositions.

passages.heading: Special Summer Curriculum Committee Report #2024-2025-03B | Page 38
passages.text:
This hands-on approach allows them to directly experiment with techniques and styles discussed in their lessons, reinforcing their understanding and skills development.
Composition students integrate the techniques learned from studying scores (Saariaho, Boulez, Webern, Harvey, Risset, Grisey, Ravel, Berio, Ligeti, Higdon, Aberdam, Revueltas) and sometimes innovate upon these techniques in their own compositions.
MUS 411 is definitely redundant for composition students.
Adjustments have been made to MUS 235, 311 and 312 DUE to a change in credits for music courses, MUS 235 from 2 to 3 credits, and MUS 311 and 312 from 1 to 2 credits.
The result is an additional 2 credits in required courses (MUS 235, and MUS 311 OR 312).
To balance the loss of 4 credits from 411, students will have the opportunity to take 7 cr. of electives instead of 5.
