The B.S. program in interdisciplinary neuroscience will provide students with foundational knowledge of the nervous system including a broad array of areas such as development of the nervous system, brain structure and function, cellular and molecular biology, neuropharmacology, neuroethics, research methods, as well as knowledge of neurodegenerative disease and psychological/psychiatric disorders.
The undergraduate program offers three major options (tracks): a B.S. degree with a major in Clinical Neuroscience from the College of Health Sciences, a B.S. degree with a major in Molecular Neuroscience from the College of Environment and Life Sciences, and a B.S. degree with a major in Neuropharmacology from the College of Pharmacy.
The option for choosing between three different neuroscience majors is a unique andstrength makesto thisthe URI majorneuroscience trulyeducational distinct with regard to undergraduate educationexperience.
Please note: students may only earn a Neuroscience degree in one track due to the overlapping of preparation and core courses needed for the major.

Careers Students who graduate with thisa B.S. in interdisciplinary neuroscience have an ever-growing choice of career options.
These include graduate school in neuroscience, medical school, graduate programs in medical and allied health professions; research positions in academic, government, biotech or pharmaceutical laboratories; and a variety of professional opportunities in science education, science writing, data science, and health care.
Requirements The B.S. program requires a minimum of 120 credits for graduation: 40-43 preparation, 31-36 core, 40 general education, (some of these credits/courses will overlap with your preparation credits/courses), and 18 in your chosen major/track (clinical, molecular, or neuropharmacology).
To transfer out of University College for Academic Success and enter your selected degree granting college, you must complete a minimum of 56 credits of the following courses with a 2.0 GPA average: BIO 101/103, BIO 102/104, BIO 220/221, BIO 222/223, CHM 101/102, CHM 112/114, CHM 124 or 227, PHY 111/185, MTH 103/131, PSY 113, COM 100, WRT 104 or 106, URI 101, NEU 101, NEU 110, NEU 210, NEU 262, and NEU 230.

Landscape Architecture Landscape architecture is a 126-credit curriculum leading to the Bachelor of Landscape Architecture (B.L.A.) degree.
Accredited by the Landscape Architecture Accreditation Board of the ASLA, the curriculum is designed to prepare undergraduates for professional careers in public and private practice.
Landscape architecture is a profession that involves the design, planning, preservation, and restoration of the landscape by applying art, science, and technology to achieve the best use of our land and water resources.
Landscape architects design and plan parks, plazas, and recreation areas; residential, institutional and commercial developments; transportation facilities, new towns and campus landscapes, and green infrastructure.
They are also involved in planning and designing landscapes in coastal areas and inland developments impacted by climate.
The requirements of this curriculum include preparation in the basic arts and sciences.

passages.heading: Curriculum & Standards Committee Report #2024-2025-01B | Page 4
passages.text:
The major includes 63-64 credits of professional core classes (LAR 101, 201, 202, 243, 244, 300, 301, 302, 343, 344, 345, 346, 353, 354, 443, 444, 445, 447, 450); 28-29 credits of supporting requirements (ART 207; GEG 101; PLS 150; CHM 100, 101 or 103 or PHY 109, or GEO 100G, or 103; CPL 410, CPL 434, 538; MTH 103; and PLS 200); and 7-8 credits of supporting electives.
Students will also take general education classes and 6-7 credits of free electives.
Students accepted into landscape architecture are required to maintain a grade point average of at least 2.50 with no landscape architecture grades below a letter C.
Students failing to maintain this minimum may be removed from the program and required to reapply once this requirement is satis�ed.
Students are required to own a P .C. laptop computer by the time they enter the program.
Speci�cations are available from the Landscape Architecture Program O�ce or from the URI Bookstore (Ramtech).
URI’s Landscape Architecture Program (LAR) is competitive.
Accreditation standards regarding staff and facilities limit the number of students accepted into the major to 20 per year.

passages.heading: Curriculum & Standards Committee Report #2024-2025-01B | Page 4
passages.text:
While enrolled in the program, students will be reviewed twice during their course of studies: �rst for admission into the lower-division design sequence and again for acceptance into the upper-division B.L.A. major.
Admission into the lower-division design sequence courses (LAR 243 and 244) requires department approval.
Approximately 75 percent of the openings are �lled by students who enter as incoming freshmen and who maintain a minimum 2.50 grade point average with no grades in LAR courses below a C.
The remaining openings are �lled by matriculated students wishing to transfer into landscape architecture from other majors.
These students are required to apply to the program and to submit an essay and transcript of grades.
Applications and transcripts are evaluated in March each year for acceptance into the lower- division (LAR 243) design sequence for the following fall.
Acceptance into the upper division (junior design sequence) is based on submission and review of a portfolio of lower-division work, a current academic transcript, and written essay.
A maximum of 20 students per year are accepted into the upper- division B.L.A. curriculum.

passages.heading: Curriculum & Standards Committee Report #2024-2025-01B | Page 4
passages.text:
Eligible applicants for upper division are students enrolled in LAR 244/returning applicants, and students wishing to transfer directly into the upper division from other accredited landscape architecture programs.
Only students who have completed comparable lower-division courses will be allowed to compete for these upper-division positions.
Such transfer applicants must �rst be accepted into the University by the O�ce of Admission and have their application package submitted to the Landscape Architecture Department Chair before the last week in February preceding the fall semester in which they wish to enroll.
Students will be noti�ed of their acceptance following a department review.
Students are eligible to transfer from University College for Academic Success to the College of Environment and Life Sciences after they have earned 24 credits with a 2.50 or higher GPA and with permission of the department chair.

No Date Chosen Changes Program Description Plant Sciences The major in Plant Sciences, offered by the Department of Plant Sciences and Entomology, prepares undergraduates for professional careers in the many public and private sectors of horticulture.
After successful completion of the major, students are awarded a degree in Plant Sciences in one of three options: turfgrass management, ornamental horticulture and sustainable crop production.
Graduates of this program pursue careers ranging from landscape contractor, golf course superintendent, director of parks, botanical gardens or arboreta, garden center or �oral shop proprietor, plant propagator, nursery production manager, vegetable or fruit grower, lawn service manager or technical representative for seed, equipment, and chemical companies, to name just a few of the opportunities available.
Other graduates enter graduate school and pursue careers in research and education at public and private institutions.
The unifying theme of the major is the development of sustainable culture and use of plants for amenity or food.
Graduates can meet the standards of several certi�cation organizations.

passages.heading: Curriculum & Standards Committee Report #2024-2025-01B | Page 11
passages.text:
Students in the ornamental horticulture option qualify for certi�cation with the Rhode Island Nursery and Landscape Association and the International Society for Arboriculture.
Graduates of the turfgrass management option qualify for certi�cation as turfgrass managers or turfgrass specialists with the American Registry of Certi�ed Professionals in Agronomy, Crops, and Soils, Ltd. of the American Society of Agronomy.
These same graduates also meet the requirements for registration with the Golf Course Superintendents Association of America.
The department manages over 50 acres of turfgrass, horticulture, and agronomy farms for teaching, research, and outreach.
The C.
Richard Skogley Turfgrass Center is the oldest turfgrass research/teaching program in the U.S.
The department also maintains a 15,000 square foot controlled environment greenhouse complex for hands-on learning and research.
These facilities are closely allied with the URI Botanical Gardens and E.P .
Christopher Arboretum.

passages.heading: Curriculum & Standards Committee Report #2024-2025-01B | Page 11
passages.text:
The Plant Sciences degree requires a total of 120 credits: 29-30 credits of pre-professional natural sciences that all majors must take including PLS 150, PLS 200, PLS 215, PLS 216, 250, PLS 255, BIO 101, BIO 103, BIO 102, BIO 104, CHM 103, CHM 105 (or CHM 101 and CHM 102) or their equivalent; 30 credits in concentration courses; and 15 credits of supporting electives approved by a faculty advisor which are speci�c to the interests of the student.
Turfgrass Management Option.
The turfgrass management option is intended primarily for students who are interested in managing golf courses, athletic �elds, commercial turf properties, sod farms or any other facilities comprised primarily of turf.
Students in this option will gain competencies in all aspects of turf production and management, with a focus on sustainable practices and integrated pest management systems.
Additionally, students interested in landscape management may also fall under this option but may take slightly different concentration courses which will address some of the other aspects of managing large, heterogeneous landscape properties.

passages.heading: Curriculum & Standards Committee Report #2024-2025-01B | Page 11
passages.text:
These students may also take a number of classes in the Landscape Architecture program, which can ful�ll their supporting electives.
Turfgrass Management students are also required to take 30 credits of concentration courses and it is suggested that in earning those credits, they take PLS 306216, PLS 322306, PLS 341322, PLS 361332, PLS 390341, PLS 440361, PLS 442, ENT 387 and ENT 411385.
Ornamental Horticulture Option.
The ornamental horticulture option is intended primarily for students who are interested in nursery management, greenhouse production, the �oral industry and the production and management of woody and herbaceous materials for landscapes and urban areas.
Students in this option will develop a wide set of skills allowing them to work in a diverse number of industries where ornamental plant production and management are practiced.
Students interested in landscape management can also select this option, instead of the turfgrass management option, if their interests are focused more on trees than on turf.
As with the turfgrass management option, these students may also take Landscape Architecture classes to ful�ll supporting electives.

Sustainable Crop Production Option. The sustainable crop production option is intended for students with an interest in growing plants for food, managing food systems and developing sustainable approaches that minimize farming impacts on the environment while maintaining or improving the quality of food and the environment, where possible. Students in this option will learn techniques and strategies for managing small, sustainable farming systems in addition to incorporating food production into the urban environment. Sustainable Crop Production students are also required to take 30 credits of concentration courses and it is suggested that in earning those credits, they take PLS 275, PLS 311, PLS 312, PLS 321, PLS 324, PLS 325, PLS 332, NRS 212, ENT 385 and ENTSAF 411400G. The undergraduate program offers three major options (tracks): a B.S. degree with a major in Clinical Neuroscience from the College of Health Sciences, a B.S. degree with a major in Molecular Neuroscience from the College of Environment and Life Sciences, and a B.S. degree with a major in Neuropharmacology from the College of Pharmacy.
The option for different neuroscience majors is unique and makes this URI major truly distinct with regard to undergraduate education.

The B.S. program in interdisciplinary neuroscience will provide students with foundational knowledge of the nervous system including a broad array of areas such as development of the nervous system, brain structure and function, cellular and molecular biology, neuropharmacology, neuroethics, research methods, as well as knowledge of neurodegenerative disease and psychological/psychiatric disorders.
The undergraduate program offers three major options (tracks): a B.S. degree with a major in Clinical Neuroscience from the College of Health Sciences, a B.S. degree with a major in Molecular Neuroscience from the College of Environment and Life Sciences, and a B.S. degree with a major in Neuropharmacology from the College of Pharmacy.
The option for different neuroscience majors is unique and makes this URI major truly distinct with regard to undergraduate education.
Please note: students may only earn a Neuroscience degree in one track due to the overlapping of preparation and core courses needed for the major.
Careers Students who graduate with this B.S. have an ever-growing choice of career options.

passages.heading: Curriculum & Standards Committee Report #2024-2025-01B | Page 30
passages.text:
These options include graduate school in neuroscience or other programs such as psychology or physical therapy and other allied health professions, medical school, research positions in academic, government, biotech or pharmaceutical laboratories, and a variety of professional opportunities in science education, science writing, data science, and health care.
Requirements The B.S. program requires a minimum of 120 credits for graduation: 40-43 preparation, 31-36 core, 40 general education, (some of these credits/courses will overlap with your preparation credits/courses), and 18 in your chosen major/track (clinical, molecular, or neuropharmacology).
In addition to an overall 2.0 GPA average, neuroscience majors must earn a 2.0 GPA average in Preparation and Core Course in order to graduate.

The program is designed for working professionals.
Typically, candidates complete the program within 8 to 9 semesters (includes summer term).
The curriculum is structured into three main components: Foundation Coursework, Methods & Application Coursework, and the Internship.
Candidates may start the program in the fall, spring, or summer semesters, beginning with Foundation Coursework.
Both Foundation and Methods & Application Coursework must be completed before enrolling in the Internship course.
Clinical experiences are completed throughout the program, providing opportunities to integrate theory and practice in real world settings.
In order to accommodate working professionals, candidates will collaborate with the program coordinator to develop an individualized course sequence for their foundational coursework.

passages.heading: Graduate Council Report #2024-2025-01C | Page 5
passages.text:
Candidates are required to take the following courses: Foundation Coursework EDC 529 Foundations of Educational Research EDL 500 Engaging Communities for Change EDL 501 Legal and Ethical Issues in Educational Leadership EDL 502 Fiscal Management for Educational Leaders EDL 503 Operations & Management for Educational Leaders Methods & Application Coursework EDL 504 Program Evaluation for School Leaders EDL 505 Supervision of Instruction EDL 506 Instructional and Curriculum Leadership EDL 507 Managing Human Capital EDL 508 Leading School & District Improvement Internship EDL 510 Internship I + Seminar EDL 511 Internship II + Seminar This program is considered a hybrid program.
Courses will be delivered online in a combination of synchronous (Zoom) and asynchronous (Brightspace) sessions.
A variety of instructional methods are used, including lectures, discussions, case studies, presentations, cooperative learning activities, Internet assignments, guest practitioner presentations (as possible), role-play, and written and verbal assignments.
Courses are taught by URI full-time and part-time faculty.

Program Learning Outcomes At the completion of this program, candidates will understand and demonstrate the capacity to promote the current and future success and well-being of each student and adult in their school community by applying the knowledge, skills, and commitments necessary to: Goal #1 - Strategic Leadership and Visioning 1.1 - Collaboratively lead, design, and implement a school mission, vision, and process for continuous improvement that reflects a core set of values and priorities, including data use, technology, equity, diversity, digital citizenship, and community. 1.2 - Demonstrate the capacity to advocate for ethical decisions and cultivate and enact professional norms. 1.3 - Develop and maintain a supportive, equitable, culturally responsive, and inclusive school culture.

Goal #3 - School Improvement 3.1 - Engage families, community, and school personnel to strengthen student learning, support school improvement, and advocate for the needs of their school and community. 3.2 - Foster a professional community of teachers and other professional staff to promote each student’s academic success and social and emotional well-being.
Goal #4 - Management and Resource Planning 4.1 - Develop coherent management, communication, technology, school-level governance, and operation systems to promote each student's academic success and well being. 4.2 - Build the school’s professional capacity, engage staff in the development of a collaborative professional culture, and improve systems of staff supervision, evaluation, and support.

Opportunities for Graduates The Educational Leadership & Policy (EDL) program at the University of Rhode Island equips graduates with the skills, knowledge, and credentials necessary to pursue a wide range of leadership roles within the education sector.
The program is designed to meet the growing demand for qualified school leaders, addressing both current workforce needs and future job market trends.
Economic Need and Workforce Data The demand for skilled educational leaders is increasing, particularly as schools and districts navigate complex challenges such as educational equity, technological integration, and community engagement.
According to the U.S.
Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), employment for elementary, middle, and high school principals is projected to grow by 4% from 2022 to 2032, which reflects the steady need for qualified individuals to fill these critical roles.
The BLS also highlights the ongoing need to replace retiring principals, further emphasizing the demand for new school leaders.
Available Jobs and Job Titles Graduates of the EDL program are well-prepared to assume a variety of leadership positions within the educational field.

passages.heading: Graduate Council Report #2024-2025-01C | Page 8
passages.text:
Some of the common job titles for program graduates include: School Principal Assistant Principal Dean District Administrator Instructional Coordinator Director of Special Education Curriculum Director Superintendent These roles are crucial in shaping the educational experiences of students and ensuring that schools operate effectively and efficiently.
The EDL program provides the comprehensive preparation necessary for graduates to excel in these positions.
Job Outlook and Growth The job outlook for educational leaders is positive, particularly in urban centers and areas with growing student populations.
The Bureau of Labor & Statistics (BLS) projects that there will be about 20,000 openings for principals each year over the next decade, mostly due to workers leaving the labor force or transferring to other occupations.
Salaries Salaries for educational leadership positions vary depending on the role and geographic location, but they generally reflect the high level of responsibility associated with these roles.
According to the BLS, the median annual wage for elementary, middle, and high school principals was $103,310 as of May 2022.

passages.text:

passages.text:
As the landscape of education continues to evolve, there is a growing need for skilled leaders who can navigate the complexities of educational institutions, implement effective policies, and drive meaningful change.
Effective principals have substantial positive impacts on student achievement.
Research demonstrates that replacing a below-average principal with an above-average one can significantly increase student learning in both math and reading annually.
Beyond student achievement, principals also affect other crucial outcomes such as student attendance, discipline, and teacher retention.
Effective principals are linked to reduced absenteeism and exclusionary discipline, as well as higher teacher job satisfaction and lower turnover rates, particularly among high-performing teachers.
Principals who engage in instructionally focused interactions with teachers, such as providing feedback, coaching, and developing a data-driven instructional program, contribute to positive school outcomes.
These practices emphasize the importance of principals being deeply involved in the instructional aspects of their schools.
Principals play a crucial role in addressing educational equity.

passages.heading: Graduate Council Report #2024-2025-01C | Page 9
passages.text:
Effective leaders are adept at creating inclusive environments that support diverse student populations.
This involves strategic hiring, fostering collaborative cultures, and ensuring equitable allocation of resources.
Rhode Island, like many other states, is facing a shortage of school administrators.
According to data collected by the Rhode Island Department of Education for the 2021-22 school year, 46 administrator vacancies were reported by 41 Local Education Agencies (LEAs), representing 8% of building-level administrator positions statewide.
Nationally, the National Center for Education Statistics (2023) found that about one in ten public school principals left the profession between the 2020-21 and 2021-22 school years.
This highlights the urgent need for strong principal preparation programs that equip future leaders with the skills required for effective school leadership.
Ongoing professional development and support are critical to ensure principals have the tools necessary to succeed (Grissom, Egalite, and Lindsay, 2021).

The EDL program is distinct from other graduate programs offered at URI, particularly those within the College of Education.

EDL 500 Engaging Communities for Change This course equips candidates with the skills to engage the community in school improvement, enhance communication, and transform support into advocacy.
Candidates learn to create a supportive school environment, promoting student success and well-being through collaborative engagement and a shared vision.
EDL 501 Legal and Ethical Issues in Educational Leadership This course examines the legal foundation of schools and educational policy, analyzing cases, statutes, and constitutional provisions affecting elementary and secondary school operations in the United States.

passages.heading: Graduate Council Report #2024-2025-01C | Page 12
passages.text:
It also explores the intersection of legal, ethical, and political issues in public administration, familiarizing educators with professional norms and ethical and legal standards.
It explores a wide spectrum of topics, including due process, discipline, freedom of speech, school safety, issues of discrimination, religion within educational contexts, and the rights of rights of marginalized and/or vulnerable students.
EDL 502 Fiscal Management for Educational Leaders This course analyzes the systems and mechanisms for �nancing public schools in the United States.
It provides both an overview of basic school �nance concepts and issues and an examination of Rhode Island’s system of �nancing schools.
This course blends the theoretical foundations of school �nance with their practical applications at state and local levels.
Candidates examine essential business functions including budgeting, facilities �nance, purchasing, and entrepreneurship as they relate to the day-to-day functions of the complex school organization.
Legal matters related to business ethics, diversity, and equity in budget allocations are prioritized.

Specialization, Music Composition (BM Music), Effective Winter 2025 Appendix D Music composition lessons are a bit different than other lessons, and the work typically done in MUS 411 is already done in the lessons.
MUS 411 is enrichment through repertoire, therefore MUS 411 is superfluous for composition students, considering they already engage in rigorous score analysis as part of their composition curriculum.

passages.heading: 24-25-04 | Page 3
passages.text:
Composition students typically undergo a curriculum that already includes regular analysis of scores relevant to their lessons, in addition to taking Counterpoint, Form and A nalysis, and Orchestration.
This means they are already exposed to a variety of Western Music styles, techniques, and structures through their coursework.
Composition lessons often involve in -depth discussions and analyses of specific compositional techniques, styles, and works.
These discussions are tailored to the individual needs and interests of the composition students, providing a more targeted and personalized learning experience.
Students not only listen and analyze scores but also actively apply what they learn to their own compositions.
This hands -on approach allows them to directly experiment with techniques and styles discussed in their lessons, r einforcing their understanding and skills development.
Composition students integrate the techniques learned from studying scores (Saariaho, Boulez, Webern, Harvey, Risset, Grisey, Ravel, Berio, Ligeti, Higdon, Aberdam, Revueltas) and sometimes innovate upon these techniques in their own compositions.
MUS 411 is definitely redundant for composition students.

Changes Summary description and rationale of proposed specialization.
Music composition lessons are a bit different than other lessons, and the work typically done in MUS 411 is already done in the lessons.
MUS 411 is enrichment through repertoire, therefore MUS 411 is superfluous for composition students, considering they already engage in rigorous score analysis as part of their composition curriculum.
Composition students typically undergo a curriculum that already includes regular analysis of scores relevant to their lessons, in addition to taking Counterpoint, Form and Analysis, and Orchestration.
This means they are already exposed to a variety of Western Music styles, techniques, and structures through their coursework.
Composition lessons often involve in-depth discussions and analyses of specific compositional techniques, styles, and works.
These discussions are tailored to the individual needs and interests of the composition students, providing a more targeted and personalized learning experience.
Students not only listen and analyze scores but also actively apply what they learn to their own compositions.

passages.heading: 24-25-04 | Page 39
passages.text:
This hands-on approach allows them to directly experiment with techniques and styles discussed in their lessons, reinforcing their understanding and skills development.
Composition students integrate the techniques learned from studying scores (Saariaho, Boulez, Webern, Harvey, Risset, Grisey, Ravel, Berio, Ligeti, Higdon, Aberdam, Revueltas) and sometimes innovate upon these techniques in their own compositions.
MUS 411 is definitely redundant for composition students.
Adjustments have been made to MUS 235, 311 and 312 DUE to a change in credits for music courses, MUS 235 from 2 to 3 credits, and MUS 311 and 312 from 1 to 2 credits.
The result is an additional 2 credits in required courses (MUS 235, and MUS 311 OR 312).
To balance the loss of 4 credits from 411, students will have the opportunity to take 7 cr. of electives instead of 5.

The major areas include neuropharmacology in the College of Pharmacy – Department of Biomedical and Pharmaceutical Science (BPS), molecular neuroscience in the College of the Environment and Life Sciences – Department Cell and Molecular Biology (CMB), and clinical neuroscience in the College of Health – Department of Psychology.

The B.S. program in interdisciplinary neuroscience will provide students with foundational knowledge of the nervous system including a broad array of areas such as development of the nervous system, brain structure and function, cellular and molecular biology, neuropharmacology, neuroethics, research methods, as well as knowledge of neurodegenerative disease and psychological/psychiatric disorders.
The undergraduate program offers three major options (tracks): a B.S. degree with a major in Clinical Neuroscience from the College of Health Sciences, a B.S. degree with a major in Molecular Neuroscience from the College of Environment and Life Sciences, and a B.S. degree with a major in Neuropharmacology from the College of Pharmacy.
The option for choosing between three different neuroscience majors is a unique andstrength makesto thisthe URI majorneuroscience trulyeducational distinct with regard to undergraduate educationexperience.
Please note: students may only earn a Neuroscience degree in one track due to the overlapping of preparation and core courses needed for the major.

Careers Students who graduate with thisa B.S. in interdisciplinary neuroscience have an ever-growing choice of career options.
These include graduate school in neuroscience, medical school, graduate programs in medical and allied health professions; research positions in academic, government, biotech or pharmaceutical laboratories; and a variety of professional opportunities in science education, science writing, data science, and health care.
Requirements The B.S. program requires a minimum of 120 credits for graduation: 40-43 preparation, 31-36 core, 40 general education, (some of these credits/courses will overlap with your preparation credits/courses), and 18 in your chosen major/track (clinical, molecular, or neuropharmacology).
To transfer out of University College for Academic Success and enter your selected degree granting college, you must complete a minimum of 56 credits of the following courses with a 2.0 GPA average: BIO 101/103, BIO 102/104, BIO 220/221, BIO 222/223, CHM 101/102, CHM 112/114, CHM 124 or 227, PHY 111/185, MTH 103/131, PSY 113, COM 100, WRT 104 or 106, URI 101, NEU 101, NEU 110, NEU 210, NEU 262, and NEU 230.

CPL 550 | Urban Design (3 crs.) Overview of the fundamentals of urban design.
Urban design concerns the arrangement, appearance and functionality of towns and cities, and in particular the shaping and uses of urban public spaces.

passages.heading: Graduate Council Report #2024-2025-02A | Page 4
passages.text: Urban design is regarded as a disciplinary practi ce that operates at the intersection of the three professions of “urban planning”, “landscape architecture”, and “architecture.” Urban design deals with the design of the community, its form and pattern; the massing and grouping of the buildings; and the design and organization of spaces between them. passages.text: FACULTY SENATE OFFICE FACULTY SENATE LEGISLATION DECEMBER 12, 2024 Curriculum & Standards Committee Report 2024-2025-04A At the November 21, 2024 meeting of the Curriculum & Standards Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate for approval. Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation By The Faculty Senate COURSE CHANGES COLLEGE OF ARTS & SCIENCES: ART 354 | Art of the Ancient Mediterranean, Effective Fall 2025 Eliminate prerequisites (3 crs.) Developments in architecture, painting, and sculpture in Greece and Rome from 800 B.C. to 400 A.D. Brief analysis of the art of the Aegean from 2500 to 1500 B.C. (Lec. 3) May be repeated once with permission of instructor. ART 356 | Medieval Art, Effective Spring 2026 Eliminate prerequisites (3 crs.) PROGRAM REPORT CURRICULUM & STANDARDS COMMITTEE Report 2025-2026-07B At the April 2, 2026 meeting of the Curriculum & Standards Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate for approval.
FOR CONFIRMATION BY THE FACULTY SENATE COLLEGE OF ARTS & SCIENCES BS – Computer Science, effective Fall 2026 Appendix A The proposed curriculum revision modernizes the B.S. in Computer Science to reflect contemporary computing practice while maintaining academic rigor.
The revision introduces a formal specialization structure with focused pathways in Artificial Intelligence and Cybersecurity; and a flexible option, while streamlining major requirements to improve time-to-degree without reducing total credits or academic standards.
The specialization structure also allows for the addition of future specializations to meet the demand of this rapidly changing field.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-07B | Page 2
passages.text: We are proposing the following changes to major requirements: - Remove CSC 106, reducing time-to-degree by one semester. - Add CSC 310 as a core requirement, ensuring all graduates gain essential expertise in data -driven decision-making and AI/machine learning, skills that are now fundamental across all computing domains. - Remove MTH 142, acknowledging that MTH 141 provides sufficient mathematical foundation for required CS courses. - Add STA 409 to ensure consistent mathematical preparation for machine learning, data analysis, and advanced study in artificial intelligence. - Reduce the science requirement from two courses to one, allowing expanded free electives while maintaining interdisciplinary science exposure. - Refine the writing requirement course list to align with general education requirements. - Implement formal specializations in Artificial Intelligence, Cybersecurity, and General Computer Science, replacing loosely defined electives with coherent learning pathways aligned with high -demand employment sectors.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-07B | Page 3
passages.text:
This curriculum revision strengthens the Computer Science major through internal reallocation of Department resources rather than expansion.
The proposed changes maintain the same total credit requirements (120 credits, 56 in major) while improving student outcomes through streamlined prerequisites and providing clearer career pathways via formal specializations in the two highest-growth computing sectors: Artificial Intelligence and Cybersecurity.
For students, the revision delivers a contemporary curriculum that reflects current industry practice without compromising academic rigor.
For the Department, the changes ensure alignment with national curriculum standards, facilitate enrollment management through reduced bottlenecks, and enhance recruitment by offering competitive specializations in the technology industry's most in-demand areas.
The clear program structure with AI and Cybersecurity pathways strengthens program identity for accreditation, assessment, and marketing to prospective students.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-07B | Page 3
passages.text:
For the University, the revision supports improved graduation rates, responds directly to workforce demand for specialized computing skills, and strengthens the institution's position in a highly competitive academic market.
The proposal requires no new resources, no additional faculty, and no changes to total credit hours.
It simply reorganizes existing offerings to better serve students and meet contemporary educational standards.
The Department respectfully requests approval of these curriculum changes to maintain the competitiveness and academic quality of the Computer Science program while positioning our graduates for success in the rapidly evolving fields of computing.
Specialization – Artificial Intelligence (CSC BS) Appendix B The specialization in Artificial Intelligence equips students with a progressive pathway from core machine learning concepts through advanced topics in deep learning, large language models, statistical learning, and scalable data algorithms.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-07B | Page 3
passages.text:
Anchored by CSC 461 (Machine Learning) as a required gateway course, the specialization ensures that every student develops foundational competency in machine learning before advancing to two upper-division electives drawn from a curated menu spanning neural networks and deep learning (CSC 561), big data algorithms (CSC 546), multivariate statistical learning (STA 441), and special topics in AI (CSC 581).
We are in the process of reactivating artificial intelligence (CSC 481), which was removed from the catalog because it had not been taught recently.
We plan to add it to the rotation of courses once it is reactivated.
Additionally, we have 2 new courses in the Kuali pipeline, large language models (CSC 455) and machine learning security and privacy (CSC 465).
These courses have been taught in the last couple of years as special topics (CSC 492/592) for undergraduate and graduate students.
Until these courses are approved, students can use them to fulfill requirements with departmental permission.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-07B | Page 3
passages.text:
Built on the program's core computer science requirements, this three -course specialization delivers the theoretical depth and applied judgment graduates need to design, evaluate, and responsibly deploy intelligent systems across diverse computing domains.
The specialization directly implements recent trends in CS education, which identify machine learning and artificial intelligence as central knowledge areas for contemporary CS graduates and implement coherent depth pathways beyond introductory ML/AI expos ure.
Critically, this specialization reflects a fundamental shift in the discipline itself: artificial intelligence is no longer a peripheral subfield, it is now core to how software systems are designed, deployed, and evaluated across virtually every application domain.
The strongest AI practitioners are not narrow specialists but professionals with deep computer science foundations in algorithms, systems, and software design, precisely what this program's core curriculum provides.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-07B | Page 4
passages.text:
The timeliness of this specialization cannot be overstated.
AI and machine learning consistently rank among the highest-demand and highest-compensating skills in the computing workforce, and regional employers, from healthcare and defense to financial services and technology, are actively seeking graduates with exactly this preparation.
Peer institutions across New England have already established formal AI tracks or majors, and the absence of a comparable pathway at URI places the program at a direct competitive disadvantage in student recruitment.
Importantly, the Department has made investments in faculty with expertise in machine learning, data science, and AI over recent years.
This specialization now formally leverages these investments into a coherent, marketable academic pathway for undergraduate students.
Specialization – Cyber Security (CSC BS) Appendix C The Cybersecurity specialization provides students with a structured pathway from foundational security concepts to advanced defensive practice.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-07B | Page 4
passages.text:
CSF 430 establishes core knowledge of security threats, defensive planning, and implementation of protective technologies, while CSF 432 builds hands-on competency in securing the networks and systems of real-world organizations.
Students then complete either CSF 434 or CSF 534, both of which advance into specialized topics including intrusion detection, penetration testing, incident response, malware analysis, and risk management, with CSF 534 incorporating a research dimension suited to students pursuing graduate study.
The Department of Computer Science and Statistics has developed substantial curricular expertise in cybersecurity over many years, reflected in a well-established sequence of CSF courses that, until now, have not been formally integrated into the B.S. in Computer Science.
This specialization rectifies that gap by leveraging existing departmental resources, faculty expertise, course infrastructure, and proven instructional design to offer students a coherent, named credential without requiring new courses or additional hiring.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-07B | Page 4
passages.text:
This is particularly timely given that cybersecurity professionals are among the most critically needed in today's workforce and organizations across every sector face a widening shortage of qualified security professionals.
By formally establishing this specialization, the Department positions its graduates to meet this demand while enhancing the University's competitiveness in recruiting students who seek purposeful, career -aligned computing education.
Specialization – General Computer Science (CSC BS) Appendix D The General Computer Science specialization provides students with a structured yet flexible pathway to tailor advanced coursework to their individual interests and career goals.
Building on the program's core curriculum, students complete three additional CSC courses: one at the 300 level or above and two at the 400 level or above.
Our department currently offers many eligible courses in areas that include, but are not limited to, algorithms, artificial intelligence, computer graphics, database systems, computer systems, programming languages, and networking.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-07B | Page 4
passages.text:
This specialization enables students to develop both depth and breadth beyond the core curriculum while aligning their studies with departmental strengths, emerging technologies, and evolving workforce demands.
Because no single specialization can encompass the full scope of modern computing, the General Computer Science pathway preserves student access to the discipline’s broad intellectual landscape.
It ensures that students whose goals lie outside established options such as Artificial Intelligence or Cybersecurity can still pursue a formally recognized course of study.
In doing so, the specialization supports preparation for diverse computing careers, interdisciplinary work, and graduate study across the field.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-07B | Page 5
passages.text:
BA – Art Appendix E Rationale for Four-Credit Studio Classes According to the University Manual, a three-credit class meets for 45 hours per semester.
In contrast, a three-credit studio class meets for 71.5 hours per semester.
Four-credit courses are designated to meet for 60 hours per semester.
If our studio courses became four-credit courses, they would still meet for 19% more time than the standard four-credit class.
Dean Riley approved that all studio courses be increased to four credits to better reflect the additional instructional hours and workload required for both students and faculty in these courses. https://web.uri.edu/manual/chapter-8/chapter-8-3/ Curriculum Changes Our revised curriculum better integrates art and design while also scaffolding professional skills for our students to be prepared for the workplace and to excel within todays and tomorrow’s environment.

COLLEGE OF BUSINESS BA – Business Studies Specialization – Human Resource Leadership (BUS BA) Appendix O The proposed Human Resources Leadership specialization within the B.A. in Business Studies is designed to prepare students to lead people and organizations in a rapidly evolving workplace.
Effective leadership today requires more than technical business kn owledge; it demands an understanding of human behavior, organizational culture, social dynamics, and the systems that shape how people work together.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-07B | Page 7
passages.text:
This specialization integrates these dimensions by combining business courses in management and leadership by using interdisciplinary coursework to deepen students’ understanding of interpersonal communication, group dynamics, diversity, equity and inclusion, and organizational systems.
Students pursuing this specialization will explore how organizations attract, develop, motivate, and retain talent, and how leaders foster environments where individuals and teams can thrive.
They will gain skills in areas such as leadership communication, conflict resolution, negotiation, and change management, while also examining the broader social and cultural factors that influence workplace relationships and organizational outcomes.
This interdisciplinary approach reflects the evolving expectations of employers, who increasingly seek graduates with the ability to manage people effectively, lead diverse teams, and navigate complex organizational challenges.
It also aligns with national trends in workforce development and talent management, where human resources leadership is emerging as a strategic driver of organizational success.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-07B | Page 7
passages.text:
By leveraging existing courses across multiple disciplines that are not currently part of the B.A. in Business Studies curriculum, this specialization can be implemented efficiently while significantly expanding the career pathways available to graduates, including roles in human resources, talent acquisition, organizational development, employee relations, an d leadership consulting.
Specialization – Sports Management (BUS BA) Appendix P The specialization is designed to help prepare students for careers in sports management, where hands-on experiences with prospective employers and relationships are a high priority.
The specialization courses build on the leadership core to emphasize comp etencies related to entrepreneurial thinking, marketing, and sports management.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-07B | Page 7
passages.text:
According to Hanover Research (11/1/2025, based on data related to 2024 completions), Bachelor's degree programs under CIP code 31.0504 Sport and Fitness Administration/Management is classified as High Growth overall; High Growth on Student Demand; High Growth in Labor Demand on the national level; and High Growth overall; Established Student Demand; and High Growth in Labor Demand in the region (New England, Mid-Atlantic states).
In 2024, 11,853 degrees were completed in the New England

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-07B | Page 8

and Mid-Atlantic regions, which reflected a 1.8% growth in completions.
The average openings are 121,500, which represents a growth rate of 9.3%.
According to URI Admissions officers, it is a program that receives many inquiries.
Currently, anecdotal information suggests student who are interested in sports management are majoring in Sports Media and Communication and Data Science; or are minoring in Business.
Establishing the specialization will provide an opportunity to be more intentional with targeted offerings that can help students prepare for careers in sports management.
Specialization – Tourism Leadership (BUS BA) Appendix Q The Tourism Leadership pathway equips students with the skills to lead organizations and communities in today’s rapidly evolving tourism sector.
Students learn how to design and deliver memorable experiences, manage destinations and hospitality services, and advance sustainability in one of the world’s most dynamic industries.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-07B | Page 8
passages.text:
The pathway emphasizes both strategic leadership and hands-on application, preparing graduates to work in areas such as destination marketing, resort and hotel management, event planning, sustainable tourism development, and cultural or heritage tourism.
Certificate – Business Leadership Appendix R Business Leadership Certificate candidates take four Honors or Honors contract courses through the College of Business.
Honors Business courses bring together motivated peers and cultivate talents of stellar students who are interested in Business.
Honors Business classes offer smaller class sizes (35 or fewer students), excellent faculty, greater academic rigor, and real-world experience.
Honors Business courses often include opportunities within a class for a student to learn new skills, receive certifications, do research, participate in project-based, experiential learning, or do other forms of projects.
Special topics courses and elective seminars will delve into cutting -edge topics, such as business innovations, leadership, sustainability, and AI and t echnologies in business, aligning with the annual Honors Colloquium theme.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-07B | Page 8

Co- curricular experiences that build transversal skills (e.g. leadership abilities, peer collaboration, and personal growth facilitated via service activities, community engagement, workshops, case competitions, and networking).
Students who are enrolled in the College of Business BSBA programs are also eligible to enroll in specially designated sections of core business courses, which will allow them to form a cohesive cohort group throughout their academic journey.

The specialization in Artificial Intelligence equips students with a progressive pathway from core machine learning concepts through advanced topics in deep learning, large language models, statistical learning, and scalable data algorithms.
Anchored by CSC 461 (Machine Learning) as a required gateway course, the specialization ensures that every student develops foundational competency in machine learning before advancing to two upper-division electives drawn from a curated menu spanning neural networks and deep learning (CSC 561), big data algorithms (CSC 546), multivariate statistical learning (STA 441), and special topics in AI (CSC 581).
We are in the process of reactivating artificial intelligence (CSC 481), which was removed from the catalog because it had not been taught recently.
We plan to add it to the rotation of courses once it is reactivated.
Additionally we have 2 new courses in the Kuali pipeline, large language models (CSC 455) and machine learning security and privacy (CSC 465).
These courses have been taught in the last couple of years as special topics (CSC 492/592) for undergraduate and graduate students.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-07B | Page 29
passages.text:
Until these courses are approved, students can use them to fulfill requirements with departmental permission.
Built on the program's core computer science requirements, this three-course specialization delivers the theoretical depth and applied judgment graduates need to design, evaluate, and responsibly deploy intelligent systems across diverse computing domains.
The specialization directly implements recent trends in CS education, which identify machine learning and artificial intelligence as central knowledge areas for contemporary CS graduates and implement coherent depth pathways beyond introductory ML/AI exposure.
Critically, this specialization reflects a fundamental shift in the discipline itself: artificial intelligence is no longer a peripheral subfield, it is now core to how software systems are designed, deployed, and evaluated across virtually every application domain.
The strongest AI practitioners are not narrow specialists but professionals with deep computer science foundations in algorithms, systems, and software design, precisely what this program's core curriculum provides.
The timeliness of this specialization cannot be overstated.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-07B | Page 29
passages.text:
AI and machine learning consistently rank among the highest- demand and highest-compensating skills in the computing workforce, and regional employers, from healthcare and defense to financial services and technology, are actively seeking graduates with exactly this preparation.
Peer institutions across New England have already established formal AI tracks or majors, and the absence of a comparable pathway at URI places the program at a direct competitive disadvantage in student recruitment.
Importantly, the Department has made investments in faculty with expertise in machine learning, data science, and AI over recent years.
This specialization now formally leverages these investments into a coherent, marketable academic pathway for undergraduate students.

Building on the core computer science curriculum, students explore fundamental security concepts drawn from industry-recognized frameworks, including threat management; vulnerability assessment; security operations; network architecture, protocols, and infrastructure defense; as well as governance, risk management, compliance, and information protection strategies. The program equips graduates with both theoretical foundations and practical skills to design secure systems and implement defense strategies across diverse computing environments. passages.text:
The Cybersecurity specialization provides students with a structured pathway from foundational security concepts to advanced defensive practice.
CSF 430 establishes core knowledge of security threats, defensive planning, and implementation of protective technologies, while CSF 432 builds hands-on competency in securing the networks and systems of real-world organizations.
Students then complete either CSF 434 or CSF 534, both of which advance into specialized topics including intrusion detection, penetration testing, incident response, malware analysis, and risk management, with CSF 534 incorporating a research dimension suited to students pursuing graduate study.
The Department of Computer Science and Statistics has developed substantial curricular expertise in cybersecurity over many years, reflected in a well-established sequence of CSF courses that, until now, have not been formally integrated into the B.S. in Computer Science.
This specialization rectifies that gap by leveraging existing departmental resources, faculty expertise, course infrastructure, and proven instructional design to offer students a coherent, named credential without requiring new courses or additional hiring.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-07B | Page 37
passages.text:
This is particularly timely given that cybersecurity professionals are among the most critically needed in today's workforce and organizations across every sector face a widening shortage of qualified security professionals.
By formally establishing this specialization, the Department positions its graduates to meet this demand while enhancing the University's competitiveness in recruiting students who seek purposeful, career-aligned computing education.

The General Computer Science specialization provides students with a structured yet flexible pathway to tailor advanced coursework to their individual interests and career goals.
Building on the program's core curriculum, students complete three additional CSC courses: one at the 300 level or above and two at the 400 level or above.
Our department currently offers many eligible courses in areas that include, but are not limited to, algorithms, artificial intelligence, computer graphics, database systems, computer systems, programming languages, and networking.
This specialization enables students to develop both depth and breadth beyond the core curriculum while aligning their studies with departmental strengths, emerging technologies, and evolving workforce demands.
Because no single specialization can encompass the full scope of modern computing, the General Computer Science pathway preserves student access to the discipline’s broad intellectual landscape.
It ensures that students whose goals lie outside established options such as Artificial Intelligence or Cybersecurity can still pursue a formally recognized course of study.

Changes How does the program align with the University’s mission and current Academic Strategic Plan?
Enhance student achievement - Increase graduate student enrollment and degree completion.
Many Art majors, especially those who become majors in their Sophomore/Junior years, struggle to complete their degrees within four years.
Over the last two years, we have been analyzing our curriculum and workload to identify factors contributing to this.
Our goal is to increase our retention and four year graduation rates without compromising our students' education.
Challenges One of the most important things for an art major is the portfolio of work that they leave the program with.
Right now, majors regularly take 3 to 4 studio classes a semester, and are therefore required to work on 3–4 creative projects at a time.
The quality of their work, and therefore the portfolio that they graduate with, suffers as a result.
A move to 4-credit classes would allow students to make a smaller amount of higher quality work, which would leave them better prepared for succeeding in creative fields.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-07B | Page 55
passages.text:
Hence, this change in credit hours would continue to increase the integrity of our program while taking away barriers that inhibit graduation.
Many of our students become Art majors after their freshman year.
This puts them at a disadvantage in completing their coursework on time.
This in addition to limited availability of 300-level classes creates additional scheduling barriers.
Converting studio courses to four credits would help students meet their credit requirements more easily, making a four- year graduation timeline more achievable.
This change would also positively impact retention rates, particularly among sophomores.

passages.text: Changes How does the program align with the University’s mission and current Academic Strategic Plan? Enhance student achievement - Increase graduate student enrollment and degree completion. Many Art majors, especially those who become majors in their Sophomore/Junior years, struggle to complete their degrees within four years. Over the last two years, we have been analyzing our curriculum and workload to identify factors contributing to this. Our goal is to increase our retention and four year graduation rates without compromising our students' education. Challenges One of the most important things for an art major is the portfolio of work that they leave the program with. Right now, majors (especially BFA students) regularly take 3 to 4 studio classes a semester, and are therefore required to work on 3–4 creative projects at a time. The quality of their work, and therefore the portfolio that they graduate with, suffers as a result. A move to 4-credit classes would allow students to make a smaller amount of higher quality work, which would leave them better prepared for succeeding in creative fields. Hence, this change in credit hours would continue to increase the integrity of our program while taking away barriers that inhibit graduation. Many of our students become Art majors after their freshman year. This puts them at a disadvantage in completing their coursework on time. This in addition to limited availability of 300-level classes creates additional scheduling barriers. Converting studio courses to four credits would help students meet their credit requirements more easily, making a four- year graduation timeline more achievable. This change would also positively impact retention rates, particularly among sophomores. From Powerbi [1] [1]

passages.text: Program Description BACHELOR OF ARTS Students in the B.A. curriculum may tailor a program to suit their individual needs and interests. The B.A. degree is popular with students pursuing a double degree in education and allows students to explore the fascinating world of mathematics. Students should meet with their advisor no later than the end of the first semester of the sophomore year to plan a complete program. This program, and any subsequent changes in it, must be approved by the advisor and the department chairperson. It must contain at least 32 credits (maximum 45) in mathematics, and include MTH 141, 142, 215, 243, 307, and 316, plus 12 or more additional credits in mathematics, at least three credits of which must be at the 400 level. Credits earned in MTH 101, 103, 104, 105, 106, 107, 108, 109, 110, 111, 208, or 209,cannot be applied toward this degree. At most one of MTH 244 or MTH 362 cannotcan be appliedcounted toward this degree. A total of 120 credits is required in the B.A. curriculum. At least 30 of these must be in courses numbered 300 or above.

Bachelor of Arts in Business Studies Specialization in Human Resources Leadership Undergraduate No No The Human Resources specialization prepares students to lead people, build inclusive and effective organizational cultures, and design systems that help employees and organizations thrive.
This pathway integrates business acumen with a deep understanding of human behavior, interpersonal dynamics, and social systems.
Students will explore how talent is recruited, developed, motivated, and retained, and they will learn to navigate complex workplace issues such as equity and inclusion, organizational change, conflict resolution, and leadership communication.
The curriculum draws on courses from management, human development and family science, education, and sociology to offer complementary perspectives on how individuals and groups function in professional environments.
By combining these insights with a foundation in organizational leadership, students will graduate ready to pursue careers in human resources, organizational development, people analytics, talent management, or leadership training across a range of industries.

passages.text:
The proposed Human Resources Leadership specialization within the B.A. in Business Studies is designed to prepare students to lead people and organizations in a rapidly evolving workplace.
Effective leadership today requires more than technical business knowledge; it demands an understanding of human behavior, organizational culture, social dynamics, and the systems that shape how people work together.
This specialization integrates these dimensions by combining business courses in management and leadership by using interdisciplinary coursework to deepen students’ understanding of interpersonal communication, group dynamics, diversity, equity and inclusion, and organizational systems.
Students pursuing this specialization will explore how organizations attract, develop, motivate, and retain talent, and how leaders foster environments where individuals and teams can thrive.
They will gain skills in areas such as leadership communication, conflict resolution, negotiation, and change management, while also examining the broader social and cultural factors that influence workplace relationships and organizational outcomes.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-07B | Page 140
passages.text:
This interdisciplinary approach reflects the evolving expectations of employers, who increasingly seek graduates with the ability to manage people effectively, lead diverse teams, and navigate complex organizational challenges.
It also aligns with national trends in workforce development and talent management, where human resources leadership is emerging as a strategic driver of organizational success.
By leveraging existing courses across multiple disciplines that are not currently part of the B.A. in Business Studies curriculum, this specialization can be implemented efficiently while significantly expanding the career pathways available to graduates, including roles in human resources, talent acquisition, organizational development, employee relations, and leadership consulting.
Students completing the Human Resources specialization will be able to: Apply theories of motivation, leadership, and organizational behavior to real-world business challenges.
Design strategies for talent development, performance management, and workforce planning.
Lead with cultural intelligence and build inclusive environments that leverage diversity as a source of innovation.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-07B | Page 140
passages.text:
Use insights from sociology and human development to address complex interpersonal and systemic issues in organizations.
Communicate effectively and resolve conflict in professional settings.
Aligned with the University of Rhode Island’s mission as the state’s flagship land- and sea-grant research institution, the Human Resources Leadership specialization advances URI’s commitment to student success, community engagement, and inclusive excellence.
This specialization prepares students to become ethical, adaptive leaders who strengthen Rhode Island’s workforce, support organizational resilience, and foster equitable and thriving workplaces in a rapidly changing global economy.
Through applied learning and interdisciplinary collaboration, students develop the capacity to lead with empathy, integrity, and strategic vision, which are qualities central to URI’s role in building informed residents and leaders who make a positive impact locally and globally.
Overlaps with BSBA with Management major.
Does not require the breadth of business courses that are required in the BSBA.

The Tourism Leadership pathway equips students with the skills to lead organizations and communities in today’s rapidly evolving tourism sector.
Students learn how to design and deliver memorable experiences, manage destinations and hospitality services, and advance sustainability in one of the world’s most dynamic industries.
The pathway emphasizes both strategic leadership and hands-on application, preparing graduates to work in areas such as destination marketing, resort and hotel management, event planning, sustainable tourism development, and cultural or heritage tourism.
Graduates will be able to Explain the importance of tourism for community and economic development, human health and quality of life, and sustainable use of natural resources.
Identify, analyze, and apply the best available information to address contemporary tourism leadership opportunities and issues.
Communicate effectively with a variety of audiences in appropriate formats.
Demonstrate leadership and collaboration skills to work effectively and professionally in groups.

The Tourism Leadership specialization in the Bachelor of Arts in Business Studies directly advances Strategy 1 of the University’s Agenda for Change by preparing students for meaningful careers through experiential, interdisciplinary, and impact-driven education.
The program emphasizes student success and workforce readiness by integrating core business knowledge with applied learning in tourism, hospitality, sustainability, and community development.
Students engage with real-world challenges through project-based coursework, internships, and collaborative experiences that strengthen critical thinking, communication, leadership, and information literacy skills.
These experiences align with Strategy 1’s focus on high-impact educational practices that improve persistence, timely degree completion, and career outcomes.
The specialization further supports the Agenda for Change by addressing pressing societal needs, including sustainable economic development, human health and quality of life, and responsible stewardship of natural and cultural resources.

The Tourism Leadership specialization under the BA in Business Studies builds on URI's bench strengths in marine affairs, resource management, and conservation; it aligns with URI's desire for hands-on learning experiences that help prepare students to make an impact on society; and it supports state-level workforce development initiatives.

Changes Program Description Biomedical Engineering The Bachelor of Science (B.S.) degree in biomedical engineering is offered by the Department of Electrical, Computer, and Biomedical Engineering (ECBE), and is open to qualified students under the New England Regional Student Program.
The biomedical engineering program is accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission (EAC) of ABET, Inc. (www.abet.org), under the commission’s General Criteria and Program Criteria for Bioengineering and Biomedical and Similarly Named Engineering Programs.
Specialization in biomedical engineering is also available within the Master of Science (M.S.) and Doctor of Philosophy (Ph.D.) programs in electrical engineering.
The Biomedical Engineering curriculum at URI is built on a rigorous foundation in mathematics, physics, life sciences, and core engineering principles, integrated with hands-on laboratory and design experiences.
The BME Program prepares students to design, evaluate, and translate technologies that improve human health while maintaining strong awareness of ethics, safety, and regulatory considerations.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-07B | Page 177
passages.text:
Additionally, students have opportunities to gain hands-on experience and training in research labs led by our nationally and internationally renowned faculty.
Students progress through a structured core that includes biomedical instrumentation, systems and signals, biomechanics, computing, and engineering design, culminating in a year-long capstone experience that emphasizes real-world problem solving and interdisciplinary collaboration.
This shared core curriculum ensures that all graduates develop strong analytical skills, technical depth, and practical experience.
All students specialize via one of three focused tracks: Bioinstrumentation and Neural Engineering, Biomechanics and Prosthetics, or Biomedical Artificial Intelligence (AI).
Program Educational Objectives.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-07B | Page 177
passages.text:
Three to five years after graduation from the B.S. in biomedical engineering, graduates will: 1) Successfully practice biomedical engineering to serve state and regional industries, hospitals, government agencies, or national and international industries ; 2) Work professionally in the areas of Biomedical Engineering including but not limited to: biomedical electronics, medical instrumentation, medical imaging, biomedical signal processing, rehabilitation engineering, neuroengineeringneural engineering, medical robotics, prosthetics, biomedical artificial intelligence (AI), and biomaterials ; 3) Achieve personal and professional success with awareness and commitment to their ethical and social responsibilities, both as individuals and in team environments ; and 4) Maintain and improve their technical competence through lifelong learning, including entering and succeeding in an advanced degree program in a field such as engineering, science, business, or medicine.
Student Outcomes.
Biomedical engineering students demonstrate knowledge in all outcomes required by ABET, Inc. which are listed in the college’s student outcomes section of this catalog.
Program Description.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-07B | Page 177
passages.text:
Biomedical engineering is an interdisciplinary areafield in which engineering techniquesprinciples are applied to problem solving in the life sciences and medicine.
The program is organized around three core tracks: Bioinstrumentation and Neural Engineering, Biomechanics and Prosthetics, and Biomedical Artificial Intelligence (AI), which collectively support innovation in medical devices, human movement analysis, and data-driven healthcare technologies.
Biomedical engineers design medical instruments and systems for diagnosis and the treatment of various diseases as well as for research in biomedical sciences.
Examples of instruments for diagnosis include electrocardiographs, electroencephalographs, automatic blood analyzers, and medical imaging systems such as X-ray imaging, radio-nuclide imaging, ultrasound imaging, computer-assisted tomography, and magnetic resonance imaging.
Examples of instruments for treatment include radiotherapy machines, pacemakers, cardiac-assist devices, intelligent drug delivery systems, dialysis machine, ventilator, and lasers for surgery.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-07B | Page 177
passages.text:
Biomedical engineers develop artificial organs for prosthesis and computer software and hardware systems to help provide high-quality, cost-effective health care.
Biomedical engineers are employed in the medical instrument industry, where they invent, design, manufacture, sell, and

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-07B | Page 178
passages.text:
service medical equipment.
They serve as clinical engineers in the hospitals, where they evaluate, select, maintain, and provide training for the use of complex medical equipment.
They also participate in medical and biological research by applying their unique analytical ability and instrumentation skills to conduct advanced research.
URI’s biomedical engineering program combines study in the biological sciences with the areas of engineering that are particularly important for the application of modern technology to medicine.
This curriculum is designed to provide students with not only a general background in biomedicalelectrical engineering,butmechanicalalsoengineering,aindustrial specialengineering,focusandoncomputerhands-on skills in electrical engineering, necessary for developing medical devices.
With a few minor elective changes, the program also satisfies the entrance requirements of most medical schools, but students who plan to go on to medical school should consult the premedical advisor and the coordinator of the biomedical engineering program.

The Biomedical Engineering program aims to provide students with a strong interdisciplinary foundation while offering structured opportunities for specialization aligned with workforce and research needs.
The revised curriculum preserves a common BME core and introduces three formal tracks--Bioinstrumentation & Neural Engineering, Biomechanics & Prosthetics, and Biomedical AI--to improve curricular clarity, advising, and career readiness.
Program goals include enhancing academic rigor, supporting timely degree completion, and preparing graduates for industry, graduate study, and professional careers through applied learning and design experiences.
These goals align with Strategy 1 of URI’s Agenda for Change, which emphasizes academic excellence and student success by strengthening curriculum relevance, improving student outcomes, and ensuring graduates are well prepared to meet evolving biomedical engineering demands.

Changes How does the program align with the University’s mission and current Academic Strategic Plan?
The proposed program aligns closely with the University’s mission and Academic Strategic Plan by advancing research excellence, interdisciplinary collaboration, student success, and societal impact.
The program strengthens the University’s research profile through innovative, externally funded work at the intersection of biomedical engineering, neuroscience, and data science.
It supports strategic priorities for interdisciplinary education and workforce preparation by providing students with hands- on training in advanced technologies, data analysis, and translational research.
Overall, the program translates institutional priorities into measurable academic, educational, and societal outcomes.

Changes Identify possible overlap with other programs offered at URI.
The proposed program has limited and complementary overlap with Electrical & Computer Engineering, Mechanical Engineering, and Kinesiology.
Overlap with Electrical & Computer Engineering includes foundational topics in signals and sensors, Python programming, AI and Machine learning.
Mechanical Engineering overlap occurs in system dynamics and dynamic fluid mechanics particularly as applied to modeling human movement and biological systems.
Kinesiology overlap arises in the context of human movement and motor control.
These overlaps are primarily foundational and contextual.

Graduates are well suited for roles such as biomedical or electrical engineer, data scientist, machine learning engineer, research engineer, and software developer in healthcare, rehabilitation, and technology industries, which offer strong job growth and competitive salaries nationwide.
In addition, the program provides rigorous preparation for graduate and professional studies (M.S./Ph.D.) in biomedical engineering, neural engineering, electrical and computer engineering, data science, and neuroscience through strong quantitative foundations, research experience, and advanced technical training.

Changes What is the demand and regional competition for this program?
There is strong demand for engineering graduates with expertise in biomedical, neurotechnology, biomechanics, data science, AI-driven healthcare, and related fields due to growth in healthcare technology and digital health sectors.
Employers in medical devices, health systems, biotech, and technology industries seek graduates with interdisciplinary skills that connect engineering and health solutions.
In the New England region, several well-established universities offer biomedical engineering programs, including the University of Connecticut, Boston University, and Brown University.
These programs represent regional competition for students but also highlight a substantial regional interest and workforce pipeline in biomedical and engineering subjects.
Rhode Island currently has no public M.D., granting medical school, but multiple feasibility studies and planning efforts suggest that establishing a medical education program at the University of Rhode Island is both viable and responsive to state health workforce needs, potentially launching in the future to address physician shortages, especially in primary care.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-07B | Page 184
passages.text:
This future opportunity could further enhance the appeal of an engineering program with strong health and medical pathways.
Overall, the regional landscape combines high student interest and established competing programs with significant opportunities for differentiation, especially by linking engineering training to future health professions, industry needs, and emerging educational paths such as a potential URI medical school.

This specialization integrates mechanics, materials science, physiology, and computational modeling to understand the structure and function of the musculoskeletal system and to develop solutions that restore or enhance mobility and physical performance.
Students gain knowledge in areas such as human motion analysis, biomechanics, prosthetic design, rehabilitation engineering, biomaterials, and assistive device development.
Emphasis is placed on ethical considerations, including patient safety, data privacy, and regulatory compliance.
