Kingston Proposed Fall 2026 Existing Fall 2024 Changes Program Description The interdisciplinary curriculum in public health leads to a Bachelor of Science (B.S.) degree.
The major is designed to prepare students for careers in public health, health promotion, health services management, for-profit companies, not-for- profit organizations, community-based health agencies, and departments of public health.
Program Requirements.
Students are required to complete the following core curriculum (120 credits): 1) At least 40 general education credits. 2) Core courses including BIO 110, or 101 and 103, or 105; CHM 100 or 103; COM 100, 202, 208, 210, or 251; HLT 101G, 201 (grade of C or higher required), 300 (grade of C or higher required) and 450 (grade of C or higher required); KIN 122 and 123; MTH 103, 107, 108, 111, 131 or 141; PHL 101, 103 or 212 and 314; PHP 405; PSY 113; and STA 307, 308, or PSY 200; URI 101; WRT 104 or 106. 3) 18-24 credits (6 courses) from one of the followingapprovedspecializations: global and environmental health, health promotion, or health serviceslist.

URI FACULTY SENATE Department Restructuring Proposal Form For two or more departments merging into a single unit General Information Current Department Names: 1) Department of Geoscience 2) Department of Landscape Architecture Proposed Department Name: Department of Earth Science s, Planning, and Design Date of Proposal Submission: Nov. 07, 2025 Effective Term & Year: Fall 2026 Proposer Name & Title: Thomas Boving – Chair Geosciences Rebecca Brown – Interim Chair Landscape Architecture Proposer Email & Phone: tboving@uri.edu 401.874.7053 brownreb@uri.edu 401.874.2755 Description & Rationale Description of Proposed Change Please briefly describe the name change being proposed.
A merger of the Department of Landscape Architecture (LAR) with the Department of Geoscience (GEO) would join two rather small departments that share expertise in areas of great research and socio-economic importance.
Specifically, our departments address climate change issues and resilience planning, management of geological resources, including protection of drinking water resources, and urban development, such as urban flooding control.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-07B | Page 251
passages.text:
A merger would create opportunities for sharing resources, collaborative grant applications, and, importantly, guarantees the continued accreditation of LAR.
Rationale Explain the reason for the merge The Department of Landscape Architecture offers the Bachelor of Landscape Architecture (BLA) and a minor in Community Planning.
The BLA is the only accredited undergraduate program of its kind in Rhode Island and will undergo re-accreditation in 2026.
By the end of the current academic year, the program will lose its last two tenured faculty members to retirement.
The absence of tenured or tenure-track faculty would jeopardize the program’s accreditation.
To demonstrate the University’s commitment to the program’s long- term success and maintain accreditation, Dean VanderGheynst has approved two tenure-track faculty searches.
The planned merger with the Department of Geosciences, which includes several tenured and

Memorandum To: Review committees From: Jean S.
VanderGheynst, Dean, College of the Environment and Life Sciences Re: Proposal to merge Department of Landscape Architecture and Department of Geosciences Date: November 7, 2025 ————————————————————————————————————— I fully support the proposed merger of the Department of Landscape Architecture (LAR) and the Department of Geosciences (GEO).
This merger aligns with the University’s strategic goals to strengthen interdisciplinary collaboration, enhance program sustainability, and advance our land and sea grant mission.
A budget and justification summarizing how existing resources will be used is included in the submission.
The Department of Landscape Architecture offers Rhode Island’s only accredited undergraduate program of its kind and is approaching re-accreditation in 2026.
The upcoming retirement of its two tenured faculty members would leave the program without tenured or tenure-track faculty, jeopardizing accreditation.
To ensure continuity and demonstrate institutional commitment, two tenure-track faculty searches focused on Environmental Planning and Urban Design and Transportation Planning have been approved.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-CASC-07B | Page 255
passages.text:
The merger with Geosciences, which includes several tenured and tenure-track faculty, provides the necessary structure to support new hires and ensure compliance with Article 15 of the collective bargaining agreement.
Both departments have voted in favor of the merger, recognizing the intellectual and operational benefits of joining two small, synergistic units.
Together, they will form a hub addressing climate change, resilience planning, sustainable development, and management of natural resources.
The merged department will enhance shared teaching, research, and outreach capacity while maintaining all existing academic programs without disruption or impact on other departments or colleges.
This merger represents a forward-looking investment in programs that exemplify URI’s strengths in environmental and community-based problem solving.
It supports the continued accreditation of the Bachelor of Landscape Architecture program and positions URI as a regional leader in sustainable design and Earth system science.

Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation By The Faculty Senate PROGRAM MODIFICATIONS COLLEGE OF ARTS & SCIENCES: ABM Applied Mathematics (MS Mathematics), Effective Spring 2025 Appendix A The purpose of this proposal is to align the accelerated BM/MS program approved in Spring 2018 with Appendix K of the graduate manual. Appendix K was approved in Fall 2018 and our original accelerated BS/MS program (Bill_17-18-35B) does not allow students to double count any credits. The current program without double counting is already successful. The purpose of this proposal is to bolster the number of graduate students in the MS in mathematics, applied track, and allow students to take advantage of Appendix K of the graduate manual. The change we propose is to allow students in this Accelerated 5-year ABM program to double count up to 4 credits of a 500-level MTH/AMS course for both the BS in mathematics and MS in mathematics, applied track. This is in addition to counting up to 12 credits in advanced standing towards the MS in mathematics, applied track. Landscape Architecture Landscape architecture is a 126-credit curriculum leading to the Bachelor of Landscape Architecture (B.L.A.) degree.
Accredited by the Landscape Architecture Accreditation Board of the ASLA, the curriculum is designed to prepare undergraduates for professional careers in public and private practice.
Landscape architecture is a profession that involves the design, planning, preservation, and restoration of the landscape by applying art, science, and technology to achieve the best use of our land and water resources.
Landscape architects design and plan parks, plazas, and recreation areas; residential, institutional and commercial developments; transportation facilities, new towns and campus landscapes, and green infrastructure.
They are also involved in planning and designing landscapes in coastal areas and inland developments impacted by climate.
The requirements of this curriculum include preparation in the basic arts and sciences.

passages.heading: 24-25-06 | Page 28
passages.text:
The major includes 63-64 credits of professional core classes (LAR 101, 201, 202, 243, 244, 300, 301, 302, 343, 344, 345, 346, 353, 354, 443, 444, 445, 447, 450); 28-29 credits of supporting requirements (ART 207; GEG 101; PLS 150; CHM 100, 101 or 103 or PHY 109, or GEO 100G, or 103; CPL 410, CPL 434, 538; MTH 103; and PLS 200); and 7-8 credits of supporting electives.
Students will also take general education classes and 6-7 credits of free electives.
Students accepted into landscape architecture are required to maintain a grade point average of at least 2.50 with no landscape architecture grades below a letter C.
Students failing to maintain this minimum may be removed from the program and required to reapply once this requirement is satis�ed.
Students are required to own a P .C. laptop computer by the time they enter the program.
Speci�cations are available from the Landscape Architecture Program O�ce or from the URI Bookstore (Ramtech).
URI’s Landscape Architecture Program (LAR) is competitive.
Accreditation standards regarding staff and facilities limit the number of students accepted into the major to 20 per year.

While enrolled in the program, students will be reviewed twice during their course of studies: �rst for admission into the lower-division design sequence and again for acceptance into the upper-division B.L.A. major.
Admission into the lower-division design sequence courses (LAR 243 and 244) requires department approval.
Approximately 75 percent of the openings are �lled by students who enter as incoming freshmen and who maintain a minimum 2.50 grade point average with no grades in LAR courses below a C.
The remaining openings are �lled by matriculated students wishing to transfer into landscape architecture from other majors.
These students are required to apply to the program and to submit an essay and transcript of grades.
Applications and transcripts are evaluated in March each year for acceptance into the lower- division (LAR 243) design sequence for the following fall.
Acceptance into the upper division (junior design sequence) is based on submission and review of a portfolio of lower-division work, a current academic transcript, and written essay.
A maximum of 20 students per year are accepted into the upper- division B.L.A. curriculum.

Only students who have completed comparable lower-division courses will be allowed to compete for these upper-division positions.
Such transfer applicants must �rst be accepted into the University by the O�ce of Admission and have their application package submitted to the Landscape Architecture Department Chair before the last week in February preceding the fall semester in which they wish to enroll.
Students will be noti�ed of their acceptance following a department review.
Students are eligible to transfer from University College for Academic Success to the College of Environment and Life Sciences after they have earned 24 credits with a 2.50 or higher GPA and with permission of the department chair.

No Date Chosen Changes Program Description Plant Sciences The major in Plant Sciences, offered by the Department of Plant Sciences and Entomology, prepares undergraduates for professional careers in the many public and private sectors of horticulture.
After successful completion of the major, students are awarded a degree in Plant Sciences in one of three options: turfgrass management, ornamental horticulture and sustainable crop production.
Graduates of this program pursue careers ranging from landscape contractor, golf course superintendent, director of parks, botanical gardens or arboreta, garden center or �oral shop proprietor, plant propagator, nursery production manager, vegetable or fruit grower, lawn service manager or technical representative for seed, equipment, and chemical companies, to name just a few of the opportunities available.
Other graduates enter graduate school and pursue careers in research and education at public and private institutions.
The unifying theme of the major is the development of sustainable culture and use of plants for amenity or food.
Graduates can meet the standards of several certi�cation organizations.

passages.heading: 24-25-06 | Page 35
passages.text:
Students in the ornamental horticulture option qualify for certi�cation with the Rhode Island Nursery and Landscape Association and the International Society for Arboriculture.
Graduates of the turfgrass management option qualify for certi�cation as turfgrass managers or turfgrass specialists with the American Registry of Certi�ed Professionals in Agronomy, Crops, and Soils, Ltd. of the American Society of Agronomy.
These same graduates also meet the requirements for registration with the Golf Course Superintendents Association of America.
The department manages over 50 acres of turfgrass, horticulture, and agronomy farms for teaching, research, and outreach.
The C.
Richard Skogley Turfgrass Center is the oldest turfgrass research/teaching program in the U.S.
The department also maintains a 15,000 square foot controlled environment greenhouse complex for hands-on learning and research.
These facilities are closely allied with the URI Botanical Gardens and E.P .
Christopher Arboretum.

passages.heading: 24-25-06 | Page 35
passages.text:
The Plant Sciences degree requires a total of 120 credits: 29-30 credits of pre-professional natural sciences that all majors must take including PLS 150, PLS 200, PLS 215, PLS 216, 250, PLS 255, BIO 101, BIO 103, BIO 102, BIO 104, CHM 103, CHM 105 (or CHM 101 and CHM 102) or their equivalent; 30 credits in concentration courses; and 15 credits of supporting electives approved by a faculty advisor which are speci�c to the interests of the student.
Turfgrass Management Option.
The turfgrass management option is intended primarily for students who are interested in managing golf courses, athletic �elds, commercial turf properties, sod farms or any other facilities comprised primarily of turf.
Students in this option will gain competencies in all aspects of turf production and management, with a focus on sustainable practices and integrated pest management systems.
Additionally, students interested in landscape management may also fall under this option but may take slightly different concentration courses which will address some of the other aspects of managing large, heterogeneous landscape properties.

passages.heading: 24-25-06 | Page 35
passages.text:
These students may also take a number of classes in the Landscape Architecture program, which can ful�ll their supporting electives.
Turfgrass Management students are also required to take 30 credits of concentration courses and it is suggested that in earning those credits, they take PLS 306216, PLS 322306, PLS 341322, PLS 361332, PLS 390341, PLS 440361, PLS 442, ENT 387 and ENT 411385.
Ornamental Horticulture Option.
The ornamental horticulture option is intended primarily for students who are interested in nursery management, greenhouse production, the �oral industry and the production and management of woody and herbaceous materials for landscapes and urban areas.
Students in this option will develop a wide set of skills allowing them to work in a diverse number of industries where ornamental plant production and management are practiced.
Students interested in landscape management can also select this option, instead of the turfgrass management option, if their interests are focused more on trees than on turf.
As with the turfgrass management option, these students may also take Landscape Architecture classes to ful�ll supporting electives.

passages.text: Ornamental Horticulture students are also required to take 30 credits of concentration courses and it is suggested that in earning those credits, they take PLS 306, PLS 331, 332, PLS 341, PLS 350, PLS 353, PLS 354, ENT 385 or ENT 387 and ENT 411385. Sustainable Crop Production Option. The sustainable crop production option is intended for students with an interest in growing plants for food, managing food systems and developing sustainable approaches that minimize farming impacts on the environment while maintaining or improving the quality of food and the environment, where possible. Students in this option will learn techniques and strategies for managing small, sustainable farming systems in addition to incorporating food production into the urban environment. Sustainable Crop Production students are also required to take 30 credits of concentration courses and it is suggested that in earning those credits, they take PLS 275, PLS 311, PLS 312, PLS 321, PLS 324, PLS 325, PLS 332, NRS 212, ENT 385 and ENTSAF 411400G. The undergraduate program offers three major options (tracks): a B.S. degree with a major in Clinical Neuroscience from the College of Health Sciences, a B.S. degree with a major in Molecular Neuroscience from the College of Environment and Life Sciences, and a B.S. degree with a major in Neuropharmacology from the College of Pharmacy.
The option for different neuroscience majors is unique and makes this URI major truly distinct with regard to undergraduate education.

Chapter 2, “The Administration,” is typicallyreviewed for routine updates by administrators led by the Provost’s office.
The Chapteraddresses the Administrative Offices of the University, the Channel of Authority, and theappointment of Administrative Officers.

The program is designed for working professionals.
Typically, candidates complete the program within 8 to 9 semesters (includes summer term).
The curriculum is structured into three main components: Foundation Coursework, Methods & Application Coursework, and the Internship.
Candidates may start the program in the fall, spring, or summer semesters, beginning with Foundation Coursework.
Both Foundation and Methods & Application Coursework must be completed before enrolling in the Internship course.
Clinical experiences are completed throughout the program, providing opportunities to integrate theory and practice in real world settings.
In order to accommodate working professionals, candidates will collaborate with the program coordinator to develop an individualized course sequence for their foundational coursework.

Candidates are required to take the following courses: Foundation Coursework EDC 529 Foundations of Educational Research EDL 500 Engaging Communities for Change EDL 501 Legal and Ethical Issues in Educational Leadership EDL 502 Fiscal Management for Educational Leaders EDL 503 Operations & Management for Educational Leaders Methods & Application Coursework EDL 504 Program Evaluation for School Leaders EDL 505 Supervision of Instruction EDL 506 Instructional and Curriculum Leadership EDL 507 Managing Human Capital EDL 508 Leading School & District Improvement Internship EDL 510 Internship I + Seminar EDL 511 Internship II + Seminar This program is considered a hybrid program.
Courses will be delivered online in a combination of synchronous (Zoom) and asynchronous (Brightspace) sessions.
A variety of instructional methods are used, including lectures, discussions, case studies, presentations, cooperative learning activities, Internet assignments, guest practitioner presentations (as possible), role-play, and written and verbal assignments.
Courses are taught by URI full-time and part-time faculty.

Opportunities for Graduates The Educational Leadership & Policy (EDL) program at the University of Rhode Island equips graduates with the skills, knowledge, and credentials necessary to pursue a wide range of leadership roles within the education sector.
The program is designed to meet the growing demand for qualified school leaders, addressing both current workforce needs and future job market trends.
Economic Need and Workforce Data The demand for skilled educational leaders is increasing, particularly as schools and districts navigate complex challenges such as educational equity, technological integration, and community engagement.
According to the U.S.
Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), employment for elementary, middle, and high school principals is projected to grow by 4% from 2022 to 2032, which reflects the steady need for qualified individuals to fill these critical roles.
The BLS also highlights the ongoing need to replace retiring principals, further emphasizing the demand for new school leaders.
Available Jobs and Job Titles Graduates of the EDL program are well-prepared to assume a variety of leadership positions within the educational field.

passages.heading: 24-25-06 | Page 71
passages.text:
Some of the common job titles for program graduates include: School Principal Assistant Principal Dean District Administrator Instructional Coordinator Director of Special Education Curriculum Director Superintendent These roles are crucial in shaping the educational experiences of students and ensuring that schools operate effectively and efficiently.
The EDL program provides the comprehensive preparation necessary for graduates to excel in these positions.
Job Outlook and Growth The job outlook for educational leaders is positive, particularly in urban centers and areas with growing student populations.
The Bureau of Labor & Statistics (BLS) projects that there will be about 20,000 openings for principals each year over the next decade, mostly due to workers leaving the labor force or transferring to other occupations.
Salaries Salaries for educational leadership positions vary depending on the role and geographic location, but they generally reflect the high level of responsibility associated with these roles.
According to the BLS, the median annual wage for elementary, middle, and high school principals was $103,310 as of May 2022.

passages.heading: 24-25-06 | Page 71
passages.text:

passages.text:
As the landscape of education continues to evolve, there is a growing need for skilled leaders who can navigate the complexities of educational institutions, implement effective policies, and drive meaningful change.
Effective principals have substantial positive impacts on student achievement.
Research demonstrates that replacing a below-average principal with an above-average one can significantly increase student learning in both math and reading annually.
Beyond student achievement, principals also affect other crucial outcomes such as student attendance, discipline, and teacher retention.
Effective principals are linked to reduced absenteeism and exclusionary discipline, as well as higher teacher job satisfaction and lower turnover rates, particularly among high-performing teachers.
Principals who engage in instructionally focused interactions with teachers, such as providing feedback, coaching, and developing a data-driven instructional program, contribute to positive school outcomes.
These practices emphasize the importance of principals being deeply involved in the instructional aspects of their schools.
Principals play a crucial role in addressing educational equity.

passages.heading: 24-25-06 | Page 72
passages.text:
Effective leaders are adept at creating inclusive environments that support diverse student populations.
This involves strategic hiring, fostering collaborative cultures, and ensuring equitable allocation of resources.
Rhode Island, like many other states, is facing a shortage of school administrators.
According to data collected by the Rhode Island Department of Education for the 2021-22 school year, 46 administrator vacancies were reported by 41 Local Education Agencies (LEAs), representing 8% of building-level administrator positions statewide.
Nationally, the National Center for Education Statistics (2023) found that about one in ten public school principals left the profession between the 2020-21 and 2021-22 school years.
This highlights the urgent need for strong principal preparation programs that equip future leaders with the skills required for effective school leadership.
Ongoing professional development and support are critical to ensure principals have the tools necessary to succeed (Grissom, Egalite, and Lindsay, 2021).

EDL 501 Legal and Ethical Issues in Educational Leadership This course examines the legal foundation of schools and educational policy, analyzing cases, statutes, and constitutional provisions affecting elementary and secondary school operations in the United States.

EDL 502 Fiscal Management for Educational Leaders This course analyzes the systems and mechanisms for �nancing public schools in the United States.
It provides both an overview of basic school �nance concepts and issues and an examination of Rhode Island’s system of �nancing schools.
This course blends the theoretical foundations of school �nance with their practical applications at state and local levels.
Candidates examine essential business functions including budgeting, facilities �nance, purchasing, and entrepreneurship as they relate to the day-to-day functions of the complex school organization.
Legal matters related to business ethics, diversity, and equity in budget allocations are prioritized.

Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation by The Faculty Senate PROGRAM MODIFICATIONS COLLEGE OF THE ENVIRONMENT & LIFE SCIENCES: Ph D Marine Affairs, Effective Spring 2025 Appendix A The proposed changes include changing the credential type to “Degree”, initiation date of Spring 2025, change in location to “Kingston”, and changing required course credits to 21 from 18 plus an additional 45 credits instead of 48 credits. We are adding a new core course requirement of MAF 521 Coastal Zone Law. We have created a 500 level version of MAF 482, which is MAF 583 Quantitative Methods in Marine Affairs. The MAF 583 requirement replaces the MAF 482 requirement, since PhD students are not able to count 400 level courses toward their degree requirements. MA Marine Affairs, Effective Spring 2025 Appendix B We are adding a new core course requirement of MAF 521 Coastal Zone Law and reducing the total number of electives from 15 to 12. We are requiring that nine of the elective credits be within Marine Affairs. We have created a 500 level version of our MAF 482 course, which is MAF 583 Quantitative Methods in Marine Affairs. The MAF 583 requirement replaces the MAF 482 requirement. We have removed the option for MAF 598 Masters Project in order to streamline course codes. GC Report 2024-2025-02B, Page 1 of 30

FACULTY SENATE OFFICE FACULTY SENATE LEGISLATIONDECEMBER 12, 2024 Graduate CouncilReport 2024-2025-3A At the November 25, 2024 meeting of the Graduate Council, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate on December 12, 2024 for approval.
SECTION IICurricular Matters Which Require Confirmation By The Faculty Senate COURSE CHANGES COLLEGE OF HEALTH SCIENCE CMD 560 | Voice Disorders Change in description, method of instruction (3 crs.) Etiology and symptomology of vocal and resonance differences and disorders for adults and children:; intervention strategies for organic, behavioral and psychogenic voice and resonance disorders:; rehabilitation team approach . (Lec.3) Pre: Graduate standing in MS-SLP program or permission of instructor.
CMD 582 | Motor Speech Disorders Change in description, method of instruction (3 crs.) Neuromotor processes and pathologies affecting speech production .
Prepares students to diagnose, assess, and treat adults with acquired motor speech disorders. (Lec. 3) Pre: Graduate standing in MS-SLP program (or permission of the instructor) ; a neuroanatomy course or concurrent registration in CMD 377.

passages.heading: Graduate Council Report #2024-2025-03A | Page 1
passages.text:
NEW COURSES COLLEGE OF EDUCATION EDC 513 | College Teaching Toolkit (3 crs.) The goal of this course is to integrate pedagogical theory with practice to provide an introduction to college teaching.
Participants will develop a toolkit for face-to-face and online college courses. (Seminar) Pre: Admitted to College of Education graduate program or Graduate standing and permission of instructor.
EDC 559 | Skill Development from Novice to Expert (3 crs.) Based upon the Dreyfus and Dreyfus Novice to Expert Skill Model, this course will examine strategies to enhance individuals and groups’ skill development in a variety of fields. (Online) EDC 664 | Equity & Inclusion in College Teaching (3 crs.) Explores theories and strategies for equity and inclusion in college teaching. (Lec. 3) Pre: Admission to COEDU graduate program or graduate standing and permission of instructor

passages.heading: Graduate Council Report #2024-2025-03A | Page 2
passages.text:
COLLEGE OF ENGINEERING EGR 404 | Building Tools with Generative AI (3 crs.) This course offers practical experience in using generative AI models to build tools that automate and optimize tasks typically managed manually. (Online) Pre: Permission of instructor.
EGR 555 | Engineering Your Startup (3 crs.) Explores the skills needed for engineers to transform innovative ideas into businesses, focusing on entrepreneurship, business model development, and bridging the gap between technical innovation and market readiness. (Lec. 3) Pre: Permission of instructor.
COLLEGE OF THE ENVIRONMENT & LIFE SCIENCES CPL 538 | Site Planning (3 crs.) Students identify and apply understanding of site planning and design, with an emphasis on the goals of smart growth and sustainability.

passages.heading: Graduate Council Report #2024-2025-03A | Page 2
passages.text:
Introduces the principles and techniques of site planning using case studies, visual presentations, reading assignments and online discussions. (Accelerated Online Program) Pre: Students enrolled in the Community Planning Graduate Certificate COLLEGE OF HEALTH SCIENCE HLT 502 | Identifying Health Disparities through Epidemiology (3 crs.) Students will learn the basic principles and methods of epidemiology as they apply to public health research and evaluation and assess public health literature.
This will be an applied course where you will have a chance to learn epidemiological skills and, more importantly, apply those skills to critically evaluate epidemiological and biomedical studies. (Online) Pre: Students admitted to MPH program, or by permission of instructor HLT 503 | Statistical Application of Public Health Research (3 crs.) The course will familiarize students with basic principles and methods of biostatistics as they apply to public health research and activities.

An emphasis of this course is the practical application of biostatistics skills to the evaluation and assessment of the public health literature. (Online) Pre: Students admitted to MPH program, or by permission of instructor HLT 507 | Program Evaluation in Public Health (3 crs.) Program evaluation is essential for public health, and this course is designed to help students develop the fundamentals of evaluation research as it applies to public health interventions/programs and policies. passages.heading: Faculty Senate Resolution #2024-2025-01 | Page 1
passages.text: FACULTY SENATE OFFICE 224 PASTORE HALL, 51 LOWER COLLEGE ROAD, KINGSTON, RI 02881 USA, P: 401.874.2616 Faculty Senate Resolution 2024-2025-01 Faculty Senate Meeting of December 12, 2024 Resolution of Appreciation and Gratitude Honoring the Estate Gift from Alumna Helen Izzi Schilling WHEREAS, Helen Izzi Schilling, a distinguished alumna of the University of Rhode Island, Class of 1954, and her late husband, Francis Schilling, have made a profound and lasting impact on the University through a historic estate gift of $65 million, the largest philanthropic contribution in the history of the University of Rhode Island; and WHEREAS, the gift establishes the Helen Izzi Schilling ’54 and Francis Schilling Scholars Program, an endowed scholarship that will provide significant financial support—up to $20,000 per year for four years—to high-achieving undergraduate students pursuing degrees in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) fields; and WHEREAS, this transformative scholarship program not only offers financial aid but also leadership development and mentoring, empowering students to achieve their academic and professional goals, and ensuring the future success of the University’s students in vital and innovative disciplines; and WHEREAS, Helen Izzi Schilling’s education in the sciences, which began at URI, laid the foundation for a distinguished career as a registered dietitian, educator, and businesswoman, making a significant impact on the healthcare community over five decades; and WHEREAS, Helen Izzi Schilling was deeply committed to the University and to making a difference in the lives of students, particularly those who, like her, sought careers in service to others; and WHEREAS, Francis Schilling, after completing his M.B.A. and pursuing a successful career in industry, including as vice president at GE Medical Systems, introduced pioneering medical technologies such as CT and MRI scanners to healthcare providers, demonstrating his commitment to innovation and progress; and WHEREAS, the Schilling’s extraordinary generosity is a testament to their unwavering belief in the power of education, their dedication to advancing STEM fields, and their desire to leave a legacy that will inspire future generations of students; passages.text: WHEREAS, the Schilling’s gift further strengthens the University’s mission of providing transformative educational opportunities, adding to the momentum of URI’s recently completed comprehensive campaign, which raised over $73 million for financial aid; and WHEREAS, the Schilling family’s deep ties to Rhode Island, dating back to the early 1900s, and their ongoing commitment to the state’s future, underscore the lasting impact of their support for the University and its students; WHEREAS, the faculty will enjoy the benefits and are ready to join in force to support the development of the scores of students who will benefit from this award far into the future, WHEREAS, collaborative work with their son, Paul Schilling, with past URI President Robert Carothers, current University of Rhode Island President Marc Parlange, and the University of Rhode Island Foundation & Alumni Engagement President Lil O’Rourke fashioned this historic arrangement to benefit high achieving students in concrete and direct ways, WHEREAS, the opportunity for life-changing support for strong students from all walks of life, including those with immigration heritages such as that of Helen Izzi Schilling herself, connotes deep concern, empathy, and intergenerational support for unknown others, NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Faculty Senate of the University of Rhode Island, on behalf of the entire University community, expresses its profound appreciation and heartfelt gratitude to the Schilling Family and the memories of Helen Izzi Schilling and Francis Schilling for their visionary generosity, their enduring legacy of support for URI students, and their commitment to ensuring that future generations have the tools and resources they need to achieve their highest ambitions; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that this resolution be entered into the official minutes of the Faculty Senate and that a copy be sent to the Schilling family as a token of our deep appreciation.

passages.heading: Faculty Senate Resolution #2024-2025-01 | Page 2
passages.text:
Unanimously adopted this 12th day of December, 2024.
Theodore Walls, URI Faculty Senate President

FACULTY SENATE OFFICE FACULTY SENATE LEGISLATION NOVEMBER 14, 2024 Cu rriculum & Standards Committee Report 2024-2025-03B At the October 31, 2024 meeting of the Curriculum & Standards Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate for approval.
Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation By The Faculty Senate PROGRAM MODIFICATIONS COLLEGE OF THE ENVIRONMENT & LIFE SCIENCES: BS Environmental and Natural Resource Economics, Effective Winter 2025 Appendix A College of Business added TMD to their programs and any course code offered by COB qualifies as concentration credits for our ENRE degree tracks (Green Markets and Sustainability option and Green Business double major).
We propose to add the TMD code to our existing list of accepted COB courses (ACC, BAI, FIN, MGT, MKT, SCA, INE).
BS Medical Laboratory Science, Effective Spring 2025 Appendix B The proposed change involves the addition of six courses that would qualify as "Professional Electives" towards the MLS degree.

passages.heading: Curriculum & Standards Committee Report #2024-2025-03B | Page 1
passages.text:
Namely, the added courses are: BIO 331 (Parasitology), CMB 312 (Introductory Biochemistry Laboratory), CMB 332 (Medical and Public Health Microbiology Laboratory), CMB 353 (Genetics Laboratory), CMB 491 (Research in Cell and Molecular Biology), and PHP 405 (Fundamentals of Epidemiology).
The addition of these courses accomplishes two goals.
First and foremost, they provide addition al opportunities for students to cultivate lab skills in areas that are relevant to MLS (BIO 331, CMB 312, CMB 332, CMB 353 and CMB 491) as well as explore MLS-related fields (BIO 331, PHP 405) that represent potential career pathways with a MLS degree.
Second, these additional courses provide more flexibility for students to successfully complete the six credit "Professional Elective" requirement of the MLS major in a timely manner.
This is due to the fact that many of the previously approved professional electives have prerequisite course requirements and limited scheduling options (i.e. offered only during fall or spring semester), which can make it challenging for students to complete this degree requirement.

NEW CERTIFICATES, MINORS, or SPECIALIZATIONS COLLEGE OF ENGINEERING: Minor - Biochemical Engineering, Effective Spring 2025 Appendix H The Biochemical Engineering minor introduces students to the fundamental chemistry and physics underlying biological processes.
Students will apply engineering principles in a biological context to control the interactions between and behavior of organic molecules, proteins, and other biomacromolecules.
With this minor, students will be prepared for industrial and research positions in the biotechnology and biomedical fields.
The Biochemical Engineering minor is comprised of a minimum of 18 credit hours, at least half of which must be earned at URI.
The required courses include two fundamental science courses (6 credits), two biochemical engineering fundamentals courses (6 credits), and two or more supporting courses (6 credits).
Up to 6 credits can double count towards a major (e.g., core courses).
Students declaring this major must earn a minimum grade point average of 2.00 in courses counted towards the minor.

passages.heading: Curriculum & Standards Committee Report #2024-2025-03B | Page 3
passages.text:
Students will need to complete the Biochemical Engineering minor form and have it signed by the minor coordinator, department chair, and ap propriate dean.
Students are responsible for meeting the prerequisite requirements for individual courses, as applicable.

Fall 2022 How can we create a sustainable society that protects the environment while maintaining a prosperous society?
Why have humans caused environmental degradation on local, regional, and global scales, and what can we do about it?
Public o�cials, nonpro�t organizations, and private businesses need professionals who can answer these questions in order to design a new sustainable world.
As a major in environmental and natural resource economics, you will acquire tools that can help answer these questions.
The environmental and natural resource economics major integrates the natural sciences with economics to help us understand why many of earth’s natural resources are under threat and how we can design policies to address these threats.
This major teaches students to weigh options and make important decisions concerning the protection, restoration, development, and use of our natural resources.
The major prepares students for graduate school or for careers in the public and private sector that address environmental and natural resource management, business, or public policy.

passages.heading: Curriculum & Standards Committee Report #2024-2025-03B | Page 8
passages.text:
Professionals in these �elds play an important role in coordinating interdisciplinary teams to address such complex problems.
Graduates gain an understanding of both natural sciences and the economy.
The degree requires a minimum of 120 credits, including 24 credits in concentration.
In addition to satisfying the general education requirements, students need nine credits in introductory professional courses, including natural resource conservation (NRS 100), introduction to resource economics (EEC 105), and environmental economics and policy (EEC 205).
The major also requires a minimum of three credits in written communication skills (WRT) at the 200 level or higher.
It is also possible to earn a double degree in environmental economics and general business, which we call Green Business (see details below).
The Environmental and Natural Resource Economics department offers multiple academic opportunities such as two curriculum options or pathways within the major, a double degree program, an energy certi�cate, a global water resource minor, and an accelerated Bachelor-Masters (ABM) program.

passages.heading: Curriculum & Standards Committee Report #2024-2025-03B | Page 8
passages.text:
The two curriculum options under the ENRE major are: Green Markets and Sustainability (GMS) and Environmental Economics and Management (EEM).
These options, the double degree program, energy certi�cate, global water resource minor, and ABM program are discussed below.
Option 1: Green Markets and Sustainability (GMS).
This option is for students who wish to develop a deep understanding of social and economic systems as they relate to a sustainable environment.
This option is designed to provide considerable �exibility so students can focus their studies to meet their professional goals.
Twenty-four credits in concentration courses are required at the 300 level or above, with 15 credits in environmental and natural resource economics (EEC), including economics of natural resource management and policy (EEC 310), bene�t-cost analysis (EEC 440), and a capstone course in environmental economics and policy (EEC 432), three credits in intermediate economic theory or intermediate microeconomics (ECN 328 or 323), and six credits in other concentration courses selected by students in consultation with their advisors.

passages.heading: Curriculum & Standards Committee Report #2024-2025-03B | Page 8
passages.text:
Up to nine concentration credits may be in economics (ECN) or business (ACC, BAI, FIN, INE, MGT, MKT, SCA).
A minimum of 21 credits in basic and supporting sciences are required in mathematics (MTH 103, 111, 131, or BAI 111), introductory statistics (STA 307, 308, 409, or BAI 210), and environmental geology or understanding the earth (GEO 100G or 103).
Applied calculus (MTH 131) is strongly recommended, especially for students who are considering going to graduate school.
Supporting sciences can be selected from a broad range of subjects including aquaculture and �sheries technology, animal and veterinary science, biology, business (BAI 210 and 212 only), cell and molecular biology, chemistry, computer science, ecology, geology, genetics, mathematics, natural resources science, oceanography, physics, plant physiology, or statistics.
An additional 27 credits in supporting electives allow the student either to develop a closely related focus area (e.g., green business) or to sample from a broad set of relevant courses.
Option 2: Environmental Economics and Management (EEM).
This option is for students who seek a balanced focus on environmental sciences and environmental economics.

passages.heading: Curriculum & Standards Committee Report #2024-2025-03B | Page 8
passages.text:
The option requires 31 credits of basic sciences, including at least eight credits in principles of biology (BIO 101/103, 102/104); four credits in general or introductory chemistry (CHM 101/102 or 103/105); four credits in introduction to soil science (NRS 212); four credits in introductory ecology (BIO 262); four credits in understanding the earth (GEO 103); three credits in applied calculus (MTH 131); and four credits in introductory statistics (STA 308).

Medical Laboratory Science This major, offered by the Department of Cell and Molecular Biology, is designed to prepare students for applied careers in the medical laboratory and biomedical sciences, as well as to prepare students for graduate or professional school.
Students are required to take the following courses as part of the curriculum: BIO 101, 102, 103, 104, 220, 221, 222, 223; CHM 101, 102, 112, 114, 124, 126; CMB 201 or 211, 311, 333, 352; MLS 102, 360, 405, 406, 409, 410, 411, 412, 413, 414, 415, 416, 451, 483; MTH 111 or 131 or 141; PHY 111, 185; STA 307 or 308; and twosix ofcredits selected from the following professional electives: BIO 341331, CMB 312, 320, 332, 334, 341, 353, 432, 435, 437, 491, PHP 405.
A total of 120 credits is required for graduation.
During the �rst three years of the program, emphasis is on general education and on basic courses in the biological, chemical, and quantitative sciences.
The courses of the senior year are taught off campus by clinical instructors from the schools of medical technologylaboratory science at a�liated hospitals.
These schools are accredited by the National Accreditation Agency for Clinical Laboratory Sciences.

passages.heading: Curriculum & Standards Committee Report #2024-2025-03B | Page 18
passages.text:
The senior year is an 11-month clinical internshipintensive program that begins in mid-June.
It is taken at one or more of the following clinical agencies: Rhode Island Hospital, Miriam Hospital, Fatima Hospital, and the Rhode Island Blood Center.
The clinical program includes lecture and laboratory instruction in clinical chemistry, clinical microbiology, hematology, immunology, immunohematology, and molecular pathology, and prepares the student for national certi�cation examinations and state licensure.
Applicants to this curriculum should have completed 60 credits and taken most of the required courses by the end of the sophomore year.
Students apply for acceptance into the clinical internship during their junior year and candidates are selected by the departmental curriculum committee and by program o�cials of the hospital schools.
Since the number of student placements in the clinical internship is limited, interested students should consult with the program director early in their college career, so they will be familiar with the requirements and application procedures.

passages.heading: Curriculum & Standards Committee Report #2024-2025-03B | Page 18
passages.text:
Flexibility in the curriculum permits students who are not admitted to the program to ful�ll requirements for other degrees in the college.
Students with a degree in a health profession, life science, or related �eld may apply to the clinical internship as a �fth year of study.

This option is for students who wish to develop a deep understanding of social and economic systems as they relate to a sustainable environment.
This option is designed to provide considerable �exibility so students can focus their studies to meet their professional goals.
Twenty-four credits in concentration courses are required at the 300 level or above, with 15 credits in environmental and natural resource economics (EEC), including economics of natural resource management and policy (EEC 310), bene�t-cost analysis (EEC 440), and a capstone course in environmental economics and policy (EEC 432), three credits in intermediate economic theory or intermediate microeconomics (ECN 328 or 323), and six credits in other concentration courses selected by students in consultation with their advisors.
Up to nine concentration credits may be in economics (ECN) or business (ACC, BAI, FIN, INE, MGT, MKT, SCA).

An additional 27 credits in supporting electives allow the student either to develop a closely related focus area (e.g., green business) or to sample from a broad set of relevant courses.

Psychology majors are required to complete a minimum of 32 (maximum 47) credits in psychology courses to be distributed as follows: PSY 113 (with a grade of C or better); a minimum of two courses from PSY 232, 235, and 254 (with a C average); both PSY 200 (300) and PSY 301 (with a grade of C or better in each); a minimum of three topics courses (9 credits) from PSY 255, 310, 324, 335, 361, 381, 384, 385, 399, 412, 425, 432, 434, 436, 442, 460, 464, 470, 479, and 480 (the average in the three courses must be C or better); a minimum of one course (3 credits) in the applied knowledge area to be selected from PSY 103, 261, 275, 324, 334, 340, 399, 465, 466, 471, and 478 (with a C or better); a minimum of one course (at least three credits) from the experiential practice and/or internships area selected from PSY 305, 473, 488, 489, 499; EDC 484; ITR 301, 302; CSV 302, with a C or better in graded courses or a satisfactory in S/U courses.
A particular course can only be used to satisfy one required program area (topics courses or the applied knowledge area).
A minimum of 32 graded psychology (PSY) credits (not S/U) are required for the psychology major.

Kingston Spring 2025 Spring 2025 The Biochemical Engineering minor introduces students to the fundamental chemistry and physics underlying biological processes.
Students will apply engineering principles in a biological context to control the interactions between and behavior of organic molecules, proteins, and other biomacromolecules.
With this minor, students will be prepared for industrial and research positions in the biotechnology and biomedical �elds.
The Biochemical Engineering minor is comprised of a minimum of 18 credit hours, at least half of which must be earned at URI.
The required courses include two fundamental science courses (6 credits), two biochemical engineering fundamentals courses (6 credits), and two or more supporting courses (6 credits).
Up to 6 credits can double count towards a major (e.g., core courses).
Students declaring this major must earn a minimum grade point average of 2.00 in courses counted towards the minor.
Students will need to complete the Biochemical Engineering minor form and have it signed by the minor coordinator, department chair, and appropriate dean.

The course requirements for the undergraduate biochemical engineering minor are as follows: Fundamental Science Courses (6 Credits): CHM 112 General Chemistry Lecture II BIO 110 Fundamentals of Biology Biochemical Engineering Fundamentals Courses (6 Credits): CHE 574 Biochemical Engineering I CMB 311 Introductory Biochemistry Supporting Courses (6 Credits): CHE 466 Biomaterials CHE 491/2 Special Problems (max 3 credits)* CHE 548 Separations for Biotechnology CHE 553 Bionanotechnology CHM 441 The Chemistry of Biological Systems CMB 210 Biochemical Aspects of Nutrition and Physiology CMB 341 Principles of Cell Biology CMB 421 Physical Biochemistry CMB 426 Structural Biochemistry CMB 482 Proteins and Enzymes CVE 472 Biosystems in Environmental Engineering PHY 430 Modern Biological Physics * Students must complete a research project related to biochemical engineering under the guidance of a faculty member and get prior permission from the Biochemical Engineering Minor Coordinator.

passages.heading: Service & Community Life Committee Resolution #2024-2025-01 | Page 1
passages.text:
Proposed Resolution for Joint Action to Redesign the Office of the Ombuds The Service and Community Life Committee (SCLC) December 12, 2024 Resolution The purpose of this resolution is to request immediate joint action by the Faculty Senate and the Office of the President as co-equal governing partners through the creation of a special joint committee.
The special joint committee will create a new Office of the Ombud.
Context In 2024, the Ombuds Dr.
Gerry Tyler and Dr.
Al Killilea were replaced by an Interim Ombud, Dr.
Charles Collyer.
An Interim Ombud role was created so that the Faculty Senate Service and Community Life Committee (SCLC), The Faculty Senate Executive Committee (FSEC), and the office of Provost could take a year to redesign and re-establish a new Office of the Ombuds.
This resolution grows out of discussions that have taken place between SCLC, FSEC, and the Office of the Provost.

passages.heading: Service & Community Life Committee Resolution #2024-2025-01 | Page 1
passages.text:
Expectations Membership of the special joint committee shall consist of advocates for those members of the campus community who may need or want to engage with the Office of the Ombuds: representatives from the faculty and delegates representing staff and student interests. ● Special joint committee co-chairs.
The committee shall be co-chaired by a designee from the SCLC and a designee from the Office of the President.
The co-chairs shall recruit committee members and manage and oversee the work of the committee until a new Office of the Ombuds is established. ● Committee charge.
The committee shall study best practices and decide the most appropriate actions for the design and creation of an effective Office of the Ombuds, including: ● Role, duties, powers and privileges.
The committee shall revise and update the policy that delineates the expectations of the Office of the Ombud and that codifies the duties, powers, and privileges of the Ombuds.

passages.heading: Service & Community Life Committee Resolution #2024-2025-01 | Page 1
passages.text: The position requires that the Ombuds are: ● Trained in how to listen and help identify issues and courses of action, mediate conflict or disputes, and guide and direct those in need ● Skilled and certified conflict mediators ● Connected to the university community, whether currently or formerly employed by the institution

passages.heading: Service & Community Life Committee Resolution #2024-2025-01 | Page 2
passages.text:
● Provided equitable compensation for their work ● Provided with appropriate space ● Provided a community infrastructure, including but not limited to a cohort of others who work in the support system of the institution (CED, EEOC, Title 9, etc.) ● Job description, nomination, application and selection process. ● Job description.
The committee will develop a new job description that must convey the following critical ideas (per section 5.88.10 of the University Manual): the Ombud role shall be to: investigate complaints from students, faculty, and administrative personnel, with the very explicit charge to handle situations that fall outside of the auspices of the usual channels (such as the Office of Community, Equity, and Diversity, the unions, office of DEI in the respective colleges, EEOC, Title IX, and Human Resources).
The Ombuds are designated to handle primarily issues that stem from interpersonal conflicts. ● Application, hiring committee, and selection process.

passages.heading: Service & Community Life Committee Resolution #2024-2025-01 | Page 2
passages.text:
The committee must also design a written application (whether it be an essay on qualifications and interest, or short answers to prompts) and an application and selection process that shall include a designated hiring committee.
The hiring committee shall include representatives of the university’s co-equal governing partnership: the Faculty Senate and the Office of the President.
The hiring committee shall review applications, interview candidates, and collectively make the final decision on the selection of at least two Ombuds.
It is important that there are at least two Ombuds, especially if they are full-time tenure track faculty, or faculty and staff, from two different colleges.
This allows for recusal from cases if necessary.
The SCLC recommends a two-person Office with one faculty representative and one staff representative. ● Nominations.

passages.heading: Service & Community Life Committee Resolution #2024-2025-01 | Page 2
passages.text:
The Manual (5.88.11) indicates that The Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs and the Faculty Senate Executive Committee shall jointly nominate one or more full-time, tenured faculty or emeritus faculty for the post of Ombuds and shall submit the names of nominees to the Faculty Senate for confirmation, no later than May 1st of the year in which the Ombuds’ term is to begin.
Revisions must make certain that it is clear that nominations are not restricted to those put forth by any member of the administration and the Faculty Senate, but will follow the nomination and selection process designed and approved by

passages.heading: Service & Community Life Committee Resolution #2024-2025-01 | Page 3
passages.text:
the special joint committee, which shall include the possibility of self-nominations. ● Visibility, privacy, and confidentiality. ● Physical space.
The committee must negotiate a new neutral space for the Office of the Ombuds that will achieve two critical goals: making the Office more visible to community members and also guarantee protections of privacy and confidentiality to those who choose to enter that space to benefit from this valuable resource. ● Communication avenues.
The committee will be charged with designing communication avenues and reporting protocols that will guarantee protections of privacy and confidentiality to those who choose to use this valuable resource. ● Digital space.
The committee will be responsible for the redesign of the Office of the Ombuds website to improve its online visibility so that the Office functions as the first stop in the reporting line.
The website must include clear messaging that is aligned with the University Manual, a more effective and reliable submission mechanism, clear expectations regarding potential courses of action and outcomes, and any other additional information that would enhance the user experience.

passages.heading: Service & Community Life Committee Resolution #2024-2025-01 | Page 3
passages.text:
It would also be helpful to link the Office of the Ombuds to the other offices that handle certain student and personnel concerns, such Title IX and the CED office’s website, to increase visibility and clarity in messaging about its services.
This includes providing clear information about what the Office of the Ombuds does (and does not do).
This information is especially pertinent for new hires and newly admitted students, as well as providing ongoing messaging directed at URI employees and students. ● Reporting and Accountability.
Record keeping and reporting are critical features of a well-functioning ombud office. ● Case Reporting and Mechanisms of Accountability.
This committee must establish a policy about reporting cases, mechanisms of accountability, report storage, etc.
The reporting must not be compromised by the bureaucratic structure and must guarantee protections of privacy and confidentiality to those who choose to use this valuable resource. ● Reporting and Accountability Cohort.
The committee must create an ecosystem/cohort of other staff who are working within reporting and resolution, such as the EEOC officer, Assistant Deans

passages.heading: Service & Community Life Committee Resolution #2024-2025-01 | Page 4
passages.text: focusing on DEI, the Office of Community Equity, and Diversity, Title 9 Officer, Dean of Students, representative from HR, among others. This cohort shall meet at least twice every semester. ● Consultancy. If supported financially, the committee will work with an outside consultancy to assist in the design and creation of the new office to achieve these goals.

passages.text: Faculty Senate Resolution #2024-2025-02

passages.heading: Faculty Senate Resolution #2024-2025-02 | Page 1
passages.text:
FACULTY SENATE OFFICE 224 P ASTORE H ALL , 51 L OWER C OLLEGE R OAD , K INGSTON , R I 02881 U SA , P: 401.874.2616 Faculty Senate Resolution 2024-2025-02 Faculty Senate Meeting of December 12, 2024 Resolution on the Implementation of Honors Contracts WHEREAS , following considerable self-study, and with significant input from external experts, the URI Honors Program has proposed the use of honors contracts at URI.
Honors contracts are formal agreements facilitated by an honors program, between a student and instructor.
They unite students and instructors to enhance non-honors courses to an honors level through additional learner-directed work tailored to the “broader, deeper, and more complex” learning experiences advocated by the National Collegiate Honors Council (NCHC); and WHEREAS , Contracts are recognized by over 60% of honors programs in the USA, where they foster community and ownership, enhancing the educational process and commitment to the programs’ success.
For example, work at the University Honors Program at the University of Kansas shows that honors contracts act as far more than stopgaps to address honors course shortages.

passages.heading: Faculty Senate Resolution #2024-2025-02 | Page 1
passages.text:
They can “facilitate access to honors, increases completion, democratize key aspects of the honors experience, provide students with structured avenues for building relationships with faculty members, and empower students to own their educational experiences;” and WHEREAS , Honors contracts may be best understood as a form of an independent study, entered into voluntarily by both students and faculty, with a contract defining outcomes, deadlines, and assessment definitions for additional work related to the course materials; and WHEREAS ,Honors contracts provide flexibility for students to align their education with their interests and goals.
They also allow programs to meet student needs when constraints of students or faculty numbers or funding limitations do not allow honors courses to be run that answer to a student’s interests and needs; and WHEREAS , Contracts provide an extra measure of curricular flexibility at institutions such as ours that are not able to field enough faculty, cannot provide an adequate number of honors courses, or do not have a large enough student body to fill honors sections.

passages.heading: Faculty Senate Resolution #2024-2025-02 | Page 1
passages.text:
Contracts can fill the gap and provide opportunities for students’ self-guided intellectual growth; NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED , that the Faculty Senate of the University of Rhode Island, calls for implementation of the following Honors Contracts Proposal.
This includes making the

passages.heading: Faculty Senate Resolution #2024-2025-02 | Page 2
passages.text: recommended changes to the University Catalog and to the eCampus system used by Enrollment Services; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED , that the Honors Program is called upon to reflect these changes on their website and in all other promotional and outreach materials promulgated by the Program. The Program is also called upon to review Chapter 8 of the University Manual (Academic Regulations, Honors Program) in light of the Contracts Proposal and bring any recommended changes to the Faculty Senate expeditiously. Adopted this 12th day of December, 2024. ____________________________________________________________ Theodore Walls, URI Faculty Senate President

passages.heading: Faculty Senate Resolution #2024-2025-02 | Page 3
passages.text: CONTRACTS: URI Catalog Information Honors Contracts Honors contracts allow students to earn Honors credit for non-Honors courses by pursuing more advanced study. This requires an agreement between the student and instructor, and approval from the Honors Program. This option is valuable for students interested in a course not offered in an Honors format or whose schedules prevent them from enrolling in an Honors section. The following restrictions apply. (Any exceptions must be approved in advance by the Honors Program): 1. Honors contract credits shall not amount to more than one-third (1/3) of a student’s total coursework required for graduation from Honors. 2. Students shall not engage in more than one honors contract per semester. 3. Honors contracts cannot be completed during the summer or J-Term. Nor can they be applied to 100-level courses, internships, independent studies, study abroad, or courses at other institutions. 4. Contracted courses must be taken for a letter grade and must be completed with a grade of B or better to count towards Honors Program requirements. 5. Students who do not complete the proposed work to the satisfaction of the instructor will not earn Honors credit for the course.

passages.heading: Faculty Senate Resolution #2024-2025-02 | Page 4
passages.text: CONTRACTS: For the Honors Program Web site. The Honors Contract Process The Honors contract process involves four stages: 1. Crafting of an individualized project with the course instructor. 2. Submission of the contract to the Honors Program for approval. 3. Completion of the agreed-upon assignments and activities. 4. Submission of the completed work and the Honors Contract completion form conﬁrming the instructor’s satisfaction with the work. 1: Crafting the Honors Contract The Honors Contract is a mutual commitment to a learning experience above and beyond normal course requirements. The student and instructor must agree on the criteria for evaluating the project and its scheduling. Instructors are under no obligation to supervise Honors Contracts. The Honors contract is intended to enrich the student's education by further work of mutual interest to the student and instructor, rather than simply adding to the course’s workload. Students would therefore be wise to consider projects where the enriched assignment or activity also suits the interests and needs of the instructor. An Honors contract should involve 6 to 7 hours per credit: A 3-credit course should, for example, involve approximately 20 hours of additional work. These estimated hours should include 2-3 hours of meetings with the instructor: one at the start, one mid-project, and one to conclude. Overall, plan for 3-5 hours of direct faculty involvement, including evaluation.

passages.heading: Faculty Senate Resolution #2024-2025-02 | Page 5
passages.text: While the details of contracted assignments and activities may vary greatly, course enrichments could include: • Collaboration with the instructor on a joint research project. • An analytical, research, or policy paper, in addition to any assigned in the "regular" syllabus, and/or more reliant on individual work with primary or original source material. • An experiential- or service-learning experience, or internship related to the course focus. • A multimedia project, performance, or artistic work related to the course focus. • Curriculum development projects, such as assisting the professor with the development and implementation of new teaching tools, class activities, or trial runs of new course projects. [INSERT CALENDAR/ TIMELINE HERE.] 2: Submission of the Contract Proposal All Honors contract proposals must be submitted no later than the end of the third week of classes. The Honors contract proposal consists of three parts: 1. The Contract Form, signed by both the student and the instructor. 2. A copy of the original course syllabus 3. A brief description of the proposed project (500-1000 words.) The following information should be included in the proposal: 1. What? Why? When? How? – A brief overview of the project, its rationale, timeline and evaluation criteria. 2. How is it "honors"? – How, precisely the project differs from the regular work of the class.

passages.heading: Faculty Senate Resolution #2024-2025-02 | Page 6
passages.text:
3.
What will we see? – What will the outcome (or deliverable) of the project be? 4.
A timetable – E.g.: Meetings with the course instructor, a mid-term check-in, submission of components or drafts of the project, and the submission of the ﬁnal product.
The ﬁnal deadline can be no later than the scheduled ﬁnal exam period for the course. 5.
Evaluation criteria – Include a clear statement of the criteria that will be used to evaluate the contracted work.
What are the minimum requirements that must be met in order to be judged acceptable?
If there are multiple elements, how do they each contribute?
Also, the following wording must be included in the proposal: "The Honors contract work will be assessed as Satisfactory or Unsatisfactory by the instructor according to the criteria described in this contract.
The rating will be entered into a Honors Contract Completion form.
A rating of Satisfactory will result in the student receiving Honors credit for the course.
A rating of Unsatisfactory will result in no Honors credit being awarded for the course.

passages.heading: Faculty Senate Resolution #2024-2025-02 | Page 6
passages.text:
Performance on the Honors Contract work will not affect the ﬁnal grade in any circumstance." The Honors Program may approve the proposal as written, request more information before making a decision, or reject it.
Once approved, the Honors Administrator will sign it and send a copy to both the student and the instructor.
Approved contracts result in a transcript notation of "Honors" for the course in question once Enrollment Services is notiﬁed by Honors that the coursework has been completed. 3: Completion of the Contracted Work Approved contract work should proceed according to the predetermined schedule.
The project may, however, evolve as it progresses.
Completed projects will not generally be expected to perfectly match the initial proposal.
However, the student and instructor

passages.heading: Faculty Senate Resolution #2024-2025-02 | Page 7
passages.text: may along the way agree on signiﬁcant alterations, deviating substantially from the approved proposal. Should this occur, the student must submit an amended Honors contract proposal outlining the new criteria for completion and assessment. If in doubt on how to proceed contact the Honors Program as soon as possible. 4: Submission of the Completed Work and Contract Completion Form To earn Honors credit for the course, students must complete the proposed work at a level deemed satisfactory by the instructor. Following that, an "Honors" designation appears on the transcript, and all credits earned for the course count towards fulﬁllment of the Honors Program, provided that the ﬁnal course grade is B or better. Work assigned by the contract is not calculated into the ﬁnal course grade. Final grades are calculated per the professor's original syllabus, reﬂecting the quality and content of all the student's coursework. As soon as the contracted work is complete and approved by the instructor, the student will submit a copy of the completed work and the Honors Contract Completion Form no later than by the end of business on the last day of the ﬁnal examination period. If, however, a presentation or performance is part of the proposal, please invite members of the Honors Program to attend.

passages.heading: Faculty Senate Resolution #2024-2025-02 | Page 8
passages.text:
Amended Text For: "Honors Program" in "Special Academic Opportunities" in URI'S catalog (Added text is in red) Honors Program The University Honors Program offers motivated students opportunities to broaden and deepen their intellectual development.
The program consists of courses that emphasize discussion and project-based learning, a colloquium that brings nationally and internationally distinguished speakers to campus, and independent research projects under the guidance of a faculty sponsor.
Honors courses at the 100 and 200 levels fulﬁll general education requirements; those at the 300 and 400 levels are more specialized and often are used to fulﬁll either a general education requirement or the requirements of a major.
Students may participate in the Honors Program if they meet the following standards: Sophomores, juniors, and seniors must have earned at least a 3.40 cumulative grade point average at URI; transfer students must have received a GPA of 3.40 or better at their previous institution to be eligible for honors courses.

passages.heading: Faculty Senate Resolution #2024-2025-02 | Page 8
passages.text:
Incoming freshmen are invited to participate in the Honors Program based on one of the following: they must have earned a cumulative grade point average (recalculated) of 3.60 or higher in high school and must have a combined score of 1,300 on the critical reading and math portions of the SAT exam (or ACT score of 27 or higher); or they must have earned a cumulative 3.80 GPA (recalculated) in high school, and SAT scores are not considered.
Eligible students may participate in the Honors Program in one of two ways: they may take honors courses on an occasional basis, registering for any number or pattern of courses that interest them; or they may do honors work on a regular basis, meeting the speciﬁc requirements to receive the transcript notation “Completed the University Honors Program.”

passages.heading: Faculty Senate Resolution #2024-2025-02 | Page 9
passages.text: No more than one third (1/3) of a student's total credits toward Honors certiﬁcation may be obtained through the use of Honors Contracts, unless an exception is granted ahead of time by the Honors Program. To achieve this certiﬁcation a student must complete a minimum of 18 honors course credits that meet the following requirements: 1) three credits in Honors at the 100 or 200 level; 2) three credits of Honors Colloquium; 3) three credits in Honors at the 300 or 400 level; 4) six credits at the 400 level, which may be either six credits of Senior Honors Project (HPR 401, 402) or three credits of Senior Honors Project (HPR 401) and three credits of Senior Honors Seminar (HPR 411/412, or other approved Senior Seminar); 5) three additional honors credits taken at any level; and 6) a 3.40 grade point average for honors courses and a 3.40 cumulative grade point average.

passages.text:
