passages.heading: Faculty Senate Resolution #2024-2025-02 | Page 11
passages.text: Honors Contracts: FAQ for Faculty For the URI Honors Program Web Page (Draft Dec. 4, 2024) What is an Honors Contract? Honors contracts allow students to earn Honors credit for non-Honors courses by pursuing more advanced study. This requires an agreement between the student and instructor, and approval from the Honors Program. This option is valuable for students interested in a course not offered in an Honors format or whose schedules prevent them from enrolling in an Honors section. Why should we use Honors Contracts? Honors Contracts offer several beneﬁts: Flexibility: They allow students to tailor their education to their interests and goals. Accessibility: They provide opportunities for honors-level work when there are limitations on the number of honors courses offered. Student Engagement: They empower students, foster motivation, and facilitate mentor-mentee relationships with faculty. Who can supervise an Honors contract? All full-time faculty may supervise an Honors contract. No one, however, is required to do so. Part-time faculty and staff may supervise contracts only in special cases if an exception is granted prior to the creation of a contract by the Honors Program. What are the faculty roles and responsibilities in an Honors contract? Faculty roles and responsibilities include: Helping the student formulate a proposal for an appropriate contract project.

passages.heading: Faculty Senate Resolution #2024-2025-02 | Page 12
passages.text:
Deﬁning the terms and timeline of the contract with the student.
Providing guidance as the student works on the contracted project, with at least one mid-project meeting.
Evaluating the contract project at the end of the semester.
How much time should faculty plan to devote to this?
Generally, a faculty member should expect to devote 3-5 hours over the course of a term on a contracted project.
How are Honors Contracts set up?
The Honors Program provides comprehensive guidelines and support for setting up contracts on its Web site (See “The Contract Process”.
Students are encouraged to communicate early with instructors and the Honors Program to explore possibilities and ensure a clear understanding of the process.
Brieﬂy: The Honors contract process involves four stages: 1.
Crafting of an individualized project with the course instructor. 2.
Submission of the contract to the Honors Program for approval. 3.
Completion of the agreed-upon assignments and activities. 4.
Submission of the completed work and the Honors Contract Completion Form confirming the instructor’s satisfaction with the work.
What should be included in an Honors Contract?
The Honors contract proposal consists of three parts: 1.

passages.heading: Faculty Senate Resolution #2024-2025-02 | Page 12
passages.text:
The Contract Form, signed by both the student and the instructor. 2.
A copy of the original course syllabus 3.
A brief description of the proposed project (500-1000 words.) The following information should be included in the proposal: 1.
What?
Why?
When?
How? – A brief overview of the project, its rationale, timeline and evaluation criteria. 2.
How is it "honors"? – How, precisely the project differs from the regular work of the class.
I.e: A clear articulation of how the contract meets the "broader, deeper, more complex" criteria of the National Collegiate Honors Council. 3.
What will we see? – What will the outcome (or deliverable) of the project be?

passages.heading: Faculty Senate Resolution #2024-2025-02 | Page 13
passages.text:
4.
A timetable – E.g.: Meetings with the course instructor, a mid-term check-in, submission of components or drafts of the project, and the submission of the final product.
The final deadline can be no later than the scheduled final exam period for the course. 5.
Evaluation criteria – Include a clear statement of the criteria that will be used to evaluate the contracted work.
What are the minimum requirements that must be met in order to be judged acceptable?
If there are multiple elements, how do they each contribute?
Also, the following wording must be included in the proposal: "The Honors contract work will be assessed as Satisfactory or Unsatisfactory by the instructor according to the criteria described in this contract.
The rating will be entered into a Honors Contract Completion form.
A rating of Satisfactory will result in the student receiving Honors credit for the course.
A rating of Unsatisfactory will result in no Honors credit being awarded for the course.
Performance on the Honors Contract work will not affect the ﬁnal grade in any circumstance." The Honors Program may approve the proposal as written, request more information before making a decision, or reject it.

passages.heading: Faculty Senate Resolution #2024-2025-02 | Page 13
passages.text:
Once approved, the Honors Administrator will sign it and send a copy to both the student and the instructor.
Approved contracts result in a transcript notation of "Honors" for the course in question once Enrollment Services is notiﬁed by Honors that the coursework has been completed.
What are some examples of positive outcomes from Honors Contracts?
When well-managed, Honors Contracts can: • Cultivate personalized learning experiences. • Develop strong mentoring relationships between students and faculty. • Enhance the overall honors experience. • Provide faculty with a new vision for their courses.
What are some potential problems with Honors Contracts, and how can they be avoided?
Some potential issues include: Routine or Casual Use: Contracts should not become commonplace or be considered a replacement of the regular honors curriculum.

passages.heading: Faculty Senate Resolution #2024-2025-02 | Page 14
passages.text: Lack of Meaningful Interaction: Although the contracted projects require only about 20 hours of work by the student and 3 to 5 hours of work by the faculty, it is important to ensure that contracts involve meaningful interaction between students and instructors. Unclear Expectations: The Honors Program provides clear guidelines and assessment criteria to students and faculty maintain high standards. Faculty are be expected to provide clear instructions to the students in the contract language. How can I ensure that Honors Contracts are effective? To ensure effectiveness: Maintain high standards and clear expectations. Ensure that the contracted work is well-connected to the course themes and outcomes. Ensure that the contracted work enhances the student’s experience of the course themes, materials, and outcomes. Will I be compensated for my work with Honors Contracts? Yes, it is essential that faculty are recognized and compensated for the additional work involved in Honors Contracts. Your work should be noted in your review portfolio. What is the difference between an Honors contract and an Honors Project? An Honors contract deﬁnes a project requiring approximately 20 hours of work, appended to an existing non-Honors course to allow the course’s credits be counted as Honors credits. An Honors project is a mentored independent study for 3 or 6 credits, devoted to a project that requires extensive research, reading, writing, creativity, or experimentation.

passages.text: How is an Honors contract satisﬁed? An Honors contract is satisﬁed when the professor notiﬁes the Honors Program that the student has completed the assigned task satisfactorily. The student must also receive a B or higher in the course in order to earn Honors credit. Approved contract work should proceed according to the predetermined schedule. The project may, however, evolve as it progresses. Completed projects will not generally be expected to perfectly match the initial proposal. However, the student and instructor may along the way agree on signiﬁcant alterations, deviating substantially from the approved proposal. Should this occur, the student must submit an amended Honors contract proposal outlining the new criteria for completion and assessment. If in doubt on how to proceed contact the Honors Program as soon as possible. What happens if a student fails to complete an Honors contract? If a student fails to complete the proposed work to the satisfaction of the instructor, they will not receive Honors credit for the course. Can Honors contracts be applied to all courses? No, Honors contracts cannot be completed during the summer or J-Term. Nor should they be applied to 100-level courses, internships, independent studies, study abroad, or courses taken at other institutions.

passages.text: FACULTY SENATE OFFICE FACULTY SENATE LEGISLATION NOVEMBER 14, 2024 Grad uate Council Report 2024-2025-02B At the November 4, 2024 meeting of the Graduate Council, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate for approval. Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation by The Faculty Senate PROGRAM MODIFICATIONS COLLEGE OF THE ENVIRONMENT & LIFE SCIENCES : PhD Marine Affairs, Effective Spring 2025 Appendix A The proposed changes include changing the credential type to “Degree”, initiation date of Spring 2025, change in location to “Kingston”, and changing required course credits to 21 from 18 plus an additional 45 credits instead of 48 credits. We are adding a new core course requirement of MAF 521 Coastal Zone Law. We have created a 500 level version of MAF 482, which is MAF 583 Quantitative Methods in Marine Affairs. The MAF 583 requirement replaces the MAF 482 requirement, since PhD students are not able to count 400 level courses toward their degree requirements. MA Marine Affairs, Effective Spring 2025 Appendix B We are adding a new core course requirement of MAF 521 Coastal Zone Law and reducing the total number of electives from 15 to 12. We are requiring that nine of the elective credits be within Marine Affairs. We have created a 500 level version of our MAF 482 course, which is MAF 583 Quantitative Methods in Marine Affairs. The MAF 583 requirement replaces the MAF 482 requirement. We have removed the option for MAF 598 Masters Project in order to streamline course codes. GC Report 2024-2025-02B, Page 1 of 30 Bill #24-25-08

passages.text: Faculty determined that all MAF graduate students should take the Coastal Zone Law course in order to develop expertise in domestic coastal law as part of their degree program. MMA Marine Affairs, Effective Spring 2025 Appendix C We are adding a new core course requirement of MAF 521 Coastal Zone Law and reducing the total number of electives from 15 to 12. We are requiring that 50% of elective credits be within Marine Affairs. This change ensures that graduates of the Master of Marine Affairs program have expertise in domestic coastal law. Change in electives ensures that students take electives from within the department. Proposed changes include initiation date of Spring 2025, location change to “Kingston”; admission requirements to 3 instead of 5 years of post-graduate equivalent experience with the removal of “in marine areas employment”. FACULTY SENATE OFFICE FACULTY SENATE LEGISLATION NOVEMBER 14, 2024 Curri culum & Standards Committee Report 2024-2025-03B At the October 31, 2024 meeting of the Curriculum & Standards Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate for approval.
Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation By The Faculty Senate PROGRAM MODIFICATIONS COLLEGE OF THE ENVIRONMENT & LIFE SCIENCES: BS Environmental and Natural Resource Economics, Effective Winter 2025 Appendix A College of Business added TMD to their programs and any course code offered by COB qualifies as concentration credits for our ENRE degree tracks (Green Markets and Sustainability option and Green Business double major).
We propose to add the TMD code to our existing list of accepted COB courses (ACC, BAI, FIN, MGT, MKT, SCA, INE).
BS Medical Laboratory Science, Effective Spring 2025 Appendix B The proposed change involves the addition of six courses that would qualify as "Professional Electives" towards the MLS degree.

passages.heading: 24-25-08 | Page 32
passages.text:
Namely, the added courses are: BIO 331 (Parasitology), CMB 312 (Introductory Biochemistry Laboratory), CMB 332 (Medical and Public Health Microbiology Laboratory), CMB 353 (Genetics Laboratory), CMB 491 (Research in Cell and Molecular Biology), and PHP 405 (Fundamentals of Epidemiology).
The addition of these courses accomplishes two goals.
First and foremost, they provide addition al opportunities for students to cultivate lab skills in areas that are relevant to MLS (BIO 331, CMB 312, CMB 332, CMB 353 and CMB 491) as well as explore MLS-related fields (BIO 331, PHP 405) that represent potential career pathways with a MLS degree.
Second, these additional courses provide more flexibility for students to successfully complete the six credit "Professional Elective" requirement of the MLS major in a timely manner.
This is due to the fact that many of the previously approved professional electives have prerequisite course requirements and limited scheduling options (i.e. offered only during fall or spring semester), which can make it challenging for students to complete this degree requirement.

NEW CERTIFICATES, MINORS, or SPECIALIZATIONS COLLEGE OF ENGINEERING: Minor - Biochemical Engineering, Effective Spring 2025 Appendix H The Biochemical Engineering minor introduces students to the fundamental chemistry and physics underlying biological processes.
Students will apply engineering principles in a biological context to control the interactions between and behavior of organic molecules, proteins, and other biomacromolecules.
With this minor, students will be prepared for industrial and research positions in the biotechnology and biomedical fields.
The Biochemical Engineering minor is comprised of a minimum of 18 credit hours, at least half of which must be earned at URI.
The required courses include two fundamental science courses (6 credits), two biochemical engineering fundamentals courses (6 credits), and two or more supporting courses (6 credits).
Up to 6 credits can double count towards a major (e.g., core courses).
Students declaring this major must earn a minimum grade point average of 2.00 in courses counted towards the minor.

passages.heading: 24-25-08 | Page 34
passages.text:
Students will need to complete the Biochemical Engineering minor form and have it signed by the minor coordinator, department chair, and ap propriate dean.
Students are responsible for meeting the prerequisite requirements for individual courses, as applicable.

Fall 2022 How can we create a sustainable society that protects the environment while maintaining a prosperous society?
Why have humans caused environmental degradation on local, regional, and global scales, and what can we do about it?
Public o�cials, nonpro�t organizations, and private businesses need professionals who can answer these questions in order to design a new sustainable world.
As a major in environmental and natural resource economics, you will acquire tools that can help answer these questions.
The environmental and natural resource economics major integrates the natural sciences with economics to help us understand why many of earth’s natural resources are under threat and how we can design policies to address these threats.
This major teaches students to weigh options and make important decisions concerning the protection, restoration, development, and use of our natural resources.
The major prepares students for graduate school or for careers in the public and private sector that address environmental and natural resource management, business, or public policy.

passages.heading: 24-25-08 | Page 39
passages.text:
Professionals in these �elds play an important role in coordinating interdisciplinary teams to address such complex problems.
Graduates gain an understanding of both natural sciences and the economy.
The degree requires a minimum of 120 credits, including 24 credits in concentration.
In addition to satisfying the general education requirements, students need nine credits in introductory professional courses, including natural resource conservation (NRS 100), introduction to resource economics (EEC 105), and environmental economics and policy (EEC 205).
The major also requires a minimum of three credits in written communication skills (WRT) at the 200 level or higher.
It is also possible to earn a double degree in environmental economics and general business, which we call Green Business (see details below).
The Environmental and Natural Resource Economics department offers multiple academic opportunities such as two curriculum options or pathways within the major, a double degree program, an energy certi�cate, a global water resource minor, and an accelerated Bachelor-Masters (ABM) program.

passages.heading: 24-25-08 | Page 39
passages.text:
The two curriculum options under the ENRE major are: Green Markets and Sustainability (GMS) and Environmental Economics and Management (EEM).
These options, the double degree program, energy certi�cate, global water resource minor, and ABM program are discussed below.
Option 1: Green Markets and Sustainability (GMS).
This option is for students who wish to develop a deep understanding of social and economic systems as they relate to a sustainable environment.
This option is designed to provide considerable �exibility so students can focus their studies to meet their professional goals.
Twenty-four credits in concentration courses are required at the 300 level or above, with 15 credits in environmental and natural resource economics (EEC), including economics of natural resource management and policy (EEC 310), bene�t-cost analysis (EEC 440), and a capstone course in environmental economics and policy (EEC 432), three credits in intermediate economic theory or intermediate microeconomics (ECN 328 or 323), and six credits in other concentration courses selected by students in consultation with their advisors.

passages.heading: 24-25-08 | Page 39
passages.text:
Up to nine concentration credits may be in economics (ECN) or business (ACC, BAI, FIN, INE, MGT, MKT, SCA).
A minimum of 21 credits in basic and supporting sciences are required in mathematics (MTH 103, 111, 131, or BAI 111), introductory statistics (STA 307, 308, 409, or BAI 210), and environmental geology or understanding the earth (GEO 100G or 103).
Applied calculus (MTH 131) is strongly recommended, especially for students who are considering going to graduate school.
Supporting sciences can be selected from a broad range of subjects including aquaculture and �sheries technology, animal and veterinary science, biology, business (BAI 210 and 212 only), cell and molecular biology, chemistry, computer science, ecology, geology, genetics, mathematics, natural resources science, oceanography, physics, plant physiology, or statistics.
An additional 27 credits in supporting electives allow the student either to develop a closely related focus area (e.g., green business) or to sample from a broad set of relevant courses.
Option 2: Environmental Economics and Management (EEM).
This option is for students who seek a balanced focus on environmental sciences and environmental economics.

passages.heading: 24-25-08 | Page 39
passages.text:
The option requires 31 credits of basic sciences, including at least eight credits in principles of biology (BIO 101/103, 102/104); four credits in general or introductory chemistry (CHM 101/102 or 103/105); four credits in introduction to soil science (NRS 212); four credits in introductory ecology (BIO 262); four credits in understanding the earth (GEO 103); three credits in applied calculus (MTH 131); and four credits in introductory statistics (STA 308).
The 24-credit concentration includes a minimum of 9 concentration credits in environmental and resource economics Program Description  Appendix A | BS Environmental & Natural Resource Economics Page 5 of 10 CASC Report 2024-2025-03B, Page 8 of 74 Bill #24-25-08

Students are also required to take a minimum of 12 concentration credits selected from ecology, soils and watersheds, and geosciences. Students choose a minimum of 20 credits in supporting electives. The Department of Environmental and Natural Resource Economics and the College of Business offer a double degree program in environmental and natural resource economics and general business. This program is designed for those interested in corporate sustainability, energy e�ciency, non-pro�t management, green marketing, renewable energy, global environmental challenges, environmental policy, and energy �nance. Students earn a B.S. in Environmental and Natural Resource Economics from the College of the Environment and Life Sciences and a B.S. in Business Administration from the College of Business. Medical Laboratory Science This major, offered by the Department of Cell and Molecular Biology, is designed to prepare students for applied careers in the medical laboratory and biomedical sciences, as well as to prepare students for graduate or professional school.
Students are required to take the following courses as part of the curriculum: BIO 101, 102, 103, 104, 220, 221, 222, 223; CHM 101, 102, 112, 114, 124, 126; CMB 201 or 211, 311, 333, 352; MLS 102, 360, 405, 406, 409, 410, 411, 412, 413, 414, 415, 416, 451, 483; MTH 111 or 131 or 141; PHY 111, 185; STA 307 or 308; and twosix ofcredits selected from the following professional electives: BIO 341331, CMB 312, 320, 332, 334, 341, 353, 432, 435, 437, 491, PHP 405.
A total of 120 credits is required for graduation.
During the �rst three years of the program, emphasis is on general education and on basic courses in the biological, chemical, and quantitative sciences.
The courses of the senior year are taught off campus by clinical instructors from the schools of medical technologylaboratory science at a�liated hospitals.
These schools are accredited by the National Accreditation Agency for Clinical Laboratory Sciences.

passages.heading: 24-25-08 | Page 49
passages.text:
The senior year is an 11-month clinical internshipintensive program that begins in mid-June.
It is taken at one or more of the following clinical agencies: Rhode Island Hospital, Miriam Hospital, Fatima Hospital, and the Rhode Island Blood Center.
The clinical program includes lecture and laboratory instruction in clinical chemistry, clinical microbiology, hematology, immunology, immunohematology, and molecular pathology, and prepares the student for national certi�cation examinations and state licensure.
Applicants to this curriculum should have completed 60 credits and taken most of the required courses by the end of the sophomore year.
Students apply for acceptance into the clinical internship during their junior year and candidates are selected by the departmental curriculum committee and by program o�cials of the hospital schools.
Since the number of student placements in the clinical internship is limited, interested students should consult with the program director early in their college career, so they will be familiar with the requirements and application procedures.

This option is for students who wish to develop a deep understanding of social and economic systems as they relate to a sustainable environment.
This option is designed to provide considerable �exibility so students can focus their studies to meet their professional goals.
Twenty-four credits in concentration courses are required at the 300 level or above, with 15 credits in environmental and natural resource economics (EEC), including economics of natural resource management and policy (EEC 310), bene�t-cost analysis (EEC 440), and a capstone course in environmental economics and policy (EEC 432), three credits in intermediate economic theory or intermediate microeconomics (ECN 328 or 323), and six credits in other concentration courses selected by students in consultation with their advisors.
Up to nine concentration credits may be in economics (ECN) or business (ACC, BAI, FIN, INE, MGT, MKT, SCA).

passages.heading: 24-25-08 | Page 58

A minimum of 21 credits in basic and supporting sciences are required in mathematics (MTH 103, 111, 131, or BAI 111), introductory statistics (STA 307, 308, 409, or BAI 210), and environmental geology or understanding the earth (GEO 100G or 103).
Applied calculus (MTH 131) is strongly recommended, especially for students who are considering going to graduate school.
Supporting sciences can be selected from a broad range of subjects including aquaculture and �sheries technology, animal and veterinary science, biology, business (BAI 210 and 212 only), cell and molecular biology, chemistry, computer science, ecology, geology, genetics, mathematics, natural resources science, oceanography, physics, plant physiology, or statistics.
An additional 27 credits in supporting electives allow the student either to develop a closely related focus area (e.g., green business) or to sample from a broad set of relevant courses.

Students majoring in psychology typically go on either to pursue a career at the bachelor’s level or study for an advanced degree.
In both cases, students should consult the department’s web site (uri.edu/psychology) and their academic advisor to select the appropriate degree option and the appropriate courses for their interests and goals.
Program Requirements.
Students who must repeat a course to meet the minimum grade requirements may use only three credits of that particular course toward graduation.
For the B.A. degree, a total of 120 credits is required for graduation.
The B.A. degree in Psychology provides students with a solid academic preparation through an overview of the current areas in the �eld of Psychology.
Students gain a better understanding of human behavior and an enhanced awareness of themselves and society, as well as skills for analyzing and evaluating information and data.
Students in this program must complete a minimum of 32 credits (maximum 47) in Psychology.

passages.heading: 24-25-08 | Page 76
passages.text: In order to transfer from University College for Academic Success to Health Sciences as a psychology major (or to be coded as such in the College of Health Sciences), a student must have completed 24 credits, have a C or better in PSY 113; a C average in two of the following courses: PSY 232, 235, and 254; and a C in PSY 200.

passages.heading: 24-25-08 | Page 76
passages.text:
Psychology majors are required to complete a minimum of 32 (maximum 47) credits in psychology courses to be distributed as follows: PSY 113 (with a grade of C or better); a minimum of two courses from PSY 232, 235, and 254 (with a C average); both PSY 200 (300) and PSY 301 (with a grade of C or better in each); a minimum of three topics courses (9 credits) from PSY 255, 310, 324, 335, 361, 381, 384, 385, 399, 412, 425, 432, 434, 436, 442, 460, 464, 470, 479, and 480 (the average in the three courses must be C or better); a minimum of one course (3 credits) in the applied knowledge area to be selected from PSY 103, 261, 275, 324, 334, 340, 399, 465, 466, 471, and 478 (with a C or better); a minimum of one course (at least three credits) from the experiential practice and/or internships area selected from PSY 305, 473, 488, 489, 499; EDC 484; ITR 301, 302; CSV 302, with a C or better in graded courses or a satisfactory in S/U courses.
A particular course can only be used to satisfy one required program area (topics courses or the applied knowledge area).
A minimum of 32 graded psychology (PSY) credits (not S/U) are required for the psychology major.

passages.heading: 24-25-08 | Page 76
passages.text:

Students pursuing the B.A. degree must complete 30 of the 120 credits required for graduation at the 300-level or higher.

Kingston Spring 2025 Spring 2025 The Biochemical Engineering minor introduces students to the fundamental chemistry and physics underlying biological processes.
Students will apply engineering principles in a biological context to control the interactions between and behavior of organic molecules, proteins, and other biomacromolecules.
With this minor, students will be prepared for industrial and research positions in the biotechnology and biomedical �elds.
The Biochemical Engineering minor is comprised of a minimum of 18 credit hours, at least half of which must be earned at URI.
The required courses include two fundamental science courses (6 credits), two biochemical engineering fundamentals courses (6 credits), and two or more supporting courses (6 credits).
Up to 6 credits can double count towards a major (e.g., core courses).
Students declaring this major must earn a minimum grade point average of 2.00 in courses counted towards the minor.
Students will need to complete the Biochemical Engineering minor form and have it signed by the minor coordinator, department chair, and appropriate dean.

CONSTITUTION, BY-LAWS, AND UNIVERSITY MANUAL COMMITTEE Report #2024-2025-1 - Proposed changes to Appendix C: By-Laws of the Faculty Senate FACULTY SENATE - November 14, 2024; REVISED - January 23, 2024 Context: The Curriculum and Standards Committee (CASC) and General Education Committee became separate committees in 2020.
Both committees have business that is related since both review curriculum with respect to their committee charges.
The proposed language seeks to reflect current operation of the two committees and includes their representation on the Joint Committee on Online and Distance Learning per UM 5.78.12.
This proposal was introduced at the 10/10/24 Faculty Senate meeting and continued to a later meeting for the required second reading.
In response to comments received at the October meeting, the proposal has been further revised to reflect current practices and to give the standing committees maximum flexibility in ensuring representation on related committees.
Please see the “Revised Proposed Language” below.

FACULTY SENATE OFFICE FACULTY SENATE LEGISLATION DECEMBER 12, 2024 C urriculum & Standards Committee Report 2024-2025-04B At the November 21, 2024 meeting of the Curriculum & Standards Committee , the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate for approval.
Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation By The Faculty Senate PROGRAM MODIFICATIONS COLLEGE OF HEALTH SCIENCES: BS - Dietetics, Effective Fall 2025 Appendix A The Nutrition department has put forth a new course, NUT 445 Medical Nutrition Therapy II, to provide a more well-balanced clinical dietetics education.
This course is currently awaiting final Faculty Senate approval with first offering in Spring 2029.
To align with this, the curriculum beginning with the 2025/2026 catalog year will be updated to reflect this change.
In addition, matriculation requirements to the major have been modified to bring students into the Dietetics degree sooner (removing STA 220 from the matriculation requirement, but still required for the degree).
Lastly, CMB 201 Intro to Medical Microbiology (4 cr) is a required course for Dietetics students.

passages.heading: Curriculum & Standards Committee Report #2024-2025-04B | Page 1
passages.text:
Beginning fall 2025, this course will now be offered as CMB 201 Intro to Medical Microbiology lecture (3 cr) and CMB 202 Intro to Medical Microbiology lab (1 cr).
Update of NFS to NUT in program description was done in Faculty Senate Bill #22 -23-27C, but seem to have disappeared from Kuali.
Course code changes are editorial only based on previously approved legislation.
BS - Psychology, Effective Fall 2025 Appendix B Earlier this year we submitted a change to add PSY260 as a required course for the BS in Psychology.
Right now, we are submitting a change to the BS program to a) make the course a matriculation requirement, and b) increase the number of credit hours requi red for the PSY BS degree from 38 credits to 41 credits.
Mi nor editorial change to fix typo (PSY 423 should have been PSY 432).
CASC Report 2024-2025-04B

passages.heading: Curriculum & Standards Committee Report #2024-2025-04B | Page 2
passages.text:
Specialization – Early Contingent Admit DPT (BS Kin), Effective Fall 2025 Appendix C Editorial Changes: NFS 207 updated to NUT 207 to align with current course naming (Faculty Senate Bill 22 - 23-27C), updating PT total credits in description from 112 to 110 based on DPT program updates (Facult y Senate Bill 22-23-26B).
Updates to requirements to stay in program: • Add clarification that grade of B (3.0) must be earned in BIO 220 and 221 before start of sophomore year.
This timing is necessary to keep students on track to complete course sequencing on time. (BIO 222/223 must be taken no later than fall of sophomore year so subsequent courses KIN 300, KIN 325, and KIN 420 can be completed within 3 years -- students who are admitted early to the D.P.T. program spend their fourth year in D.P.T. courses so they must complete KIN courses within 3 years) • Change end of freshman year GPA to 3.3 and end of sophomore year GPA to 3.4 to increase transparency and give students a more realistic assessment of their current progress toward a GPA that will be competitive for D.P.T. program admission.

passages.text:

It is an old track that was last offered in the 2012 -2013 catalog and has been fully taught out.
Specialization – Health Fitness (BS Kin), Effective Winter 2025 Appendix E Delete this specialization.
It is an old track that was last offered in the 2012 -2013 catalog and has been fully taught out.
DEPARTMENT NAME CHANGE COLLEGE OF ENGINEERING: Department name change from “Chemical Engineering” to “Chemical, Biomolecular and Materials Engineering”, Effective Winter 2025 Appendix F A change in department name is proposed from "Chemical Engineering" to "Chemical, Biomolecular, and Materials Engineering" to better reflect the fields chemical engineering students enter after graduation, the research expertise in our department, and the content in our courses and minors.

Course codes and names of degrees will not change.
CASC Report 2024-2025-04B

Program Description This curriculum leads to a Bachelor of Science (B.S.) degree.
This major prepares undergraduates for a career as a Registered Dietitian/Nutritionist (RDN).
The M.S. in Nutrition includes an Accelerated Bachelors to Masters of Science (ABM) option for students enrolled in the B.S. degree, described below.
This Dietetics degree is required for all students planning to become RDN'sRDNs.
URI's Dietetics program is accredited by the Accreditation Council for Education in Nutrition and Dietetics (ACEND), 120 South Riverside Plaza, Suite 2190, Chicago, IL 60606. 800.877.1600, ext. 5400; https:/ /www.eatrightpro.org/acend/.
Please see the department website for complete program information (https://web.uri.edu/nfsnutrition/).

passages.heading: Curriculum & Standards Committee Report #2024-2025-04B | Page 7
passages.text:
The dietetics major requires 27 credits in sciences (four in general chemistry [CHM 103/105], four in organic chemistry [CHM 124/126], three in biochemistry [CMB 210], twelve in biology [BIO 110/103; 220/221; 222/223], and four in microbiology [CMB 201/202]), 4 credits in applied general nutrition (NFSNUT 207/210), 4 credits in introductory professional courses (NFSNUT 110 and 212G); and 41 credits in the concentration including the following courses: NFSNUT 336, 337, 375, 376, 394, 395, 410, 440, 441, 443, 444, 445, and 458 [capstone].
Additionally, MGT 341 is required and COM 100, MTH 103, PSY 113, SOC 100, STA 220, and WRT 104 are required and may be used to ful�ll general education requirements.
There are 16-1917 credits of free electives.
Students are encouraged to use free electives to study disciplines related to the �eld.
Students must maintain a 3.00 average in all required courses (NFSNUT courses, science courses, and the remaining degree courses), with no less than a C in any one class, in order to graduate.
A total of 120 credits is required for graduation.

passages.heading: Curriculum & Standards Committee Report #2024-2025-04B | Page 7
passages.text:

Students must havemaintain earned a 3.00 average in theseall classesrequired courses (NUT courses, science courses, and the remaining degree courses) completed when being evaluated for admission, with no less than a C in any one class, in order to be admittedgraduate.
Students may repeat NFSNUT courses once.
After completing their B.S. requirements, students can qualify for the professional title of Registered Dietitian/Nutritionist by completing supervised practice requirements and graduate degree, and passing a national credentialing exam.
The supervised practice requirement can be met by completing an ACEND-accredited dietetic internship program, individualized supervised practice program, future education graduate program, or coordinated dietetic internship/graduate program.
Programs are available to students on a competitive basis nationwide.

Changes What are the program goals?
Include any connections to Strategy 1 in the Agenda for Change.
Goal 1: Graduates will be prepared to enter research-focused graduate programs based on their knowledge of empirically- supported psychological processes and how to apply this knowledge to promote health and welfare.
Goal 2: Graduates will be competent in intermediate level critical thinking and behavioral data analysis skills.
Goal 3: Graduates will be able to work ethically in settings that emphasize diversity and global thinking.
The BS in Psychology is described to students as a program that focuses on the empirical and methodological aspects of psychology, that emphasizes math, science, and research methods in creating and applying psychological knowledge, and that includes a requirement in hands on research experience.
This program addresses Strategy 1 of the Agenda for Change (Infuse Anti-Racism, Social Justice and DEI Perspectives) in the Curriculum in several ways.
The introductory course (PSY 113) required of all majors, includes sections on anti-racism.
The lead instructor for this course has published multiple papers on teaching anti-racism and social justice.

passages.heading: Curriculum & Standards Committee Report #2024-2025-04B | Page 18
passages.text:
Goal 3 of the BS program focuses on teaching students to work ethically in settings that emphasize diversity.
The addition of PSY260GPSY260 Psyched About Cultured: Introduction to Cross Cultural Psychology is designed to address this need.
This course is currently approved as GCH 102G: Interdisciplinary Topics in Diversity and Inclusion and has been offered by Assistant Professor Ceren Gunsoy.
We wish now to make it a required course for all PSY BS majors.
Mission Statement: The BS in Psychology aligns well with the University's mission statement with its focus on the public- learner centered research university, quest for knowledge, and the educational opportunities of the research university.
This program's focus on training students in empirical knowledge foundations of Psychology and expertise in the research and methods of the field is an important addition to the mission of URI.
The values cited in the mission statement including scholarship, diversity, engaged learning, and intellectual and ethical leadership are also important values for the department of Psychology and the BS major (see for example learning outcome 3.2: Be able to discuss psychology-related issue in ethics).

The BS program in the current proposal requires students take a 3 credit course to obtain hands-on experience with psychological research.
Goal 3 Strategy 3 : Create opportunities for the internationalization of the curriculum and co-curriculum to ensure that all students are exposed to global perspectives and build global competence.

Mark Robbins A BS in psychology prepares students for a wide variety of career options.
According to the website of the American Psychological Association ( https://www.apa.org/ed/precollege/psn/2018/01/bachelors-degree ), about 25 percent of psychology baccalaureates go to graduate school in psychology, about 18 percent go on for more education but not in psychology, and 57 percent are workforce graduates (Lin, Christidis & Stamm, 2017).
The BS degree prepares graduates especially well to apply to doctoral or other research-oriented advanced degrees in Psychology or other fields.

passages.heading: Curriculum & Standards Committee Report #2024-2025-04B | Page 19
passages.text:
For those who do not wish to obtain an advanced degree, there are many job opportunities.
The above referenced website lists 70 job titles that students with a BS in Psychology are prepared for.
The BS degree with its focus on methodology, scientific writing, and statistical analysis especially trains graduates for any type of position requiring analytic, scientific writing, or data analytic skills, such as data base design analyst, research assistant, systems analyst, technical writer, information specialist, or data base manager.
A number of these occupations are considered high impact jobs in RI.
The Occupational Outlook Handbook of the Bureau of Labor ( https://www.bls.gov/ooh/field-of- degree/psychology/psychology-field-of-degree.htm ) indicates that the median salary for those with a degree in Psychology is $50,000 and that 60% are employed in occupations requiring at least a bachelor's degree.
Many department faculty offer students the opportunity to serve as undergraduate teaching assistants for course credit.
There are no paid undergraduate assistantships.
Graduate teaching assistantships are offered to assist instructors with PSY 200, PSY 301, and PSY 435.

passages.text:
Among peer institutions (UMass, UConn, UVM, UNH, U of Maine, and U of Delaware) BS degrees in Psychology are offered by three (UMASS, UCONN, and UVM).
The University of Delaware offers a BS in Neuroscience but not Psychology.
UNH and U of Maine offer only BA programs.
It does not make URI unique in our region to offer this degree, but if we did not offer it, we would not be keeping up with the more research/science oriented institutions in our region.
There is a trend among peer institutions to emphasize the scientific basis of psychology, which the proposed changes to the program are designed to accomplish.

passages.text: V. 24.01.26 CURRICULUM & STANDARDS COMMITTEE FACULTY SENATE OFFICE URI Curriculum & Standards Committee Department Name Change Proposal Date: September 30, 2024 Person to contact during review: Geoff Bothun, gbothun@uri.edu GENERAL INFORMATION 1. Name of Institution: University of Rhode Island 2. Name of administrative unit: Department: Chemical Engineering College: Engineering 3. Current Department Name: Chemical Engineering 4. Proposed Department Name: Chemical, Biomolecular, and Materials Engineering 5. Intended date of change: January 1, 2025 6. Documentation of review & approval process. Please attach approvals from the following approval bodies: · Department approval by faculty vote · College Dean Approval by the CASC/Graduate Council, Faculty Senate, and the University President will be facilitated by the Faculty Senate Office. 7. Summary of Proposed Change: A change in department name is proposed from "Chemical Engineering" to "Chemical, Biomolecular, and Materials Engineering" to better reflect the fields chemical engineering students enter after graduation, the research expertise in our department, and the content in our courses and minors. The name change will also provide a platform for department growth and aid recruiting efforts at the undergraduate, graduate, and faculty levels. Course codes and names of degrees will not change. Appendix F | Department Name Change, Chemical Engineering Page 1 of 4 CASC Report 2024-2025-04B

passages.heading: Curriculum & Standards Committee Report #2024-2025-04B | Page 48
passages.text:
V. 24.01.26 RATIONALE There should be a demonstrable purpose and documented need for the proposed name change. 1.
Explain why the change of department name is being proposed.
The proposed new name of "Chemical, Biomolecular, and Materials Engineering" accurately reflects the career and technological fields that graduates enter and the research and scholarly expertise of the department faculty.
For example, the department has many graduates working at Amgen, which is a biotechnology company producing biological molecules (i.e., biomolecules), as well as Toray Plastics America, which produces polymeric materials.
The new name also reflects topics that are taught in our courses and the newly formed department Minor in Materials Engineering.
An additional Minor in Biochemical Engineering has been proposed (expected launch in Spring 2025) and a minor in Pharmaceutical Manufacturing and Formulation (includes biomolecular topics) is offered by the Department of Biomedical and Pharmaceutical Sciences for chemical engineering majors.

passages.heading: Curriculum & Standards Committee Report #2024-2025-04B | Page 48
passages.text:
The proposed new name aligns with similar department names of URI's peer and aspiring institutions, which include terms such as "bioengineering", "biomedical", and "biological engineering" in their names preceded by the term "chemical".
Changing the department name at URI is expected to make us more competitive in undergraduate student recruiting and, coupled with the new name reflecting our research expertise, more competitive at recruiting graduate students and faculty.
INSTITUTIONAL ROLE The department name change should be clearly related to the published role and mission of the institution and be compatible with the organizational structure of the institution. 1.
Explain how the name change is consistent with published role and mission of the institution, and how it is related to institutional planning.
As with our current name, the new name will continue to align with the role and mission of the institution in providing high-quality education and solving the world's most challenging problems (the new name explicitly extends this to biomolecules and materials).

passages.heading: Curriculum & Standards Committee Report #2024-2025-04B | Page 48
passages.text:
It also aligns with institutional planning, providing new opportunities to increase student recruiting, to create new degree and/or certificate programs, and to pursue interdisciplinary collaboration (funding agencies/proposal review panels link department names to expertise). 2.
Explain how the organizational change impacts other units and programs within the institution.
Have you communicated with the other units and programs and have any concerns been raised relative to the organizational change?
Describe the concerns.
The proposed name change was formally presented to the department chairs in the College of Engineering and no concerns were raised - they were collectively enthusiastic.
The potential for the most overlap is with the Biomedical Engineering program in the Department of Electrical, Computer, and Biomedical Engineering.
The CHE chair discussed the name change with the program lead for Biomedical Engineering and the only concern was with the abbreviation, CHE changing to CBME. "BME" is the abbreviation for Biomedical Engineering and the BME lead thought this could lead to confusion during registration.

passages.heading: Curriculum & Standards Committee Report #2024-2025-04B | Page 48
passages.text:
After explaining that the course codes would remain "CHE" there was no longer a concern.

passages.text:
FACULTY SENATE OFFICE FACULTY SENATE LEGISLATIONDECEMBER 12, 2024 Graduate CouncilReport 2024-2025-3B At the November 25, 2024 meeting of the Graduate Council, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate on December 12, 2024 for approval.
Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation By The Faculty Senate PROGRAM CHANGES COLLEGE OF EDUCATION College Student Personnel - MS Proposed changes include removal of “in College Student Personnel” in the degree title and reducing total credits required to 30 with 21 core courses.
Per the URI Grad school initiative to reduce total required credits for masters degrees, we have evaluated the CSP curriculum for duplicated content.
We also compared curricular content to national CAS standards to ensure that the program is in alignment with best practices.
The result is the removal of one class: EDC 529.
The course, in its entirety, no longer meets the needs of current CSP students.
The old curriculum map shows EDC 529 as only “R”einforcing Program Student Learning outcome #4.
And, that outcome is reinforced in two other courses and evaluated in EDC 580.
The program outcomes have not changed.

passages.heading: Graduate Council Report #2024-2025-03B | Page 1
passages.text:
The existing outcomes can still be introduced, reinforced, and evaluated via the new changes.
Additionally, other CSP programs tend to have fewer credits than our current program.
The streamlining of our curriculum, particularly in regards to credit hours, aligns us with other programs nationally.
COLLEGE OF THE ENVIRONMENT & LIFE SCIENCES Environmental and Natural Resource Economics - PHD 3.
Reduce the number of credits required.
The graduate school now only requires 64 credits, so we are adjusting our program accordingly.
We are reducing credits to allow students to take advantage of the increased availability of ABD semesters. 4.
Allow for equivalent class to be taken in place of EEC502.
When teaching capacity is strained in our department, we have found several suitable replacements for this class, and we want them to be able to count when we are unable to offer EEC502. [A note to the reviewers: Our program description and admission requirements in Kuali did not reflect recent changes that had been approved.
We copied and pasted the current program description and admission

passages.heading: Graduate Council Report #2024-2025-03B | Page 2
passages.text:
requirements into Kuali and then added items 2-4 above. 2-4 are the only changes we are requesting to the program description; all other changes have already been approved, as can be seen in the current catalog.] Proposed changes include removing “in Environmental and Natural Resource Economics” from the degree title and an initiation date of Spring 2025.
COLLEGE OF NURSING Nursing Practice - DNP Our current Program started as a BS to DNP Program and was put on hold about five years ago.
After that, we only accepted Post-Masters students for the in-person DNP Program.
Our current change to an Online Program will close both the Post BS to DNP and Post Masters to DNP in-person Programs.
Our current in-person DNP program attracts a small number of applicants each year.
Converting our program to an online, asynchronous, program offers expansion of the student pool from local to national.
There will be an overlap between teaching-out the in-person program and the start of the online offering.
We anticipate the last graduating class from the live program to be in the Spring Semester of 2027, while the first cohort to enter the online offering will be fall of 2025.

passages.heading: Graduate Council Report #2024-2025-03B | Page 2
passages.text:
The proposed online program remains essentially the same with updates to some of the courses being delivered and a few new courses to enhance topical areas of integrative healthcare.
Teach-Out Plan: Students will be notified of the online plan and offered an LOA or postpone entry if they choose the online option.
Otherwise, the in-person DNP program will continue until students have completed which is anticipated to be Spring 2027.
To work in the URI online format, the 7-week sequence was required but the College wanted the extended time for each course for doctoral-level work (14 weeks), thus, the A/B model evolved for each course which is denoted with "A" 7 weeks plus "B" 7 weeks taken sequentially.
Attached is a sample of the course sequence for the NursingPractice-DNP Online.
Proposed program description: The Doctor of Nursing Practice (DNP) is an innovative, online, post master’s program that prepares advanced practice nurses as leaders in evidence based principles of traditional, complementary, and integrative health (TCIH) to transform health care systems.

passages.heading: Graduate Council Report #2024-2025-03B | Page 2
passages.text:
Program Requirements: Program requirements include a minimum of 68 credits obtained as follows: 30 credits from a post MS degree and 38 credits to be completed to complete the DNP degree.
Program prerequisites include a master’s degree in nursing, completion of a 300- to 500-level statistics course, and a master’s level introduction research course.
DNP required NUR courses (32 credits) including NUR 662 (A&B), 664 (A&B), 672 (A&B), 673 (A&B), 674 (A&B), 675 (A&B), 676 (A&B), 677 (A&B) and 679 (A&B).
Also required are PHP XXX (A&B) and MBA XXX (A&B).
The program culminates with the clinical immersion practicum and a practice improvement project associated with NUR courses 677, 678, 679 (A&B sessions).
The Doctorate of Nursing Practice_DNP is a cohort model starting each fall and each cohort will complete the course sequence according to their program plan.

passages.heading: Graduate Council Report #2024-2025-03B | Page 2
passages.text:
Proposed admission requirements: A master’s degree in nursing (GPA minimum 3.30); minimum R.N. licensure in the state student resides; completion of a 300- to 500-level statistics course; completion of a master’s level introduction to research course; completed application package with all transcripts; three letters of reference attesting to the applicant’s capability for doctoral study (academic and professional, at least one from a doctorally prepared nurse); one scholarly paper or a master’s thesis or equivalent; a statement of purpose indicating goals that are congruent with those of the program and institution and a curriculum vitae/resume.
Acceptance is based on a full review of the applicant’s record and not any single component.

passages.heading: Graduate Council Report #2024-2025-03B | Page 3
passages.text: NEW CERTIFICATES FEINSTEIN COLLEGE OF EDUCATION College Teaching - Cert The 12 credit graduate certificate in college teaching is designed to prepare individuals to effectively teach in post-secondary settings–including college and community settings with adult learners. The graduate certificate will provide a knowledge base of adult learning theory and skills for instructional design, implementation and evaluation. It will also provide a solid foundation of teaching for equity and inclusion. COLLEGE OF THE ENVIRONMENT & LIFE SCIENCES Community Planning - Cert (online) The Graduate Certificate in Community Planning (CPL), composed of 3 required classes and one elective, is an asynchronous online "stackable certificate" provides the pathway for working professionals to develop core competencies in sustainable Community Planning. Through this program, students will gain a foundation in the principles and practices of community planning and development, specifically in areas of site planning and environmental planning. Students can earn their certificate in four sessions, maximizing flexibility and convenience for career enhancement and professional growth. Class content in this certificate is geared towards working professionals who do not have prior knowledge in planning. Completion of the certificate will provide a basic knowledge of planning that can be augmented with certificate programs in other departments, such as the Master of Public Administration (MPA), and the Master of Environmental Management (MEM) program.

The College Student Personnel (CSP) program’s mission is to prepare equity minded and reflective practitioners for careers in student affairs.
Graduates seek primarily entry-level positions such as advisors, coordinators, and assistant directors/deans at institutions of higher education.
The CSP curriculum is designed to teach emerging professionals’ best practices in student affairs and is designed in accordance with the guidelines established by the Council for the Advancement of Standards (CAS) in Higher Education.
These goals are enacted through DEI infused pedagogy and content throughout the courses in the program.
The CSP program aligns with numerous goals within Strategic priority 2: Enhance student achievement by cultivating an engaged and inclusive learning environment.
This is a unique program tied to a specific field of education.
The program is specifically dedicated to professional preparation in the field of College Student Personnel and does not overlap with any other programs at URI.

For the past thirty years, there has been a consistently high demand that reflects interest within the region and beyond.

Admission requirements: Online submission of an application through the Graduate School website.
Supporting materials must include two letters of recommendation (one preferably a faculty member from your undergraduate major and one student affairs professional), transcripts of all previous college course work, a current résumé, and a Personal Statement.
For guidance on the Personal Statement, see https://web.uri.edu/education/academics/csp/.https://web.uri.edu/education/academics/csp/.
The completed application package, including supporting materials, is due for priority fall admission by January 15; materials received after this date and prior to April 1 are reviewed on a space-available basis.
After initial screening, admitted students will receive information on applying for Graduate Assistantships or other direct links to practice in college student affairs settings.
Selection for admission to this program is competitive and enrollment is limited; preference is given to applicants with experience in college student affairs.
Diversity among students is valued by the program and student affairs profession.

passages.text:
The Graduate Certificate in Community Planning (CP) is an online program that helps students develop core competencies in sustainable Community Planning.
Through this program, students will gain a foundation in the principles and practices of community planning and development, specifically in areas of land use and environmental planning.
The history of planning has many examples of environmental injustice, in which land use decisions have privileged some communities over others.
A commitment to anti-racism, inclusiveness, equity, as well as spatial and social justice perspectives is an integral part of a planning education.
Students can earn their certificate in four sessions, maximizing flexibility and convenience for career enhancement, leadership positions in the industry, and professional growth.
The Community Planning online certificate aligns with the University's commitment to urban initiative, community engagement and solving the world's most important challenges by equiping students with practical knowledge and understanding of how to plan for and enable equitable and sustainable communities.

passages.heading: Graduate Council Report #2024-2025-03B | Page 49
passages.text:
This 4-course asychonous online graduate certificate also creates a learning opportunity for students who may not be able to attend graduate school in person on a full time basis, thereby creating a diverse learning opportunity (goal 3 of the URI Stragic Priority 2) and increase graduate student enrollment (goal 2 of Strategic Priority 2).
The impact of a working public better informed in values and strategies of community planning should contribute to healthier and more sustainable communities environmentally, socially and economically.
The online graduate Community Planning certificate will open doors for recent college graduates as well as working professionals; they will become eligible for positions and promotion in a growing job market.
By combining this online certificate with other stackable certificates such as Public Administration, MEM and GIS, students will be well equipped to engage in the significant planning challenges of our time.
Our department currently offers an in-person Graduate Certificate in Community Planning.
This proposed new program will be offered in the 7-week online format and require 4 classes with 3 required classes and one elective (12 credits).

passages.heading: Graduate Council Report #2024-2025-03B | Page 49
passages.text:
Our existing Community Planning Graduate Certificate requires 5 courses to complete the certificate (15 or 16 credits).
The asychonous online certitificate is intended for a different student population from our in-person gradute certificate and provides somewhat different content.
The online certificate content is pragmatically planned to be useful for working professionals, adapted for online delivery, and geared towards working professionals who do not have prior knowledge of planning.
The purpose of the Certificate is to give these students a way to quickly and remotely attain a basic knowledge of planning, and to stack that knowledge with other certificates, such as Public Policy, Marine Affairs, GIS, etc.
By contrast, the full semester, in-person planning program encompasses a wide and in-depth disciplinary space, with opportunities to learn from in-person university relationships and pursue independent research, while still providing future planners with knowledge and tools for professional work.

passages.text: FACULTY SENATE OFFICE F ACULTY SENATE LEGISLATION January 23, 2025 Gr aduate Council Report #2024-2025-04 The following matter was discussed and recommended by the Graduate Council at their November, 2024 meeting after similar legislation was advanced in a joint action by the Faculty Senate Executive Committee (FSEC) and the Curriculum and Standards Committee (CASC) last November. Their intent was to ensure a streamlined curricular approval process for online undergraduate courses, regardless of their calendar format The Graduate Council now requests that the Faculty Senate approve the same measure for graduate-level courses. Con text: Currently, courses approved for online formats during the traditional academic calendar (Fall/Spring 14-weeks, J-Term, and Summer 5- and 10-weeks) must complete a full curricular review to be added to the URI Online Accelerated calendar (7-week Fall, Spring, and Summer sessions). Pr oposed: Any course approved for online instruction is thereby approved for being offered in all online calendars: 14-week, J-Term, Summer (5 and 10 week), and accelerated 7-week terms. GC 2024-2025-04

Faculty Senate Executive Committee Report #2024-2025-2 January 23, 2025 Faculty Senate Meeting Context (from JCODL 2022-2023 final report): “Several years ago (circa 2013), URI adopted definitions of online and blended learning (Face to face [< 25% online], Blended [25-75% online], and Online [75-100% online]), with the implicit, but unstated, assumption that the online portion was asynchronous.
The COVID era of remote instruction gave rise to additional approaches to remote instruction and the need to reflect all available modality options and to provide clear, comprehensible and accessible definitions and descriptions for the benefit of faculty and students.” Rationale: The “adopted” definitions are not memorialized in the University Manual and the current need to update modality-related descriptions provides an opportunity to provide standardized language in the University Manual, where it will be easily found and understood.
The language is proposed for insertion into Chapter 8, Academic Regulations (Regulations for Students), Section 30, Courses.

passages.heading: Faculty Senate Executive Committee Report #2024-2025-02 | Page 1
passages.text:
Existing modalities will translate into new modalities as follows: 1. ‘In-person’ � ‘In-person’ 2. ‘Blended’ � ‘In-person and online asynchronous’ or ‘In-person and online synchronous’ 3. ‘Online’ � ‘Online synchronous’ or ‘Online synchronous and asynchronous’ or ‘Online asynchronous’.
Because current ‘online’ and ‘blended’ modality courses will need to be assigned to a new modality (perhaps more than one if multiple faculty teach the same course using different modalities), faculty/departments will be allowed to update the modality of current ‘online’ and ‘blended’ modality courses directly with the registrar without going through the standard course modification process.
A course change proposal will not be necessary if faculty/departments teaching a class in one of the three ‘in-person’ modalities (‘In-person’, ‘In-person and online asynchronous’, ‘In-person and online synchronous’) wish to adopt (or add, in the case of a multi-section class) another of the ‘in-person’ modalities.

passages.heading: Faculty Senate Executive Committee Report #2024-2025-02 | Page 1
passages.text:
A course change proposal will not be necessary if faculty/departments teaching a class in one of the three ‘online’ modalities (‘Online synchronous’, ‘Online synchronous and asynchronous’, ‘Online asynchronous’) wish to adopt (or add, in the case of a multi-section class) another of the ‘online’ modalities.
As per current practice, course change proposals will continue to be necessary for courses with one of the three ‘in-person’ modalities that wish to adopt (or add, in the case of a multi-section class) one of the three ‘online’ modalities.
This is also true for ‘online’ modality courses that wish to adopt/add an ‘in-person’ modality.
Because of the volume of required changes, the new modalities will take effect starting in the Fall 2026 semester.

passages.heading: Faculty Senate Resolution #2024-2025-03 | Page 1
passages.text:
FACULTY SENATE OFFICE 224 PASTORE HALL, 51 LOWER COLLEGE ROAD, KINGSTON, RI 02881 USA, P: 401.874.2616 Faculty Senate Resolution 2024-2025-03 Faculty Senate Meeting of January 23, 2025 Resolution on the Implementation of Honors Contracts WHEREAS, following considerable self-study and significant input from external experts, the URI Honors Program has proposed the use of honors contracts at URI.
Honors contracts are formal agreements, facilitated by an honors program, between a student and instructor.
They allow students and instructors to enhance non-honors courses to an honors level through additional learner-directed work tailored to the “broader, deeper, and more complex” learning experiences advocated by the National Collegiate Honors Council (NCHC); and WHEREAS, contracts are recognized by over 60% of honors programs in the USA, where they foster community and ownership by enhancing the educational process and commitment to the programs’ success.
For example, work at the University Honors Program at the University of Kansas shows that honors contracts act as far more than stopgaps to address honors course shortages.

passages.heading: Faculty Senate Resolution #2024-2025-03 | Page 1
passages.text:
They can “facilitate access to honors, increases completion, democratize key aspects of the honors experience, provide students with structured avenues for building relationships with faculty members, and empower students to own their educational experiences”; and WHEREAS, honors contracts may be best understood as a form of an independent study, entered into voluntarily by both students and faculty, with a contract defining outcomes, deadlines, and assessment definitions for additional work related to the course materials; and WHEREAS, honors contracts provide flexibility for students to align their education with their interests and goals.
They also allow programs to meet student needs when student/faculty constraints or funding limitations preclude offering stand-alone honors courses that fit student interests and needs; and WHEREAS, Contracts provide an extra measure of curricular flexibility at institutions such as ours that are not able to field enough faculty, cannot provide an adequate number of honors courses, or do not have a large enough student body to fill honors sections.

passages.heading: Faculty Senate Resolution #2024-2025-03 | Page 1
passages.text:
Contracts can fill the gap and provide opportunities for the self-guided intellectual growth of students; NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Faculty Senate of the University of Rhode Island calls for implementation of the following Honors Contracts Proposal.
This includes making the

passages.heading: Faculty Senate Resolution #2024-2025-03 | Page 2
passages.text: recommended changes to the University Catalog and to the eCampus system used by Enrollment Services; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the Honors Program is called upon to reflect these changes on their website and in all other promotional and outreach materials promulgated by the Program. The Program is also called upon to review Chapter 8 of the University Manual (Academic Regulations, Honors Program) in light of the Contracts Proposal and bring any recommended changes to the Faculty Senate expeditiously; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the authority to offer Honors Contracts enabled by this resolution shall not extend beyond the Fall 2025 semester; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that no instructor may participate in more than three Honors Contracts in a single semester. Adopted this 23rd day of January, 2025. ____________________________________________________________ T heodore Walls, URI Faculty Senate President

passages.text: FACULTY SENATE OFFICE F ACULTY SENATE LEGISLATION January 23, 2025 Gr aduate Council Report #2024-2025-04 The following matter was discussed and recommended by the Graduate Council at their November, 2024 meeting after similar legislation was advanced in a joint action by the Faculty Senate Executive Committee (FSEC) and the Curriculum and Standards Committee (CASC) last November. Their intent was to ensure a streamlined curricular approval process for online undergraduate courses, regardless of their calendar format The Graduate Council now requests that the Faculty Senate approve the same measure for graduate-level courses. Con text: Currently, courses approved for online formats during the traditional academic calendar (Fall/Spring 14-weeks, J-Term, and Summer 5- and 10-weeks) must complete a full curricular review to be added to the URI Online Accelerated calendar (7-week Fall, Spring, and Summer sessions). Pr oposed: Any course approved for online instruction is thereby approved for being offered in all online calendars: 14-week, J-Term, Summer (5 and 10 week), and accelerated 7-week terms. The median annual wage for sales managers was $127,490/year in May 2021. (5% growth; fast as average) The demand for Master of Science in Management (MSM) programs has been on the rise due to the increasingly complex business landscape and the need for advanced management skills.
These programs are particularly attractive because they are typically open to recent graduates or those early in their careers, unlike MBA programs which often require prior work experience.
MSM programs offer specialized tracks in fields like project management, leadership, analytics, or strategy, allowing students to tailor their education to specific career paths.
Furthermore, the shorter duration and generally lower tuition fees compared to traditional MBA programs make MSM degrees more accessible and financially appealing.
In addition to their growing popularity among domestic students, MSM programs are also sought after by international students who wish to gain a business education in the U.S.
These programs provide essential technical skills and management training which are attractive for those looking to work in global markets.

passages.text:
The competition among MSM programs is intense, with a large number of institutions offering these degrees.
Programs strive to differentiate themselves by emphasizing unique curricular components such as leadership development modules, capstone projects, or global immersion experiences, which are designed to enhance employability and prepare graduates for management roles.
The rise of digital learning technologies has also led many institutions to offer MSM programs in online or hybrid formats, further increasing their reach and intensifying competition as geographic barriers to enrollment are reduced.
To stand out in a crowded market, programs often seek accreditation from prestigious bodies like AACSB, AMBA, or EQUIS and aim to secure favorable rankings from notable publications.
Many programs also forge partnerships with businesses and other organizations to help in curriculum development, provide real-world learning opportunities, and facilitate networking and job placements for graduates.

passages.heading: Graduate Council Report #2024-2025-04C | Page 7
passages.text:
Recent trends in MSM programs include an increased emphasis on technology and analytics to integrate digital technologies in business, a focus on sustainability and social responsibility reflecting broader societal concerns, and more customizable and flexible learning paths to attract a diverse student body with varying needs and career goals.
Overall, the market for MSM programs remains robust, driven by their relevance, accessibility, and adaptability to market needs and educational technologies, though programs must continuously innovate and adapt to remain competitive.

It is now presented to the Faculty Senate for approval. Context: Currently, courses approved for online formats during the traditional academic calendar (Fall/Spring 14-weeks, J-Term, and Summer 5- and 10-weeks) must complete a full curricular review to be added to the URI Online Accelerated calendar (7-week Fall, Spring, and Summer sessions). Proposed: Any undergraduate course approved for online instruction is thereby approved for being offered in all online semester calendars: 14-week, J-Term, Summer (5 and 10 week), and accelerated 7-week terms. FACULTY SENATE LEGISLATION April 16, 2026 Graduate Council Report 2025-2026-6B At the April 6, 2026 meeting of the Graduate Council, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate for approval.
Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation By The Faculty Senate PROGRAM MODIFICATIONS COLLEGE OF BUSINESS Professional Science Masters - PSM, Effective Spring 2027 The Professional Science Masters (PSM) program is a non-thesis graduate degree program that prepares students for leadership and management roles in science- and technology-driven organizations.
Housed in the College of Business, the PSM integrates advanced scientific or technical coursework with professional skills in leadership, project management, communication, and applied problem solving that are broadly applicable in rapidly evolving scientific fields.
This 30–33 credit interdisciplinary degree combines a graduate certificate in a science or technical field with professional business coursework and applied experiential learning.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-GC-06B | Page 2
passages.text:
Students develop practical interpersonal, leadership, communication, and critical thinking skills, and apply these competencies in real-world organizational and industry contexts.
The PSM requires the completion of a graduate certificate in a science field, and four professional courses, including at least one capstone/practicum, and an additional relevant graduate-level course(s) from the URI Online portfolio as elective with Program Director approval.
PSM program tracks that have been certified by the National Professional Science Master's Association should have Industry Advisory Boards and include an integrative, hands-on experiential learning project or applied internship.
The menu of professional courses includes BUS532, BUS506, BUS509, BUS515, MBA540, and BUS557 (MBA557).
Other online courses may be approved by the program director.
At least one 3-credit course must be a capstone/practicum.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-GC-06B | Page 2
passages.text: If a student does not take BUS515 and the certificate program does not contain a capstone experience, they should take another capstone course from the URI Online portfolio (e.g., PSC592 or MPS598) In addition to the graduate certificate courses, the four professional courses, and the capstone/practicum, students must complete relevant graduate-level course(s) from the URI Online portfolio as electives with Program Director approval (up to 6 credits).

passages.heading: 2025-2026-GC-06B | Page 3
passages.text:
Textiles, Fashion Merchandising and Design - ABM, Effective Fall 2026 Textiles, Fashion Merchandising and Design (TMD) Department offers an Accelerated Bachelor of Science to Master of Science Degree in Textiles, Fashion Merchandising and Design (ABMTMD) to allow undergraduates to complete a BS/BA and an MS degree in 5 years.
The program would allow students currently receiving a Bachelor’s of Science in Textiles, Fashion Merchandising and Design; or a Bachelor’s of Science in Textile Marketing; or Bachelor’s degree in any other major combined with a TMD minor Under certain circumstances, students enrolled in programs leading to degrees in related areas may be considered for admission into the TMD program, for example, Business, Chemistry, History, Art History, or Psychology.
In such cases, half of the total credits must be in TMD.
As part of the program, ABMTMD students will need to earn a total of 33 credits (including 11 credits double-counted from their undergraduate degree) Students will also complete industry-oriented capstone project as an independent study (for example, complete an industry-focused case study or an industry-sponsored project).

passages.heading: 2025-2026-GC-06B | Page 3
passages.text:
Finally, students will also successfully complete comprehensive exams on two TMD elective courses.
Courses eligible for double-counting: TMD403 Textile Performance TMD413 Dyeing and Finishing Textiles TMD424 Retail Product Trend Forecasting TMD426 Historic and Contemporary Furniture TMD432 Fashion Retail Supply Chain Management TMD433 Textile Markets TMD434 Branding Fashion Industry TMD440 Historic Textiles TMD441 History of Western Dress TMD442 Fashion Promotion TMD458 Fashion Retail Analytics URI courses outside the TMD Department that are cataloged as eligible for graduate credits can double-count.
COLLEGE OF HEALTH SCIENCE Mental and Behavioral Health Counseling - MS, Effective Summer 2026 The Master's in Mental and Behavioral Health Counseling program prepares graduates to work with clients in settings including counseling agencies, hospitals, community mental health centers, and private practice.
Students gain training in evidence-based practice, measurement-based care, develop practical skills in individual and group therapy approaches, as well as career counseling with diverse populations.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-GC-06B | Page 3
passages.text:
This 66-credit program meets curricular requirements for the State of Rhode Island's Licensed Mental Health Counselor (LMHC).
Course Requirements: HDF450, HDF551, HDF570, PSY507, PSY603, PSY615 (3 credits), PSY642, PSY643, PSY644, PSY660, PSY666, PSY670 (18 credits), and PSY672 (12 credits).
A minimum of 66 credits is required to graduate.
