Master of Science (M.S.) in Human Development and Family Science The Human Development and Family Science (HDF) Department offers a Master’s of Science degree with two specialization pathways. 1) Specialization in Couple and Family Therapy This program provides skills for students become licensed couple and family therapists.
This program involves intense clinical practice, including a year-long clinical placement at approved agencies and the department’s Family Therapy Clinic.
A minimum of 60 credits is required for completion of the Couple and Family Therapy pathway within the Human Development and Family Science Program, with an option for 66 credits with thesis. 2) ABM Specialization in Prevention Science Through the Accelerated Bachelor's to Master's (ABM) program, students are able to complete their master’s degree within one year after completion of their Bachelor of Science (B.S) degree.

This program provides skills for students to work for organizations designed to improve the well-being of families (e.g., non-profit organizations and state agencies.) NEW CERTIFICATES OR SPECIALIZATIONS Leadership in Sports Management - Graduate Certificate, Effective Summer 2026 The Graduate Certificate in Leadership for Sports Management (12 credits) is designed for professionals who are moving into or occupying management roles in sports who seek to develop the strategic leadership, business acumen, and inclusive mindset required to thrive in today’s dynamic sport industry.
Through a flexible format where courses are available online, in person, or students can flex between formats, this certificate blends core leadership development with sports-specific business skills.
Students will explore sport as a dynamic venue for social equity, brand-building, revenue generation, and community partnership, while strengthening their capacity to lead diverse teams, shape culture, and drive organizational transformation.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-GC-06B | Page 7
passages.text:
On completion, graduates will be prepared to apply leadership strategies, ethically navigate sport management challenges, and promote inclusive and sustainable sports organizations at the local, national or global level.

It is designed for working professionals who hold a bachelor’s degree and seek to strengthen their leadership capabilities across a variety of organizational contexts.
Offered fully online, the certificate emphasizes practical leadership, organizational decision making, operations and project management, and the human dynamics of organizations.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-GC-06B | Page 8

The Organizational Leadership Graduate Certificate consists of 12 graduate credits.

Multilingual or non-English-speaking people in Rhode Island, across the country or abroad interested in enhancing their English communication skills for personal and professional growth. - The program provides advanced English language skills training, including academic writing, reading and vocabulary, oral communication, and a seminar course tailored to a specific field of graduate study.
Through a combination of intensive coursework and applied learning experiences, participants develop the ability to communicate effectively in academic and professional settings.
Our specialized seminar—ELS 453 English for Specific Purposes —allows students to refine language skills relevant to their disciplines.

This program is structured to prepare working professionals for the rigorous task of preventing, predicting, and reacting to hazards in a variety of operational environments.
Our students will gain experience in assessing risk within the framework of engineering and managerial principles, as well as regulatory requirements and benchmarks.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-GC-06B | Page 9

This curriculum will cover areas related to engineering leadership and communication, industry safety standards, quality and safety, as well as various special interest topics (e.g., marine safety, construction zones, and wind energy safety).
Following a hybrid model, this course will include online lectures and deliverables.
This 12-credit program allows students to earn their certification in one year or less.
Eligible students must have a Bachelor’s degree or advanced standing in a STEM field.
A prerequisite of ISE311 or equivalent is also needed for this program.
Program Requirements: - ISE517, Fundamentals of Industrial Safety (1) - ISE518, Engineering Leadership & Communication (1) Four (4) credits of the following course, taken under different topics: - ISE519, Special Topics for Systems Safety Certificate (1) Two (2) of the following courses: - ISE513, Quality & Safety (3) - ISE515, Production Safety (3) - ISE520(PSY520), Human Factors & Ergonomics (3)

We propose a flexible master’s program that offers an attractive path to an interdisciplinary graduate degree to current students in the URI online certificate programs and post-graduate professionals looking to bolster their skill sets and attain higher leadership positions and salaries.
The program would require students to successfully complete a graduate certificate program offered through URI Online, two elective courses, and four professional skills courses.
The mix of professional and discipline-specific skills and knowledge aims to prepare professionals for a broad range of careers across private industry, local, state, federal agencies, and community organizations.
Graduates of the program will be prepared to implement impactful societal, cultural, and economic initiatives.
The program speaks directly to the desire to foster a 21st-century, 24/7 learning environment.
Offered completely online and asynchronously, this program targets working professionals across various disciplines who wish to obtain their credentials while still holding full-time jobs.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-GC-06B | Page 16
passages.text:
The ‘a la carte’ nature of this program highlights the intersection of specialties employers are currently looking for while offering a flexible path to obtaining a master's degree.
Furthermore, the appeal of the in-state competitive tuition speaks to the accessibility of the program nationwide and beyond.
This program provides intellectual development for a diverse community of students.
The professional courses and graduate certificates push students to discover the synergies within their certificate areas and business/public administration to foster meaningful and impactful solutions and leadership.
The program integrates online certificate programs offered.
Students completing the certificates are accounted for within their respective programs, so it would not be considered an overlap but rather more of an inclusion.
This proposal describes a PSM framework under which focused tracks will be developed.
There are other master's degree programs that incorporate certificates into the masters (Master's of Public Administration, Masters of Science in Healthcare Management, and proposed Masters of Science in Health Outcomes and Data Analytics).

passages.heading: 2025-2026-GC-06B | Page 16

Capstone projects will take one of the following forms, depending on availability in a given year: RITIN-affiliated or industry-sponsored projects, in which an external organization presents a real-world problem, and students analyze the issue and propose viable solutions (similar in structure to MBA capstone projects).
These projects will be sourced by graduate faculty advisors, with support from the College’s Professional and Executive Business Education (PEBE) team.
If such projects are not available in a given year, students will complete an industry-focused case study, such as a Harvard-style or Fashion Scholarship Fund (FSF)–inspired case, to be submitted to the department.

The current need for mental and behavioral health care in RI is well-documented (i.e., opiate and substance use crises, need for mental health services with emergent needs in child and adolescent mental health).
Furthermore, RI is designated as a Health Professional Shortage Area (HPSA).
Therefore, there exists an urgent need for master’s level mental and behavioral health clinicians to meet workforce needs in RI and nationally to address these mental health and behavioral health needs.
The Department of Psychology currently has more than 1000 undergraduate majors whose bachelor’s degrees are not sufficient for entry into mental or behavioral health counseling positions.
Students who wish to work in delivery of mental and behavioral services require masters-level training that prepares them for state licensure.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-GC-06B | Page 32
passages.text:
The Psychology Department proposes to develop a professional non-thesis master’s degree in Mental and Behavioral Health Counseling at URI to help prepare committed applicants from psychology and related fields for employment opportunities in our field, helping to address the workforce needs of RI employers and, most importantly, supporting the development of these students into an essential resource to meet the critical mental and behavioral health needs of Rhode Islanders.
Graduates of this program will be eligible, with appropriate post-degree supervision hours, for licensure in the state of Rhode Island to become licensed mental health counselors (LMHCs).
These individuals can work in a range of settings (e.g., hospitals, private practice, community mental health centers) and, when licensed, provide services that can be reimbursed by all major insurance providers.
The Psychology Department has a 50-year history of applied graduate programs in Clinical (PhD) and historically School (master’s and PhD) focus areas.
Our PhD program in Clinical Psychology has been fully accredited by the American Psychological Association since 1972.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-GC-06B | Page 32
passages.text:
It is expected that a new professional Master's degree program will easily fit into pre- existing resources and structures: 1) our existing graduate curriculum for our Clinical PhD program currently meets the Discipline-Specific Knowledge, Profession-Wide Competencies, and Learning/Curriculum Elements required by the American Psychological Association for Master’s degree program accreditation, 2) faculty and staff are already teaching the majority of the required courses (didactic and experiential supervisory training), as well as 3) the Psychology Department has an in- house training clinic, the Psychological Consultation Center, that is directed by a full-time PhD clinical psychologist and is a principal training site for current doctoral students.
Psychology’s Master’s Program in Mental and Behavioral Health Counseling proposed here aligns with several elements of the URI’s Strategic Plan including: 1.
Strategic Priority 1; Broadening URI’s Impact - Goal 1.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-GC-06B | Page 32
passages.text:
This program is designed to contribute to broad and deep impacts on the social, cultural, and economic ecosystems across Rhode Island, the nation and beyond – by increasing the number of Master’s-trained license-eligible well prepared mental health professionals added to the RI and regional workforce to address pressing mental and behavioral health needs. 2.
Strategic Priority 2; Enhance Student Achievement- Goal 2: This new master’s program at URI will be a career preparation track that will be attractive to Psychology’s large pool of undergraduate majors as well as to regional applicants.
The significant need for well-trained license-eligible master’s students in RI, regionally, and nationally is likely to continue given mental illness upward trends. 3.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-GC-06B | Page 32
passages.text:
Strategic Priority 3; Foster an Inclusive Culture - Goal 2: This new master’s program will continue the Psychology Departments deep commitment to and significant ongoing efforts (e.g., standing departmental Inclusion and Diversity Committee) to build an innovative, contemporary, and professional learning environment and workplace that values diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility with leadership that is principle-centered and effective. 4.
Strategic Priority 4; Power the University of the Future - Goals 3 & 4: This new master’s program will help URI secure the necessary resources to sustain and grow the university and will generate a new revenue stream for years to come.

URI has the potential to be a major player in addressing our state’s mental health workforce needs as well as helping to address the national mental health crisis.
There would be modest overlap with the Master of Science program in the Human Development and Family Science department insofar as both Programs would lead to licensure at the Master's level.
However, the HDF program's graduates are eligible only to be licensed as Marriage and Family Therapists (LMFTs) whereas the graduates of the Masters in Mental and Behavioral Health Counseling will be eligible only to be licensed as Mental Health Counselors (LMHCs).
Although the two programs provide training in counseling and use external placements for their training, the two programs differ in terms of the requirements for licensure of the supervisors providing the training (students in the HDF Master's require supervisors to be LMFTs; students in the Masters in Mental and Behavioral Health Counseling program will have supervisors who are LMHC, MSWs, or PhDs).
The two programs are working together to share resources to the benefit of both programs (e.g., students in each program will be required to take class(es) in the other program).

passages.heading: 2025-2026-GC-06B | Page 33
passages.text:
The Masters in Mental and Behavioral Health Counseling program will also overlap with the Clinical Psychology doctoral program; yet, we see this as tremendously advantageous to both programs.
Many courses in the Doctoral program will be shared with the Masters program ensuring fully enrolled classes that run each year (currently, several classes in the clinical program run every other year due to low enrollments).
In addition, the doctoral program has an excess of clinical externship sites requesting students for training.
The new Master's program would help to meet this demand and offer training opportunities to students in placements that have long-standing training collaborations with the doctoral program.
Finally, the Masters program will offer courses (e.g., Group Counseling) that students in the doctoral program may wish to take.

Regional competition includes a three-year Clinical Counseling Program with a specialization in either rehabilitation counseling or holistic mental health at Salve Regina University.
Roger Williams offers a Forensic Mental Health Counseling masters program geared to those wanting to provide services in forensic settings with populations including incarcerated individuals, those court-ordered to treatment, etc.
Both of these programs, however, offer education and training that is more specialized than the proposed Mental and Behavioral Health Counseling program.
Rhode Island College (RIC) offers a three-year Masters in Clinical Mental Health Counseling.

PHP571 Methods in Epidemiology, Systematic Review, and Meta-Analysis.
This course introduces epidemiology, the study of health and disease in populations.
It emphasizes epidemiologic methods and research design for conducting and interpreting health research.
Additionally, the course will provide a detailed description of the systematic review process, discuss the strengths and limitations of the method, and provide step-by-step guidance on how to perform a systematic review and meta-analysis using statistical software.
PHP572 Measuring Outcomes and Identifying Causal Effects.
This course introduces students to the foundations of health outcome measurement and causal inference.
We will examine how clinical, humanistic, and economic outcomes, including patient-reported outcomes, are defined, measured, and validated, drawing on classical psychometric theory.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-GC-06B | Page 83
passages.text:
Students will also learn the potential outcomes framework for assessing whether interventions cause changes in health outcomes in both randomized trials and observational studies.
Examples from epidemiology and medical research will illustrate how accurate outcome measurement and rigorous causal reasoning support evidence-based decision-making in health care.
PHP670 Advanced Epidemiologic and Economic Methods in Health Sciences.
This course provides advanced training in pharmacoepidemiologic and pharmacoeconomic research methods and statistical analyses for evaluating health and cost outcomes, with emphasis on applied exercises utilizing contemporary approaches in the field.
Key aspects of the course include multivariable methods for common study designs, addressing bias, deriving and interpreting measures of effect, and economic modeling for assessing cost-effectiveness.
Course exercises utilize SAS and MS Excel to provide students with hands-on experience with various statistical models.

Online - Academic Year Summer 2026 Fall 2026 The Graduate Certificate in Leadership for Sports Management (12 credits) is designed for professionals who are moving into or occupying management roles in sports who seek to develop the strategic leadership, business acumen, and inclusive mindset required to thrive in today’s dynamic sport industry.
Through a flexible format where courses are available online, in person, or students can flex between formats, this certificate blends core leadership development with sports-specific business skills.
Students will explore sport as a dynamic venue for social equity, brand-building, revenue generation, and community partnership, while strengthening their capacity to lead diverse teams, shape culture, and drive organizational transformation.
On completion, graduates will be prepared to apply leadership strategies, ethically navigate sport management challenges, and promote inclusive and sustainable sports organizations at the local, national or global level.

Online - Academic Year Spring 2027 Spring 2027 The Graduate Certificate in English Language Development is designed to meet the needs of non-English language speakers who are: - International graduate students who have either been conditionally admitted into a graduate degree program OR are considering graduate level study but lack the English proficiency to matriculate into a U.S. higher education institution; - International graduate students who are already matriculated in a U.S. college or university who are interested in enhancing their English communication skills for personal and professional growth.
Multilingual or non-English-speaking people in Rhode Island, across the country or abroad interested in enhancing their English communication skills for personal and professional growth. - The program provides advanced English language skills training, including academic writing, reading and vocabulary, oral communication, and a seminar course tailored to a specific field of graduate study.

Graduates will demonstrate advanced English proficiency in writing, grammar, discourse, reading comprehension, vocabulary acquisition, oral communication (including classroom interactions, debates, and presentations) for academic research and presentations across content areas.
Graduates will communicate confidently in professional contexts within their academic discipline, utilizing effective registers, discourse, and vocabulary in written and oral communication genres.
Graduates will enhance their career readiness through discipline-specific language training, needs analysis, and genre analysis.
The Graduate Certificate in English Language Development reflects the University of Rhode Island’s role as the state’s flagship land-and sea-grant research institution and its commitment to global engagement and inclusive education.
As a student-centered research university, URI partners locally and globally to advance knowledge and prepare informed leaders.
This program supports URI’s mission by providing high-quality, accessible language education that empowers international graduate students to succeed academically and professionally.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-GC-06B | Page 106

By fostering linguistic proficiency and cultural competence, the certificate contributes to URI’s goal of solving global challenges through collaboration and innovation.
It also aligns with URI’s dedication to creating a diverse and inclusive environment for learners, ensuring equitable opportunities for success in graduate education and beyond.
The program also advances the goals of FOCUS URI: Strategic Plan 2023–2033.
Specifically, it: Broadens URI’s Impact (Priority 1) by attracting and supporting international students, strengthening URI’s global presence, and fostering cross-cultural collaboration that extends URI’s contributions to research and workforce development.
Enhances Student Achievement (Priority 2) by providing intensive, discipline-specific English language training in a flexible, asynchronous online and in-person formats, ensuring students have the tools to excel academically and professionally.
Fosters an Inclusive Culture (Priority 3) by reducing language barriers and creating equitable opportunities for diverse learners to thrive in graduate education.

passages.heading: 2025-2026-GC-06B | Page 106

Through this alignment, the Certificate contributes directly to URI’s mission and strategic priorities, while advancing the University’s role as a leader in global education and professional development.

To what extent will the program attract new students or draw students from existing programs?
Attracting New Students: The Graduate Certificate in English Language Development is designed to attract new international graduate students who would otherwise be unable to enroll due to English proficiency barriers.
By offering a conditional admission pathway, URI can tap into a global pool of academically qualified applicants who need language support before matriculating.
This program aligns with URI’s goal to increase international enrollment from 3% to 10% by 2033, making it a key driver for new student recruitment.
Impact on Existing Programs: The certificate is not expected to draw students away from existing URI graduate programs.
Instead, it serves as both a feeder program, preparing students for successful entry into those programs and a means to improve their academic success in those programs.
It complements URI’s current English Language Program by offering a credit-bearing, graduate-level certificate.
Students who complete the certificate will likely transition into URI master’s or doctoral programs, strengthening enrollment in those areas.

Online - Academic Year Fall 2026 Spring 2027 Risk management has become an integral part of today’s fast-paced industries, and leaders qualified in creating a culture of safety in their organization are in high demand. This program is structured to prepare working professionals for the rigorous task of preventing, predicting, and reacting to hazards in a variety of operational environments. Our students will gain experience in assessing risk within the framework of engineering and managerial principles, as well as regulatory requirements and benchmarks. This curriculum will cover areas related to engineering leadership and communication, industry safety standards, quality and safety, as well as various special interest topics (e.g., marine safety, construction zones, and wind energy safety). Following a hybrid model, this course will include online lectures and deliverables. This 12-credit program allows students to earn their certification in one year or less. Eligible students must have a Bachelor’s degree or advanced standing in a STEM field. A prerequisite of ISE311 or equivalent is also needed for this program. Program Requirements: - ISE517, Fundamentals of Industrial Safety (1) - ISE518, Engineering Leadership & Communication (1) Four (4) credits of the following course, taken under different topics: - ISE519, Special Topics for Systems Safety Certificate (1) Two (2) of the following courses: - ISE513, Quality & Safety (3) - ISE515, Production Safety (3) - ISE520(PSY520), Human Factors & Ergonomics (3) Is this program offered in the accelerated online calendar? What are the program goals?
Goal 1: Graduates will be prepared to lead safety initiatives and programs for their organizations. 1.1 Operationalize a Safety Management Systems approach through an understanding of how technology, human performance, and organizational factors influence safety outcomes. 1.2 Communicate effectively the plans and methods for safety assessment and risk to non-safety educated leaders.
Goal 2: Graduates will have the technical skills necessary to understand and assess safety standards and practices. 2.1 Demonstrate strong fundamentals in statistics, data management, and safety performance indicators. 2.2 Apply hazard identification, risk assessment, and failure analysis tools including failure mode analysis, fault tree analysis, gap analysis and job task/hazard analysis.

passages.text: Faculty Senate Executive Committee Report #2024-2025-09 Motion Regarding Honors Representation in the Faculty Senate March 6, 2025 Faculty Senate Meeting MOTION - That the Honors Program gain representation in the Faculty Senate per the following: Over the last year, the Faculty Senate, through its standing and special committees, has worked with Honors to restructure the program, and continues to actively pursue an option that would create a University-Sponsored Institute to house Honors. Until such time as this Institute is created or Honors is otherwise restructured, it is important that the program be represented formally in the university’s shared governance structure. While the program is undergoing a significant transition, it seems prudent to have an Honors representative actively participating in meetings where the future of the program is being discussed. Analogous to the way that deans and other administrators serve as ex officio members of the Faculty Senate, i.e. without the right to vote, but with the right to make and second motions and participate in debate, the Faculty Senate Executive Committee proposes that that the Honors Program Director become an ex officio member of the Faculty Senate effective immediately. Inclusion of the Honors representative in the Faculty Senate is a temporary measure which shall expire at the end of the 2025-2026 academic year.

These changes were approved in Bill #21-22-21B: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1XlqSOuKERd_Y6K0WFIExcj3piek-0k3z/view Information Equity, Diverse Communities, and Critical Librarianship - Specialty, Effective Summer 2025 Appendix B Equity, diversity, and inclusion are fundamental values of the American Library Association and are one of ALA’s committed key action areas which act as guiding principles for investment of energies and resources.
ALA’s Office for Diversity, Literacy and Outreach Services also encourages using a social-justice framework of diverse perspectives within LIS to advocate for equitable access to library services for all people.
In an increasingly diversifying country, library and information professionals are in need of critical thinking skills, cultural competency approaches, and new social justice approaches to executing equitable information spaces.

passages.heading: Graduate Council Report #2024-2025-04B | Page 2
passages.text:
Currently, LIS programs, professional organizations, and LIS-based companies are competitively offering trainings around Information Equity, Diverse Communities, and Critical Librarianship approaches to LIS.
For example, the New England Library Association (NELA) held a one-day diversity summit in the summer of 2017 with full enrollment, heavily focused on discussing race, racism, gender, sexuality, ability, immigrant and migrant rights, and social justice applications to diverse groups.
The University of North Carolina’s School of Information and Library Science offers a Diversity Advocate Certificate, the LIS press “Library Juice Press Academy” offers a course titled “Exploring and Applying Critical Theory: An Introduction for Librarians,”, and Library Journal has a number of diversity based professional development workshops such as “Diversity and Cultural Competency Training: Collections & RA,” to name a few.
This graduate track is a highly manageable 12-credit program from an accredited institution of higher education.

passages.heading: Graduate Council Report #2024-2025-04B | Page 2
passages.text:
The proposed track in Information Equity, Diverse Communities, and Critical Librarianship approaches will prepare LIS graduates for diverse workplaces, serving and collaborating with diverse populations, and recruiting a more diverse workforce, as well as creating equitable information institutes.
This proposed track will be the only such track in New England and as a track, it will also serve librarians across the United States COLLEGE OF THE ENVIRONMENT & LIFE SCIENCES Environmental and Natural Resource Economics - MS, Effective Winter 2025 Appendix C 1.

Equity, diversity, and inclusion are fundamental values of the American Library Association and are one of ALA’s committed key action areas which act as guiding principles for investment of energies and resources.
ALA’s Office for Diversity, Literacy and Outreach Services also encourages using a social-justice framework of diverse perspectives within LIS to advocate for equitable access to library services for all people.
In an increasingly diversifying country, library and information professionals are in need of critical thinking skills, cultural competency approaches, and new social justice approaches to executing equitable information spaces.
Currently, LIS programs, professional organizations, and LIS-based companies are competitively offering trainings around Information Equity, Diverse Communities, and Critical Librarianship approaches to LIS.
For example, the New England Library Association (NELA) held a one-day diversity summit in the summer of 2017 with full enrollment, heavily focused on discussing race, racism, gender, sexuality, ability, immigrant and migrant rights, and social justice applications to diverse groups.

passages.heading: Graduate Council Report #2024-2025-04B | Page 13
passages.text:
The University of North Carolina’s School of Information and Library Science offers a Diversity Advocate Certificate, the LIS press “Library Juice Press Academy” offers a course titled “Exploring and Applying Critical Theory: An Introduction for Librarians,”, and Library Journal has a number of diversity based professional development workshops such as “Diversity and Cultural Competency Training: Collections & RA,” to name a few.
This graduate track is a highly manageable 12-credit program from an accredited institution of higher education.
The proposed track in Information Equity, Diverse Communities, and Critical Librarianship approaches will prepare LIS graduates for diverse workplaces, serving and collaborating with diverse populations, and recruiting a more diverse workforce, as well as creating equitable information institutes.
This proposed track will be the only such track in New England and as a track, it will also serve librarians across the United States.

The Graduate Track in Information Equity, Diverse Communities, and Critical Librarianship will especially foster URI’s values of diversity, fairness and respect in students.
Information Equity, Diverse Communities, and Critical Librarianship supports URI’s mission by supporting diverse communities.
Additionally, the track will foster the leadership and critical thinking skills needed in a diversifying country and workforce.

Presently, MBA students can earn our Online Ocean Science Graduate Certificate and use these credits towards the MBA degree.
An in-person program will benefit the in-person Blue MBA program because there is a much larger number of in- person elective class offerings than there are online.
Taking online classes is cumbersome for in-person MBA students as URI Online requires separate tuition and is on a different academic calendar than the in-person calendar.
Effectively, the present situation requires students to disenroll from the in-person MBA program and enroll in the online certificate program to complete the Blue MBA program.
The present cumbersome situation was recognized as a problem in conversations between GSO and the College of Business and it was jointly agreed that GSO would propose an in-person certificate to streamline and enhance the Blue MBA program.
The URI Strategic Plan explicitly calls for an increase in graduate student enrollment and creating a diverse learning community which ensures that a URI education is within reasonable reach for all students.

FACULTY SENATE OFFICE FACULTY SENATE LEGISLATIONDECEMBER 12, 2024 Graduate CouncilReport 2024-2025-3B At the November 25, 2024 meeting of the Graduate Council, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate on December 12, 2024 for approval.
Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation By The Faculty Senate PROGRAM CHANGES COLLEGE OF EDUCATION College Student Personnel - MS Proposed changes include removal of “in College Student Personnel” in the degree title and reducing total credits required to 30 with 21 core courses.
Per the URI Grad school initiative to reduce total required credits for masters degrees, we have evaluated the CSP curriculum for duplicated content.
We also compared curricular content to national CAS standards to ensure that the program is in alignment with best practices.
The result is the removal of one class: EDC 529.
The course, in its entirety, no longer meets the needs of current CSP students.
The old curriculum map shows EDC 529 as only “R”einforcing Program Student Learning outcome #4.
And, that outcome is reinforced in two other courses and evaluated in EDC 580.
The program outcomes have not changed.

passages.heading: 24-25-10 | Page 2
passages.text:
The existing outcomes can still be introduced, reinforced, and evaluated via the new changes.
Additionally, other CSP programs tend to have fewer credits than our current program.
The streamlining of our curriculum, particularly in regards to credit hours, aligns us with other programs nationally.
COLLEGE OF THE ENVIRONMENT & LIFE SCIENCES Environmental and Natural Resource Economics - PHD 3.
Reduce the number of credits required.
The graduate school now only requires 64 credits, so we are adjusting our program accordingly.
We are reducing credits to allow students to take advantage of the increased availability of ABD semesters. 4.
Allow for equivalent class to be taken in place of EEC502.
When teaching capacity is strained in our department, we have found several suitable replacements for this class, and we want them to be able to count when we are unable to offer EEC502. [A note to the reviewers: Our program description and admission requirements in Kuali did not reflect recent changes that had been approved.
We copied and pasted the current program description and admission

passages.heading: 24-25-10 | Page 3
passages.text:
requirements into Kuali and then added items 2-4 above. 2-4 are the only changes we are requesting to the program description; all other changes have already been approved, as can be seen in the current catalog.] Proposed changes include removing “in Environmental and Natural Resource Economics” from the degree title and an initiation date of Spring 2025.
COLLEGE OF NURSING Nursing Practice - DNP Our current Program started as a BS to DNP Program and was put on hold about five years ago.
After that, we only accepted Post-Masters students for the in-person DNP Program.
Our current change to an Online Program will close both the Post BS to DNP and Post Masters to DNP in-person Programs.
Our current in-person DNP program attracts a small number of applicants each year.
Converting our program to an online, asynchronous, program offers expansion of the student pool from local to national.
There will be an overlap between teaching-out the in-person program and the start of the online offering.
We anticipate the last graduating class from the live program to be in the Spring Semester of 2027, while the first cohort to enter the online offering will be fall of 2025.

passages.heading: 24-25-10 | Page 3
passages.text:
The proposed online program remains essentially the same with updates to some of the courses being delivered and a few new courses to enhance topical areas of integrative healthcare.
Teach-Out Plan: Students will be notified of the online plan and offered an LOA or postpone entry if they choose the online option.
Otherwise, the in-person DNP program will continue until students have completed which is anticipated to be Spring 2027.
To work in the URI online format, the 7-week sequence was required but the College wanted the extended time for each course for doctoral-level work (14 weeks), thus, the A/B model evolved for each course which is denoted with "A" 7 weeks plus "B" 7 weeks taken sequentially.
Attached is a sample of the course sequence for the NursingPractice-DNP Online.
Proposed program description: The Doctor of Nursing Practice (DNP) is an innovative, online, post master’s program that prepares advanced practice nurses as leaders in evidence based principles of traditional, complementary, and integrative health (TCIH) to transform health care systems.

passages.heading: 24-25-10 | Page 3
passages.text:
Program Requirements: Program requirements include a minimum of 68 credits obtained as follows: 30 credits from a post MS degree and 38 credits to be completed to complete the DNP degree.

passages.text: NEW CERTIFICATES FEINSTEIN COLLEGE OF EDUCATION College Teaching - Cert The 12 credit graduate certificate in college teaching is designed to prepare individuals to effectively teach in post-secondary settings–including college and community settings with adult learners. The graduate certificate will provide a knowledge base of adult learning theory and skills for instructional design, implementation and evaluation. It will also provide a solid foundation of teaching for equity and inclusion. COLLEGE OF THE ENVIRONMENT & LIFE SCIENCES Community Planning - Cert (online) The Graduate Certificate in Community Planning (CPL), composed of 3 required classes and one elective, is an asynchronous online "stackable certificate" provides the pathway for working professionals to develop core competencies in sustainable Community Planning. Through this program, students will gain a foundation in the principles and practices of community planning and development, specifically in areas of site planning and environmental planning. Students can earn their certificate in four sessions, maximizing flexibility and convenience for career enhancement and professional growth. Class content in this certificate is geared towards working professionals who do not have prior knowledge in planning. Completion of the certificate will provide a basic knowledge of planning that can be augmented with certificate programs in other departments, such as the Master of Public Administration (MPA), and the Master of Environmental Management (MEM) program.

The College Student Personnel (CSP) program’s mission is to prepare equity minded and reflective practitioners for careers in student affairs.
Graduates seek primarily entry-level positions such as advisors, coordinators, and assistant directors/deans at institutions of higher education.
The CSP curriculum is designed to teach emerging professionals’ best practices in student affairs and is designed in accordance with the guidelines established by the Council for the Advancement of Standards (CAS) in Higher Education.
These goals are enacted through DEI infused pedagogy and content throughout the courses in the program.
The CSP program aligns with numerous goals within Strategic priority 2: Enhance student achievement by cultivating an engaged and inclusive learning environment.
This is a unique program tied to a specific field of education.
The program is specifically dedicated to professional preparation in the field of College Student Personnel and does not overlap with any other programs at URI.

passages.text:
The Graduate Certificate in Community Planning (CP) is an online program that helps students develop core competencies in sustainable Community Planning.
Through this program, students will gain a foundation in the principles and practices of community planning and development, specifically in areas of land use and environmental planning.
The history of planning has many examples of environmental injustice, in which land use decisions have privileged some communities over others.
A commitment to anti-racism, inclusiveness, equity, as well as spatial and social justice perspectives is an integral part of a planning education.
Students can earn their certificate in four sessions, maximizing flexibility and convenience for career enhancement, leadership positions in the industry, and professional growth.
The Community Planning online certificate aligns with the University's commitment to urban initiative, community engagement and solving the world's most important challenges by equiping students with practical knowledge and understanding of how to plan for and enable equitable and sustainable communities.

passages.heading: 24-25-10 | Page 50
passages.text:
This 4-course asychonous online graduate certificate also creates a learning opportunity for students who may not be able to attend graduate school in person on a full time basis, thereby creating a diverse learning opportunity (goal 3 of the URI Stragic Priority 2) and increase graduate student enrollment (goal 2 of Strategic Priority 2).
The impact of a working public better informed in values and strategies of community planning should contribute to healthier and more sustainable communities environmentally, socially and economically.
The online graduate Community Planning certificate will open doors for recent college graduates as well as working professionals; they will become eligible for positions and promotion in a growing job market.
By combining this online certificate with other stackable certificates such as Public Administration, MEM and GIS, students will be well equipped to engage in the significant planning challenges of our time.
Our department currently offers an in-person Graduate Certificate in Community Planning.
This proposed new program will be offered in the 7-week online format and require 4 classes with 3 required classes and one elective (12 credits).

passages.heading: 24-25-10 | Page 50
passages.text:
Our existing Community Planning Graduate Certificate requires 5 courses to complete the certificate (15 or 16 credits).
The asychonous online certitificate is intended for a different student population from our in-person gradute certificate and provides somewhat different content.
The online certificate content is pragmatically planned to be useful for working professionals, adapted for online delivery, and geared towards working professionals who do not have prior knowledge of planning.
The purpose of the Certificate is to give these students a way to quickly and remotely attain a basic knowledge of planning, and to stack that knowledge with other certificates, such as Public Policy, Marine Affairs, GIS, etc.
By contrast, the full semester, in-person planning program encompasses a wide and in-depth disciplinary space, with opportunities to learn from in-person university relationships and pursue independent research, while still providing future planners with knowledge and tools for professional work.

Program Description This curriculum leads to a Bachelor of Science (B.S.) degree.
This major prepares undergraduates for a career as a Registered Dietitian/Nutritionist (RDN).
The M.S. in Nutrition includes an Accelerated Bachelors to Masters of Science (ABM) option for students enrolled in the B.S. degree, described below.
This Dietetics degree is required for all students planning to become RDN'sRDNs.
URI's Dietetics program is accredited by the Accreditation Council for Education in Nutrition and Dietetics (ACEND), 120 South Riverside Plaza, Suite 2190, Chicago, IL 60606. 800.877.1600, ext. 5400; https:/ /www.eatrightpro.org/acend/.
Please see the department website for complete program information (https://web.uri.edu/nfsnutrition/).

passages.heading: 24-25-10 | Page 63

The dietetics major requires 27 credits in sciences (four in general chemistry [CHM 103/105], four in organic chemistry [CHM 124/126], three in biochemistry [CMB 210], twelve in biology [BIO 110/103; 220/221; 222/223], and four in microbiology [CMB 201/202]), 4 credits in applied general nutrition (NFSNUT 207/210), 4 credits in introductory professional courses (NFSNUT 110 and 212G); and 41 credits in the concentration including the following courses: NFSNUT 336, 337, 375, 376, 394, 395, 410, 440, 441, 443, 444, 445, and 458 [capstone].
Additionally, MGT 341 is required and COM 100, MTH 103, PSY 113, SOC 100, STA 220, and WRT 104 are required and may be used to ful�ll general education requirements.
There are 16-1917 credits of free electives.
Students are encouraged to use free electives to study disciplines related to the �eld.
Students must maintain a 3.00 average in all required courses (NFSNUT courses, science courses, and the remaining degree courses), with no less than a C in any one class, in order to graduate.
A total of 120 credits is required for graduation.

After completing their B.S. requirements, students can qualify for the professional title of Registered Dietitian/Nutritionist by completing supervised practice requirements and graduate degree, and passing a national credentialing exam.
The supervised practice requirement can be met by completing an ACEND-accredited dietetic internship program, individualized supervised practice program, future education graduate program, or coordinated dietetic internship/graduate program.

Goal 1: Graduates will be prepared to enter research-focused graduate programs based on their knowledge of empirically- supported psychological processes and how to apply this knowledge to promote health and welfare.
Goal 2: Graduates will be competent in intermediate level critical thinking and behavioral data analysis skills.
Goal 3: Graduates will be able to work ethically in settings that emphasize diversity and global thinking.
The BS in Psychology is described to students as a program that focuses on the empirical and methodological aspects of psychology, that emphasizes math, science, and research methods in creating and applying psychological knowledge, and that includes a requirement in hands on research experience.
This program addresses Strategy 1 of the Agenda for Change (Infuse Anti-Racism, Social Justice and DEI Perspectives) in the Curriculum in several ways.
The introductory course (PSY 113) required of all majors, includes sections on anti-racism.
The lead instructor for this course has published multiple papers on teaching anti-racism and social justice.

passages.heading: 24-25-10 | Page 74
passages.text:
Goal 3 of the BS program focuses on teaching students to work ethically in settings that emphasize diversity.
The addition of PSY260GPSY260 Psyched About Cultured: Introduction to Cross Cultural Psychology is designed to address this need.
This course is currently approved as GCH 102G: Interdisciplinary Topics in Diversity and Inclusion and has been offered by Assistant Professor Ceren Gunsoy.
We wish now to make it a required course for all PSY BS majors.
Mission Statement: The BS in Psychology aligns well with the University's mission statement with its focus on the public- learner centered research university, quest for knowledge, and the educational opportunities of the research university.
This program's focus on training students in empirical knowledge foundations of Psychology and expertise in the research and methods of the field is an important addition to the mission of URI.
The values cited in the mission statement including scholarship, diversity, engaged learning, and intellectual and ethical leadership are also important values for the department of Psychology and the BS major (see for example learning outcome 3.2: Be able to discuss psychology-related issue in ethics).

passages.heading: 24-25-10 | Page 74
passages.text:

The BS program in the current proposal requires students take a 3 credit course to obtain hands-on experience with psychological research.
Goal 3 Strategy 3 : Create opportunities for the internationalization of the curriculum and co-curriculum to ensure that all students are exposed to global perspectives and build global competence.

The BS major includes learning outcome 3.1 be able to discuss psychology-related issues in diversity.

Mark Robbins A BS in psychology prepares students for a wide variety of career options.
According to the website of the American Psychological Association ( https://www.apa.org/ed/precollege/psn/2018/01/bachelors-degree ), about 25 percent of psychology baccalaureates go to graduate school in psychology, about 18 percent go on for more education but not in psychology, and 57 percent are workforce graduates (Lin, Christidis & Stamm, 2017).
The BS degree prepares graduates especially well to apply to doctoral or other research-oriented advanced degrees in Psychology or other fields.

passages.heading: 24-25-10 | Page 75
passages.text:
For those who do not wish to obtain an advanced degree, there are many job opportunities.
The above referenced website lists 70 job titles that students with a BS in Psychology are prepared for.
The BS degree with its focus on methodology, scientific writing, and statistical analysis especially trains graduates for any type of position requiring analytic, scientific writing, or data analytic skills, such as data base design analyst, research assistant, systems analyst, technical writer, information specialist, or data base manager.
A number of these occupations are considered high impact jobs in RI.
The Occupational Outlook Handbook of the Bureau of Labor ( https://www.bls.gov/ooh/field-of- degree/psychology/psychology-field-of-degree.htm ) indicates that the median salary for those with a degree in Psychology is $50,000 and that 60% are employed in occupations requiring at least a bachelor's degree.
Many department faculty offer students the opportunity to serve as undergraduate teaching assistants for course credit.
There are no paid undergraduate assistantships.
Graduate teaching assistantships are offered to assist instructors with PSY 200, PSY 301, and PSY 435.

passages.heading: 24-25-10 | Page 75
passages.text:
Among peer institutions (UMass, UConn, UVM, UNH, U of Maine, and U of Delaware) BS degrees in Psychology are offered by three (UMASS, UCONN, and UVM).
The University of Delaware offers a BS in Neuroscience but not Psychology.
UNH and U of Maine offer only BA programs.
It does not make URI unique in our region to offer this degree, but if we did not offer it, we would not be keeping up with the more research/science oriented institutions in our region.
There is a trend among peer institutions to emphasize the scientific basis of psychology, which the proposed changes to the program are designed to accomplish.

passages.text: V. 24.01.26 CURRICULUM & STANDARDS COMMITTEE FACULTY SENATE OFFICE URI Curriculum & Standards Committee Department Name Change Proposal Date: September 30, 2024 Person to contact during review: Geoff Bothun, gbothun@uri.edu GENERAL INFORMATION 1. Name of Institution: University of Rhode Island 2. Name of administrative unit: Department: Chemical Engineering College: Engineering 3. Current Department Name: Chemical Engineering 4. Proposed Department Name: Chemical, Biomolecular, and Materials Engineering 5. Intended date of change: January 1, 2025 6. Documentation of review & approval process. Please attach approvals from the following approval bodies: · Department approval by faculty vote · College Dean Approval by the CASC/Graduate Council, Faculty Senate, and the University President will be facilitated by the Faculty Senate Office. 7. Summary of Proposed Change: A change in department name is proposed from "Chemical Engineering" to "Chemical, Biomolecular, and Materials Engineering" to better reflect the fields chemical engineering students enter after graduation, the research expertise in our department, and the content in our courses and minors. The name change will also provide a platform for department growth and aid recruiting efforts at the undergraduate, graduate, and faculty levels. Course codes and names of degrees will not change. passages.heading: 24-25-10 | Page 104
passages.text:
V. 24.01.26 RATIONALE There should be a demonstrable purpose and documented need for the proposed name change. 1.
Explain why the change of department name is being proposed.
The proposed new name of "Chemical, Biomolecular, and Materials Engineering" accurately reflects the career and technological fields that graduates enter and the research and scholarly expertise of the department faculty.
For example, the department has many graduates working at Amgen, which is a biotechnology company producing biological molecules (i.e., biomolecules), as well as Toray Plastics America, which produces polymeric materials.
The new name also reflects topics that are taught in our courses and the newly formed department Minor in Materials Engineering.
An additional Minor in Biochemical Engineering has been proposed (expected launch in Spring 2025) and a minor in Pharmaceutical Manufacturing and Formulation (includes biomolecular topics) is offered by the Department of Biomedical and Pharmaceutical Sciences for chemical engineering majors.

passages.heading: 24-25-10 | Page 104
passages.text:
The proposed new name aligns with similar department names of URI's peer and aspiring institutions, which include terms such as "bioengineering", "biomedical", and "biological engineering" in their names preceded by the term "chemical".
Changing the department name at URI is expected to make us more competitive in undergraduate student recruiting and, coupled with the new name reflecting our research expertise, more competitive at recruiting graduate students and faculty.
INSTITUTIONAL ROLE The department name change should be clearly related to the published role and mission of the institution and be compatible with the organizational structure of the institution. 1.
Explain how the name change is consistent with published role and mission of the institution, and how it is related to institutional planning.
As with our current name, the new name will continue to align with the role and mission of the institution in providing high-quality education and solving the world's most challenging problems (the new name explicitly extends this to biomolecules and materials).

passages.heading: 24-25-10 | Page 104
passages.text:
It also aligns with institutional planning, providing new opportunities to increase student recruiting, to create new degree and/or certificate programs, and to pursue interdisciplinary collaboration (funding agencies/proposal review panels link department names to expertise). 2.
Explain how the organizational change impacts other units and programs within the institution.
Have you communicated with the other units and programs and have any concerns been raised relative to the organizational change?
Describe the concerns.
The proposed name change was formally presented to the department chairs in the College of Engineering and no concerns were raised - they were collectively enthusiastic.
The potential for the most overlap is with the Biomedical Engineering program in the Department of Electrical, Computer, and Biomedical Engineering.
The CHE chair discussed the name change with the program lead for Biomedical Engineering and the only concern was with the abbreviation, CHE changing to CBME. "BME" is the abbreviation for Biomedical Engineering and the BME lead thought this could lead to confusion during registration.

passages.heading: 24-25-10 | Page 104
passages.text:
After explaining that the course codes would remain "CHE" there was no longer a concern.

FACULTY SENATE OFFICE 224 P ASTORE H ALL , 51 L OWER C OLLEGE R OAD , K INGSTON , R I 02881 U SA , P: 401.874.2616 Faculty Senate Resolution 2024-2025-02 Faculty Senate Meeting of December 12, 2024 Resolution on the Implementation of Honors Contracts WHEREAS , following considerable self-study, and with significant input from external experts, the URI Honors Program has proposed the use of honors contracts at URI.
Honors contracts are formal agreements facilitated by an honors program, between a student and instructor.
They unite students and instructors to enhance non-honors courses to an honors level through additional learner-directed work tailored to the “broader, deeper, and more complex” learning experiences advocated by the National Collegiate Honors Council (NCHC); and WHEREAS , Contracts are recognized by over 60% of honors programs in the USA, where they foster community and ownership, enhancing the educational process and commitment to the programs’ success.
For example, work at the University Honors Program at the University of Kansas shows that honors contracts act as far more than stopgaps to address honors course shortages.

passages.heading: 24-25-10 | Page 112
passages.text:
They can “facilitate access to honors, increases completion, democratize key aspects of the honors experience, provide students with structured avenues for building relationships with faculty members, and empower students to own their educational experiences;” and WHEREAS , Honors contracts may be best understood as a form of an independent study, entered into voluntarily by both students and faculty, with a contract defining outcomes, deadlines, and assessment definitions for additional work related to the course materials; and WHEREAS ,Honors contracts provide flexibility for students to align their education with their interests and goals.
They also allow programs to meet student needs when constraints of students or faculty numbers or funding limitations do not allow honors courses to be run that answer to a student’s interests and needs; and WHEREAS , Contracts provide an extra measure of curricular flexibility at institutions such as ours that are not able to field enough faculty, cannot provide an adequate number of honors courses, or do not have a large enough student body to fill honors sections.

passages.heading: 24-25-10 | Page 112
passages.text:
Contracts can fill the gap and provide opportunities for students’ self-guided intellectual growth; NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED , that the Faculty Senate of the University of Rhode Island, calls for implementation of the following Honors Contracts Proposal.

passages.text: CONTRACTS: URI Catalog Information Honors Contracts Honors contracts allow students to earn Honors credit for non-Honors courses by pursuing more advanced study. This requires an agreement between the student and instructor, and approval from the Honors Program. This option is valuable for students interested in a course not offered in an Honors format or whose schedules prevent them from enrolling in an Honors section. The following restrictions apply. (Any exceptions must be approved in advance by the Honors Program): 1. Honors contract credits shall not amount to more than one-third (1/3) of a student’s total coursework required for graduation from Honors. 2. Students shall not engage in more than one honors contract per semester. 3. Honors contracts cannot be completed during the summer or J-Term. Nor can they be applied to 100-level courses, internships, independent studies, study abroad, or courses at other institutions. 4. Contracted courses must be taken for a letter grade and must be completed with a grade of B or better to count towards Honors Program requirements. 5. Students who do not complete the proposed work to the satisfaction of the instructor will not earn Honors credit for the course.

passages.heading: 24-25-10 | Page 115
passages.text: CONTRACTS: For the Honors Program Web site. The Honors Contract Process The Honors contract process involves four stages: 1. Crafting of an individualized project with the course instructor. 2. Submission of the contract to the Honors Program for approval. 3. Completion of the agreed-upon assignments and activities. 4. Submission of the completed work and the Honors Contract completion form conﬁrming the instructor’s satisfaction with the work. 1: Crafting the Honors Contract The Honors Contract is a mutual commitment to a learning experience above and beyond normal course requirements. The student and instructor must agree on the criteria for evaluating the project and its scheduling. Instructors are under no obligation to supervise Honors Contracts. The Honors contract is intended to enrich the student's education by further work of mutual interest to the student and instructor, rather than simply adding to the course’s workload. Students would therefore be wise to consider projects where the enriched assignment or activity also suits the interests and needs of the instructor. An Honors contract should involve 6 to 7 hours per credit: A 3-credit course should, for example, involve approximately 20 hours of additional work. These estimated hours should include 2-3 hours of meetings with the instructor: one at the start, one mid-project, and one to conclude. Overall, plan for 3-5 hours of direct faculty involvement, including evaluation.

passages.heading: 24-25-10 | Page 116
passages.text: While the details of contracted assignments and activities may vary greatly, course enrichments could include: • Collaboration with the instructor on a joint research project. • An analytical, research, or policy paper, in addition to any assigned in the "regular" syllabus, and/or more reliant on individual work with primary or original source material. • An experiential- or service-learning experience, or internship related to the course focus. • A multimedia project, performance, or artistic work related to the course focus. • Curriculum development projects, such as assisting the professor with the development and implementation of new teaching tools, class activities, or trial runs of new course projects. [INSERT CALENDAR/ TIMELINE HERE.] 2: Submission of the Contract Proposal All Honors contract proposals must be submitted no later than the end of the third week of classes. The Honors contract proposal consists of three parts: 1. The Contract Form, signed by both the student and the instructor. 2. A copy of the original course syllabus 3. A brief description of the proposed project (500-1000 words.) The following information should be included in the proposal: 1. What? Why? When? How? – A brief overview of the project, its rationale, timeline and evaluation criteria. 2. How is it "honors"? – How, precisely the project differs from the regular work of the class.

passages.heading: 24-25-10 | Page 117
passages.text:
3.
What will we see? – What will the outcome (or deliverable) of the project be? 4.
A timetable – E.g.: Meetings with the course instructor, a mid-term check-in, submission of components or drafts of the project, and the submission of the ﬁnal product.
The ﬁnal deadline can be no later than the scheduled ﬁnal exam period for the course. 5.
Evaluation criteria – Include a clear statement of the criteria that will be used to evaluate the contracted work.
What are the minimum requirements that must be met in order to be judged acceptable?
If there are multiple elements, how do they each contribute?
Also, the following wording must be included in the proposal: "The Honors contract work will be assessed as Satisfactory or Unsatisfactory by the instructor according to the criteria described in this contract.
The rating will be entered into a Honors Contract Completion form.
A rating of Satisfactory will result in the student receiving Honors credit for the course.
A rating of Unsatisfactory will result in no Honors credit being awarded for the course.

passages.heading: 24-25-10 | Page 117
passages.text:
Performance on the Honors Contract work will not affect the ﬁnal grade in any circumstance." The Honors Program may approve the proposal as written, request more information before making a decision, or reject it.
Once approved, the Honors Administrator will sign it and send a copy to both the student and the instructor.
Approved contracts result in a transcript notation of "Honors" for the course in question once Enrollment Services is notiﬁed by Honors that the coursework has been completed. 3: Completion of the Contracted Work Approved contract work should proceed according to the predetermined schedule.
The project may, however, evolve as it progresses.
Completed projects will not generally be expected to perfectly match the initial proposal.
However, the student and instructor

passages.heading: 24-25-10 | Page 118
passages.text: may along the way agree on signiﬁcant alterations, deviating substantially from the approved proposal. Should this occur, the student must submit an amended Honors contract proposal outlining the new criteria for completion and assessment. If in doubt on how to proceed contact the Honors Program as soon as possible. 4: Submission of the Completed Work and Contract Completion Form To earn Honors credit for the course, students must complete the proposed work at a level deemed satisfactory by the instructor. Following that, an "Honors" designation appears on the transcript, and all credits earned for the course count towards fulﬁllment of the Honors Program, provided that the ﬁnal course grade is B or better. Work assigned by the contract is not calculated into the ﬁnal course grade. Final grades are calculated per the professor's original syllabus, reﬂecting the quality and content of all the student's coursework. As soon as the contracted work is complete and approved by the instructor, the student will submit a copy of the completed work and the Honors Contract Completion Form no later than by the end of business on the last day of the ﬁnal examination period. If, however, a presentation or performance is part of the proposal, please invite members of the Honors Program to attend.

Amended Text For: "Honors Program" in "Special Academic Opportunities" in URI'S catalog (Added text is in red) Honors Program The University Honors Program offers motivated students opportunities to broaden and deepen their intellectual development.
The program consists of courses that emphasize discussion and project-based learning, a colloquium that brings nationally and internationally distinguished speakers to campus, and independent research projects under the guidance of a faculty sponsor.
Honors courses at the 100 and 200 levels fulﬁll general education requirements; those at the 300 and 400 levels are more specialized and often are used to fulﬁll either a general education requirement or the requirements of a major.
Students may participate in the Honors Program if they meet the following standards: Sophomores, juniors, and seniors must have earned at least a 3.40 cumulative grade point average at URI; transfer students must have received a GPA of 3.40 or better at their previous institution to be eligible for honors courses.

passages.heading: 24-25-10 | Page 119
passages.text:
Incoming freshmen are invited to participate in the Honors Program based on one of the following: they must have earned a cumulative grade point average (recalculated) of 3.60 or higher in high school and must have a combined score of 1,300 on the critical reading and math portions of the SAT exam (or ACT score of 27 or higher); or they must have earned a cumulative 3.80 GPA (recalculated) in high school, and SAT scores are not considered.
Eligible students may participate in the Honors Program in one of two ways: they may take honors courses on an occasional basis, registering for any number or pattern of courses that interest them; or they may do honors work on a regular basis, meeting the speciﬁc requirements to receive the transcript notation “Completed the University Honors Program.”

passages.heading: 24-25-10 | Page 120
passages.text: No more than one third (1/3) of a student's total credits toward Honors certiﬁcation may be obtained through the use of Honors Contracts, unless an exception is granted ahead of time by the Honors Program. To achieve this certiﬁcation a student must complete a minimum of 18 honors course credits that meet the following requirements: 1) three credits in Honors at the 100 or 200 level; 2) three credits of Honors Colloquium; 3) three credits in Honors at the 300 or 400 level; 4) six credits at the 400 level, which may be either six credits of Senior Honors Project (HPR 401, 402) or three credits of Senior Honors Project (HPR 401) and three credits of Senior Honors Seminar (HPR 411/412, or other approved Senior Seminar); 5) three additional honors credits taken at any level; and 6) a 3.40 grade point average for honors courses and a 3.40 cumulative grade point average.

passages.text: Honors Contracts: FAQ for Faculty For the URI Honors Program Web Page (Draft Dec. 4, 2024) What is an Honors Contract? Honors contracts allow students to earn Honors credit for non-Honors courses by pursuing more advanced study. This requires an agreement between the student and instructor, and approval from the Honors Program. This option is valuable for students interested in a course not offered in an Honors format or whose schedules prevent them from enrolling in an Honors section. Why should we use Honors Contracts? Honors Contracts offer several beneﬁts: Flexibility: They allow students to tailor their education to their interests and goals. Accessibility: They provide opportunities for honors-level work when there are limitations on the number of honors courses offered. Student Engagement: They empower students, foster motivation, and facilitate mentor-mentee relationships with faculty. Who can supervise an Honors contract? All full-time faculty may supervise an Honors contract. No one, however, is required to do so. Part-time faculty and staff may supervise contracts only in special cases if an exception is granted prior to the creation of a contract by the Honors Program. What are the faculty roles and responsibilities in an Honors contract? Faculty roles and responsibilities include: Helping the student formulate a proposal for an appropriate contract project.

passages.heading: 24-25-10 | Page 123
passages.text:
Deﬁning the terms and timeline of the contract with the student.
Providing guidance as the student works on the contracted project, with at least one mid-project meeting.
Evaluating the contract project at the end of the semester.
How much time should faculty plan to devote to this?
Generally, a faculty member should expect to devote 3-5 hours over the course of a term on a contracted project.
How are Honors Contracts set up?
The Honors Program provides comprehensive guidelines and support for setting up contracts on its Web site (See “The Contract Process”.
Students are encouraged to communicate early with instructors and the Honors Program to explore possibilities and ensure a clear understanding of the process.
Brieﬂy: The Honors contract process involves four stages: 1.
Crafting of an individualized project with the course instructor. 2.
Submission of the contract to the Honors Program for approval. 3.
Completion of the agreed-upon assignments and activities. 4.
Submission of the completed work and the Honors Contract Completion Form confirming the instructor’s satisfaction with the work.
What should be included in an Honors Contract?
The Honors contract proposal consists of three parts: 1.

passages.heading: 24-25-10 | Page 123
passages.text:
The Contract Form, signed by both the student and the instructor. 2.
A copy of the original course syllabus 3.
A brief description of the proposed project (500-1000 words.) The following information should be included in the proposal: 1.
What?
Why?
When?
How? – A brief overview of the project, its rationale, timeline and evaluation criteria. 2.
How is it "honors"? – How, precisely the project differs from the regular work of the class.
I.e: A clear articulation of how the contract meets the "broader, deeper, more complex" criteria of the National Collegiate Honors Council. 3.
What will we see? – What will the outcome (or deliverable) of the project be?

passages.heading: 24-25-10 | Page 124
passages.text:
4.
A timetable – E.g.: Meetings with the course instructor, a mid-term check-in, submission of components or drafts of the project, and the submission of the final product.
The final deadline can be no later than the scheduled final exam period for the course. 5.
Evaluation criteria – Include a clear statement of the criteria that will be used to evaluate the contracted work.
What are the minimum requirements that must be met in order to be judged acceptable?
If there are multiple elements, how do they each contribute?
Also, the following wording must be included in the proposal: "The Honors contract work will be assessed as Satisfactory or Unsatisfactory by the instructor according to the criteria described in this contract.
The rating will be entered into a Honors Contract Completion form.
A rating of Satisfactory will result in the student receiving Honors credit for the course.
A rating of Unsatisfactory will result in no Honors credit being awarded for the course.
Performance on the Honors Contract work will not affect the ﬁnal grade in any circumstance." The Honors Program may approve the proposal as written, request more information before making a decision, or reject it.

passages.heading: 24-25-10 | Page 124
passages.text:
Once approved, the Honors Administrator will sign it and send a copy to both the student and the instructor.
Approved contracts result in a transcript notation of "Honors" for the course in question once Enrollment Services is notiﬁed by Honors that the coursework has been completed.
What are some examples of positive outcomes from Honors Contracts?
When well-managed, Honors Contracts can: • Cultivate personalized learning experiences. • Develop strong mentoring relationships between students and faculty. • Enhance the overall honors experience. • Provide faculty with a new vision for their courses.
What are some potential problems with Honors Contracts, and how can they be avoided?
Some potential issues include: Routine or Casual Use: Contracts should not become commonplace or be considered a replacement of the regular honors curriculum.

passages.heading: 24-25-10 | Page 125
passages.text: Lack of Meaningful Interaction: Although the contracted projects require only about 20 hours of work by the student and 3 to 5 hours of work by the faculty, it is important to ensure that contracts involve meaningful interaction between students and instructors. Unclear Expectations: The Honors Program provides clear guidelines and assessment criteria to students and faculty maintain high standards. Faculty are be expected to provide clear instructions to the students in the contract language. How can I ensure that Honors Contracts are effective? To ensure effectiveness: Maintain high standards and clear expectations. Ensure that the contracted work is well-connected to the course themes and outcomes. Ensure that the contracted work enhances the student’s experience of the course themes, materials, and outcomes. Will I be compensated for my work with Honors Contracts? Yes, it is essential that faculty are recognized and compensated for the additional work involved in Honors Contracts. Your work should be noted in your review portfolio. What is the difference between an Honors contract and an Honors Project? An Honors contract deﬁnes a project requiring approximately 20 hours of work, appended to an existing non-Honors course to allow the course’s credits be counted as Honors credits. An Honors project is a mentored independent study for 3 or 6 credits, devoted to a project that requires extensive research, reading, writing, creativity, or experimentation.

passages.heading: 24-25-10 | Page 126
passages.text: How is an Honors contract satisﬁed? An Honors contract is satisﬁed when the professor notiﬁes the Honors Program that the student has completed the assigned task satisfactorily. The student must also receive a B or higher in the course in order to earn Honors credit. Approved contract work should proceed according to the predetermined schedule. The project may, however, evolve as it progresses. Completed projects will not generally be expected to perfectly match the initial proposal. However, the student and instructor may along the way agree on signiﬁcant alterations, deviating substantially from the approved proposal. Should this occur, the student must submit an amended Honors contract proposal outlining the new criteria for completion and assessment. If in doubt on how to proceed contact the Honors Program as soon as possible. What happens if a student fails to complete an Honors contract? If a student fails to complete the proposed work to the satisfaction of the instructor, they will not receive Honors credit for the course. Can Honors contracts be applied to all courses? No, Honors contracts cannot be completed during the summer or J-Term. Nor should they be applied to 100-level courses, internships, independent studies, study abroad, or courses taken at other institutions.
