Proposed Resolution for Joint Action to Redesign the Office of the Ombuds The Service and Community Life Committee (SCLC) December 12, 2024 Resolution The purpose of this resolution is to request immediate joint action by the Faculty Senate and the Office of the President as co-equal governing partners through the creation of a special joint committee.
The special joint committee will create a new Office of the Ombud.
Context In 2024, the Ombuds Dr.
Gerry Tyler and Dr.
Al Killilea were replaced by an Interim Ombud, Dr.
Charles Collyer.
An Interim Ombud role was created so that the Faculty Senate Service and Community Life Committee (SCLC), The Faculty Senate Executive Committee (FSEC), and the office of Provost could take a year to redesign and re-establish a new Office of the Ombuds.
This resolution grows out of discussions that have taken place between SCLC, FSEC, and the Office of the Provost.

passages.heading: 24-25-10 | Page 127
passages.text:
Expectations Membership of the special joint committee shall consist of advocates for those members of the campus community who may need or want to engage with the Office of the Ombuds: representatives from the faculty and delegates representing staff and student interests. ● Special joint committee co-chairs.
The committee shall be co-chaired by a designee from the SCLC and a designee from the Office of the President.
The co-chairs shall recruit committee members and manage and oversee the work of the committee until a new Office of the Ombuds is established. ● Committee charge.
The committee shall study best practices and decide the most appropriate actions for the design and creation of an effective Office of the Ombuds, including: ● Role, duties, powers and privileges.
The committee shall revise and update the policy that delineates the expectations of the Office of the Ombud and that codifies the duties, powers, and privileges of the Ombuds.

passages.heading: 24-25-10 | Page 127
passages.text: The position requires that the Ombuds are: ● Trained in how to listen and help identify issues and courses of action, mediate conflict or disputes, and guide and direct those in need ● Skilled and certified conflict mediators ● Connected to the university community, whether currently or formerly employed by the institution

passages.heading: 24-25-10 | Page 128
passages.text:
● Provided equitable compensation for their work ● Provided with appropriate space ● Provided a community infrastructure, including but not limited to a cohort of others who work in the support system of the institution (CED, EEOC, Title 9, etc.) ● Job description, nomination, application and selection process. ● Job description.
The committee will develop a new job description that must convey the following critical ideas (per section 5.88.10 of the University Manual): the Ombud role shall be to: investigate complaints from students, faculty, and administrative personnel, with the very explicit charge to handle situations that fall outside of the auspices of the usual channels (such as the Office of Community, Equity, and Diversity, the unions, office of DEI in the respective colleges, EEOC, Title IX, and Human Resources).
The Ombuds are designated to handle primarily issues that stem from interpersonal conflicts. ● Application, hiring committee, and selection process.

passages.heading: 24-25-10 | Page 128
passages.text:
The committee must also design a written application (whether it be an essay on qualifications and interest, or short answers to prompts) and an application and selection process that shall include a designated hiring committee.
The hiring committee shall include representatives of the university’s co-equal governing partnership: the Faculty Senate and the Office of the President.
The hiring committee shall review applications, interview candidates, and collectively make the final decision on the selection of at least two Ombuds.
It is important that there are at least two Ombuds, especially if they are full-time tenure track faculty, or faculty and staff, from two different colleges.
This allows for recusal from cases if necessary.
The SCLC recommends a two-person Office with one faculty representative and one staff representative. ● Nominations.

Revisions must make certain that it is clear that nominations are not restricted to those put forth by any member of the administration and the Faculty Senate, but will follow the nomination and selection process designed and approved by

The committee must negotiate a new neutral space for the Office of the Ombuds that will achieve two critical goals: making the Office more visible to community members and also guarantee protections of privacy and confidentiality to those who choose to enter that space to benefit from this valuable resource. ● Communication avenues.
The committee will be charged with designing communication avenues and reporting protocols that will guarantee protections of privacy and confidentiality to those who choose to use this valuable resource. ● Digital space.
The committee will be responsible for the redesign of the Office of the Ombuds website to improve its online visibility so that the Office functions as the first stop in the reporting line.
The website must include clear messaging that is aligned with the University Manual, a more effective and reliable submission mechanism, clear expectations regarding potential courses of action and outcomes, and any other additional information that would enhance the user experience.

Instead of a prescribed sequence of environmental related courses, student will be able to concentrate in an area of interest utilizing pre-existing environmentally-related courses across the curriculum.

passages.heading: 24-25-16 | Page 2
passages.text:
However, upon inception of the bachelor's degree program, the department was hesitant to use the long degree name.
Over time, the exclusion of the biomedical sciences in the name has led to a false perception by students and potential employers that the area is not a focus of the program.
A name change for the program to Biomedical and Pharmaceutical Sciences is being proposed to more fully characterize the program, its offerings, and potential student opportunities.
Biomedical sciences and pharmaceutical sciences have alway been included in the program description.
The changes being made to the program description involve the changing of the degree name.
The addition of health professions programs as an opportunity for graduates has also been added.
Other minor edits to clarify catalog language have been made.

For example, pre-health professional students can now take PSY or SOC courses to meet basic requirements for applying to medical, dental, or other health profession schools while students wishing to minor in business could continue to take ECN 201. Edited curriculum sheets are attached to reflect the removal of ECN 201 as a requirement. Freshman and sophomore year students will identify and describe the influences of social, economic, and cultural identity on access to and engagement in environmental education programs and services, with particular attention to barriers faced by historically underrepresented populations.
In addition, they will learn how development has negatively and positively impacted human relationships with the environment and the developed environment's impacts on the quality of life.
As juniors and seniors they will learn how data science is changing what we know about environmental justice.
They will engage in critical conversations, service learning projects, and research to collect and display data to influence policy makers, and to educate people of all ages and abilities to take positive actions toward a healthy and just society.
An Environmental Education Major at URI supports URI's mission to enrich the lives of students, the community, and beyond through the values of a land and sea grant institution.
Students and faculty will learn and lead together to sustain and improve the conditions for all people locally and across the globe.

passages.heading: 24-25-16 | Page 10
passages.text:
The new program will offer unique, creative and interdisciplinary research experiences by embedding students with an education focus into current STEM research and into the work of environmental community partners.
The program will step beyond traditional classroom lectures to engage students in place-based learning experiences and civic involvement projects.
The program will support FOCUS URI, the Strategic Vision for the University priorities.
A few examples of how this program would meet those priorities are: Priority 1 Broaden Our Impact: Goal 1 Contribute to broad and deep impacts on the social, cultural, and economic ecosystems across Rhode Island, the nation, and beyond.
Action 1: Position URI as a vital partner and dynamic leader in solutions-based societal change.
The program aims to create leaders who are capable and confident to promote knowledge and skills to a wide audience to broaden participation in solution-based action.
Action 2: Strengthen relationships with local, state, and federal agencies, as well as community organizations, to identify and implement impactful societal, cultural, and economic initiatives.

passages.heading: 24-25-16 | Page 10
passages.text:
The EE program was initiated by community organizations such as the Roger Williams Park Zoo, Save the Bay, and Audubon Society who would like to (1) work more closely with URI on research and outreach (2) would like to have knowledgeable and skilled people apply to their entry level positions and (3) partner as leaders to influence local policy.
Field experiences and internships would develop partnerships with 54 organizational members of the Rhode Island Environmental Association.
In addition, the program would work closely with the North American Association of Environmental Education to become one of the few (less than 5) undergraduate accredited programs in the country.
Action 3: Foster meaningful engagement with alumni, parents, and friends of URI.
Designed into the new program will be a 21st century portfolio assessment system that will include students in a leadership role during a community event day in which students of the program engage alumni, parents, friends, AND future URI generations in learning about research and local impacts on the environment.

passages.heading: 24-25-16 | Page 10
passages.text:
Priority 2 Enhance Student Achievement Goal 1 Continuously invigorate the learning environment to reflect active learning; student agency; and contemporary, high-impact learning pedagogies.
The EE program will intentionally break traditional teaching methods by using the forests, the coastlines, and other natural and designed environments as classroom spaces.
The high-impact place-based instruction has potential to attract and retain a more diverse student population and may provide a model and tools for other additional programs to move toward flexible use of classroom space.

Kingston Proposed Fall 2025 Existing No Date Chosen Changes Program Description The four-year program offers students a solid foundation in the basic sciences and expertise within the pharmaceutical and biomedical sciences.
It is designed to provide educational and training experiences that prepare students for careers in the pharmaceutical, consumer product, and biomedical industries, and health professions.
Graduates of the B.S.P.S.in Biomedical and Pharmaceutical Sciences program will be qualified to seek a diverse range of career options that include: research and development, manufacturing, product marketing, sales, quality, and administrative positions within the pharmaceutical industry; research and regulatory oversight careers within government agencies; and research and teaching positions in academia.
As a prelude to many of these career opportunities, the program prepares students for graduate studies in the expanding fields of pharmaceutical and biomedical sciences.

passages.heading: 24-25-16 | Page 18

In addition, the program will fulfill basic science requirements and provide further expertise for students applying to health professional schools.
The science component of the curriculum is consistent with the admission requirements of many basic science graduate programs and health professional schools.
Biomedical and Pharmaceutical Sciences courses offered in the third and fourth year are taught by Department of Biomedical and Pharmaceutical Sciences (BPS) and Department of Pharmacy Practice (PHP) faculty.
They provide solid, fundamental training in the biomedical and pharmaceutical sciences.
Students have the option to tailor their academic program to prepare them for the specific career paths that they choose by taking 18 credits of pre-approved B.S.P.S.
Professional Electives.
At least 9 of the 18 credits of Professional Electives must be under BPS, PHP, or PHC course codes.
The Associate Dean, in consultation with the BPS Department Chair and the B.S.P.S.BPS Program Director, will maintain a list of approved Professional Electives so that the list can be updated regularly to reflect new and obsolete courses.

A minimum total of a 120 credits is required for graduation.
The curriculum can be described in three distinct components.
One component consists of University General Education which is required of all University graduates.
The second component consists of science and mathematics pre-requisite courses that will deliver a firm foundation in the life and physical sciences and satisfy admission requirement for many basic science graduate programs and health professional schools.
The third component is the B.S.P.S. upper-level courses and labs in the major offering students a strong understanding of the pharmaceutical and biomedical sciences.
Within the third component, students have the option to tailor their academic program to prepare them for the specific career paths that they choose by applying up to 18 credits of pre- approved Professional Electives toward the minimum 120 credits required for the degree.
At least 9 of the 18 credits of Professional Elective credits must be under the BPS, PHP, or PHC course codes.

Experiential Education Experiential education can lead to a deeper understanding of subject matter than is possible through classroom study alone and can increase the capacity for critical thinking and application of knowledge in complex situations.
By using structured reflection, students have the opportunity to link experience with theory and, thereby, deepen their understanding and ability to use what they know.

passages.heading: 24-25-16 | Page 20
passages.text:
In addition, experiential education has value building inter-personal skills, work ethic, and practical expertise that are critical for students seeking employment in the pharmaceutical science industry.
Experiential Education requirement may be satisfied through one of the following: (1) 6-credits of BPS 497/498 (Pharmaceutical Science Independent Study), (2) 6-credits of BPS 460 (Pharm Science Internship), or (3) an approved external internship with minimum of 260 hours and enrollment in BPS 460 for zero credits.
Credit-bearing experiences should consist of 43 hr of work per credit.
All courses and/or internships must be approved by the pharmaceutical sciences Experiential Education Coordinator.
A standardized learning contract must be completed for each experience regardless of attached credits.
Course codes CHE491/492, CHM353/354, CMB499, HPR401, PHP497/498 with collaborating faculty may be accepted with prior approval.
Must earn Satisfactory in an S/U graded course.
Must earn passing (>D) in A-F graded course.

Combined Degrees Working in collaboration with the College of Arts and Sciences, B.S.P.S. students can earn a second degree (B.A.) in a foreign language while in the College of Pharmacy.
Earning the two degrees extends the program of study from 4 years to 5 years and includes an international year of study abroad where the student takes general education, language, and field experience courses in the pharmaceutical sciences.
Upon graduation, students are able to compete in the global marketplace and are fluent in a second language.
Present opportunities exist for experiences in Italy and Germany.

passages.text: FACULTY SENATE OFFICE FACULTY SENATE LEGISLATION JANUARY 23, 2025 Curriculum & Standards Committee Report 2024-2025-05B At the December 19, 2024 meeting of the Curriculum & Standards Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate for approval. Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation By The Faculty Senate PROGRAM MODIFICATIONS COLLEGE OF ARTS & SCIENCES: BA Criminology & Criminal Justice, Effective Fall 2025 Appendix A CCJ seeks to add 3 new elective classes to its curriculum. CCJ 285 and CCJ 456 have been approved by the CCJ faculty as criminal justice elective options for majors and CCJ 334 has been approved as a criminology elective. CCJ 285 (Fac Sen Bill # 23-24-19) and 456 (Fac Sen Bill # 24-25-01) have been fully routed and approved through the curriculum process. CCJ 334 is currently being routed through the process (submitted for the October 14 A&S curriculum committee meeting) but we seek to include the class in this NOC of change to reduce the need for curriculum modifications moving forward as the department intends to offer this class as soon as the 25-26 AY. BFA Theatre, Effective Fall 2025 Appendix B Changes approved for addition of THE200 to the curriculum per Faculty Senate Bill # 22-23-39A passed and signed by President on 23.04.20. This course (THE200) replaces two previous courses: THE291 (2 cr) and THE391 (2 cr). It is intended to make the production courses less complicated and confusing for students, allowing for consistency of the numbering system.

COLLEGE OF EDUCATION: BS Health & Physical Education, Effective Fall 2025 Appendix C Curricular changes are intended to align with national norms and availability of university course offerings.
The changes will offer students flexibility to select professional electives that closely align with their unique career goals in health and physical education.
COLLEGE OF THE ENVIRONMENT & LIFE SCIENCES: BS Geology & Geological Oceanography, Effective Fall 2025 Appendix D The current program has two options (Geology option and Geological Oceanography option).
We propose to add the Water and Climate Sciences as a third option.
The total number of credits in intro & professional courses, core geosciences and option specific courses, electives and supporting sciences is not changing, i.e. the number of credits will be comparable to the currently existing options.
However, option specific core course GEO 200, GEO 234 and GE0 280 replace GEO 210, GEO 320, GEO 370 and GEO 450.
Please refer to the advising sheet for the new Water and Climate Sciences option.
Copies of the existing (unchanged) advising sheet for the other two options are included for reference.

passages.text:

Existing courses added to the revised core program are taught at a frequency that ensures degree completion in four years.
All existing classes have the capacity to accommodate additional inflow of students or, if needed, new class sections can be opened.
Students in the current options will not be affected by the proposed changes.
NEW SPECIALIZATIONS COLLEGE OF THE ENVIRONMENT & LIFE SCIENCES: Specialization in Water & Climate Science (BS Geology & Geological Oceanography), Effective Fall 2025 Appendix E The specialization in Water and Climate Sciences allows students the flexibility to define their own area of concentration within the water and climate sciences.
Example areas of concentration include environmental geology/ hydrogeology, and climate.
Students will be well prepared to pursue careers in environmental consulting, water resource management, sustainability initiatives, climate adaptation and resilience, and the emerging field of climate analytics.
These career opportunities are available with national and international government agencies, non-profit organizations, and the private sector.

passages.text: COLLEGE OF HEALTH SCIENCES: Specialization in Kinesiology (BS Kinesiology), Effective Fall 2025 Appendix F The Kinesiology Track provides flexibility to choose professional electives appropriate for a wide range of health and exercise science related careers. It is appropriate for students interested in pursuing health care professions such as physical therapy, chiropractic, medical doctor, or physician’s assistant or in becoming an exercise physiologist, strength and conditioning specialist, occupational therapist or health coach. Career opportunities exist in corporate, community, commercial and hospital-based fitness and wellness centers. The Kinesiology track will also prepare students for graduate study in clinical exercise physiology, cardiac rehabilitation, exercise science, health fitness, health promotion, preventive medicine and related fields. Kinesiology students will be prepared to become a certified professional in specialty areas including exercise physiology, strength and conditioning and/or personal training. The Kinesiology Track requirements include: 1. One of: PSY 200, STA 220, 307, or 308 2. 12 credits from the list of professional electives, with a minimum of 6 credits from KIN courses: CHM 105, 124, 126; CMB 210; EDC/HLT 401; KIN 125, 243, 369, 375G, 414, 425, 464G, 482; NUT 360; PSY 255. Other KIN or health-related courses may apply with approval from the KIN Department Chair. Additionally, there are free electives. Any student interested in graduate education should check programs of interest for prerequisites. Free electives can be used to satisfy those prerequisites.

The Department of Criminology and Criminal Justice offers a Bachelor of Arts (B.A.) degree.
The interdisciplinary degree in Criminology and Criminal Justice provides students with a wide range of course options so that students may tailor their learning to their educational and professional interests.
Our purpose is to empower our graduates to meaningfully consider, contribute to, and reimagine discourses and decisions about crime and justice.
The CCJ Department does this by making intentional choices about our work and remaining committed to continual professional growth and community building.
The program requires 30-49 credits in the major including CCJ/SOC 230(H) (with a grade of C or better), CCJ/PSC 274(H) (with a grade of C or better), and one of three capstone classes: CCJ 403, CCJ 410 or CCJ/PSC 476.
Students must select one research methods course from the following: ECN 306, PSC 310, PSY 200, or SOC 301.

passages.heading: Curriculum & Standards Committee Report #2024-2025-05B | Page 8
passages.text:
Students are required to take six elective courses selected from the following two areas: criminology electives – AAF 230; CCJ 200 (approved topics), 334, 370, 400 (approved topics), 403, 410, 450, 476; AAF/HIS 366; PHL 318; PSY 254, 466; SOC 420; criminal justice electives – AAF 230; CCJ 200 (approved topics), 280, 285, 290,,, 332, 333, 381 (must be taken in combination with CHM 391 and/or ITR 305 for a total of 3 credits to count as 1 elective class), 456, 480, 490, 400 (approved topics), 403, 410, 476; CHM 391 (must either be repeated 3 times or taken in combination with CCJ 381 and/or ITR 305 for a total of 3 credits to count as 1 elective class); CCJ/HIS 361, AAF/HIS 366; ITR 305 (must be taken in combination with CHM 391 and/or CCJ 381 for a total of 3 credits to count as 1 elective class) PSC 334, 371, 388, 472; PSY 465; SOC 303.
At least two courses must be taken from each elective area and no more than four courses can be taken in either area.
All electives must be a minimum of 3 credits.
While CCJ 403, 410, and CCJ/PSC 476 are each capstone classes and electives, students may not use the same course to count as both a capstone and an elective class.

passages.heading: Curriculum & Standards Committee Report #2024-2025-05B | Page 8
passages.text:
When appropriate, and by permission of the Department Chair, students may substitute internship credit (SOC 477, PSC 375/376, PSY 305, or GWS 300) or independent study credit (CCJ 485, SOC 498/499, PSC 455/456, PSY 489, or GWS 450) for one of their elective courses listed above.
No more than 3 credits may be used toward the major from internship or independent study.
Internal transfers into the CCJ major form a different major, or students wishing to add the CCJ major to their current major, must have a minimum 2.50 GPA.
A total of 120 credits is required for graduation.
At least 30 of these credits must be in courses at the 300-level or above.
In order to transfer into the criminology and criminal justice B.A. program from University College for Academic Success, a student must have completed at least 24 credits and have an earned a minimum of a 2.0 GPA.

As the interests and career opportunities for our students have become more diverse, we are seeking to allow more flexibility in selecting professional electives most appropriate for each individual.
The best preparation for many students is something in between our existing Pre-Professional Exercise Science and Applied Exercise Science specializations.
Additionally, it is currently difficult for students who begin in the Pre-Professional Exercise Science specialization and then realize it is not the best fit to change to the Applied Exercise Science specialization without impeding progress toward graduation.
This proposal combines the Professional Content Area courses from each of those specializations into a single list of Professional Electives students can select from.
It will replace the existing Pre-Professional and Applied Exercise Science specialization options in the catalog, but in practice will allow students to choose Professional Electives aligning with either of those specializations or a combination of the two.

passages.heading: Curriculum & Standards Committee Report #2024-2025-05B | Page 58
passages.text:
The Kinesiology program is currently accredited by the Committee on Accreditation for the Exercise Sciences and this proposal will not change anything associated with that accreditation.
This specialization continues to provide opportunities for students to participate in the department's active research program and community engagement opportunities through active learning courses and internships in alignment with the University's Mission.
It provides the basic science and core kinesiology content area background as well as professional elective options necessary to prepare students for careers that have a great impact on social, cultural, and economic ecosystems in RI and beyond (Strategic Plan Goal 1) including many in healthcare.
The specialization allows students opportunities for study abroad and international internship experiences such as the TEAN program placing our majors in internships in Australia (Strategic Plan Goal 2 Action 3).
Students will also be able to gain hands on research experience working with faculty throughout the department (Strategic Plan Goal 3).

passages.heading: Curriculum & Standards Committee Report #2024-2025-05B | Page 58
passages.text:
The only specializations this overlaps with are our department's current specializations of Pre-Professional Exercise Science and Applied Exercise Science.
This proposal will replace both of those with this single Kinesiology specialization, so there will be no lasting conflicts or overlaps.
Students currently in the Pre-Professional Exercise Science and Applied Exercise Science specializations will be able to complete the programs they have already started, and incoming students will be entered into the new Kinesiology specialization.

COLLEGE OF HEALTH SCIENCES: BS Human Development and Family Science, Effective Fall 2025 Appendix H Proposals to change the number of course credits in HDF 306, 308, 310, 312, and 314 from 4 to 3 have been approved at the department and college levels, and are now in progress through Faculty Senate.
Thus, updates are needed to the total number of credits for these courses.
Also, the language referring to "experiential I, II" can be deleted because HDF is now referring to these courses as "applied development;" this terminology is more consistent with use in the academic discipline.
Because of the change of these classes from 4 to 3 credits, the HDF undergraduate major credits would be reduced by 2 credits; thus, the department approved adding one 3-credit HDF elective--for a total of 12, instead of 9, HDF elective credits.
This means that instead of 50 total major credits, students will take 51 major credits.
Additionally, students no longer are restricted from taking additional applied development courses as HDF electives.
Finally, because of the increase of HDF elective credits, no more than 6 (instead of 3) may be at the 200 or lower level.

passages.heading: 24-25-14 | Page 4
passages.text:
To clean up other changes that are not yet reflected in the HDF undergraduate major description, the following updates can be made to the list of gen ed courses: -add HDF 200 (previously approved through Faculty Senate); -add HDF 250 (recently approved by department and college; now in progress through Faculty Senate); and -delete 412 (previously approved to move from HDF to LDR through Faculty Senate).
Certificate in Early Intervention, Effective Fall 2025 Appendix I We, along with the Part C Coordinator at the RI Executive Office of Health and Human Services, propose to eliminate HDF 342 (Working with Families in Early Childhood) from the required Early Intervention Certificate Courses.
Upon running HDF 342 along with the other core EI Certificate courses for the first time during the 2024-2025 academic year, it became apparent that the content in HDF 342 greatly overlapped with the 4 other EI courses.
For example, the main purpose of HDF 342 was to introduce students to best practices in working with families (e.g., effective communication).
These strategies are covered in depth in HDF 341 and 343.

passages.heading: 24-25-14 | Page 4
passages.text:
In fact, students in HDF 341 and 343 will receive hands-on practice with these strategies through the application of relevant screening and assessment tools used in the field of Early Intervention.
Another key emphasis in HDF 342 is cultural competence.
However, cultural competence and humility is already emphasized in each of the other four core courses, especially HDF 306.
For example, students in HDF 306 complete a paper on using a cultural competence framework in working with families of infants and toddlers.
Considering the overlap in content amongst HDF 342 and all other core courses, it is recommended to remove HDF 342 as a requirement from the EI certificate.
The changes proposed here include: 1). removing HDF 342 from the certificate, and 2). reflecting that change in the program description (i.e., from "five course" to "four", and "16 credits" to "12 credits".
Please note that our department has another Kuali proposal to move HDF 306 from 4 credits to 3 credits.
The changes reflected here assume that HDF 306 will be only 3 credits beginning in the fall of 2025.
These changes are supported by the Rhode Island Executive Office of Health and Human Services.

passages.text: Please see the attached email from the RI Part C Coordinator, Jennifer Kaufman who confirms that removing HDF 342 from the URI Early Intervention Certificate will not impact how the state appraises graduates with the certificate from URI.

The Master of Science (M.S.) and the Accelerated Bachelor's to Masters (ABM) programs are described below and in the Graduate Programs section.
The Textile, Fashion Merchandising and Design major is open to prospective students who have a professional interest in the artistic and technical aspects of the subject.
Specialized programs of study prepare students for careers in the design, development, manufacture, and merchandising of textiles, apparel, and interior furnishings.
Qualified students can prepare for graduate studies.
The following core courses are required: TMD 103G, 123, 126, 203, 213, 224, 232, 390, 433; one of the following: TMD 240, 426, 440, or 441; ART 101, 120, 207, 251, or 252; CHM 101 and 102 or 103 and 105; ECN 201 and 202; one of the following natural sciences: AFS 190, PLS 190, PHY 111/185, PHY 112/186, or NFS 207/210, and CSC 101.

passages.heading: 24-25-14 | Page 29

Students should choose TMD electives and professional electives in consultation with an academic advisor.
Students must complete 24 credits,including TMD 103G and 123, with an overall 2.0 GPA to transfer from University College to the College of Business (The same requirements apply to students wishing to transfer into TMD from other majors.).
To complement classroom and laboratory/studio instruction, internships and study abroad are encouraged.
A total of 120 credits and a 2.0 GPA is required for graduation.

Fall 2024 Changes Program Description Civil Engineering The Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering (CVE) offers a curriculum leading to the Bachelor of Science (B.S.) degree in civil engineering.
The civil engineering program is accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission (EAC) of ABET, Inc.(www.abet.org) under the commission’s General Criteria and Program Criteria for Civil and Similarly Named Engineering Programs.
The department also offers a minor in environmental engineering and the Master of Science (M.S.) and Doctor of Philosophy (Ph.D.) degrees in civil and environmental engineering.
Faculty: Faculty: Professor Baxter, Chairperson; Professors Bradshaw, Gindy, Lee, Oyanedel-Craver, Parlange, and Tsiatas; Associate Professors Akanda, Das, Goodwill, Hunter, Thiem, and Thomas; Assistant Professors Abbas and Amini; Associate Teaching Professor Rahmani; Professors Emeriti Marcus, McEwen, Poon, Silva, Urish, and Wright.
Department Mission Statement.

passages.heading: 24-25-14 | Page 39
passages.text:
Consistent with the missions of the University of Rhode Island and the College of Engineering (COE), the department of civil and environmental engineering seeks to prepare students to practice professionally in the national and international marketplace in the field of civil and environmental engineering through the provision of high quality undergraduate and graduate educational programs and research opportunities; provide an environment that encourages and supports faculty career development and professional/community service; actively promotes diversity; and maintain a nationally recognized research program.
Program Mission Statement.
Consistent with the mission of the department of civil and environmental engineering, the B.S. in civil engineering (BSCE) program will prepare graduates for successful careers, advanced studies at the graduate level, and lifelong learning based upon a solid foundation of technical ability, high standards of professional ethics, and strong communication skills.
Program Educational Objectives.

passages.heading: 24-25-14 | Page 39
passages.text:
Three to five years after graduation from the B.S. in civil engineering, graduates will : 1) Practice and actively contribute to the civil engineering profession in one or more of the technical areas of environmental, geotechnical, structural, transportation, and water resources engineering. 2) Practice civil engineering with an awareness of and commitment to ethics and social responsibility, sustainability, and diversity both as individuals and in team environments. 3) Pursue life-long learning through graduate education, professional licensure, or advanced training in civil engineering or related fields.
Student Outcomes.
Civil engineering students demonstrate knowledge in all outcomes required by ABET, Inc. which are listed in the college’s student outcomes section of this catalog.
Program Description.
Civil engineers are responsible for researching, developing, planning, designing, constructing, and managing many of the complex systems and facilities essential to modern civilization.

passages.heading: 24-25-14 | Page 39
passages.text:
These include environmental engineering systems; water supply and pollution control systems; all types of transportation systems, from pipelines to city streets; structural systems from residential buildings to city skyscrapers, power plants, and offshore platforms; and all types of geotechnical systems from foundations to dams.
Civil engineers play important roles in planning and administration with government agencies at all levels, especially those dealing with public works, transportation, environmental control, water supply, and renewable energy.
The curriculum provides students with an excellent background to pursue graduate study or to enter directly into professional Appendix D Page 5 of 11

passages.heading: 24-25-14 | Page 40
passages.text:
practice in industry or government after graduation.
The first year is devoted largely to courses in mathematics, chemistry, physics, and engineering science common to all engineering curriculums.
During the sophomore year, students take three courses in civil engineering including mechanics of materials and two laboratories.
In their last two years, students develop a proficiency in environmental engineering, geotechnical engineering, structural engineering, and transportation engineering.
They can also meet their own professional goals through the selection of professional electives in these areas as well as construction management.
Professional electives are selected in consultation with the student’s advisor.
The civil engineering major requires 126 credits.
Freshman Year First semester: 15 credits CHM 101 (3), 102 (1); ECN 201 (3); EGR 105 (1); MTH 141 (4); and general education outcome(s)1 (3).
Second semester: 17 credits EGR 106 (2); GEO 103 (4); MTH 142 (4); PHY 203 (3), 273 (1); and general education outcome(s)1 (3).
Sophomore Year First semester: 17 credits CVE 205 (1); MCE 262 (3); MTH 243 (3); and PHY 204 (3), 274 (1); STA 409 (3); and WRT 332 (3).

passages.heading: 24-25-14 | Page 40
passages.text:
Second semester: 16 credits CHM 112 (3); CVE 220 (3), 230 (1), 250 (3); MCE 263 (3); and MTH 244 (3).
Junior Year First semester: 17 credits CVE 346 (3), 354 (3), 355 (1), 374 (3), 381 (3), 382 (1); and MCE 354 (3).
Second semester: 14 credits CVE 347 (3), 348 (1), 370 (3), 375 (1); ISE 304 (3) ; and professional elective2 (3).
Senior Year First semester: 15 credits CVE 400 (1), 465 (3), 483 (3), 497 (2) [capstone]; and professional electives2 (6).
Second semester: 15 credits CVE 498 (3) [capstone]; professional electives2 (6); general education outcome(s)1 (6); and take the Fundamentals of Engineering (FE) Examination3. 1 General Education Outcomes (A1-D1): if all outcomes are satisfied in fewer spaces than provided, you must take a course(s) of your choice (Free Elective) to ensure you have earned at least 120 credits as required to earn a BS degree.
A complete detailing of these requirements are listed in the college’s curriculum requirements section of this catalog. 2 Professional Elective Requirements: Three (3) of the fifteen (15) credits must be selected from the following courses: CVE 470, 471, 475, 477.

passages.heading: 24-25-14 | Page 40
passages.text:
The remaining twelve (12) credits can be any 300-level and above CVE courses and may include three (3) credits from the following courses: CHE 333, ELE 220, MCE 341, or MTH 215.

Changes Program Description Computer Engineering The Bachelor of Science (B.S.) degree in computer engineering is offered by the Department of Electrical, Computer, and Biomedical Engineering (ECBE).
The computer engineering program is accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission (EAC) of ABET, Inc. (www.abet.org), under the commission’s General Criteria and Program Criteria for Electrical, Computer, Communications, Telecommunication(s), and Similarly Named Engineering Programs.
Specialization in computer engineering is also available within the Graduate Certificate in Embedded Systems, as well as the Master of Science (M.S.) and Doctor of Philosophy (Ph.D.) programs in Electrical Engineering.
The department also offers the Bachelor of Science (B.S.) in Electrical Engineering and Bachelor of Science (B.S.) in Biomedical Engineering. & Department Faculty: Professor Sun, Chairperson; Professors Besio, He, Kumaresan, Lo, Mankodiya, Sendag, Sunak, Swaszek, Vaccaro, and Yang; Associate Professors Shahriari, Stegagno, and Vetter; Assistant Professors Abiri, Adhikari, Bi, Jeong, Jia, Kim, and H.

Program Educational Objectives.
Three to five years after graduation from the B.S. in Computer Engineering, graduates will: 1) Successfully practice computer engineering to serve state/regional industries, government agencies, or national/international industries;2) Work professionally in the areas of Computer Engineering including but not limited to: computer hardware and software design, embedded systems, computer networks and security, cloud computing, machine learning, robotics, IC design; Achieve personal and professional success with awareness and commitment to their ethical and environments ; and 4) social responsibilities, both as individuals and in team Maintain and improve their technical competence through lifelong learning, including entering and succeeding in an advanced degree program in a field such as engineering, science, or business.
Student Outcomes.
Computer engineering students demonstrate knowledge in all outcomes required by ABET, Inc. which are listed in the college’s student outcomes section of this catalog.

passages.heading: 24-25-14 | Page 50
passages.text:
Program Description.
Digital computer and communication systems have transformed society in a profound way.
The examples range from super powerful scientific computers, to embedded systems such as smart phones, internet of things (IoT), and smart cities.
Traditionally, computer engineering has been a discipline that combines both electrical engineering and computer science.
The URI computer engineering program is thus designed so the students will have a strong foundation in the relevant fields of electrical engineering and computer science, while establishing themselves with the latest computer engineering topics, such as advanced computer architecture, computer network and cyber-physical security, big data learning and processing, and field programmable gate array (FPGA).

passages.heading: 24-25-14 | Page 50
passages.text:
The computer engineering core courses can be categorized as follows: (1) ELE 208/209, 305, and 408/409 are core courses for computer system architecture and hardware and software organization and interaction. (2) ELE 201/202, 301/302, and 405/406 are the core courses for digital design with electronic design automation and rapid prototyping, and for computer system integration. (3) ELE 313 and 437 are core courses for computer communication and networks.
The computer engineering program has three professional electives in the senior year so students can further expand into areas such as signals and systems, digital control, electronics, and computer software.
The computer engineering program culminates in the senior year with two major design experiences.
ELE 408/409 is where all the skills accumulated through the curriculum will be employed in a group senior design project.
ELE 480 and 481 provide each student with the opportunity to work in a multi-disciplinary team in a senior capstone design project.

passages.text:
Graduates from the program go on to positions in both government agencies and the private sector, or enter graduate school for further study.
Many computer engineering undergraduate students work with faculty on research projects before entering graduate school.
The computer engineering major requires 121–124 credits.

Second semester: 15 credits CSC 211 (4); ELE 212 (4), 215 (1); MTH 243 (3); and general education outcome(s)1 (3).

Second semester: 16 credits ELE 301 (3), 302 (1), 305 (3); MTH 451 (3); and general education outcome(s)1 (6).
Senior Year First semester: 14–15 credits ELE 400 (1), 405 (3), 406 (1), 437 (3), 480 (3) [capstone]; and approved professional elective2 (3-4).

International Engineering Program (IEP).
In conjunction with the College of Arts and Sciences, the COE offers a five-year program in which students earn two degrees: a Bachelor of Science (B.S.) in engineering and a Bachelor of Arts (B.A.) in a foreign language.
Minor in Computer Engineering.
Minors require the completion of 18 or more credits.

passages.heading: 24-25-14 | Page 51
passages.text:
A minimum grade point average of 2.00 must be earned in the minor courses, and at least 12 of the 18 credits must be at the 200 level or above.
At least half of the credits required for the minor must be earned at the University of Rhode Island.
General education requirements may be used for the minor, but no course may be used for both the major and minor field of study.
Minor courses may not be taken on a pass-fail basis.
Students interested in pursuing a minor in computer engineering should speak with the department chairperson to discuss specific course requirements.

No Date Chosen Changes Program Description Biological Sciences BACHELOR OF SCIENCE IN BIOLOGICAL SCIENCES A B.S. in Biological Sciences prepares students for careers in the life sciences and health professions.
Graduates are employed in the public and private sectors or continue their training for careers in medicine, dentistry, veterinary medicine, or other professions that require post-graduate training.
The major provides foundational training in biological and physical sciences with flexibility to specialize in sub-disciplines such as biodiversity, ecology, evolution, genetics, physiology, or molecular, cellular, or developmental biology.
Laboratory, field, and seminar courses build skills in experimental design and interpretation and promote awareness of the impacts of science on humans and the environment.
Students selecting a major in biological sciences must complete at least 35 credits in BIO including 101 or 101H/103, 102/104 and 352 (12 credits).

passages.heading: 24-25-14 | Page 60
passages.text:
The remaining 23 credits must include at least one course from each of three of the following five core areas: cell and development (BIO 302, 311, 341); ecology and evolution (BIO 262, 272); molecular biology (BIO 437); organismal diversity (BIO 308, 310, 321, 323, 354, 365, 366, 385, 404, 412, 417); physiology (BIO 201, 220/221, 222/223, 242/244, 346).
These 23 credits must also include at least one course from list A (plant biology), one course from ist B (animal biology), and at least three BIO laboratory courses in addition to 103 and 104 and excluding 491 and 492.
BIO 105, 181G, 286 and 498 are not for major credit.
Students must complete CHM 101, 102, 112, 114 or CHM 191, 192; CHM 226, 227, 228 or CHM 124, 126, CMB 311; CMB 201 or 211; MTH 131 or 141; MTH132 or 142 or STA 308; PHY 111, 112, 185, 186 or PHY 203, 204, 273, 274; and WRT 104 or 106.
Up to three credits of independent study or special topics (491 and 492) in the following disciplines may be applied toward the major requirements: AFS, AVS, BIO, CMB, NRS, and PLS.
List A (plant biology): BIO 308, 310, 311, 321, 323, 332, 346, 365, 416.

passages.heading: 24-25-14 | Page 60
passages.text:
List B (animal biology): BIO 121, 201, 220, 221, 222, 223, 242, 244, 300, 301, 302, 354, 350, 355, 366, 385, 388, 404, 412, 417, 419, 422, 425G, 444, 467.
Students must maintain a 2.00 grade point average in BIO courses used to meet the major requirements.
A total of 120 credits is required for graduation.
In order to transfer from University College for Academic Success to the College of the Environment and Life Sciences as a Biological Sciences major (or be coded as such in the College of the Environment and Life Sciences), a student must have earned 30 credits including BIO 101 or 101H, 103, 102, 104 with grades of C or better; CHM 101 with a grade of C- or better.
May not be combined with a B.A. in Biology.

BACHELOR OF SCIENCE IN MARINE BIOLOGY The B.S. in Marine Biology allows students to explore the vast world of marine biology while providing an important foundation in modern biological sciences.
It is designed for students who plan to work in marine biology, biological oceanography, marine conservation, or related fields at a professional level, or who wish to apply their training to a wide range of other exciting careers in the public and private sectors.
We encourage students to participate in lab, field, and shipboard research with faculty members.
Graduates work in marine and environmental science and policy, or continue their education in veterinary school or in graduate school in a wide range of fields.
A minimum of 36 credits is required and must include BIO 101 or 101H/103, 102/104, 130, 352 and 360 (17 credits) and at least one course from each of three of the following five areas: cell and developmental biology (BIO 302, 311, 341); ecology and evolution (BIO 262, 272); molecular biology (BIO 437); organismal diversity (BIO 308, 310, 321, 323, 354, 365, 366, 385, 404, 412, 417, 425G; CMB 211); physiology (BIO 201, 346).

passages.heading: 24-25-14 | Page 69
passages.text:
The balance of the 36 credits must be selected from among the marine biology electives: AFS 415, 486; AVS 440, BIO 256G, 308, 310, 345, 354, 355, 365, 412, 416, 422, 425G, 455, 457, 469, 475, 485, 563; NRS 475; OCE 575; OCG 420, 480, 561, 576.
Students are encouraged to participate in research; up to three credits of independent study or special topics (BIO 491, 492, 495) in the following disciplines may be applied toward this requirement: AFS, AVS, BIO, CMB, NRS, OCE, OCG and PLS.
Students must take at least two BIO laboratory courses in addition to 103, 104 and 360, and excluding 491, 492, and 495.
In addition, students must take CHM 101, 102, 112, 114 or CHM 191, 192; CHM 226, 227, 228 or CHM 124,126, CMB 311; MTH 131 or 132; MTH 141 or 142 or STA 308; OCG 301 or 451; PHY 111, 112, 185, 186 or PHY 203, 204, 273, 274; and WRT 104 or 106.
Students must maintain a 2.00 grade point average in BIO courses used to meet the minimum of 36 credits for the major.
A total of 120 credits is required for graduation.

May not be combined with a B.S. in Biological Sciences or a B.A. in Biology The Minor.
The minor in marine biology requires at least 20 credits, including 8 credits of general biology (BIO 101/103 and 102/104, or equivalent, e.g., Advanced Placement), marine biology (BIO 360), and at least 8 additional credits chosen from among courses counted as marine biology electives for the B.S. degree in marine biology.
A maximum of 3 credits in research (e.g., BIO 491, 492) may be counted towards the minor.
At least half of the credits for the minor must be earned at URI.
A minimum GPA of 2.00 must be earned in the credits required for the minor.
Application for a minor must be filed with the coordinator of the Marine Biology Program prior to the completion of the first semester of the senior year.

The curriculum in human development and family science (HDF) leads to a Bachelor of Science degree.
HDF also offers a Master of Science degree with the following concentrations: Couple and Family Therapy, and Developmental Science.
The M.S. in Developmental Science includes an Accelerated Bachelors to Masters (ABM) option for students enrolled in the Bachelor of Science in HDF degree, described below.
The Master of Science program is described in the Graduate Program section of this catalog.
The undergraduate B.S. curriculum provides a general background for work with children, families, and adults with multiple practicum and internship opportunities.
Many professions in human development and family science require academic work beyond the bachelor’s degree for continuing professional work and advancement.
Individuals with a baccalaureate degree are employed as professionals in preschools, early intervention programs, child care centers, senior centers, health institutions and hospitals, and in recreational, child guidance, social service, family financial services, and other community agencies.

Summary description and rationale of proposed changes to program.

We, along with the Part C Coordinator at the RI Executive Office of Health and Human Services, propose to eliminate HDF 342 (Working with Families in Early Childhood) from the required Early Intervention Certificate Courses.
Upon running HDF 342 along with the other core EI Certificate courses for the first time during the 2024-2025 academic year, it became apparent that the content in HDF 342 greatly overlapped with the 4 other EI courses.
For example, the main purpose of HDF 342 was to introduce students to best practices in working with families (e.g., effective communication).
These strategies are covered in depth in HDF 341 and 343.
In fact, students in HDF 341 and 343 will receive hands-on practice with these strategies through the application of relevant screening and assessment tools used in the field of Early Intervention.
Another key emphasis in HDF 342 is cultural competence.
However, cultural competence and humility is already emphasized in each of the other four core courses, especially HDF 306.

passages.heading: 24-25-14 | Page 90
passages.text:
For example, students in HDF 306 complete a paper on using a cultural competence framework in working with families of infants and toddlers.
Considering the overlap in content amongst HDF 342 and all other core courses, it is recommended to remove HDF 342 as a requirement from the EI certificate.
The changes proposed here include: 1). removing HDF 342 from the certificate, and 2). reflecting that change in the program description (i.e., from "five course" to "four", and "16 credits" to "12 credits".
Please note that our department has another Kuali proposal to move HDF 306 from 4 credits to 3 credits.
The changes reflected here assume that HDF 306 will be only 3 credits beginning in the fall of 2025.
These changes are supported by the Rhode Island Executive Office of Health and Human Services.
Please see the attached email from the RI Part C Coordinator, Jennifer Kaufman who confirms that removing HDF 342 from the URI Early Intervention Certificate will not impact how the state appraises graduates with the certificate from URI.

The primary goal of this certificate program is to ensure students: Develop comprehensive and collaboratively defined individualized family service and delivery plans to support families of children with diverse needs (birth to 3 years old).
This goal directly maps onto Strategy 1 of the Agenda for Change as all core courses teach strategies to promote inclusion of diverse families and parents in decision-making, goal setting, and service planning and delivery.
Further, all courses articulate a strengths-based approach to understanding and promoting growth and functioning for young children with disabilities.
Changes How does the program align with the University’s mission and current Academic Strategic Plan?
The certificate program strongly aligns with the URI’s mission to educate and enrich the lives of URI students and the broader Rhode Island community around issues related to diversity, fairness, and equity for one of the most vulnerable populations: young children with disabilities and their families.
Specifically, the program will align with URI’s goals to enhance student success and embrace diversity (see below).

passages.heading: 24-25-14 | Page 91
passages.text:
Goal 1 – Enhance student success Strategy 2 – Expand experiential learning opportunities The certificate program will enhance student success by offering an early experiential opportunity working in close proximity with infants and toddlers, as well as an optional experiential internship working with families and children receiving EI services.
Adoption of this certificate will greatly expand access to internship placements at EI programs in Rhode Island.
In our current work placing interns with EI programs, EI directors have been reluctant to offer internship opportunities to undergraduates because the state has few positions at the Early Interventionist I level, a position for those with a bachelor’s degree only.
With this certificate, students can be hired as provisional Early Interventionist IIs after their internship, a position with many openings in RI.
EI directors in Rhode Island have confirmed at interagency meetings that they will be greatly interested in providing internship opportunities to URI students in this certificate track, with the goal of hiring the student intern for full-time employment at the end of the internship or upon graduation.

passages.heading: 24-25-14 | Page 91
passages.text:
Goal 4 – Embrace diversity and social justice Strategy 3 - Create an active learning community among students, faculty, staff, and administrators that engages in open discourse and enhanced understanding about what it means to be a diverse and socially just community.
This certificate offers courses specifically addressing how to engage in inclusive and collaborative relationships with EI families, and with other professionals working with those family.
Readings, class discussions, and assignments across all courses have been developed to promote active consideration of the practices, knowledge, and perspectives needed to develop trust and respect for diverse families, and to ultimately foster culturally responsive partnerships that can address a family’s unique needs with cultural sensitivity.

These foci distinguish this program from any URI program including URI’s teacher education programs, which train educators for school-based delivery and focus on typically developing and older aged children, and EDC 402 (The Education of Special Needs Students), which does not emphasize developmental disabilities for children ages birth to three.

Graduates with BA/BS in relevant fields, such as Human Development, Communicative Disorders, Kinesiology who do not possess an additional degree or recognized certificate or licensure can only be hired for an entry level position (Early Interventionist I) and cannot advance without further education.

This proposed state recognized certificate program would allow bachelor’s degree graduates who have completed the certificate requirements to be initially hired at the Early Interventionist II level for a 1000 hour probationary period.
Upon successful completion of the probationary work, the individual would be hired as a regular employee at the EI II level.
Due to the Medicaid reimbursement formula, Early Interventionist I positions do not translate into fully billable hours at the same level as Early Interventionist II positions.
According to the RI Executive Office of Health and Human Services, the majority of EI programs in Rhode Island are phasing out the entry-level Early Interventionist I positions and replacing them with Early Interventionist II/specialist jobs.
Thus, there is a demand for Early Interventionist II specialists in Rhode Island and nationally.
The app, Indeed, shows multiple job openings in Rhode Island for positions that come under the Early Interventionist II umbrella, including Service Coordinator II, Early Intervention Educator, and Early Intervention Practitioner, with salaries ranging from $41,200 to $72,000.
The U.S.

Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) does not provide specific statistics on the growth in EI but a relevant career, early childcare special education teachers, is projected to experience an 8% increase in between 2016 and 2026 (BLS, 2022).
This certificate will provide a path to the Early Interventionist II position, by providing URI graduates with the specific qualifications needed for this position.
None.
We have developed this certificate in conjunction with the RI Executive Office of Health and Human Services’ Part C Coordinator, to directly meet the need for demand for qualified early intervention personnel in RI.
The EI Training and Technical Assistance office at the Paul V.

passages.heading: 24-25-14 | Page 93
passages.text:
Between 2019 and 2020, EI programs in RI reported a 33% average of staff turnover, with the highest turnover for Early Interventionist I (the lowest paid position in EI).
Due to the shortage of qualified applicants for Early Interventionist II positions, programs in RI such as Meeting Street are offering signing bonus to recruit applicants.
In terms of overall need for these services, there was an 88% delay or interruption of services to children due to staff turnover and shortages, as well as 88% of families withdrawing from EI services due to staff challenges and turnover in 2021 (RI KidsCount, 2021).
This shortage of qualified early intervention personnel places children in Rhode Island at higher risk for developing delays and/or disabilities.
Studies indicate that the severe staff shortage has made it difficult for Early Intervention programs to accept all children in need of help (Nesi & Sherman, 2022).
In terms of state competition, Rhode Island College currently offers two options: a master’s degree in Early Childhood Special Education and an Early Intervention Certificate program.

passages.heading: 24-25-14 | Page 93
passages.text:
The master program includes course work designed to enhance specific knowledge of Early Intervention: a course on working with families in EI, and a required internship in EI.
Other course work addresses develop and assessment of young children (birth through age 8) with special needs.
The inclusion of EI related courses in the Masters was designed to increase skills and interest relative to EI.
However, pay scales differences between public educational systems and EI programs appear to dampen enthusiasm for the EI jobs.
RIC’s EI certificate is designed and limited to current EI employees who have at least two years in EI and are seeking to advance in EI.
In contrast, the URI Certificate in Early Intervention is targeted to undergraduates and therefore does not conflict with either RIC programs instead, it creates an additional pathway to become qualified personnel in EI.
The only regional competitor is Northeastern University.
Northeastern offers a Certificate in Early Intervention, with coursework similar to URI’s EI certificate proposal, that the state of Massachusetts has approved for provisional certification with advanced standing (PCAS) in Early Intervention.

passages.heading: 24-25-14 | Page 93
passages.text:
Applicants who possess the PCAS must then complete 1440 hours of supervised employment in an EI setting before applying for permanent standing.
It is likely that the proposed certificate in EI at URI would allow graduates to obtain this provisional certification in Massachusetts.

Service and Community Life Committee Report #2024-2025-01 April 10, 2025 Faculty Senate Meeting Constitutional Amendment to Appendix B of the University Manual, Article III, “Membership” Rationale: The University of Rhode Island’s Retired Faculty Association (‘RFA’) is recognized by the office of the President and the Provost as the official representative of faculty members who have retired from the University of Rhode Island.
The RFA is housed within the office of the Provost and recently authored URI’s “Retired Faculty Handbook”.
Many RFA members are interested in remaining active on campus and contributing their time and talents to assist current faculty.
As part of that involvement, the RFA has requested their organization be represented on the Faculty Senate by an ex officio member (the RFA president or, if unavailable, their designee).
As with other ex officio members, this person would have the right to make and second motions but would not be able to vote.
This provides the RFA a voice in academic and organizational matters while maintaining the current policy that only active faculty elected as Senators shall be accorded the right to vote in Faculty Senate meetings.

1 PROPOSED CHANGE TO OFFICER AND FSEC ELECTIONS Faculty Senate Executive Committee Report #2024-2025-7C April 10, 2025 Faculty Senate Meeting (Friendly amendments reflected) Rationale: The original version of this legislation proposed changing the one-year term of one of the four Executive Committee positions to a two-year term, altering the timing of nominating committee formation, and amending how we vote for officers and FSEC members.
The original legislation was proposed at the 3/6/25 meeting; comments made at that meeting and subsequent extended conversations with several senators convinced us to drop the proposed changes to FSEC term lengths and nominating committee dates.
The amended version of the legislation thus only addresses the fact that it is currently possible for senators who attend Faculty Senate meetings in person to vote twice in officer/FSEC elections: once electronically and once in person via anonymous paper ballot.
We propose adopting a standard electronic ballot system for elections held both virtually and in person (hybrid), while maintaining a paper ballot system for elections held only in person.

Election of Officers 5.3 At the meeting(s) at which elections are conducted, nominations from the floor shall be in order.
All candidates may offer a brief oral statement during the meeting regarding their interest and experience.
Paper ballots shall be used in the election for all eligible Senators attending in person and an electronic poll will be administered to all eligible Senators attending remotely.
All ballots/polls shall include a “write-in” option.
A majority of the legal votes cast shall be required to elect. 5.4 The election of officers shall be in accordance with the following procedures: When more than two candidates are nominated for a single office, a candidate shall be declared elected on the first ballot if a majority of the votes cast are received.

The Board of Trustees By-Laws (adopted 2021, specifically Section 1.2), on the other hand, do not require that the BOT approve Certificates.

passages.text:
The prevention sciences graduate certificate combines skills with methods to understand how to reduce risk and promote health and healthy development.
There is an emphasis on examining social determinants of health with the aim of enhancing equity and decreasing disparities.
Additionally, this program provides intellectual development and training to a diverse community of students who can benefit from foundational and applied skills in health promotion and disease prevention but require flexible academic pathways (Strategic priority 2; Goal 1; Action 1).
This certificate can be completed to meet requirements in the Master's of Professional Studies program and the Master's of Public Administration program.
For the Master's of Professional Studies (30 credits total), students complete two certificates, and six additional credits of coursework.
The Prevention Science certificate can be included as one of the certificates toward completion of the degree.
For the Master's of Public Administration (36 credits total), students complete three certificates to complete the degree.

passages.heading: 24-25-16 | Page 9
passages.text:
The Prevention Science certificate can be included as the third certificate the students complete towards their degree.
The certificate could also be taken as a stand-alone certificate for any interested students.
One of the key elements of prevention science is the partnership with key community stakeholders (both public and private) who can work together to develop and implement appropriate interventions that address today’s health-related challenges.
Using evidence-based practices, applied learning, and real-world scenarios, students will be able to explore a range of issues through the lens of promoting and protecting health (e.g., social justice, family trauma, substance abuse and/or other addictions).
Therefore, the interdisciplinary nature of the program aims to foster meaningful interactions amongst students who bring expertise from a variety of health backgrounds.

passages.heading: 24-25-16 | Page 9
passages.text:
This program aligns with the URI strategic plan priorities and goals in several ways to include: 1) Strategic Priority 1 (Broaden Our Impact), Goal 1: Contribute to broad and deep impacts on the social, cultural, and economic ecosystems across Rhode Island, the nation, and beyond. 2) Strategic Priority 2 (Enhance Student Achievement), Goal 2: Increase graduate student enrollment and degree completion. 3) Strategic Priority 4 (Power the University of the Future), Goal 4: Expand research and new academic programs and services through an increased focus on revenue generation.
Offered completely online and asynchronously, this program targets working professionals across a myriad of health sectors who wish to advance within the workforce while still holding full-time jobs.
This will be attractive to students while meeting employers’ needs.
Additionally, the stackable design of this program highlights the intersection of specialties that employers look for while offering a flexible path for students.
Furthermore, the appeal of the in-state competitive tuition speaks to the accessibility of the program nationwide and beyond.

passages.heading: 24-25-16 | Page 9
passages.text:
We currently offer a Developmental Science Master's program as a traditional face-to-face graduate program.
We are proposing this graduate certificate in Prevention Science to offer a new pathway for working professionals and other individuals seeking an online Master's degree focused on health sciences and health prevention.
The Developmental Science Master’s degree program will pause enrollment for the 2023/2024 academic year until we decide the future of the program.
One of the primary drivers for our decisions regarding the future of the Developmental Science program’s future will be based on the PhD in Health Sciences Program and its possible plan to add a Master’s degree pathway for PhD students.

Accelerated online certificates are an attractive option for prospective students to upgrade their skillset; and the variety of certificates offered and anticipated through URI Online reflect diverse subject areas.
This proposed certificate supports students achieving an additional graduate credential while also offering multiple degree pathways that meet individual student needs within a flexible structure.
Furthermore, this program complements other existing professional master’s degree programs through URI Online including the Master of Professional Studies (MPS), Professional Science Masters (PSM), Master of Public Administration (MPA), and the planned Master of Public Health.
Graduates of programs with the foundational Prevention Science certificate should have an ability to work across the health arena and social services in areas such as health education, health promotion, lifespan development, healthcare administration, public health, behavioral sciences, and case management.

Applicants to the ABM need to have earned a minimum of 75 credits toward their BSBA and 90 credits to start the ABM, have a current GPA of 3.2 or higher, and have completed an internship.

The sports management track emphasizes sport-specific creative problem-solving, experiential learning, and hands-on experiences in business and leadership to prepare students up for dynamic careers within the diverse and growing sport industry.
The sports industry is growing rapidly, with global revenues projected to grow from $403.1 billion in 2022 to $680.7 billion in 2028. 2024 Average Annual Salaries Director of Corporate Partnerships: $84,714 Sports Marketing Manager: $149,200 Sales Manager: $141,690 Athletic Director: $68,226 The MSM program is designed for professional growth, building business knowledge and skills, insights, confidence, and interpersonal skills that can be used immediately to differentiate our graduates on the job market and, in the case of this specialization, in their sport management careers.
The program will continue to help professionals and aspiring professionals upskill and prepare for advanced organizational leadership positions.
The program is most aligned with Priority 2 (Enhance Student Achievement); Goal 1: Continuously invigorate the learning environment to reflect active learning; student agency; and contemporary, high-impact learning pedagogies.

Chapter 1 – The University of Rhode Island Land Acknowledgement, Mission, Board of Trustees and the President of the University #22-23-2
The University of Rhode Island
1.10.10 Land Acknowledgement. “The University of Rhode Island occupies the traditional stomping ground of the Narragansett Nation and the Niantic People. We honor and respect the enduring and continuing relationship between the Indigenous peoples and this land by teaching and learning more about their history and present-day communities, and by becoming stewards of the land we, now too, inhabit.” #22-23-2

passages.heading: Presidential Administrative Report #2024-2025-01
passages.text: 1.10.20 Background. The University of Rhode Island, the state’s land and sea grant research institution began as the state of Rhode Island’s Agricultural Experiment Station and agricultural school chartered in 1888. In 1892, the institution’s name was changed to the Rhode Island College of Agriculture and the Mechanic Arts. This name was subsequently changed to Rhode Island State College in 1909. The current name- the University of Rhode Island— was adopted in 1951 by an act of the State of Rhode Island’s General Assembly. For a complete history of the University, refer to https://www.uri.edu/about/history/.

passages.heading: Presidential Administrative Report #2024-2025-01
passages.text:
1.10.30 Mission. The University of Rhode Island is the state’s flagship land and sea grant research institution, with a commitment to urban initiatives. A student-centered research institution, URI actively partners with other organizations globally and locally to advance knowledge and to develop informed residents and leaders. URI is committed to high-quality education, community engagement, and solving the world’s most important challenges. Situated on the traditional land and territories of the Narragansett Nation and the Niantic People, URI strives to create a diverse and inclusive environment for researchers, teachers, learners, and community members.
1.10.40 Values. The University of Rhode Island is committed to the following foundational values:
* Freedom to learn, teach, create, and conduct research with integrity in the pursuit and dissemination of new knowledge aimed at contributing to the public good.
* An inclusive, accessible, equitable and diverse community whereby we respect the rights and dignity of all.
* Intellectual curiosity, lifelong learning, leadership, and scholarship in creating a thriving URI community in service to Rhode Island and the world.

Teaching, Advising, and Assessment Committee Report #2024-2025-01 May 1, 2025 Faculty Senate Meeting Amends the University Manual: Appendix C, Sections 4.30-4.34.
RATIONALE During Academic Year 2023-2024, the University created a new permanent committee known as JAPROA (The Joint Committee on Academic Program Review and Outcomes Assessment, per Faculty Senate Bill #23-24-8).
The Committee essentially merged the activities of two former standing committees, the Academic Program Review Committee (APRC) and the Learning Outcomes Oversight Committee (LOOC).
Given the new Committee’s inclusion of Assessment in its charge, the Teaching, Advising, and Assessment Committee’s (TAAC) charge seems ripe for revision to reduce overlap and eliminate any confusion or lack of clarity concerning committee scope and authority.
Around the same time, FSEC had separately taken note that no standing committee at the university is assigned to review admissions and retention data and advise the administration regarding admissions.
Adoption of the proposed language would incorporate university admissions into the charge of the TAAC.

1.10.30 Mission. The University of Rhode Island is the state’s flagship land and sea grant research institution, with a commitment to urban initiatives. A student-centered research institution, URI actively partners with other organizations globally and locally to advance knowledge and to develop informed residents and leaders. URI is committed to high-quality education, community engagement, and solving the world’s most important challenges. Situated on the traditional land and territories of the Narragansett Nation and the Niantic People, URI strives to create a diverse and inclusive environment for researchers, teachers, learners, and community members. Administrative Report July, 2024
1.10.40 Values. The University of Rhode Island is committed to the following foundational values:
Freedom to learn, teach, create, and conduct research with integrity in the pursuit and dissemination of new knowledge aimed at contributing to the public good.
An inclusive, accessible, equitable and diverse community whereby we respect the rights and dignity of all.

1.20.11 Composition of the Board Trustees and Quorum Requirements .
Initial membership of the Board of Trustees is defined in the original R.I. Gen. Laws §16 – 32 – 2.2.
The Board of Trustees shall consist of seventeen (17) voting members and five (5) non-voting ex officio members, including:

The President of the University of Rhode Island will appoint one (1) faculty member and one (1) student member who shall be a full-time student in good standing at the University, and who shall both serve in non-voting, ex officio capacity for a single two (2) year term.
