MINUTES
FACULTY SENATE MEETING
Thursday, May 7, 2026
Hope Room, Higgins Welcome Center
Remote option via ZOOM
Please find the Acronym Glossary here
1. Call to order - The meeting was called to order by President Williams at 3:05 pm. All AY 25-26 Senators were on hand except Senators Bevan, Chadha, Ghonem, Kusz, Liu, Lundy, Matson, Palter, Porto, Shahriari, Thomas, and Yuan (sabbatical). Ex officio members and others in attendance included: President Parlange, Vice Provost Adams, Vice Provost Johnson, VP’s Reynolds, Benson, Mello, Associate VP’s Libutti and Lavan, Deans Dennis, VanderGheynst, Meyerand, LaPlante, Rogers, and DeBoef, and RFA Representative Honhart.
2. Land Acknowledgement Statement -The statement was read by President Williams.
3. REPORT OF OFFICERS AND EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE
1. Announcements - Senate President Williams
1. Today’s reception is being sponsored by the College of Arts and Sciences - Thank you Dean DeBoef!
2. Welcome new Senators! Farewell to all outgoing Senators! - Newly elected senators who will begin their terms in the fall were welcomed by the group. Outgoing senators were thanked for their service.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text:
3. Disposition of the minutes of the 04/16/26 Faculty Senate meeting. The minutes were approved.
4. Informational Item: President Williams reminded those convened that the Executive Committee has the authority to approve curriculum proposals and other initiatives over the summer on behalf of the full Senate for matters deemed urgent/essential. (Per UM Appendix C, By-Laws of the Faculty Senate, Section 4.3)
5. Reminder of Faculty Senate Meeting Dates for AY 2026-2027 - Senators were reminded to get all senate meetings into their calendars well in advance.
6. Other reminders:
1. Summer Kuali maintenance/submissions pause - VP Preisser reminded faculty that the Kuali CMS will be closing soon to new submissions so that needed upgrades can be made. Drafts will not be lost, however, and proposers will be alerted when the system re-opens for new submissions to be made.
2. 9/1/26 curriculum meeting - VP Preisser reminded relevant curriculum committee chairs and other approvers of the ‘all-hands’ curriculum process information session that will be held on 9/1/26. Invitees are strongly urged to attend in person.
1. Activities of the Executive Committee - Senate Vice President Preisser

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text:
1. Executive Committee Meetings - Minutes of the April 3, 10, 17 and 24, 2026 meetings. A question was raised about the minutes as a senator tried to follow the progress of the JCODL bill that was discussed last month and which is back on today’s docket. VP Preisser noted that the minutes provide a broad-brush summary of FSEC activities and they are not intended to address finite details or refer to specific individuals by name. Regarding the JCODL bill specifically, written comments on the legislation that were provided to the Faculty Senate President were shared by e-mail and FSEC had commented and discussed as needed.
2. Report from the Nominating Committee (Sens. Krieger, Moore, and Roberts) - Election to fill vacancies on the Faculty Senate Executive Committee (FSEC) - Pres. Williams introduced the nominating committee and nominees were given one minute each to explain their interest and qualifications. There were no nominations from the floor.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text:
i. Two vacancies for a two-year term on FSEC - Nominated were: Noah Daniels, College of Arts and Sciences; Laura Meyerson, College of the Environment and Life Sciences; and Damon Rarick, College of Arts and Sciences. Sens. Daniels and Meyerson were elected by electronic ballot. Sen. Rarick agreed to be added to the ballot for the one-year term (item ii below).
ii. One vacancy for a one-year term on FSEC - Nominated are: Nominated are: Ying Chen, College of Business; Amanda Crego-Emley, University Libraries. Sen. Chen was elected via electronic ballot following a run-off.
d. Recommendations of the Faculty Senate Executive Committee

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text: i. Bill 2025-2026-FSEC-09: Amendments to UM 5.78.10 - 5.78.12 regarding the Joint Committee on Online and Distance Learning - Continued from the 2/19/26, 3/12/26, and 4/16/26 meetings. A motion to approve the bill was seconded and debate was managed by VP Preisser. Senate President Williams offered an overview of the bill and its travel to the senate floor. A question was raised from the floor by a senator from Engineering who noted he had provided a memo outlining seven specific concerns with the bill that he would like addressed individually. Not all voting senators had seen the memo, which was very detailed, however. Vice Provost Adams spoke in favor of the proposal as drafted, noting that a committee had worked collaboratively for almost two years on the draft, with a special eye toward accreditation standards and best practices in online education. The first of the seven proposed amendments was discussed in detail and a motion was made to make the language change that it recommended, but it was not approved. A subsequent motion was made to table the proposal, along with the six remaining suggested amendments. As part of the motion, it was noted that the areas of concern addressed by the memo deserved serious consideration. The motion to table was approved.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text:
ii. Bill 2025-2026-FSEC-13: Amendments to UM 8.60.10 - 8.65.12 regarding the Honors Program. Senate President Williams explained the proposal, noting that the legislation is designed to bring the University Manual into alignment with the the restructuring of Honors that was approved by the Faculty Senate back on January 22, 2026 (Bill #2025-2026-TAAC-01). The FSEC and Honors Program Directors worked on the bill together and it had been reviewed by TAAC and CBUM. The bill was moved by the FSEC, seconded from the floor and approved.
4. REPORT OF THE PRESIDENT and OTHER ADMINISTRATORS

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text:
1. President’s Remarks - President Parlange noted several recent events, including the April 30 Academic Excellence Awards Ceremony and the success of the URI Day of Giving, during which the overall fundraising goal was exceeded. It was also announced that the university had set a new record in terms of new applications for enrollment and the overall economic impact of the university on the state of RI is currently estimated at over $2 billion. The President reminded all faculty that they are strongly encouraged to participate in commencement ceremonies coming up May 15 - 17 and he made a special point of thanking outgoing Faculty Senate President Travis Williams, whom he praised as a strong, diplomatic, and effective leader.
2. Status of Actions Forward to the President:
1. The following bills were signed by the President on 05/06/26.
* Curriculum & Standards Committee Bill #25-26-07B and 7C
* Graduate Council Bill #25-26-06B
* Joint Bill #25-26-01, Reorganization of the Office of the Ombuds
* Faculty Senate Executive Committee Bill #25-26-12, regarding use of Veteran’s Day as an instructional day.
* Administrative Report on UM Chapter 2 and related Chapter 9 amendments.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text: 3. Administrative Report on UM Chapter 5 - amends Secs 5.41.10 and 5.41.11 to update the Space Allocation Committee for alignment with current practice. Senate President Williams explained the bill, noting that it was administrative in nature, designed to bring Manual language into comportment with current practices in terms of the committee’s charge and composition, and it will also update or correct various titles and roles. Vice President Benson was on hand to support the bill. There was a motion and second to accept the report and update the University Manual accordingly. The motion was unanimously supported.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text:
4. Annual Athletics Presentation - Vice President and Director of Athletics Pat Lyons introduced his co-presenters, including student athletes and Associate Athletics Directors. The presentation began with a snapshot of the academic performance of the student athletes and it was noted that the 2025 cumulative gpa for URI athletes was the highest ever achieved. Several teams were highlighted for their strong conference finishes, especially the women’s basketball, men’s football, and track and field teams. Updates were provided on various facilities upgrades, including to the track and field complex and Meade Stadium, along with a summary of NCAA compliance issues, ongoing fundraising initiatives, and athlete development issues like mental health, financial literacy, and sports gambling training.
5. AWARDS AND HONORS
1. Faculty Senate Awards

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text: 1. Presentation of the Fritz Wenisch Award for Exceptional Contribution to the Faculty Senate - President Williams announced that this year’s winner is Furong Xu (College of Education), who served as this year’s Curriculum and Standards Committee (CASC) Chair. The presentation included details about CASC’s record number of proposals processed this year. The task would have been made immensely more challenging but for Chair Xu’s ability to keep atop myriad details, organize information and meetings so as to come to good decisions, and communicate well with colleagues. As a result, CASC was a remarkably productive committee this year, due in large part to Sen. Xu’s smooth and skillful handling of the process, during which her good humor and collegiality never waned.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text:
2. Presentation of the Sheila Black Grubman Faculty Outstanding Service Award - President Williams presented the award to Douglass Reed (Arts and Sciences, Philosophy), who served as Administrator Evaluation Coordinator (AEC) for the past two years. Pres. Williams highlighted Dr. Reed’s spirit of ‘calm industriousness’ that he brought to the AEC role and noted that he received praise from his colleagues for his diplomacy, tact, and resourcefulness. Pres. Williams further noted that before being appointed as AEC, Dr. Reed had served in the Faculty Senate on the Teaching, Advising and Assessment Committee (TAAC) and had brought the same ambitious and proactive energy to that role. Concluding his remarks, Pres. Williams noted that in addition to today’s award, Dr. Reed is a 2022 Arts and Sciences Teaching Excellence Winner and also winner of the URI Excellence in General Education Award for 2026.
6. REPORTS OF JOINT, STANDING, AND SPECIAL COMMITTEES
1. Announcement of Election Results - See item 3c above.
2. Curriculum and Standards Committee - Chair Xu was on hand to field questions about the reports. The following were advanced by the Committee, seconded from the floor, and approved.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text:
i. Bill No. 2025-2026-08A, Courses, covering course modifications in five colleges, and new courses in the Colleges of Business, Pharmacy and Arts and Sciences.
ii. Bill No. 2025-2026-08B, Programs, covering multiple programs in several colleges.
The following proposal was tabled:
iii. Bill No. 2025-2026-08C, covering the new BS in Interdisciplinary Artificial Intelligence proposed by the College of Business. An objection was raised by a Senator from the Department of Computer Science and Statistics, who asserted that their department had not been given an opportunity to comment on possible overlap. A second question was raised about the extent to which ethics will be addressed by the new program and it was suggested that ethical use of AI should be integrated. CASC Chair Xu noted that her committee has a duty to address overlap, but typically, by the time a proposal reaches CASC, overlap should have been addressed or resolved at the level of the department and college curriculum committees. In the subject case, appropriate documentation from the affected colleges was included.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text:
c. General Education Committee - Acting Chair Stark was on hand to field questions about the report. The following was advanced by the Committee, seconded from the floor, and approved.
i. Bill No. 2025-2026-07A, Courses, covering course modifications in three colleges, and three new courses in the College of Arts and Sciences.
d. Curricular Reports from the Graduate Council to the Faculty Senate - Chair Hans Saint-Eloi Cadely was on hand to field questions about the reports. The following were advanced by the Committee, seconded from the floor, and approved.
i. Bill 2025-2026-07A, Courses, covering several course changes across multiple colleges, and new courses in the Colleges of Arts and Sciences, Engineering, and the Environment and Life Sciences.
ii. Bill 2025-2026-07B, Programs, covering and new specialization in the College of Business and a new online certificate in the College of the Environment and Life Sciences.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text: e. Centers and Institutes Review Committee Report - The CIRC is required to present annually on any new Centers and Institutes and on the rechartering status of other C/I’s reviewed. Committee member Julia Lovett presented the report, thanking her fellow committee members and highlighting their key accomplishments. In addition to reviewing three existing centers for renewal and authorizing creation of a new Institute, the Committee also worked to revise their forms in light of recent legislation, provided feedback on proposed University Manual language in Chapter 8, Section 90, and continued their tracking and oversight functions per their charge, among other things. A motion to accept the report was made, seconded and approved.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text: f. Research and Creative Activities Committee (CRCA) and SubCommittee Reports – Chair D’Agata thanked the members of her committee and reviewed the committee’s charge. Highlights of AY 25-26 activities included providing support to faculty during an era of rapid change in the research environment. The Committee had also prioritized supporting graduate students who faced unique and exacerbating housing and other financial challenges this year. The Committee has outlined proposed changes to its scope, structure, and strategic alignment with institutional governance over research functions which they hope to formalize during AY 26-27. Subcommittee Chair Wei also thanked fellow committee members, as well as the volunteer reviewers who assisted in reading and ranking applications for Career Enhancement, Proposal Development, and Collaborative Research Development grants. Proposals were due in January and awards were announced on April 6. A total of 51 submissions were received (significantly higher than in recent years) and 18 were awarded. In looking ahead to next year, the Committee noted a need for more reviewers if the number of applications exceeds expectations again. They also noted a need for more explicit guidance to be provided to both proposers and reviewers, which would help to streamline and improve consistency across submissions and evaluations. The reports were accepted.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text: g. General Education Committee (GEC) Report - GEC Acting Chair Stark explained that the Committee was focused on assessing the C2 (Global Responsibilities) and D1 (Integrate and Apply) outcomes this year. An ongoing challenge with outcomes assessment for the committee continues to be participation in the process, with only between 13 and 37 percent of relevant courses participating this year. The low level of participation constrains the degree to which conclusions about findings can be drawn. The results seemed stronger for the D1 outcome than the C2, as students more often approach competency in the D1 areas. Students assessed for C2 outcomes consistently struggle with communicating in a language other than English, considering multiple perspectives, and examining global responsibilities. Questions from the floor centered around C2 findings and whether they represent a structural weakness in foreign language proficiency within the current GenEd framework. Chair Stark, Associate Teaching Professor in Languages, suggested that it appears to be so. He advocated for treating language proficiency as a central pathway to achieving the university’s goals, rather than as optional enrichment for students. The report was accepted.

passages.text:
7. NEW BUSINESS - A Senator from the College of Business moved that Bill CASC 8c, introduced and tabled earlier in the agenda, be revisited. The motion was seconded. Several senators spoke from the floor before the question was called. Points made included the fact that practices differ from department to department in terms of how engaged faculty are on curricular proposals from outside their own college or department, and the degree to which they actually get a voice in advancing those proposals. It was also noted that the community is likely ripe for a forum or larger conversation with faculty about how best to integrate AI across the curriculum at the university. Pres. Williams called for a vote on whether or not to lay the issue back on the table for substantive consideration. The motion to reconsider was defeated.

Heather Sharpes-Smith, Executive Director of URI Online, JCODL Chair Purpose of the Committee The purpose of the Joint Committee on Online and Distance Learning (JCODL) is to propose, examine, and recommend institutional policies and practices for developing, planning, and evaluating online and distance learning with a focus on quality, sustainability, and connection to the University’s mission, with approval of the Faculty Senate and Provost.
Further, JCODL considers faculty training, quality in delivery of online offerings, student learning outcomes, and ADA compliance regarding online and distance learning, as well as develops and implements strategic plans for online courses, certificate, and degree programs. (University Manual 5.78.10 - 5.78.11).
Executive Summary The committee discussed several topics internally (listed in the next section) during the 2025-2026 academic year.
The committee did not bring forward any proposals for consideration and a vote to the university’s Faculty Senate.
However, the Faculty Senate did discuss a new structure for the committee during the spring 2026 semester.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 1
passages.text:
As of the April 2026 Faculty Senate meeting, no changes had been made to the committee’s structure.
Internal Topics of Discussion During the 2025-2026 Academic Year Fall 2025 With the addition of new members added to the committee this year, the fall semester served as a regrounding and educational opportunity to ensure that all of the members of the committee were aware of the current structure and professional development opportunities available to

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 2
passages.text:
faculty who want to teach online at URI.
During this semester, Joannah Portman-Daley, Director of URI Online’s Online Education & Instructional Design team, led presentations to ensure that all members of the committee were aware of current opportunities related to online learning professional development that are available on the campus including the list of qualified instructors and the 4 current pathways for becoming qualified to teach online .
Spring 2026 At the start of the spring 2026 semester, Chris Lavan resigned as chair of the committee and moved to the role of Provost Office’s designee.
This was done for 2 reasons.
First, to fully recognize URI Online as the unit holding the university’s expertise for online learning and instructional design.
Second, to provide the committee with the leadership it needed to properly engage in the current strategic needs of the university related to online learning.
Subsequently, Heather Sharpes-Smith became the chair of the committee during this semester.
The spring semester also included continued discussion of the upcoming alignment and merging of accelerated and traditional academic calendars and the broader implications for online learning.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 2
passages.text:
The committee discussed how this transition affects online course scheduling, student registration patterns, faculty planning, instructional design timelines, student support, and operational coordination across academic and administrative units.
These conversations also reinforced URI Online’s expanded scope, with all online programs — whether 14-week traditional online offerings or 7-week accelerated offerings — falling under URIO’s purview.
This alignment is intended to support clearer governance, more coordinated planning, consistency in the online student experience, and stronger institutional oversight of online learning across the university.

passages.text: The spring semester also included: ● Information about the proposed Brightspace Change process led by Michelle Rogers, Director of Teaching & Learning Services. ● Information about the new program process led by Joannah Portman-Daley to ensure that all members of the committee were aware of the forthcoming process that academic departments and colleges must complete to propose a new academic program online. ● Information about training opportunity to support faculty in making courses in Brightspace more accessible, led by Michelle Rogers. ● Multi-factor authentication being turned on in Engage, the university’s LMS for non-degree related educational opportunities, by Michelle Rogers. ● Awareness of the renewal of the university’s NC-Sara members by committee chair and URI Online Executive Director, Heather Sharpes-Smith. ● Information about ADA compliance procedures and digital course content, as well as an overview of the Provost Office’s faculty resource site in Brightspace led by Heather Sharpes-Smith and Joannah Portman-Daley ● Information about the university’s “Digital Accessibility: Understanding Your Rights and Responsibilities” event on March 30, 2026, including URI’s new digital accessibility webpage , led by Heather.

passages.text: PROGRAM REPORT Special Summer Curriculum Committee Report 2026-2027-SSCC-02-B At the July 14, 2026 meeting of the Special Summer Curriculum Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate Executive Committee for approval. for confirmation by the senate PROGRAM MODIFICATIONS Communicative Disorders - Minor, Spring 2027 Appendix A Change description, course requirements NEW MINOR Ocean Innovation - Minor, Spring 2027 Appendix B The minor in Ocean Innovation is designed for students who want to apply innovation and problem-solving skills in ocean-based contexts and industries. The minor is intended for students pursuing majors across the University who are interested in creating new ventures, innovating within established organizations, or contributing to interdisciplinary teams addressing challenges and opportunities connected to the ocean, coasts, and related systems. Students completing the minor develop skills to identify and evaluate opportunities, apply innovative thinking to complex systems, and translate scientific, technical, and environmental knowledge into viable solutions. The minor emphasizes innovation in areas such as ocean and coastal industries, food and energy systems, climate and resilience, data-driven decision-making, and sustainability-focused business models. In addition to fulfilling all the basic requirements for a minor (see Minor Fields of Study), students declaring an Ocean Innovation minor must complete 18 credits. The College of Business administers the Ocean Innovation minor in collaboration with academic units across the University. Interested students should contact their academic advisor for further information.

passages.text: NEW PROGRAM REPORT curriculum & standards committee Report 2025-2026-casc-08-c At the April 23, 2026 meeting of the Curriculum & Standards Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate for approval. for confirmation by the senate NEW PROGRAM Interdisciplinary & Applied Artificial Intelligence - BS, Spring 2026 Appendix A The Interdisciplinary & Applied Artificial Intelligence (AI) program prepares students to apply AI technologies to complex, interdisciplinary real-world challenges. The program is grounded in technical foundations and interdisciplinary collaboration. Students develop hands-on skills in data management, analytics programming, machine learning, visualization, and generative AI tools. They also examine the broader implications of AI for organizations. Emphasis is placed on fairness and responsible AI use. Through project-based coursework, innovation and entrepreneurship experiences, and an applied internship, students learn to work in cross-functional teams and translate AI insights into actionable solutions. Graduates of the program are prepared for roles that require technical fluency and critical thinking, including positions in analytics, innovation, and emerging AI-enabled fields, as well as for graduate study. passages.text:
The primary goal of the BS in Interdisciplinary Applied Artificial Intelligence is to prepare graduates who can apply artificial intelligence responsibly, creatively, and effectively across domains, integrating technical skills with ethical reasoning, interdisciplinary collaboration, and real-world problem solving.
The program emphasizes applied and lifelong learning, workforce relevance, and societal impact, ensuring that graduates are prepared for both immediate employment and long- term career adaptability.
It advances student success, retention, timely degree completion, and career readiness.
The program’s applied focus, interdisciplinary design, and integration of experiential learning opportunities support students in developing market- relevant skills that align with workforce needs.
By embedding internships, project-based learning, and applied AI coursework throughout the curriculum, the program enhances students’ engagement, persistence, and post-graduation outcomes while positioning URI graduates to succeed in a rapidly evolving, AI-enabled economy.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 9
passages.text:
The vision is to provide students with deep knowledge of AI systems and expertise in transferring and applying AI to a variety of problem types.
This program will cover knowledge of the AI ecosystem including the ability to work in interdisciplinary teams with data and domain experts to collect, clean organize, and sample data, match the problem and data to the right intelligent computational tool (there are many types of AI, each with its strengths and weaknesses), tailor, build on top of, and adapt these tools to the problems at hand, support the safe, secure, ethical and accurate reporting of the results to domain experts, and guide teams in deciding if the analytical results make sense.
Students will learn how to use, tailor and augment AI so that the AI can serve as assistants in problem solving, with the human as the master, well versed in the interpretation, and ethical and societal implications of the use of the powerful AI that they will wield.
All of this is in the context of a world in which educators and potential employers are concerned with the lack of digital skills among today’s students and graduates.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 9
passages.text:
To be well educated and prepared for the modern workplace, students must learn to acquire applied technology skills and also to transfer these technologies to specific problems as they arise.
Thus this program is not intended to train students to develop new AI, but to become experts in mastering, adapting, building upon, and deploying existing and evolving intelligent computational artifacts.
We will help students to master the AI tools of today but also help them to understand that these are only contemporary examples to sharpen their problem solving, and learning skills, and give them a leg up as they enter the workplace.
As the world changes and embraces new technologies such as digital twins, and quantum computing, both already inextricably intertwined with AI, we propose a major that is flexible enough that it can evolve with emerging intelligent technologies.
The program advances the University’s goals by preparing students to address complex real-world challenges through the responsible and creative application of emerging technologies.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 9
passages.text:
The curriculum integrates applied coursework, project-based learning, and internships, ensuring that students develop both technical expertise and transferable skills that support career readiness and lifelong learning.
The program reflects the University’s commitment to interdisciplinary problem-solving and collaboration across colleges and departments.
The program also contributes to the University’s role in supporting economic development, innovation, and the future of work in Rhode Island and beyond.

At the end of week six, they need to have 10 extenuating circumstances with supporting documentation for approval of a late drop. Many - 11 most - courses do not post midterm grades by week six, however, making students predict their 12 success in the course before they have any real data. Students either drop the course for fear of 13 not doing well and miss the chance to succeed or stay in and try and succeed when they should 14 have dropped it. When students ask for a W too late, without extenuating circumstances, their 15 late drop petition gets denied even if their reasoning is sound. 16 For regular session classes, this legislation would extend the “Withdraw without 17 extenuating circumstances” deadline from 6 weeks to 11 weeks. 18 19 DATA 20 Ten comparable universities were reviewed: half allow late drops without extenuating 21 circumstances until the eleventh week, and all have a later date than URI*. 22 23 *See “Addendum to Proposal Change to URI’s Late Withdrawal of a Course Policy” 24 document to review the comparable universities and their full policies 25 Potential impacts: This proposal has been vetted by ESAC (Enrollment Services 26 Advisory Committee), a URI internal administrative body that includes academic deans or 27 representatives from each degree-granting college and the directors of student-supporting service 28

To ensure that students understand the academic and/or financial implications of a ‘W’, 29 ESAC recommended that course withdrawal forms remain required between the end of the add 30 period and the last day of classes. Each form must be signed by the class professor and the 31 academic affairs office before being processed by enrollment services. 32 Although this will increase the number of forms being processed, the processing time will 33 be reduced significantly due to the lack of extenuating circumstances evidence needed. There 34 will be fewer meetings and less work put on students for finding documentation to support 35 extenuating circumstances. 36 This change will also greatly benefit staff working in areas such as Health Services, 37 Student Support & Advocacy Services, and Disability, Access, & Inclusion. Over the past four 38 Fall semesters (see below), an average of 1,379 “Withdraw with extenuating circumstances” 39 requests were processed each semester. However, the 111 current structure gives administrative officers voting authority on a committee whose purview 112 extends to academic policy, faculty development, online teaching practices, class size, and 113 instructional conditions.
That dilutes the faculty voice and shifts the balance of authority toward 114 the administrators.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 3
passages.text:
In matters affecting academic governance, administrators should advise, 115 inform, and support implementation, but faculty should retain primary voting authority. 116 Summary response to amendment proposed at 5/7/26 meeting: 117 A joint committee is, by definition, one in which both faculty and administration have 118 voting rights.
JCODL has been a joint committee since its 2012 inception and has worked well in 119 that capacity.
This amendment would change that, and we recommend against its adoption. 120 The proposed amendment states that allowing administrators voting authority “…dilutes 121 the faculty voice and shifts the balance of authority toward the administrators”.
Bill 2025-206-09 122 specifies, however, that seven of 13 voting JCODL members are faculty while four are 123

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 4
passages.text:
4 administration.
Making administrators less than one-third of the voting membership thus ensures 124 that “…faculty should retain primary voting authority”. 125 If the amendment is approved, the Senate Parliamentarian recommends that JCODL be 126 dissolved.
This is because both the original JCODL legislation and bill 2025-2026-09 was 127 developed jointly by a faculty/administrator committee.
Creating a faculty- and 128 student-representative-only Committee on Online and Distance Learning would require the 129 formation of a special faculty committee tasked with bringing forward legislation establishing 130 such a body. 131 Detailed response to amendment proposed at 5/7/26 meeting: 132 Rationale for Maintaining Joint Voting: The proposed revision of the membership 133 structure is designed to preserve JCODL as a meaningful joint governance body while ensuring 134 strong faculty leadership and representation. 135 Faculty hold a majority of the voting membership.
Seven of the 13 voting members are 136 faculty appointed by the President of the Faculty Senate in consultation with the Faculty Senate 137 Executive Committee.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 4
passages.text:
The proposal also establishes a Senate-appointed faculty co-chair and 138 faculty liaisons to the Curriculum and Standards Committee, Graduate Council, and Teaching, 139 Advising, and Assessment Committee.
The remaining voting membership includes four 140 institutional representatives whose areas have direct responsibility for the delivery and support of 141 online and distance education, as well as graduate and undergraduate student representatives. 142 This structure protects a strong faculty role in academic governance while recognizing 143 that the work of JCODL also intersects with institutional responsibilities for the delivery and 144 support of online education.
The institutional members do not participate solely as technical 145 resources; they represent areas with direct responsibility for implementing and supporting 146 matters within the committee’s charge.
Their voting participation allows those responsibilities 147 and faculty academic perspectives to be considered as recommendations are developed. 148 The proposed structure also deliberately distinguishes between voting membership and ex 149 officio participation.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 4
passages.text:
Two senior administrators may participate as non-voting ex officio 150 members.
This demonstrates that the proposed structure does not assume that every administrator 151 connected to online education requires a vote.
Rather, voting membership is limited to the 152 faculty, students, and institutional roles identified as core participants in the committee’s work. 153 Joint Voting and Faculty Authority: Maintaining voting participation by institutional 154 members does not diminish Faculty Senate authority.
JCODL is an advisory and recommending 155 body.
Under the proposed §5.78.11, it provides advice and guidance to both the Provost and 156 Faculty Senate and consults appropriate committees, units, and personnel. 157 Matters requiring Faculty Senate approval continue through Faculty Senate governance, 158 while matters requiring administrative authority remain subject to the appropriate administrative 159 processes.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 4
passages.text:
Joint voting therefore allows JCODL to develop informed recommendations through 160 meaningful participation by both faculty and institutional representatives without changing 161 where final authority resides. 162 Governance Consideration: If there is interest in changing JCODL from a Joint 163 Committee of the Faculty Senate and the President to a Faculty Senate committee, that represents 164 a broader governance question concerning the status and purpose of the committee. 165 Making the institutional members non-voting would materially alter the joint governance 166 structure proposed in Bill 2025-2026-09.
A change of that nature should be considered directly 167

FY ‘24 Overhead Report - The Committee for Review of the Distribution of Facilities and Administrative (Overhead) Funds is chaired by the Chair of the Committee for Research and Creative Activities (CRCA).
Chair Meenach explained the committee structure and noted that the group had advanced several significant recommendations that she hopes will be enacted in the near future.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 4
passages.text:
There seems to be a need to restructure the committee in a big-picture way.
There is also a need for an overhead funds “best practices guide” that would set the stage for more uniform policies and practices across colleges and guarantee more uniform approaches to distribution and utilization of F&A funds.
Additional oversight is recommended as the new budget model is implemented. ii.
Center Review Subcommittee Report - The Committee was busy throughout the year as an initiative to create an entirely new framework for Centers and Institutes (C/I) was pursued.
The initiative is ongoing, but the committee structure will be different next year.
In addition to the required reviews for C/I renewals, the committee also approved the creation of one new institute and the dissolution of another. iii.
Competitive Grants Subcommittee Report - The Committee reviewed and approved similar numbers of proposals for career enhancement and proposal development as in past years.
However, the total funds awarded this year marked an increase in investment from the VPAF’s office.
The Subcommittee this year was smaller in membership that last year’s committee and outside faculty reviewers were relied upon.

Overview.
There is renewed interest in ocean acoustics due to undersea defense applications as well as concerns about the effects of anthropogenic noise (e.g., from offshore wind farms) on marine animals.
The US Navy recently began a five-year, $2.4 billion investment in industrial base and workforce development support, including nearly $750 million in FY23 for the submarine industrial base.
In the realm of offshore renewable energy, the US has a goal of installing 30 gigawatts of offshore wind farms by 2030, or enough to power more than 10 million homes for a year.
One of the major objectives of the graduate certificate is to provide an option for students from engineering, oceanography, or other fields who would like to have graduate preparation in ocean acoustics.
Many of the courses below are already offered in a hybrid mode indicated by the asterisks.
We propose that an adequate number of hybrid courses be available for this certificate.
A concern for the public and environmentalists is the ocean noise impact of wind farm construction on marine mammals and fish.
Both the defense and offshore wind industries need people with expertise in ocean acoustics.

URI's mission includes a commitment to high-quality education, community engagement, and solving the world’s most important challenges.
This graduate certificate in underwater acoustics will support that mission by educating engineers, oceanographers, marine biologists, and others in the important aspects of sound in the ocean.
No overlap with any programs at URI.

MINUTES
FACULTY SENATE MEETING
Thursday, April 16, 2026

Hope Room - Higgins Welcome Center
Remote option via ZOOM
1. Call to order of the General Faculty - Graduate Faculty meeting by President Parlange at 3:02 pm.
2. Call to order of the Faculty Senate Meeting immediately following the General Faculty - Graduate Faculty Meeting by Faculty Senate President Williams. All Senators were on hand except Senators Burns, Deng, Ghonem, Liu, Lundy, Martin, Matson, Porto,Thomas, Zhang, and Yuan (sabbatical). Ex officio members and others in attendance included: President Parlange, Vice Provost Adams, Vice Provost Johnson, VP’s Reynolds, Jenkins, Benson, Mello, Associate VP’s Libutti and Lavan, Deans Dennis, VanderGheynst, Meyerand, LaPlante, and DeBoef, Past President Walls, and RFA Representative Honhart.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text:
a. SPECIAL REMEMBRANCE of Faculty Member, Faculty Senator, and General Education Committee Chair Kathy Quick - Faculty Senate President Travis Williams paid tribute to former GEC Chair and A&S faculty member Kathy Quick, and he read a statement from her Department of Art and Art History colleagues who could not be present. The statements emphasized the jolt and collective sorrow experienced by the community with the loss of a colleague in the prime of their career. Chair Quick’s strong work ethic, willingness to serve and to lead, and her thoughtfulness and good nature will be missed by all, students, faculty, and staff alike.
3. REPORT OF THE UNIVERSITY PRESIDENT/OTHER ADMINISTRATORS

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text:
1. Updates and Announcements - President Parlange thanked all faculty who participated in URI Day at the Statehouse, as well as other recent events, like World Quantum Day. Faculty were reminded that Budget Model Town Halls are ongoing in the Colleges, and other notable events, like the Excellence Awards and the annual Day of Giving, are also coming up this month. The spring commencement ceremonies are set for May 15 - 17 and all faculty are strongly encouraged to participate. President Parlange provided a brief update on the proposed Medical School, noting the initiative has moved into ‘Phase 2 of exploration,’ which involves detailed financial feasibility investigations, analysis of existing gaps in service provision and training pipelines, and other studies and assessments. He also provided a brief update on his and VP Abby Benson’s efforts to ‘undo’ the state-imposed cap on FTE’s at URI, which has been in place for far too long.
2. Administrative Report on UM Chapter 5 - amends Sec. 5.41.11 to update the Space Allocation Committee for alignment with current practice - The report was tabled pending possible revisions.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text:
3. Report on results of College of Education Dean Dennis’ evaluation, consistent with Chapter 10 of the University Manual. (Sec. 10.90.15) A point of order was raised about the senate’s authority to hear the report but it was overruled. Vice Provost Adams, filling in for Provost Wolfe, provided a summary of the evaluation, noting results were generally favorable across all metrics.
4. Presidential Administrative Report on Chapter 2 with related additions to Chapter 9 of the University Manual. Vice Provost Adams presented the report, noting it had been introduced and discussed at the January 22, 2026 meeting. The legislation was moved, seconded, and approved.
5. Status of Actions Forwarded to the President:
* The following Bills were signed by President Parlange on 3/18/26
* Curriculum & Standards Committee Bill #25-26-6B
* Graduate Council (GC) Bill #25-26-5B
* FSEC Bills #25-26-10 and#25-26-11
* Administrator Bill #25-26-02
* CASC Bill #25-26-6C and GC Bill #25-26-5C, which require final approval by the Board of Trustees.
4. REPORTS OF OFFICERS AND THE EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE
1. Announcements - Faculty Senate President Williams

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text:
i. Today’s reception is being sponsored by the College of Pharmacy - Thank you Dean LaPlante!
ii. Call for Nominations: At the October Faculty Senate meeting, Sens. Kendall Moore, William Krieger, and Alison Roberts were chosen as this year’s Nominating Committee. Per Section 5.2 of the Senate By-Laws, the Nominating Committee shall prepare a slate of candidates for one (1) one-year and two (2) two-year vacancies on the Executive Committee. The Executive Committee Election shall be held May 7, 2026. Please reach out to a member of the Nominating Committee if you are interested in this role.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text: iii. Announcement regarding making rooms available to rent to grad students - VP Preisser offered a reminder about concerns recently shared by the Graduate Student Association related to the temporary closure of Graduate Village. Dozens of students remain on a waitlist for housing. In an effort to ensure that all enrolled students have access to appropriate housing, FSEC encourages faculty and staff, especially those who live in close proximity to campus, to consider offering a room to rent. VP Preisser encouraged faculty to spread the word, and suggested that they explore relevant housing webpages or reach out to him directly for more information.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text:
iv. ‘All-hands’ curriculum meeting prior to the start of fall semester 2026 - VP Preisser announced that the Faculty Senate and Vice Provost Adams are co-hosting a mandatory meeting on September 1, at 1 pm, aimed at improving curriculum proposal quality and review process consistency in Kuali. The meeting would be required for Deans and Associate Deans who have approval roles in the CMS and it is strongly recommended that the faculty chairs of college-level curriculum committees also attend. More information will be forthcoming but affected parties need to make sure this meeting is in their calendars.
2. Disposition of the Minutes - Faculty Senate President Williams
i. Minutes of the Faculty Senate Meeting of 3/12/26 were approved.
3. Activities of the Executive Committee - Senate Vice President Preisser noted the important work of FSEC reflected in the following minutes. There were no questions.
i. Executive Committee Meetings of March 6, March 13, and March 27, 2026 meetings. (No meeting on 3/20 due to Spring Break.)
d. Recommendations of the Faculty Senate Executive Committee: FSEC recommends the following bills:

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text:
i. Approval of Faculty Senate Meeting Calendar for AY 2026-2027. Pres. Williams noted that FSEC has recommended a meeting calendar that prioritizes ‘third Thursdays’ for consistency, while avoiding holidays, breaks, and cultural or religious celebrations that preclude work. The calendar was approved.
ii. Bill 2025-2026-FSEC-09: Amendments to UM 5.78.10 - 5.78.12 regarding the Joint Committee on Online and Distance Learning - Continued from the 2/19/26 And 3/12/26 meetings. Pres. Williams noted the proposal had been discussed by the faculty senate at previous meetings and is now offered for approval. It was moved to the senate docket for action by FSEC and was seconded. Questions were raised from the floor about some particulars of the bill and FSEC members responded. Comments were also offered from the floor noting one senator’s outstanding concerns about the bill as written. A motion was made to table the bill in its entirety. Pres. Williams noted a motion to table is not debatable or amendable and requires a ⅔ majority for approval. The motion to table passed.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text: iii. Ratification of appointment to the Space Allocation Committee: Leon Thiem, representing the College of Engineering. A motion to ratify was approved.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text: iv. FSEC Bill 2025-2026-12 regarding precluding use of the Veteran’s Day holiday as an instructional day - VP Preisser noted that while State and Federal calendars list Veteran’s Day as a holiday, language in the University Manual does not preclude its use as an instructional day. FSEC sought to clear up any confusion via the proposed amendment, which was moved for action by FSEC and seconded from the floor. College of Education senators inquired whether or not the current proposal was the result of their petition last month to amend the University Manual to preclude the use of Indigenous People’sDay/Columbus (IP/C) Day as an instructional day. VP Preisser answered affirmatively, explaining that the detailed review of UM Sec. 8.70.25 that occurred with their proposal marked the first time the ACC, CBUM and FSEC had all taken an in-depth look at the relevant language in quite some time, and the question of Veteran’s Day seemed to warrant clarification independent of what happens with the IP/C Day legislation, which is still under consideration. In response to further questions, VP Preisser confirmed that approval of the subject bill does not preclude approval of the IP/C Day bill, but he acknowledged that the constrained number of available instructional days in certain fall semesters certainly makes the Calendar Committee’s work more challenging.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text:
5. SPECIAL REPORTS:
1. Bill 2025-2026-Joint-01, a joint proposal of the University Administration, FSEC, and the SCLC regarding reorganization of the Office of the University Ombuds. Faculty Senate President Williams explained that the proposal was the result of work done by multiple committees and individuals over the course of more than a year. Also, the plan to professionalize the Office of the Ombuds had been discussed at previous senate meetings, including, most recently, the March 12 meeting. With no further questions or discussion, there was a motion and second to approve the proposal. The motion was approved.
2. Student Senate Resolution on Accessible Education Material, as approved by the Student Senate on March 25, 2026. Tabled.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text: 3. Kuali pause for proposal submissions, summer 2026 - Faculty Senate Specialist Spitale, FSEC member Trimm, and Enrollment Services Assoc. Director Humphrey. Specialist Spitale explained that a pause in new Kuali submissions is planned for the summer months to allow system administrators the opportunity to make much-needed updates to workflows and user experience features. All proposals entered by 5/15 will still advance through the approval process to the Dean-level of review. Any proposal not approved by the relevant dean by 6/1 will revert to draft form. Such drafts will remain in the system and will still be viewable, but will need to be resubmitted at a later date to advance toward approval. Normal proposal submission procedures and workflows will resume on 8/15. Additional information is available via the Curriculum Toolkit on the Faculty Senate’s webpage. Questions from the floor were offered, including inquiries about the degree to which suggestions from the various college curriculum committees factor into the update. It was noted that the current effort is focused more on compliance with the curricular streamlining initiative approved by the faculty senate earlier this year, but it is hoped that this year’s initiative will lay the groundwork for future short pauses wherein incremental process improvements like those that would be suggested by the curriculum committees might be made.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text:
6. REPORTS OF STANDING AND SPECIAL COMMITTEES
a. Curriculum and Standards Committee - Chair Furong Xu was on hand to field questions about the reports. The following were advanced by the Committee, seconded from the floor, and approved.
i. Bill No. 2025-2026-07A, Courses, covering one new temporary course and fifteen new permanent courses, as well as numerous course modifications across five colleges.
ii. Bill No. 2025-2026-07B, Programs, covering multiple program modifications, including to specializations and minors, in the Colleges of Arts and Sciences, Business, Engineering, Health Sciences, and the College of the Environment and Life Sciences.
iii. Bill No. 2025-2026-07C, covering two new programs, one in the College of Arts and Sciences and one in the College of the Environment and Life Sciences.
b. Curricular Reports from the Graduate Council to the Faculty Senate - The following bills were advanced by the Committee, seconded from the floor, and approved.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text:
i. Bill 2025-2026-06A, Courses, covering multiple course modifications across seven colleges, along with several new courses in the the Colleges of Arts and Sciences, Business, Education, Engineering, Pharmacy, and the College of the Environment and Life Sciences.
ii. Bill 2025-2026-06B, Programs, including several program modifications, along with new certificates and specializations.
c. Centers and Institutes Review Committee - Chair Porto - The CIRC is required to present annually on any new Centers and Institutes and on the rechartering status of other C/I’s reviewed. Tabled to the May 7 meeting.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text: d. Teaching, Advising, and Admissions Committee Annual Report- Chair Romanow praised her fellow committee members and noted they have had a very busy and productive year. The TAAC was involved in the review and approval of several key pieces of legislation this year, including the creation of a President’s List and modernizing the Second Grade Option. They were also involved in the curricular streamlining initiative and the reconfiguration of the Honors Program. As a result of legislation approved last year, the Committee now has a role to play in Admissions and is still determining, with AVP Libutti’s help, how that new charge will be implemented. In terms of future priorities, the Committee has been tasked with looking at UM provisions related to academic dishonesty, especially where it intersects with grade disputes. The Committee hopes to craft relevant amendments for consideration next year.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text:
e.
Budget and Administration Committee Annual Report - Chair Triki explained that his committee’s primary task this year has been to try to measure faculty sentiment toward the new budget mode via a survey distributed broadly to the community.
As of now, the Committee intends, according to Chair Triki, to share their results with the Financial Strategy and Planning Office so that a conversation about improving messaging might be had.
It has not yet been decided how the data collected might otherwise be shared or disseminated.
Based on the survey results, the Committee had concluded that there seems to be a serious disconnect between the actual outcomes of the budget model roll-out and the faculty’s perception of those outcomes.
As examples, a majority of those surveyed did not see the new model as improving transparency or ensuring a more fair allocation of resources across colleges.
Chair Triki suggested that expanding dissemination of information about the details and mechanics of the budget might result in more positive perceptions.
VP Jenkins asked if current sentiment around higher education generally might have colored the survey results.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text:
She enumerated several recent and ongoing concerns and challenges facing universities around the country (constrained research funding, various Federal actions, outside influence and interference in curricular matters, etc.) and suggested that the current landscape likely has a negative ‘baseline mood’ undercurrent that would be hard to measure.
Chair Triki agreed that the survey probably did roll out at an unfortunate time for measuring faculty understanding and satisfaction.
He noted that one positive takeaway from the results was the degree to which faculty are engaged and paying attention, and he praised their resilience in the face of unrelenting bad news.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text:
f. Committee on Technology and Infrastructure Annual Report - Chair Wallace noted the many projects his committee tackled this year, including providing input to improve Brightspace and EdTech operations, helping to recreate a searchable classroom database, and suggesting strategies for improving the IT contracts/software approval process. They also provided important outreach to faculty about their roles in website editing, and helped raise awareness about current IT Policies. Priorities for next year will include understanding faculty needs and habits around responsible AI use in research, and aiding in Brightspace file recovery and migration, among other things.
7. CALL for NEW BUSINESS - None.
8. ADJOURNMENT - The meeting adjourned at 4:35 pm.

COLLEGE OF NURSING: BS – Accelerated Online R.N. to B.S., Spring 2026 Appendix B - Accelerated online version of existing in-person RN to BS degree program. The University of Rhode Island College of Nursing’s Accelerated Online R.N. to B.S. program is dedicated to providing an education that will broaden your view of the world and create opportunities to transform healthcare in your own community. Building upon your clinical experience, the R.N. to B.S. program expands your scientific knowledge base, giving you a set of skills that allows you to integrate clinical practice, scientific inquiry and critical, creative thinking. You’ll graduate fully prepared for a whole new world of healthcare opportunities. Progression and Graduation Requirements Students are expected to achieve a C or higher in all required courses. In addition, students must maintain a minimum GPA of 2.2 to progress through and graduate from the College of Nursing.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 2
passages.text: Students who achieve less than a grade of C must repeat the course, obtaining a C grade or higher, before progressing in the nursing curriculum. Permission to retake the course will be granted on a space-available basis only. Even if successfully repeated, the initial grade remains on record as the first unsuccessful attempt. There are no further allowances for repeating a NUR course, and any subsequent NUR coursework of C- or below will result in dismissal. If the student should achieve a C- or less in two NUR courses in a single session or semester, he or she will be immediately dismissed from the College of Nursing. A total of 120 credits is required to earn a B.S. in Nursing. This includes program specific courses as well as general education requirements. R.N. to B.S. A grade of C or higher is required in each of these courses. General Education. All College of Nursing Students must meet the University's General Education requirements. 1 University of Rhode Island Board of Trustees Regulations Regarding Use of University Property [DRAFT 20241008 CC] Introduction As noted in the University of Rhode Island’s Mission Statement and consistent with University values, the University of Rhode (also “University” or “URI”) is committed to high- quality education, community engagement, and the freedom to learn, teach, create, and conduct research with integrity in the pursuit and dissemination of new knowledge aimed at contributing to the public good.
The management of University Property and other resources is paramount to meeting that mission.
Authority and Applicability Pursuant to Rhode Island General Laws §§ 16-32-2 and 16 -32-2.1, the University of Rhode Island Board of Trustees is empowered to make rules and regulations for the control and use of Univ ersity Property while the President of the University is responsible for the general management of University Property.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 1
passages.text:
These regulations apply to all users of University Property , including all members of the University community (students, faculty, staff, and affiliates) and third parties (individuals, groups, and members of the public) who wish to use any University Property for any purpose.
Definitions University Operations.
All teaching , research, community engagement, and business functions, as well as any other official activity of the University.
University Property.
Property belonging to the State of Rhode Island and held in trust by the University of Rhode Island Board of Trustees; property held by the University of Rhode Island or any of its component units in its own name; and property owned by third parties but assigned to, occupied by, or managed by the University or any of its component units.
University Property includes all real property, including without limitation land, buildings and other structures, fences, driveways and walkways, and other permanent improvements and associated infrastructure .
For the purposes of these regulations, property leased or licensed to a third party is excluded from the definition of University Property. 1.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 1
passages.text:
General The primary purpose of University Property is to support the University’s mission.
Every individual and group using University Property is expected to use it in a manner that (i) complies with all applicable laws, policies, procedures, rules, and regulations; (ii) is safe and responsible; (iii) maintains and protects the integrity, cleanliness, and functionality of the University Property; (iv) does not materially and substantially disrupt or interfere with University Operations; and (v) does not impinge upon the individual rights of another person or group.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 2
passages.text:
2 Access to and use of University Property is governed by the University, not by colleges, departments, or administrative units.
Individual colleges, departments, and administrative units may adopt guidelines governing the use of University Property allocated for their specific use provided that such guidelines are consistent with these regulations.
Space is allocated pursuant to the University’s policy on Allocation and Utilization of Space. 2.
Limitations and Prohibited Activities The University may establish reasonable standards and limitations regarding the time, place, and manner of use for any University Property, including access to certain areas within a building, entire buildings themselves, or specified areas of University Property, by both the general public and the University community.

Laura Meyerson, Professor Natural Resources Science Having served on the URI faculty for over two decades, I bring deep institutional knowledge, commitment to shared governance, and a record of working across departments, colleges, and national and international organizations to advance the mission of higher education.
URI is navigating a period of significant institutional complexity, including a new budget model, changing federal priorities, pressures on research and teaching, and the continuing need to protect academic freedom, faculty voices, and transparent decision-making.
I would welcome the opportunity to help the Faculty Senate meet these challenges.
My previous Faculty Senate service (2019-22) gave me a broad understanding of Senate processes and responsibilities.
I served on the Curriculum Affairs Committee, chaired the University Calendar Committee, served on the Faculty Senate Executive Committee (FSEC), and the Joint Committee on Academic Planning and the Academic Freedom Committee (JCAP).

My Senate service was recognized through the URI President David and Reverend Lynn Dooley Faculty Senate Award for Important Contributions to the Faculty Senate and the Fritz Wenisch Award for Exceptional Contributions to the URI Faculty Senate.

My broader leadership experience includes serving as Editor-in-Chief of Biological Invasions , as a Coordinating Lead Author for the IPBES Invasive Alien Species Assessment, as a member of IUCN and national advisory groups, US National Invasive Species Council Invasive Species Science Advisory Board.

If elected, I would bring that same level of commitment to the Executive Committee: a commitment to transparent governance, academic freedom, equity across disciplines, responsible curriculum processes, and strong faculty participation in decisions that shape URI’s future.

Candidate Statement I would like to boast that my work on committees spanning the curriculum, assessment, general education, academic planning, technologies, and accreditation has given me a keen ability to understand the inner workings and needs of the Faculty Senate and the University itself.

They remind us of the importance of taking care of one another, working constructively across academic and institutional boundaries, and protecting shared governance, academic freedom, and advocacy itself during tumultuous times.
URI has weathered past transformational challenges, including the complete reform of the General Education Program, the global pandemic, and the ﬁrst years of the intensifying demographic cliff we are facing.

Uncertainty seems to be the word that best encapsulates the challenges we face today — challenges that affect the process of decision-making itself.

passages.text: Faculty Senate Constitution, By-Laws and University Manual Committee Report #2001-02-1 November 19, 2001 As approved by the Faculty Senate on December 13, 2001 Amendments to the Constitution of the Faculty Senate Recent changes of titles and/or responsibilities of administration officials have affected certain ex officio members of the Faculty Senate listed in the membership paragraph (Article III) of the Faculty Senate Constitution. The Faculty Senate Executive Committee has asked the CBUM Committee to consider the constitution's membership article in light of these changes. At a meeting on November 7, 2001, the consensus of the CBUM Committee members was that no changes to the Senate Constitution are to be made without a referendum as provided for in Article VII of the Faculty Senate Constitution. That constitution, stating the Senate's fundamental principles, is too important a document to permit its being changed editorially; among other things because there may be disagreement on whether a change is editorial or substantive. This implies that changes to the titles and/or responsibilities of members of the administration who are also ex officio members of the Faculty Senate ought not to occur by administrative fiat, but are to be preceded by consultation with the body whose constitution they affect. Nevertheless, the CBUM Committee's consensus was that the following Senate Constitution changes required to make the document consistent with recent administrative action are comparatively non-controversial: From Vice Provost for Academic Programs and Services to Vice Provost for Academic Affairs. CBUM #1 http://www.uri.edu/facsen/CBUM 01-02-1.html 1 of 5 1/23/14, 1:59 PM

Accordingly, the CBUM Committee recommends that the Senate approve a future referendum authorizing those changes to the Senate Constitution. GEC End-of-Year Report for the May 7, 2026, Faculty Senate Meeting
General Education Assessment: C2 and D1 Outcomes
This is a summary of the key findings and recommendations from the General Education assessment, focusing on the C2—Global Responsibilities—and D1—Integrate and Apply—outcomes.
Starting with C2: the expectation is that all students reach competency by graduation. The outcome is designed to position students within a global framework by asking them to engage with histories, cultures, institutions, and languages, and to move beyond understanding toward identifying and analyzing responsible action in response to complex global issues. In principle, it’s one of the most ambitious components of the GenEd program: it aims to cultivate knowledge and foster a sense of ethical responsibility and purpose within an interconnected world. Among the most urgent findings, which is echoed in both assessment data and anticipated student feedback, is the persistently low level of proficiency in a language other than English among our students. This isn’t a marginal issue; it represents a structural weakness in the current GenEd framework.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text:
What we see in the data is partial progress toward that goal. Most students place at the level of approaching competency, with stronger performance in applying regional knowledge, understanding global systems, and reflecting on their own cultural perspective. These are important strengths that suggest our curriculum is building foundational global awareness effectively.
However, there are consistent gaps. Students struggle most with communicating in a language other than English, considering multiple perspectives, and—most notably—examining global responsibilities. Even at the upper levels, where we see developmental gains, these areas remain underdeveloped. The data suggest that students are better at knowing than at doing—that is, they can describe global issues but are less prepared to engage them critically or propose solutions.
We also note a structural limitation: only about 37% of courses participated in the C2 assessment. That level of participation constrains how broadly we can generalize these findings.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text:
Turning to D1: this outcome is intended to move students beyond disciplinary silos by emphasizing the interconnectedness of knowledge and its application to complex, real-world problems. Positioned primarily at the 300- and 400-level, it assumes that students will draw on prior learning across the GenEd curriculum to synthesize ideas, transfer skills, and respond effectively to new academic and professional challenges. In this sense, D1 represents the culminating logic of GenEds: not just the accumulation of knowledge, but its integration and use.
Here the results are stronger. Students most often meet or approach competency, particularly in transferring skills, connecting knowledge, and engaging in integrative learning. This is encouraging and suggests that, where integration is explicitly built into coursework, students perform well.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text:
That said, the D1 data come with even more significant limitations. Only 13% of courses participated, and the sample is heavily weighted toward upper-division courses, limiting representation of earlier stages in the undergraduate experience and our ability to assess developmental progression. So, while the results are positive, they are not yet comprehensive.
Across both outcomes, student performance is closely tied to assignment design. Where assignments are well aligned with GenEd outcomes, students demonstrate competency. Where that alignment is unclear—or where assignments do not explicitly ask for reflection, perspective-taking, or application—student performance drops accordingly.
So, what’s next?
* First, GEC recommends clearer and more explicit guidelines for aligning assignments with GenEd outcomes, particularly in Kuali submissions.
* Second, we recommend investment in faculty development—workshops and resources that help instructors design assignments that elicit the kinds of learning we are trying to measure.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text:
* Third, and critically, we need to find a way to increase faculty participation in assessment. Without broader participation, we risk turning assessment into a compliance exercise rather than a meaningful tool for program improvement.
* Finally, we recommend that certain criteria be revisited—especially––and I emphasize this: language use within C2, to see how criteria are defined and implemented across disciplines, to ensure they are both rigorous and applicable.
A Key Emerging Concern: Language Proficiency
Among the most urgent findings echoed in both assessment data and anticipated student feedback, is the persistently low level of proficiency in a language other than English among our students. This isn't a marginal issue; it represents a structural weakness in the current GenEd framework.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text:
At a time when we position global competency, intercultural awareness, and cross-cultural communication as central institutional goals, the fact that relatively few students graduate with functional proficiency in another language reveals a misalignment between our stated outcomes and our curricular realities. We're asking students to demonstrate global understanding without consistently providing them the most fundamental tool required to achieve it.
This raises a set of unavoidable questions for the committee and for the university: What is the role of language study within General Education? And more importantly, can we credibly claim to prepare students for global citizenship and an increasingly multilingual workforce if language proficiency remains peripheral to the curriculum?

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text:
Without sustained and meaningful engagement in language learning, our claims of intercultural competence risk remaining aspirational rather than demonstrable. If C2 is to function as more than a conceptual framework, then we need to treat language proficiency as a central pathway to achieving its goals, not as an optional enrichment. Despite our stated goals of fostering global understanding and communication across cultures, relatively few students graduate with functional proficiency in another language. This disconnect raises fundamental questions about:
* The role of language study within our GenEd requirements
* Whether GenEd is adequately preparing students for global citizenship and workforce demands
In short, the program is working, but unevenly. Students are learning, but not always in the ways we intend to measure. With stronger alignment, clearer expectations, and broader participation, we can close that gap.

It advances student success, retention, timely degree completion, and career readiness.
The program’s applied focus, interdisciplinary design, and integration of experiential learning opportunities support students in developing market- relevant skills that align with workforce needs.
By embedding internships, project-based learning, and applied AI coursework throughout the curriculum, the program enhances students’ engagement, persistence, and post-graduation outcomes while positioning URI graduates to succeed in a rapidly evolving, AI-enabled economy.
The vision is to provide students with deep knowledge of AI systems and expertise in transferring and applying AI to a variety of problem types.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 8
passages.text:
This program will cover knowledge of the AI ecosystem including the ability to work in interdisciplinary teams with data and domain experts to collect, clean organize, and sample data, match the problem and data to the right intelligent computational tool (there are many types of AI, each with its strengths and weaknesses), tailor, build on top of, and adapt these tools to the problems at hand, support the safe, secure, ethical and accurate reporting of the results to domain experts, and guide teams in deciding if the analytical results make sense.
Students will learn how to use, tailor and augment AI so that the AI can serve as assistants in problem solving, with the human as the master, well versed in the interpretation, and ethical and societal implications of the use of the powerful AI that they will wield.
All of this is in the context of a world in which educators and potential employers are concerned with the lack of digital skills among today’s students and graduates.
To be well educated and prepared for the modern workplace, students must learn to acquire applied technology skills and also to transfer these technologies to specific problems as they arise.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 8
passages.text:
Thus this program is not intended to train students to develop new AI, but to become experts in mastering, adapting, building upon, and deploying existing and evolving intelligent computational artifacts.
We will help students to master the AI tools of today but also help them to understand that these are only contemporary examples to sharpen their problem solving, and learning skills, and give them a leg up as they enter the workplace.
As the world changes and embraces new technologies such as digital twins, and quantum computing, both already inextricably intertwined with AI, we propose a major that is flexible enough that it can evolve with emerging intelligent technologies.
The program advances the University’s goals by preparing students to address complex real-world challenges through the responsible and creative application of emerging technologies.
The curriculum integrates applied coursework, project-based learning, writing-intensive experiences, and internships, ensuring that students develop both technical expertise and transferable skills that support career readiness and lifelong learning.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 8
passages.text:
The program reflects the University’s commitment to interdisciplinary problem-solving and collaboration across colleges and departments.
The program embeds ethical reasoning, equity, and societal impact throughout the curriculum, aligning with the University’s emphasis on responsible scholarship, civic engagement, and public good.
The program also contributes to the University’s role in supporting economic development, innovation, and the future of work in Rhode Island and beyond.
