passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 9
passages.text:
The Applied AI Major is justified by a fundamental shift in how artificial intelligence is developed and used in practice.
Innovation in AI is no longer driven primarily by building algorithms from scratch; instead, it increasingly relies on the creative and programmatic use of existing models, platforms, and tools to design new products, services, and decision systems.
Modern workplaces expect graduates who can integrate pretrained models, APIs, and data pipelines into real- world applications,d combining technical fluency with domain knowledge to solve practical problems.
This requires more than traditional computer or data science or statistics training: it demands an applied understanding of how to select appropriate models, adapt them to specific contexts, validate their outputs, and embed them into larger systems responsibly.
An Applied AI Major addresses this need by preparing students to work at the intersection of data, models, and applications.
Students learn how to manipulate and orchestrate existing AI tools programmatically, that is, fine-tuning models, designing prompts and workflows, building intelligent pipelines, and translating outputs into usable products.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 9
passages.text:
Equally important, they learn how to evaluate model limitations, detect bias, protect privacy, and communicate results clearly to nontechnical stakeholders.
This combination of technical practice and critical judgment reflects how AI is actually deployed in industry, government, and research labs.
Research on Human–AI teaming [Vanshika Vats, et al. (2024)] shows that integrating large pretrained models with human decision making enhances applied problem solving and decision quality across domains underscoring the importance of skills to programmatically manipulate and integrate existing AI models.
By focusing on the intelligent use of existing AI models rather than solely on algorithm development, the major equips students with transferable competencies: problem formulation, tool selection, system integration, and ethical reasoning.
These skills enable graduates not only to build AI- driven products today, but also to adapt quickly as new “d” technologies emerge.
The Applied AI Major therefore fills a distinct and timely educational need, preparing students to have practical knowledge of AI, and to be creators and integrators of intelligent systems rather than passive users of them.

The Graduate Certificate in Community Development & Planning is an online program that helps students develop core competencies in sustainable Community Planning.
Through this program, students will gain a foundation in the principles and practices of community planning and development, specifically in areas of legal, historical, and community-focused dimensions of planning.
The history of planning has many examples of environmental injustice, in which land use decisions have privileged some communities over others.
A commitment to anti-racism, inclusiveness, equity, as well as spatial and social justice perspectives is an integral part of a planning education.
Students can earn their certificate in four sessions, maximizing flexibility and convenience for career enhancement, leadership positions in the industry, and professional growth.

Community Development & Planning — Topical Coverage Certificate 2: Social Planning provides graduate students with an integrated foundation in the theoretical, analytical, legal, and applied dimensions of contemporary planning practice.
The certificate is structured around four required courses that collectively emphasize how planners understand communities, analyze conditions, design interventions, and operate within institutional and legal frameworks.
The Theory and History of Planning course introduces students to the intellectual foundations of the planning profession, examining key theories, movements, and historical contexts that have shaped planning thought and practice.
This course provides critical perspective on the social, political, and ethical dimensions of planning.
The Introduction to Planning Methods course focuses on the analytical and technical tools used by planners to assess community conditions, support decision-making, and evaluate planning outcomes.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 17
passages.text:
Students develop foundational skills in planning analysis and learn how methods inform policy and practice.
The Community Revitalization course emphasizes applied planning strategies aimed at strengthening communities, particularly in contexts experiencing social, economic, or physical challenges.
Students examine approaches to revitalization that address equity, economic development, housing, and the built environment.
The Planning Law course provides essential instruction in the legal frameworks that authorize and constrain planning practice.
Students learn how constitutional principles, statutes, and judicial decisions shape land use regulation, development review, and public decision-making, and how planners must integrate legal reasoning and ethical judgment into professional practice.
Together, these four courses provide a comprehensive preparation in social planning by linking planning theory, analytical methods, applied community interventions, and legal frameworks.
The certificate is designed to support students seeking professional planning knowledge applicable across public, nonprofit, and private-sector contexts.

Noah M.
Daniels I ask you to consider my candidacy for the Faculty Senate Executive Committee for a 2-year term, 2026-2028.
I am an associate professor of computer science, and will have been a member of the faculty for 10 years as of Fall 2026.
I am beginning my second term on the Faculty Senate, and just completing my first 1-year term on FSEC.
In my first term on Faculty Senate, I served two years as chair of the Committee on Technology and Infrastructure.
In that time, my primary focus was on developing consensus policies for ITS to replace unilaterally-developed policies set forth by the administration which hindered academic freedom, research, and teaching.
I have continued this effort as the FSEC liaison to CTI.
This has culminated in a draft of the new ITS policy (with several flaws noted by the faculty) presented for comment in the last month.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 1
passages.text:
In my time on CTI and FSEC, I have served on the IT Governance committee, on the search committees for the Chief Information Officer as well as the University Librarian, and am a founding member of the ad-hoc committees to proactively evaluate whether the technologies on which we depend are effective before the administration signs lengthy contracts.
I enjoy bringing my own perspective to these intellectually diverse working groups, and reconciling that perspective with those of others.
I see the particular strengths I bring to FSEC as including a deep understanding of both technology and how people use technology, as well as a bulwark to efforts to corporatize university ITS and other aspects of university life.
In a tumultuous time when new cybersecurity threats lead to sometimes-draconian policies that can impact research and teaching, as well as the rise of “AI” everywhere (sometimes without the needed critical thinking), I believe I can bring expertise and reasoned argument to addressing these issues.
Beyond technology, I see the adoption of the new budget model and the recent, eye-opening budget committee survey as being a key concern of FSEC going forward.

Committee for Research and Creative Activities End-of-Year Annual Report May 2026 Committee Membership Geoff Bothun, COE, CRCA Member Sen.
Bridget Buxton, CAS Sen.
Amy D’Agata, CON, Chair Sen.
Ruitang Deng, COP Bethany Jenkins, VPRED, Ex Officio Gaurav Khanna, CAS, CRCA Member Dave Rowley, COP, CRCA Member Sen.
David Smith, GSO Sen.
Cynthia Thomas, COB Sen.
Matt Wei, GSO Committee Overview Structure The Committee for Research and Creative Activities (CRCA) consists of six faculty senators and five non-senator research-active faculty.
The Vice President for Research and Economic Development (VPRED) is an ex officio (non-voting) member of the committee.
The Faculty Senate Executive Committee appoints six senators and the VPRED appoints five research-active non-senators to the committee.
The CRCA also comprises a subcommittee, the Competitive Grants Subcommittee.
The CRCA was restructured in 2024 to include non- senators, expanding the committee from 6 to 11 faculty members.
Charge The full committee serves as the representative voice of the university community in all matters related to research, creative, and scholarly activities.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 1
passages.text:
It seeks to improve the environment for research at URI in all ways possible.
The committee oversees the following areas related to research: Advocacy of Research and Creative Activities The committee is to promote a comprehensive understanding of the notion of research, creative, and scholarly work in order to enhance the well-being of all such work at URI; seek to identify all challenges that do or could hinder research, creative, and scholarly efforts at URI and provide recommendations to correct them; review and recommend policies for the management of research affairs at URI and serve as the advisory committee for the Vice President for Research and Economic Development; upon request, advise all campus groups and offices on matters relating to research, creative, and scholarly work.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 1
passages.text: Library and Open Access The committee acts as a liaison between the University Libraries (Library) and the faculty as a whole and advise the Library on matters of general faculty concern; consult with the Library faculty on long-range needs of the Library and the adequacy of budget provisions to meet those needs; serve in an advisory capacity to the Faculty Senate regarding the implementation and interpretation of the University of Rhode Island Open-Access Policy, resolving disputes concerning the interpretation and application of the policy and recommending changes of the policy to the Faculty Senate.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 2
passages.text:
Competitive Grants Subcommittee The subcommittee solicits proposals from the faculty and awards, on a competitive basis, financial support for a “Faculty Development” program (using guidelines developed together with the full committee) to support faculty salary and fellowships, student support, operating expenses, travel, and equipment; advises the Vice President fo r Research and Economic Development concerning the allocation among faculty, on a competitive basis , of financial support for a “Proposal Development” program (using guidelines developed by the Vice President for Research and Economic Development in consultation with the full committee) to support faculty salary and fellowships, student support, operating expenses, travel, and equipment. 2025 –26 Activities The Committee for Research and Creative Activities (CRCA) membership included 6 senators and 3 non- senators.
The committee met regularly throughout Academic Year 2025–2026 to address key issues impacting the University’s research and creative enterprise.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 2
passages.text:
The committee’s work this year focused on three primary areas: (1) supporting faculty success in a shifting federal funding landscape, (2) identifying and addressing challenges facing graduate students, and (3) evaluating and redefining the committee’s role, structure, and alignment within the University.
Throughout the academic year, CRCA engaged in regular, productive exchanges with VPRED Bethany Jenkins, who provided timely and transparent updates on the evolving federal research landscape, institutional responses, and emerging challenges affecting faculty.
These discussions were both informative and collaborative, with committee members sharing on-the-ground perspectives that informed committee discussions and the institution's understanding of research-related challenges for faculty.
CRCA also contribut ed to the interview process for the next AVP of Research Development.
Below is an overview of what was discussed and planned during this period: 1.
Faculty Support in a Changing Research Environment A central theme throughout the year was the evolving federal funding landscape and its implications for faculty research productivity and evaluation.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 2
passages.text:
Early in the year, the committee identified the need for clearer guidance on promotion and tenure expectations in light of funding uncertainties.
This led to discussions and initial drafting efforts to develop peer-review and evaluation guidance that accounts for structural shifts in funding availability.
During the winter, the committee engaged directly with Sue Adams, Vice Provost for Academic and Faculty Initiatives.
These conversations reinforced the need for flexibility and a more holistic approach to faculty evaluation.
The committee also explored the proposed “Achievement Relative to Opportunity” supplement, ultimately determining that existing mechanisms, particularly the applicant statement, were sufficient and more appropriate for contextualizing faculty contributions. 2.
Graduate Student Support The committee identified graduate student support as a priority area, particularly amid the rising cost-of-living concerns and housing challenges.
Discussions highlighted the intersection of financial constraints, housing availability, and the recruitment/retention of graduate students.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 3
passages.text:
In December, CRCA hosted Ellen Reynolds, Vice President for Student Affairs, and Thomas Cooley, Associate Vice President for Student Affairs, to discuss graduate housing initiatives and broader financial challenges facing students.
Key takeaways included the importance of transparent communication with prospective students about the cost of living and the potential need to revisit graduate stipend structures, including budgeting practices for externally funded grants.
The committee also emphasized the importance of continued engagement with Graduate School leadership and plans to revisit these discussions in the coming academic year to further develop actionable recommendations. 3.
Committee Structure, Scope, and Strategic Alignment A portion of the committee’s work this year focused on a critical evaluation of its structure, charge, and institutional role.
Early discussions identified the need to formalize term limits for non -senator members and to more clearly define the committee’s scope, particularly regarding creative activities, intellectual property, and its interface with other university entities.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 3
passages.text:
These conversations reflected a broader recognition that the current structure does not fully position CRCA to meet the evolving needs of the research enterprise.
Building on this assessment, the committee discussed potential restructuring to strengthen its impact and clarify its role in institutional governance.
Two primary models were explored: (a) a joint committee operating in formal partnership between the Faculty Senate and the Division of Research, or (b) a committee housed within the Division of Research with formal Faculty Senate representation.
Both models would more intentionally position CRCA as a strategic, bidirectional conduit for faculty input on rese arch-related issues and as a responsive advisory body to institutional leadership.
Preliminary discussions with Bethany Jenkins and the Faculty Senate Executive Committee indicated openness to advancing a restructuring proposal.
Given the significance of these changes, the committee determined that further development, stakeholder input, and alignment with Faculty Senate processes are needed.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 3
passages.text:
As such, formal proposals and decisions have been intentionally deferred to the next academic year to ensure thoughtful planning and broad engagement.
For continuity and efficiency, d rafted documents developed this year will be carried forward and shared with next year’s committee, providing a foundation for continued refinement and timely progress. 4.
Competitive Grants Subcommittee See subcommittee report. 5.
Key Themes and Looking Ahead Across all areas of work, several consistent themes emerged: ● The need for adaptable faculty evaluation frameworks in response to external funding variability ● The importance of strengthening institutional support for graduate students ● The value of clear, coordinated structures connecting faculty governance and research administration ● Increasing demand for internal research support mechanisms 6.
F&A Report As part of the CRCA charge, an annual F&A report is typically included in the committee’s end-of-year report to the Faculty Senate.
However, the most recent FY25 data currently available are already approximately 11 months old, raising questions about the usefulness and timeliness of reporting those figures this spring.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 3
passages.text:
In addition, changes in the University’s budget structure have limited the level of detail available for reporting.
While the business office can still provide F&A distributions and proportional research administration assessments by college, other research -related expenses are now aggregated with broader non -research operational costs, limiting the ability to provide the same level of reporting detail as in prior years.
Given both the timing and reporting limitations, the committee believes the Senate would be better served by shifting the F&A reporting

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 4
passages.text: cycle to the fall, when more current and complete data are available. The committee plans to revisit this issue as part of its broader restructuring discussions in the coming academic year. Conclusion CRCA played an important role this year as a forum for identifying emerging challenges, facilitating communication between faculty and research leadership, and laying the groundwork for structural improvements. The committee is well -positioned to build on this work in the coming year, with a focus on implementing changes that strengthen the research environment and support faculty and student success.

COMMITTEE REVIEW PROCESS The committee were able to continue the practice established by the 2022-3 committee of seeking three reviews per proposal for the Career Enhancement proposals.
However, due to the significant increase of proposals in Proposal Development and Collaborative Proposal Development, the committee must reduce to two reviews per proposal for these two categories.
This year’s committee only has 4 members, much smaller than previous years (7 members in 2024-5 and 10 members in 2023-4).
For that reason, the committee relied on 6 other members of the Committee for Research and Creative Activities as well as 25 previous awardees to contribute reviews.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 7
passages.text:
Each committee member (10 total) reviewed 5-6 proposals, and each external reviewer reviewed 2-3 proposals.
Proposals were assigned so that at least one committee member reviewed each proposal.
The committee attempted to assign knowledgeable reviewers to each proposal while avoiding conflicts of interest.
The nature of the competition, however, means that most proposals were reviewed by faculty outside their discipline.
The committee created rankings of the proposals in each funding category based on the reviewer scores and comments, but the committee discussed the merits of each proposal, focusing particularly on proposals with variable scores and on proposals close to the funding threshold.
In situations where ratings were very similar, the committee gave preference to junior faculty.
The committee created a written summary of the deliberation for each proposal in the Career Enhancement category and most proposals in the Collaborative Proposal Development category.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 8
passages.text:
We acknowledge that reviewers are likely to differ in the range of scores assigned and checked the possibility that a reviewer might give consistently “high” or “low” scores respectively.
Because the number of proposals reviewed per reviewer is low, our ability to correct for reviewer “leniency” was limited.
RECOMMENDATIONS FOR 2027 Be prepared to handle more proposals The number of proposals increased substantially in both Proposal Development and Collaborative Proposal Development, while remaining relatively stable in Career Enhancement.
This growth has made it challenging for the subcommittee to manage the workload and secure enough qualified reviewers.
We anticipate that proposal volume will remain at this level or continue to rise next year.
To address this, we may need to (1) expand the size of the committee and (2) seek additional review support from colleagues who are not previous awardees.
Emphasize the expectations in more detail The RFP states that this is a campus-wide competition and that proposals will be reviewed by non-experts.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 8
passages.text:
While most PIs appeared to understand and appreciate this, some submissions seemed to be revised versions of proposals originally prepared for specific agencies and therefore included a level of technical detail that may not be accessible to a generalist audience.
Regarding plans for future external submissions, reviewers expected applicants to identify not only a specific target agency or program but also a realistic timeline.
Several proposals did not include a timeline and were consequently scored lower.
Placing additional emphasis on this requirement in future RFPs would help applicants avoid unnecessary point deductions.
Communicate expectations from reviewers Reviewers may benefit from more explicit guidance on both the criteria and process for evaluating proposals.
For example, using prior external funding as an example some reviewers assigned lower scores to applicants with extensive previous awards, while others scored them more favorably.
Similarly, for the Career Enhancement category, some reviewers assumed that awards are primarily intended for assistant professors, which is not the case.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 8
passages.text:
Providing more detailed and standardized review criteria would help improve consistency across evaluations.

UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND FACULTY SENATE REPORT OF THE EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE March 2006 During the 2003-04 academic year, the Faculty Senate Executive Committee urged the JSPC and the President to develop a procedure for reviewing academic programs that would include both qualitative and quantitative measures. (See http://www.uri.edu/facsen/JSPC_MIN_12_18_03.html).
In January 2004, President Carothers hired Mr.
Thomas Murphy to adapt his model to the University of Rhode Island (See http://www.uri.edu/facsen/JSPC_Min_1_22.html).
In February of that year the JSPC agreed to replace the Program Contribution Analysis (PCA) with an instrument that would include qualitative as well as quantitative measures (See http://www.uri.edu/facsen/JSPC_Min_2_5.html).
Shortly thereafter, a small group comprising members of the JSPC began working with Mr.
Murphy to refine and revise his model.
This work continued through the 2004-2005 academic year and in the summer of 2005 under the auspices of a Faculty Senate Executive Committee- Administration working group (2004-05 Senate Chair Faye Boudreaux-Bartels, Senators Michael Rice and Celest Martin, Assistant Provost Cliff Katz and Ms.

passages.heading: Linked from Faculty Senate Executive Committee Report #2024-2025-01 | Page 1
passages.text:
Ann Morrissey, Co-Director of Planning Services and Professional Development and Executive Assistant to the President).
This group continued to revise, refine, and test the model originally developed by Mr.
Murphy, and eventually renamed the AIIM Model (See http://www.uri.edu/facsen/AIIM_Home.html for details on the process and the development of the model) In the fall 2005, faculty members from all academic departments were asked to complete the AIIM Survey.
At that time, the Faculty Senate Executive Committee asked the Constitution, By-Laws and University Manual Committee to review the existing sections of the University Manual on Program Quality Review and to revise them to accommodate a combined quality-cost process (such as the AIIM) and to establish a standing joint committee to oversee the process and the development of any future instrument.
After some discussion between members of the working group and the Constitution, By Laws and University Manual Committee, it was agreed that the Faculty Senate Executive Committee should develop a proposal in consultation with the CBUM Committee.

passages.heading: Linked from Faculty Senate Executive Committee Report #2024-2025-01 | Page 1
passages.text:
It is clear to the Faculty Senate Executive Committee that the Program Contribution Analysis (PCA) and the Program Quality Review (PQR) process as outlined in the UNIVERSITY MANUAL are no longer viable.
Therefore, after consulting with the Constitution, By-Laws and University Manual Committee, the FSEC now proposes revisions to sections of the University Manual on Program Quality Review and the establishment of a Joint Committee of the Faculty Senate and the Administration which would be responsible for maintaining faculty oversight and review of an academic assessment process, including developing and revising an appropriate instrument as the University’s needs evolve.
The Executive Committee recommends that the Faculty Senate adopt the following legislation as the University’ official procedure for academic program review.

passages.heading: Linked from Faculty Senate Executive Committee Report #2024-2025-01 | Page 2
passages.text:
Recommendations I.DELETE EXISTING SECTIONS 8.86.12, 13, 14, 20, 21, 22, 31, 32, 33 34, 41 and 50, which refer to the detailed Program Quality Review Process: 8.86.12 The Chair of the Graduate Council, the Chair of the Curricular Affairs Committee, and the Vice Chair of the Faculty Senate shall have general responsibility for determining a program review cycle conforming to the guidelines specified for carrying out other oversight functions of the University's program quality review process.
This includes notifying affected parties and publishing schedules of reviews to allow effective planning and workload assignment for the review.
This group shall meet at least once each year, early in the fall semester, and as often as necessary to accomplish their assigned responsibilities. 8.86.13 In general, programs should be reviewed at least every seventh year, that is, reviews should be scheduled so that the completion date of successive reviews for a given program should be no more than seven years apart.

passages.heading: Linked from Faculty Senate Executive Committee Report #2024-2025-01 | Page 2
passages.text:
Programs may be reviewed after an interval of less than this at the mutual agreement of the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs and the chair or person responsible for the program. 8.86.14 In consultation with the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs, the group specified in 8.86.12 may schedule a number of related programs to be reviewed simultaneously and may make special arrangements to this end. 8.86.20 Program Review Steering Committees.
Each program identified for review shall have its own three member Program Review Steering Committee appointed to oversee and coordinate the review of that specific program.
The Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs shall appoint one person to the committee, the program being reviewed shall appoint one person to the committee, and the third person shall be an individual agreed upon by both the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs and the program.

passages.heading: Linked from Faculty Senate Executive Committee Report #2024-2025-01 | Page 2
passages.text:
The Provost's appointee shall chair the committee. 8.86.21 A basic responsibility of a Program Review Steering Committee for a particular program shall be to meet with the members of that program in order to design and determine the specific procedures and formats that will be followed in the current review.
General guidelines for reviews are given below, but adjustments or modifications to them can be recommended by a Program Review Steering Committee.
For example, the Program Review Steering Committee may decide that outside reviewer should be consulted in a particular review or that a recent accreditation review document prepared by the program can serve as the primary component of the current review. 8.86.22 Each Program Review Steering Committee shall prepare a brief program review plan in consultation with members of the program and submit it to the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs for approval.
If the program review plan contains a recommendation to use outside reviewers in a program review, a mechanism for selecting them shall also be included as part of the plan.
An approved plan shall

passages.heading: Linked from Faculty Senate Executive Committee Report #2024-2025-01 | Page 3
passages.text:
be the basis for a specific program review.
This plan should normally be submitted and approved in the semester prior to the beginning of the review.
The review process itself normally shall extend over the two semesters of an academic year, with a report being submitted to the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs in the spring semester. 8.86.31 Description.
The descriptive section may be comprised largely of departmental material produced on an annual basis such as past annual reports, supplemented by curricular proposals submitted since the last review, updated vitae of all tenure- track faculty members and other personnel, other than graduate assistants teaching on a part-time and/or non-continuing basis, the latest accreditation report, if applicable, and such other documentation as the department considers pertinent.
The Program Review Steering Committee shall determine what specific information may be used or must be included in the descriptive section. (See 8.86.21). 8.86.32 Evaluation.

passages.heading: Linked from Faculty Senate Executive Committee Report #2024-2025-01 | Page 3
passages.text:
The members of the program, in cooperation with their Program Review Steering Committee, shall use the information contained in the descriptive section to assess the strengths and weaknesses of the program including a quantitative and qualitative assessment of the teaching, research, service, and/or other creative accomplishments of the faculty. 8.86.33 Recommendations.
On the basis of the assessments made in the evaluative section, the members of the program, in cooperation with their Program Review Steering Committee and the Dean or academic administrator to whom the program director or chair reports shall develop a plan to help direct the future efforts of the program.
The plan should include: goals, steps to be taken to achieve those goals, and a timetable. 8.86.34 Summary.
The Steering Committee shall prepare a short summary of the most important points in the report and any observations or thoughts on the evaluation and recommendations contained in the report.

passages.heading: Linked from Faculty Senate Executive Committee Report #2024-2025-01 | Page 3
passages.text:
These observations shall serve as a peer assessment of the process and its outcome and shall be conveyed with the report as described in 8.86.40-41. 8.86.41 In general, the written report submitted to the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs as a result of the program review process shall be made available upon request to any interested parties.
Any individual or group of standing in a particular program review may request that some portions of the report, especially those relating to specific personnel issues, not be made public.
The Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs shall have the final authority to decide whether or not to withhold any portions of the report from public distribution. 8.86.50 Follow-Up.
Each Steering Committee, in consultation with the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs, the Dean or academic administrator to whom the program director or chair reports and the program director or chair, shall determine the length of a follow-up period.

passages.heading: Linked from Faculty Senate Executive Committee Report #2024-2025-01 | Page 3
passages.text:
This period, usually two years, should allow for implementation of at least some of the recommendations made in the report or subsequently agreed to as a result of discussions with the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs.
At the end of the follow-up period, the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs, the program director or chair, the Dean or academic administrator to whom the program director or chair reports and such members of

passages.heading: Linked from Faculty Senate Executive Committee Report #2024-2025-01 | Page 4
passages.text:
the Program Review Steering Committee as are available, will review the recommendations and assess progress.
Further recommendations, including recommendations to schedule subsequent follow-up meeting(s) may be negotiated at this time.
II.REVISE the following sections (Changes in boldface): 8.86.10 Academic Program Quality Review.
In this section the term "program" shall be understood to include academic departments, as well as any curriculum or University sponsored activity requiring the assignment of one or more faculty to serve in a teaching, research, or service capacity and intended to result in the conferral of an undergraduate or graduate degree or of a certificate or other credential. 8.86.11 The primary purpose of the academic program quality review shall be to assess both the academic quality of and the financial aspects of a program.
The academic program review shall be used to inform decision-makers with regard to resources in academic departments and programs and to provide the University with information that will lead to improved program focus and quality.

passages.heading: Linked from Faculty Senate Executive Committee Report #2024-2025-01 | Page 4
passages.text:
In addition, it is intended to help the University gain greater degrees of efficiency and effectiveness in the delivery of the academic curriculum. 8.86.12 (8.86.23) During the course of the academic program review and during the formulation of the review instrument, an Academic Program Review Steering Committee shall help coordinate the steps of the review, shall lead in the formulation of the evaluation instrument, and shall continue to modify previous instrument versions or develop new instruments to accommodate the changing needs of the faculty and administration. (See sections 5.86.10-11 on the Academic Program Review Committee.) 8.86.13 (8.86.30) Report.
In general terms, The report, prepared as a result of an academic program quality review, shall be available to the University Community; however, responses to the evaluation instrument submitted by individual participants shall remain confidential. 8.86.14 (8.86.40) Presentation of the Report.

passages.heading: Linked from Faculty Senate Executive Committee Report #2024-2025-01 | Page 4
passages.text:
The Steering Committee for each review, the program director or chair and the Dean or academic administrator to whom the program director or chair reports shall meet with the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs to examine and discuss the results of the review present and explain the report, and to discuss the recommendations made in the report. as soon as feasible, but no longer than one hundred and eighty calendar days following the dissemination of the results.
The Academic Program Review Committee shall serve in an advisory capacity during this process. the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs shall provide the program director or chair and the Dean or academic administrator to whom the program director or chair reports with a written response to the report and the meeting including what support can be expected to help implement recommendations made in the report or subsequently agreed to.

passages.heading: Linked from Faculty Senate Executive Committee Report #2024-2025-01 | Page 5
passages.text: III.ADD NEW SECTIONS 5.86.10 and 5.86 11 as follows: 5.86.10 The Academic Program Review Committee (APRC) shall develop and maintain the academic program review instrument. The committee shall coordinate the administration of the review, oversee the collection of data, and compile and disseminate information resulting from the review as outlined in sections 8.86.10-14. When academic program reviews are conducted, the committee shall serve as a resource to departments and programs being reviewed. The committee shall receive and respond to comments regarding the program review process, including, but not limited to, the academic program review instrument. 5.86.11 The committee shall be comprised of at least four faculty members appointed by the Faculty Senate, two representatives of the Provost and a representative of the President. Faculty members shall serve three-year terms, shall be appointed on a staggered basis and may succeed themselves for one additional three-year term.

passages.text:
Announcements - Faculty Senate President Nassersharif offered remarks about theFaculty Senate budget, noting that the Faculty Senate leadership, including committeechairs, are faced with the difficult task of balancing Senate service with their regularfaculty duties.
These leaders rarely receive course release or other support.
Any time thatthe Senate has required additional resources, members had to make a special requestfrom the Provost.
Without a budget model that provides for adequate and reliablesupport, the Senate’s autonomy and ability to engage in shared governance fully has beencompromised.
Fortunately, Provost Wolfe has recently agreed to meet with Senateleadership for a meaningful discussion about providing the Senate its own budget andempowering officers and chairs to engage in their leadership roles.
Provost Wolfe wasthanked for her leadership on this issue and the Faculty Senate will be kept abreast ofthese developments.
The entirety of President Nassersharif’s remarks can be found here. i.
Today’s reception is being sponsored by the College of Pharmacy - Thank you DeanLarrat! 1

FSEC recently discovered that in the process, an error wasintroduced in Appendix G, where Policy #80-1 on Faculty Senatejurisdiction over policies was inadvertently deleted in the process.

The report was informational and no otheraction was required. iii.

REPORT OF THE PRESIDENT a.
Announcements and Budget Presentation - The President highlighted someevents and gatherings around campus so far this year.
Of special note were eventsinvolving Hillel and the Middle Eastern Students Association in response to thecrisis in Gaza.
President Parlange emphasized the need to foster a welcomingcommunity at URI where everyone feels respected and free to speak without fear.Fall events also included a very successful Quad Fest, coinciding with the AnnualDay of Giving, which exceeded all fundraising expectations.

passages.heading: Linked from LOOC Annual Report, December, 2023 | Page 3
passages.text:
President Parlangemoved on to address URI’s global rankings and praised US News and WorldReport for revising their methodology.
This has resulted in a number of publicuniversities, URI included, moving up in rank.
In terms of the annual budget presentation, the President noted that while URIdid not get everything it asked for from the State of RI, its allocation did increasefor 2024, which gives the university some momentum to carry out someimportant initiatives.
Increased state funding comes in the form of the standardbudget allocation as well as special funds (ARPA, bonds, etc).
President Parlangethen outlined spending priorities for the year, including essential services, capitalprojects, and certain strategic investments.
The university is transitioning to anincentive-based budget model which will be new for the URI community.
It is theBOT’s and the administration’s position that this model will reward innovationand entrepreneurship, improve transparency and accountability, and incentivizeimproved academic quality. c.

PRESENTATIONS/REPORTS FROM OTHER ADMINISTRATORS a.
Updates from Provost Wolfe - Provost Wolfe provided updates in three broadareas: the future of UCAS, the status of current Dean searches, and changescoming to URI Online.
A steering committee met throughout 2021 to formulaterecommendations about UCAS and implementation of recommendations isstarting now.
The University’s new Strategic Plan includes some of therecommendations which now have KPI’s associated with them.
For example,additional investment in advising is forthcoming and the administration expectsthis to positively impact retention and graduation rates.
A new ExecutiveDirector of Student Success is being hired to lead change in UCAS.

passages.heading: Linked from LOOC Annual Report, December, 2023 | Page 4
passages.text:
As for Deansearches, a new Pharmacy Dean was announced this week and the Deans ofNursing and CHS are expected to be announced within the next two weeks.Regarding URI Online, the University is currently recruiting a new Vice Provostfor Online and Strategic Educational Initiatives which will be a new position.
Thenew Vice Provost is expected to steward expansion of non-traditionaleducational initiatives and should be on board by the end of the year. b.
Athletics Annual Presentation, Athletic Director Thorr BjornAssisting in the presentation will be Jeff Johnson, Associate Athletic Director, 4

passages.heading: Linked from LOOC Annual Report, December, 2023 | Page 5
passages.text:
and the following student athletes: Olivia Dumeer, Catie Castle, Sam Gumprecht,Jarret Young and Irma Accius.
AD Bjorn and the student athletes presented dataprofiling the athletics program at the university and providing academic anddemographic information on student athletes by sport.
Recent team andindividual accomplishments were highlighted along with goals for the future.The Athletics Program has established the objective of seeing more than half ofits teams win a conference championship by 2032 and has a number ofimprovement initiatives planned in furtherance of that goal.
Physical facilityimprovements along with recruiting and retaining top athletes and coaches willplay a role.
The Annual Athletics Report was accepted by consensus. 7.

This update toChapter 8 would wrap up work began by the CASC last year to clarifylanguage regarding Minors.

CASC Chair Preisser responded tosubstantive questions, noting the intention was to ensure thatstudents pursuing a Minor obtained course credit beyond therequirements of their chosen major.
The report was approvedunanimously. ii.
CBUM Report #2023-2024-3 - Chair Ward proposed changes toChapter 5 of the University Manual to create a new committee.
Thiseffort also grew out of work done in AY 22-23 when AVP Veeger’soffice suggested the merger of the Academic Program ReviewCommittee (APRC) with the Learning Outcomes and OversightCommittee (LOOC).
The new committee would be known as the JointCommittee on Academic Program Review and Outcomes Assessment(JAPROA).
Current TAAC Chair Lofgren asked for a friendlyamendment to include language indicating the new committee willwork with the TAAC.
CBUM Chair Ward accepted the amendment andnoted she will make the modification to the language.
AVP Veegermade a motion to amend the draft language to remove the referenceto NECHE, noting there are other offices and committees existing toadvise the university regarding accreditation and this new committeewould likely not be involved.
Her motion was seconded by Sen.
Kosterand approved via voice vote.

passages.text:
Informational Report on Curricular Processing Timelines - Chair Preisserdeferred to Faculty Senate Specialist Genvieve Spitale to present the report.
The report made clear that the CASC is a very hard working group, havingreviewed 142 course proposals last academic year.
Of those, 140 wereapproved and 91% were acted upon by the Faculty Senate at the meetingimmediately following the CASC meeting.
It was hoped that this datawould help to dispel the myth that the Faculty Senate approval process iscumbersome and slow.
Most proposals spend the majority of their reviewtimeline under the purview of the departments and colleges involved, i.e.before they reach the level of the Faculty Senate and its committees.Proposers need to keep in mind that review workflows arecollege-specific and timelines can vary a great deal from college tocollege.
The Faculty Senate office is in the process of modernizing its webpages and curricular processing deadlines will be clearly posted to helpproposers better manage their schedules and expectations. ii.
Report No. 2023-2024-1A, Courses - Chair Preisser presented the report fromhis committee’s October 6 meeting.
It included one informational item, three 6

The informational report makesclear that Chinese, Portuguese and Italian, in addition to German, Spanish,Latin and French are covered by the approved program. The report wasunanimously accepted. d. General Education Committee - Chair Fogelmani. Report No. 2023-2024-2A - Chair Fogelman presented the report from theCommittee’s October 3 meeting. It included two courses in the College of Arts andSciences for action. It was unanimously approved. e. Academic Calendar Committee - Chair Kovoori. Informational Report - Update the December Commencement CeremonyDate - Chair Kovoor explained that the University of Rhode Island has nothad a December Commencement Ceremony in the past but will begin to doso this year and the official Academic Calendar should be amended to reflectthese dates. The report is informational but acceptance of the report willmemorialize the change. The report was accepted via voice vote. 8. CALL for NEW BUSINESS - None. 9. World Wide Web-enhanced courses combine traditional classroom and World Wide Web-based instruction. Courses that are web-enhanced require a classroom and are scheduled in the usual manner. When appropriate, proposals for new courses should address the extent to which and how the course is Web-enhanced. Web-based courses are delivered entirely online. The CAC believes that this delivery method has a significant impact on learning and teaching and thus (a) a separate curricular approval process is required; and (b) Web-based courses should be designated as such in the catalog, and in scheduling materials. 6 Early Contingent Admission to the Doctor of Physical Therapy (DPT) Program.
Students who major in Kinesiology will have the opportunity to complete non-elective coursework for their degrees by the end of their third year at URI.
If the student has a minimum 3.4 GPA, a minimum of a 3.0 in Biology 121, and meets all other requirements for admission to the DPT program, the student can apply for early contingent admission to the DPT program.
If admitted on early contingency, these students would take the first year courses for the DPT.
These courses would count as the elective courses in the bachelor's degree.
Once students have completed the required number of credits, they will receive their bachelor's degree.
The student would then continue on in the DPT program and complete both programs in 6 rather than the usual 7 years.
This option will be limited to outstanding students only.
Students in this program would have to have a minimum GPA of 3.2 at the end of the first year, a minimum of 3.30 GPA at the end of the second year, and a minimum GPA of 3.40 for early contingent admission to the DPT program.

passages.heading: #05-06–28 | Page 6
passages.text:
Additionally, all students must have achieved a minimum of 3.0 in Biology 121 and meet all requirements for admission to the DPT program.
Students who meet the benchmarks are not guaranteed acceptance into the DPT program.
Students who meet the benchmarks but are not accepted into the DPT program can easily complete their B.S.

The proposal is in the format required by the Board of Governors for Higher Education. A.GENERAL INFORMATION 1. Name of institution University of Rhode Island 2. Names of administrative units Kinesiology Department College of Human Science and Services 3. Title of proposed organizational unit Physical Therapy Department 4. Summary description of the proposed organization change. The purpose of this proposal is to change the standing of the Physical Therapy Program from a program within the Kinesiology Department to a separate Department within the College of Human Science and Services. 8. Signature of the President ______________________________ Robert L. Carothers 9. Resources The organizational changes proposed herein require no new resources. The Physical Therapy Program has its own director, faculty, secretarial support, facilities, and operating budget. 10. passages.heading: #05-06–16 | Page 3
passages.text:
3 B.RATIONALE This organizational change is being proposed because the Physical Therapy Program can better fulfill its mission to educate competent doctors of physical therapy who can provide skilled patient care in a variety of settings, conduct clinical research, and provide service to the community at large if it is an academic department within the College of Human Science and Services rather than a program within the Kinesiology Department.
The mission of the Physical Therapy Program focuses on professional, graduate rather than undergraduate education as is the case in the Kinesiology Department.
There are no common students between the two units nor does faculty teach across the units.
The reorganization will allow PT faculty to focus their efforts on continued development and advancement of the program, clinical and basic science research related to the profession and provision of service to the community and profession.
The Physical Therapy Program has functioned autonomously within the (Department of Physical Education now renamed) Kinesiology Department since its inception in 1991.

passages.heading: #05-06–16 | Page 3
passages.text:
It has had its own faculty, support staff, facilities, and budget from the very beginning as a requirement of professional accreditation.
Further, due to accreditation requirements, the Program Director has maintained direct communication with the Dean of the College and was a regular participant at College Management meetings.
A self-study report for the Commission on Accreditation in Physical Therapy Education was recently completed in preparation for a site visit that occurred in September 2005.
It was during this self- evaluation that the faculty recognized that the Program was intended to be a separate entity within the college from its development and that separation would allow for better overall functioning of the program.
With the recent move from the masters of physical therapy to the doctor of physical therapy, the program is even more out of place being located within the Kinesiology Department.
Separation will allow better collaboration between the Physical Therapy Program and other departments such as Communicative Disorders and Biology.

passages.heading: #05-06–16 | Page 3
passages.text:
This re- organization will simplify day-to-day operations and clarify evaluation of program activities because data will no longer be combined with that of the Kinesiology department.
Please note that no new resources are needed to affect this organizational change.
C.INSTITUTIONAL ROLE This organizational change is consistent with the published role and mission of URI.
The Department of Physical Therapy will have all of the responsibilities of a Department.
In addition, it will provide added value to the University through its recognition as the only Physical Therapy Program in the state and via the clinic, which provides physical therapy to citizens of Rhode Island.

passages.heading: #05-06–16 | Page 4
passages.text: 4 D.INTERINSTITUTIONAL CONSIDERATIONS The projected impact of this organizational change on the other public higher educational institutions in Rhode Island is nil. Other institutions in Rhode Island will not be affected by this change because the Physical Therapy Program is not a new program and is not competing with other programs in the state for students or resources. There are no cooperative arrangements with other institutions relative to this organizational change. E.EVALUATION The Physical Therapy Program is fully accredited through the Commission on Accreditation in Physical Therapy Education (CAPTE). Evaluation of the program is on going and includes both direct and indirect measures of clearly defined outcomes. Examples of outcome measures include the percentage of students who pass the National Physical Therapy Licensure Exam, the percentage of students who receive outstanding grades on the clinical performance instrument, a tool that is used nationally to evaluate the performance of students in the clinical setting, and responses from employers gathered both on surveys and in focus groups. Effective this semester, the PT program will begin using the electronic portfolio system recently purchased by URI called “True Outcomes”. Data from these evaluations will be used to make necessary changes in the doctor of physical therapy degree program.

Name of Institution University of Rhode Island 2. Institutional Review and Approval Process Date Approved College of Pharmacy October 2003 Curricular Affairs Committee, Faculty Senate January 2004 Faculty Senate President of the University 8. Summary of Proposed Organizational Change The College of Pharmacy presently consists of three Departments: The Department of Applied Pharmaceutical Science (APS); The Department of Biomedical Science (BMS) and the Department of Pharmacy Practice (PHP). The Department of APS consists of two sections, a Pharmaceutics Section and a Pharmacoepidemiology / Pharmaceconomics Section. During the 2002-2003 academic year the Dean of the College established a committee with representation from all three departments. The committee was charged to consider ways of optimizing the administration, research program and teaching activities of the College. After discussions with the Dean of the College, it was recommended that the College be reorganized into two departments. It was proposed that the Pharmaceutics Section of APS and the whole of BMS should be merged to form a new Department of Biomedical and Pharmaceutical Sciences (BPS). It was further proposed that the Pharmacoepidemiology and Pharmacoeconomics section of APS become part of the Department of PHP. 9. Resources 420CAC http://www.uri.edu/facsen/420CAC.html 2 of 4 1/6/14, 5:35 PM

Carothers 11.
Person to Contact During the Review Judith Swift Interim Vice Provost for Academic Programs and Services 874-4408 B.
RATIONALE The College of Pharmacy presently consists of three Departments: The Department of Applied Pharmaceutical Science (APS); The Department of Biomedical Science (BMS) and the Department of Pharmacy Practice (PHP).
Faculty in PHP are primarily clinicians, who are directly involved in patient care and as a result are primarily based at clinical sites throughout the state.
In contrast, faculty in APS and BMS are based at the Kingston campus.
Furthermore, with the exception of the Pharmacoepidemiology and Pharmacoeconomics (PE/PE) Section of APS, the research activities of APS and BMS are primarily laboratory based.
As pharmaceutical science and biomedical science has evolved in the last decade there has been an increasing overlap in the research activities of the two departments.
However, the present departmental structure discourages collaboration and hinders interaction between and among faculty.

passages.heading: #03-04–18 | Page 3
passages.text:
The proposed departmental structure would address this problem and hopefully lead to cross-fertilization of research efforts between the two existing departments.
Owing to the more practice oriented research activities of the PE/PE section of APS, a more logical placement for this section would be within the department of PHP.
These organizational changes will also enable the College to address its graduate program and consider ways to make the program more cost-effective and to better prepare the graduates for careers in pharmaceutical and biological science.
The new structure would have minimal effect on the courses offered in College of Pharmacy.
The College of Pharmacy's main teaching responsibility is delivery of the Doctor of Pharmacy curriculum.
Since this is a College-wide integrated curriculum, the proposed restructuring would only lead to some recoding and renumbering of courses.
It is anticipated that the improved communication associated with the proposed changes will enhance the coordination of course content and reduce overlap between courses. 420CAC http://www.uri.edu/facsen/420CAC.html 3 of 4 1/6/14, 5:35 PM

passages.heading: #03-04–18 | Page 4
passages.text: Overall it is anticipated that the proposed re-structuring would: increase collaboration between and among faculty in the College of Pharmacy; promote cross-disciplinary research projects; improve the quality and cost-effectiveness of the graduate program and improve the delivery of the Doctor of Pharmacy curriculum. Finally, given the size of the College of Pharmacy, which has about 35 full-time faculty, a two department system would be more in-keeping with other College structures on campus. The net loss of one chair in the College will result in the following annual savings: $3,000.00 chair supplement 1/9 to 3/9 of the contract salary for a summer salary. C. INSTITUTIONAL ROLE The merger is consistent with the University's efforts to promote efﬁciencies and increase productivity through restructuring. D. INTERINSTITUTIONAL CONSIDERATIONS None E. CONTENT No change in content F. EV ALUATION The functioning of the Departments of BPS and PHP will be monitored by the Chairperson of each department, the Associate Dean for Research, the Associate Dean of Academic Affairs in the College of Pharmacy, the Dean of the College of Pharmacy and the Provost of the University in accordance with the standard management practices of the institution. 420CAC http://www.uri.edu/facsen/420CAC.html 4 of 4 1/6/14, 5:35 PM

passages.heading: Chapter 8 – Academic Regulations
passages.text:
Assessment of Student Learning Outcomes
8.59.10 Assessment of student learning outcomes shall be coordinated by the Assistant Director of Student Learning, Outcomes Assessment and Accreditation (see 2.22.21 ) with the oversight of the JAPROA (see Sections 5.84.10 – 5.84.14). The following policies shall apply to this process: #23-24-7
8.59.11 Academic Program Engagement: All undergraduate, professional, and graduate academic programs, including General Education, shall be actively engaged in student learning outcomes assessment as evidenced by, but not limited to:
a) Published student learning outcomes that are clear statements of what students are expected to gain, achieve, demonstrate, or know at the completion of the academic program. These student learning outcomes shall be published on the program’s website as well as on the website for the Office of Student Learning, Outcomes Assessment, and Accreditation (SLOAA). These student learning outcomes shall be periodically reviewed by the academic program for ongoing relevance.

passages.heading: Chapter 8 – Academic Regulations
passages.text:
b) A plan of student learning outcomes assessment that is endorsed by the program’s faculty. Plans should include a regular and predictable cycle for collecting and analyzing assessment data, for discussing curricular and programmatic changes, for implementing interventions, and for re-assessing the impact of implemented changes. Outcomes assessment plans will be published on each program’s website as well as on the SLOAA website.
c) Reports of student learning outcomes assessment that are provided to SLOAA using staggered cycles of no more than 3 years. Cycles for accredited programs will be adjusted to decrease redundancy of effort. #09-10–29

passages.heading: Chapter 8 – Academic Regulations
passages.text:
8.59.12 SLOAA Guidance for Academic Programs: Guidelines and schedules for preparation of outcomes assessment plans and reports shall be provided by SLOAA with the assistance and approval of the Joint Committee on Academic Program Review and Outcomes Assessment (JAPROA). SLOAA shall offer advice on the logistics of collecting assessment data, support for analyzing the results, and feedback on designing curricular and programmatic changes. Rubrics for evaluating the plans and reports shall be generated by SLOAA and posted on its website. #09-10–29 #23-24-7
8.59.13 Evaluation of Plans and Reports: Student learning outcomes assessment plans and reports shall be submitted through SLOAA for evaluation and recommendations by JAPROA. Programs shall be notified directly of the results of the evaluation and whether modification is needed. Summary reports shall be published on the SLOAA website. JAPROA shall provide a general summary of outcomes assessment in its annual report. #09-10–29 #23-24-7

passages.heading: Chapter 8 – Academic Regulations
passages.text: 8.59.14 University-Wide Student Learning Outcomes Assessment: With guidance from JAPROA, SLOAA shall work with the Office of Institutional Research and other university offices to collect, maintain, analyze, and distribute student learning outcomes assessment findings, derived from a variety of local and national sources. SLOAA shall identify patterns of student performance to inform ongoing program and institutional improvement. #09-10–29 #23-24-7

1 Constitution, By-laws and University Manual Committee Informational Report on Changes to Administrative Portions of University Manual Chapters 4 and 7 Submitted on behalf of President Dooley January 2013 Modified at Faculty Senate Meeting of January 24, 2013 The informational report presented here is a first step in the effort to update, in cooperation with the President and other administrative officers, those parts of the University Manual which are under the jurisdiction of the President (see UM 11.10.11).
For the most part, the report concerns position descriptions in Chapters 4 and 7 of the University Manual.
The Committee employed the following procedure: During the Spring 2012 semester, we met with Vice Provost Katz who provided valuable input; on the basis of that input, a draft of changes was constructed and, during the Summer of 2012, submitted to the President, the Provost, and other administrative officers, including all the academic deans, with a request for feedback.
Based on the feedback and on conversations with some of the administrative officers who had responded, this document has been prepared.

passages.heading: Administrative January 2013 | Page 1
passages.text:
Although it is presented as an informational report, senators are encouraged to suggest improvements.
Part I of this report contains the University Manual sections in their modified form; Part II documents the changes that have been made.

The rights and privileges of faculty status, excepting the rights of tenure and of election to the Faculty Senate, and with other stated exceptions, shall be extended to the following categories (4.12.11-12): 4.12.11 Administrative.
The Vice Presidents and the directors of major University divisions, with the further exception of the right of salary increment as defined for faculty ranks. 4.12.12 Coaching positions shall be based on appointment by the Director of Athletics and shall be related to the coaching of intercollegiate athletics.

PROGRAM REPORT CURRICULUM & STANDARDS COMMITTEE Report 2025-2026-08B At the April 23, 2026 meeting of the Curriculum & Standards Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate for approval.
FOR CONFIRMATION BY THE FACULTY SENATE COLLEGE OF ARTS & SCIENCES BA – Computer Science, effective Fall 2026 Appendix A This curriculum revision represents a strategic modernization that strengthens the B.A. in Computer Science through internal reallocation of Department resources while preserving its distinctive character as a flexible, interdisciplinary degree option.
The proposed changes maintain 120 total credits while prescribing a 36-credit core.
The B.A. requires nine core CS courses compared to eleven core and three specialization courses in the B.S. program, providing a lighter computing load while ensuring foundational competency in software development, algorithms, systems, and machine learning.
BA – Film Media, effective Summer 2026 Appendix B Film media is deleting courses that have been removed from the URI catalog and adding new FLM courses to the appropriate elective pools.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 1
passages.text:
BA – Journalism, effective Fall 2026 Appendix C During a curriculum retreat, members of the journalism faculty evaluated both the program learning outcomes and the curriculum for the B.A in Journalism degree program.
Based on our retreat and our focus on experiential learning in the program, we voted to adopt new requirements for our major.
These changes include eliminating the conceptual/skills designation in our current curriculum, adding additional core requirements, and altering JOR elective options so that students may pursue recommended, but not required, pathways in print, photojournalism, and multimedia/video journalism.
Several advanced courses will work directly with our new Community News Lab, which provides real-world experience to our students by having them produce news content for local media organizations.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 2
passages.text:
BA – Public Relations, effective Fall 2026 Appendix D The Public Relations degree program was developed within the Communication Studies department.
In the Fall of 2024, the program moved into a new department.
The Department of Journalism and Public Relations now manages both the Journalism BA and Public Relations BA degrees.
While the PR program stands on its own, it shares many courses with Communication Studies, particularly in the three focus areas.
As the two programs have become more distinct, scheduling and course management issues have arisen.
Public Relations majors have trouble enrolling in Communication Studies courses to fulfill their focus areas.
We are proposing to amend the focus areas so s tudents have more flexibility in their elective courses.
Both the JOR/PR faculty and the Communication Studies faculty support the proposed changes (please see attached).
Please note the focus area course list remains the same with one exception, we added an additional course COM 321G.
BA – Theatre, effective Fall 2026 Appendix E The Theatre BA is currently suspended and only open to those students who are pursuing a degree in Elementary Education.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 2
passages.text:
We propose reinstating the BA for all eligible students in order to serve the shifting demographic of our student body as well as refine our BFA program to introduce more rigorous standards appropriate to a pre-professional training program.
The Rhode Island Promise Act has increased the number of transfer students considerably, making it highly difficult for those students to complete a BFA in 4 years.
Additionally, the number of double majors/minors has increased making it equally difficult for those students to complete the very narrow BFA curriculum without impact to their other majors (particularly those, such as Nursing, who also have to meet clinical requirements that tend to conflict with our required courses).
A BA offers more flexibility for order of courses, thus making it more feasible for our transfer students and those completing more than one major.
URI Theatre completed an External Review in Spring of 2024.
Among their recommendations was to standardize evaluation tools across our curriculum and instate more rigorous standards for degree completion, including capstone performances and projects.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 2
passages.text:
Many BFA programs also involve standards that, if not met, result in dismissal from the program.
It has never been the policy of URI theatre to dismiss students from our program except in very rare cases of academic failure.
Introducing this type of standardization is possible if we have the option to invite students to our BA program in the event that the BFA curriculum is not a good fit.
Bifurcating our program in this way allows URI Theatre to serve the widest number of students while also introducing more clear standards for our BFA students.
The reinstatement of the BA does not require any new courses or staffing.
Students in the BA program will be taking courses already offered in our existing curriculum but have more choice in terms of when and what they take.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 2
passages.text: Because our program has undergone some changes to course codes since the suspension of the BA, we include here the courses we propose for completion of the BA in Theatre: Core Courses (total of 33 credits): THE111 (Introduction to Acting), THE161 (Introduction to Stagecraft), THE181 (Script Analysis), THE221 (Introduction to Stage Management), THE250 (Costume Laboratory), THE251 (Introduction to Design), THE307 or THE338G ( Creative Dramatics or Ethics in Theatre), THE321 (Orientation to Directing), THE381 (Theatre History to 1642), THE382 (Theatre History:

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 3
passages.text:
Neoclassical through 19th century), and either THE351, 352, 383, 384 OR 481 (these are advanced design or special topics courses) for a total of 33 required credits.
Optional electives within the major include THE112, THE200, THE300, THE400.
For many students, this would include participating in our production season for which they receive course credit (THE200/300/400).
Students must complete a minimum of 30 credits at the 300-level or above (these may include 300-level courses offered inside the major or courses offered outside the program).
COLLEGE OF HEALTH SCIENCES BS – Clinical Neuroscience, effective Fall 2026 Appendix F INP Curriculum Committee voted unanimously in favor of having this course, BPS/PSY 436: Psychotropic Drugs and Therapy as a track elective for clinical neuroscience students.
This course would benefit our clinical neuroscience students from knowledge regarding psychotropics medications that are used to treat clinical disorders (depression, anxiety, OCD, etc.) Many of the clinical neuroscience students pursue healthcare, graduate PhD programs in psychology, and medical school.
Support letter from PSY is attached.

For the Department, the changes ensure consistent preparation across all B.A. graduates, simplify advising by replacing complex course menus with prescribed requirements, and create clear differentiation between the B.A. and the B.S.

Film Media - BA Arts and Sciences Film/Media No BA Film Media No 1.
Kingston Proposed Summer 2026 Existing Fall 2025 Changes Program Description The Major.
Film/Media is an interdisciplinary major offering hands-on experience in documentary, experimental, narrative, and new media production, balanced with an emphasis on international cinemas, film/media history, criticism, and theory.
Our curriculum reflects the dynamic and diverse nature of this field, approached from a perspective of film history and media theory.
Students learn to work with the evolving and overlapping technologies involved in the production of moving images (including film, digital video, 3D animation, game design, and new media), with an understanding of the broadening and globalization of their cultural and aesthetic contexts.
A wide range of courses is available to the film/media student—courses that examine the historical, theoretical, and global approaches to the analysis and creation of moving images.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 19
passages.text:
The film/media program prepares students for careers in such areas as independent filmmaking; animation and media design; film and television industries; advertising, marketing, and public relations; and media criticism.
Graduates of this program are also prepared to continue with graduate studies, either in film and media production for an M.F.A., or in a master’s or doctoral program in film and media studies.
Students majoring in film/media must complete a minimum of 31 credits (maximum 46) in approved courses toward the major.
FLM 101 or FLM 101H is a required prerequisite.
All students must complete the core courses: FLM 110, FLM 203 (or ENG 302), FLM 204 (or FLM 205 or 206), including the senior-level seminar FLM 495 (or FLM 496); a minimum of 6 credits from the production and technique category and 6 credits from the critical studies category; a minimum of 3 elective credits in courses that count toward the film major from the Production and Technique and Critical Studies categories (see below).
This wide range of choices in film/media courses permits students to design a major that will meet both personal and professional goals.

Based on our retreat and our focus on experiential learning in the program, we voted to removeadoptnew requirements for our major.

passages.text:
We would like our students to demonstrate proficiency in news writing across multiple platforms (print, digital, broadcast, and emerging technologies); practice professional reporting skills, including sourcing and verification, to produce original and in-depth news content; recognize the vital role that journalism plays in upholding democratic values such as transparency, accountability, and the free exchange of ideas; understand local, national, and global affairs, with the ability to contextualize news within broader social, political, and economic frameworks, and report on issues of significance to diverse communities; practice ethically and socially responsible journalism, with a particular emphasis on fair and inclusive reporting; and demonstrate knowledge of the legal, regulatory, and economic dimensions of the media.
These new program goals reflect our commitment to offering innovative, experiential opportunities in an inclusive learning environment.

Rationale for Proposed Changes perThe23Theatre BA is currently suspended and only open to those students who are pursuing a degree in Elementary Education.
We propose reinstating the BA for all eligible students in order to serve the shifting demographic of our student body as well as refine our BFA program to introduce more rigorous standards appropriate to a pre-24professional training program.
The Rhode Island Promise Act has increased the number of transfer students considerably, making it highly difficult for those students to complete a BFA in 4 years.
Additionally, the number of double majors/minors has increased making it equally difficult for those students to complete the very narrow BFA curriculum without impact to their other majors (particularly those, such as Nursing, who also have to meet clinical requirements that tend to conflict with our required courses).
A BA offers more flexibility for order of courses, thus making it more feasible for our transfer students and those completing more than one major.
URI Theatre completed an External Review in Spring of 2024.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 52
passages.text:
Among their recommendations was to standardize evaluation tools across our curriculum and instate more rigorous standards for degree completion, including capstone performances and projects.
Many BFA programs also involve standards that, if not met, result in dismissal from the program.
It has never been the policy of URI theatre to dismiss students from our program except in very rare cases of academic failure.
Introducing this type of standardization is possible if we have the option to invite students to our BA program in the event that the BFA curriculum is not a good fit.
Bifurcating our program in this way allows URI Theatre to serve the widest number of students while also introducing more clear standards for our BFA students.
The reinstatement of the BA does not require any new courses or staffing.
Students in the BA program will be taking courses already offered in our existing curriculum but have more choice in terms of when and what they take.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 52
passages.text:
Because our program has undergone some changes to course codes since the suspension of the BA, we include here the courses we propose for completion of the BA in Theatre: Core Courses (total of 33 credits): THE111 (Introduction to Acting), THE161 (Introduction to Stagecraft), THE181 (Script Analysis), THE221 (Introduction to Stage Management), THE250 (Costume Laboratory), THE251 (Introduction to Design), THE307 or THE338G (Creative Dramatics or Ethics in Theatre), THE321 (Orientation to Directing), THE381 (Theatre History to 1642), THE382 (Theatre History: Neoclassical through 19th century), and either THE351, 352, 383, 384 OR 481 (these are advanced design or special topics courses) for a total of 33 required credits.
Optional electives within the major include THE112, THE200, THE300, THE400.
For many students, this would include participating in our production season for which they receive course credit (THE200/300/400).
Students must complete a minimum of 30 credits at the 300-20level or above (these may include 300-level courses offered inside the major or courses offered outside the program).

Include any connections to Strategy 1 in the Agenda for Change.
Strategy 1 of the Agenda for Change asks us to broaden our impact on social, cultural, and economic systems in Rhode Island and beyond.
This proposed change allows URI Theatre to serve the broadest number of students, in particular, those students for whom completing a BFA in four years may be less feasible due to their status as transfer students or students who need to work or provide critical care to their families.
The BFA is a credit-heavy degree that requires students to take coursework at nights and on weekends.
This can be a major barrier to students who work, commute, and/or have families to care for.
By offering the BA, we diversify our student body to include those types of students who would otherwise be unable to pursue a degree in theater.
Further, by making it more possible for double majors to add the Theatre degree, we see this program as an exciting opportunity to broaden the impact the arts has on other disciplines such as the sciences, math, business, and other disciplines not typically associated with the performing arts.

By introducing the BA program, we are able to turn our attention to the academic and creative standards of our BFA students in new and important ways.
