passages.text:
Appendix E: General Information Curricular Procedures Curricular procedures have been developed in order to facilitate the integration of curricular proposals, legislative action, the e-Campus Course Schedule, and the University Catalog.
Faculty, department chairs, and college curriculum committees are asked to give very careful consideration to the completion of curricular forms.
The information provided is used to directly inform the course schedule (e-Campus), academic advising, the Catalog, and in some cases, admission materials.
Signatures of approval verify that the information provided on a proposal is factually accurate and that all possible curricular impacts both within and outside of the originating department have been considered.
Faculty proposers, department chairs, and college curriculum committees must ensure that proposals are prepared according to guidelines and are complete prior to submission.

passages.heading: 2016-2017 University Manual | Page 172
passages.text:
In planning for the first offering of 1) a newly proposed course or academic program, or 2) the implementation of changes to an existing course or academic program, please be aware that the review and approval of a proposal is a multi-step process that can take several months and is not complete until the course/course change is officially listed in e-Campus or, with regard to programs, until notification has been received from the Rhode Island Office of the Postsecondary Commissioner.
It is advisable to think "a year ahead." The length of time for full approval of program proposals often depends on the complexity of the proposal.
Generally, a course proposal that is intended to be effective in a fall semester should be submitted the prior fall.
There may not be sufficient time for proposals submitted in the spring to be fully approved before the end of the academic year (see important academic year deadlines).
Note: only existing courses, approved for scheduling, may be listed in program proposals. • Fully approved course changes will be made in e-Campus for the subsequent semester up to, but not a fter, the start of pre-registration for that semester (on or about mid-semester).

passages.heading: 2016-2017 University Manual | Page 172
passages.text:
Pre-registration for t he Spring semester starts in mid-October; pre-registration for the Fall semester starts in early March.
Contact the Senior Associate Director of Enrollment Services for exact dates. • Fully approved course changes to Learning Community courses for the subsequent academic year will be made in e-Campus only up to the second week of February. • Fully approved new courses and temporary courses may be added to the Course Schedule (classroom s pace and available meeting times permitting) up to the start of the semester in which they are to be first offered and will appear in the subsequent catalog only if officially listed in e-Campus before July 1. • Projected effective dates for proposals will be implemented as requested if the curricular approval process has been fully completed within the appropriate time to meet that deadline. • NOTE: Per Section 8.81.62 of the University Manual, courses not taught for two successive calendar years and not scheduled to be taught for the third year will be deleted from the public list of curricular offerings (Official Un iversity Catalog).

passages.heading: 2016-2017 University Manual | Page 172
passages.text:
General Principles The Curricular Affairs Committee reviews undergraduate curriculum matters, including proposals for courses at the 100-, 200-, 300-, and 400-levels.
The Graduate Council processes graduate curriculum matters, including proposals for courses at the 400-, 500-, 600-, and 900-levels.
If a proposal for a 400-level course indicates that it is to be offered for graduate credit as well as undergraduate credit, it is processed by both committees.
These review committees, which meet monthly, submit approved proposals to the Faculty Senate for action (approval at a Faculty Senate meeting).
Program proposals 172

passages.heading: 2016-2017 University Manual | Page 173
passages.text: approved by the Senate require the President's approval; new courses and course changes do not require the President's approval. Some program proposals also require review by the Council on Postsecondary Education. 173

passages.heading: 2016-2017 University Manual | Page 174
passages.text:
Appendix F: Transfer Policies Part I: Rhode Island Office of the Postsecondary Commissioner Policy for Articulation and Transfer Between and Among Public Institutions of Higher Education in Rhode Island (Amended 6/18/1998) I.
Introduction Articulation between the educational programs of the Rhode Island public institutions of higher education is a matter of considerable importance.
The relationships among the academic disciplines and between levels of coursework require clear understandings about content and purpose so that students may make progress toward their educational objectives without unnecessary disruption.
Institutions within the system, therefore, are obliged to observe these guidelines and procedures for course and program articulation, and the transfer of credit.
II.
Purpose Articulation and transfer guidelines facilitate cooperation between higher education institutions for the purpose of accommodating the needs and interests of students who earn credit at one institution and choose to transfer to another.
Successful transfer minimizes loss of time and duplication for students and optimizes the use of institutional resources.

passages.heading: 2016-2017 University Manual | Page 174
passages.text:
The policy recognizes that each institution has a separate and distinct mission, and that each has the responsibility to establish and to maintain academic quality within that mission.
Underlying the policy is an attitude of mutual respect and cooperation among the institutions and recognition that the primary objective of articulation agreements is to benefit students.
III.
Guidelines and Procedures Institutional Requirements Each higher education institution has the responsibility of establishing, maintaining and communicating requirements to students seeking to complete courses and programs and to earn certificates and degrees at the institution.
Transfer Student Admission Admission of transfer students will be determined by the receiving institution following an assessment of academic performance and standing as well as eligibility for entrance to a specific program.
Students holding associate of arts degrees oriented toward the baccalaureate degree with a grade point average of 2.4 from the Community College of Rhode Island shall be assured admission to Rhode Island College and the University of Rhode Island.

passages.heading: 2016-2017 University Manual | Page 174
passages.text:
If the number of transfer students seeking admission to a particular program exceeds the number that can be accommodated, program admission decisions will be based on criteria and promulgated by the institution; these criteria developed shall provide fair treatment for institutional students and for transfer students.
Direction of Transfer The direction of student transfer (two-year to four-year college or university, four-year to two-year, and four-year to four- year) shall not affect the transferability of credit, unless so noted. 174

passages.heading: 2016-2017 University Manual | Page 175
passages.text:
Academic Transcript Institutions shall keep a complete student academic transcript.
The transcript shall clearly identify each student and include all academic work for which the student was enrolled during each semester, the end-of-semester status in each course, grade and credit awarded.
The transcript shall clearly indicate the source of credit (e.g., examination, course, assessment of experiences).
A statement explaining the grading policy of the institution shall be part of each transcript.
Course Prerequisites All requirements and prerequisites for entrance into courses and programs shall be stated in the official catalog in a consistent manner.
The determination of such requirements and prerequisites is the responsibility of the institution awarding the degree.
Transfer students who have completed equivalent prerequisite courses and achieved an acceptable grade should not be required to repeat such prerequisite courses.
Earned Credits College-level credit earned with minimally acceptable grades at one public higher education institution shall be transferable to another as earned credit.

passages.heading: 2016-2017 University Manual | Page 175
passages.text:
Specified prerequisite-equivalent courses may require a "C" grade to serve as the equivalent prerequisite at the receiving institution; for non-equivalent prerequisite courses, a higher grade may be required.
Pass/Fail Credit The application of pass/fail grading systems to transfer students shall be consistent with the application of those systems to students who entered the institution as freshmen.
Transfer students should consult the catalog of the institution to which they are transferring regarding these policies.
Non-Traditional Learning and Evaluation for Credit The determination of the credit value of non-traditional learning is typically achieved through an examination or other standardized or institutionally-accepted form of assessing prior learning.
An institution which examines or otherwise assesses extra-institutional learning shall clearly state its criteria for measuring and awarding credit and publish information about its credit by examination/assessment policies in its official catalog.

passages.heading: 2016-2017 University Manual | Page 175
passages.text:
For credit by examination, information must be available that includes names of tests for which credit by examination is given (Advanced Placement, general and subject matter CLEP, ACT, institutional, etc.), and score levels which indicate that course work requirements comparable to classroom situations have been met.
For the College-Level Examination Program (CLEP), the receiving institution will accept the American Council on Education (ACE) recommended credit- granting score for the year in which the examination was taken.
Credit awarded through examination or other forms of assessment shall be identified as such on the transcript.
These transcripted credits will be honored by the receiving institution.
Graduate and Advanced Professional Credit Decisions regarding the transfer of credit toward advanced degrees (master's, CAGS, doctorate) or advanced professional degrees rests with the faculty of the degree-granting division. 175

passages.heading: 2016-2017 University Manual | Page 176
passages.text:
Resolution of Equivalency Disputes From time to time there may be inter-institutional disagreements among the faculty of subject matter disciplines.
These disagreements will normally be resolved at the chairperson level.
Conflicts not resolved by the chairperson will be referred to the Articulation/Transfer Committee.
The committee will resolve the dispute or forward a recommendation to the Postsecondary Education Executive Council (PEEC).
PEEC may accept the recommendation or seek an alternate resolution.
IV.
Transfer Guide Inter-institutional agreements on course and program equivalencies shall appear in appropriate institutional publications and be compiled regularly in a single document entitled: Transfer Guide for Students (hereafter, the guide).
The guide is an integral part of the articulation/transfer policy and procedures and shall be made available for use by students, faculty and staff.
Course Equivalencies The institutions shall identify specific courses that are equivalent.
This identification shall be on a discipline-by-discipline basis and shall appear in the guide.

passages.heading: 2016-2017 University Manual | Page 176
passages.text:
Information about course additions, changes or deletions by an institution shall be communicated by the appropriate chairperson to the corresponding chairpersons at other institutions for equivalency evaluation before or during the annual meeting of departmental chairs.
Program Equivalencies The institutions shall specify transfer agreements on a program-to-program basis; these agreements shall appear in the guide.
Program transfer plans will consist of the sequence of courses to be completed to fulfill associate degree requirements at the community college and the equivalent sequences at the college and the university, where appropriate.
Chairpersons shall agree on program-to-program equivalencies before or during the annual meeting of department chairs.
General Education Requirements General education programs are determined by individual institutions, each of which has the continuing responsibility for determining the character of its own program, for its own degree purposes.
General education program requirements shall be clearly stated in the institutional catalog and in the guide.

passages.heading: 2016-2017 University Manual | Page 176
passages.text:
Students who intend to transfer to another institution should review that institution's general education requirements and discuss their plans with admissions counselors or advisors in their intended majors.
V.
Student Rights and Responsibilities Students who intend to transfer must inform themselves of the transfer admission requirements, and the program and degree requirements of the institution to which they expect to transfer.
Students who through no fault of their own encounter legitimate difficulties in transferring from one institution to another must seek resolution of these difficulties through institutional procedures, with the assistance of academic advisors.
Students who have exhausted all administrative remedies available at the institution to which transfer credit is being sought and who have been unable to satisfactorily resolve the problem may appeal in writing to the articulation/transfer officer at the institution that awarded the credit.

passages.heading: 2016-2017 University Manual | Page 176
passages.text: The articulation/transfer officer shall receive and consider all relevant materials and shall review the cases with appropriate representatives of the receiving institution so that a determination may be made as to the transferability of the courses or earned credits being contested. 176

passages.heading: 2016-2017 University Manual | Page 177
passages.text:
Cases which cannot be satisfactorily resolved may be reviewed by the Articulation/ Transfer Committee.
When a student transfers under the course-to-course option, the articulation/ transfer agreement in place when that student initiates the second half of the associate's degree program (31 credit hours or more) will be the agreement that governs course equivalencies for that student.
When a student transfers under a program-to-program agreement, the student is governed by the requirements in effect at the beginning of the academic year in which the student was officially accepted into the program.
These requirements will remain in effect for that student for five years regardless of changes to individual course equivalencies.
VI.
Inter-institutional Articulation/Transfer Committee Composition of the Committee To assure compliance with and the continuing viability of the Articulation/Transfer Policy, a permanent inter-institutional committee on articulation/transfer was established.

passages.heading: 2016-2017 University Manual | Page 177
passages.text:
This Articulation/Transfer Committee is comprised of eleven members: three from each of the three public institutions of higher education plus a chairperson and a staff person from the RI Office of the Postsecondary Commissioner.
The institutional representatives are appointed by the president and are to include the institutional articulation/transfer officer.
The chairperson is appointed by the Postsecondary Commissioner.
Committee appointments shall be reviewed every three years.
Committee Responsibilities The Committee is responsible to the Postsecondary Education Executive Council (PEEC) for the following tasks: * Soliciting suggestions from administrators, faculty and students matters of articulation/transfer; * Providing continuous evaluation and review of institutional programs, policies and procedures, and inter-institutional relationships affecting transfer of students; * Recommending such revisions as are needed in institutional programs, policies, and procedures to promote the success and general well-being of the transfer student.

passages.heading: 2016-2017 University Manual | Page 177
passages.text:
The Committee shall fulfill these responsibilities in the following ways: * Recommending policy or procedural changes that would improve articulation/transfer in higher education institutions; * Recommending resolution of course equivalency disputes between cooperating institutions; * Conducting reviews as needed of the Articulation/Transfer Policy; * Planning and executing the annual meeting of department chairpersons and assisting in the production of the guide.
Committee Meetings The Articulation/Transfer Committee shall be convened, as necessary, by its chairperson.
PART II: Undergraduate Transfer Policy (Amended 1999-00) 177

passages.heading: 2016-2017 University Manual | Page 178
passages.text:
The University of Rhode Island prepares a formal transfer credit evaluation only after an applicant has been accepted as a degree student.
Evaluations are prepared in a course-by-course manner with the course number and course title of the former school displayed on the left side of the page and the University course equivalent on the right.
Most of the course evaluations are made from catalog course descriptions.
An equivalent University of Rhode Island course number is assigned wherever possible provided the other college work requires the same prerequisites as those required by University departments and provided the work is comparable in content, scope, and level to University courses.
If no equivalent URI course can be designated, departmental elective credits or free elective credits may be awarded.
A departmental elective may be used to fulfill major or minor credit requirements in the specific department, but may not be used for General Education.
A free elective fulfills credit hours needed for graduation but does not meet department or General Education requirements.
The University usually awards the credit value of the sending institution.

passages.heading: 2016-2017 University Manual | Page 178
passages.text:
Excess credits are used as free electives.
Courses taken in disciplines that are not represented at the University of Rhode Island are awarded free elective credit unless the courses are equivalent or nearly equivalent to courses offered by URI.
Transfer credit may be given in those courses in which the student received a grade of "C" (2.00) or better, but no credit shall be given for courses in which a "C-" or lower was earned.
However, the RI Office of the Postsecondary Commissioner Policy for Articulation/Transfer (Appendix F, Part I) mandates that college level credit earned with minimally acceptable grades at another public postsecondary education institution in Rhode Island shall be transferable as earned credit.
Credit transferred from a community or junior college is limited only by the provision that the student must earn at least half the credits required for the University of Rhode Island degree at a baccalaureate granting institution.
No course credit earned at the University or at other institutions shall be counted for graduation after eight years, except by consent of the dean of the degree granting college involved.
Advanced Placement.

passages.heading: 2016-2017 University Manual | Page 178
passages.text:
The University awards credits and/or course exemptions to freshmen and transfer students who present scores of 3 or higher on the College Board Advanced Placement Tests.
Art, Music, Theatre courses offered by an accredited institution are referred to respective departments for evaluation for students majoring in those areas.
Athletics.
The University does not grant credit for participation in intercollegiate athletics.
Business Administration Courses.
The University grants direct transfer credit for equivalent business administration courses taken at institutions that are accredited by the American Assembly of Collegiate Schools of Business.
Upper level business courses taken at an institution not accredited by this Association must be validated by examination.
Those courses not validated will be awarded free elective credit.
College Level Examination Program (CLEP).
The University grants transfer credit for CLEP examinations taken prior to enrollment at the University of Rhode Island provided the scores meet University standards and the CLEP credit does not duplicate other transfer credit.
Regulations regarding CLEP may be found in the University Manual.

passages.heading: 2016-2017 University Manual | Page 178
passages.text:
CLEP credit and score minimums are delineated in the University Catalog.
Correspondence Courses offered through an accredited institution shall be evaluated for transfer provided course titles, grades and credit values appear on an official college or university transcript.
Foreign Credits.
Each foreign transcript shall be evaluated independently. 178

passages.heading: 2016-2017 University Manual | Page 179
passages.text:
International Baccalaureate Diploma Program.
Academic credit may be awarded for most higher-level examinations passed with a score of 5, 6, or 7.
Course credit is awarded at the discretion of individual departments.
The University grants no credit for standard level examinations.
Non-collegiate Educational Experiences.
Academic credit may be awarded for knowledge and skills gained in non- collegiate settings.
Only assessment procedures approved by academic departments, colleges and the Faculty Senate may be used.
Pass/Fail Courses.
The University accepts credits offered by an accredited institution that were taken on a pass/fail basis.
However, such credit cannot be used for concentration or General Education requirements.
Pre-collegiate, Remedial, Personal Development or Self-improvement Courses.
The University grants no credit for these courses.
Professional Courses. (e.g.
Computer Science, Dental Hygiene, Engineering, Medical Technology, Nursing, Pharmacy) as well as courses of an advanced nature, independent studies, practicums and seminars offered by an accredited institution shall be referred to appropriate faculty for evaluation and course equivalency.
Proficiency and Waiver Examinations.

passages.heading: 2016-2017 University Manual | Page 179
passages.text:
A student who successfully passes a departmental proficiency examination shall earn credits as well as exemption from the course.
A student who successfully passes a department waiver examination shall be exempted from the course, but shall earn no credit.
Religion Courses.
Only those courses offered by accredited institutions which are planned and taught from a strictly historical, literary or comparative viewpoint as determined by the appropriate faculty shall be awarded transfer credit.
Technical, Vocational Courses.
The University grants no credit for technical or vocational courses.
College parallel courses taken at technical institutions may be granted credit.
Veterans.

Center and Institute Application (Non-Research) Question 1: Describe the mission and vision for the Center or Institute.
Mission The URI Honors Institute values and creates diverse active-learning approaches, including foundational and experiential learning, insights from national experts via the Honors Colloquium, and policy-rooted education.
It emphasizes integrative learning, connecting disciplines, and supports students’ self-development and self-directed learning through honors-level electives and projects, which can be taken in students’ majors.
The Institute encourages self-advocacy and lifepath learning through fellowship and scholarship applications, empowering students to shape their academic journey.
The URI Honors Institute is designed to create a dynamic learning environment for all students within its scope, encouraging them to engage with and address local manifestations of global issues.
This setting facilitates meaningful interactions with nationally and internationally renowned experts, oﬀering students a unique opportunity to explore major contemporary challenges.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 13
passages.text:
Within the institute, students can actively pursue Honors work in their respective majors, contributing to the overall enhancement of the college experience.
The URI Honors Institute fosters a community of individuals with diverse backgrounds, perspectives, and majors, all united by a shared objective: leveraging their talents to address some of the most critical challenges confronting our world.
Within this community, engaged learners are driven by a passion for making meaningful contributions to positive change and sustainable solutions, both within their local communities and on a global scale.
The Institute serves as an incubator for faculty and students who are thinkers and doers of all stripes, whether in the arts, sciences, professional Page 11 Application: URI Honors Institute | February 2024

February 26, 2024 Dear Institute Proposal Evaluators, I have seen the proposal for a URI Honors Institute titled “Application: URI Honors Institute” and, on behalf of the College of Arts and Sciences, I am pleased to endorse the initiative.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 48
passages.text:
I would like to thank the Oﬃce of the Provost for aﬀording us the opportunity to conduct a self study and external review of the URI Honors Program.
Through this process of self-study, using the “NCHC Program Review Instrument,” we have been able to learn in depth the best practices of mature honors programs.
This report constitutes the ﬁrst formal self study of our URI Honors Program conducted for external review.
Prior to this 2023 report, there were two other self-studies that provide useful historical information regarding the evolution of URI “Honors”: a 2013 informal self-study and a 2005 study of the relationship between the Scholarship Oﬃce and the Honors Program.
Due to an evolution that is speciﬁc to the resource allocation history at the University of Rhode Island, “URI Honors'' is actually comprised of four distinct entities: the Honors Program; the Honors Colloquium; the Oﬃce of National Fellowships and Academic Opportunities; and the Pre-Health Professions Advising Program.
The Honors Colloquium will celebrate its sixtieth anniversary in Fall 2023.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 48
passages.text:
The Colloquium spawned the URI Honors Program, roughly forty years ago, and it was about twenty years ago that the Honors Program took its current form.
While advising for national fellowships existed informally within the Honors Program, in 2013, Honors formalized fellowship advising with the creation of an Oﬃce of National Fellowships and Academic Opportunities (ONFAO).
This oﬃce also conducted pre-health advising until 2016, when fellowships advising was formally uncoupled from pre-health advising. (Honors took over Pre-health advising from the College of the Environment and Life Sciences in 2009.) Currently, one person is staﬃng the ONFAO and serving as its director.
She also served as the pre-health advisor until the position was uncoupled from national fellowships advising.
Pre-health has both a director and a half-time advisor line, currently ﬁlled with an interim advisor.
This report is designed to be read alongside the NCHC Program Review Instrument, which provides a rubric for evaluation for honors programs and colleges.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 48
passages.text:
Since this self-study has been scaﬀolded by the NCHC Program Review Instrument, which is dedicated speciﬁcally to Honors Program education, it will primarily present reﬂections on and evaluations of the URI Honors Program.
For reviewer consideration, we have included in the Appendix a Pre-health Professions Advising Program self-study as well as the last annual report of the ONFAO.
The Honors Program is currently at a juncture of change.
In the past year, the previous director of the program, Lynne Derbyshire, retired after nine years of service to the program; the Honors Program Coordinator of thirty-seven years, Deborah Gardiner, also retired; and the half-time continuing pre-health advisor left.
The departures of both Lynne Derbyshire and, especially, Deborah Gardiner have left an information gap that we are struggling to ﬁll.
Coupled with these departures will be the exiting of two (of three) associate directors – Kathleen McIntyre, who will be

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 49
passages.text:
returning to Gender & Women’s Studies; and Smita Ramnarain, whose one-year sabbatical next year will coincide with the last year of her term.
The term of Jill Doerner, the remaining associate director, is also ending in spring 2023.
At the macro level, the University welcomed a new President, Marc Parlange, in Fall 2021 and a new Provost, Barbara Wolfe, in January of 2023.
It also rolled out a new Strategic Plan in 2023.
And in September 2022, I stepped in as the new director of the Honors Program, charged with bringing strategic vision.
This report thus represents our Honors Program at a locus of transition.
It presents and evaluates the program as it was, based on the history that we have available to us, with an eye to where we are heading.
There are a number of key takeaway points that we highlight throughout this study in textboxes and quotes.
Below I call attention to two of the most salient ones: ●The Honors Program is a key recruitment and retention tool for the University in order to attract high-achieving students, thereby enhancing the University’s student population, proﬁle of its graduates, and quality of its alumni.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 49
passages.text:
Over the past ﬁfteen years, the program has grown tremendously in terms of incoming Honors-eligible freshmen, reaching almost 1,500 incoming eligible Honors students, or one third of the admitted freshman class.
In the last ﬁve years alone, we have seen a thirty-six percent increase in the number of Honors-eligible students.
Roughly 1,000 of these 1,500 Honors-eligible students seek seats in Honors courses their ﬁrst semester of college.
The focus in the past has been to provide a multitude of 100- and 200-level courses that fulﬁll General Education requirements so that as many ﬁrst- and second-year Honors-eligible students as possible can experience the intimate, high-impact nature of the Honors curriculum, thereby enhancing retention of top-performing ﬁrst- and second-year students. ●The Honors Program as it currently exists is unsustainable The unsustainability of the Honors Program as it currently exists is rooted in a number of factors including unmet student expectations; an unclear mission; a lack of programmatic goals; no assessment or evaluation processes and procedures; an opaque budget structure; funding limitations; and major structural challenges.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 49
passages.text:
The goal of this self-study and external review is to produce a strategic plan, to be presented to and approved by the President and the Provost, that will guide the Honors Program and resource allocation for the program over the next ﬁve years.
The new strategic direction of Honors is already sketched and can be found in the Appendix as a presentation entitled“New Strategic Direction.”We refer to our “new strategic direction” often in this report.
As best as we could, we attempted to work within the existing budgetary parameters so that the “new strategic direction” will not require signiﬁcant additional resources; however, it was diﬃcult to concretely determine these parameters because the current budgeting structure for Honors is opaque at best and unsustainable at worst.
I refer readers to “Section 5 - Infrastructure” formore on budget and funding.
We are very excited about our new strategic direction, which is organized both around the mission of “Imagining Sustainable, Equitable Societies” and the most visible and distinguishing centerpiece of Honors: our Honors Colloquium.
Our students and our children are facing unparalleled challenges –

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 50
passages.text:
climate change, biodiversity collapse, irreversible pollution, looming food instability, declining democracy, mass migrations, a rising reign of artiﬁcial intelligence, and maybe even nuclear war.
It is essential that they go forth into their professional lives knowingwhat they can do.
The Honors Colloquium has typically tackled these challenges yearly with nationally, and sometimes internationally, renowned speakers.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 50
passages.text:
We would like to build on the Colloquium by structuring our Honors Program around stackable Honors Certiﬁcates that provide real-world experiential learning around themes like: sustainable, equitable food systems; sustaining our shores; business for the common good; resilient, equitable democracies; sustainable design; and sustainable, equitable healthcare. (Almost all of these themes are either prior or future Colloquium topics with interested faculty members and deans already sketching the contours of these future “certiﬁcates.”) We believe that this new structure of Honors will not only distinguish our URI Honors Program from Honors programs and colleges at peer institutions but it will also attract serious changemakers, leaders and activists, and provide them with the tools to become the engaged citizens that we need.
This new structure will also allow us to build on existing academic strengths of the University of Rhode Island and to launch certiﬁcates that can become campus-wide after their initial pilot runs in Honors.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 50
passages.text:
According to theNCHC Program Review Instrument, amature Honors Program “is a permanent and highly regarded unit that contributes centrally and substantially to the overall traditions of excellence on campus.” The history of Honors at the University of Rhode Island has provided us with a robust foundation from which we can grow.
It is our hope that our New Strategic Direction will take us into a new era of substantial and central contributions to the overall traditions of excellence on campus.
In conclusion, I would like to thank the whole Honors team for their work on this report. ●Anna Blake – Honors Program Coordinator ●Melissa Stevens – Honors Program Specialist ●Jill Doerner – Associate Director of Honors ●Kathleen McIntyre – Associate Director of Honors ●Smita Ramnarain – Associate Director of Honors ●Kathleen Maher – Assistant Director of Honors, Director of ONFAO ●Andrew Simmons – Assistant Director of Honors, Director of Pre-health Advising

The current Honors Program mission statement does not represent that of a mature honors program, as per theNCHC Program Review Instrument,but rather of a developing honors program.
Furthermore, it does not align with the newly announced Mission, Foundational Values and Goals of the University, copied below.

URI MISSION, FOUNDATIONAL VALUES, AND VISION In February 2023, URI oﬃcially launched its new Strategic Plan entitled “Focus URI: A Strategic Vision for the University of Rhode Island (2023-2033).” Beloware the mission, foundational values and vision for the University.
Mission The University of Rhode Island is the state’s ﬂagship land and sea grant research institution, with a commitment to urban initiatives.
A student-centered research institution, URI actively partners with other organizations globally and locally to advance knowledge and to develop informed residents and leaders.
URI is committed to high-quality education, community engagement, and solving the world’s most important challenges.
Situated on the traditional land and territories of the Narragansett Nation and the Niantic People, URI strives to create a diverse and inclusive environment for researchers, teachers, learners, and community members.

1.5 Engagement in continuous “closed-loop” assessment and evaluation 1.6 Qualiﬁed peers regularly and periodically review the program ASSESSMENT AND EVALUATION Assessment and evaluation is currently undeveloped in our Honors Program and also in our Honors Colloquium.
In Fall 2022, we initiated a conversation with the URI Oﬃce of the Advancement of Teaching and Learning about course-level and program-level assessment as well as about assessment of the Honors Colloquium.
As a result of this conversation, we have immediately begun work on creating a closed-loop assessment and evaluation process for courses and the program (but not yet for our Honors Colloquium).
This closed-loop assessment and evaluation process will be built into the new strategic plan for Honors once we conﬁrm the programmatic goals.
Since a number of our courses count for General Education learning outcomes, they are subject to assessment by the University-wide General Education Assessment Committee.
Every once in a while, one of our courses is selected.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 56
passages.text:
We do not currently have a mechanism in place for the Program to follow up with these assessments, as the assessments conducted by General Education are submitted directly by the faculty.
Further, faculty have not been given feedback by the General Education Assessment Committee and we are not aware of a public report outlining the ﬁndings of these assessments.
Evaluation of courses We have put in place a provisional evaluation procedure for new and existing Honors courses that is based on what we are calling, for now, the “Course Proposal Cover Sheet.” This cover sheet links to theNCHC Course Design Pageand it lists the ﬁve learning objectives generally typical of Honors courses.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 56
passages.text:
It then asks faculty members to respond to four questions: 1) How does your course incorporate high-impact learning practices; 2) How does your course meet learning objectives 3-5 as articulated by the NCHC; 3) How is your course interdisciplinary; 4) If you are proposing an H-section of an existing course, how is your H-section diﬀerent from the regular section? (See Appendix for full call for course proposals.) As we move to the new incarnation of the Honors curriculum, we will build in a course evaluation procedure for the four categories of courses that will be its main features: the foundational course, the Colloquium course, the experiential course and the position paper course.

Section 2 - Enrollment Management and Scholarships 2.1 The program has clear and eﬀective recruitment strategies and practices 2.2 A clearly articulated set of admissions criteria (e.g., GPA, test scores, a written essay, satisfactory progress, etc.) identiﬁes the targeted student population served by the Honors Program The Honors Program and Pre-Health staﬀ participate in a variety of university events to recruit new students (events are usually held in person, but began virtually during the height of Covid-19 and continue to the present as a supplement to in person events).
During the Fall semester, staﬀ participate in several Open House events aimed at disseminating information to prospective students and their families.
Prospective students are given a chance to ask questions as well as meet current Honors Program and Pre-Health students and staﬀ.
During the Spring semester, staﬀ and students also participate in several events to recruit accepted students.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 57
passages.text:
For the last three years, Honors and Pre-Health staﬀ and students have participated virtually in ‘An Evening with Honors’ in conjunction with the Oﬃce of Admissions.
This event was launched during the height of the Covid-19 pandemic when restrictions on campus visits existed.
The event worked so well that we have since continued it because it gives admitted students and their families the ability to come together via Zoom to meet University Admissions staﬀ, our staﬀ, and current students, and to learn about student experiences in the Honors Program.
In addition, one of our Honors Faculty gives a mini-teaching demonstration.
This event has been very well attended, with 700-800 people signed on from across the United States and abroad.
We have been recording these events and uploading them to ourHonors Program YouTube channel.
Laterin the Spring semester, our staﬀ and students participate in Welcome Day events, attended by accepted students and their families.
We present them with information about the Honors Program, planned courses for the coming Fall semester, and give them the opportunity to ask questions and talk individually with Honors Program students and staﬀ.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 57
passages.text:
High school students are automatically invited to join the Honors Program if they have a weighted recalculated high school GPA of 3.8 or weighted recalculated high school GPA of 3.6 and a combined SAT score of 1300 or higher or an ACT composite score of 27 or higher.
Weighted recalculated high school GPAs are determined by the Oﬃce of Admissions and once students meet the eligibility requirements, they receive an oﬃcial letter of invitation from the Honors Program Director (sent by Admissions).
These criteria are posted on our website and in print materials, and are shared widely Page11 URI Honors Program Self-Study | March 2023

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 58
passages.text:
during University recruitment events.
Roughly one-third of the incoming class of students are eligible for the Honors Program each year.
The Honors Program also has the ability to admit students who are close to meeting the Admissions requirements.
Students who transfer to the University of Rhode Island with a cumulative GPA of 3.40 or higher from their previous college or university are eligible to enroll in Honors courses.
Admission criteria for transfer students are also available on our website.
The Honors Program works closely with the Special Populations Oﬃce within the Oﬃce of Admissions and the Transfer Resource Center to inform students about the Honors Program.
Further, Honors has worked closely over the last several years with the Transfer Resource Center to inform Assistant and Associate Deans and others working to evaluate transfer credits about the potential for Honors transfer credit and future participation in Honors.
Lastly, the Honors Program works with the Oﬃce of International Students and Scholars to identify eligible international students.
In terms of yield, of 1,500 Honors-eligible incoming students, roughly 1,000 seek seats in Honors courses their ﬁrst semester.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 58

We have consistently struggled to ﬁll this demand and have encouraged students who cannot ﬁnd a seat in an appropriate course to take their ﬁrst course in the spring semester.
In its new incarnation, the Honors Program will change the admissions criteria, thereby changing recruitment strategies.

5.regular conversations with the Associate Vice President for Enrollment and Student Success to determine numbers of seats needed for incoming freshmen; 6.reserving seats in 100-level and 200-level courses for incoming freshmen; 7.priority registration for Ryan and Verrechia scholars (Ryan and Verrechia scholars receive 4-year scholarships from the University with a number of perks, including automatic admission into the Honors Program.
More about these scholarships can be foundhere.).
In its new incarnation, the Honors Program will change admissions criteria, provide more holistic advising, consistently provide enough seats for students seeking to complete the program, and provide more realistic pathways for completion.
We will also aim to integrate Ryan and Verrechia scholars more meaningfully into the program.
Unfortunately, we don’t have control over the enrollment management software that URI uses, so this will continue to be a challenging area.

In terms of retention and probation policies: To maintain eligibility and continue participation in the Honors Program, students must maintain a cumulative GPA of 3.40 or higher (the minimum GPA has been increased over time to match with average GPAs of incoming students).
Any student who falls below those requirements is able to re-enroll in Honors courses once their cumulative GPA reaches a 3.4 or higher.
Records of students who are close to but below the required GPA are pulled by the Coordinator and examined by the Honors Director and staﬀ to determine continued participation in Honors in the semester after they fall below the requirement.
These criteria are posted on our website and are clearly articulated to students who fall below the required GPA.
Students who fall below the required GPA are contacted by the Coordinator. 2.5 The program clearly speciﬁes the requirements needed for satisfactory completion To receive a milestone notation on their transcripts stating they have “completed the University Honors Program,” students must take at least 18 credits in Honors Program courses and have a cumulative GPA of 3.4 or higher.

Determination is made on the basis of academic merit with preference given to students with ﬁnancial need who otherwise qualify. ●The Dr.
Mary A.
Silverman Ravin ‘44 Endowed Scholarshipis awarded annually to the highest ranking female pre-medical student at the close of her junior year. 2.8 When appropriate, two-year and four-year programs have articulation agreements by which honors graduates from two-year programs who meet previously agreed-upon requirements are accepted into four-year honors programs 2.9 When applicable, articulation agreements are based on clearly delineated SLOs oﬀering exceptional and enhanced educational opportunities to honors students We do not currently have articulation agreements by which honors graduates from two-year programs are accepted into our Program.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 62
passages.text:
However, as stated above, we do work closely with the Special Populations Oﬃce within the Oﬃce of Admissions and the Transfer Resource Center to inform eligible transfer students about the Honors Program and their possible participation.
Further, Honors has worked closely over the last several years with the Transfer Resource Center to inform Assistant and Associate Deans and others working to evaluate transfer credits about the potential for Honors transfer credit and future participation in Honors.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 62
passages.text:
Section 3 - Administrative Structures 3.1 The place of Honors in the administrative structure is appropriate to the mission and functions of the program 3.2 The Honors director reports to the chief academic oﬃcer of the institution The administrative situation of the Honors Program within the University is as follows: The director of the Honors Program reports to the Provost; the program does not report to a college or department; and the Honors Program is deemed “University-wide.” Historically, the Provost’s Oﬃce – comprised of the Provost and Vice-Provosts – has been strongly supportive of Honors education, and this strong support has been demonstrated by increased funding over the years; a strong push to advertise Honors to prospective, incoming and existing students; and commitment to the URI Honors Colloquium, both in funding and in regular in-person attendance.
Page16 URI Honors Program Self-Study | March 2023

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 63
passages.text:
This structure and support is squarely in line with best practices in Honors education, and the program is very lucky to have enjoyed this support.
As our program is growing, there are areas of concern, though.
These areas pertain largely to how the program is under-represented in administrative structures.
Representation issues ●Dean’s level: Currently, the Honors Program is notrepresented at Deans’ council meetings where policy and budgets are discussed, although upon request, the program can be invited to a meeting.
Since the Honors Program serves all colleges, it should be invited regularly to deans’ level meetings where policy and budgets are discussed. ●Assistant Dean and Budget Manager level: The HonorsProgram is not represented at University-wide meetings for assistant deans and budget managers, and thus does not receive relevant information in a systematic and timely manner.
Additionally, there is no formal budget training for staﬀ who oversee the Honors budget. ●Faculty Senate: In a similar vein, the Honors Programis not represented in the Faculty Senate through (an) Honors-designated faculty senator(s).

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 63
passages.text:
As a result, the Honors Program is not formally represented on any Faculty Senate committees and has no voice or voting rights in curricular or policy matters.
Historically, the Honors Program has been invited to present an annual report to the Faculty Senate but this report is also easily tabled if other Faculty Senate agenda items demand attention.
The report before the Faculty Senate, once a year, is currently the only standing opportunity that the Honors Program has to communicate with colleges and faculty members from across the campus. ●AAUP Collective Bargaining: The Honors Program interestsare not represented at AAUP Collective Bargaining negotiations.
A recent issue related to the Honors Program and the AAUP Contract is the annual review process for a teaching professor line that is situated within the Honors Program.
With no dean or acting dean for the Honors Program, the University must ﬁnd a “friendly dean” workaround.
This is not a sustainable practice.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 63
passages.text:
The Honors Director should serve as dean for the annual review process, and this should be written into the AAUP contract. ●Budget requests: Historically, it has been the normfor the Honors Program to be invited to strategic allocation and reallocation presentations as part of the annual budget process but it is not policy for the Honors Program to be involved in this process.
Honors budget requests are scheduled after the requests from the Colleges. ●Fundraising and the URI Foundation: The Honors Programlacks a designated development person in the URI Foundation.
As such, prior to this year, the URI Foundation has not engaged in any concerted eﬀort to fundraise for the Honors Program despite the fact that many of the top students at URI over the years have been Honors students, and that they undoubtedly have giving capacity. ●Admissions events: Honors has a good relationshipwith Admissions and is well integrated into the URI Admissions process.
It is not as well integrated into prospective- and Page17 URI Honors Program Self-Study | March 2023

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 64
passages.text:
new-student events such as the Fall Open Houses, Welcome Days and Orientation.
Deans can speak in large-event settings with students who might or will be attending their colleges; Honors does not have a time to present to students that is not in competition with the College presentations.
Structural issues Honors is situated in its own University-wide administrative node, which is a best practice in Honors education.
Honors falls through other cracks in University-wide policies and practices, due to its inconsistently integrated structure. ●Basic staﬃng resources: The Honors Program does not currently have professional advisors; a designated ﬁscal clerk or access to a budget manager; access to an enrollment management specialist; access to a designated study abroad advisor; or to a designated information technology support person. ●Building resources: The Honors Program has its ownspace, which includes oﬃce space, lounge space, meeting space and classrooms.
All of this is in line with best practices in Honors education.
It does not, however, receive any funding for the upkeep of these spaces.
Our technology is out of date.
Furniture needs to be replaced.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 64
passages.text:
Carpets need to be replaced and the third ﬂoor needs an aesthetic overhaul to avoid looking dated and depressing. ●Unit deﬁnition: Academic and personnel forms andprocesses at URI are predicated on Colleges as the sole academic units.
Thus these forms and processes require Dean’s level signature.
The Honors Director is not institutionally recognized as having dean’s level signature authority, which complicates many daily tasks. ●Course fees: Honors cannot assign course fees likeColleges because the course fees would go back to the Colleges who hold the course code for the H-section. ●Assessment and Evaluation: Unlike all other academicprograms on campus, Honors is not required to submit regular program assessments and it is not required to conduct regular external review. ●Information systems: Our enrollment management system,E-campus, requires that Honors fall under a College in terms of coding; as such, all Honors courses are coded under the College of Arts & Sciences in the E-Campus system back end.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 64
passages.text:
This creates information- and enrollment-management challenges such as the assignment of seat credits, the mapping of classes for General Education requirements and prerequisites, and access to teaching evaluations of Honors teaching faculty.
Another major challenge related to E-campus is that there is no automatic way to code students who are pursuing the Honors program.
In other words, there is no way to code students as Honors-declared.
Admissions sends our Coordinator a list of all the students who are eligible based on our criteria and she codes them; yet, not all students who are Honors-eligible pursue the Honors program.
As a Page18 URI Honors Program Self-Study | March 2023

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 65
passages.text:
consequence, there is no automated way to follow students who are actively pursuing program completion or identify students who are close to completion but maybe need a little more encouragement to start/ﬁnish an Honors project. 3.3 The Honors program is a permanent, stable and highly regarded academic unit that contributes to a lasting tradition of excellence The URI Honors Program is most well known at the University for the annual fall HonorsColloquium, which is the premier speaker series at URI, attended regularly by the President and the Provost of the University.
As a former administrator once said jokingly, “unless you live under a rock, you know about the Colloquium.” The program is also well known for attracting high-caliber prospective students and for retaining these students; for oﬀering small classes taught by engaging faculty; for impactful student Honors projects; for helping students apply and be accepted in competitive health programs; and for the scholars and fellows that the Oﬃce of National Fellowships and Academic Opportunities produces, which, last year alone, brought students over $850,000 in combined funding.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 65
passages.text:
All of these elements contribute to the reputation of academic excellence enjoyed by the program.
The Provost’s Oﬃce has historically held the Honors Program in high regard and has viewed it as “one of the crown jewels of the University” (correspondence with Provost Emeritus, Donald H.
DeHayes).
Indeed, the Honors Program has grown considerably over the past ﬁfteen years to the point where we are now admitting roughly 1,500 Honors-eligible students into the University, one thousand of whom take courses with us within their ﬁrst year.
These admission numbers are a testament to the value that students and their parents place on being admitted into an honors program.
The program is at a juncture, though, where a focus on admissions has led the program to lose sight of its mission and vision in terms of serving the admitted student population.
This loss of focus can be most acutely gleaned from the inconsistent support of Honors by Colleges and departments.
Some colleges collaborate actively and intentionally with the Honors Program, and demonstrate high regard for the program, while other colleges support and/or collaborate minimally and inconsistently with the Honors Program.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 65
passages.text: The three most committed colleges to the Honors program, in terms of collaboration, outright funding and in-kind funding are the College of Arts & Sciences, College of Business and the College of Page19 URI Honors Program Self-Study | March 2023

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 66
passages.text:
Engineering. 45% of Honors teaching faculty came from the College of Arts & Sciences this year.
The College of Business is actively collaborating with Honors on a new concentration/future certiﬁcate that will be tied to their upcoming Honors Colloquium: Business for Good.
The College of Engineering has worked actively with Honors to adapt its curriculum to encourage engineering students to complete the Honors program.
Both colleges also commit the largest amount of funding – $5,000 – to the Honors Colloquium every year.
The other colleges engage to varying degrees – from little support or involvement to allowing faculty to teach Honors courses or H-sections of existing courses.
It is our hope that the new strategic direction that we have elaborated will appeal to all colleges equally and will also provide a much needed strategic vision and mission to the program.
Section 4 - Curriculum 4.1 The program oﬀers carefully designed educational experiences that meet the needs and the abilities of the undergraduate students it serves Since there have not been prior comprehensive self-studies, we cannot know the history behind the architecture of the Honors program requirements.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 66
passages.text:
To the extent that we require courses at each level and also a capstone experience – the Honors project – we can assume that the program requirements were probably scaﬀolded onto Bloom’s taxonomy, with the Honors project capstone experience representing the tip of the taxonomy: the creation of new knowledge.
Also, to the extent that the Honors program evolved out of the Colloquium, we can assume that the architects of the program sought to include the Colloquium as a unique element in the larger program design through the dedicated Honors Colloquium course.
In terms of requirements for courses that have historically been included in the program, prior calls for course proposals, like the 2021 call below, have sought courses that: …include one or more of the following criteria: interdisciplinary approach to the subject matter, emphasis on developing critical thinking, reading, and writing skills, project-based learning, work with primary sources rather than textbooks, more emphasis on cooperative learning, and providing a core content area to a primarily competency-based course (for Page20 URI Honors Program Self-Study | March 2023

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 67
passages.text: example, writing or communication competencies) or other criteria that you feel identiﬁes your course as an Honors course.(See Appendix forfull call) As a reminder, to receive a notation on their transcripts stating they have “completed the University Honors Program,” students must take at least 18 credits in Honors Program courses and have a cumulative GPA of 3.4 or higher.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 67
passages.text: Honors Program credits must include the following: ●One Honors course at the 100/200 level ●One Honors Colloquium course (HPR 2XX) ●One Honors course at the 300/400 level ●One Elective Honors Course at any level ●One Honors project - HPR 401 ●One Honors course at the 400-level, either HPR 411 or HPR 412 OR one Honors project—HPR 402 (HPR 402 is for those students who choose to do a six-credit, full academic year Honors Project) In sum, the design of the program is clear but it lacks focus and precise programmatic learning outcomes, which is why we are designing a new Honors program around the precise focus of “imagining sustainable, equitable societies.” In consultation with the Oﬃce for the Advancement of Teaching and Learning, we will determine precise programmatic learning outcomes associated with the training of future engaged citizens and societal changemakers. 4.2 The honors curriculum purposefully aligns with and enhances the mission of the Honors Program As a reminder, the Honors Program mission as it is currently articulated reads: “The mission of the Honors Program is to develop and maintain an interdisciplinary intellectual community; to stimulate intellectual excitement for all participants; to inspire and enhance critical, creative, and integrative thinking; and to foster opportunities to broaden intellectual development.” This mission statement was last updated on January 26, 2017.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 67
passages.text:
It is our opinion that the Honors Program is not purposefully aligned with its mission nor with the institutional mission.
Indeed, the curriculum embodies the spirit of the Honors mission.
However, purposeful alignment between the institutional mission and a clear Honors mission is necessary to create eﬀective programmatic learning outcomes.
Purposeful alignment is also necessary in order to ensure student achievement and success.
The new Honors program will have a focused mission with which the curriculum will be purposefully aligned.
Page21 URI Honors Program Self-Study | March 2023

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 68
passages.text:
Perhaps the most notable innovation to the Honors Program in recent years is to ensure that students can meet many of their general education outcomes through the Honors program.
It was also a strategy in the past to create an Honors version of the general education curriculum. 4.3 The curricular design leads to mastery of identiﬁed learning outcomes Our program does not currently have clearly deﬁned programmatic learning outcomes.
See 4.1 and 4.2 above. 4.4 The pedagogic practices of the program are based on clearly identiﬁed learning outcomes No scaﬀolding practices currently exist because there are no clear programmatic outcomes but they will exist in the new incarnation of the Honors Program. 4.5 The Honors program exercises considerable control over the Honors curriculum The Honors Program has partial control over course oﬀerings each semester.
Oﬀerings are signiﬁcantly dependent upon approval by other collegiate units.
Each semester a call for course proposals for the following year is sent to the URI Community via email.
We review the course proposals in our Fall Curriculum Committee meeting.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 68
passages.text:
Then, when approved, we work with the faculty member, the chairperson of the faculty member’s department and the faculty member’s college to determine whether the college/department is willing to contribute the course “in kind,” whether it requires buyout, or whether the college/department is not willing to let the faculty member teach the course for the Honors Program.
Under the former Provost, Donald H.
DeHayes, it was written into all new hire letters that newly appointed faculty members could be requested to teach in the Honors program.
Unfortunately, we have not been able to track all the new hires and their appointment letters in order to keep colleges and departments “on the hook,” so to speak, for oﬀering Honors courses.
In sum then, it is the unclear, opt-in funding structure for course oﬀerings that is prohibitive in terms of the Honors Program controlling its own curriculum.
We hope to change this funding structure in the new incarnation of the Honors program. (For more on funding and budget, seesection 5.) Page22 URI Honors Program Self-Study | March 2023

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 69
passages.text:
4.6 The program oﬀers specialized active learning courses, seminars and colloquia Honors Program courses include a range of diﬀerent types and levels of courses to provide extensive options for our students.
Students can choose from two types of Honors courses: Honors sections of courses that exist across the university or Honors Program courses (HPR course code) that are available only to Honors eligible students.
Honors courses emphasize enriched rather than accelerated learning, adding depth and dimension to students’ learning experiences.
Class size is limited to 20 students at the introductory level and 15 students at the upper level to allow for discussion and active and project-based learning and to create a seminar-type environment for students and faculty.
TheHonors Colloquiumis the program’s signature course that students can choose to take either in the Fall or Spring semester.
The fall Honors Colloquium combines a topical series of speakers and events with a 200-level Honors course that averages between 50 and 80 students.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 69
passages.text:
Scholars from all over the world, who are leading experts on contemporary and controversial topics, are brought in to share their thoughts and work with both the class and the wider community.
In addition to the Colloquium lectures and panel discussions that take place on Tuesday evenings throughout the semester, related URI theater productions, ﬁlms, readings and exhibitions are often featured to complement the weekly events in the series.
Since it was ﬁrst held in 1963, the URI Honors Colloquium has played an important role in the intellectual life of both the URI campus and the State of Rhode Island.
Colloquium topics have included inequality and the American Dream, new ways to think about gender, the origins of life, healthcare, race in America, global environmental change, hunger, understanding India, and the rise of China.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 69
passages.text:
Prominent speakers who have participated in the series include Coretta Scott King; Pete Seeger; feminist thinker, Jessica Valenti; actor and activist Christopher Reeve; Robert Reich; Earth scientist Robert Hazen; basketball great Bob Cousy; author Tracy Kidder; novelists Chris Cleave, Geraldine Brooks and Jhumpa Lahiri; Cory Booker; professor and MSNBC personality Melissa Harris-Perry; inventor Ray Kurzweil, and Jane Goodall, just to name a few.
Since the Honors Colloquium has played such a deﬁning role in the Honors Program, we now seek to bring it to the forefront of our curricular redesign, as reviewers will note in ournew Strategic Direction for Honors.
A full list of course oﬀerings can be found in our appendix, and on ourwebpage, which includes courses oﬀered from Fall 2018 to the present.
Page23 URI Honors Program Self-Study | March 2023

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 70
passages.text:
4.7 The program oﬀers class-based experiential learning opportunities 4.8 The program oﬀers undergraduate research or independent-study 4.9 The program promotes internships, service learning, and ﬁeld experiences The Honors Project provides a capstone research, scholarly and creative experience for students completing the Honors Program.
It oﬀers our talented and motivated undergraduate students the opportunity for independent, distinguished research and creative work that is oftentimes not available until graduate studies.
This project is done under the guidance of both a faculty sponsor and the Associate Director for Honors Projects and culminates in a presentation at the annual Honors Project Conference.
Students are able to complete their project on any topic; there are no formulas or limits.
Students have produced videos; mounted photography, sculpture, and art exhibits; written poetry manuscripts, novellas, and scientiﬁc papers; designed an aerodynamically advanced golf putter; volunteered in health centers; practiced nursing in the Dominican Republic; done ﬁeld research in California; and explored topics such as cultural competency in the classroom.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 70
passages.text:
The goal of the project is to challenge students creatively and cognitively, capture their heart and mind, and be original work.
We oﬀer an array of courses that include service learning, ﬁeld experience, etc. but we haven’t yet integrated them into programmatic outcomes in any systematic way.
For example, we have an administrative internship experience; honors projects can be experiential or service-centered in nature; many classes have service-learning components like Carolyn Hames’ HPR 124 Loss in the Lives of Children and Adolescents where students work with a local organization on bereavement counseling, Sara Murphy’s classes HPR 411: AIDS in America where students do civic outreach projects as part of their course work, Tom Zorabedian’s HPR 344: Experiencing Film in Rhode Island – an experiential class that involves meeting with Rhode Island ﬁlm-related professionals and viewing ﬁlms in various movie theaters in RI.
SeeSection 8 for more details.
In the new incarnation of the Honors Program, experiential learning, undergraduate research, and service learning/ﬁeld experiences will be explicitly and meaningfully incorporated into the program.

4.10 The program requirements constitute a substantial portion of the participants’ undergraduate work 4.11 The curriculum is designed so that honors requirements can, when appropriate, also satisfy general education requirements, major or disciplinary requirements, and pre-professional or professional training requirements On average, students at the university must take 120 credits to graduate.
This includes courses in three areas: major courses, General Education courses, and electives.
Students electing to complete a second major and/or minor, study abroad, or complete the Honors Program often use elective credits to manage those requirements.
However, Honors courses most often fulﬁllGeneral Educationrequirements and can sometimes fulﬁll arequirement in the student’s major or minor area of study.
To complete the Honors Program, students must take at least 18 credits in Honors courses.
This constitutes 15% of a student’s overall credit requirement to graduate.
In the new incarnation of the Honors Program, we will oﬀer three tracks to maximize ﬂexibility for students: 12 credit, 18 credit and 30 credit tracks.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 71
passages.text:
We will move away from attempting to help students satisfy major requirements and pre-professional/professional training requirements because we do not have the resources to be able to meet these goals in any truly meaningful and systematic way.
Section 5 - Infrastructure 5.1 The program is allocated an annual budget that adequately supports the mission of the program. 5.2 The program is allocated personnel resources that adequately support the mission of the program For FY 2023, the Honors Program was allocated roughly $950,000 to cover administrative salaries; some teaching expenses; operating expenses; and both the Colloquium and the end-of-year Honors poster presentation. (As a reminder, “the Honors Program” comprises the Oﬃce of National Fellowships and Academic Opportunities, the Pre-Health Oﬃce, the Honors Colloquium and the Honors Program.) The $950,000 allocation was from the central budget.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 72
passages.text:
$657,138.20 is paid out in salary and fringe, as is detailed below. $70,000 is allocated for the URI Honors Colloquium. $10,000 is allocated for Honors projects and the spring Honors Poster Conference. $11,000 was allocated for interim coverage for the Honors position director during the summer.
Fixed cost operating expenses total roughly $32,470.
For teaching support, we are allocated $165,381.
This leaves us with roughly $4,000 in extra operating funds for the full ﬁscal year.
Most of this $4,000 will be absorbed by travel to national conferences and costs of membership to professional organizations for the Oﬃce of National Fellowships and Academic Opportunities and Pre-Health Advising.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 72
passages.text:
To consider whether the Honors Program is allocated a base budget that adequately supports the teaching, operational and extracurricular facets of the program (from URI’s permanent and recurrent budget), we must consider several factors: teaching support; personnel support (salary, personnel needed, professional development funding); Colloquium and Honors Poster Conference support; ﬁxed cost support; general operational support (including building and technology maintenance) TEACHING SUPPORT The funding model for Honors is unsustainable.
URI does not fund Honors teaching directly from the central budget allocation, which makes us reliant on “loaned” or “in kind” contributions from colleges.
As an example of this unsustainable model of funding, this FY ‘23, we oﬀered 232 credits of Honors courses.
We were allocated $165,381 from the central budget.
If we calculate the outright minimal cost of 232 credits worth of courses at the lowest part-time-faculty per-credit rate ($1575/credit PTF1), it is $365,400.
At the lowest part-time faculty rate, we would be short $200,019 in order to cover our curriculum.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 72
passages.text:
Clearly, the Honors program depends upon contributions from the Colleges in order to exist.
Obviously, a dynamic Honors program should not be relying at all on part-time faculty but rather on full-time faculty who have demonstrated excellence in their teaching.
If we were to begin to extrapolate what it would cost for Honors courses, taught by full-time faculty members, to be funded entirely from the central budget, we could use the College of Arts & Sciences contributions as a starting point, with the caveat that full-time faculty members in the A&S are among the lowest paid, if not the lowest paid, at the University.
According to A&S budget calculations (see Appendix), this ﬁscal year, in percentage salary contribution, A&S contributed $361,568.63 for 105 credits of the Honors program. (This represents 45% of the total Honors credits oﬀered in FY 23.) The per-credit rate for full-time continuing A&S faculty averages then at $3443.51/credit hour.
If we calculate the outright cost of 232 credits worth of courses at the A&S full-time continuing faculty average rate, it would be $798,894.32.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 72
passages.text: Given that the A&S contribution to the total number of credits oﬀered by Honors is only 45%, the real number of how much central budget would need to provide to cover 232 credits worth of courses would certainly be considerably higher given that the other contributions to Honors come from the College of Business, the College Page26 URI Honors Program Self-Study | March 2023

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 73
passages.text:
of the Environment and Life Sciences, the College of Engineering, the College of Health Sciences, the College of Nursing, and the College of Pharmacy.
Challenge - Reliance on part-time faculty The following charts depict the composition of our teaching faculty.
Note that at URI we have two full-time continuing tracks: Tenure and Teaching Professor.
PTF designates part-time faculty.
Unfortunately, these charts show partial reliance on part-time faculty/staﬀ to deliver our curriculum, which is not a best practice in Honors education.
Challenge - The calculation of funding for Honors and garnering commitment to funding teaching for Honors are becoming increasingly diﬃcult A major challenge that we are currently facing is that we would like to calculate the cost of the new Honors curriculum that we are proposing, but we cannot get numbers from the Colleges, except for the College of Arts & Sciences, on the value of their “loaned” or “in kind” contributions.
Further, since it seems that Colleges calculate workload diﬀerently, it may be that even if we were to receive value numbers, they might not be comparable.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 73
passages.text:
We would like to work within the parameters of the existing funding (both outright and in-kind) that we are receiving so that our new Honors Program does not cost the University more that it is currently funding, but a lack of central funding for Honors teaching, and the reliance on in-kind contributions from colleges that are growing more reluctant to “loan” full-time faculty is making the calculation and planning of this new program very diﬃcult.

Challenge - additional staﬃng needed Staﬀ Additional staﬀ lines are needed, and speciﬁcally: 1) an advisor to assist in the Oﬃce of National Fellowships and Academic Opportunities, which in the new incarnation of the Honors Program will become the Oﬃce of Honors Opportunities and Fellowships; 2) a half-time professional advisor for the Honors Program; 3) a half-time ﬁscal support person.
