passages.text: 1 Bylaws of the University of Rhode Island Board of Trustees Created 6/26/2020 Amended 6/25/2021 Amended 11/4/2022 Amended 11/8/2024 Preamble The University of Rhode Island is the State flagship research university and the State’s leading public institution of higher education. As a land and sea grant institution with global reach, the University of Rhode Island carries out its mission for the benefit of the people of the State of Rhode Island (“State”), the United States, and the world. In all aspects of its work, the University of Rhode Island maintains unshakable commitments to academic freedom and expression, shared governance, diversity and inclusion, and active outreach to its many communities of interest. The University of Rhode Island also engages active partnerships for mutual benefit with Rhode Island College and the Community College of Rhode Island and other private higher education institutions. These bylaws establish the principles, structures, and procedures to ensure the University of Rhode Island remains true to its mission and meets the mandate of applicable statutes, while performing its important work at the highest possible level. Article I Duties of the Board of Trustees 1.1 Fundamental Purpose. The Board of Trustees (“Board”) is established by act of the Rhode Island General Assembly as the exclusive fiduciary authority for the University of Rhode Island (“University” or “URI”). In that capacity, the Board is legally entrusted with the institution’s care and has the critical responsibility for protecting the integrity of the institution’s mission as Rhode

passages.heading: Bylaws | Page 2
passages.text: 2 Island’s premier institution of higher education and overseeing compliance with all provisions of the law. 1.2 Duties of the Board.

passages.heading: Bylaws | Page 2
passages.text: To meet its statutory mandate as the ultimate governing authority for the University of Rhode Island, the Board of Trustees performs a number of critical functions, including but not limited to: (a) Appointment and evaluation of the President of the University (“President”); (b) Recommend trustees for appointment in accordance with RIGL Section 16- 32-2.2 and Section 2.2 hereof. (c) Review and approval of the Strategic Plan and the three-year funding plan for the University, which is to be developed and submitted to the Board by the President; (d) Upon receipt of the recommendations of the President and appropriate faculty bodies, approval of the awarding and revocation of degrees, including honorary degrees, diplomas, certificates, and honors to be conferred by the President; (e) Approval of recommendations made by the President regarding the awarding of tenure to qualified members of the University faculty; (f) Review of the University’s performance under the institution’s Strategic Plan developed and reported by the President and University community; (g) Stewardship of University physical, financial, and human resources consistent with the provisions of all applicable statutes and regulations and policies of the Board of Trustees; (h) Promoting and enforcing integrity and effectiveness of all aspects of the University’s budgeting and financial management, including changes in tuition and fees, submission and approval of the University’s annual budget and three-year financial projections; (i) Approve the creation or termination of new academic majors and the creation, consolidation or termination of academic departments, schools and colleges based on the recommendations of the President who shall have followed the appropriate University process.

passages.heading: Bylaws | Page 3
passages.text:
3 Article II Membership 2.1 Membership.
The membership of the Board shall consist of seventeen (17) voting members and five (5) non-voting members, including one (1) URI faculty member and one (1) URI student to be appointed by the President, and the President, the chair of the Rhode Island Board of Education and the chair of the Rhode Island Council on Postsecondary Education serving ex officio. 2.2 Appointment.
The members shall be appointed in accordance with RIGL Section 16-32-2.2, which specifies that the governor will appoint the members with the advice and consent of the senate, and with due consideration to recommendations from the President and the chair of the Board.
At least three (3) of the members appointed by the governor shall be residents of the State of Rhode Island, at least one (1) of those members shall be selected after due consideration of a list of names of at least five (5) individuals submitted by the speaker of the house of representatives, and at least one (1) of those members shall be selected after due consideration of a list of names of at least five (5) individuals submitted by the president of the senate. 2.3 Appointments of the President.

passages.heading: Bylaws | Page 3
passages.text:
The President will appoint one (1) faculty member who shall serve in a non-voting capacity for a single two (2) year term and one (1) student member who shall be a full-time student in good standing at the University who shall serve in a non-voting capacity for up to two (2) one-year terms. 2.4 Initial Terms.
Six (6) of the members initially appointed pursuant to RIGL Section 16-32-2.2 shall serve terms of three (3) years; seven (7) members initially appointed pursuant to this section shall serve terms of two (2) years, including the member appointed from the list submitted by the speaker of the house of representatives and the member appointed from the list submitted by the president of the senate; and four (4) members initially appointed pursuant to this section shall serve terms of one (1) year. 2.5 Terms.
After the initial terms of appointment have expired, the governor shall appoint members as provided in Section 2.2 hereof for terms of three (3) years and members shall be eligible for reappointment.

passages.heading: Bylaws | Page 4
passages.text:
4 2.6 Removal.
Public members shall be removable by the governor for cause only, and removal solely for partisan or personal reasons unrelated to capacity or fitness for the office shall be unlawful.
In making decisions to remove a member, the governor shall give due consideration to recommendations from the chair of the Board.
RIGL Section 16-32-2.2 (d) provides details about the process for removal for cause. 2.7 Vacancies.
If a vacancy occurs because of death, resignation, or removal among board members appointed by the governor, the secretary of the Board shall inform the governor of the vacancy, and the governor shall make an appointment of a member to serve the unexpired term.
If a vacancy occurs among the non-voting faculty or student Board members, the secretary of the Board shall inform the President of the vacancy so the unexpired term may be filled as provided in the bylaws.
If a vacancy occurs because a member’s term has expired, that member shall serve until a successor is appointed. 2.8 Compensation.
Board members shall receive no compensation for their service on the Board. 2.9 Conflicts of interest.

passages.heading: Bylaws | Page 4
passages.text:
Board members are subject to the State Code of Ethics and shall sign annually a statement documenting the absence of any conflicts of interest.
Board members shall disclose any actual or potential conflict of interest that they may have relating to any matter under the jurisdiction of the Board and shall recuse themselves from discussion or action on any such matter.
No member of the Board (with the exception of the President and the non-voting faculty member and student member) shall be employed in any position under the jurisdiction of the Board, nor contract in any manner for any purpose with the Board or the University; nor shall the Board purchase, sell, or lease any land, property, or supplies from or to any firm or business association of which any member of the Board is owner, part owner, or officer or director.
No person related by consanguinity or affinity in the first degree to any member of the Board shall be employed in any capacity under the Board’s jurisdiction.
Article III Meetings 3.1 Open public meetings.
All meetings, including special meetings, shall be convened pursuant to the provisions of RIGL Chapter 42-46, the Rhode Island

passages.heading: Bylaws | Page 5
passages.text:
5 Open Meetings Act.
Executive (closed) session may be held as provided for in RIGL Chapter 42-46 and Section 42-46-5. 3.2 Quorum.
A quorum shall consist of a majority of voting members of the Board, but less than a quorum may adjourn any meetings.
A majority of those present and voting shall be required for action.
For purposes of these Bylaws, the term “present” includes participation remotely in accordance with the Open Meetings Act. 3.3 Regular meetings.
Regular meetings shall be held at least four times during each calendar year at the call of the Board chair at the time and place within the State of Rhode Island specified in the notice of the meeting in accordance with RIGL Section 42-46-6.
The Board shall give supplemental written notice of any meeting within a minimum of forty-eight (48) hours, excluding weekends and State holidays in the count of hours, before the date as required by law. 3.4 Notice to members.

passages.heading: Bylaws | Page 5
passages.text:
In addition to providing notice of meetings as required by law, written notice of regular meetings and the agenda for such meetings, or in lieu of an agenda, a written statement of the substance of the business to be transacted shall be sent by the Board secretary to each Board member at least one (1) week prior to the date of the meeting. 3.5 Special meetings.
Special meetings may be called by the Board chair with supplemental written notice of any meeting with a minimum of forty-eight (48) hours, excluding weekends and State holidays in the count of hours, compliance with RIGL Section 42-46-6.
Notice of special meetings shall specify the date the notice was posted, the date, time, and place of the meeting and the nature of the business to be discussed or acted upon, and shall also be sent via electronic communication to each Board member not less than forty-eight (48) hours prior to each meeting. 3.6 Waiver of notice.

passages.heading: Bylaws | Page 5
passages.text:
Any member may waive notice of any regular or special meeting by instrument in writing signed by him/her prior to or after such meeting, and the presence of a member at a meeting shall in any event constitute a waiver of notice as to that member. 3.7 Agenda for regular meetings.
The agenda shall be prepared by the Board chair in consultation with the President of the University.
The agenda shall include

passages.heading: Bylaws | Page 6
passages.text:
6 any matter that the Board has at a prior meeting voted to include in such agenda and, further, shall include a provision such that any item requested by any seven (7) members in writing delivered to the chair not less than seven (7) days prior to the date of the meeting shall be placed on the agenda of such meeting.
Any member may introduce a matter to be put on the agenda at the meeting upon the majority vote of the members present, provided such matters shall be for informational purposes only and may not be voted upon except when necessary to address an unexpected occurrence that requires immediate action to protect the public or to refer the matter to the appropriate committee or to another body or official. 3.8 Conduct of meetings.
All meetings, including special meetings, shall be convened pursuant to the provisions of RIGL Section 42-46, the Rhode Island Open Meetings Act.
The affirmative vote of the majority of the members present shall be required for the adoption of any motion or resolution.
All members, including the Board chair, shall have the right to offer motions or resolutions, discuss questions, and to vote.
The chair shall declare the outcome of all votes.

passages.heading: Bylaws | Page 6
passages.text:
A roll call vote shall be taken upon the demand of any member present.
Any member desiring to speak shall address the chair, and after his/her right to speak has been recognized, he/she shall confine remarks to the question under debate.
Other than a member of the Board or staff members, no person shall speak at or address a meeting, except in Open Forum, unless invited to do so by the chair.
Except in unusual circumstances, no more than twenty (20) minutes will be set aside on each Board meeting agenda for persons, other than members or staff, to address the board during Open Forum; such persons must limit their remarks to three (3) minutes or less.
Board members will not respond directly to the topics being raised, but may refer the matter to the Board and the University staff for follow-up where appropriate.
Nothing contained herein shall require the Board to have an Open Forum or to have an Open Forum at any specific meeting. 3.9 Minutes.
Minutes of open meetings shall be deemed public records.

passages.heading: Bylaws | Page 6
passages.text:
Minutes of executive (closed) sessions shall be confidential if the Board has voted to seal them pursuant to RIGL Section 42-46-7 otherwise they shall be made available at the next regularly scheduled meeting of the Board.
Final action taken in executive session shall be reported by the Board chair once the open session reconvenes; provided, however, a vote taken in an executive (closed) session need not be

passages.heading: Bylaws | Page 7
passages.text:
7 disclosed for a period of time during which its disclosure would jeopardize any strategy, negotiation or investigation undertaken pursuant to discussions conducted under that section of the Rhode Island Open Meetings Act that sets forth the purposes for which a meeting may be closed (RIGL Section 42-46-5 (a). 3.10 Records.
The records of all business transacted at each meeting shall be kept under the direction and supervision of the Board.
Article IV Officers of the Board and Duties 4.1 Officers of the Board.
The officers of the Board shall be a chair, vice chair and secretary.
Other officers may from time to time be established with such powers as determined by the Board, and the persons named to such offices shall serve at the pleasure of the Board. 4.2 Election of Officers.
A majority of the members of the Board shall elect the chair of the Board (the “chair”) in accordance with RIGL Section 16-32-2.2(c) from among the voting members of the Board.
In addition, the members of the Board shall elect a vice chair.
The terms of office shall be three years or until a duly appointed successor is elected. 4.3 Duties of the Chair.

passages.heading: Bylaws | Page 7
passages.text:
The chair shall preside at meetings of the Board, exercise the powers and perform the duties set forth in statute and these bylaws and such other duties as usually devolve upon the presiding officer of a deliberative body, and, unless otherwise ordered, shall appoint all committees and all special committees.
The chair shall execute, on behalf of the Board, all contracts and documents approved by the Board, unless otherwise ordered by the Board.
The chair serves as the spokesperson for the Board on matters voted on and approved by the Board. 4.4 Duties of the Vice Chair.
In the absence of the chair, the vice chair shall perform the duties of the chair, including any authorities delegated to the chair by the Board.
In the absence of both the chair and the vice chair, a chair pro tempore shall be elected from among the members of the Board. 4.5 Duties of the Secretary.
The secretary is a university staff member selected by the University President subject to Board approval.
The secretary is responsible for supporting the Board and the Board committees, including issuing required notices of Board meetings and preparing the minutes.
Working with the Board

passages.heading: Bylaws | Page 8
passages.text:
8 chair and University President, and in consultation with other senior leaders of the University, the secretary plans and manages the meetings of the Board and its committees, and in consultation with the University General Counsel is responsible for compliance with all relevant legal requirements and sound governance practices.
The secretary serves as the key liaison between the Board and the President and the University administration.
The secretary is responsible for communication on Board-related policy and procedural matters.
In addition, the secretary shall perform other duties assigned by the Board.
Article V Committees of the Board 5.1 Expectations for Board Committees.
The Board adopts best governance practices that its duties should be grounded in the work of its standing committees.
The Board shall define the duties of each committee by approving a committee charter which declares clearly the purposes of the committee.
Further, the committee work should be accomplished in accordance with an annual work plan which is aligned with the University’s strategic vision and priorities.

passages.heading: Bylaws | Page 8
passages.text:
Committee agendas should be developed in consultation with the committee chair and the University staff member assigned as the liaison to the committee. 5.2 Standing Committees.
The Board shall establish standing committees comprising an Executive Committee, including a compensation subcommittee; an Academic Affairs and Research Committee; a Finance and Facilities Committee; a Governance Committee; an Institutional Risk and Compliance Committee; and a Student Life and Athletics Committee.
Other standing committees may be established by the Board from time to time. 5.3 Special Committees.
The Board shall establish special committees that it considers appropriate and necessary to fulfill its responsibilities. 5.4 Appointment to Committees.
Standing committees shall be appointed by the chair.
Special committees shall be appointed by the chair from time to time.
The chair may request recommendations for committee appointments from the University President and the Governance Committee.

passages.heading: Bylaws | Page 8
passages.text: The chair and vice chair shall be voting members of the Executive Committee and of any other standing or special committees to which they are appointed pursuant to this Section 5.4 and shall be invited to attend, without vote, all meetings of other standing

passages.heading: Bylaws | Page 9
passages.text:
9 committees, special committees and subcommittees.
The University President shall be an ex officio non-voting member of all standing committees, special committees and subcommittees with the exception of the Compensation Subcommittee. 5.5 Conduct of Committee Meetings.
All standing committee meetings and, except as otherwise allowed by law, special committee meetings, shall be convened and conducted pursuant to the provisions of RIGL Chapter 42-46, the Rhode Island Open Meetings Act. 5.6 Quorum and Action by Committees.
Committees shall act by majority vote of members present and voting.
A quorum shall consist of a majority of voting committee members, but less than a quorum may adjourn any meetings. 5.7 Committee Liaisons.
The President, with the concurrence of the Board, shall appoint at least one University staff member for each committee as a liaison between the Board and the University.
Article VI.
President of the University 6.1 Appointment of the President.
The President of the University shall be appointed by the Board to a fixed term of service determined by the Board.

passages.heading: Bylaws | Page 9
passages.text:
The President may be reappointed to an additional term, or terms, following a finding by the Board of satisfactory performance in the position.
In the case of the death, termination, resignation, or disability of the President, the Provost shall serve as Interim President until another interim or permanent replacement is appointed by the Board of Trustees. 6.2 Duties of the President.
The President is the chief executive officer of the University and in addition to any powers granted to the President by law or regulation, the President shall have full power and authority to manage the institution in a manner consistent with its mission, Strategic Plan, and policies established by the Board of Trustees.
The President shall exercise this authority by carrying out responsibilities that include, but are not limited to: (a) In consultation with appropriate internal and external stakeholders, develop the Strategic Plan for the University, including appropriate performance metrics, for approval by the Board;

passages.heading: Bylaws | Page 10
passages.text: 10 (b) Appoint the Officers of the University (see Article VII); (c ) Report regularly, and upon special request from the chair of the Board, to the Board on the general condition of the University, including progress on the strategic plan, bring attention to the Board any matter, including risks, that may affect the Board in pursuit of their obligations under Article I and the authorizing legislation; (d) In consultation with appropriate officials of the University, prepare the annual budget of the University, including recommendations of adjustments in tuition and fees and state appropriations, for consideration by the appropriate committees and the full Board; (e) Report annually to the Board on institutional progress in regard to the institution’s performance metrics related specifically to State of Rhode Island performance funding model and recommend, as appropriate, alternative performance metrics specifically relevant to this funding model; (f) In consultation with appropriate faculty bodies and academic leadership, recommend the creation or termination of academic majors and the creation, consolidation or termination of academic departments, schools, and colleges; (g) Together with the annual budget, prepare and submit a three-year funding plan for the University; and (h) Act, or through delegation to designated representatives, as the authoritative voice of the University in all matters pertaining to the mission, outreach, and philanthropic goals of the institution, including, but not limited to, interactions with key constituencies, government officials, and the media.

passages.heading: Bylaws | Page 10
passages.text:
Article VII Officers of the University 7.1 President.
See Article VI of the Bylaws for information about the duties of the President. 7.2 Provost and Executive Vice President for Academic Affairs.
The Provost is the chief academic officer of the University and is responsible for academic programs and faculty actions.
During brief periods when the President is unavailable or incapacitated, and in the absence of specific action to the contrary by the URI

passages.heading: Bylaws | Page 11
passages.text:
11 Board of Trustees, the Provost shall discharge presidential responsibilities as necessary. 7.3 Vice President for Administration and Finance.
The vice president is the chief financial officer of the University and is responsible for financial and business affairs and the physical and technological infrastructure. 7.4 University General Counsel.
The general counsel is the chief legal officer of the University and advises the Board and the University President about the laws, rules and regulations affecting education. 7.5 Vice President for Research and Economic Development.
The vice president is the chief research officer of the University with overall supervision for the research and economic development missions of the University.
Article VIII The Faculty The faculty of the University of Rhode Island play a central and important role in the governance of the institution in multiple ways, as specified in the University Manual and in the policies of the University, but generally through the work of the Faculty Senate.

passages.heading: Bylaws | Page 11
passages.text:
As stated in the University Manual, “Faculty participation in the government of the University of Rhode Island is essential to its sound development and to the successful performance of its role in the life of the state.
The basic functions of the University – teaching and research – are performed by a community of scholars who must exercise sound judgment in the planning and execution of their assigned responsibilities.
The collective judgment of the scholars who comprise the faculty is a resource of great value which properly utilized will help to guarantee that University policy will be wisely established and effectively carried out. “ The collective knowledge, skills and experience of the faculty enable the University to carry out its mission, to develop and implement strategic plans, and, especially to achieve the academic goals of the Strategic Plan, which is the central document that guides the University towards achieving its overall goals.
This Article affirms the importance of shared governance and faculty responsibility and leadership for matters affecting the core academic mission of the University of Rhode Island.

passages.heading: Bylaws | Page 12
passages.text:
12 8.1 Membership.
Criteria and procedures for membership in the General Faculty of the University of Rhode Island are established in Chapter 4 of the University Manual 8.2 Faculty Senate.
The Faculty Senate is the duly authorized deliberative body representing the General Faculty of the University of Rhode Island.
The Faculty Senate is the ultimate legislative body for matters that fall within the roles and responsibilities of the General Faculty. 8.3 Roles and Responsibilities of the Faculty.

passages.heading: Bylaws | Page 12
passages.text:
In keeping with shared governance, the university faculty, subject to the provisions of applicable law and regulation and the policies of the Board of Trustees and with the concurrence of the President of the University, are responsible to formulate, review, or recommend policy and actions in the following areas: (a) Faculty role in shared governance; (b) Teaching, research, and faculty committee structures and purposes; (c) Academic curricula, programs, requirements, and standards; (d) Intellectual property and patents; (e) Academic integrity and scholastic standards; (f) Recommendations to the Board of Trustees on students’ completion of academic requirements for the awarding of undergraduate and graduate degrees. 8.4 Student welfare and activities.
The University Manual notes that in carrying out these responsibilities the Faculty Senate avoids interference with the authority and responsibility of administrative officers in the conduct of their duties.

passages.heading: Bylaws | Page 12
passages.text:
The Faculty Senate also gives due consideration to the authority and actions of Presidential committees and joint committees of faculty and administrators as well as the faculties of the Colleges and the Graduate Faculty. 8.5 Academic Freedom.
As specified in Chapter 6 of the University Manual, the freedom of expression in general, and academic freedom as defined in Chapter 6, are essential to research, scholarship, creative work, and teaching at the University of Rhode Island.

passages.heading: Bylaws | Page 13
passages.text:
13 Article IX Indemnification 9.1 Conditions.
Each person who at any time is threatened to be or is made a party to any threatened, pending, or completed action, suit, or proceeding, whether civil, criminal, administrative, or investigative (other than an action by or in the right of the Board) by reason of the fact that he/she is, or was, a member of the Board or an officer, employee, or agent of the Board, or is or has served at the request of the Board, as director, officer, employee, or agent of another enterprise of any type, shall be indemnified against expenses (including attorney’s fees), judgments, fines, and amounts paid in settlement actually and reasonably incurred by him/her in connection with any such action, suit, or proceeding, if the Board determines he/she acted in good faith and in a manner he/she reasonably believed to be in or not opposed to the best interests of the Board, and with respect to any criminal action or proceeding, had no reasonable cause to believe his/her conduct was unlawful.

passages.heading: Bylaws | Page 13
passages.text:
No indemnification shall be made in respect to any criminal action or proceeding as to which such person shall have been judged guilty, unless and only to the extent that the court in which such action or proceeding was brought shall determine upon application that, despite the adjudication of guilty, in view of all the circumstances of the case, such person is entitled to indemnification for such expenses or fines which the court shall deem proper.
Determination of any action, suit, or proceeding by judgment order, settlement, conviction, or upon a plea of nolo contendere or its equivalent, shall not, of itself, create a presumption that a person did not act in good faith in the manner which he/she reasonable believed to be in or to opposed to the best interest of the Board, and with respect to any criminal action or proceeding had reasonable cause to believe that his/her conduct was unlawful. 9.2 Notice.
This indemnification shall be conditioned on due written notice of any such claims being given to the Board which shall be entitled to be present at all hearings, proceedings, and negotiations relative to such claims. 9.3 Miscellaneous.

passages.heading: Bylaws | Page 13
passages.text: The provisions of this article shall in no way be exclusive of any other rights of indemnification to which such person shall be entitled, shall continue as to a person who has ceased to be a member, officer, employee, or agent of the Board, and shall inure to the benefit of the heirs, executors, and administrators of such a person.

passages.heading: Bylaws | Page 14
passages.text: 14 Article X Miscellaneous 10.1 Seal. The seal of the University of Rhode Island shall be the seal of the University of Rhode Island Board of Trustees. The seal may be used by causing it or a facsimile thereof to be impressed or affixed or reproduced or otherwise. 10.2 Fiscal Year. The University operates on a fiscal year defined as July 1 through June 30. Article XI Amendment of Bylaws 11.1 Process. These bylaws may be amended, suspended, or altered by vote of two-thirds (2/3) of the members present taken at any regular meeting or special meeting, provided that written notice of the substance of the proposed change has been emailed to the members of the Board at least one (1) week prior to such meeting. 11.2 Suspension of Rules of Order. Those parts of these bylaws that are in the nature of rules of order may be suspended by a two-thirds (2/3) vote of those present.

2 / UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND ANNUAL REPORT 2021 / 3 OVERVIEW Preparing for URI’s Future THE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND The University of Rhode Island is the state’s flagship research university and the state’s leading public institu- tion of higher education.
As a land and sea grant institution with global reach, the University of Rhode Island carries out its mission for the benefit of the people of Rhode Island, the United States, and the world.
In all aspects of its work, the University of Rhode Island maintains unshakable commitments to aca- demic freedom and expression, shared governance, diver- sity and inclusion, and active outreach to its many commu- nities of interest.
The University of Rhode Island also devel- ops and maintains partnerships for mutual benefit with Rhode Island College, the Community College of Rhode Island, and other private higher education institutions.

passages.heading: Annual Report 2021 | Page 3
passages.text:
THE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND BOARD OF TRUSTEES The Board of Trustees is the University’s governing body charged with oversight of critical academic and administra- tive issues, including appointing the University president, annually setting tuition rates, approving the budget, awarding degrees, and formally approving the awarding of tenure to faculty.
BOARD OF TRUSTEES HIGHLIGHTS New University President The selection process for the new University president was global, comprehensive, rigorous, and inclusive, involving every facet of the University community.
The board orga- nized town hall meetings with all University stakeholders and virtual open forums with presidential candidates.
It conducted a totally virtual search and selected the 12th president of the University.
The board is proud of the open and thorough process that led to the hiring of President Marc Parlange, who has already begun strengthening and expanding the Universi- ty’s research mission, including a University-wide call to develop a culture of scholarship and service, which will improve collaboration and communication across colleges, disciplines, and departments.

passages.heading: Annual Report 2021 | Page 3
passages.text:
Even though he is in his early days as president, President Parlange is focusing on expanding URI’s strengths in oceanography, agriculture, engineering, and the arts, along with the importance of student athletes.
He is expected to deliver a new strategic plan in 2022 that will outline the University’s vision over the next several years, which will be shared with you and Rhode Island leaders.
COVID-19 Operations and Response As with other public boards, our work was conducted remotely and in accordance with executive orders during the pandemic.
At every meeting, the trustees reviewed the University’s response to the pandemic and supported its actions to ensure the health and safety of students, staff, faculty, and visitors to campus.
The board praised the entire University community for its outstanding efforts during the pandemic, resulting in 95 percent vaccination rate and a continued very low positivity rate.
Importantly, the University was able to manage its financial resources quite effectively throughout the crisis, and, unlike many other higher education institutions, URI has come through the pandemic quite well.

passages.heading: Annual Report 2021 | Page 3
passages.text:
Ten-Y ear Strategic Plan The University will engage the entire community and key constituencies in the development of a new Universi- ty-wide, 10-year strategic plan (2022–2032) designed to create a vision for the future and what the University aspires to achieve.
A University-wide Steering Committee will oversee the process, develop key performance indica- tors (KPIs) to measure progress of the goals, and analyze trends, challenges, and opportunities impacting the higher education landscape currently and into the future.
Social Justice, Equity, and Inclusion at URI The board is keenly interested in the advancement of social justice, equity, and inclusion at URI.
In October 2020, the board heard from University leaders on one of URI’s transformational goals for the 21st century—to build a community that values and embraces equity and diversity.
At its January, June, and November board meetings, dis- cussions focused specifically on this issue and how to con- tinue to improve the environment at URI.

passages.heading: Annual Report 2021 | Page 3
passages.text:
At its November 2021 meeting, the board reviewed the results of the “Uni- versity of Rhode Island Assessment of Climate for Learning, Living, and Working, ” URI’s first Campus Climate Survey conducted in spring 2021.
The report provides baseline data on diversity and inclusion and may be used to guide decision-making regarding policies and practices at URI to realize its commitment to an inclusive campus and to insti- tute organizational structures that respond to the needs of its dynamic campus community.
Rhode Island’s Blue Economy The Board of Trustees sees tremendous opportunity in marshalling the research and economic development engines of the University to help drive and grow the Rhode Island economy.
URI has been especially engaged in providing the scientific and technical basis for renewable energy, fisheries and aquaculture, environmental quality, marine and coastal conservation, and management efforts in conjunction with stakeholders and Rhode Island government agencies.

passages.heading: Annual Report 2021 | Page 3
passages.text:
The University and the state of Rhode Island are investing mil- lions of dollars in improvements at the Narragansett Bay Campus, home to URI’s world-renowned Graduate School of Oceanography, to advance its efforts in ocean science.
Rhode Island Workforce Efforts The board is focused on the University’s investment in workforce development opportunities, including continu- ing education/certificate programs, professional develop- ment, the URI Online degree program, and 24/7 learning opportunities.
Polaris MEP , a business unit of the URI Research Foundation, is a manufacturing industry partner for the Governor’s Workforce Board providing competitive manufacturing business improvement programs to grow the state’s manufacturing industry.
Innovate@URI helps entrepreneurs and startups access the vast resources of the University to help grow their ideas and their business, with URI’s Business Engagement Center serving as the front door to industry since 2013.

2 / UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND ANNUAL REPORT 2022 / 3 OVERVIEW Building the University of the Future UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND The University of Rhode Island is the state’s flagship research university and the state’s leading public institution of higher education.
As a land- and sea-grant institution with global reach, the University carries out its mission for the benefit of the people of Rhode Island, the United States, and the world.
In all aspects of its work, the University maintains unshakable commitments to academic freedom and expression, shared governance, diversity and inclusion, and active outreach to its many communities of interest.
The University also maintains partnerships for mutual benefit with the state’s two other public institutions— Rhode Island College and Community College of Rhode Island—and other public, private, and nonprofit entities.

passages.heading: Annual Report 2022 | Page 3
passages.text:
UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND BOARD OF TRUSTEES The Board of Trustees is the University’s governing body charged with oversight of critical academic and administrative issues, including appointing the University president, annually setting tuition rates, approving the budget, awarding degrees, and formally approving the awarding of tenure to faculty.
BOARD OF TRUSTEES HIGHLIGHTS Approved a new 10-year strategic plan The Board of Trustees unanimously approved the University’s 10-year strategic plan, Focus URI.
The plan outlines a strate- gic vision for the University of Rhode Island for the next decade—articulating the institution’s aspirations and the actions that will be taken to achieve them.
The agile, dynamic plan will necessarily evolve, enabling the University to respond to changes in the state and world, while maintaining a firm commitment to its land- Advanced initiatives to drive Rhode Island’s leadership in the Blue Economy Under the board’s leadership, in partnership with the Gen- eral Assembly and the governor, and with the strong sup- port of Rhode Island voters, the University passed Ques- tion 1 on the November ballot.

passages.heading: Annual Report 2022 | Page 3
passages.text:
The initiative provides a $100 million general obligation bond to revitalize URI’s Narragansett Bay Campus by improving outdated facilities and constructing new facilities to support research and educational programs, ensuring that the state of Rhode Island remains a global leader in the Blue Economy.
The Blue Economy—which includes the defense industry, tour- ism, marine trades, fisheries, and offshore wind—is a criti- cal driver of the state’s economy, generating more than $5 billion every year.
By 2030, that total is projected to double.
A modern URI Bay Campus will help create the innovative jobs critical to Rhode Island’s future.
Welcomed key academic and administrative leaders The board welcomed the appointment of Barbara Wolfe as provost and executive vice president for academic affairs.
Wolfe was appointed by President Parlange after an exten- sive national search and will work closely with stakeholders on advancing the University and implementing the 10-year strategic plan.
Wolfe is a successful scholar, researcher, and educator, who skillfully led the College of Nursing since joining the Uni- versity in 2016.

passages.heading: Annual Report 2022 | Page 3
passages.text:
At the college, she built research strength and raised the level of federal research and training grant funding.
She is an innovative academic administrator with a track record of success and led URI into the U.S.
News and World Report’s Top 50 rankings for master’s nursing education.
She is nationally respected in her field, holding leadership positions in several national associations. and sea-grant missions, institutional vision, and founda- tional values.
The ideas in the plan are intended to unify the community, inspire new ideas and actions, and acceler- ate URI’s exciting forward trajectory.
Development of the plan was led by a diverse steering committee comprised of faculty, staff, students, and community members, and incorporates input from hundreds of stakeholders across all URI campuses and the community.
The plan focuses on four strategic priorities with action items and corresponding key performance indicators to track and measure the plan’s progress.
The four strategic priorities are, “broaden our impact, ” “enhance student achievement, ” “foster an inclusive culture, ” and “power the university of the future. ”

passages.heading: Annual Report 2022 | Page 4
passages.text:
4 / UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND ANNUAL REPORT 2022 / 5 Celebrated the opening of the Talent Development Achievement House In January, the University opened the Talent Development Achievement House fulfilling an institutional goal of establishing a dedicated residence facility for Talent Development Scholars.
URI’s Talent Development—or TD— program recruits and serves Rhode Island high school graduates with college potential who come from historically disadvantaged backgrounds, a majority of whom are scholars of color.
From its first class of 13 students in 1968 to the 1,100 current scholars and more than 4,000 alumni, TD has formed a community of accomplished individuals across the state and around the world.
Approved new degree programs to meet the needs of Rhode Island The board approved several new degree programs in 2022 that meet the demands of students and the needs of the state and citizens of Rhode Island.

passages.heading: Annual Report 2022 | Page 4
passages.text:
The new programs include: • A Bachelor of Science in early childhood education, PK-2, administered online and developed in conjunction with the Community College of Rhode Island, that will give the incumbent workforce of early childhood educators accessible, high-quality, and meaningful pathways toward credential attainment, career advancement, and higher compensation. • A Bachelor of Arts in world language education designed to meet changes in the Rhode Island Department of Education’s credentials for world language instructors in PK-12.
The new program ensures that URI graduates are certified to teach in Rhode Island at all levels of elemen- tary, middle, and secondary education. • A master’s degree in data science offered through URI Online. • A Bachelor of Science in nutrition within the College of Health Sciences.
Approved record financial aid support for students Recognizing the inflationary pressures faced by students and families, the board approved an increase in ins- titutional financial aid for undergraduate and graduate students to more than $140 million—a record high for the University.

passages.heading: Annual Report 2022 | Page 4
passages.text:
The significant investment in URI students and student success ensures that the University will remain among the most affordable flagship state universities in the Northeast.
Made significant investments in the student-athlete experience The board approved strategic investments in intercolle- giate athletics to enrich the overall student-athlete experi- ence and leverage the considerable visibility athletics gen- erates to enhance the national and global reputation of the University.
In March, URI welcomed Archie Miller as men’s basketball head coach.
Miller joined the University after holding head coaching positions at Indiana University, of the Big Ten, and the University of Dayton.
At Dayton, Miller built the Flyers into a perennial Atlantic 10 Conference power, making four NCAA tournament appearances in six seasons.
The University also retained Tammi Reiss as wom- en’s basketball head coach.
Reiss has reinvigorated the women’s basketball program, leading the Rams to 20 wins in a season for the first time in 25 years and setting the program on a course for sustained success.

passages.heading: Annual Report 2022 | Page 4
passages.text:
And, the board approved the addition of women’s lacrosse, adding important athletic opportunities for female students at the University.
Endorsed the University’s first land acknowledgment statement The University worked closely with the Narragansett Tribal Council on several initiatives, including a land acknowledgment.
The acknowledgment represents months of important conversations between the Univer - sity and members of the tribe, and it reads: The University of Rhode Island occupies the traditional stomping ground of the Narragansett Nation and the Niantic People.
We honor and respect the enduring and continuing relationship between the Indigenous people and this land by teaching and learning more about their history and present- day communities, and by becoming stewards of the land we, now too, inhabit.
Several additional programs are underway or in develop - ment to continue to strengthen the University’s close partnership with the Narragansett Tribe and support and celebrate the tribe’s culture and traditions.

passages.heading: Annual Report 2022 | Page 4
passages.text:
Formed new board committees to advance research and University facilities The board approved the creation of two new special ad hoc committees: the Sponsored Research Committee and the Real Estate Committee.
These committees are designed to address specific needs of the University and accelerate progress in these priority areas.
Contributed to important legislative changes Members of the board successfully testified in favor of legislation, including a bill that provides the board the flexibility to participate remotely in open public meetings of the board.
The board extends its appreciation to the General Assembly for this key legislative decision that enables the University and board to nimbly and effectively address emerging needs and opportunities.

He previously served as director of state govern- ment affairs for the Toy Association, leading the group’s legislative and reg- ulatory efforts at the state level, on issues related to product safety, chemical regulation, and environ- mental sustainability across multiple states in the Northeast.
Lenz previ- ously served as senior pol- icy advisor to R.I.
Attorney General Peter Kilmartin.
He is appointed from the list submitted by the president of the Senate.
Roby Luna Term expires: Feb. 1, 2022 Roby Luna ’04 is the presi- dent of Aretec Inc. and serves as a member of the URI College of Business Dean’s Advisory Council.
As a founding member of Aretec, he oversees the technical vision and stays attuned to the needs of the data science and cybersecurity industry, working to ensure the company meets or exceeds those needs.
While at URI, he was a member of the Army Reserve and assisted a combat support hospital in Massachusetts.

David J.
Martirano Term expires: Feb. 1, 2023 David J.
Martirano ’91 is the co-founder and man- aging partner of Point Judith Capital, which was officially rebranded as PJC nearly two decades later.
PJC, an early-stage venture capital fund, is investing out of its fifth fund.
Before PJC, Martirano co-founded Rex Capital Ventures, which invested interna- tionally in early-stage com- panies.

He currently sits on the Investment Com- mittee for Lifespan, was previously a member of the URI College of Business Advisory Council, and was on the founding board of Year Up Providence.

Cortney M.
Nicolato Term expired: Feb. 1, 2021 Cortney M.
Nicolato ’01 is the president and CEO of United Way of Rhode Island, a nonprofit agency with more than 80 employ- ees and an operating bud- get of $19.2 million.

passages.heading: Annual Report 2022 | Page 6
passages.text:
United Way of Rhode Island invests in proven programs that address community issues to strengthen Rhode Island.
Last year, it awarded $6.5 million to 72 nonprofit agencies that support programs for childhood literacy, work- force development, and more.
Before United Way, she held several high-level, national management positions, each building upon the effectiveness of her transformational lead- ership style.
Most recently, Nicolato served as presi- dent and CEO of the Senior Source, the largest non- profit agency for seniors in North Texas.
Her previous experience also includes being senior advisor and director of new business initiatives at the National Center of the American Heart Association/Ameri- can Stroke Association.

passages.text: RECOMMENDATIONS ON WINTER J-TERM SESSION The following recommendations are the combined efforts of the Academic Standards and Calendar Committee and discussions among members of the Faculty Senate Executive Committee, the Office of Enrollment Services and the Office of the Provost SECTIONI Guidelines for Winter J-Term Session Courses and Scheduling A. I-Term Course Guidelines: Department Chair and Dean approve. The instructor's syllabus shall reflect the provisions of sections 8.32.10-13. The Curricular Affairs Committee and the Graduate Council shall be informed of the decision. Approved topics for open-ended courses may be offered as outlined above. department chair may be offered if posted and approved by the CAC or Graduate Council. New Courses must follow all procedures for approval of new courses and must include a syllabus that reflects the provisions in 8.32.10-13. B. I-Term Scheduling Guidelines Courses shall be scheduled for the Winter J-Term Session no later than October 15 of the preceding fall semester. Registration shall be permitted up to the first meeting of the J-Term course. After the first day, students may only drop or add the course through the petition process with the approval of the student's academic dean. Resulting tuition and fee adjustments will be subject to approved billing and adjustment scales. Faculty members shall not be required to teach during Winter J-Term Session and shall be compensated for such teaching. Compensation may take the form of overload salary or agreed-upon release time during the fall or spring semester.

information regarding the Administrative Councils for inclusion on the University Manual 5.52.10 The President's Executive Council is a core team of university senior leaders tasked with addressing include at minimum Provost/Vice President for Academic Affairs, Vice President for Administration and Finance, General Counsel, and the Senior Advisor and Chief of Staff to the President. 5.53.10 The academic and administrative leaders responsible for purposeful information sharing, effective and inclusive decision-making, clear and timely communications, and overall university stewardship. FSEC (Faculty Senate Executive Committee) Meeting Minutes Date: Wednesday September 16, 2026 - Time: 10:00 am to 12:00 Pastore Hall Room 224 - Remote option via ZOOM Find the Acronym Glossary here Action Items: Staff will work with the FS President to clean up slides and scripts for the 9/17 FS meeting.
Pres.
Preisser will continue to refine the JCODL bill amendment language in advance of the meeting.
Staff will start reaching out to potential speakers/presenters tentatively scheduled for the October senate meeting so that the agenda can be firmed up. 1.
Call to Order - Pres.
Preisser called the special meeting to order at 10:01 pm.
VP Trimm and Senators Van Wyk, Daniels, Meyerson, and Chen were present. 2.
Minutes for approval 2.1 Minutes of the 9/9/26 FSEC meeting.
The minutes were approved. 3.
Priority Items and New Business 3.1.
Recap - 9/10 senate meeting - FSEC members were pleased with how the Orientation event went.
Although the attendance felt sparse in the room, there were a number of attendees on Zoom and staff confirmed that nearly all newly elected senators were on hand.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 1
passages.text:
The idea of providing Orientation purely for new members was discussed with the pros being that experienced senators will not feel pressured to attend during the demanding first week of classes, and such a protocol would help adjust the expectation that the room will be full of senators, which it typically is not for Orientation. 3.2.
Meeting Prep - 9/17/26 Faculty Senate Meeting - see also microphone duties.
The spreadsheet showing microphone responsibilities was shared and staff noted a hard copy will always be in the meeting room.
The agenda and accompanying slides were discussed in detail.
Regarding the curricular reports, it was noted that SSCC Chair Furong Xu will be on hand to answer any questions about summer approvals.
Several announcements were added for inclusion before FSEC moved on to discuss specific legislation. 3.2.1 Discuss Proposed Legislation: ● Reintroduction of JCODL Legislation - VP Trimm will act as presiding officer during this item as Pres.
Preisser will present the legislation substantively.
Amendments have been proposed, which Pres.
Preisser has discussed with the proposer, and draft alternative text is being inserted into the slides for presentation.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 1
passages.text:
Staff will prepare electronic ballots in case a voice vote is inadequate for determining approval of the proposal and related amendments. ● Course withdrawals legislation and back-up - It was noted that the current proposal applies to regular session courses only.
There were suggestions regarding clarity on some of the slides and it was questioned whether a faculty member’s signature indicated an approval or simply an acknowledgment of withdrawal.
Pres.
Preisser noted that one important take-away from this agenda item will be that good ideas for enactment by the senate can come from anywhere on campus, not just from faculty members (the bill was proposed by an advisor in CELS). 1

The COB has been advised to run a special election and transmit the results asap.

Faculty Senate Executive Committee Bill #2026-2027-01
October 15, 2026 Faculty Senate Meeting - FOR ACTION
(Introduced at the September 17, 2026 Faculty Senate Meeting)
Creates standard process for committee formation
Approved by FSEC 08/31/26 and 10/7/26 (as amended)
Reviewed by CBUM 09/28/26 and 10/8/26 (as amended)
Legislation effective date: Spring semester 2027
Rationale: The limited number of faculty senators, in combination with University-Manual-mandated committee staffing requirements, can make it difficult to staff an expanding number of standing committees. This makes it important to ensure that additional standing committees and subcommittees, whose charges and memberships are proscribed in the University Manual, are created only in response to a significant and sustained need. In contrast, special committees can be created by the Faculty Senate to address pressing issues. While there is no limit to the length of time a special committee can exist, the faculty senate must vote to reauthorize each special committee each year.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text:
This legislation mandates that a newly formed committee must exist as a special committee for at least three (3) years before legislation reconstituting it as a standing committee or subcommittee can be considered by the Faculty Senate. Such legislation must be accompanied by language specifying the charge and membership of the standing committee for inclusion in the University Manual. This change provides time for the Faculty Senate to 1) consider whether a new standing committee or subcommittee is truly warranted; and 2) craft an appropriate and achievable charge for the body.
This legislation does not mandate that a special committee must be reconstituted as a standing committee after three years. It is also not retroactive, i.e., all existing standing committees and subcommittees remain unchanged.
This original version of this legislation was introduced for discussion at the 9/17/26 Faculty Senate meeting. The final version has been revised as follows in response to faculty/staff comments.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text:
1. Remove language mentioning joint committees. Joint committees are, by definition, created in concert with the administration (staffing, wording, charge, power balance). While the faculty and administration may choose to designate a joint committee as a special joint committee subject to the rules and procedures detailed below, the power to do so does not rest exclusively with the faculty senate.
2. Identify the assessment process and who conducts it. Added language to §4.12.1 specifying that the Special Committee’s self-assessment shall be reviewed by FSEC. FSEC which shall use it as the basis for a recommendation to the Faculty Senate to vote on whether the Committee should dissolve, continue as a Special Committee, or be reconstituted as a permanent Standing Committee or Subcommittee.
3. What happens if no reauthorization vote is taken before the end of the AY? Added language to §4.11.1 specifying that all Special Committees are annually authorized by vote of the Faculty Senate. A Special Committee that has not received an affirmative reauthorization vote (assuming that no duly authorized extension has been granted) within one year of authorization shall be dissolved.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text:
4. After the third-year review, can a reauthorized Special Committee apply to change its status? Added language to §4.12.1 specifying that a Special Committee must wait at least two years after its third-year review (i.e., be in its fifth consecutive year of operation) before requesting that the Faculty Senate reconsider reconstituting it as a Standing Committee or Subcommittee.

Graduate student-related concerns - follow up - Sen.
Daniels noted that part-time graduate students are addressed in four sections in the University Manual but their status is not defined (except through their exclusion from the defined class of full-time students).
He has met with the Graduate School Dean about the need to provide explicit definitions and guidance regarding part-time students so that Enrollment Services does not continue to impose enrollment holds on them.
Although the graduate school dean is very good about getting the holds lifted, they should not be happening in the first place.
FSEC members suggested other programs wherein students might be affected like Sen.
Daniels students are and it was suggested he collaborate with them as well as the Grad School Dean’s office to find a solution.

New Business – Open for additional items not listed in the agenda. 7.1 Curricular Practical Training (CPT) concerns - Senator Daniels noted that recent guidance from DHS is causing confusion and concern around student internships, especially with regard to the level of scrutiny the agency can give to the necessity of the work experience as an integral part of the curriculum.
There are differing interpretations within the colleges and departments about what DHS actually requires, and whether internships must be required as part of a degree program, or if the option of an internship as just one of several paths to program completion is sufficient to meet the DHS standard.
It is expected that the Office of General Counsel will weigh in on the approach the University should take.

passages.heading: Minutes | Page 3
passages.text:
FSEC members agreed that a crucial perspective to bring to bear in this inquiry would be that of Vice Provost for Global Initiatives Kristin Johnson.
It was suggested that she be approached as a partner in gleaning clear and comprehensive guidance about how to proceed.
Past President Williams noted that this seems to be an area in which the role of the faculty senate is not a formal one, i.e. it is not within the senate’s jurisdiction.
The senate can and should, however, play an informal role by focusing attention and energy on the issue and facilitating an exchange of information that might help the university solve the problem.
Past President Williams added that the FSEC should be guided by three central questions as they consider whether or not to advance an issue: 1) what is the problem? 2) What does a solution look like?
And 3) What can the senate do to achieve the solution, i.e. what is the appropriate level and type of senate involvement?
FSEC members agreed this is a good framework for figuring out how to triage and prioritize new issues and concerns. 8.

Creation of a College Liaison Special Committee
Effective starting spring 2027
The College Liaison Special Committee shall consist of ten senators, one from each college that elects Faculty Senators and one from the Library, who are referred to as the ‘Liaison’ from their unit to the Faculty Senate. If the Faculty Senate votes to approve creation of this Special Committee in fall 2026, senators from each college/Library will select one of their number to serve during the spring 2027 semester in the role of Liaison. Following senate elections in May 2027, senators from each college/Library will again select one of their number in August to serve during the 2027-2028 academic year in the role of Liaison. Liaisons may be re-elected but must be a current senator. The Senate President and FSEC will ask for volunteers to chair this committee on a one-year basis and identify a chair for vote by the Faculty Senate at its September meeting.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda
passages.text:
College Liaison Committee members are charged with ensuring that faculty in each college are informed of pertinent university-level matters and communicate senate- and college-level concerns in both directions. Liaisons attend all-college faculty meetings and will be given the opportunity to give a report on senate activities. The Liaison also attends meetings of the Faculty Senate in their role as a current senator.
Liaisons have two responsibilities in addition to attending college- and senate-level meetings. First, Liaisons provide a brief monthly update regarding senate/university-level matters to faculty in their college. Second, Liaisons represent their college on the College Liaison Committee. This committee meets at least once per semester to address issues requiring inter-college coordination. The College Liaison Committee is a Special Committee of the Faculty Senate, chaired by the Vice President of the Faculty Senate who serves as a non-voting member.

FSEC Proposal - Introduction Only - Bill #2026-2027-FSEC-02 - Changing deadlines for course withdrawals.
Kristy Snow, CELS Academic Advisor, presented her draft bill which has been favorably reviewed and advanced by FSEC.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 3
passages.text:
It was noted that advisors are attuned to students’ frustration with early withdrawal deadlines because, in many instances, they have yet to glean a robust assessment of whether or not they can be successful in a course.
They are forced to make guesses about how they might perform and many withdraw too soon, in an abundance of caution, which often has grave consequences.
Because withdrawals can impact things like full-time status, housing and financial aid, graduation date, etc. students would benefit from a more complete snapshot of how they are doing before making such decisions.
There were a number of questions from the floor and, while most senators were supportive of the move to extend the "withdraw without extenuating circumstances" period, there was concern that changing the deadline from three to eleven weeks was a bit extreme.
Data was presented from peer institutions who all have later deadlines than URI.
Other concerns centered around possible increased demand for faculty signatures, whether or not deadlines for accelerated and summer/J-term courses will also be adjusted (the current proposal only addresses 3

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 4
passages.text:
regular semester-long courses), and what impacts later withdrawals might have on group work of fellow students and on IDEA completions for faculty.
Sen.
Buxton suggested that the bill proposers perhaps also consider expanding the deadlines and relaxing the requirements for taking courses Pass-Fail rather than for a letter grade.
Students could then still keep earning credits so impacts on full-time status, degree completion dates, financial aid, etc. are somewhat mitigated.
Advisor Snow noted the usefulness of the feedback and she hopes to address many of the concerns in the next draft of the bill. d.
FSEC Proposal - Introduction Only - By-Laws Amendment - Bill #2026-2027-FSEC-01: Transitioning Special Committees to Standing Committees.
Senate President Preisser presented the draft bill which will be reviewed by CBUM before the next senate meeting when it will return for a vote.
He explained that, in recent memory, the senate has created new permanent committees without a complete understanding of their long-term need, the durability of their charge and resources available to help them address it, and the most appropriate membership composition to ensure the committee’s enduring success.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 4
passages.text:
The proposal calls for a three-year “trial period,” wherein a special committee is created (through senate action, but without requiring an amendment to the university manual or by-laws) that performs a self-assessment during its third year and makes recommendations to the senate about whether to continue as a special committee, disband, or convert to a permanent committee.
This new process would apply to joint and sub-committees as well as senate standing committees.
Feedback was generally positive and it was noted that once a permanent, standing committee makes its way into the university manual and/or by-laws, it becomes difficult and cumbersome to refine its mission, charge and membership.
The new process would provide time to adopt the best possible manual language for new committees and ensure that practical concerns which can only be understood by seeing a committee in action are addressed from the start. e.

passages.text: SECTION 1. ABOUT THE ACADEMIC PROGRAM REVIEW 4

passages.heading: Linked from Linked from Agenda | Page 5
passages.text:
Introduction The Academic Program Review (APR) at the University of Rhode Island is a valuable opportunity for all academic departments/units to celebrate achievements, shape the future of their academic department/units (referred to as departments herein), and ensure lasting impact for students, faculty, and the broader institution and community.
Through a systematic and structured process, APR engages faculty and staff in retrospective reflection and prospective planning to showcase program impact in ways that have shaped institutional priorities and investments with contributions to teaching, learning, research, scholarship, and student success, and to identify opportunities for growth and innovation.
APR fosters meaningful collaboration that is necessary to develop a shared vision and chart an inspiring course forward.
The Program Review Process and Report Development The program review process consists of several essential components, each playing a vital role in shaping the final report: 1.
Orientation: The APR journey begins with an orientation session designed to introduce faculty to the support structures available to them throughout their report writing effort.

passages.heading: Linked from Linked from Agenda | Page 5
passages.text:
At this first session, hosted by the Joint Committee on Academic Program Review and outcomes Assessment (JCAPROA), departments will also receive a preliminary program data packet provided by the Office of Institutional Research. 2.
Self-Study: Departments are asked to prepare a detailed Self-Study that examines how their activities in several areas (teaching, outcomes assessment, research, service and resource utilization, etc.) are aligned with the University’s Mission and Strategic Plan. (See Self Study Guidelines, Section 2) 3.
External Review: Departments are asked to invite a peer reviewer from a similar or aspirational department at another institution to provide an external perspective on the program’s strengths and identified growth areas.
The external reviewer’s report will include recommendations for improvement which should be integrated into the department’s Action Plan response. (See External Review, Section 3) 4.
Action Plan (Response and Strategic Planning): The Department Chair and Dean meet to discuss the external reviewer’s feedback, set response actions, 5

passages.heading: Linked from Linked from Agenda | Page 6
passages.text:
and develop a strategic Action Plan for the next six years. (See Action Plan, Section 4) Oversight and Support In addition to ongoing support available through the Office of the Provost, there are two key resources available to support departments throughout the APR process: ● Faculty Senate Joint Committee on Academic Program Review and Outcomes Assessment (JCAPROA) is responsible for overseeing, guiding and supporting the academic program review process, coordinating the scheduling of program reviews and maintaining the guidelines for reporting (University Manual 8.85.14) ● Office of Institutional Research disseminates university-level data and supports the departments with the interpretation of data.
Level of Organizational Evaluation URI Academic Program Review is at the department or academic program degree level, and at the college level for colleges without departments or with departments having fully integrated academic degrees.

passages.heading: Linked from Linked from Agenda | Page 6
passages.text:
For clarity within this document, the terms “department” or “unit” are used instead of “academic program.” Guidance for Specialized Accredited Units The APR process for units with specialized accreditation will be coordinated to avoid a duplication of effort.
These departments may also be reviewed independently of others within their academic unit.
Units with a combination of accredited and non- accredited programs are only required to address those areas not covered within their accreditation report within their Self-Study.
The Dean and Provost should receive both the accreditation report and the Self-Study when the APR report is submitted on behalf of the unit.
The proposed Action Plan should cover all programs within the unit (reference Action Plan, Section 4).
APR Review Cycle Departments are notified of an upcoming Academic Program Review reporting expectation the two semesters before the APR is due (e.g., notification in Fall of 2026 for APR due in Spring 2027).
The review cycle is intended to be every six years, with approximately 1/6 of the academic units reviewed each year.
Typically, all or most departments within a college are reviewed simultaneously.

passages.heading: Linked from Linked from Agenda | Page 6
passages.text: The master schedule and timeline will be maintained by JCAPROA and available on the Provost’s Brightspace page. 6

passages.heading: Linked from Linked from Agenda | Page 7
passages.text: Deferring Academic Program Review A one-year, one-time extension can be requested, with prior agreement from the Dean’s Office, by emailing the Vice Provost for Academic and Faculty Initiatives and the Chair of JCAPROA (See Appendix A: Extension Request Form). Reasons for extensions can include, but are not limited to: leadership transitions, major curriculum changes, specialized accreditation review, institutional or strategic priorities, data availability and institutional changes, faculty workload and capacity, significant external changes (mergers, reorganizations, or new programs). Extensions beyond one-year will be considered on a case by case basis. Submission of the APR Departments should work in conjunction with their Dean’s Office to determine the method (e.g., email) and format (.pdf, word, etc.) the Dean prefers in order to receive and review the draft report. The Department Chair should upload the final APR report package to the Vice Provost for Academic and Faculty Initiatives. 7

passages.text: APR Orientation Meeting (Spring) The Orientation to Academic Program Review is designed to provide faculty with information about the process, resources, and access to the support available to undertake a successful Academic Program Review within a department. Orientation includes: ● Guidelines for writing the report ● Best practices in review ● Review of the recommended timeline ● Priorities to consider now! Institutional Data Sources ● Data from URI’s Office of Institutional Research: university- and department- level data collected over the prior six years form the cornerstone for how programs will document progress on performance goals and benchmarks. ● A table of data the program may need is included in Appendix C. The table includes sources for institutional data as well as external and benchmarking resources. ● IR is available to support chairs in using the data. 9

passages.heading: Linked from Linked from Agenda | Page 10
passages.text: SECTION 2. THE SELF-STUDY 10

passages.heading: Linked from Linked from Agenda | Page 11
passages.text:
The Self-Study Academic Program Review includes a self-reflection on research and scholarly activities, teaching and curriculum development activities, public engagement activities and resource utilization.
The self-study is both a retrospective and a prospective activity which summarizes the current state of a department, analyzes trends since the last program review (when applicable), compares the academic program’s activities with benchmark data of similar academic programs (provided by URI’s Office of Institutional Research), and outlines an assessment process for continuous quality improvement of these programs and activities.
This retrospective analysis allows departments to explain how their past activities support their program’s strategic plan, the University’s mission and the curricular/academic plan.
Using data provided through the university data (e.g., data provided by Institutional Research and Enrollment Management), Hanover Data Reports, and internal department data collection over the past six years, programs examine progress on their performance goals and benchmarks.

passages.heading: Linked from Linked from Agenda | Page 11
passages.text:
The self-study will also present a plan for the future that includes ways to ensure improvement in the quality of academic programs and their services to the college, university, and community.
This prospective analysis allows academic programs to articulate response strategies to the opportunities and challenges within their discipline, university and higher education, and to establish forward-looking goals and benchmarks to be pursued during the next planning cycle.
The audience for the self-study includes the Dean, Provost, Vice Provost, the external reviewer(s) (see External Review, Section 3), and the faculty, staff, and administrators within the college.
Guidelines for Completion of the Self-Study Report: 1.
The 20-30 page report (plus appendices) should be an honest evaluation, providing feasible mechanisms for advancing quality. 2.
The report should be comprehensive yet succinct, focusing on key issues, with each section being descriptive and evaluative. 3.
The report should reflect the views of the faculty for the department/unit under review. 4.
Two main criteria should structure the review: Quality/Effectiveness and Efficiency. 11

passages.heading: Linked from Linked from Agenda | Page 12
passages.text: a. Program quality/effectiveness addresses how well the Department does what it sets out to do. For example, how do the goals and objectives of the Department in terms of teaching, research, and public engagement compare to other benchmark programs, and how well are these achieved? Does it effectively serve the mission and strategic goals of the University? Is the Department innovative and of high quality? b. Program efficiency addresses the cost effectiveness of offerings of the Department. For example, what are the costs associated with its teaching, research, and public engagement activities? How effective is the Department in generating resources through attracting students, teaching and generating external funding in comparison to the level of institutional investment? Is it productive? Does it use its resources efficiently? c. SEE APPENDIX B FOR A TABLE OF DATA THAT DEPARTMENTS WILL USE TO INFORM THE SELF-STUDY 12

passages.heading: Linked from Linked from Agenda | Page 13
passages.text: Outline of the Self-Study Report See the following sections of the APR handbook for detailed information about each of the sections below. I. Executive Summary II. Brief history of Department (include mission statement) III. Brief summary of prior program review and actions (when available) IV. Brief description and summary of current state of degree programs (graduate, professional, and undergraduate) A. Brief description and summary of current teaching, learning and outcomes assessment processes B. Brief description and summary of current research programs C. Brief description and summary of current service and public engagement programs V. Institutional effectiveness VI. Future plans and priorities VII. Appendices (should include: faculty vitae, learning outcomes assessment curriculum map/reports/feedback, Annual Central Data Reports, Data Collection Summaries, Department strategic plan, etc.) 13

passages.heading: Linked from Linked from Agenda | Page 14
passages.text: Self-Study Report Part I. Executive Summary Executive Summary ● A 1-2 page summary highlighting the key points of the self-study, external review, and action plan. It should restate the purpose of the APR, highlight the major points of the APR, and describe any conclusions or recommendations from the APR. Part II: Background History of the Department ● Overview of the unit and background including the work to complete the Shared Values ● What is our unifying and overarching goal (mission)? ● What is the unit mission and purpose? ● To what degree/in what ways are the unit’s activities linked to the mission of the unit, the college, and URI’s strategic plan? ● When was the mission last reviewed and discussed? Is there a process for reviewing the mission and purposes of the unit? ● Does the mission effectively link unit strengths in research and teaching with societal needs and opportunities for the future? ● How deep and extensive is knowledge of the unit’s mission, vision, goals among its faculty members, staff, and stakeholders? Alignment with College and University Strategic Goals and the Academic Plan ● How is your department aligned with the University’s strategic goals to provide value in terms of program quality and efficiency? 14
