passages.heading: Linked from Linked from Agenda | Page 30
passages.text:
The External Review Process The external review (ER) process is designed to provide an outside perspective on the program’s strengths and areas for improvement.
The review is conducted by a peer from a similar program at another institution and results in a formal summary report.
Guidelines for the External Review Process: 1.
The unit lead identifies qualified individuals from peer institutions, ensuring any potential conflicts of interest are addressed early in the process. 2.
The department chair and Dean discuss possible external reviewers with the Dean.
External reviewers are chosen with the concurrence of the Dean. 3.
It is recommended that invitations to reviewers be sent by the department chair or Dean no less than eight months in advance of the scheduled site visit.
Chairs and Deans should determine who will send the email invitation. 4.
The External Reviewer discusses expected outcomes with the unit lead and sets a schedule for the site visit.
The unit lead prepares and provides a draft itinerary for the campus visit. 5.
The unit lead provides the External Reviewer with access to key documents, including the Self-Study, data reports, and strategic plans. 6.

passages.heading: Linked from Linked from Agenda | Page 30
passages.text:
During the site visit, the External Reviewer meets with faculty, students, and key stakeholders to assess the program.
Following the visit, the reviewer submits a formal written report with evaluative findings and recommendations, which are incorporated into the department’s action plan response.
Stakeholder meetings should be conducted without the chair present. 7.
The department and dean meet to discuss the reviewer’s findings and develop a formal response, including an action plan to address areas for improvement. 8.
The Provost’s Office will support a $1250 stipend plus travel expenses for one External Reviewer.
Colleges and departments can opt to contribute additional funds to support a larger stipend or to bring a second reviewer to campus.
Qualifications of External Reviewers 1.
Reviewer is from a comparable R1 program in quality, size and ranking. 2.
Reviewer has an arm’s length relationship with the URI program. 3.
Emeriti faculty from other universities who retired within the past year can be reviewers.
Providing context about how this person provides a visionary approach to the APR is helpful. 4.

passages.heading: Linked from Linked from Agenda | Page 30
passages.text: Reviewers’ curriculum vitae should be shared with the dean before an invitation is extended to the prospective reviewer. 30

During the visit, the review team will meet with faculty, students, department leadership, and other university stakeholders.

passages.heading: Linked from Linked from Agenda | Page 40
passages.text: Overview of the Action Plan The Action Plan outlines the strategic plan of the Department for the next six years including annual benchmarks used to assess progress. The plan addresses major issues raised in the self- study and by the external reviewer(s), and relates these to the strategic plan of the Department. The plan also includes specific goals, their rationale, and estimates of resources required. ● Faculty review and discuss the external reviewer’s self-study, and the Department Chair collaborates with the faculty to develop a draft Action Plan that is submitted to the Dean. ● The Dean meets with the Department chair (and/or the self-study chair, if a different person) to develop a mutually agreeable proposed Action Plan that is submitted to the Provost with the Self-Study and the External Reviewer Report. ● The Department chair, the Dean, the Provost and representatives from the Provost’s office meet to discuss the Action Plan for the Department which outlines the strategic plan for the next six years, addressing any major issues raised in the self-study and external review, and includes specific goals and resource estimates. ● To promote continuous quality improvement, the Provost may request a follow up, Interim Report from the department. Interim reports will be submitted to the Dean who will present them to the Provost for discussion. ● The approved Action Plan is complete following this discussion and represents an agreement between the Department, the college Dean, and the Provost for actions to be taken over time, benchmarks used to assess progress, and a plan for allocation of resources. 40

passages.heading: Linked from Linked from Agenda | Page 41
passages.text: Action Plan Guidelines Action Plan Development, Milestones and Implementation Plan Action Planning is a continuous and multi-year process. See the table below for a detailed timeline of milestones associated with Action Plan Development and Implementation. Timeline Activity Description Initial Development Year 1, Months 1-3 Faculty Engagement Faculty review and discuss the findings from the external review and the self-study, kickstarting the development of the Action Plan. Year 1, Months 4-6 Drafting the Plan The Department Chair collaborates with faculty to create a draft Action Plan. This draft is then submitted to the Dean for initial feedback. Review and Approval Process Year 1, Months 7-9 Collaborative Refinement The Dean and the Department Chair (including the self-study chair if different) refine the draft Action Plan into a mutually agreeable proposal. Year 1, Month 10 Strategic Submission This proposed Action Plan, together with the Self-Study and the External Reviewer Report, is submitted to the Provost for preliminary approval. Year 1, Months 11-12 Comprehensive Discussion The Department Chair, Dean, Provost, and representatives from the Provost’s office meet to discuss, finalize, and approve the Action Plan. Implementation and Monitoring Year 2-5 Action The approved Action Plan is implemented, 41

passages.heading: Linked from Linked from Agenda | Page 42
passages.text: Implementation setting the course for the department’s actions. Departments initiate projects and strategies outlined in the plan and start monitoring their impact. Year 2-5 Regular Monitoring Departments conduct annual reviews to monitor progress against the benchmarks set in the Action Plan. Adjustments are made based on these reviews to ensure the plan remains responsive to both achievements and challenges. Goals and progress toward goals are discussed annually with the Dean. Year 6 Evaluation and Preparation for Next Cycle A comprehensive evaluation of the Action Plan’s outcomes is conducted to assess its effectiveness and gather insights for the next APR cycle. This evaluation informs the upcoming self-study and the development of a new Action Plan. Cycle Repeats Year 6, Months 1-3 Start New Cycle The next cycle begins with updated orientation and data collection, reflecting the latest developments and priorities in the department’s discipline and the broader institutional context. 42

Goals should be specific, measurable, realistic and the most appropriate goals for this unit at this time. 1) Address major issues raised in the self- study and by the external reviewer(s), and relate these to the strategic plan of the unit and university. 2) Identify at least 6 strategic priorities for the next 6 years, classifying them as short term (1-2 years), medium term (3-4 years), and long term (5-6 years)?

2025-26 Academic Year Annual Report of the Joint Committee for Academic Program Review & Outcomes Assessment to the Faculty Senate May 2026 The 2026 update on learning outcomes assessment (2025-2026 academic assessment reporting year) reaffirms that student learning outcomes and academic program assessment is acknowledged as a shared responsibility and demonstrates a regular and ongoing commitment to understanding student learning and student success.
Data and results from outcomes assessment activities are examined in the aggregate only and are not used to evaluate individual faculty nor students, but to improve learning opportunities for all students.
This report is submitted by the Office of Student Learning Outcomes Assessment and Accreditation in the Office for the Advancement of Teaching & Learning , and in partial fulfillment of the charge outlined for the Joint Committee on Academic Program Review and Outcomes Assessment ( JCAPROA , Spring 2024).

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 1
passages.text:
SUMMARY OF INSTITUTION WIDE ASSESSMENT ACTIVITIES The summary of outcomes assessment reporting presents the assessment activities of the Joint Committee for Student Learning Outcomes Assessment & Accreditation (JCAPROA) that took place during the 2025-26 academic year.
Often throughout the year, and in support of this committee and its charge, members of the Office for the Advancement of Teaching & Learning (ATL) through the Office of Student Learning Outcomes Assessment and Accreditation (SLOAA) acted in partnership to ensure specific objectives were met and certain expertise related goals were achieved.
The following items describe the work accomplished by this committee.
Item #1: New Program Assessment Plans 1 During the 2025-26 academic year, the JCAPROA continued to partner with members of ATL through SLOAA to ensure that new assessment plan proposals received timely support and guidance as part of new degree program and certificate offerings.
This process has ensured compliance with the Faculty Senate current new program proposal process. (ref: University Manual 8.85.14 .).

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 1
passages.text:
The review of assessment plans includes the articulation of program goals, learning outcomes, curriculum map support, and a plan for long-term learning for each program.
This year, 8 degree program assessment plans were reviewed and supported, and 11 certificate assessment plans were reviewed and supported as well.
Please see Appendix A for a complete list of those degree and certificate programs.
Item #2: New Program Process Workflow Part of the charge given to JCAPROA from the Faculty Senate’s Executive Committee this year was to support and provide additional clarification about the process that new programs (degrees and certificates) must follow in order to attain Faculty Senate support from their originating department.
Members of this committee took on that charge and the following workflow visual was developed.
Please see Appendix B to review the newly created resource.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 1
passages.text:
Item #3: Student Learning Outcomes Assessment Process Review and Update For years, the Student Learning Outcomes Assessment and Accreditation team in the Office for the Advancement of Teaching & Learning has provided support to all URI colleges and departments as it relates to the effective evaluation of student learning outcomes in the undergraduate curriculum.
Historically, the evaluation of student learning outcomes at URI happened on a 2-year cycle, until the fall of 2024 when the university’s largest college, the College of Arts & Sciences, was collaboratively shifted by request to a 3-year cycle.
Since then, our team has listened to other university leaders (Deans, Associate Deans, and Department Chairs, and individual faculty) from other colleges across URI regarding this topic.
During the fall 2025 semester, members of our team reached out to more than 50 other universities to learn more about their 1 Not all programs will have completed the approval process at the time of this update. 1

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 2
passages.text:
assessment processes.
From those conversations, along with receiving support from the Office of the Provost, we worked during the 2025-2026 academic year to reset the university’s undergraduate academic program assessment cycle to a 3-year schedule.
A timeline of those events is below.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 2
passages.text: Timeline ● Fall 2023: The College of Arts & Sciences petitioned the Provost’s Office for an additional year to be added to the undergraduate assessment cycle in order to complete a deeper and richer analysis of the student learning outcomes across programs in the college. ● Fall 2023: Conversations were ongoing to identify a positive solution to the opportunity raised by the CAS. ● Spring 2024: The Provost’s Office supported the proposed additional year, and a pilot began during the Fall 2024 semester. ● Fall 2024: The College of Arts and Sciences 3-y pilot assessment cycle begins. ● Spring 2025: Other college leaders begin to see the benefits of moving to a 3-year cycle and they express their desire to move to a 3-year cycle. ● Fall 2025: The undergraduate academic program assessment cycle schedule is paused to allow the Student Learning Outcomes Assessment and Accreditation (SLOAA) team time to research the potential implications for a university-wide change in the assessment schedule, The SLOAA team contacts more than 50 universities to learn more about their assessment cycles for evaluating student learning outcomes. ● Spring 2026: The updated 3-year cycle is supported by the Office of the Provost, and the updated cycle is shared with the university.

Shane Tutwiler moved to create 3 working groups (listed below) to ensure progress of specific committee goals for this academic year.
Members of the JCAPROA have been asked to participate in at least 1 of the working groups based on their experience and expertise as it relates to the committee’s overall charge. 1.
Learning Outcomes Oversight (LOO) working group - Supporting review of LOO related policies, inventorying LOO documents across academic programs, synthesizing information into templates and timelines, developing a LOO FAQ with reporting instructions, and evaluating criteria for final packets 2.

Appendix D - JCAPROA and the updated NECHE Standards and Indicators (2026 revision) NECHE–JCAPROA Crosswalk Table •2025–2026 Updated to reflect NECHE 2026 Standards for Accreditation Standard 1: Mission, Organization, Governance, and Planning NECHE Focus: Governance structures, faculty role in curriculum, institutional planning and evaluation.
NECHE Indicator NECHE Expectation (2026) JCAPROA Responsibility 1.12 Internal governance provides for appropriate participation of constituencies and maintains regular, effective communication channels.
JCAPROA committee structure and communication processes model faculty-shared governance; webpage, FAQs, and timelines support constituent engagement. 1.13 Faculty hold primary responsibility for curriculum content, quality, and effectiveness; faculty have a substantive voice in academic policy.
JCAPROA policy development and APR process place program review authority with faculty through college-level structures. 1.14 The institution demonstrates systematic planning beyond the short term, evaluates the effectiveness of its planning, and aligns resources with strategic priorities.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 12
passages.text:
Development and maintenance of APR cycle guidance, multi-year review calendars, and templates for documenting planning outcomes and improvement actions.
Standard 2: The Academic Program, Faculty, and Students NECHE Focus: Academic program quality, coherence, learning outcomes, program review.
NECHE Indicator NECHE Expectation (2026) JCAPROA Responsibility 2.4 The institution publishes learning goals and requirements for each program.
LOO policy requires programs to develop, document, and make public explicit student learning outcomes; JCAPROA templates support compliance. 2.10 The institution reviews academic programs on a regular cycle, incorporates external perspectives, and uses results for program improvement.
APR handbook oversight, review timelines, external review expectations, and integration of LOO evidence into program review cycles. 2.13 The institution demonstrates clear and ongoing administrative oversight for academic elements of all courses for which it awards credit.
APR process provides structured mechanism for colleges to demonstrate oversight of curriculum content, delivery, and credit integrity. 12

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 13
passages.text:
Standard 4: Educational Effectiveness and the Success of All Students NECHE Focus: Evidence of student achievement, systematic assessment, use of results for improvement, transparency.
NECHE Indicator NECHE Expectation (2026) JCAPROA Responsibility 4.1 The institution identifies mission-appropriate goals for student learning and success at institution, program, and course levels; establishes metrics including retention, graduation, and success rates.
LOO policy framework defines scope of outcome development; university-wide policy establishes required levels (institution, program, course) and documentation standards. 4.2 The institution uses a variety of quantitative and qualitative, direct and indirect measures to assess mission-appropriate goals and evaluate program quality and effectiveness.
LOO reporting structure requires programs to document multiple assessment methods; JCAPROA templates prompt direct and indirect evidence collection. 4.3 The institution regularly and systematically collects and analyzes data aligned with its mission and uses findings to identify and address areas for improvement.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 13
passages.text:
APR and LOO processes together create a systematic data collection and use cycle; JCAPROA coordinates inventory, templates, and reporting timelines. 4.4 The institution demonstrates progress toward achieving mission-appropriate goals based on results of its inquiry, evidence, and evaluation.
LOO reporting templates emphasize closing-the-loop documentation; APR handbook requires programs to present evidence of improvement over review cycles. 4.5 The institution defines and demonstrates post-enrollment/post-graduation success of students using mission-appropriate metrics (e.g., transfer, employment, return on investment, social mobility).

BFA Film - BFA The Major.
The BFA in Film/Media is an intensive, experiential degree that integrates advanced creative practice with critical and historical study.
The curriculum emphasizes sequential training in film and media production alongside rigorous engagement with theory, research, and analysis.
Students develop technical and conceptual proficiency through sustained coursework, collaborative projects, and advanced culminating work that reflects professional standards and disciplined artistic inquiry.
FLM 496 (Capstone Seminar in Film/Media) and FLM 397 (1 Credit) BFA portfolio are required in the junior year; and FLM 497 (BFA Capstone) is required in the senior year.
Students learn to work with the evolving and overlapping technologies involved in the production of moving images.
A wide range of courses is available to the Film/Media student—courses that examine the historical, theoretical, and global approaches to the analysis and creation of moving images.
The Film/Media program prepares students for careers in such areas as independent filmmaking; animation and media design; film and television industries, advertising, marketing, public relations, and media criticism.

passages.heading: Linked from Agenda | Page 11
passages.text:
Graduates of this program are also prepared to continue with graduate studies in film and media production for an M.F.A.
Students majoring in the Film BFA must complete a minimum of 52 credits (maximum 67) in approved courses toward the major.
FLM 101 or FLM 101H is a required prerequisite.
We recommend that students take at least one film production course per semester beginning with FLM 110 in their freshman year, establishing a regular and consistent creative process.
The wide range of choices in Film/Media courses permits students to design a major that will meet both personal and professional goals.
Students must have a plan of study approved by an academic advisor in the Film/Media program before beginning their coursework in the major.
Degree Requirements: 120 total credits required for graduation, with minimum 30 credits numbered 300 or above.

passages.heading: Faculty Senate FAQ — FAQ-Page-3.jpg
passages.text:
Who may attend Faculty Senate meetings and where are they held?
Any member of the URl community or the general public may attend a Faculty Senate
meeting.However,only voting members of the Senate may vote on legislation,resolutions,
officer elections,and any other business raised at the meeting.Bylaws stipulate that only
Senators and ex officio members have the RIGHT to speak during meetings.Exofficio
members participate in discussions,ask questions,and make and second motions;theyare
not,however,allowed tovote.Non-senators may request to speak at a meeting beforehand
via the online Permission To Speak”form found on the Faculty Senate website.To facilitate
the meeting itself
Meetings take place throughout the academic year in the Hope Roomof the Higgins
Welcome Center from3-5p.m.monthly on a Thursday.A brief reception with refreshments is
provided at every meeting.This is a wonderful opportunity for in-person attendees to network
colleges
How are agenda items determined?
The meeting agenda is set by the Faculty Senate Executive Committee.Agenda items may
can also be suggested to the Executive Committee via an anonymous form on the Faculty

passages.heading: Faculty Senate FAQ — FAQ-Page-3.jpg
passages.text:
can also be suggested by a committee or introduced at a Senate meeting during the New
Business'portion.
While agenda items maybe suggested at anytime,inclusion of an item at the monthly
meeting requires the Executive Committee approve adding it to the agenda atleast one week
in advance of the scheduled senate meeting.This is necessary for timely agenda posting and
motion in realtime are typically considered for inclusion on a future agenda or referred to a
standing or special committee for further exploration.Exceptions to this timeline are reserved
for unusually urgent or time-sensitive Issues.
Doesthe Faculty Senate use parliamentary procedures to conduct meetings?
The Senate relies upon the American Institute of Parliamentarians Standard Codeof
Parliamentary Procedure.Guidebooks and other reference materials are available in the
Faculty Senate Office.Training on procedural basics is provided during the annual
Orientation meeting.This meeting is held each September and is required for all new
Senators(and highly recommended as a refresher for ALL Senators).
